title: Will Trump be Burnham’s undoing, or the making of him? The answer lies in Europe | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: In an increasingly dangerous world, Europe is finding safety in numbers – but Britain is on the outside. The new PM’s task is to change that, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: In an increasingly dangerous world, Europe is finding safety in numbers – but Britain is on the outside. The new PM’s task is to change that, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Shutterstock/APView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Shutterstock/APOpinionAndy BurnhamWill Trump be Burnham’s undoing, or the making of him? The answer lies in EuropeJonathan FreedlandIn an increasingly dangerous world, our European neighbours are finding safety in numbers – but Britain is on the outside. The new PM’s task is to change thatFri 31 Jul 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 13.54 EDTShareThere is an orange cloud in the sky. I’m not referring to the wildfires ravaging parts of Europe and East Anglia, though they are connected. I mean the looming pall from across the Atlantic that threatens to spoil the sunny start to the premiership of Andy Burnham – and whose name isDonald Trump.Burnham’s first 10 days or so in office have gone about as well as he or any of his team could have dared hope. His net approval rating has risen by 17 points, according toone early poll,gaining groundwith every category of voter except supporters of Reform UK, though they too like some of what they see. His easy manner, no-notes speech-making and agility on social media have won plaudits, including from a usually sceptical press.But the new prime minister will know that all this could be upended at a stroke, with a single move by the man in the White House. Keir Starmer watched as the earliest green shoots of economic growth emerged earlier this year, only to be crushed by Trump’s decision to combine with Israel and attack Iran. What can Burnham do to ensure he does not suffer that same fate? As it happens, the answer to that question answers another: what might constitute a Burnham foreign policy that would match the spirit and ethos of the agenda he has set out at home?So far most of the discussion in this area has concentrated on how the new PM should handle his counterpart in Washington. Some suggest his best bet is to emulate Starmer: swallow your pride, ladle on the flattery, avoid overt confrontation. Maybe tickle Trump’s tummy by promising to drill in the North Sea, even as Suffolk is engulfed in the flames of the climate breakdown. Others say the US president is a bully who only respects strength: therefore, stand up to him, even if that means a row.All this owes more to the realm of animal psychology than political analysis. Different world leaders have tried both approaches – nice guy and tough guy – and both have failed. And sometimes succeeded. Trump has an attention span measured in seconds; he is erratic and impulse driven; he changes his mind without warning, logic or consistency.Those at the sharp end have come to understand this, which helps explain the muted reaction to Trump’s announcement late on Thursday of a breakthrough in Gaza. “There is scepticism and cautiousness among Palestinians,” reported Al Jazeera after Trump said Hamas was ready to disarm in return for an Israeli withdrawal from the territory. As anyone who has followed his zigzagging engagement with the Middle East has come to learn, the safest response to any development heralded by the US president is: don’t hold your breath.Faced with such a man, it’s foolish to imagine a British prime minister can have much impact on American decisions. Even senior US administration officials have been known to admit privately that they have next to no sway over Trump, so why would a British PM fare any better? Brits do have access – I’m told that national security adviser Jonathan Powell is in regular contact with Trump’s personal envoy and golfing buddy Steve Witkoff – but that is not the same as influence.The remedy, then, is not to hope to change a president who won’t change, but rather to be less exposed to his whims. And that points to a much larger strategy, one that makes sense in terms of both policy and politics – and which just so happens to fit Burnham’s approach to a T.The prime minister’s opening pitch has been that he will speak to voters candidly, that he will confront the big problems that his predecessors ducked and that he is ready to break from orthodoxies that have held too long. He has already made a start in that vein domestically, withhis promise this weekto tackle social care. But why not extend it to the international realm?It would begin with a stark admission that the foundation of postwar UK foreign policy is no longer stable – that we cannot rely on the US as the guarantor of our security. A US president who muses out loud about abandoning Nato, whothreatens to seize the territory(Greenland) of a Nato ally (Denmark) and whose support for a country (Ukraine) invaded by an enemy (Russia) is so inconstant, is less a guarantor than a danger. It is clearly reckless to remain in a state of dependence on such a power.Luckily, there is a group of allies close at hand who have reached that same conclusion and are already acting on it. Our European neighbours are coming together to defend themselves, without relying on Washington. They are borrowing money collectively, which makes it cheaper, and pooling resources, which makes arms spending more efficient. Add theSafe loan programme, funding joint defence procurement to the tune of €150bn (£128bn), to the EU arming of Ukraine, and you can see why Mark Leonard, director of the European Council on Foreign Relations, tells me: “The EU is becoming a security community.”It is security broadly defined too. Witness joint EU action on energy, to plug the gap previously filled by Russian gas; vaccines during the Covid pandemic; cybersecurity and election interference; the climate crisis and immigration. In an increasingly dangerous world, the Europeans are finding safety in numbers. And we, though they are our nearest neighbours, are on the outside.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is an economic dimension to this. Spending your defence budgets closer to home, rather than on US-made hardware, serves pretty well as what Burnham might call a reindustrialisation strategy. The French have long understood that; the Germans increasingly so. Not for nothing has Berlin decided to spendonly 8%of its massive €80bn rearmament drive on US weapons. As the EU moves to a “buy European” approach, it will be European industry that benefits – but not us.The economic dimension goes further, because our security is threatened in that sphere too. As Mark Carney of Canada correctly diagnosed in hisDavos speech, globalisation, and the economic interdependence it entails, can easily be turned into a weapon. Trump’s US wields it through the imposition of tariffs, China by controlling access to rare earth metals. The best way for a country to protect itself is to stop being dependent on either of those two titans. The UK’s only shot at such independence is, perhaps paradoxically, to be part of a group large enough to aim for resilience and self-sufficiency – and that means the EU.It will look politically daring, but that’s only if you adopt the view from Westminster – where Brexit seems untouchable and all anyone can see are red lines. Among the people of Britain, it’s a very different picture.A major survey by the ECFRin June found that Britons now regard Brexit as a “disaster”, with three-quarters wanting a closer relationship with the EU. One striking number: when asked to choose, 63% said they would prioritise the relationship with the EU over the US, with only 19% making the opposite choice. A plurality even favours the creation of that one-time tabloid spectre: a European army with British troops in it. As Leonard puts it: “The waters are much warmer than people realise.”This, then, is what Burnhamism could look like abroad – a willingness to face the world as it now is, to break from the old, Atlanticist default setting and to pursue a new approach that will make us both militarily and economically more resilient. The answer is no longer to put our trust in a single, unreliable friend – but rather to combine with our nearest neighbours. The new prime minister has so much to do, but he can do almost none of it without challenging a status quo that has done so much damage in a single decade. He will have to undo the folly of 2016 – and look to Europe.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionEuropeEuropean UnionDonald TrumpForeign policyDefence policyBrexitcommentShareReuse this content

title: Ariana Grande: Petal review – calm, controlled anger at exes, fans and the media | Ariana Grande | The Guardian
description: Casting herself as a flower trampled underfoot, the superstar’s eighth album swaps the ​glitz of her Wicked years ​f​or dark blooms of haunted electronics
Author: Katie Hawthorne
Headline: Casting herself as a flower trampled underfoot, the superstar’s eighth album swaps the ​glitz of her Wicked years ​f​or dark blooms of haunted electronics
Content: Measured neutrality … Ariana Grande.Photograph:  Katia TemkinView image in fullscreenMeasured neutrality … Ariana Grande.Photograph:  Katia TemkinAriana GrandeReviewAriana Grande: Petal review – calm, controlled anger at exes, fans and the media(Republic)Casting herself as a flower trampled underfoot, the superstar’s eighth album swaps the ​glitz of her Wicked years ​f​or dark blooms of haunted electronicsKatie HawthorneFri 31 Jul 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 13.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Tell me who’s to blame?”Ariana Grandeasks, exasperated, on the title track of her eighth album, Petal. “Is it the people or myself?” As bleary, fuzzed-up drums threaten to drown her out, this shadowy carousel-ride of a song cycles through more questions than answers. Does her success only make her need more of it? Can her new record of No 1 singles stave off heartbreak? Does Grande’s life shape her music, or does her music shape her life?View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Petal.Photograph: Republic Records/APMoody and muted, Petal is a riposte to the glitz and sparkle of the pop star’s Oscar-nominated turn inWickedand the theatre kid energy of her last album, 2024’sEternal Sunshine. She describes this record as one of “unfiltered rage”, and there’s plenty Grande could be angry about: just this weekshe filed a lawsuitagainst hackers who allegedly stole and sold numerous unreleased songs.Intrusive fans are raked over the coals on the icily aloof lead single Hate That I Made You Love Me – a huge global hit since its release in May – while whispery Oh Well casually dispatches “bad guys” (read: exes) to hell. Like I Do opens with panicky gasps, stylised as a vocal exercise, and ruminates on co-dependence with the press – along with a possible dig at years of clickbait headlines pedalling faux concern about her weight: “I’ve got shit to talk, keeps me well fed.”The album’s central metaphor of a petal on the pavement – something delicate getting trampled underfoot – is mirrored in production that is unusually dark by Grande’s standards. Written and produced by Grande and longtime collaborator Ilya Salmanzadeh, Petal buries her soft, sparkling voice under bass, rattling percussion and a raft of crackling, distorted electronic textures. It sounds lonely: a haunted house of a pop record with Grande’s usual R&B vocal fireworks locked in the basement.Dread-soaked opener Kiss Me is a crisis of faith, with Grande’s gleaming voice the only light in the dark as she demands, vampirically, for a lover to “bring her to life”. Water drips from the ceiling on Hate That I Made You Love Me, as if her chilly dismissal of her fans’ obsession was recorded in some kind of sewer.Snatches of shuffling UKG percussion suggest that Kelela’s eerie fusion of club, R&B and alt-rock has replaced Mariah Carey’s glam on Grande’s mood board, but there’s still a shiny, theatrical bent to her new grunge. Sirens wee-woo melodramatically on Never Get Over Me, which threatens another ex over campy, villainous piano. In a similar vein, Big Feelings claims femme fatale status via generically stomping synths and a wide-eyed rendition of a line from Rizzo’s big ballad in Grease: “There are worse things that I could do.”Through it all, Grande maintains a measured neutrality to her voice. Shelving the powerhouse vocal runs she’s famous for, she leans towards lacy, translucent harmonies and stacked layers (in the vein of her longtime inspiration Imogen Heap), which turn into ghostly cathedrals of sound. The closest we get to an old-school Ariana moment is on interlude Warning Signs, which escalates into a rare outburst: “I wish someone could hear me,” she cries, before the track cuts out.Ariana Grande review - glittering hits and powerhouse vocals in stunning return to stageRead morePetal is an album of quiet, controlled, vetted anger; there’s no rush of blood to the head. Maybe it’s because Grande is rehashing familiar topics – it’s far from the first time she’s dissected fame, romance or self-worth in her music – that she sounds numb to it, tired of treading the same ground. Or maybe it’s because performing anger in public is a new challenge for her. While singing the title track live for the first time this week, she clenched her fists: Anger 101. But as she demanded those answers – from herself, from a sea of screaming fans and phone screens – her voice had real bite.Explore more on these topicsAriana GrandePop and rockR&Balbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: A World Cup with no participants – it could be Gianni Infantino’s boldest move yet | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: You’ve got to admire the Fifa president’s chutzpah in trying to flog off football’s greatest prize. If only Uefa wasn’t being so pesky about it all, says Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: You’ve got to admire the Fifa president’s chutzpah in trying to flog off football’s greatest prize. If only Uefa wasn’t being so pesky about it all, says Marina Hyde
Content: Fifa president Gianni Infantino during the World Cup 2026 play-offs draw in Zurich, Switzerland, 20 November 2025.Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPAView image in fullscreenFifa president Gianni Infantino during the World Cup 2026 play-offs draw in Zurich, Switzerland, 20 November 2025.Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPAOpinionGianni InfantinoA World Cup with no participants – it could be Gianni Infantino’s boldest move yetMarina HydeYou’ve got to admire the Fifa president’s chutzpah in trying to flog off football’s greatest prize. If only Uefa wasn’t being so pesky about it allFri 31 Jul 2026 08.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 08.48 EDTShareImagine a plan so distasteful that even the Americans and a Middle Eastern nepo-royal football boss can’t be doing with it. Such is the status of Fifa president Gianni Infantino’s scheme tosell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors. More historically, perhaps, the 55 nations that make up Uefa have reacted to this horror show byvoting unanimously to boycott Fifa tournaments, including World Cups, if Infantino presses ahead. That would mean Spain and Portugal boycotting their own men’s World Cup next time around, which you’d think – not to call it too soon – would come off as slightly bad vibes.A testing moment, then, for the haunted cue-ball. Again. Can it really already be time to turn to Infantino once more, even after he appeared in this spotonly on Tuesday, after his 15-page Instagram crash-out about his haters? Yes. Yes, I’m afraid it can. Demanding the federations of the world sell off the World Cup to some fund led byDonald Trump’s son-in-law’s brotherwill regrettably draw attention to you in ways that will prove difficult to control. As indicated, the Fifa president’s plan has contrived to appear vulgar to the North American confederation, Concacaf, as well as the Asian Football Confederation (AFC).Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, the Bahraini royal who leads the AFC,has issued a statement, declaring that “the AFC is deeply concerned that Fifa’s unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football, which are based on solidarity, cooperation and transparency”. He went on to call for “the highest standards of ethics and good governance”. And certainly, it’s always a pleasure to take an ethics lesson from a guy like this. A number of human rights organisations claim that during the Arab spring,Salman busied himself with identifying dissident players and other athletes, many of whom were imprisoned and tortured. (He denies this.) Yet even he simply cannot force himself through Infantino’s latest show of full-spectrum amorality.It’s hard to escape the sense of gathering momentum against not only Infantino’s plan but the man himself, even from federations he has showered with disproportionate amounts of development cash over the years. A hotly defensive new statement declaring that “Nobody is selling football” emanated overnight from Fifa, which, to repeat, is proposing literally selling stakes in football to private investors.It’s a testing moment, too, for one of the most extravagant pieces of corporate bullshit of our entire era – the post-binfire promise: “We will learn from this.” And so to the involvement of JP Morgan in Infantino’s scheme. Five years ago, JP Morgan ended up apologising to fans after its part in the imploded plan to create a breakaway European Super League.Back then, it said: “We clearly misjudged how this deal would be viewed by the wider football community and how it might affect them in the future.” Then, it was time to deploy the mother lode: “We will learn from this.” Will you though? JP Morgan evidently regards time as a great healer, because it is once again the bank at the centre of the firestorm, having been working with Fifa to raise $4.2bn with the new commercial vehicle.At time of writing, Infantino was still insisting that he was pressing ahead with the scheme despite Uefa’s boycott pledge, which is certainly bold, given he would be trying to sell stakes in a tournament in which most of the best sides would not be playing. One intervention that has yet to materialise is any comment on the idea from Trump. The US president has, of course, been quite taken up over the past few days with his Middle East peace manoeuvres, creditinghis “historic” agreement to disarm Hamasand other militant groups in Gaza to the machinations of his Board of Peace – a body whose inauguration, you might recall, Infantino showily attended. Perhaps the most excruciatingly on-brand move for the Fifa president now would be to post a 15-page Insta meltdown about how he was way more concerned with the slightly more important matter of Middle East peace as brought about by his special friend, than about trifling matters such as flogging the World Cup to private equity. Certainly wouldn’t put it past him.But it is hard not to conclude that it is too much time with his special friend that has caused Infantino to overplay his hand in precisely the way he has. Maybe the real Trump derangement syndrome is the betas who suck up to the alpha in the apparent belief they will somehow osmotically absorb his unique characteristics and political gifts, and then themselves get away with the sort of stuff that only he has historically been able to pull. It’s personality cult as cargo cult.We see it in Nigel Farage, a man who threw a byelection to which no one turned up, and is now having to chomp his way through a long hot summer of wasting time and money. And we see it in Infantino, a man who has spent the past year or two getting as up close and personal as possible with Trump, and presumably concluded that the US president’s ability to defy various laws of politics had rubbed magically off on him. But that isn’t how it has worked at all, as he is now finding out, presumably to his own bemusement. The first rule of politics, famously, is to learn how to count – and Infantino’s failure to do so now suggests his own days are numbered.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMarina Hyde is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoOpinionFifaUefaFootball politicsDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: The best ice-cream makers in the UK for gelato, soft serve and sorbets – tested | Ice-cream and sorbet | The Guardian
description: Our writer spent the hottest weeks of the year churning through the top ice-cream makers, from compressor models to the cult favourite Ninja Creami. Here’s the scoop
Author: Danielle Amato
Headline: Our writer spent the hottest weeks of the year churning through the top ice-cream makers, from compressor models to the cult favourite Ninja Creami. Here’s the scoop
Content: View image in fullscreenThe FilterIce-cream and sorbetReviewThe best ice-cream makers in the UK for gelato, soft serve and sorbets – testedOur writer spent the hottest weeks of the year churning through the top ice-cream makers, from compressor models to the cult favourite Ninja Creami. Here’s the scoopKitchen gadgets top chefs can’t live withoutDanielle AmatoFri 31 Jul 2026 12.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Ilove a scoop or two of the good stuff, even more so when the mercury hits 30C and ice-cream starts feeling less like an indulgence and more like an essential survival tool. This is why owning an ice-cream maker has always made sense to me. I’ve been using the original Ninja Creami for years now, but before that I was spending a small fortune on gelato, fruity sorbets, frozen yoghurt and other such desserts from the frozen aisle.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Some might argue that the best ice-cream makers are a luxury, but if you’re a true dessert devotee, I believe they can earn their keep in no time. A tub of Häagen-Dazs will set you back almost £6 nowadays, which is an expensive habit if you’re getting through a pot a week during the hottest months of the year.With your own ice-cream machine, you get an endless supply whenever you fancy it, and you can get creative with flavours, tweaking as you go. It’s also ideal if you have allergies or follow a dairy-free diet, as good allergy-friendly ice-cream can be harder to find. Better still, making your own means you can skip the emulsifiers, artificial flavours, sweeteners and stabilisers found in many shop-bought tubs, so it’s a great option if you’re trying to move away from ultra-processed foods.But with so many options available, where do you start? I’ve taken one for the team – and no doubt my waistline – to test the best ice-cream makers available right now, from trendy soft-serve ice-cream machines to professional-style compressor models.At a glanceBest ice-cream maker overallCasoIceCreamer£278.97 at AmazonBest budget ice-cream makerCuisinartSolo Scoops£33.99 at AmazonBest freeze-first ice-cream makerNinjaCreami NC300£199.99 at SharkNinjaBest ice-cream maker for small freezersNutribulletChill£169.99 at CurrysBest soft-serve ice-cream makerGreenPanFrost ice-cream maker and slushie machine£328.99 at AmazonWhy you should trust meI’ve spent almost a decade researching, testing and reviewing kitchen appliances, which means I’m aware of the very best (and worst) the industry has to offer. I’ve seen appliance trends come and go, and I know what people actually want in their kitchens.I’m also an avid home cook and dinner party host. When I’m not in my kitchen testing appliances on the clock, I’m still there whipping up feasts for my willing partner and friends.How I testedView image in fullscreenWhipping up a storm … each ice-cream maker was assessed on everything from texture to ease of cleaning.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianThe research for this article meant making – and eating – a lot of ice-cream and sorbet (someone had to do it). I put 13 machines through their paces with three recipes on each: Felicity Cloake’sperfect vanilla ice-cream, herlemon sorbetand, where the machine allowed, a more basic throw-it-all-in recipe for strawberry ice-cream made with milk, cream, sugar and macerated strawberries. All the machines also came with their own recipe booklet or app, so I also tested one of these, usually a standard vanilla recipe with double cream.Testing a variety of recipes gave me a sense of how capable and versatile each machine really was, helping to decide whether it’s worthy of taking up precious space on your worktop.As well as making lots of ice-cream, I put on my technical hat to measure churning speeds, record noise levels using a decibel meter, and assess ice crystal formation, as well as the general taste and texture of the results after some time in the freezer.As a certified chore hater, I found that ease of assembly and cleaning were just as important. Waiting 24 hours to taste the results of your prep is one thing; spending another hour to disassemble and scrub clean the machine afterwards is quite another.All ice-cream makers sourced for this article will be donated to charity.The best ice-cream makers for your homeView image in fullscreenCool contenders … the ice-cream machines that went head-to-head in the tests.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianBest ice-cream maker overall:Caso IceCreamerCasoIceCreamerfrom£278.97£280 at Argos£278.97 at AmazonWhat we loveFamily-friendly and easy to useWhat we don’t loveIt’s a worktop hogView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£280 at Argos£278.97 at AmazonA real surprise standout, this model from the little-known brand Caso turned out to be not only the best compressor ice-cream maker, but also my favourite overall. It may be big and bulky, but that shouldn’t put you off (as long as you have the space).Why we love itCaso’s IceCreamer was the easiest machine I used, with very little that can actually go wrong. It has a generous two-litre capacity, and as it’s a compressor model, there was no need to prefreeze anything. Caso recommends chilling any mixture beforehand to improve churning times, but that can be as little as an hour – I’m impatient, and I still got great results after about 30 minutes.I was testing on one of the hottest June days on record, and so I wasn’t expecting miracles when it came to churn times. Impressively, though, the machine produced rich, velvety ice-cream in about 60 minutes using Felicity Cloake’s vanilla recipe. I imagine on a slightly cooler day it would have been even quicker. Unfortunately, the heat did mean my ice-cream began to melt almost instantly once out of the machine, but I managed to get it in the freezer before all the hard work was undone.Despite this, the ice-cream that initially emerged was well frozen yet buttery smooth and had few ice crystals. After a couple of days in the freezer in an airtight container, it still tasted fantastic. It also made light work of the lemon sorbet recipe in about 40 minutes.The IceCreamer has post-churn settings that keep the ice-cream at a frozen temperature for up to 60 minutes, or it just churns without freezing. It also comes with an ice-cream scoop and measuring cup. The bowl was easy to clean and, unlike some other machines here, there weren’t any fiddly parts to handle.It’s a shame that …it’s on the large side – and quite pricey, when not on offer.Machine type:compressorCapacity:2lAverage churn time:1hrNoise level: 67dBDimensions:43 x 28.5 x 28cm (WDH)Wattage:180WWarranty:two yearsCasoIceCreamerfrom£278.97£280 at Argos£278.97 at AmazonWhat we loveFamily-friendly and easy to useWhat we don’t loveIt’s a worktop hogBest budget ice-cream maker:Cuisinart Solo ScoopsCuisinartSolo Scoopsfrom£33.99£39.99 at Lakeland£33.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s compact and easy to useWhat we don’t loveStruggles to produce a good consistencyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£39.99 at Lakeland£33.99 at AmazonLet me temper your expectations here – if you’re spending this little on an ice-cream maker, you’d be silly to expect the world. However, I’m making a case for this mini motor-based machine because it’s so ridiculously simple to use.Why we love itIf you’re short on counter space or can’t justify the £200+ spend on a more premium machine, this is a great option. For occasional ice-cream indulgers who prefer to make their desserts from scratch – I’m thinking people with allergies and dairy-free dessert fans – the Solo Scoops is a compact, low-risk buy.The ice-cream maker comes with a small bowl that makes up to 475ml of ice-cream. It needs to be popped in the freezer for at least 24 hours before use, but takes up very little space. You’ll know it’s ready when you can no longer hear the liquid in the walls of the bowl moving around.Its small size is both a strength and a limitation. Because it relies on the frozen bowl staying cold for as long as possible (which proved a challenge in my furnace-like kitchen), I struggled to achieve the same firm, scoopable texture as the other models here despite using the same vanilla recipe throughout. With a little patience, though, you can get a soft-serve-style ice-cream in about 30 minutes. I got the best results by freezing the bowl for a minimum of 36 hours, chilling the ingredients first, and opting for sorbets over richer, higher-fat ice-creams.If you’re at all worried about longevity given the price (I was), the good news is that parts are easy to replace or repair. The Solo Scoops’ simple design means there’s less to go wrong, and replacement parts are available throughCuisinart’s website.It’s a shame that …while it’s not overly loud, the noise it makes is a bit grating.Machine type:freeze-firstCapacity:475mlAverage churn time:30minsNoise level:66dBDimensions:machine,25 x 21 x 21cm (WDH); bowl, 15 x 15 x 10cm (WDH)Wattage:12WWarranty:three yearsCuisinartSolo Scoopsfrom£33.99£39.99 at Lakeland£33.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s compact and easy to useWhat we don’t loveStruggles to produce a good consistencyBest freeze-first ice-cream maker:Ninja Creami NC300NinjaCreami NC300from£199.99£199.99 at SharkNinja£199.99 at CurrysWhat we loveMakes ice-cream easy; good for healthier optionsWhat we don’t loveIt’s noisy and freakishly tallView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£199.99 at SharkNinja£199.99 at CurrysNinja’s first iteration of the Creami might be getting on a bit now, with newer models featuring improved designs and new settings, but I’ve owned it for years, and it still produces good results.Why we love itNinja’s ice-cream makers are popular for a reason. While some find the brand’s products a little gimmicky (and some are, in my opinion), the Creami stands out because it makes homemade ice-cream genuinely achievable – even for the most reluctant cooks.Over the years, I’ve used my Creami to create all kinds of frozen desserts, from the brand’s signature strawberry ice-cream, which you’ll find in the accompanying booklet, to gelato-style mixes and even frozen smoothie bowls. Unlike other brands on this list, I really rate Ninja’s recipes, too.All recipes I tested, including Felicity’s sorbet and frozen vanilla ice-cream, were fully churned in about three minutes – a couple of minutes faster than the Nutribullet Chill below. I also like the Creami’s flat blade, as it allows it to get right to the end of the tub with ease. The compact tubs are also a plus, fitting easily into the freezer without taking up too much space.I found the Creami easy to clean, and some parts are dishwasher-safe. That’s not to say there aren’t any nooks where mixture can hide, but I haven’t had any problems as long as I’ve cleaned the machine straight away.The machine comes with two 493ml tubs as standard from SharkNinja, although some retailers offer three, and you canbuy more either directly from the manufactureror at otheronline retailers. Spare parts are available throughthe brand’s website, so if anything does go wrong, it’s usually easy to fix at home.It’s a shame that …it’s quite loud, and it’s unusually tall, so might not fit under some kitchen cabinets.Machine type:freeze-firstCapacity: 2 x 493mlAverage churn time:3minsNoise level:81dBDimensions:machine, 40.5 x 16.5 x 27cm (WDH); cup only, 11 x 11 x 10.31cm (WDH)Wattage:800WWarranty:two years (needs to be registered if bought from a third-party retailer)NinjaCreami NC300from£199.99£199.99 at SharkNinja£199.99 at CurrysWhat we loveMakes ice-cream easy; good for healthier optionsWhat we don’t loveIt’s noisy and freakishly tallBest ice-cream maker for small freezers:Nutribullet ChillNutribulletChillfrom£169.99£169.99 at Currys£169.99 at AmazonWhat we loveEasy to use and comes with two tubsWhat we don’t loveIt’s ear-shatteringly loudView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£169.99 at Currys£169.99 at AmazonNutribullet’s Ninja Creami-esque machine makes ice-cream, sorbet and frozen yoghurt with minimum fuss after 24 hours of freezing the mixture in the tub. I was won over by its simple design, and much like the Caso, it was an underdog that surprised me in testing.Why we love itThe Nutribullet Chill isn’t your classic churning ice-cream maker, but it’s easy to use and produced great results with my vanilla ice-cream and lemon sorbet test mixtures. You make and prefreeze your mixture in a compact 470ml tub, then the machine uses a powerful blade to churn it all up from frozen.The texture isn’t quite the same as a classic compressor machine – it’s less velvety – but for its compact size and ease of use, the trade-off is one I’d be happy to make.In performance, it’s similar to the Ninja Creami. The vanilla ice-cream and sorbet recipes came out as expected – less smooth than a compressor but still delicious – although I did find that the recipes in Nutribullet’s accompanying booklet and app do need a little tweaking. Using too much fat in your recipe will give you grainy, greasy-tasting results, as the fat from the cream isn’t stable and solidifies. I had better luck swapping out the double cream in Nutribullet’s recipes with a 40:60 split of double and single cream. It also did a great job making vegan ice-cream.The Nutribullet Chill comes with two 470ml tubs, withextras available to buy. In addition, the blade comes away for easy cleaning, plus replacement parts are available for repairing at home.It’s a shame that …it’s ear-shatteringly loud: I found myself having to leave the room while noise levels were being measured. Something to bear in mind if you’re noise-sensitive like I am.Machine type:freeze-firstCapacity: 2 x 470mlAverage churn time:5minsNoise level:96dBDimensions:machine,19.6 x 20.5 x 43.1cm (WDH); cup only, 10.5 x 10.5 x 15cm (WDH)Wattage:500WWarranty:two years if you keep your receiptNutribulletChillfrom£169.99£169.99 at Currys£169.99 at AmazonWhat we loveEasy to use and comes with two tubsWhat we don’t loveIt’s ear-shatteringly loudBest soft-serve ice-cream maker:GreenPan Frost ice-cream maker and slushie machineGreenPanFrost ice-cream maker and slushie machinefrom£328.99£328.99 at Robert Dyas£328.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMakes soft serve, slushies, milkshakes and moreWhat we don’t loveExpensive and tiresome to cleanView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£328.99 at Robert Dyas£328.99 at AmazonLooking for an all-in-one appliance that will keep both kids and adults happy? Then GreenPan – best known for, well, itspans– turns out to make a surprisingly capable ice-cream maker, too.Why we love it:The GreenPanFrost really impressed in tests. I used it to make a custardy vanilla soft serve using Felicity Cloake’s recipe and a soft-serve “sorbet” – essentially, a lemon slushie. My chilled mixture achieved soft-serve consistency in about 25 minutes, but I did have to tweak the recipe a few times to get it right.Some research revealed that soft serve works best with an additional stabiliser, such as xanthan gum. I tested this with other batches and found it did indeed help the ice-cream hold its shape better. That said, it’s not essential if you’d rather skip it – you’ll simply get a more traditional soft-serve texture. The GreenPan Frost also has settings for making milkshakes, slushies (of the booze and booze-free variety) and similar treats.Unfortunately, one of the downsides of this style of machine is cleaning: it was definitely trickier to clean than others on this list. The Frost has a self-cleaning cycle, while its numerous parts can be disassembled for cleaning in the dishwasher – a bonus for convenience and repairability. My advice is to run the clean cycle with two to three rinses of warm water and a bit of washing-up liquid before taking apart the machine.It’s a shame that …it’s the priciest model on this list.Machine type:compressor/soft serveCapacity: 1.9lAverage churn time:30-40 minsNoise level:58dBDimensions:22.2 x 44.1 x 43.8cm (WDH)Wattage:150WWarranty:two yearsGreenPanFrost ice-cream maker and slushie machinefrom£328.99£328.99 at Robert Dyas£328.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMakes soft serve, slushies, milkshakes and moreWhat we don’t loveExpensive and tiresome to cleanThe best of the restView image in fullscreenSide by side … the Lakeland (right) excelled at gelato-style recipes, while the Cuisinart Frost Fusion (left) took more trial and error.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianLakeland Compressor ice-cream makerLakelandCompressor ice-cream maker£199.99£199.99 at LakelandWhat we loveMakes amazing ice-creamWhat we don’t loveControls aren’t very intuitiveView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£199.99 at LakelandBest for:gelato-style recipesThis is another great classic compressor machine – simple, with gentle churning that’s ideal for gelato. It performed well in tests, with results in about an hour. It’s also easy to clean.Unlike the Caso IceCreamer, the Lakeland Compressor machine doesn’t allow you to adjust the timing mid-cycle. When I set it to 40 minutes and realised halfway through that my mixture needed longer, I couldn’t simply press the “+” button to add more time – I had to stop and restart the machine instead.Thankfully, this didn’t affect the quality of the ice-cream – it was still excellent and held its texture well in the freezer. It was just frustrating that I had to use a workaround for something that should have been a simple adjustment.It didn’t make the final cut because …I found the controls counterintuitive and a pain to use. The Caso IceCreamer offered a slightly better user experience.Machine type:compressor;capacity:1.8l;average churn time:30-40mins;noise level:58dB;dimensions:49.8 x 38.6 x 30.4cm (WDH);wattage:150W;warranty:three yearsLakelandCompressor ice-cream maker£199.99£199.99 at LakelandWhat we loveMakes amazing ice-creamWhat we don’t loveControls aren’t very intuitiveCuisinart Frost Fusion soft-serve ice-cream maker and drinks machineCuisinartFrost Fusionfrom£199.99£299.99 at Lakeland£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMore affordable than some; easy to useWhat we don’t loveThe soft-serve recipe provided doesn’t workView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£299.99 at Lakeland£199.99 at AmazonBest for:familiesI had high hopes for this machine: it’s cheaper and easier to clean than the GreenPan, but I found it more difficult to achieve the right ice-cream consistency. It was always just a bit too soft, even after many tweaks to the recipe.I started with Cuisinart’s own soft-serve recipe from the accompanying booklet, which uses 100% double cream, sugar and vanilla. Unfortunately, the result was less soft serve, more homemade butter. I initially assumed it was my fault, particularly as I’d halved the quantity – but when it happened a second time, I realised something was up.Swapping to a 60:40 mix of single and double cream fixed this – as it did with other machines – but the whole experience was rather unpleasant. I wouldn’t recommend using your soft-serve maker to churn butter, by the way – it’s not particularly easy to clean.However, the slushies were amazing, and the standard vanilla recipe I used throughout testing was decent, although it lacked the structure I would have liked for soft serve. While there’s nothing catastrophically wrong with the machine itself, be prepared for a lot of trial and error.It didn’t make the final cut because …performance wasn’t up there with the GreenPan, although it is slightly more affordable.Machine type:compressor/soft serve;capacity:1.6l;average churn time:30-40mins;noise level:58dB;dimensions:16.4 x 41.4 x 41.8cm (WDH);wattage:150W;warranty:three years at LakelandCuisinartFrost Fusionfrom£199.99£299.99 at Lakeland£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMore affordable than some; easy to useWhat we don’t loveThe soft-serve recipe provided doesn’t workWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenWorth the wait: freeze-first machines, such as the Cuisinart Solo Scoops, need planning ahead, but can produce excellent ice-cream and sorbet.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianFreeze first vs compressor ice-cream makers – what’s the difference?There was a time when you could only get two types of ice-cream maker. The first was a classicfreeze-firstmodel, where you needed to prefreeze the coolant-filled bowl for at least 24 hours before starting. The other was acompressormodel, using a built-in refrigeration unit that freezes the chilled mixture as it churns, taking up to 60 minutes.While these two options are still popular today, others have joined the ice-cream-making party. These include soft-serve and slushie machines, which also use a compressor but churn faster to produce softer, Mr Whippy-style ice-cream. Another type is often described as a “frozen dessert maker” (such as the Ninja Creami, Nutribullet Chill, and so on). These machines require you to combine ingredients and prefreeze in a tub, after which the mix is processed from frozen with a sharp blade.These newer models are more flexible in terms of what you can make, but they require more experimentation to get the best results and are often trickier to clean.How to make ice-cream in an ice-cream makerI quickly learned during testing that many of the recipes in the ice-cream makers’ accompanying booklets aren’t very good. Most suggest using double cream exclusively, which doesn’t freeze that well and often creates a greasy, grainy texture when it does.My advice is to stick to tried-and-tested recipes that use stable, lower-fat ingredients. While you need some fat to achieve that delicious, creamy feel, if it’s too much, it goes the other way.Compressor machinesView image in fullscreenKeep your cool: compressor models often mean simply adding the chilled mixture and letting the machine do the rest.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianYou’ll get great results with most recipes – I found sorbet and custard-based ice-creams worked best. Simply chill the mixture, then throw it in. In general, mix-ins aren’t advised while freezing and should instead be added at the end using the “churn-only” setting, which simply spins the paddle.Freeze-first machinesThese require you to freeze the included bowl for at least 24 hours before making ice-cream (I found 36 hours works best as a minimum), as well as chill your mixture in the fridge separately. With this done, you can churn as usual – but, like compressor models, leave mix-ins until the end.Soft-serve and slushie machinesThese can be a bit trickier to master, especially if the recipes included with your machine aren’t quite right. For best results, stick to stable, medium-fat recipes (eg not just double cream); otherwise you risk making butter. You can use a chilled mixture straight from the fridge, though – it chills even quicker than a traditional compressor model, so no 24-hour waits.Blade machinesThese work a bit like freeze-first machines, but instead of freezing the bowl overnight, you freeze the mixture in the tub provided. Again, if it’s too high in fat, your mixture will become grainy, so stick to a custard or single-cream base. You can also freeze certain mix-ins directly within the ice-cream base with these models, as the blade will chop right through them.How repairable are ice-cream makers?Repairability varies. If you want a machine that lasts for years, look for one with easily replaceable parts and a simple design. Models with fewer hidden electronics or that can be disassembled into several pieces for cleaning are generally easier to repair at home or by a local professional. In that light, the Nutribullet Chill and Cuisinart Solo Scoops are two of the most easily repairable machines on this list in terms of the spare parts that are available.However, spare parts won’t always cover you for issues with electrical components. It’s always worth checking whether the manufacturer of your model offers a repair service. Some have dedicated support pages on their websites where you can buy replacement parts, and of course, don’t overlook warranties when you’re making a buying decision, for valuable peace of mind if anything should go wrong.For more, read thebest (and worst) chef’s knivesand thebest blenders for smoothies, soups and frozen dessertsDanielle Amato is a consumer reviews journalist with almost a decade of experience covering kitchen and home appliances. She’s an avid ice-cream and pasta enthusiast (not at the same time, though she wouldn’t judge) and loves nothing more than getting stuck into a new recipe or appliance in her unofficial test kitchenExplore more on these topicsIce-cream and sorbetThe FilterDessertFoodGadgetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Alien erotica, football coaching and making Meryl Streep cry: Ted Lasso’s new star Tanya Reynolds opens up | Television | The Guardian
description: She lit up screens as Sex Education’s steamy sci-fi writer, wowed Streep in the West End and now she’s starring in the return of TV’s feelgood footie hit. The star talks about pretending to be sporty – and why she’s a total cheese string
Author: Lucinda Everett
Headline: She lit up screens as Sex Education’s steamy sci-fi writer, wowed Streep in the West End and now she’s starring in the return of TV’s feelgood footie hit. The star talks about pretending to be sporty – and why she’s a total cheese string
Content: ‘The thought of me being tough is hilarious’ … Tanya Reynolds, photographed in London for the Guardian.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The thought of me being tough is hilarious’ … Tanya Reynolds, photographed in London for the Guardian.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianTelevisionInterviewAlien erotica, football coaching and making Meryl Streep cry: Ted Lasso’s new star Tanya Reynolds opens upLucinda EverettShe lit up screens as Sex Education’s steamy sci-fi writer, wowed Streep in the West End and now she’s starring in the return of TV’s feelgood footie hit. The  star talks about pretending to be sporty – and why she’s a total cheese stringFri 31 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy the time its third season came to an end in 2023, Ted Lasso was a Big Deal. The cosy comedy about an indefatigably positive American football coach gee-whizzing his way into the hearts of a London football team had won 13 Emmys and racked up more than 25bn minutes ofviewing.Contributing exactly zero minutes to this staggering stat wasTanya Reynolds, who joins the series in its fourth season as Ted’s assistant coach, Alice.“I don’t know where I was!” she tells me with a helpless shrug as we chat. “I mean, I am a bit of a hermit. I do sort of live under a rock, so it’s not surprising I missed it.” She had heard of it, she assures me, and accepted the invitation to audition because it was “so unlike anything I’ve done before. I just was like: ‘Football coach. Mad. Yeah, OK.’” A week after sending her tape and thinking nothing more of it “because I didn’t think it was very good”, Tanya had a Zoom with the show’s co-creator, writer and titular star, Jason Sudeikis, who offered her the part on the spot. She swiftly watched all three seasons and realised “I really want to be part of this world”.She’s speaking from her north London home on a Monday morning – every hermit’s favourite time to meet a prying journalist who is snooping at your background (I spot candles, books – Tanya recommends her favourites on Instagram – and a huge painting of sunflowers, which she swings her camera towards so I can get a better look). In a sleeveless red top, her hair in a scrunchy, Reynolds is blissfully free of media-training gloss – her answers are peppered with pauses and rephrasings (or perhaps they’re just a result of her being a “nervous person”). She is also warm, never far from a face-splitting laugh and, like all self-respecting Brits, mocks herself routinely and expertly.View image in fullscreen‘I am a bit of a hermit. I do sort of live under a rock’ … says Reynolds.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianAs we settle, amid apologies about her whirring washing machine (“I’m hoping it chills out. You know when it goes mental?”), I ask aboutMeryl Streep and Martin Shortcoming to see1536, the play she is starring in when we speak, with Margot Robbie as co-producer.“We’d known they were coming for weeks. We actually graffitied it backstage: MERYL STREEP IS COMING ON THE TENTH!” she says. “We all stood on the stage, lined up like …” she does her best impression of an old-timey family portrait, “and couldn’t speak. But they were so kind … We all cried. Meryl cried. It was lovely.”She adds that “Margot’s input has been huge … It’s so wonderful that someone with that amount of power is championing really important work, new work.” And how beautiful is she in real life, on a scale of one to obscene? Reynolds laughs. “She’s like a painting that’s come to life.”1536 is the latest entry on Reynolds’s impressive theatrical CV, which also includes playing Masha inThe Seagulllast year opposite Cate Blanchett, and being nominated for an Olivier award in 2024 for her performance inA Mirrorat the Almeida. But many will still know her best for her breakout role in Netflix’sSex Educationas Lily Iglehart – the space-bun sporting, cosplaying teen writer of alien erotica (The Trial of Glenoxi: Fucklord of the Universe being one of her efforts). The show proved a hotbed for young talent, with Ncuti Gatwa and Aimee Lou Wood among the cast. “I remember feeling in my very first days: ‘I am in the presence of superstars,’” says Reynolds.View image in fullscreenReynolds with Siena Kelly in 1536.Photograph: Helen MurrayShe has since become a TV fixture, starring in Netflix’s bubonic plague rompThe Decameron, in which she stole the show as wild maid turned “noblewoman” Licisca, and the BBC’sThe Other Bennet Sister, where she played a deliciously disdainful Caroline Bingley (pleaseGoogle the primrose-eating scene). There have been films, too, including Alice Lowe’s era-hopping comedy Timestalker.Encouraged by Lowe, Reynolds wrote her own film,Dog Person, which she will direct (“I’m definitely terrified, for sure”) and star in, alongside Hugh Bonneville and James Norton. “Hopefully” shooting this year, it follows a thirtysomething woman, exhausted by life’s pressures, who “discovers this desire to be a dog”. (As if by magic, her own dog, a shaggy rescue called Borage, pads in at this point, after a trip to the vet).Born in Hemel Hempstead into “not a theatrical family at all” (her Italian dad was a builder and her mum a sign painter – both were “quite quiet and quite shy”), Reynolds decided, aged four “or maybe six”, to be an actor. Where did that come from?“I don’t.Know,”she enunciates. “I was always showing off and I remember my mum saying: ‘You’re brilliant at acting,’ and something in my brain was like: ‘Oh, I’ll do that.’ My parents, even though they we were not even adjacent to that world … never made it seem like it would be hard.” She was the first person in her family to go to university before winning a fully funded scholarship to the Oxford School ofDrama– the only way she could afford to go.Given that she “never had a backup plan”, what does she think about thedecline of drama in schools? “It’s crazy to me that drama’s even on the chopping block of the curriculum,” she says. “That breaks my heart … The drama department was always my safe space. It’s so upsetting to me that there are kids that may not be able to explore that side of themselves because of government cuts. What is happening? It’s absolutely mad.”If there is a through-line in Reynolds’s career, it is refreshingly complex characters – flawed, forthright, spiky, violent. Playing Licisca, she says, helped her find her “feral” side. “It’s always been there but it never comes out – unless in a medieval costume!”View image in fullscreenReynolds with Jason Sudeikis in Ted Lasso’s fourth season.Photograph: Colin Hutton/AppleCoach Alice is another complicated proposition. She glowers through much of my allotted four episodes, eyeing Ted’s proffered high fives as if she might catch rabies, or worse, fun. But there are glimmers of an unfurling. “I was quite scared at the thought of playing someone tough. The thought of me being tough is hilarious. Because I am a cheese string,” she laughs. “[But] she’s almost performing at the beginning … Particularly in fields that have been historically male-dominant, I think women can often feel they have to present as the opposite to what is typically regarded as feminine. Alice is trying to be this sturdy, unemotional, humourless machine. But what the show is so good at is showing that, beneath any exterior, no matter how tough or spiky, there’s complexity and depth and tenderness.”Indeed, the show is still a wholesome delight: reliably funny, big on cockle-warming, and this season with a great dollop of female empowerment thanks to its new storyline, in which Ted coaches Richmond’s women’s team. It is also a welcome break from the incessant violence against women on our screens, and indeed in all art forms. I mention last month’s revelation that nine out of 10 bestselling novels in the UKfeature a murdered woman. “Yes!” shouts Reynolds, head in hands in exasperation.“A big part of why I loved Ted Lasso so much was that it’s exactly the kind of TV I want to watch right now,” she says. “Personally, and maybe this is because of my own slightly nervous, anxious disposition …” a pause, “or maybe it’s because I’m justfuckingexhausted, like so many women out there are just exhausted of ... yeah,” she trails off, rubbing her eyes wearily. “But I can’t watch things that are violent, and especially violent towards women. I just can’t,” she concludes.“1536,” she adds, “is basically a play about how history is repeating itself [and asking] how far have we moved on from that time that a king [Henry VIII] decided to start changing the laws so he could kill his wives.” A gallows laugh. “Take us out of our huge dresses and put us in jeans, and you could have the same script, essentially.” She adds: “Ted Lasso is very different but its whole thing is about optimism and positivity and … communicating with each other. That’s the kind of telly I’m craving.”Others who have been craving Ted will be pleased to see many of the original cast returning. In fact, outside of the footballers, Reynolds is the only new lead. How was her first day on set?“I was so nervous. And they write as they go, so it wasn’t like we had 10 scripts in advance. By the time I started, I had read two,” she says. “They know where they would like to go but they’re also so open to collaboration and they write for the actors, so everything’s getting built as you’re going.”A lot of her scenes were with “genius improvisers” Sudeikis and Brendan Hunt (the co-creator and writer who plays Coach Beard). “So much of the improv was just them being hilarious, and me trying not to laugh. The whole shoot felt like an exercise in ‘Don’t laugh. Just don’t laugh.’”They also helped Reynolds find her footballing feet. “Like a lot of people, I definitely have gotten into women’s football in the last couple of years but I had to up the ante getting this [job].” Despite watching “more football than I’ve probably ever watched”, the match scenes proved tricky. “They filmed the coaches separately, so we’re not actually watching any football. The lads would improv and shout things out. I just was like ‘Er, kick! Go on, um, kick the ball!’ I had to constantly ask Brendan and Jason: ‘What’s a good football-coachy thing to say?’”The release of Ted Lasso will no doubt catapult Reynolds to a new level of stardom. But despite being “obnoxiously sure of [herself]” at primary school, she has been dogged by imposter syndrome throughout her career. Surely it’s getting better with all her successes, I ask?“To be honest, I think it’s maybe getting worse!” she laughs a ‘what you gonna do?’ laugh. “It gets worse every year. The way I’m dealing with it currently is to take every job as it comes, do my best with it, and then afterwards I don’t watch anything. I just think: ‘I’m just gonna keep going until they tell me I can’t.’”Ted Lasso is on Apple TV from5 August.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionDramaTV comedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A bitter pill: are you wasting your money on supplements? | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: Will collagen make you look younger? Could magnesium help you sleep better? Or are the benefits overstated? A dietitian reveals which are worth taking
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Will collagen make you look younger? Could magnesium help you sleep better? Or are the benefits overstated? A dietitian reveals which are worth taking
Content: Photograph: Anil Akkus/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Anil Akkus/Getty ImagesHealth & wellbeingA bitter pill: are you wasting your money on supplements?Will collagen make you look younger? Could magnesium help you sleep better? Or are the benefits overstated? A dietitian reveals which are worth takingJosie PorterFri 31 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMultivitaminsMultivitamins are one of the most commonly used supplements worldwide – but for most people, there isn’t evidence of a huge benefit.One of the largest trials to date found a smallimprovement in memoryamong older adults taking a daily multivitamin. But the difference was tiny, amounting to roughly a quarter of a word in a 20-word recall test. Other outcomes such as mood, immune function and overall wellbeing have generally shown little to no improvement in people who are already meeting their nutritional needs through food.That doesn’t mean multivitamins are pointless. They may be helpful during life stages with higher nutrient requirements, such as pregnancy, or when intake or absorption is lower. But multivitamins are not standardised, so check with your doctor or dietitian what’s best for you.Your best return on investment will always come from real food. Aim to include fruits, vegetables, whole grains, beans, nuts, seeds, dairy (or fortified alternatives) and protein-rich foods every day in order to give your body a good blend of the vitamins, minerals, fibre and plant compounds that supplements can’t fully replicate.CreatineCreatine has been getting a lot of hype lately, even though it’s been around for years. It’s a compound that your body naturally produces, though you can also get very small amounts from red meat and fish.Creatine is stored in your muscles, where it helps provide energy during short bursts of high-intensity exercise. The effects of taking extra creatine are not dramatic, but when combined with training well, eating enough protein and prioritising recovery, it may help you modestlylift heavier weightsorsprint better.Unlike many nutrients, where dietary changes can often achieve similar results to supplementation, there isn’t a practical food-first way to maximise creatine stores.CollagenCollagen is the main structural protein in skin, tendons and connective tissue, and production starts to gradually decline from your mid-20s.Most collagen supplements come in the form of hydrolysed collagen peptides, meaning the protein has been broken down into smaller fragments that are easier to dissolve and digest. They are typically sold as powders that can be mixed into drinks or foods. Several randomised controlled trials suggest that taking these supplements daily for about three months may lead to smallimprovements in skin hydration and elasticity, particularly in women in their 40s and 50s.Collagen supplements are also being studied for tendon and joint health, with some trials suggesting modest improvements. However, these are best seen as a potential edge for very specific groups, such as people withexercise-related joint injuriesor those withhigher training loads, rather than a magic fix or a replacement for food-first strategies.Before thinking about supplements, it’s crucial to make sure you are eating enough protein overall, which for most people is about 30g per meal, to provide the amino acids needed for tissue repair and collagen production, including glycine and proline, alongside adequate vitamin C from fruit and vegetables, which is required for collagen synthesis.Vitamin DOur skin makes vitamin D from sunlight, but in the UK this only really works between late March and early October, when UVB is strong enough. Outside these months, even on bright or warm days, our exposure to the sun is too weak. This is why low vitamin D is more common in winter, and also more likely year-round in people with darker skin, older adults, those who cover their skin, and people who spend most of their time indoors.There are food sources, but they’re limited and usually not enough on their own, which is why it’s recommended to supplement10 micrograms (400 IU) dailyduring autumn and winter. This is mainly for bone health, supporting calcium absorption and reducing the risk of conditions such as rickets and osteomalacia. But more is not better – vitamin D is fat soluble and stored in the body, so avoid very high intakes as these can build up and may cause harm.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Yagi Studio/Getty ImagesMagnesiumMagnesium supplements are getting a lot of attention for improving everything from sleep and muscle cramps to blood pressure and brain health, but the evidence is more underwhelming than the marketing. Most benefits are seen in people with low magnesium intake. This is relevant because the National Diet and Nutrition Survey shows that many people in the UKfall below recommended intakes, largely due to low consumption of nuts, seeds, legumes, whole grains and leafy green vegetables.These foods, which are naturally high in magnesium, also contain other key nutrients from which we can benefit: fibre, healthy fats, vitamin E, or minerals such as iron.Meeting your recommended allowance is easier than it might seem. For example, a bowl of porridge with pumpkin seeds or wholewheat pasta with chickpeas and spinach can provide almost half of your daily magnesium needs.ElectrolytesElectrolyte supplements contain minerals such as sodium, chloride and potassium that help regulate fluid balance. They’re often marketed as a daily hydration essential, but for most people this isn’t supported by science.In reality, our body tightly regulates electrolytes, particularly sodium, which we lose when we sweat. Outside situations involving significant fluid loss, such as long endurance exercise, heavy sweating or illness, most people maintain electrolyte balance throughfood and simply drinking enough water.When sweating a lot, sodium and chloride are the main electrolytes we lose, and these can usually be replaced by adding salt to meals or drinks, which is far cheaper than supplements. As a rough guide, during heavy sweating, sodium losses are around the equivalent of 1g to 3g of salt per hour, which is roughly equivalent to between a couple of pinches and half a teaspoon.Omega-3In the UK, most people don’t meet the recommendation of at leastone portion of oily fishper week, which contains vital omega-3s, including eicosapentaenoic Acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic Acid (DHA), alongside protein, iodine, selenium and vitamin D. Good sources include mackerel, salmon, trout, sardines and anchovies.We can also get omega-3s from plant sources, known as alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), but this is a less efficient way of meeting our needs, as conversion to EPA and DHA is limited. For people who don’t eat fish, algae-based omega-3 supplements can be a practical alternative. Check the label for adequate levels of EPA and DHA, aiming for about 250-500mg combined.AshwagandhaAshwagandha is a herbal supplement with a long history in Ayurvedic medicine. The strongest evidence of any effectiveness relates to stress. People taking ashwagandha often report improvements in stress and sleep quality, alongsidereductions in cortisol levelsof about 10-30%.But most people in these studies don’t have high cortisol levels to begin with. And because cortisol naturally rises and falls throughout the day and plays an important role in the body, it’s not clear whether lowering it when it’s already within a normal range has any meaningful long-term health benefit.Before turning to supplements, it’s worth remembering that eating regular meals with enough protein and fibre helps provide steady fuel for the brain and body and supports more stable blood sugar levels, which can help combat energy dips, irritability and sudden pangs of “hanger”.Fibre (psyllium husk or blends)Fibre supplements can be useful in specific contexts, particularly for symptom management, with psyllium husk having good evidence for bothconstipation and diarrhoea, and modest improvements incholesterol levelslinked to heart health.Outside these targeted uses, we tend to benefit more when we get fibre from a wide range of plant foods. Large observational studies, including data from the American Gut Project, have found eating30 or more different plant foods a weekis associated with greater gut microbiome diversity.This is probably because whole plant foods such as fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds and whole grains provide fibre alongside a range of other compounds, including polyphenols, that aren’t present in isolated supplements. You don’t need to obsess over eating 30, as more research is needed to confirm this number. Just focus on eating as many plants as possible.IronIron is an essential mineral that’s most often low in menstruating women, endurance athletes and people following plant-based diets. It plays a key role in oxygen transport, energy production and cognitive function, so when levels are low, you can feel it.That said, symptoms such as fatigue can be down to many different factors, so a blood test is essential, as more iron is not better. Higher intakes can cause gastrointestinal side effects such as constipation, nausea and abdominal discomfort, and in rare cases can contribute to iron overload.Reduce your risk of deficiency by eating red meat, fish and poultry, and plant-based iron found in lentils, beans, tofu and fortified cereals. Iron from plants is less readily absorbed, but smart pairings with vitamin C-rich foods such as red peppers and kiwis canincrease absorption by up to 300%. Think beans on toast with tomatoes, or overnight quinoa with strawberries.How to build a balanced plateMost of your needs over time can be covered by a simple repeating structure: one protein (for maintenance and repair); two different-coloured plants (for micronutrients and fibre); one fibre-rich starchy carb (for energy); two flavour boosters such as herbs and spices (for polyphenols); and one source of fat (for vitamin absorption). This framework helps you quickly sense-check whether a meal is broadly balanced, without needing to track, measure or optimise every detail.Aim for protein variety across the week by rotating three to five sources – such as eggs, yoghurt or kefir, chicken or turkey, tofu or tempeh, fish, and beans or lentils – in your weekly shop. This also provides a balance of different vitamins, minerals and compounds.Curate a colourful freezer because frozen fruit, vegetables and herbs are often cheaper, just as nutrient-dense and require zero prep. Think mango chunks stirred into yoghurt, edamame added to salads or rice bowls, raspberries on porridge, spinach blended into sauces, or mixed veg folded into egg fried grains.Aim to try one new ingredient, recipe or meal combination each week. Small, repeated exposures to different foods is one of the simplest ways to naturally increase diversity in your diet and broaden your intake of micronutrients.HowNot toTakeSupplements:ADietitian’sGuide toThriving onRealFood by Josie Porterispublished byEburyat £17.99.
