title: Burnham risks first revolt as PM over apparent support for North Sea drilling | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Labour MPs fear No 10 team lack up-to-date energy insight and don’t fully recognise voters’ climate concerns
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Labour MPs fear No 10 team lack up-to-date energy insight and don’t fully recognise voters’ climate concerns
Content: Andy Burnham has said this week that he intends to take a pragmatic approach to the question of the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham has said this week that he intends to take a pragmatic approach to the question of the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAAndy BurnhamBurnham risks first revolt as PM over apparent support for North Sea drillingLabour MPs fear No 10 team lack up-to-date energy insight and don’t fully recognise voters’ climate concernsFiona Harvey,Aletha Adu,Josh HallidayandPeter WalkerFri 31 Jul 2026 13.38 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham was told he could face the first revolt of his premiership as Labour MPs and climate experts condemned his apparent support for renewed drilling for oil and gas.As the UKsuffersthrough drought, fires and heatwaves, the prime minister gave the strongest indication yet on Friday he was minded to allow new drilling. His comments came just hours before the UN secretary-general warned “every new fossil fuel project” made heatwaves more dangerous.Speaking at a community centre in Sheffield on Friday, Burnham repeated hewould be “pragmatic” about oil and gasand that decisions on new drilling would be made “in due course”. But he added: “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is where does it come from.”But manyLabourMPs are increasingly worried about how support for expanded drilling will play with an electorate alarmed by the worst drought since 1976, soaring temperatures, wildfires, and climate-related food inflation and potential supply shortages.They worry about losing more voters to the Greens: Zack Polanski’s party hasstressed its oppositionto further new licences for the North Sea, including the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea and the Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland. A decision to go ahead with the projects could trigger a new surge in defectors from Labour.View image in fullscreenClimate activists protest outside the office of the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, last week.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersRachael Maskell, the Labour MP for York Central, urged ministers to “keep carbon in the ground”, and watch the recentnational emergency climate briefing. She added: “We’re seeing ice caps melting, seas warming up, hotter and hotter summers. This summer has been a warning that we have to go towards a sustainable future fast.”Clive Lewis, the Labour MP for Norwich South, said there was “no legitimate reason” topress ahead with Jackdawbecause it would make only a negligible difference to energy prices while sending the wrong signal internationally as Europe experienced record heat.Lewis said approving the field would show Burnham was “not looking at the evidence” and that Labour risked adding “the stain of the climate crisis” to the party’s record, alongside Gaza.Graph showing projected production and demand for North Sea gasChris Murray, the Labour MP for Edinburgh East and Musselburgh, said the UK must stay the course on decarbonisation. “Britain was the first country to industrialise and we have a duty to lead the world on net zero. We must be wary of the self-interest from which oil and gas companies are arguing, while the future of the planet is at stake.”António Guterres, the UN secretary-general, did not single out the UK but gave a pointed warning on Friday, as the World Meteorological Organisationforecasthotter temperatures from August to October. “Every new fossil fuel project approved today makes tomorrow’s heatwaves more dangerous, and our world less secure,” Guterres said.“Yet some governments still plan to produce more than twice as much fossil fuel in 2030 as the 1.5-degree limit allows. More coal, oil and gas will lead to a more combustible future.”These warnings are hitting home with voters, several Labour MPs told the Guardian. One source said “there will be a revolt” if there is a chance for Labour MPs to vote on new licences for the North Sea.Jackdaw and Rosebank are already in the planning system, and so could be argued to fall outside Labour’s manifesto promise to halt new licensing.Despite these loopholes, the source said Burnham would need “support from the Conservatives and possibly the SNP rather than Labour unity” if it came to a vote, though Burnham is likely to try to avoid this by taking any decisions as an administrative measure after consultations on the fields conclude in mid-August.Concerns over thenegative impact of allowing new North Sea drillingextend across the Labour party, transcending factions and “tribes”. The Guardian has contacted or been told of concerned MPs including ministers and junior members of government, longstanding senior backbench MPs and committee figures and new MPs from the 2024 general election intake.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA decision on Rosebank and Jackdaw will not come before the consultations end in mid-August, but the issue of whether further drilling could be allowed is likely to still be live when thebudget comes on 28 October. In a video message on social media on Friday announcing the date, the chancellor, John Healey, said it would be “a budget that moves money and power out of Westminster, and into every postcode around Britain”, and that it would be “built on fiscal discipline”.Graph showing projected production and demand for North Sea oilPart of the North Sea problem, according to some insiders, is that Burnham has assembled an older economic team with traditional views on industry, lacking knowledge of the climate and the rapidly changing dynamics of energy around the world.Several influential economists told the Guardian that increased drilling would not help the UK economy. Mariana Mazzucato, who worked closely with Burnham on the lauded transformation of transport in Manchester, and who has been a key influence on his thinking, said: “Drilling the North Sea won’t help people across the UK struggling with their energy bills – most of the oil and gas from these new sites would be sold to the highest bidder on international markets.“But the bigger picture is that green industrial strategy requires coherent and credible policy signals, to give investors confidence that the ‘clean energy superpower’ mission of Labour’s manifesto is still the direction of travel – which this drilling would undermine.”‘It’s too fast, too big’: speed of climate crisis is devastating crops, say farmersRead moreDaniela Gabor, a professor of economics at SOAS, added: “It’s a terrible idea. The Burnham government is caving to the fossil lobby just as we experience some of the most intense heatwaves of recent times.”Nicholas Stern, the economist, said new drilling would not alleviate pressure on energy bills and dismissed arguments that UK North Sea oil would lead to fewer carbon emissions than imports. “Extra output leads to extra use and more greenhouse gases. Further, and importantly, it would send a dangerous signal to the world,” he said.However, some backbench MPs are also wary of the “massive bear trap”, as one described it, of allowing the climate to become a wedge issue for voters, as the Tories and Reform party are seeking to do. They are prepared to keep the peace by accepting the go-ahead for the Jackdaw gasfield, and potentially even the more controversial Rosebank oilfield, if a line can then be drawn against any further licences and if Burnham reaffirms his commitment to pushing forward urgently with net zero.That is still in question. “[There is] growing concern among MPs that No 10 don’t realise this [new drilling] won’t help with bills at all and will cause political damage,” said another Labour backbencher. “A pragmatic approach can help us navigate this but the fundamentals need to be understood.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamLabourFossil fuelsEnergyOilGasAntónio GuterresShareReuse this content

title: Fifa scraps proposal to sell off stakes in World Cup after widespread backlash | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Gianni ⁠Infantino has said Fifa ​has scrapped plans to ⁠sell a stake in the World ⁠Cup to private ​investors ‌after widespread ‌backlash
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Gianni ⁠Infantino has said Fifa ​has scrapped plans to ⁠sell a stake in the World ⁠Cup to private ​investors ‌after widespread ‌backlash
Content: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has said plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup have been scrapped after a furious backlash.Photograph: Buda Mendes/FIFA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFifa president Gianni Infantino has said plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup have been scrapped after a furious backlash.Photograph: Buda Mendes/FIFA/Getty ImagesFifaFifa scraps proposal to sell off stakes in World Cup after widespread backlashGianni ⁠Infantino issues statement on controversial plan‘This proposal will not proceed,’ confirms Fifa presidentNick AmesFri 31 Jul 2026 19.55 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGianni Infantino’s proposal to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors has sensationally collapsed, with the Fifa president admitting the project “has created divisions of a nature that are no longer of the interest of the objective”, amid widespread anger globally.The plan had caused ructions within football around the world, leading Uefa to threaten a boycott of futureFifatournaments if it was not shelved. Other confederations had also come out in opposition while one of Infantino’s senior advisors, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned on Friday in protest at the scheme. The Fifa chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, had also aimed a scathing rebuke at Infantino’s “serious lack of respect” in seeking to force it through with minimal consultation.Andy Burnham calls on Infantino to resign over ‘outrageous’ World Cup plansRead moreIt has led Infantino to back down amid speculation the venture capital firm Thrive Capital, which was leading the proposed investor group, had also expressed doubts after a week that threatened to tear the sport apart. Infantino’s previously secure presidency has come under severe pressure and it remains to be seen whether his climbdown will be enough to save his position.“Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place,” Infantino said in a statement.“Our purpose has always been – and will always be – to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed. Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support.”The proposed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), unveiled earlier this week, had been intended to raise hundreds of millions of dollars by selling a significant stake in the commercial rights of the men’s and women’s World Cups, and the Club World Cup, to investors. It promised an increase in distribution to “over $10bn” (£7.5bn) being spread back among Fifa’s 211 member associations. A deadline of 19 September had been set for member associations to sign up to the scheme, which offered an optional $20m (£14.8m) to those participating.But the plan was roundly rejected by European countries’ FAs, who agreed upon a boycott at an emergency meeting on Thursday. Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation, the latter with a stinging statement on Friday morning, had also made their distaste clear. While Infantino retains a stronghold in Africa he was left with nowhere to go, the numbers to push through the plan in any credible form having eluded him.Attention will now turn to Infantino’s future given the scale of the internal revolt within Fifa and the severe hit his standing has taken elsewhere. It is unlikely his withdrawal of the plan will sway member associations who had already become deeply disenchanted by his handling of the Folarin Balogun affair, which unfolded three weeks previously during the World Cup. But some observers have wondered whether recourse to Fifa’s reserves, which stand at around $4bn (£2.97bn), for the promised FFE cash would convince enough federations to save his skin.Uefa and other confederations have stepped up their search for candidates to run against Infantino in next year’s Fifa election, in which he had been expected to comfortably win a fourth term. Their appetite is unlikely to change and time will tell whether Infantino can turn his fortunes around after an episode that has had a shattering impact on his credibility.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour wins decisive victory in Greater Manchester mayoral byelection | Mayoral elections | The Guardian
description: Bev Craig succeeds Andy Burnham and wins back support in areas where Reform made gains in May
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Bev Craig succeeds Andy Burnham and wins back support in areas where Reform made gains in May
Content: Bev Craig defeated Reform UK by 66.3% to 33.7% in the second round of the Greater Manchester mayoral byelection.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBev Craig defeated Reform UK by 66.3% to 33.7% in the second round of the Greater Manchester mayoral byelection.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianMayoral electionsLabour wins decisive victory in Greater Manchester mayoral byelectionBev Craig succeeds Andy Burnham and wins back support in areas where Reform made gains in MayJosh HallidayNorth of England editorFri 31 Jul 2026 18.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLabour has stormed to a decisive victory in theGreater Manchestermayoral byelection, seizing back areas that recently fell to Reform UK and the Greens.Labour’s Bev Craig, theManchestercity council leader, will now succeed Andy Burnham and hold one of the most powerful political positions outside Westminster.Labour won 47% of first-preference votes, withReform UKway behind on 21% and the Greens in third on 12%.The contest took place under the supplementary vote system, meaning that, as no candidate achieved more than 50%, voters’ second preferences were counted.When voters’ second choices were counted and other parties were eliminated, Labour’s share rose to 66.3% and Reform UK’s to 33.7%.In her victory speech at Co-op Live in Manchester, Craig urged society to “move away from divisive politics that try to pit neighbour against neighbour”.The scale of the victory is a significant boost for the new prime minister, suggesting Labour can win back both left- and right-leaning voters who deserted the party under Keir Starmer.It also poses troubling questions for Nigel Farage, whose party has surrendered its year-long lead in the national polls and is in a deepening crisis over questions about its funding.A poll last month had Labour and Reform UK virtually neck and neck in the battle for the mayoralty.In the May elections, Farage’s party won more than 100 seats across Greater Manchester, including all but one of the 25 up for grabs in Wigan – the borough of Burnham’s new constituency – and 18 out of 19 in Tameside, both once solidly Labour areas.However, Farage scuppered the party’s mayoral campaign when he announced he was standing down as an MP in order to fight aself-imposed parliamentary byelectionin Clacton after scrutiny over his funding.Before the result was officially declared, Labour sources said it had won in every ward in boroughs including Bury, Tameside and all but one in Trafford, where both Reform UK and the Greens made inroads in May.In Oldham, where Reform UK gained 13 councillors and ended Labour’s 15-year grip on power two months ago, Labour won 17 of the 20 wards in the mayoral contest, it is understood. Sources said Labour had won every ward in Gorton and Denton, the constituency won by the Green party’s Hannah Spencer in February.One senior Labour source said it looked as if Reform UK had “massively underperformed” and that the result was a combination of Burnham’s prime ministership signalling “you can vote Labour again” and voters feeling confident they could vote for Craig.‘This is the dream job’: Labour’s Bev Craig on the battle to be Greater Manchester mayorRead moreThe result will also worry Reform UK as its hard-right rival Restore Britain won 8.7% of the vote to beat the Conservatives into fourth place.Rupert Lowe’s anti-immigration party, which only launched six months ago, focused its campaign on child sexual abuse gangs and its approach appeared to pay off, taking a share of Reform UK’s vote while potentially galvanising lapsed voters who might otherwise have stayed at home.Its support was strongest in more deprived outer boroughs like Tameside, where Restore got 14% of the vote – almost 6,000 voters – and Rochdale and Oldham where it won 12%.Speaking from the podium after the result was announced just after 11pm on Friday, Craig said that during the campaign she had met “fantastic people doing incredible things against the odds every single day – rejecting the politics of hate but standing with their neighbours, looking out for each other”.For the Greens, which won 7% of the vote against Burnham when the Greater Manchester mayoralty was last contested in 2024, the result may be a disappointment after its recent electoral successes.Geraldine Coggins, the Green party candidate, said she was pleased with its campaign and that there had been a “surge” of support for the party under Zack Polanski’s leadership.She claimed the result was “not a ringing endorsement” of Craig, comparing her 47% vote share with Burnham whonever won less than 60% of the vote in each of his three victories since 2017.“The fact this has even gone to the second round is devastating for them,” Coggins said. “To have lost this much support in the honeymoon period of a new prime minister is not a positive sign for them.”The contest was triggered by Burnhamwinning the Makerfield byelectionon 18 June, meaning he had to step down as mayor of the most powerful combined authority outside London.The byelection was the biggest contest of its kind in British political history, with more than 2 million eligible voters.However, the turnout was down on previous Greater Manchester mayoral contests – only 25%, the third lowest of any mayoral byelection to date – due to a combination of low voter awareness and it taking place in the summer holidays.Explore more on these topicsMayoral electionsGreater ManchesterBev CraigLabourManchesterReform UKGreen partynewsShareReuse this content

title: At least 57 people die as tens of thousands cross to Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco | Spain | The Guardian
description: Pedro Sánchez decries ‘violation of territorial integrity’ as other EU countries criticise Madrid over incident
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Pedro Sánchez decries ‘violation of territorial integrity’ as other EU countries criticise Madrid over incident
Content: People try to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on Thursday.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/APView image in fullscreenPeople try to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on Thursday.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/APSpainAt least 57 people die as tens of thousands cross to Spanish enclave of Ceuta from MoroccoPedro Sánchez decries ‘violation of territorial integrity’ as other EU countries criticise Madrid over incidentSam Jonesin Madrid,Angela Giuffridain Rome andJakub KrupaFri 31 Jul 2026 13.52 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 03.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 57 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after as many as 50,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco in what Spain’s prime minister,Pedro Sánchez, called “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”.The huge influx, which took place over the course of just 24 hours, overwhelmed the city of 85,000 people, triggered a political crisis for Madrid and led to a mixed reaction from other EU countries, including calls forSpainto be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.3:37Tens of thousands of migrants cross into Spanish enclave Ceuta from Morocco - videoSánchez, who arrived in Ceuta on Friday morning, said he would use all the resources at his disposal to guarantee the safety of the city’s population.He attributed the mass crossing to “human trafficking mafias” that had taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta, or Spain’s other north African enclave of Melilla, could not be summarily returned under special rules.Sánchez said: “That has spread like wildfire during these last few hours through the networks of mafias that traffic in human beings and has produced an avalanche of the characteristics and dimension that we experienced yesterday.”Sánchez said a temporary reception centre would be established to facilitate the documentation, registration, triage and “expedited” expulsion of people with no legal claim to be in Spain.Hundreds of migrants run and cheer as they enter Spain’s enclave of CeutaHe also said the government would erect a visible barrier – a line of buoys – near the breakwater at Ceuta’s Tarajal beach to make it clear where the border was, and to legally comply with the court’s ruling.Although the Spanish government said about 50,000 people had crossed the border on Thursday and in the early hours of Friday, the president of Ceuta put the figure at about 60,000.Spain’s interior ministry, which has deployed additional police officers and soldiers to the enclave, said more than 48,300 people had voluntarily returned toMoroccoby 6pm on Friday.The Irish presidency of the EU has convened a meeting of member states on Saturday, under the Integrated Political Crisis Response mechanism.EU sources said this will provide experts from member states with an opportunity “to discuss the movements into Ceuta over the last two days, the numbers of people who have returned to Morocco today, the supports being provided by the EU to Spain and diplomatic engagement with Morocco”.A further meeting of EU ambassadors has been called in Brussels on Monday.The latest incident dwarfs the last mass border crossing in May 2021, when Morocco loosened its border controls, allowing about 10,000 people to enter the territory over the course of two days.Map showing location of Ceuta between Spain and Morocco, and another map showing location of Tarajal breakwater in CeutaThat crossing came amid heightened tensions between Madrid and Rabat over Spain’s decision to allow the leader of the Western Sahara independence movement, the Polisario Front, to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. Morocco and the Polisario Front both lay claim to Western Sahara, which was under Spanish rule until 1975, when colonial authorities handed over the territory to Morocco and Mauritania.That diplomatic crisis ended in 2022 when Madrid reversed its longstanding policy of neutrality and backed Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara – a move that had caused a diplomatic rift between Spain and Algeria, which had supported the Polisario group.Sánchez visited Algiers on 20 July – the first such visit by a Spanish head of government in four years – marking a thaw in relations with Algeria.Moroccan government sourcestold the Europa Press news agencythat the surge of people entering Ceuta was down to “criminal organisations” and insisted that Rabat’s cooperation with Spain remained “exemplary”.Morocco’s ambassador to Spain, Karima Benyaich, was quoted by the Associated Press as saying that “we have always prioritized legal, orderly and safe migration for all” and indicated that the situation had developed against Rabat’s wishes.View image in fullscreenSpain’s interior ministry said more than 48,300 people decided to return to Morocco from the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on Friday.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/APRachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers’ association representing officers of the Spanish Guardia Civil – which patrols Spain’s borders – described the situation as a “serious humanitarian crisis”.Without shelter, thousands of people, including unaccompanied children, had been left sleeping in parks and on pavements, while others roamed the streets aimlessly. “It’s chaotic,” said Sbihi.Among those who died, many drowned, but some were killed in a crush to cross the breakwater fence at Tarajal beach, Sbihi said.View image in fullscreenPeople waiting on the Moroccan side of the border for a chance to cross to Ceuta.Photograph: ReutersVideo footage on Thursday showed crowds of people walking around the breakwaters at Tarajal beach on to local roads. While most appeared to be young men, there were also families with women and small children.Ceuta and Melilla have the E​U’s only land border with ​Africa. ‌Both cities ​periodically ​experience surges in attempted crossings by people seeking to reachEurope.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCrowds in downtown Ceuta on Friday after making the crossing.Photograph: Fabian Bimmer/ReutersThe events in Ceuta led some EU countries to issue strong threats or rebukes.Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, summoned Italy’s ambassador to Madrid on Friday after Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, blamed the situation in Ceuta on the Sánchez government’s decision to offer a now closed schemeto regularise the statusof more than 1 million undocumented migrants and asylum seekers. He said the programme had incentivised human trafficking and was “profoundly wrong”.Tajani’s remarks prompted a sharp response from Albares, who said the comments were “unbecoming” and accused Italy of “partisan demagoguery”.Italy announced on Friday evening that it would be suspending its Schengen arrangements with Spain, but the practical impact of the move was not immediately clear.Meloni said the measure would be kept in force only as long as needed, adding: “In parallel, Italy is ready to support every European initiative to assist Spanish institutions as needed to restore full control of the union’s external borders and to address the ongoing situation with determination.”View image in fullscreenSpanish soldiers patrolling the Spanish-Moroccan border in Ceuta on Friday.Photograph: Fabian Bimmer/ReutersResponding to Italy’s unilateral decision, aEuropean Commissionspokesperson said a member state “may exceptionally and temporarily reintroduce internal border control as a matter of last resort, to address serious threats to public order or national security”. But they added that the member state would need to notify the commission and explain how the situation in Ceuta constituted such a threat.The Guardian understands that Italy has not yet formally notified any of its EU partners of its decision.The Swedish prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, urged Spain to “act swiftly to regain control of the situation and fulfil its commitments within Schengen cooperation”.The Finnish interior minister, Mari Rantanen,saidthat as Spain had “completely failed to protect the Schengen area’s external border”, all EU countries should support Italy’s proposal to suspend its Schengen status.However, in a statement later on Friday, the European Commission said Ceuta and Melilla were subject to special Schengen rules that prevented onward movement within the zone.View image in fullscreenBelongings float in the sea after they were left behind by people crossing from Morocco into Ceuta.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/APThe EU’s migration commissioner, Magnus Brunner, called the situation in Ceuta “unacceptable” and said he was in close contact with the Spanish authorities. But he also confirmed there was no onward route from Ceuta given the enclave’s unique status under the Schengen rules.He said: “The Schengen borders code provides for special rules that apply to Ceuta and Melilla. Border checks on persons departing from Ceuta and Melilla remain in force.”But there were also shows of unity. The European Council president, António Costa, expressed his “solidarity with Spain in the current situation of illegal migration in Ceuta”.The French president, Emmanuel Macron, said he had been in touch with the Spanish government to express his solidarity and to offer assistance to Spain. But, as a precautionary measure, Macron said he had asked the interior ministry to strengthen the French controls on its border with Spain with four mobile units and drones.In Spain, the opposition People’s party (PP) called on Sánchez to come up with a tough response, saying the military and police reinforcements announced on Thursday night were insufficient.In a post on X, the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, wrote: “People have continued to arrive in Ceuta throughout the night, and those on the ground describe an occupied city, with nothing sufficient being done to prevent it.” The far-right Vox party called the incident “an invasion”.On Friday evening, hundreds attended an anti-migrant rally outside the Moroccan embassy in Madrid, with images showing some protesters performing Nazi salutes and waving flags with far-right insignia.Explore more on these topicsSpainMoroccoPedro SánchezEuropean UnionEuropean CommissionMigrationItalynewsShareReuse this content

title: High court clears way for clinical trial giving puberty blockers to children | Transgender | The Guardian
description: Legal challenge to King’s College London research study claimed it could harm participants but was rejected
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Legal challenge to King’s College London research study claimed it could harm participants but was rejected
Content: King's College London says particular care will be taken over the safety of participants, who will be aged between 11 and 16.Photograph: camberwell.camera/AlamyView image in fullscreenKing's College London says particular care will be taken over the safety of participants, who will be aged between 11 and 16.Photograph: camberwell.camera/AlamyTransgenderHigh court clears way for clinical trial giving puberty blockers to childrenLegal challenge to King’s College London research study claimed it could harm participants but was rejectedKevin RawlinsonFri 31 Jul 2026 13.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA clinical trial of drugs that can delay puberty can go ahead after a high court judge threw out a legal challenge on Friday.Campaigners had launched the attemptto halt the planned research into puberty blockers, to be run by researchers at King’s College London (KCL), on the grounds that they believed it could harm the children taking part.But Mr Justice Chamberlain refused the application for a judicial review, saying none of their claims had a realistic chance of success in court. He said each patient involved in the Pathways trial would have been assessed over “many months” by specialist doctors who would have “formed the opinion that a child has a reasonable prospect of receiving a clinical benefit from the treatment”.The university welcomed the court’s decision on Friday, saying particular care would be taken over the safety of participants of the trial, which will start recruiting more than 220 children aged between 11 and 16 years old from 1 August.But opponents, including the psychotherapist James Esses and Keira Bell, who began taking puberty blockers as a teenager before later detransitioning, expressed sadness at the ruling.Bell told the BBC: “It’s a tragedy that the court has refused permission for this challenge to proceed. The medical profession and morality do not always walk hand in hand. If they did, this trial would be out of the question.”The Bayswater Group, which works with parents of gender-questioning children and was also part of the legal challenge, said:“We remain of the view that the Pathways trial does not meet the legal and ethical thresholds required for research on children.“The design and scale of the study, the known and potential harms of the intervention, and the absence of a sufficient prior evidence base of benefit raise fundamental questions about whether the protective framework for minors has been properly implemented.”A spokesperson for KCL said: “Pathways trial is a carefully designed study to give much needed evidence about the potential benefits and risks of puberty suppression to improve NHS care.“A small number of young people with long-term gender incongruence, who have already received comprehensive psychological and social support through NHS gender services, will be eligible.”The spokesperson added that the study would have “strict eligibility requirements” and that the trial’s design had been “carefully reviewed by independent researchers and has been approved by the UK’s health research regulators, the HRA and MHRA”.The study was originally commissioned in response to a 2024 review of gender identity services by Dr Hilary Cass, which found that gender medicine was an “area of remarkably weak evidence” and“built on shaky foundations”. Initially used to treat early onset puberty,puberty blockershad been prescribed off-label to children with gender dysphoria until the NHS banned their use last year after the Cass review.Explore more on these topicsTransgenderChildrenMedical researchYoung peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Drifting SpaceX rocket heading for accidental collision with moon | SpaceX | The Guardian
description: Scientists and sky gazers will watch intently as rocket’s upper stage slams into lunar surface on Wednesday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Scientists and sky gazers will watch intently as rocket’s upper stage slams into lunar surface on Wednesday
Content: The SpaceX rocket expected to smash into the moon is seen lifting off from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on 15 January 2025.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAView image in fullscreenThe SpaceX rocket expected to smash into the moon is seen lifting off from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on 15 January 2025.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPASpaceXDrifting SpaceX rocket heading for accidental collision with moonScientists and sky gazers will watch intently as rocket’s upper stage slams into lunar surface on WednesdayAssociated PressFri 31 Jul 2026 09.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA driftingSpaceXrocket is on a collision course withthe moonafter launching a pair of lunar landers more than a year ago.The rocket’s upper stage will unintentionally slam into the moon on Wednesday, carving out a crater and sending up a plume of dust and rubble that scientists – and sky gazers – are eager to observe.Space tracking expert Bill Gray predicts an impact of 5,400mph (8,700km/h) – seven times the speed of sound – near Einstein Crater on the moon’s sunlit western limb. With the action unfolding in the wee hours of the morning for the US, the eastern portions of the US and Canada, and much of South America, should have the best views.While scientists are not too concerned about this particular piece ofspace junk, it highlights the growing threat as more and more items cram into orbit.One small pen for one giant fee: Buzz Aldrin’s mission-saving felt-tip sells for over $850,000Read more“Things are getting crowded up there,” said Gray, who plans to view the aftermath from New Brunswick, Canada.It was never SpaceX’s intent to hit the moon. But space experts said the crash could have been avoided if the upper stage had been nudged into orbit around the sun.It will be the second dead rocket known to crash into the moon accidentally. A Chinese rocket segment dug out a pair of craters on the lunar far side in 2022.The new smashup will occur on the moon’s near side, packing the equivalent energy of three tons of TNT explosives.The impact flash, lasting less than a second, will probably be too dim to see from Earth, according to experts. But the stream of ejected material could stretch for several miles into space and remain visible to telescopes for tens of minutes.“Gravity on the moon is low and there is no wind to blow the dust away,” said Los Alamos national laboratory’s Benjamin Fernando, who is encouraging observations by professionals and amateurs alike.“Part of the reason for our interest in this event is to figure out how much of a hazard debris impacts pose to future astronauts,” he added in an email.Fernando anticipates an impact crater nearly 90ft across and 16ft deep (27 meters across and 5 meters deep), too small to see from Earth but visible to spacecraft.Nasa’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and South Korea’s Danuri lunar orbiter will gather before-and-after shots of the crash scene.Explore more on these topicsSpaceXThe moonSpacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran strikes tankers under US escort in Hormuz strait as Trump gathers cabinet to discuss war | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Energy prices have soared again since fighting between US and Iran resumed two weeks ago as conflict spreads across Middle East
Author: William Christou
Headline: Energy prices have soared again since fighting between US and Iran resumed two weeks ago as conflict spreads across Middle East
Content: Donald Trump en route to Camp David where he and his cabinet are meeting to discuss the war and its fallout.Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump en route to Camp David where he and his cabinet are meeting to discuss the war and its fallout.Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/APUS-Israel war on IranIran strikes tankers under US escort in Hormuz strait as Trump gathers cabinet to discuss warEnergy prices have soared again since fighting between US and Iran resumed two weeks ago as conflict spreads across Middle EastWilliam Christouin BeirutFri 31 Jul 2026 10.48 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 10.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran has said it struck two tankers trying to pass through the strait of Hormuz under the escort of the US military asDonald Trumpgathered his cabinet to discuss the stalling war and rising prices as midterm elections in the US loom.Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Friday that the “non-compliant oil tankers … were struck and brought to a halt, while four other oil tankers quickly changed course and returned to their previous positions”. The military body said the ships had tried to pass through the strait via an “undeclared route” and under US aerial escort.Iran and the US have said ships should pass through the strait via two competing routes, with Iran bombing ships that take the southern route, close to the coast of Oman, and the US bombing ships that violate its blockade of Iranian ships and ports.View image in fullscreenVessels in the strait of Hormuz near Oman. The strait has been almost completely closed to traffic for the last two weeks.Photograph: ReutersThe strait has been almost completely closed to traffic since Iran and the US returned to fighting two weeks ago, sending energy prices soaring. On Thursday, the price of crude oil pushed past $90 a barrel when the US struck Iran in retaliation for its targeting of US bases in Jordan.Fighting continued on Friday, with the Kuwaiti defence ministry reporting that it had shot down Iranian drones targeting “vital and military facilities” without any casualties.In Lebanon, the Israeli military carried out a huge detonation overnight near the ancient Beaufort Castle. It said it was targetingHezbollahtunnels and infrastructure. The explosion was heard across south Lebanon and covered nearby towns in ash, while photos showed the affected area levelled by the force of the blast.Lebanese officials accusedIsraelof violating the ceasefire by carrying out the detonation. The Israeli military said it was ensuring the security of its northern residents.View image in fullscreenSmoke rises behind Beaufort Castle in Lebanon after an Israeli military strike in June. The area was hit by Israel again on Friiday in a massive explosion that covered towns in ash.Photograph: Léo Corrêa/APTrump has tried to open the strait of Hormuz by force, butincreasingly intense US strikes on Iran have yielded few results. The price of gas and groceries remain high in the US as a result of the energy disruption, complicating Republicans’ chances at the ballot box in November’s midterm elections.On Friday, Trump brought his cabinet together at the Camp David retreat in Maryland to try to chart a path forward for the war. The White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, said at a briefing last week that the cabinet meeting would be “a lot of fun and something different for the cabinet to experience together”.Top of the agenda will be the Iran war, which Trump promised would last a few weeks but has now dragged on for five months. A Reuters-Ipsos poll this week found that one in three Americans support the war, the lowest polling since the war began.View image in fullscreenA gas station in Miami. Energy companies have posted record profits as a result of the war in Iran.Photograph: Marta Lavandier/APSupport in Congress is also waning, with the US Senate narrowly rejecting a symbolic vote to express disapproval of the war. The war powers resolution asking the president to stop the war failed in a 49-50 vote.Inflation caused by the war is a boon for Democrats, who are hoping to wrest control of the house from the Republicans.Energy companies have posted record profits as a result of the conflict, with ExxonMobil’s profits doubling and Chevron reporting more than five times its profits in the same time period last year.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranStrait of HormuzTrump administrationDonald TrumpIranUS politicsMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He lived here a long time, so it feels poignant’: Nick Cave thrills Brighton passersby with secret rooftop gig | Nick Cave | The Guardian
description: Prior to playing huge outdoor show in city’s Preston Park, Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds set up on a record shop balcony – and play to fans visiting from across the world
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Prior to playing huge outdoor show in city’s Preston Park, Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds set up on a record shop balcony – and play to fans visiting from across the world
Content: Onstage commitment is his trademark … Nick Cave performing with the Bad Seeds on the roof of Resident Records in Brighton.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOnstage commitment is his trademark … Nick Cave performing with the Bad Seeds on the roof of Resident Records in Brighton.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/The GuardianNick Cave‘He lived here a long time, so it feels poignant’: Nick Cave thrills Brighton passersby with secret rooftop gigPrior to playing huge outdoor show in city’s Preston Park, Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds set up on a record shop balcony – and play to fans visiting from across the worldAlexis PetridisFri 31 Jul 2026 12.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNick Cave and the Bad Seeds’ only advertised UK live performance of 2026, a show in Brighton’s Preston Park, arrives with other events across the city attached. The Duke of York’s Picturehouse cinema is hosting a weekend-long Nick Cave takeover, featuring films curated and introduced by the singer-songwriter. There is a pop-up shop replete with exclusive merchandise, and a postbox where physical letters can be sent toThe Red Hand Files, the website Cave started in 2018 where he answers fans’ questions on topics ranging from faith and grief to his favourite brand of hair dye (L’Oreal, apparently). Even the announcements at the train station have been changed: arrivals are temporarily greeted by the sound of Nick Cave welcoming them to Brighton.All these have been well-publicised, but judging by the crowd gathering in Kensington Gardens, a narrow pedestrian road in North Laine – not far from Jubilee Street, the subject of a Cave song – word also seems to have leaked out about a theoretically secret event: a live performance on the roof of Resident Records, which is hosting the two-dayNick Cavepop-up shop.View image in fullscreenBy 10.30am the street is packed … the view of Resident Records, with the band performing on the balcony.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/The GuardianA substantial group has already assembled, an hour before the performance is scheduled to begin. Some have been tipped off in advance (“My mate told me about it last night, he’s very well connected”). Others simply arrived in order to avail themselves of an exclusive Cave picture disc. (It sold out yesterday and there are already copies on eBay for £60, one disgruntled punter notes, before suggesting that the enterprising soul behind the eBay listing is “a bastard”.) After seeing the musical equipment on the roof, they put two and two together.By 10.30am, the street is packed. A security guard manages to keep a narrow flow of pedestrians moving through its centre, but no one seems to have considered Snoopers Paradise, the vintage market across the road. The crowd jams its doorways and shoppers can’t get out: “What’s going on?” asks a plaintive voice. “Oh, I can’tstandNick Cave.”Said voice is clearly in the minority. The startling thing about the crowd is that it largelyisn’tcomprised of curious locals: there are people here from Germany, Norway, France, all of whom have flown in specially for the Preston Park gig. There is talk of visitors from the US and east Asia. A couple from Oslo are enjoying what they call “a Nick Cave summer”, following the Bad Seeds around Europe: “Well, we’re going to four shows – he’s playing 32”. TheBrightonshow has extra appeal, says Lisa, who has travelled down from Edinburgh with her partner because it’s a kind of a hometown gig, although “former adopted hometown” gig would be more accurate. “He lived in Brighton for a long time – he moved when his son died,” she says, referring to Arthur Cave, who fell from a cliff in Ovingdean in 2015. “So it feels quite poignant.”View image in fullscreenEclectic and winningly chaotic … Nick Cave.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/The GuardianThe distance some people in the crowd have travelled reflects Cave’s ongoing purple patch. The music he has released in the last decade – most notably 2019’s extraordinary mediation on loss,Ghosteen– has been some of the most acclaimed of his career. The harrowing documentary filmOne More Time With Feelingmet with similar acclaim, as didFaith Hope and Carnage, a book containing an astonishingly frank series of interviews with journalist Sean O’Hagan.Cave has courted controversy over his opposition to the cultural boycott of Israel, although it doesn’t seem to have impacted his popularity. Improbably, the Bad Seeds began playing arena-sized venues at the exact moment their music took a turn towards the abstract, with 2016’sSkeleton Tree, although Lisa suggests the crowds may have been swelled by those only familiar with his most famous songs. “I think there were a lot of Peaky Blinders fans in the audience when he played Glasgow,” she says, “just waiting to hear Red Right Hand.” She wrinkles her noise, irritably. “They were quite chatty during the rest of it.”By the time Cave and the Bad Seeds arrive, there are people gathered not just on the street but on the roofs of adjacent shops. The set is eclectic – lurching from the apocalyptic clatter of 1985’s Train Long Suffering to a piano-led cover of T Rex’s Cosmic Dancer – and winningly chaotic, as perhaps any performance involving seven musicians and four backing singers on a tiny balcony is wont to be.View image in fullscreenFans on Kensington Gardens watching Nick Cave.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/The GuardianCave occasionally grins at the absurdity of it all (“Fucking Brighton!” he smiles at one point) or issues frantic instructions to his bandmates mid-song, but the really striking thing is how committed his performance is, despite the peculiar circumstances. He hangs precariously over the balcony to conduct the crowd in call-and-response vocals. Singing Henry Lee as a duet with Janet Ramus, he performs it as if wracked by a desire for both the backing vocalist and his wife, Susie, who is watching from an adjacent balcony. Then again, onstage commitment regardless of the circumstances is something of a Cave trademark, as our Norwegian friends enjoying their summer of Nick note. “In Antwerp, the show was in the middle of a heatwave and he played for two and a half hours wearing a three-piece suit.”It ends with a version of Papa Won’t Leave You, Henry. The police arrive shortly afterwards – one suspects the gig was not officially sanctioned – but the crowd are already dispersing, most of them in the direction of Preston Park. It’s hours before the Bad Seeds are due on stage, but the real lure seems to be the opportunity to outwit the bastards on eBay: a rumour suggests remaining copies of the exclusive picture disc are on sale there, and people scurry off.Explore more on these topicsNick CavePop and rockBrightonShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s OK to mess around’: how ‘mop man’ stole the show at Glasgow’s Commonwealth Games | Commonwealth Games | The Guardian
description: CJ Miller from West Lothian has delighted global audiences with ‘sheer stupidity’ of his half-time routines
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: CJ Miller from West Lothian has delighted global audiences with ‘sheer stupidity’ of his half-time routines
Content: CJ Miller, the man behind the mop, says he is enjoying ‘a lovely 50 minutes of fame’.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCJ Miller, the man behind the mop, says he is enjoying ‘a lovely 50 minutes of fame’.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianCommonwealth Games‘It’s OK to mess around’: how ‘mop man’ stole the show at Glasgow’s Commonwealth GamesCJ Miller from West Lothian has delighted global audiences with ‘sheer stupidity’ of his half-time dancesPriya BharadiaFri 31 Jul 2026 12.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe 2026Commonwealth Gamesin Glasgow have already provided plenty of highlights. But fans across the world have been dazzled by one particular breakout star: the “mop man”.When a cleaner came out at half-time during a netball match to wipe down the court before the restart, everything appeared normal. But as the cleaner swept, and the first bars of Queen’s I Want to Break Free rang out in the venue, he went from sweeping to a standing split.A full dance routine set to the 1984 hit then followed, much to the surprise and delight of the audience at the OVO Hydro. The crowd watched him do the worm, splits and front handsprings. He has since entertained crowds during breaks in play at a number of other events and clips of his performances have gone viral online.View image in fullscreen‘It’s Doris the mop now’: CJ Miller isn’t the only one to have been given a surprising nickname.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAThe man behind the mop is CJ Miller, 25, from Livingston, West Lothian, a trained dancer who was hired by the Games to keep crowds entertained during intermissions.He considers himself more of an introvert than his cleaning alter ego. “I’m an anxious and paranoid queen,” said Miller. “And I’m so grateful for the turn of events. It’s been a lovely 50 minutes of fame. I wish I’d had a haircut before it happened.”Miller was initially told he would be part of a flashmob at the Games with other dancers. “Then it was, ‘oh, here’s a mop. Here’s the song.’ It wasn’t until the Tuesday before the Games I found out it was gonna be Boo Boo the Fool here, on his own,” Miller laughed, pointing to himself.View image in fullscreenFreddie Mercury in Queen’s video for I Want to Break Free, the song Miller dances to.Photograph: QueenWhen choreographing the routine, Miller was inspired by “the concept of a volunteer … a cleaner that had been possessed by the music and just exploded.”But the character soon took on a life – and fanbase – of his own. “People have messaged being like, ‘Thank you for making me smile, I really needed that today.’”For Miller, the universal charm of his performance comes from “the sheer stupidity, the sheer bonkersness of it all”. “It just made people feel like it’s OK to mess around,” he said. “Sometimes, people need to be reminded to just take a break. Just take a minute to smile at someone else being so bloody ridiculous.”Miller’s performance was soon picked up by broadcasters and newspapers around the world. There was particular praise for the unexpected chemistry with his dance partner: Doris the mop.“Phil [Goodlad] from the BBC had named the mop Doris – so I didn’t even name the bloody mop!” said Miller. “He asked me, and I went: ‘The mop is a mop, Phil.’ And he was like: ‘I think it looks like a Doris.’ I went: ‘Brilliant. It’s Doris the mop now, Phil, spectacular.’”Did he have a name in mind for his other dance partner, the vacuum? “It was a Vax vacuum, so I think the vacuum should be called Vaxtina – like Xtina. You can write that one down.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA new start after 60: stuck in a hospital bed, I decided to retire. Now I’m a tap dancerRead moreGoing into the Games, Miller felt nervous about performing in front of a sports crowd for the first time. “Basketball, for me, was a scary one. I was like: ‘I don’t think the basketball crowd are going to want to see my flamboyant ass, giving them a dance to Freddie Mercury. And I was wrong. The basketball crowd were incredible.”View image in fullscreenMiller with his dance partner, Doris the mop.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian“It was a lesson for me to check my own prejudice,” he said. “It doesn’t excuse the point of view I had of sports fans, and that has been changed now from the immense support I’ve received from the sports fans at the Commonwealth. Thank you for proving me wrong, sports fans.”Going forward, Miller is soon to join Newcastle College as a dance tutor and continue building his career as a choreographer. But will the world ever see more of mop man?“I think it would be fun,” said Miller, who has been approached by one company about taking his performance further. “If I were to do it again, let’s get some other professions in there,” said Miller. “Referee, waiter, bloody construction worker. Let’s get inventive with it.”While mop man’s performances may have come to an end, Miller hopes viewers can be inspired by his character’s self-confidence and sense of whimsy. “Be messy, fail, screw up,” he said. “That’s what makes us human. Get your mop and shake your ass, you know what I mean?”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth GamesCommonwealth Games 2026DanceQueenScotlandGlasgownewsShareReuse this content
