title: Release schedule: when to wee and when to wait during this summer’s biggest movies | Movies | The Guardian
description: With run-times hitting three hours, you will probably need to take a bathroom break during this season’s blockbusters. Here’s a handy guide for your urination calculations
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: With run-times hitting three hours, you will probably need to take a bathroom break during this season’s blockbusters. Here’s a handy guide for your urination calculations
Content: A quick dash … Matt Damon in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesView image in fullscreenA quick dash … Matt Damon in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesMoviesRelease schedule: when to wee and when to wait during this summer’s biggest moviesWith run-times hitting three hours, you will probably need to take a bathroom break during this season’s blockbusters. Here’s a handy guide for your urination calculations‘An intermission is a must’: why Greek cinemas are adding a loo break to The OdysseyStuart HeritageFri 31 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe OdysseyYou will almost certainly need to urinate during Christopher Nolan’s epic. Do not make the same mistake I did, and sneak off after the big cyclops setpiece. You might assume that the plot will relax after this, but you will be wrong. If your cinema’s toilet is as far from the screen as my cinema’s, you will end up missing most of the Trojan Horse section. Much better would be to cling on until after the horse, because then you’ll only miss the Laestrygonians. These are the giants depicted on the film’s poster but you pretty much get the gist of the scene from the poster anyway.Minions and MonstersThis feels bizarre to say, but do not go to the toilet at any point during the first half of this movie, because it is somehow the most lovingly observed tribute to the early days of Hollywood in recent years. It almost exclusively deals with the bumpy transition from silent films to talkies, with such carefully observed tenderness that it is genuinely quite moving. If you think that sounds a lot like Damien Chazelle’s Babylon, then you would be right (including the elephant). However, since that film didn’t have minions in it and this film does, this is better. Anyway, this element burns out after about an hour, at which point you can wee at will.View image in fullscreenHold it … Toy Story 5.Photograph: Disney/PAToy Story 5Plenty of choices here, depending on why you went to see the film in the first place. If you want to find yourself emotionally engaged with the heart of the film, then get up and go to the toilet whenever the army of Buzz Lightyears arrive on the screen. Until close to the very end, these scenes are just superfluous fan service that have no bearing whatsoever on the plot. However, if you went purely because you love superfluous fan service, then you should probably get up and go as soon as Jessie unearths the lunchbox full of Emily’s memories, you heartless monster.BackroomsLook,Backroomsderives a lot of its power from the sustained eeriness of its tone – which is to say that the film essentially bores you into terror. As such, any trip to the toilet has the potential to ruin the effect. But needs must, so perhaps try to go about halfway through when Renate Reinsve enters the shop. You’ll miss a long scene of her wandering around. If you’re invested in the film, the scene serves to ratchet the tension even higher. If you’re busting for the toilet, though, it will feel so endless that you’ll convince yourself that the film is punishing you for having a bladder.Disclosure DayView image in fullscreenTake your toilet time … The Super Mario Galaxy Movie.Photograph: Nintendo and Illumination/AP‘An intermission is a must’: why Greek cinemas are adding a loo break to The OdysseyRead moreAt two-and-a-half hours,Disclosure Dayfeels a little longer than it needs to be, and this will go double if you managed to slurp down an entire large Sprite before the trailers finished. I checked the trusty RunPee app for this, and I am in broad agreement that the best time to go involves some counterintuitive thinking. A little over halfway through, there is an action sequence where Emily Blunt’s car gets pushed on to some train tracks. What follows is a long and not particularly interesting sequence, the likes of which you will have seen many times before.The Super Mario Galaxy MovieI don’t know if you’ve ever taken a 98-minute pee, but nothing in this film is good or memorable, so why not try? Heck, you may as well walk all the way back home and use your own toilet. You literally won’t miss anything.Explore more on these topicsFilmThe OdysseyToy Story 5Disclosure DayBackroomsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Hold the front page! Marilyn Monroe is Dakota Johnson’s ninth cousin three times removed | Movies | The Guardian
description: The vogue for celebrity ancestors can be traced back to Robert Pattinson descending from Dracula and Benedict Cumberbatch being related to just about everyone
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The vogue for celebrity ancestors can be traced back to Robert Pattinson descending from Dracula and Benedict Cumberbatch being related to just about everyone
Content: Family resemblance? … Dakota Johnson as Marilyn Monroe in Flesh ImpactView image in fullscreenFamily resemblance? … Dakota Johnson as Marilyn Monroe in Flesh ImpactMoviesHold the front page! Marilyn Monroe is Dakota Johnson’s ninth cousin three times removedThe vogue for celebrity ancestors can be traced back to Robert Pattinson descending from Dracula and Benedict Cumberbatch being related to just about everyoneStuart HeritageFri 31 Jul 2026 10.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 10.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.To mark Marilyn Monroe’s 100th birthday, a short film will premiere at this year’s Venice film festival. Entitled Flesh Impact, the film has been written and directed by Maggie Gyllenhaal, and will star two versions of Monroe. The first, played by Ellen Burstyn, will apparently be “a version of Monroe the world never got to see”, while Dakota Johnson will play Monroe in her pomp.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Ahead of its premiere, a photo of Johnson dolled up as Monroe has been released. And it has to be said that the resemblance is actually pretty good. This could be down to one of two reasons. The first is that Monroe is so iconic that you could slap a wig and a beauty spot on Phil Mitchell and you’d immediately see who he was trying to emulate. Or it could be because Marilyn Monroe andDakota Johnsonare literally related.View image in fullscreenBig news … Monroe in Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953).Photograph: 20th Century Fox/AllstarNo, really. A new press release from MyHeritage has revealed that Marilyn Monroe is Dakota Johnson’s ninth cousin three times removed. According to the release, “their shared ancestry traces back to Richard and Charity Tydings, 17th-century English settlers in Maryland. Marilyn descends from their daughter Pretitia, while Dakota and [her father] Don Johnson descend from her younger sister, Mary.”This is incredible news indeed. What a scoop, casting one of Marilyn Monroe’s own relatives in a film about Marilyn Monroe. And a close relative, too. Ninth cousins three times removed. Take that, anyone who is only the 12th cousin six times removed of Marilyn Monroe. This is the real deal.However, if you can believe such a thing, Johnson and Monroe are not the only miraculous relatives in Hollywood. For example, in the 2017 BBC seriesGunpowder, Kit Harington played Robert Catesby, the leader of a Catholic group who planned the failed gunpowder plot in 1605. It’s a great, grim character to play – spoiler, he ends with his head on a spike – but the biggest news about the series was the fact that Harington was a descendant of Catesby. The website Famouskin claims that Harington isCatesby’s sixth cousin 11 times removed, although it’s worth pointing out that Harington’s family is so well to do that his10th great-grandfather was James I– meaning that he is simultaneously related to a failed assassin and the assassin’s intended victim.Another actor related to royalty is Benedict Cumberbatch. In 2016, Cumberbatch playedRichard III in The Hollow Crown, a year after genealogists revealed that the actor was Richard’ssecond cousin 16 times removed. However, it turns out that Cumberbatch is also related to basically every other character he has ever played.View image in fullscreenBenedict Cumberbatch as Alan Turing in The Imitation Game.Photograph: Black Bear Pictures/Sportsphoto/AllstarAfter appearing inSherlock, Ancestry revealed that Cumberbatch was the16th cousin twice removed of Arthur Conan Doyle. When the Alan Turing biopicThe Imitation Gamewas released in 2014, Ancestry went to work again, declaring thatCumberbatch and Turing were 17th cousins, sharing an ancestor in the first Earl of Somerset. You may also remember that Cumberbatch starred in12 Years a Slave. While not directly related to his character, Cumberbatch’s fifth great-grandfather Abraham was nevertheless an enslaver with a Barbados sugar plantation in his name.As you can see, Ancestry really comes into its own on matters like this. For example, just one month after Taylor Swift announced her 2024 albumThe Tortured Poets Department, the website managed to discover that Swift was in fact related to a notoriously tortured poet, being thesixth cousin three times removedof Emily Dickinson. Last year, it was also claimed that Swift was theeighth cousin 11 times removedof King Louis XIV of France. Perhaps this will be a link covered in a future album called The Hubristic Monarchs Department.View image in fullscreenTaylor Swift and her sixth cousin three times removed, Emily Dickinson.Composite: Getty Images for TAS Rights Management, Culture ClubBut being related to royalty is boring. Being related to something supernatural, on the other hand, is much more fun. And so it came to pass in 2009 that Emma Watson, famous for playing a witch in the Harry Potter films, is actually related to a witch. The news came out of yet another Ancestry deep dive, revealing that Watson’sdistant ancestor was Joan Playle, a woman who was convicted of witchcraft in 1592. Although she wasn’t executed for her crimes, Playle was nevertheless excommunicated from the church, although it might be worth pointing out that the evidence for her being a witch essentially begins and ends with the fact that she was unmarried.Finally, the greatest ancestral link of them all. Shortly before the release of The Twilight Saga: Eclipse, Ancestry managed to work out that Robert Pattinson, who played a vampire in the film, wasdistantly related to Vlad III, known as Vlad the Impaler or Vlad Dracula. Being a screen vampire who is literally related to Dracula is quite a flex, although it should also be pointed out that other relatives of Vlad include Prince William and Prince Harry, and George W Bush, so hopefully they’ll band together for any further sequels.Explore more on these topicsFilmDakota JohnsonMarilyn MonroeBenedict CumberbatchKit HaringtonRobert PattinsonTaylor SwiftfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Change is happening! I can cut off my hair and misbehave’: Vicky Krieps on rage, rebellion, and rejecting Hollywood | Movies | The Guardian
description: After her star turn in Phantom Thread, everyone expected a move to Tinseltown – but the actor embraced indie European films instead. It’s because of a lifelong instinct to be bold, she says
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: After her star turn in Phantom Thread, everyone expected a move to Tinseltown – but the actor embraced indie European films instead. It’s because of a lifelong instinct to be bold, she says
Content: Risky business … Vicky Krieps.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRisky business … Vicky Krieps.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty ImagesMoviesInterview‘Change is happening! I can cut off my hair and misbehave’: Vicky Krieps on rage, rebellion, and rejecting HollywoodFiona SturgesAfter her star turn in Phantom Thread, everyone expected a move to Tinseltown – but the actor embraced indie European films instead. It’s because of a lifelong instinct to be bold, she saysFri 31 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 09.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBack when she was a rising actor, Vicky Krieps had her fill of people telling her what not to do. When she got pregnant in her 20s, she was advised not to have the baby as it would derail her career, but she did it anyway. When, after playing a fashion designer’s muse in Paul Thomas Anderson’sPhantom Thread, she went back to making low-budget French films, she was, she says, “actually laughed at. It just seemed absurd to these people that I would turn my back on Hollywood and invest so much energy and passion in something that wasn’t giving me money.”Yet Krieps’s determination to forge her own path has reaped rewards. For the last decade she has had one foot in the Hollywood mainstream, appearing in Fede Álvarez’s The Girl in the Spider’s Web and M Night Shyamalan’sOld, while keeping the other firmly in independent cinema where she has freedom to experiment. Krieps also does her utmost to avoid the pantomime of red-carpet events. On the occasions she does make an appearance, she will stick out her tongue or give photographers the finger. “I always smile when I’m doing it. But I’m telling them: ‘Guys, this is really ridiculous and the shouting is a bit much. Just talk nicely to me.’”It comes as no surprise to learn that Krieps, 42, who was born and raised in Luxembourg and speaks four languages, has declined to make the obligatory move to Los Angeles. For the past 15 years, she has lived in Berlin – though, when we speak over video call, she is in Greece, which she regularly visits since marrying her husband, the Greek film production assistant Lazaros Gounaridis, last year. (They met on the set of the 2023 film Hot Milk.)Sporting a pixie cut and a crisp white shirt, Krieps is open, thoughtful and speaks with unusual seriousness and candour about her job which, for her, is all-consuming. “Sometimes I feel less like an actor and more like a scientist who is experimenting on my own body,” she says.View image in fullscreenKrieps in Love Me Tender.Photograph: Peccadillo PicturesThis immersive approach can take a toll. Two weeks after wrapping her forthcoming film Love Me Tender, in which she plays a woman who loses custody of her young son, Krieps began feeling “really bad in my body. I was lying on my bed, and I couldn’t move my arms and my neck. I thought I had a serious disease.” She saw doctors and had an MRI, and found everything was fine but the pain itself was real. “I think I had assembled so much psychological pain that it became physical. You know the saying ‘My heart is aching’? I feel that in my whole chest.”Directed by Anna Cazenave Cambet and based on the autobiographical novel by Constance Debré, Love Me Tender challenges the unfair expectations foisted upon mothers. Krieps plays Clémence, who has given up a well-paid legal career to write books. After separating amicably from her husband, Laurent, she gives away most of her belongings, immerses herself in the club scene and explores her sexuality. When she eventually tells Laurent that she is dating women, he appears to accept it. But afterwards, he makes dark allegations about her and questions her mental stability in a bid to secure sole custody of their eight-year-old son, Paul.“Laurent,” says Krieps, “is an example of when the male ego starts to rage because it is hurting and doesn’t understand what is happening. He’s thinking: ‘Why am I not included in this? Why did this train leave without me?’” When “there is no real dialogue between men and women, men like this can become mean, sour and self-righteous”.As their case creaks through the courts, Clémence is denied permission to see Paul. When they finally meet after nearly 18 months apart, it’s for an hour every fortnight under supervision. Those meetings, where Clémence must hold in her grief and keep it together for her son, are devastating. The tension of those scenes, Krieps realised, “caused me to hit a wall. But it was good for me to learn that the next time I work on something like this I will need to look after myself and take longer breaks while filming.”View image in fullscreenCouture club … Krieps with Daniel Day-Lewis in Phantom Thread.Photograph: Focus Features/AllstarKrieps has spent much of her career playing women trying to break out of the boxes that others have put them in. In Phantom Thread, she is Alma, a serving maid who is expected to remain meek in front of Daniel Day-Lewis’s dictatorial dressmaker but instead stands her ground and answers back. In 2022’s terrificCorsage, she is Elisabeth, Empress of Austria, celebrated in the 19th century for her beauty and her tiny waist (made tinier by ruthless corsetry), who rebels against her tightly controlled existence. In Emily Atef’sMore Than Ever, she is a terminally ill woman fighting for the right to live out her days on her own terms.“I talked to Charlotte Rampling about this after we worked on the Jim Jarmusch movieFather Mother Sister Brother,” Krieps reflects. “We realised what we have in common is that we are constantly drawn to exploring the edge of a [character], the place where it starts to hurt. I think I take this to every part.”Where possible, Krieps tries to work with female directors – or rather, she clarifies, directors who preside over “feminine sets. I’ve worked with men where the set was not masculine and there was no male ego. And there are female directors who unfortunately operate with a male ego. A lot of film sets are run like the military and are very hierarchy-driven. It’s incredibly loud and it’s about pushing. But take a director like [Corsage’s] Marie Kreutzer: her set is extremely quiet and calm. No one is shouting. And the positive side to that is when you create silence, you start hearing each other.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPicking apart societal roles and rejecting authority is in Krieps’s blood. Her grandfather was in the resistance during the second world war and survived internment at Dachau. He later became a socialist politician in Luxembourg and successfully mounted a campaign to abolish the death penalty. “Knowing that someone so close almost lost his life to fight for humanity, this is something you can’t forget,” reflects Krieps. Meanwhile, her mother “is just a crazy hippy, in the best way, and raised me to question everything: how do I know this is what they say it is? I think this made me dare to be brave and risk my livelihood.”That daring surfaced when a teenage Krieps attended her school graduation ceremony and thanked her teachers for giving her “proof that I know how to learn off by heart, that I know how to copy and how to shut my mouth”. The incident made the papers in Luxembourg. It is also evident in her habit of tweaking the words and actions of her characters mid-scene. In Corsage, she launched herself out of a window in frustration at her onscreen husband (she emerged unscathed; the scene was filmed on the ground floor). The moment was not in the script but nonetheless made the final cut, with Krieps’s character sustaining a fracture from the fall. “These things are not premeditated but sometimes you just feel something that feels like the truth, and it wants to come out,” Krieps says.True to her straddling of popular and arthouse entertainment, this autumn Krieps can be seen in Ryan Murphy’s series Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story playing the Borden family’s maid Bridget Sullivan. She has also just finished work on Emma Doucet, a film by the French director Élise Girard about a single mother who falls in love with the French prime minister and which, she says, is “close to a poem. It’s very nouvelle vague.”Krieps acknowledges that her questing spirit and single-mindedness as an actor wouldn’t have been possible even 20 years ago. “You wouldn’t have a woman who’s allowed to do all these different movies, and not give a fuck, cut off her hair and generally misbehave. The fact that I exist shows me change is happening and is possible.”Love Me Tender is in UK and Irish cinemas from7August.Explore more on these topicsFilminterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hobbies can improve your health – here are four tips for choosing one | Well actually | The Guardian
description: From sea swimming to painting, doctors are ‘prescribing’ hobbies – but you don’t need a doctor’s note to get started
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From sea swimming to painting, doctors are ‘prescribing’ hobbies – but you don’t need a doctor’s note to get started
Content: ‘Research has long linked hobbies involving exercise, arts and nature to a wide range of health benefits.’Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Research has long linked hobbies involving exercise, arts and nature to a wide range of health benefits.’Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesWell actuallyHobbies can improve your health – here are four tips for choosing oneFrom sea swimming to painting, doctors are ‘prescribing’ hobbies – but you don’t need a doctor’s note to get startedJulia HotzFri 31 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2020, the year Amanda lost her mother, husband, job and pre-pandemic normalcy, she was diagnosed with major depressive disorder. “My life was just spiraling down and down and down,” she says.To help with her symptoms, in addition to an antidepressant prescription, Amanda was given a “social prescription”: a referral to a non-medical, community-based activity, typically involving movement, nature, art or service. Amanda lives near Devon, England, and became curious about sea swimming after reading about its health benefits and watching other women do it at her local beach all year round. When she told this to her mental health nurse, she was prescribed a spot inChill Therapy, an eight-week course that teaches swimming, floating and breathing techniques to build skill and confidence navigating the open water.Six years later, Amanda turns to swimming in the sea whenever she feels stressed. “It invigorates me and makes me feel I can cope with anything,” she says. “I can’t do without it, to be honest.” She is now down to the lowest dose of her antidepressant, and has made a ton of friends along the way: “I feel refreshed in body and soul.”Though research has long linked hobbies involving exercise, arts and nature to a wide range of health benefits, social prescribing now lets people like Amanda participate in them as part of their healthcare, typically covering barriers like cost and transportation. While the practice is more common in the UK,some insurersin the USarestarting to participatein social prescribing.But you don’t need a doctor’s note to get started. We asked experts in the social prescribing field for tips on picking a hobby that will actually improve your health.Match your symptom to the scienceWhen choosing a hobby, think about how you’re feeling now, and how you’d like to feel in the future.For instance, if you’ve been feeling tired or down, like Amanda, science suggests you should move your body; for example, multiple studies show sea swimming can help reducedepressionanddepressive symptoms.On a physiological level, this makes sense: aerobic exercise has been linked with gains in mood-boostingendorphinsandserotonin. Additionally, time spent in nature is linked with lower levels of cortisol, astress hormone.Feeling distracted? Nature is also good at improving focus. According to theAttention Restoration Theory, nature is uniquely equipped to restore our depleted mental resources by providing “soft fascination”, a state of effortless focus that captures our attention without draining it. This could explain why nature has been shown to improve ourexecutive functioningandconcentration.Creative activities can help with getting through sadness, isolation or pain. “Art is a human experience – it helps folks get out of their loneliness and into aflow state, which can rewire their brain from trauma,” says Holly Jacobson, CEO of Path With Art, a Seattle-based non-profit that offers free arts-based community programming. Anew small studyfound that Path with Art participants experienced statistically significant gains in mental wellbeing and efficacy, and reductions in loneliness. Earlier small studies found thatpainting can reduce anxiety, and that art-making canreduce cortisol levels after 45 minutes.Ask yourself what matters to youSome people can’t see themselves knitting, while others might rule out sports because of injury.Researchsuggestswe are more likely to follow through on an activity if we have intrinsic motivation – the internal drive to do something because we find it genuinely enjoyable or satisfying, rather than an external reward, like losing weight.That’s what worked for Amanda. Instead of receiving a finger-wagging recommendation to exercise, she says she was intrinsically motivated to go sea swimming. “When I could not go in the sea while waiting for hip replacement for two years, I used to picture myself in the waves with my friends and it always cheered me up,” she says.To help uncover a patient’s intrinsic motivation,professionalscalled link workers are tasked with listening to patients and helping them uncover their unique curiosities. Many aretrainedin motivational interviewing, an evidence-based, person-centered conversational technique that helps people work within their own value system and reasons for change, says Dr Tim Anstiss, a medical doctor who helped to develop the training, which recommends questions like: how might your life change if you joined that group? Who or what gives your life meaning and purpose?Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’Doing what gives us purpose and meaning is “vital” to our health and wellbeing, agrees Dr Ivory Rose, a California-based occupational therapist and lead within Social Prescribing USA. “Leisure pursuits are a very important part of [our health], but often get forgotten in the face of an illness or busy schedule,” she says, referencing studies that linkmeaningful activity to greater health.Rose aims to rebuild this association for clients with questions like: what is something you used to enjoy doing that you haven’t done in a while? What is important to you to be able to do?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUse mindfulness to identify activities that naturally capture your attentionMindfulness is “the very simple process of noticing”, says Dr Ellen Langer, a psychology professor at Harvard University. In her most recent book,The Mindful Body,she explores the wide-ranging benefits of being more mindful, which include improving your memory, creativity and energy, and strengthening your social relationships.Langer says to start by noticing three new things about something familiar – say, a person, place or object. Every time you notice you are on autopilot, you build “a healthy mindset for uncertainty”, she says. This is important because people who are stressed or in pain often “believe the symptoms they have are going to stay the same or get worse”, and that suffering is constant, Langer says. But according to research, people can feel better when they notice improvements and reflect on why they feel better.Try small steps and set the bar low: how to find the meaning of lifeRead moreDr Rachel Zoffness, a pain psychologist teaching at Stanford and the University of California at San Francisco, similarly points to research showing that pain can increase or decrease, depending on where we direct our attention.In her recent book, Tell Me Where It Hurts, she offers tips for pain relief. She says she sometimes asks patients directly: “Will you tell me about a time you were so absorbed in an activity that you briefly forgot about your pain?”Just say ‘yes’If you’re not sure what brings you meaning or what captures your attention in adulthood, try reflecting on what brought you joy in childhood. “When we were kids, playing did not relate to a specific goal, but it’s the most natural form of learning,” says Purvi Shah, founder ofPlayRx.life, a wellness platform. Shah advises clients to “say ‘yes’ to something new, especially when they are stuck in a rut and problems seem overwhelming”.Caitlin Marshall, a licensed clinical social worker and co-author of Creative First Aid, agrees. In her work leading creative workshops on activities including beekeeping and watercolor painting, she focuses on helping people who are experiencing psychological distress rediscover a sense of childlike joy. “It’s about learning to help people do what feels good and inspiring to them,” she says.Encouraging participants to be open-minded helps them to discover new things about themselves. “Some of them will arrive and say: ‘I hate cooking.’ Then those people are the ones that end up loving it,” Marshall says. “It’s hard to be judgmental and curious at the same time.”Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyHobbiesHealthMental healthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Will Burnham fix our barbaric prisons – or cave to rightwing populism? The answer is a tragedy | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: England and Wales’s prisons are overcrowded, drug-infested and barbaric. Labour has halted a once-in-a-generation effort to change that sorry state, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: England and Wales’s prisons are overcrowded, drug-infested and barbaric. Labour has halted a once-in-a-generation effort to change that sorry state, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: Prisoners in Pentonville prison being released early in September 2024, as part of the attempt to tackle overcrowding issues.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenPrisoners in Pentonville prison being released early in September 2024, as part of the attempt to tackle overcrowding issues.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAOpinionPrisons and probationWill Burnham fix our barbaric prisons – or cave to rightwing populism? The answer is a tragedySimon JenkinsEngland and Wales’s prisons are overcrowded, drug-infested and barbaric. Labour has halted a once-in-a-generation effort to change that sorry stateFri 31 Jul 2026 06.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.18 EDTShareAndy Burnham’s“pausing”of the Starmer government’s prisoner release scheme and theresignation of its architect, James Timpson, are disasters. They indicate a Downing Street that puts populism ahead of policy. England and Wales’s prisons are a total disgrace. Timpson was the first justice minister in 15 years prepared to handle them. Now he has gone. Although he said it had been an “honour” to serve in the government, it is reasonable to assume he resigned in disgust.InAugust 2024, the prison population in England and Wales hit a record high. The following March, a savagereport from the public accounts committeewarned that prisons, already full to bursting, could not cope with such numbers and would overflow by the start of 2026.Theearly release of 16,000 prisoners in the last three months of 2024eased pressure on the system, but now another crisis is forecast for this November. Under Timpson’s law passed in January, a surge in electronic tagging was being frantically prepared for another bout of early releases in September. But pressure fromprobation unions, parliamentary opponents and victim groups, backed by the rightwing press, has persuaded Burnham to call a halt.Chaos beckons.Victims of crime may deserve sympathy and support, but they should not dictate justice policy.Kemi Badenoch, meanwhile, should not do anything but apologise for her party in government reducing prisons to their current state.The facts cannot be repeated too often. England and Wales’s penal policy is the most backward in western Europe. They imprisonroughly twice the proportion of the population as Germany, and three times as many as Italy and Spain. Prisoner numbers in England and Wales havedoubled in 30 years.In 2024, a quarter of prisoners in England and Wales were having toshare cells designed for one person. Two-thirds were estimated to spend most of their days in their cells with little to occupy them, fuelling reports from prisoners of mental health problems and self-harm. In the 21st century, this is indefensibly primitive.Prisoners are some of the nation’s most assiduous consumers of drugs. About 40% of prisoners in England and Wales say it iseasy to access drugs while inside, cells are simplyawash in illegal substances. As for training and rehabilitation to prepare for release, curbed budgets and staff shortages have seen them collapsing.Half of short-term prisoners reoffendas a result. Rehabilitation – the one sure way to cut reoffending – is a farce. Community sentences such as Timpson’s favouredintensive supervision courtsoffer an alternative but are still in their infancy.As for England and Wales’s fixation with incarcerating women, in December 2024, aquarter of thosein prison were on remand, awaiting what might not have been imprisonment at all. Most need help, not separation from their families and loved ones, with many said to be victims of worse crimes than they commit. The Prison Reform Trust has pleaded for sentences totake account of family stability, but to no effect. Even Reform UK’sColin Sutton, the new police and crime commissioner for Norfolk, has said most women in custody should be released.To allow prisons policy to be led by public opinion is absurd. It should be led by evidence of what works. Manynon-violent prisoners will be drug and alcohol addictschronically in need of effective treatment in the community. There are also the kind of prisoners I used to visit prisons in the London area. They are victims of family or personal breakdown, poverty, homelessness or sheer misfortune. Above all they needed hostels and help.Nothing more infuriates the pro-prisons lobby than mention of Norway. The reason is thatNorway’s prisons work. In the 1990s, the country suffered a dire 70% recidivism rate. It examined evidence and opted for drastic reform. This tied new “correction centres” to local communities, relating rehabilitation to local jobs and family ties. Prisoners were treated with dignity. Reoffending plummeted and Norway’s prison population has been drastically reduced.The late Ann Widdecombe, a former Tory prisons minister, boldly went to Norway in 2020 with a television crew to see what she calledThe World’s Most Luxurious Prison.She called it a holiday camp. She admitted it “worked” but was appalled at the absence of what she regarded as penal retribution. Loss of liberty was combined with a total lack of humiliation.Nothing more typified the British approach to social policy than Widdecombe’s reaction. Foreigners must be wrong, even if she could not explain why. To her, as to many of her compatriots, the survival of our Dickensian prisons embodied justice. Their harshness was an appropriate response to crime. Even if they did not “work”, they must be right.A liberal society must be able to look abroad, examine evidence and be open to reform. Even in the prison-loving US, states from Texas to Oregon and North Dakota have visited Norway and are professing tolearn from it.They know it makes no sense to imprison but not rehabilitate.Our justice policy is crippled by changes of leadership. Catherine McKinnell, appointed as Timpson’s replacement, is the 13th prison minister in the past decade – a ludicrous number, as if it was a hobby rather than a job. Policy is left at the mercy of rightwing sentiment, fed by victims groups and the press. They are now joined by the prime minister. Beware the autumn.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsPrisons and probationOpinionUK criminal justiceLabourJames TimpsonAndy BurnhamCrimecommentShareReuse this content

title: Think our basic rights are safe? In the age of oligarchs and corporate lobbying, think again | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: The global assault on our freedoms is coming ever closer to home. Just look at the sinister prosecution of UK lawyer Rajiv Menon, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: The global assault on our freedoms is coming ever closer to home. Just look at the sinister prosecution of UK lawyer Rajiv Menon, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Illustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianOpinionLawThink our basic rights are safe? In the age of oligarchs and corporate lobbying, think againGeorge MonbiotThe global assault on our freedoms is coming ever closer to home. Just look at the sinister prosecution of UK lawyer Rajiv MenonFri 31 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 03.11 EDTShareNo more resistance in the US. The era of human rights is over, and dissent is once more forbidden. This is what certain billionaires and their concierges want, and this is the model they’re also seeking to project across the world. If we fail to resist, if our new prime minister is as weak and suggestible as the last one, this is what we will get. In fact, we are halfway there already.Why? Because successive governments in the UK have succumbed to a global campaign to cancel our fundamental freedoms, a campaign led by oligarchs and corporations, the media they own and the junktanks they fund. A campaign that has become definitional for the second Trump presidency.At aglobal summitconvened by the US government earlier this month, the Trump administration officials Marco Rubio, Stephen Miller and Scott Bessent explained that they were redirecting counterterrorism efforts away from Islamic jihadism and towards “the political left”. Most of the examples they cited to justify this shift were more than 30 years old. Several times they had to dig down to the 1970s to find a sufficiently menacing threat. You could hear the barrel being scraped.Without producing a shred of evidence, Rubio, the secretary of state, claimed that the Cuban government is “inextricably linked to the far-left groups and movements across and beyond the west”. The following week, his department sought to justify this claimwith a reportcontaining a long list of leftwing legislators, journalists and activists that attempted tolink them to Cubain ways that ranged from the tenuous to the hilarious. This is a well-honed tactic, used prolificallyby the Nazisamong others: they claimed dissenters, by definition, were part of an international communist conspiracy. They insisted, as Rubio did, that “it is time to crush this evil for ever”.That wasn’t the only crude reminder. Miller, Donald Trump’s deputy chief of staff, maintained that when you see antifascist protests, “not one of the people that is demonstrating looks like a normal person. Not one looks normal. They’re all deformed in some way – in their appearance, in their dress, in their mannerism … their outer appearance becomes a manifestation of their inner hatred.” I’m just surprised he didn’t say “untermenschen”. The US government, by contrast, promotes “normal, healthy, ordered living”.But what hit me even harder was Miller’s attack on “jury nullification”: jurors acquitting people who, he said, were “obviously guilty”. Shutting down this possibility has been an aim of illiberal governments and conservative judges around the world. We saw it in the UK in theprosecution of Trudi Warnerand others for holding signs that state an ancient principle in English law: “Jurors have an absolute right to acquit a defendant according to their conscience.”View image in fullscreenRajiv Menon KC, who is facing prosecution for contempt of court.Photograph: Garden Court ChambersWe see it in theastonishing prosecution, being pursued at the moment, of Rajiv Menon KC, who reminded jurors of this right at the trial of the Palestine Action campaigners he was defending. He became, as a result, the first lawyer in English history to becharged with contempt of courtfor a closing speech. If convicted, he faces up to two years’ imprisonment and will be struck off. Prosecuting lawyers for defending their dissident clients is more or less the definition of authoritarianism.We also saw it in the assault Keir Starmerlaunched on jury trialsas a whole, greatly curtailing, without any coherent justification, our strongest defence against injustice.Starmer was a weak man, without a clear vision of his own, who was rolled by any powerful state or corporate lobby. He was no match for a well-funded and highly effective international campaign. A network of groups such as theAmerican Legislative Exchange Council, funded by corporations and billionaires, has been producing “model legislation”. The groups test these laws in sympathetic jurisdictions. If they are found to work, they then press for their adoption elsewhere. The result is a sustained assault on our rights to protest, to political equality and to ahabitable planet.The globalisation of this attack on our fundamental rights is a key conservative aim. As capital operates everywhere, so should its ability to crush our objections. The long series ofvicious anti-protest lawsin the UK is an outcome of sustained lobbying by junktanks, the media and other governments. The result is a country that now keepshundreds of political prisoners, a country in which you can getsix months in jailfor marching slowly down the street.These oppressive laws have culminated – so far – in an act of parliament passed in April that enables the police to shut down any protestthey deem to havea “cumulative” impact on the community. The only protests that have ever succeeded are those with acumulative impact. Protest is acceptable as long as it’s useless. Let the people have their say, but only if we can’t hear them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne day, your life and future may depend on a jury. The integrity of that legal process is in peril right now | Imran KhanRead moreThe new laws have been accompanied by that age-old trick, traditionally associated with fascist regimes, of smearing leftwing dissidents as terrorists. As the rights groupLiberty has pointed out, the definition of terrorism here has greatly expanded, to incorporate tactics formerly regarded as civil protest. This is what enabled Starmer’s government toban Palestine Action.The judge who referred Menon for contempt, Mr Justice Johnson, was also the first – at the same trial – to use theextraordinary powersquietly inserted by the Conservatives into the Sentencing Act 2020. These enable someone tried for one crime to be sentenced for another. The four Palestine Action protesters were convicted of ordinary crimes. But, without informing the jury, Johnson marked the case as having a “terrorist connection”. He then sentenced them for terrorist offences, which means much more prison time.Already, his example has been followed by another judge: a different group of pro-Palestine protesters, who sprayed red paint and broke some windows of a branch of Barclays Bank, are about to besentenced as terrorists, though neither they nor the jurors were told of this possibility during their trial for criminal damage. This means, of course, that they were unable to defend themselves against this far more serious charge.Nothing is safe from the billionaire assault on humanity. None of our rights, however ancient and familiar, are impregnable. Fight for them now or lose them, perhaps for ever.George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Digested week: As wildfires rage, should I buy a helicopter or marry a guy with a bunker? | Lucy Mangan | The Guardian
description: Plus, train toilet roulette, an astonishingly stoic hiker and the tradwife paradox
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Plus, train toilet roulette, an astonishingly stoic hiker and the tradwife paradox
Content: Home sweet home? Oh, to have bunker money.Photograph: DoxaDigital/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHome sweet home? Oh, to have bunker money.Photograph: DoxaDigital/Getty ImagesDigested weekReese WitherspoonDigested week: As wildfires rage, should I buy a helicopter or marry a guy with a bunker?Lucy ManganPlus, train toilet roulette, an astonishingly stoic hiker and the tradwife paradoxFri 31 Jul 2026 07.47 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 06.39 EDTShareMondayAs I read the headlines about Europe on fire, and imagine – or is it true? – I can smell smoke from theSuffolk wildfireencroaching on a nuclear power facility a county away from me, I’m remembering the wisdom of a friend who told me years ago that she wasn’t aiming to buy a house but a helicopter. “Because,” said Sarah, gesturing around us, “it’s going to be no good trying to getacrossflood waters or dusty plains or great drifts of virus-ridden corpses. You’re going to need to goup.”However. I have noticed a trend emerging among the true oracles, the true bellwethers of society – our lady film stars. The likes ofReese Witherspoon, Nicole Kidman and Jennifer Garner are all taking up not with fellow stars but financiers – usually tech financiers – who are the very richest of the rich. And you know what this means. It means they do not have just helicopter money (even a lady film star has helicopter money) – they have bunker money.The parameters have subtly shifted. The dream is not lifelong luxury in a mansion or two. It is survival in subterranean safety with whoever can fund it. I now have to decide between buying a helicopter or marrying a bunkerman. I hope I haven’t left it too late.View image in fullscreenReese Witherspoon survives by taking a long hike in the 2014 film Wild.Photograph: Anne Marie Fox/APTuesdayThe sex toy retailer Pulse & Cocktails has taken over Little Chef. This is an unhappy sentence. But it is, alas, true. Or rather, it is true that Pulse & Cocktails has taken over the service station chain’s former venues to allow its customers more privacy.I have many questions. One: have drivers to Kettering never heard of the internet? Two: is selling roadside gimp masks really more profitable than hash browns and American-style pancakes? Am I so detached from the national appetite? And, most importantly, three: what is going on with this name? Pulse & Cocktails? It’s terrible. Rhythmically awful and in its evocations, worse. “Pulse” suggests checking for one and unless this is a terrifically niche roadside sex shop (and again, I would point you to the financial viability issue with which we are already struggling in an interwebbed world), is not a fabulously sexy opener. And “cocktails” is meh.Or it suggests you are throwing one in the face of the unresponsive body upon which you, for reasons best known to yourself, have designs. Or am I missing a pun? There should surely be a pun here. And no, the first syllable of “cocktails” is not enough. Answers, of a semantic nature only, on a postcard to the usual address please.WednesdayTrain drivers are considering strike action over a lack of loo facilities. Now look. Up the working man and all that, but let’s extend that.I am travelling by train a lot at the moment and I think it’s time customers got a turn. What is the equivalent of customers striking until we get not just working toilets but – and this is a vital detail – guaranteed working toilets?As someone who needs to wee about every 12 minutes, each time I step on to a train, I also step into a vortex of anxiety and unknowns. And do you know what anxiety isn’t good for? Yes, exactly.We can’t withhold our journeys – we need to get to places. We can’t withhold our fares because we’d get very arrested and still not get to our places. I’m on the verge of suggesting just protest-weeing where you sit if there isn’t a working convenience conveniently close by, but I think I’m edging too near niche Little Chef territory again, so we’ll stop here.ThursdayA hiker in Montana’s Beartooth Mountains made a 10-mile, six-hour descent after being impaled through the chest by his walking pole, rather than call out the medical rescue team. “I’m pretty confident this is outside my chest wall,” 32-year-old David Cifaldi told the two friends he was crossing the Froze-to-Death Plateau (no, really) with on the way to Granite Peak of the 44in metal stick piercing his torso.Now, Cifaldi is a nurse but “I’m pretty confident this 44in metal stick that entered under my left arm and came out of my back isn’t going to move and kill me so let’s tra-la-la down this ice-covered mountain to save everyone’s time and resources” is still a ballsy move. If this guy’s got bunker money too, I think he could be The One.View image in fullscreenDavid Cifaldi in hospital in Billings, Montana, before his walking stick is removed from his chest.Photograph: Jesse Ross/David Cifaldi/APFridayThis week I have spent a lovely afternoon playing with and kissing the delectable face off a friend’s baby, picked nearly seven homegrown tomatoes from my garden and defrosted the fridge. Am I … Am I atradwifenow? On the one hand, I have quite enjoyed myself. On the other, I don’t believe in God, am too short for prairie dresses, and when I bake I kill people.Tradwives obsess me. The convolutions of the thought processes involved. Celebrating traditional domesticity while monetising every moment of it in the most modern way possible. Doting on a brood of children who are being raised the old-fashioned way while being paraded on the internet.Selling a vision of effortless ease and fulfilment while keeping a schedule that periodically puts you in bed with exhaustion (as the leader of the tradwife pack Hannah Neeleman once mentioned).Ostentatiously deferring to your husband while building an empire that rests entirely on your work, talents and looks and would disappear overnight without you. Amazing. Women – not for the first time, I feel we really need to get together and talk about a few things.Digested week in picturesView image in fullscreen‘Could you not, for once, just hand me the remote?’Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/GettyView image in fullscreen‘We call it scissors, paper, drone.’Photograph: Simon Jones/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreen‘Fighting? Or the other thing? You’ve got one second to decide!’Photograph: Anadolu/GettyExplore more on these topicsReese WitherspoonDigested weekNicole KidmanParents and parentingWalkingWildfiresHealth & wellbeingcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Burnham bounce is eclipsing the Green surge – and Zack Polanski’s radical hope is being tested | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: The new PM is enjoying a honeymoon period but the Greens have the freedom to say whatever Labour won’t, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: The new PM is enjoying a honeymoon period but the Greens have the freedom to say whatever Labour won’t, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Zack Polanski, leader of the Green party, 10 July 2026Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/LNPView image in fullscreenZack Polanski, leader of the Green party, 10 July 2026Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/LNPOpinionGreen partyThe Burnham bounce is eclipsing the Green surge – and Zack Polanski’s radical hope is being testedGaby HinsliffThe new PM is enjoying a honeymoon period but, longer-term, the Greens have the freedom to say whatever Labour won’tFri 31 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 03.11 EDTShareCackling happily into their pints, the two most powerful men in the country scoff their way through a selection of pub snacks.Pork scratchings or scampi fries? Or maybe old-school peanuts? It’s hardly the toughest choice currently facing Andy Burnham andthechancellor, John Healey, so some may find this week’s made-to-go-viral Instagram reel of themgleefully ranking crispsa bit silly. (I’m writing this, laptop balanced on my knee, beside a hospital bed; right now I couldn’t care less whether the chancellor likes bacon fries.) But I do care, intensely, about a government that ispromising once-in-a-generation reform of care for elderly peoplewinning the public’s confidence for long enough to actually carry out that promise, and weirdly in 2026 that means chomping crisps on camera to establish your bona fides with people who’d scroll straight past conventional political content.Pulling off this kind of freewheeling, seemingly casual content actually takes surprising skill, as the compulsively online Green leader, Zack Polanski – until now the reigning king of leftwing British TikTok – has just inadvertently demonstrated. On Wednesday, the policecleared Polanski of any wrongdoingover reposting a picture of a man in a T-shirt emblazoned with a guillotine and the words, “We’re only making plans for Nigel”. (Polanski says it was among a bunch of images he uploaded without looking properly first, and he deleted it as soon as he realised.) An innocent mistake but a sloppy one, coming days after the alleged murder of the Reform spokeswoman Ann Widdecombe; the kind he can no longer afford to make too often.The unexpected resurgence of hope, joy and radical energy in the Labour party over the last week and a half poses an unmistakable threat to the leader who until now has had a virtual monopoly on those things. Hardened Green voters – those for whom Burnham’s “business-friendly socialism” will never be socialist enough, or who see the new prime minister’s support for more drilling in the North Sea as environmental vandalism – are going nowhere. But newcomers who migrated to the Greens because they felt Keir Starmer’s government had lost its moral compass, or become too relentlessly miserable, are now squarely in Burnham’s sights. Interestingly, the More in Common poll this week, whichput Labour back in the leadfor the first time since last March, found that “Burnham bounce” coming if anything more at the Greens’ expense than Reform’s.When the new prime ministerapologisesfor the way his predecessor approached the Gaza war, orcondemnswhat he calls 40 failed years of neoliberalism, he’s signalling that it’s safe for those lost Labour voters to come home. When he’s messing about on Instagram, he’s reaching out to younger people unused to seeing Labour politicians doing anything interesting on Green-dominated feeds. And when heholds cross-party talkson fixing social carewithout either Polanski or Farage, then intentionally or not, he is sending a message about who he takes seriously. Polanski,whose partner works in palliative care, has spoken movingly about the issue. But it was only the Lib Dems and the Tories, Downing Street says, who actually wrote to the prime minister expressing interest in his call for a non-partisan approach to this difficult issue.It would be ridiculous, of course, to think this Labour honeymoon can last. Keir Starmer was popular, right up until his first spending cut.The Green surgemay be receding for the moment but it’s only five months since they left Labour for dust in theGorton and Denton byelection, and it would be a surprise if they don’t at least improve on their 2024 performance in this week’s Manchester mayoral elections.Yet something has clearly shifted. As recently as early May, 22% of Britons thought Polanski would be a better prime minister than Starmer, according to YouGov. Butonly 9% now prefer him to Burnham. The guillotine T-shirt affair, meanwhile, was merely the latest in a string of mistakes – from Polanski’sfailure to register to votein May’s local elections, toconfusion over whether he paid enough council taxwhile living on a houseboat in London, to a spate ofantisemitism allegationsinvolving Green candidates at the local elections – that together raise questions about Polanski’s readiness for the remorseless scrutiny that wannabe main parties of the left inevitably face.The Greens’ defence is to argue that only they can offer a “full fat” socialist revolution, not some watered down Burnhamite version. If he won’t imposerent controlsor newproperty taxes– both ideas circulating around the sprawling Burnham camp that have died an unceremonious death since he entered Downing Street – then they will. Unconstrained by the realities of government, their freedom to say whatever Labour won’t could easily become a powerful weapon again given time and the inevitable disappointments of office, though it’s unclear how much time Burnham intends to give them. (He has publiclyruled out a snap election, but the current strategy – a blitzkrieg of exciting but vague announcements, starving Reform and the Greens of political oxygen but without giving them much to fight him on – wouldn’t half be good preparation for one.)But for the next few weeks at least, it’s Burnham on whom the fickle political sun shines: Burnham who has the priceless opportunity to actuallydosomething about what ails the country, rather than simply talk – however fluently or winningly – about it. Political careers, as he should know, are notoriously short these days. He should make the most of every moment while it lasts.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsGreen partyOpinionZack PolanskiAndy BurnhamSocialismcommentShareReuse this content

title: My family is coming apart – so it’s time for one last video game session | Games | The Guardian
description: I wanted our last family games night to be the best fun we’ve ever had. Maybe we should have stuck with Mario Kart …
Author: Dominik Diamond
Headline: I wanted our last family games night to be the best fun we’ve ever had. Maybe we should have stuck with Mario Kart …
Content: ‘Games remind us that we always have more things in common than we sometimes feel’ …Photograph: Interfoto/Alamy Stock PhotoView image in fullscreen‘Games remind us that we always have more things in common than we sometimes feel’ …Photograph: Interfoto/Alamy Stock PhotoGamesMy family is coming apart – so it’s time for one last video game sessionDominik DiamondI wanted our last family games night to be the best fun we’ve ever had. Maybe we should have stuck with Mario Kart …Fri 31 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 19.16 EDTShareIt is the end of an era for the Diamond family. For 20 years, there have been five of us living together. It has not been easy. Militant vegan daughters, sons who have inherited Scottish tempers, and a youngest child who attracts trouble like an industrial magnet, have meant our house has been conflict-laden at times. Throw in the fact that we are beset with all manner of mental health bobbins and chronic illnesses that resulted in two of our three kids almost dying in hospitals and you get a family that is combustible – but extremely close.Through it all, we had games. They always brought us back together. Not just us all hunkering over Super Mario Kart like some kind of UN-mandated family therapy, but the conversations that happen when any of us spy another playing something new.Gamesare a cultural touchstone that helped us crack through the veneer of disagreements and distrust and remind us that we have more things in common than we sometimes feel.View image in fullscreen‘UN-mandated family therapy’ … Mario Kart 8 Deluxe.Photograph: NintendoBut now we are moving out of the house we have shared for years. My wife has to go back to the UK for family reasons, #1 Child is moving in with her boyfriend and youngest child is moving in with a friend. This leaves the Son and I – we are moving into an apartment for the next few months, which Charlie is already dubbing the bro-tel. (I am filled with equal parts excitement and dread about this.)So I wanted one last family games night to remind us of simpler times before we all go our separate ways. I wanted it to be the best fun we have ever had. I wanted … Quiplash!Quiplash is one of the most important games in the history of our family, because I view it as the game that trained my kids to be funny. Seeing them all become fairly high-level comedy beings has been the greatest thrill of my life as a dad.It’s a simple “fill in the blanks or answer the question with something funny to get the most votes” game, the beauty of it being you can play using mobile phones as controllers and five people can play. That’s why I have it as a go-to. Getting any family together to do anything is like herding particularly wilful sheep, and when was the last time you saw a shepherd try that while hunting for 10 working batteries for gaming controllers? Exactly.It’s not just the genuinely funny answers that get votes: there is also a lot of love for old family running gags, most of which are at my expense, usually my baldness or my rigidity with rules.However, while I am impressed by my grownup kids’ quick-thinking quippery, I am still appalled by some of their spelling. So for our final game, I introduce a rule that you can only vote for answers spelt correctly. This rule is not just ignored but aggressively mocked with answers that are part punchline and part Welsh street name.I am in last place because they can tell which answers are from me. So, I start deliberately entering badly spelt answers to confuse them, so they give up trying to play the game seriously and while I am writing quality punchlines such as “God said ‘wrong door’” (you had to be there), I am faced with answers from them such as “pee pee poo poo”.And then the rows break out. My two youngest kids work at the same trendy bar/restaurant, and they have issues with each other. One suggested a role for the other there that they are not happy about, so they declare they never want to work in the same place together again. Impressively, during the argument, my son still manages to answer “skittle flavour that just missed the cut” with “narly Netenyahu nectarine”. Which almost got my vote until I noticed that neither Netanyahu nor gnarly are spelt like that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe row escalates. Wife and #1 Child have reverted to doomscrolling on their phones instead. No one wants to play. It’s all falling apart. Not just this desperate attempt at one final family gaming session, but the family itself. In one week, our matriarch, the most important one of us, will be on the other side of the Atlantic. In a couple of months, #1 Child could be the only one still actually living on this side of it.View image in fullscreenMemories flooded back … Kirby’s Return to Dream Land Deluxe.Photograph: NintendoMemories start flooding back: the summer I spent playing Super Mario Sunshine with #1 Child when she was five. Evading guard dogs in the snow with my son on Call of Duty: Modern Warfare when he wasn’t much older. Seeing my youngest child fall in love with Kirby. The years of Mario Kart, Mortal Kombat and Just Dance. The conversations. The debates. The windups. There is such joy in those moments but now they are spilling through my fingers like water.I think of all the times in recent years when one of the kids has asked me if I want to play a game with them. And I’ve been “too busy”. I wish I had all those moments back to create more memories.My wife, ever the peacemaker of the family, declares the next day that we will have one more go at this the night before she goes back to Blighty. That prospect seems as good as it gets right now.Explore more on these topicsGamesFamilycommentShareReuse this content

title: After teargas, protests and legal strife, Turkey has a new opposition party. Is this the man who can defeat Erdoğan? | Kaya Genç | The Guardian
description: Under Özgür Özel, the CHP became Turkey’s most popular party. Now his Yeni (New) movement is growing fast, says the Istanbul-based novelist Kaya Genç
Author: Kaya Genç
Headline: Under Özgür Özel, the CHP became Turkey’s most popular party. Now his Yeni (New) movement is growing fast, says the Istanbul-based novelist Kaya Genç
Content: Özgür Özel, former leader of Turkey’s CHP opposition party, now leader of the Yeni (New) party, Ankara, 24 July 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenÖzgür Özel, former leader of Turkey’s CHP opposition party, now leader of the Yeni (New) party, Ankara, 24 July 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionTurkeyAfter teargas, protests and legal strife, Turkey has a new opposition party. Is this the man who can defeat Erdoğan?Kaya GençUnder Özgür Özel, the CHP became Turkey’s most popular party. Now his Yeni (New) movement is growing fastFri 31 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 05.15 EDTShareIn May this year, police in Ankara stormed the headquarters of the Republican People’s party (CHP), the oldest political party in Turkey. Officersused teargas to enforcea controversial appeal court decision that reinstated the CHP’s 77-year-old former leader Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu–seen as less of a threat to the ruling Justice and Development party (AKP). CHP members aligned with Kılıçdaroğlu’s successor, Özgür Özel, placed furniture at the building’s entrance, creating a barrier to prevent police from entering. It didn’t work. Hours later, party members loyal to Özel were physically removed from the premises.Entering the offices of Turkey’s leading opposition party in such a fashion was a spectacular act with historic consequences. Last Friday, Özel and 90 CHP deputiesresigned from their partyand declared the founding of the New (Yeni) party. The CHP had served as Turkey’s main opposition since 2002. But not any longer: with the exodus of members to the New party, the CHP is reduced to just 44 legislators in the 600-seat parliament, its third smallest party out of seven.Over the past week, Turkey’s new main opposition, with its 91 legislators, enjoyed strong winds in its sails. Throughout Turkish political history, those who have suffered legal injustices have gone on to benefit from them at the ballot box. In 1999,Recep Tayyip Erdoğanhimself spent four months in prison. Four years later, he was prime minister. If managed well, the ousting of Özel from the CHP will probably boost the popularity of Turkey’s progressives overall.But what of the CHP itself? This is the party MustafaKemal Atatürkfounded in 1923, which played a crucial role in establishing the modern republic of Turkey. In the past 18 months, it has witnessed a stunning reversal of fortunes.At Turkey’s nationwide local elections in March 2024, the CHP was Turkey’smost popular political party. Özel’s leadership engineered that success: the CHP won37.8% of the vote, beating Erdoğan’s AKP on 35.4%. This was the first national election since the AKP’s establishment in 2001 in which it wasn’t the largest party – a decisive moment in Turkish politics and one with worrying implications for Erdoğan in the run-up to 2028’s presidential elections. The CHP victory, on a platform of municipal socialism, has raised the profile of a generation of young, charismatic leftwing mayors who, like Zohran Mamdani in New York, won office in Turkey’s wealthiest and most populous cities: Istanbul, Ankara, İzmir.Their proximity to power must have raised concerns among the country’s ruling elites, who have profited from an economic order that prioritises the construction, defence and tourism industries. Three weeks after he announced his candidacy for the presidential elections, in March last year, Istanbul’s CHP mayor, Ekrem İmamoğlu, wasremoved from office. He has been accused of142 offences, including accepting bribes, unlawfully obtaining personal data, racketeering, leading a criminal organisation, interfering with public tenders and aiding the outlawed Kurdistan Workers’ party (PKK). His charges could lead to 2,430 years behind bars, and it looks extremely unlikely that he will be able to run for president in 2028. Writing inthis newspaper from jaillast September, İmamoğlu claimed Erdoğan was “weaponising the courts against the democratic opposition”. (The government has denied putting pressure on the courts to prosecute CHP mayors.)Since İmamoğlu’s arrest, a different CHP city or district mayor has beenarrested almost every month. One after another, politicians have been sent to jail or threatened with prosecution. Several detained CHP mayors have since been released, including İnan Güney, the suspended mayor of Istanbul’s touristic hub, Beyoğlu.View image in fullscreenA protest against the arrest and imprisonment of then mayor of Istanbul, Ekrem İmamoğlu, 25 March 2025.Photograph: Francisco Seco/APOver time these developments led to apathy among opposition supporters: for months, it felt almost impossible to keep up with CHP’s legal troubles, which dominated the Turkish media.When İmamoğlu was arrested in March 2025, ittriggered nationwide protests, the largest in Turkey in more than a decade. But since then, court cases against the CHP have largely been met with silence. In April, I went tofollow İmamoğlu’s casein a courtroom in Silivri, 83km (52 miles) away from Istanbul’s city centre; I saw no supporters inside or outside the courtroom. The cab driver who took me to the court that day said he wished to see the CHP mayor of Silivri in jail next. While holidaying on Büyükada island off the coast of Istanbul two months later, I heard of theSilivri mayor’s arrest. By the end of June, Büyükada’s CHP mayor had been jailed too.After his reinstatement as party leader, Kılıçdaroğlu implied, in a public statement, that those CHP mayors could indeed be guilty. Likening the CHP to a tree, he said: “The shade of this mighty tree can never, ever be a refuge for the forbidden and the polluted. When necessary, it knows how to purify itself and conduct its inner accounting.” Kılıçdaroğlu’s call for purification has led to fury among opposition supporters, protests and an exodus of party members.Despite the excitement over Özel’s New party, it faces challenges: it lacks CHP’s resources, personnel, history and financial support from Turkey’s treasury. Breakaway parties have often suffered defeat in Turkish politics: the Good party, established in 2017 by disgruntled Turkish nationalists, has little support among the electorate. The Future party and the Democracy and Progress party (DEVA), founded by former AKP leaders in 2019 and 2020, fared poorly in elections, failing to distinguish themselves from the AKP.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI was elected mayor of Istanbul, but I write this from jail: Turkish democracy is under grave threat | Ekrem ImamoğluRead moreThe CHP is a similar colossus, with an unsurpassable brand name in Turkish politics. It is the Republic of Turkey’s founding party, the party of Atatürk, and its history carries a lot of weight.Özel has defined the New party as “social democrat”, and theparty programmeacknowledges Turkey’s different religions, ethnicities and languages. It also references gender and sexual orientation, terms that have become taboo in Turkey in recent years. The New party embraces full membership of the EU and promises to increase Turkey’s role at the Council of Europe and Nato.If Özel can position his party as not just another splinter party but the new CHP, that would be an attractive proposition. A century ago, the CHP implemented a flurry of social, cultural and political reforms across Turkey, from the abolition of the caliphate to significant advancements in women’s rights. In the 1960s and 1970s it found support from students, the underprivileged and the marginalised with its leftist turn.The New party should promise an equally bold and progressive agenda. That way it won’t just emerge as the victor of the 2028 elections but will be in a position to truly transform Turkey.Kaya Genç is a novelist and essayist from Istanbul, and the author ofThe Lion and the Nightingale: A Journey Through Modern TurkeyExplore more on these topicsTurkeyOpinionRecep Tayyip ErdoğanEuropeKemal AtatürkcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on England’s centralised state: Andy Burnham must unbundle it | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Devolution should finance transport, skills and industry, not become a rightwing contest to promise the largest tax giveaway
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Devolution should finance transport, skills and industry, not become a rightwing contest to promise the largest tax giveaway
Content: Andy Burnham and Oliver Coppard, the mayor of South Yorkshire, at a family centre in Sheffield on Friday.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/Pool PA/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Oliver Coppard, the mayor of South Yorkshire, at a family centre in Sheffield on Friday.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/Pool PA/APOpinionDevolutionThe Guardian view on England’s centralised state: Andy Burnham must unbundle itEditorialDevolution should finance transport, skills and industry, not become a rightwing contest to promise the largest tax giveawayFri 31 Jul 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTShareThat England is among the rich world’s most centralised countries underpins Andy Burnham’s critique of the economic history of the past 40 years. Only post-communist Europedeindustrialisedas rapidly as Yorkshire and the Midlands did in the 1980s. Centralisation did not close every factory or pit, but left regions without the powers, finance or institutions to cushion the shock or build a resilient, replacement economy. Hence Mr Burnham’s radical and welcome plan to unbundle English government.There are three facets to his devolution programme. The first are the detailed and concrete proposalscontainedin a cabinet paper Mr Burnham released on Friday. This appears to be a blueprint to create a decentralised state organised around mayors as the key regional economic actors, while jointly governed pan-regional agencies could emerge, say for transport, energy, investment and industrial systems, that cross mayoral boundaries. Regions without mayors will get a chance to have one – or limit themselves to weaker powers.View image in fullscreenBen Houchen, mayor of Tees Valley.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesThe second,outlined in the Guardianand laterconfirmedby No 10, is that mayors will be able to keep income-tax and business-rate revenues, with the forthcoming budget and spending review deciding on how much. Before entering No 10, Mr Burnhamproposeda third pillar: a duty, modelled on Germany’s Basic Law, requiring English regions to pursue equivalent living conditions nationwide.Following this logic, a mayoral authority would receive a share of tax revenues and benefit when its economy and tax base grow. But the national government would continue redistributing resources so that poorer places can provide comparable services and possess meaningful investment capacity. Without such an equalisation measure, disparities would widen. One thinktank pointed out that if mayorsreceived2.5% of the 20p basic rate of income tax, London would get £2.3bn in 2026-27 while Hull and East Yorkshire would get £135m.Ben Houchen, the Tory mayor of Tees Valley,wantsto turn devolved income-tax revenues into new powers to offer tax rebates. That mistakes a regional investment settlement for a tax-cutting competition: poorer places would forfeit the cash needed to rebuild transport links as well as skills and industrial capacity. What some rightwingers seek is to turn regional elections into tax-cutting auctions over who can return the most public money. But cash giveaways now would just mean the bill of the underinvestment would land later.England’s devolution map remains incomplete, but Mr Burnham wants to finish it. New mayors are due inCumbria, and Cheshire and Warrington, in 2027, followed by ones in southern and eastern regions in 2028. The rest of the country will be asked to choose between mayoral strategic authorities with stronger powers or non-mayoral “foundation” bodies operating with more limited controls.Anew Harvard Kennedy School and King’s College London paper, co-authored by the former Labour minister Ed Balls, argues that Britain’s weak productivity stems from persistent regional divides, with the gap between south-east England and the rest of the nation wider than that separating east and west Germany today. One reason this has not been tackled is that Britain has never had bothNo 10 and the Treasurycommitted to regional growth. Now it does. The country may finally discover what happens when the centre pulls in the same direction.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
