title: The Guardian view on the Lovell telescope: budget cuts to physics are bad science and worse politics  | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Funders have picked a damaging fight with scientists and the public. They should reconsider their plans
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Funders have picked a damaging fight with scientists and the public. They should reconsider their plans
Content: The Lovell telescope at Jodrell Bank Observatory.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Lovell telescope at Jodrell Bank Observatory.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAOpinionScience policyThe Guardian view on the Lovell telescope: budget cuts to physics are bad science and worse politicsEditorialFunders have picked a damaging fight with scientists and the public. They should reconsider their plansFri 31 Jul 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe iconic Lovell telescope, housed at the Jodrell Bank Observatory in Cheshire, has always expanded our view of the universe – from tracking the Sputnik launch in 1957 to its current contributions to the study of dark matter. It is now threatened with closure afterit was announced thatgovernment funding will not continue past March 2028. Theprojected savingsare just £2.8m a year.This is just the latest in arolling package of cutsfrom the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC) – which disperses government funding to particle, astro and nuclear physics, among other disciplines – aimed at saving about £160m over the next four years. The STFC has insisted that the measures are a result of cost overruns. That may be true, but it is hard not to see this as part of a larger shift in what kind of science the government funds and prioritises, and what areas it allows to wither.There is no doubt that physics is expensive. From telescopes to synchrotron beams, its instruments are increasingly large-scale and power-hungry. And scientists are not immune to the cost of living crisis. If households are feeling the pinch of electricity costs, just imagine getting the monthly bill for a particle accelerator. However, UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), of which the STFC is a subsidiary, has just gone through a revamp of its funding model, one thatclearly prioritiseseconomic growthand measureable outcomes. Looking acrossthe programmes cut, which include international collaborations with other telescope arrays and the Cern facility in Switzerland, many scientists believe that long-term, fundamental research is under specific threat.View image in fullscreenIan Chapman.Photograph: PR Company HandoutThe UKRI and STFC have not helped the situation by badly misreading the politics. In a session at theHouse of Lordsearlier this month, the UKRI chief, Ian Chapman, seemed surprised by the scientists’ “hyperbolic” reaction, and noted that they “feel that they have been cut” when, in fact, overall physics funding has increased. But scientists have reason to feel slighted when valued ongoing projects and collaborations – rather than future plans – are axed, and when what appear to be relatively small cost savings (the UKRI budget will be £10bn by 2030) fall on their shoulders. There are shades of the departed Starmer government in this saga: the UKRI wants to tell a big story about science funding going up, but instead is mired in a row over a fairly minor sum that has angered scientists and sections of the public. One does not have to be an astronomer to know that optics matter.The UKRI and STFC are technically arm’s‑length bodies, but it hasn’t escaped notice that the ministers who set its funding priorities,Liz Kendalland Patrick Vallance, are no longer in office, whileAndy Burnham has abolishedthe Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. It would seem a good time for the current course to be reconsidered, whether by the funding councils or the new government itself.There is a conversation to be had about what research we fund with limited resources, and the balance between so-called blue sky projects and those expected to yield commercial returns. But when physicists warn that the UK could lose a “generation of scientists” to these cuts – in one of the few fields in which we can credibly claim to be world-leading – they should be heeded. It’s time to refocus, and look again.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Andy Burnham’s first step towards fairer social care for all | Social care | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to the prime minister’s pledge to spend his ‘political capital’ and find cross-party consensus on reforming social care
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to the prime minister’s pledge to spend his ‘political capital’ and find cross-party consensus on reforming social care
Content: Andy Burnham visiting a care home in north London on 29 July.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham visiting a care home in north London on 29 July.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PASocial careLettersAndy Burnham’s first step towards fairer social care for allReaders respond to the prime minister’s pledge to spend his ‘political capital’ and find cross-party consensus on reforming social careFri 31 Jul 2026 13.11 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 13.12 EDTShareI write as someone whose disabilities mean that I will be in receipt of social care support my whole life (Andy Burnham seeks cross-party agreement on future of social care, 27 July). For too long, people like me have been cannon fodder for politicians who routinely forget that their highest duty in providing social care is to protect those less able, or unable, to care for themselves. Investing in the right support for us unlocks our often-forgotten abilities. When we are successful, it is often because we have had opportunity to be because of that support, and when we aren’t, as so often happens, it is because society writes us off.Andy Burnham’s intervention is welcome news as it shows that he considers us a priority. Reform of the social care system has to be taken hand in hand with disability groups and people with lived experience of being disabled. Too often the system traps people into dependency on temporary accommodation rather than providing them with the means to receive support in their own home.Six years ago, this was the case for me, but not any more. I am now studying at university and have settled into a life that is light years better than what I had before.The prime minister’s own experience of dealing with this issue is also helpful in this. In his first five years as the mayor of Greater Manchester, rough sleeping wasreduced by two-thirds. If he wants to be bold, he only needs to look north and to his prior success in delivering this for Manchester.Robbie BentleyBristolDespite economists saying that it is too hard to tax wealth rather than income, there is already a wealth tax in place paying for social care in this country. The trouble is that it’s only levied on those who have the misfortune to need it. As yourexplainerpoints out, disabled and elderly people in England with assets over £23,250 have to pay the full cost of their social care.Why shouldn’t the super-rich be taxed on a similar basis – all assets over a threshold – and then they can pay for a functional and decent social care system for all the people who they made their money from by charging extortionate profits and paying sub-living wages?If the working class isn’t allowed to pass down generational wealth, why should anyone else be?Rachel PowildManchesterRightwing politicians and newspapers screaming about inheritance grabs and new taxes to fund social care are missing the point, probably deliberately. Socialising the cost of social care does not increase the cost, but spreads it more fairly. At present it is a lottery: if you get a losing ticket and you or a family member needs long-term care for dementia, all your savings, and the capital tied up in your house, could disappear. If you are lucky and die quickly, your children get a windfall.It is clearly fairer that everyone gives up a share of their wealth rather than some all and some none. Not only that, it removes the stress about whether a lifetime’s savings will suffice. A properly designed national care service will share risk, which is what a civilised society should value.Mike CushmanLondonAny attempt to pay for the broken social care system should start with the abolition of the triple lock on pensions. I welcome the moves towards achieving a cross-party consensus, but fear that political point-scoring and manoeuvring will defeat them, as they have done in the past.Michael LeeStockton on Tees, County DurhamIn the debate on how to fund care costs, can all parties drop “no one should have to sell their home” mantra? If you are the sole occupant and need residential care, why shouldn’t you sell it to pay the costs? After all, you’re not using it. Is it fair to receive financial support and still be able to pass your biggest asset on to your children?John TraynerLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: We are shocked that Palestine Action barrister faces contempt proceedings | Contempt of court | The Guardian
description: Letters: Former clients of Rajiv Menon KC, including Tariq Ali and Hillsborough family members Margaret Aspinall and Sue Roberts, say the charges against him must be dropped. Plus a letter from Andrew Smith
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Former clients of Rajiv Menon KC, including Tariq Ali and Hillsborough family members Margaret Aspinall and Sue Roberts, say the charges against him must be dropped. Plus a letter from Andrew Smith
Content: ‘At some of the most traumatic times in our lives Rajiv Menon has represented us with professionalism, integrity and compassion.’Photograph: Garden Court ChambersView image in fullscreen‘At some of the most traumatic times in our lives Rajiv Menon has represented us with professionalism, integrity and compassion.’Photograph: Garden Court ChambersContempt of courtLettersWe are shocked that Palestine Action barrister faces contempt proceedingsFormer clients of Rajiv Menon KC, includingTariq Aliand Hillsborough family membersMargaret AspinallandSue Roberts, say the charges against him must be dropped. Plus a letter fromAndrew SmithFri 31 Jul 2026 13.09 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 13.11 EDTShareThe fight for truth and justice can too often be a hard and long struggle. Navigating the law is complex, and justice depends on lawyers who we can trust – lawyers who listen to our voices, stand up for us, and pursue the truth on our behalf.Rajiv Menon KC is an experienced and highly respected barrister who has spent his career representing people like us. At some of the most traumatic times in our lives he has represented us with professionalism, integrity and compassion, ensuring that our voices were heard in inquests, inquiries and criminal trials.We are all deeply shocked that Rajiv is facing contempt proceedings (Palestine Action barrister’s prosecution criticised as ‘chilling’, 23 July). As clients we must have confidence that our lawyers can represent us fearlessly and independently. This case risks undermining the fundamental relationship of trust and confidence between clients and their lawyers without which meaningful participation in the justice system is impossible.We stand with Rajiv and believe that these proceedings must be dropped immediately.Tariq AliWitness, undercover police inquiry;Margaret AspinallMother of James Aspinall, who diedin the Hillsborough disaster;Sue RobertsSister of Graham Roberts, who died in the Hillsborough disaster;Marieha HussainProtester acquitted over “coconut” placard;Tippa NaphtaliCousin of Mikey Powell, who died in police custody;Selma Taha, Divina Riggon, Danae Thomas(King’s Cross Three)Imran Khan makes a valid case against the charge of contempt against Rajiv Menon KC (One day, your life and future may depend on a jury. The integrity of that legal process is in peril right now, theguardian.com, 23 July). I wonder how this charge would stand up to theHillsborough law, where state actors are required to tell the whole truth when giving evidence.The disparity of justice meted out toPalestine Actionseems to point to inevitable fines or prison when the above law should be giving everyone the opportunity of a fair trial. Apart from that, no advocate should be concerned for their own freedom when defending another citizen, no matter what they have done.Andrew SmithBoltonExplore more on these topicsContempt of courtTrial by juryPalestine ActionlettersShareReuse this content

title: Don’t let Jodrell Bank Observatory become another industrial museum | Science policy | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to reports that the world-famous big dish is facing closure due to spending cuts by UK Research and Innovation
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to reports that the world-famous big dish is facing closure due to spending cuts by UK Research and Innovation
Content: Jodrell Bank Observatory. ‘It seems odd that there is a squeeze of government investment in this area of soft power.’Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenJodrell Bank Observatory. ‘It seems odd that there is a squeeze of government investment in this area of soft power.’Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAScience policyLettersDon’t let Jodrell Bank Observatory become another industrial museumReaders respond to reports that the world-famous big dish is facing closure due to spending cuts by UK Research and InnovationFri 31 Jul 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.47 EDTShareThroughout my long life, Jodrell Bank Observatory has been a source of wonder and pride (Jodrell Bank Observatory facing closure after major funder cuts support, 27 July). Sir Bernard Lovell’s inspirational creation never ceases to awe with its combination of cutting-edge space exploration and heroic engineering structure. A tour of its welcoming visitor centre with my grandchildren confirmed that this sense of awe is being passed on to future generations.Yes, it would make another fine museum. But here in the north we have quite a few museums of our glorious industrial past. We have only one Jodrell Bank, probing the mysteries of the universe right now. So I’m afraid it is over to my fellow English graduateAndy Burnhamto reverse the philistine decision of UK Research and Innovation, reminding him of his poetic hero Philip Larkin’s fear for the possible future of the UK: “Our children will not know it is a different country./ All we can hope to leave them now is money”.Dr Ken SmithMacclesfield, CheshireThe one thing that Britain can still claim to be a top-division power in is science and technology. From numbers of Nobel laureates, to startups being funded then absorbed by global enterprises, and our universities and research establishments attracting the best minds from all over the world, the evidence is there. When trade delegations travel the world, the selling point is our science and technology. So it seems odd that there is a squeeze of government investment in this area of soft power.One of the symbols of Britain’s scientific prowess is the big dish at Jodrell Bank. Generations in Britain and around the world have grown up seeing it as the backdrop to space travel and astronomical discoveries. Reducing its funding will draw attention to the reduced circumstances of Britain’s scientific endeavour and a lack of ambition to keep Britain as a world leader. If the government wants to quietly cut spending on scientific research, reducing Jodrell Bank to a museum is not the best route. £2.8m a year seems a small price to pay for keeping an international symbol of Britain’s prowess going.John SommerSaltford, SomersetI’m dismayed at the news that Jodrell Bank Observatory is under threat. I enjoyed an enlightening day at the visitor centre recently, and was planning a return visit. Could I suggest that the relevant funding body dig out their own telescopes and take a long hard look at the future of British science and those young people looking forward to careers in science, engineering and technology?Peter BaddeleyPainswick, GloucestershireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Georgia Hunter Bell outruns Odira to win Commonwealth Games 800m gold | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Hunter Bell clocked 1min 59.51 to beat the world champion in Glasgow, a victory that secured a full set of major medals for the English woman
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Hunter Bell clocked 1min 59.51 to beat the world champion in Glasgow, a victory that secured a full set of major medals for the English woman
Content: Georgia Hunter Bell takes in her achievement after winning the women's 800m final in Glasgow.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGeorgia Hunter Bell takes in her achievement after winning the women's 800m final in Glasgow.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Georgia Hunter Bell outruns Odira to win Commonwealth Games 800m goldHunter Bell clocks 1min 59.51 to beat world championWin secures full set of major medals for English runnerSean Ingleat Scotstoun StadiumFri 31 Jul 2026 17.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are late developers in sport, and then there is the brilliant Georgia Hunter Bell, who continues to defy sporting gravity at the age of 32.And on Friday night under the Glasgow lights, she gave a tactical masterclass to outwit – and then outpace – the 800m world champion Lilian Odira and complete her set of global medals.Commonwealth Games 2026: Hunter Bell wins 800m gold; athletics and boxing on day eight – liveRead moreIncredibly it was only two years ago that she made her international debut here in Scotland’s biggest city. Back then she was a part-time runner working in tech. Now, staggeringly, she is one of Britain’s biggest sports stars and the proud owner of Olympic, World, European and now Commonwealth medals.“There were some tears on the podium,” Hunter Bell said afterwards. “That showed me how much that meant.”Hunter Bell’s story loses nothing in its retelling. As a teenager she was among the best runners in Britain. Then came a series of injuries, setbacks and heartaches. By her mid-20s she had retired. Then came a second act not even Hollywood would dare write.It started with long cycle rides during lockdown, then a series of parkruns in Bushy Park. By November 2022 Hunter Bell had got in contact with her old coaches, Trevor Painter and Jenny Meadows, who guided Keely Hodgkinson to glory and had regarded Hunter Bell as “the one who got away”. Soon her injuries were long behind her – along with most of her opponents.By March 2024 she was wearing her first GB vest in the world indoor championships in Glasgow. That August she won an Olympic 1500m bronze medal in a British record 3min 52.61sec. Since then she has given up her job and got even better. This medal, in an England vest, was her sixth time on a global podium.“Lots of people reflect on being a kid and doing it for the kid version of yourself,” she said after. “But I ­actually think of the young woman version of myself, who was like 23, 24, and gave up and really didn’t know what she was doing with her life.“I feel sorry for that girl, and then I feel proud of making it through that and coming back here,” she added. “That’s what makes me emotional.”View image in fullscreenGeorgia Hunter Bell crosses the finishing line well clear of Lilian Odira and Sarah Billings.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APGoing into the final, most thought that Odira, the Kenyan who had defied Hunter Bell and Hodgkinson to win gold at last year’s world championships, was the one to beat.But Hunter Bell had other ideas, leading from tape to gun, to take an easy victory in 1min 59.51sec. Odira took silver, more than a second back, with the Australian Sarah Billings claiming bronze.“I felt calm,” Hunter Bell said. “I really feel like I was composed. It didn’t go to plan as in the race. I did not think I would go gun-to-tape and lead it for the whole thing. I wanted to lead with 200m to go. But I found myself at the front, and so I thought ‘I’ll just control it, keep it relaxed, not too fast’, and then when I feel that pressure on me with the move being made, I’ll be ready to go.”The thing is nobody came. They were through halfway in a slow 60.32sec, and the race had barely sped up when Hunter Bell finally powered clear with 200m to go. At this point Odira was five metres back and had no chance of closing.“I’m really happy with that, it worked perfectly,” Hunter Bell said. “I really felt my legs were going in the last few steps and I couldn’t see where anyone was, but the crowd really pulled me home. It was great.”There were also two silver medals for England on the night through Emily Newnham and Jake Minshull in the women’s and men’s 400m hurdles. But this was a night that belonged to Hunter Bell.Elsewhere, Adaejah Hodge of the British Virgin Islands gave a small hint of her talent by storming to the women’s 200m title in 22.07.The 20-year-old has already run 10.63 for the 100m this year, making her the fifth fastest woman in history. For good measure she has a personal best of 21.68 for the 200m, putting her joint-ninth of all time. But on a cold night in Glasgow, a more modest time was enough as she took gold ahead of Shaniqua Bascombe, of Trinidad and Tobago, with Jamaica’s Alana Reid picking up bronze.In the men’s javelin Sri Lanka’s Rumesh Pathirage continued his annus mirabilis by winning gold with a huge throw of 89.75m, ahead of India’s Olympic champion, Neeraj Chopra.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Echoes of 1954 as Kerr, Wightman and rising star Myers face off in mile race | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Roger Bannister’s ‘Miracle Mile’ race 72 years ago is set to gain a worthy successor as Scottish pair take on the prodigious Australian
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Roger Bannister’s ‘Miracle Mile’ race 72 years ago is set to gain a worthy successor as Scottish pair take on the prodigious Australian
Content: Josh Kerr’s mile world record in London has heightened the anticipation around Saturday’s final in Glasgow.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAView image in fullscreenJosh Kerr’s mile world record in London has heightened the anticipation around Saturday’s final in Glasgow.Photograph: Adam Davy/PACommonwealth Games 2026Echoes of 1954 as Kerr, Wightman and rising star Myers face off in mile raceRoger Bannister’s ‘Miracle Mile’ race 72 years ago is set to gain a worthy successor as Scottish pair take on the prodigious AustralianSean Inglein GlasgowFri 31 Jul 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThey call it the Miracle Mile: the race still regarded as the greatest inCommonwealth Gameshistory. And 72 years later in Glasgow, it finally has a worthy successor.Rewind to 1954. In May Sir Roger Bannister had become the first man to run a mile in under four minutes. Six weeks later, the Australian John Landy lowered his mark by more than a second. Then came their epic clash in Vancouver.Australian runner Olli Hoare clarifies he did not witness murder in GlasgowRead more“I felt it was a piece of unfinished business to be able to reproduce the performance of my sub-four-minute mile in a race,” Bannister later said. “However, at the half-mile … he was 15 yards ahead and I thought either he’s going to break a world record in 3min 56sec or he’s going to have to slow.”Somehow Bannister dragged himself back into it by the bell, yet Landy was still leading as they turned into the home straight. But there was to be a dramatic late twist.Because the roar of the crowd was so great, Landy was unable to hear his pursuer, so he looked over his left shoulder. At which point Bannister attacked and flew past his great rival on his right shoulder before storming to gold in 3:58.8.On Saturday night the men’s mile should provide another contest for the ages, with Scotland’s Josh Kerr and Jake Wightman facing Australia’s new superstar Cameron Myers.Everyone knows about Kerr. Since the 28-year-old ran an astonishing 3:42.66 tobreak the world mile record, there have been profiles in the New York Times and Wall Street Journal, and he has become joint favourite with Jude Bellingham to win the BBC’s Sports Personality of the Year.View image in fullscreenRoger Bannister’s breaking of the four-minute mile in May 1954 kickstarted a compelling summer that culminated in his Commonwealth Games triumph.Photograph: APPlenty of non-athletics fans will also be aware of Wightman, given that he won the world 1500m title in Eugene in 2022 while his dad, Geoff, wascommentating in the stadium,and followed it up with aworld silver in Tokyoin September 2025.And while the 20-year-old Myers might be a new name to some, everyone in track and field is in awe of his talent. “I got beaten by him in 2024 in Australia,” says Wightman. “And I was like, ‘man, he’s going to be good.’ But he just kept getting better every year. He’s the future of the sport.”How good might he be? “This is a crazy era,” says Wightman. “But we’re potentially racing against someone who’s going to be the best of all time – that’s the way I look at him.”That is extraordinary praise given Myers was still a teenager at the start of June. But Wightman is just as effusive about Kerr’s mile world record. “It’s insane,” he says. “It’s like 54-second laps. The average person will get nowhere near running 100 metres at that pace, and I thought it was impossible to do that.“The world record’s amazing and I’m sure that will stand for a long, long time. But the worst bit about it was I watching, thinking: ‘Christ, I’ve got to race him in a couple of weeks’ time.’”View image in fullscreenCameron Myers (right) in the mile heats. He has been hailed as ‘the future of the sport’ by Jake Wightman.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPThe race tactics will be fascinating. Over 1500m this year, Kerr and Myers have run more than a second quicker than anyone else. But this is championship racing, with no pacemakers or wavelights. And that, as Kerr acknowledges, brings different challenges.“It is very different to go from racing a clock to racing these guys,” he says. “They are some of the best milers in the world. But I thrive in a pressure environment. I’m here to show up and get a gold medal for Scotland.”Most believe that Kerr will want a truly run race and will go to the front early if no one pushes the pace. But the slower the first two laps are, the more likely Wightman’s sprint finish will come into play.“I pride myself on being good at champs,” says Wightman, who also ran the fifth fastest 1000m in history last month. “I know that I couldn’t do what Josh did in that world record. But I love the fact you come to champs and it becomes both a physical and mental battle. I’d love it to be cagey, others I’m sure wouldn’t.”View image in fullscreenJake Wightman seals his famous 1500m gold in 2022. ‘I pride myself on being good at champs,’ he says.Photograph: Adam Warżawa/EPAThe great unknown is how much Kerr’s thrilling run in London has affected him. As Wightman says, it isn’t always easy to reset after a massive high. In 2022 he won the 1500m world title only to suffer a shock defeat to Olli Hoare in the Commonwealth Games 10 days later.And while gold is surely between the big three, Kenya’s 2019 world champion, Timothy Cheruiyot, and Wales’ Jake Heyward, who is in the shape of his life, have medal chances too.Wightman also points out another complicating factor. While much of Britain is enjoying a heatwave, the temperature when the race starts will be only 13C and gusty.“It’s not the stillest track and the Glasgow weather’s not the kindest,” he says, smiling. “The potential is that if you go and take it out hard you might be ending up working a lot harder than you think you are. It’s going to be a battle.”The echoes of 1954 will be heard loud and clear in Scotstoun on Saturday night.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Commonwealth Games 2026 medal table | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Follow the latest standings for the Glasgow Games as 74 countries compete for the 645 medals on offer
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Follow the latest standings for the Glasgow Games as 74 countries compete for the 645 medals on offer
Content: Commonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth Games 2026 medal tableFollow the latest standings for the Glasgow Games as 74 countries compete for the 645 medals on offerGuardian sportFri 31 Jul 2026 17.43 EDTFirst published on Thu 23 Jul 2026 10.48 EDTShareMedal tableCountryThe 23rdCommonwealth Gamesare taking place in Glasgow between 23 July and 2 August. There are 74 Commonwealth Games Associations eligible to compete, all of whom are expected to send athletes to the championships.Medals will be available in 215 events, spread across 10 sports. Six of them include Para sport competition: 3x3 basketball, athletics, bowls, cycling, swimming and weightlifting. The other four sports are artistic gymnastics, boxing, judo and netball.Australia toppedthe medal table in Birmingham four years ago,thanks to a 179-medal haul that included 67 golds. They were followed by England, Canada, India and New Zealand in the standings, with these nations taking the top five spots in the competition’s all-time medal table in the same order. They are likely to be among the most dominant once again.The table is sorted by number of gold medals, then silvers and then bronzes, rather than by the overall total. Hosts Scotland will hope to improve on the 13 gold medals they collected in 2022.Last updated: 22.45pm (BST) Friday 31 July

title: Arsenal’s title defence: keeping tired players fit and the Vinícius question | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Key players have piled up extra minutes at the World Cup and signing Vinícius Júnior would smash their wage structure
Author: Andrew Beasley
Headline: Key players have piled up extra minutes at the World Cup and signing Vinícius Júnior would smash their wage structure
Content: Gabriel Magalhães has played 4,210 minutes since the start of last season, and is one of several Arsenal players who have had heavy workloads.Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/GettyView image in fullscreenGabriel Magalhães has played 4,210 minutes since the start of last season, and is one of several Arsenal players who have had heavy workloads.Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/GettyArsenalArsenal’s title defence: keeping tired players fit and the Vinícius questionKey players have piled up extra minutes at the World Cup and signing Vinícius Júnior would smash their wage structureAndrew BeasleyFri 31 Jul 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter beating MK Dons 3-0 in a training-ground friendly last weekend,Arsenaltruly begin their pre-season programme against Girona on Saturday evening. It marks a return to action for the Premier League champions, who will want to show their success last season was not a one-off.Retaining the English title is incredibly difficult if you are not Manchester City. No other club has done it since Manchester United won three in succession from 2007 to 2009. Chelsea have done it once, Liverpool have not managed it for more than 40 years, and it is the best part of a century since Arsenal retained the crown. Mikel Arteta faces a sizeable challenge.Reaching a second successive Champions League final will not be simple either. Manchester City in 2021-22 are the only one of England’s previous five finalists who made it as far as the semi-finals the next season. With the Premier League stronger than ever, competing on two fronts has never been tougher. Transfer business may improve Arsenal’s chances, though their spending has been modest to this point. More than half of the £79m spent was on making Piero Hincapié’s loan permanent.Elsewhere Arsenal have replaced Leandro Trossard with Christos Tzolis, a Greek winger, from Club Brugge. Seven years younger than the Belgian, his arrival is a logical move in future-proofing the squad. However, the left side of Arsenal’s attack would be elevated to truly elite level if they could secure reported target Vinícius Júnior. The on-field argument speaks for itself. Vinícius made 92 carries of at least five metres that ended with him either taking a shot (49) or creating a chance (43) last season, the most of anyone in Europe’s top five leagues. Open-play threat, for a side that has often relied on set pieces, would be considerably increased.Those holding the purse strings at Arsenal may have pause for thought. Capology’s wage data estimates that Vinícius is the joint-third highest paid player in Europe’s top five leagues, earning in excess of £100,000 a week more than anyone at his potential new club. Would Arsenal be willing to rewrite their wage structure? They should expect calls from the agents of their current players if they are. In this sense, Bradley Barcola, with whom they have also been linked, makes a more plausible target. The issue there would be competition fromLiverpool, who are in far greater need of wingers.Chart comparing Vinícius Júnior’s salary with Arsenal’s top paid playersThis is the test facing Andrea Berta, Arsenal’s sporting director. Improving a squad that is already one of the best around is not easy. WhenBerta’s arrived last year, the club’s primary targets were said to be Alexander Isak and Benjamin Sesko, both of whom joined rivals instead. The pool of players who could add something significant to Arteta’s options is drying up.Keeping existing players fit may be more beneficial than enhancing the squad. Arsenal did well to win the league given only a handful of clubs had players that missed more games. Kai Havertz was reportedly their top earner beforeBukayo Saka signed a contract extensionin February, but he only started seven league games. The captain, Martin Ødegaard, was also unavailable for spells, meaning he and Saka started only 10 Premier League matches together in 2025-26. One of them coincided with the only game for which Declan Rice was injured (the 4-1 home win over Aston Villa), another (another home win, 2-1 against Brighton) when he started at right-back.View image in fullscreenMikel Arteta indulges in a bit of training-ground banter with first-team coach Miguel Molina in Girona.Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesThis meant Arteta was rarely able to give key men a breather. Arsenal have five of the Premier League’s top 20 players for club minutes in all competitions since the start of last season. Granted, the goalkeeper David Raya is one of them. But their outfield players with more than 4,200 minutes were Rice (4,456 minutes, the 11th most for a Premier League club), Martín Zubimendi (4,298, 15th), William Saliba (4,254, 17th) and Gabriel Magalhães (4,210, 19th), all vital components of the side’s spine.Saliba also played 795 minutes for France, pushing him past 5,000 minutes before his World Cup was prematurely ended by a back injury that looks likely to sideline him for some time. It is remarkable Rice was able to play 1,026 minutes for England on top of his Arsenal commitments, not least as he hasmanaged nerve pain in a hamstring throughout 2026.This workload clearly impacted his ability to contribute at his best for Thomas Tuchel this summer, and that will be a concern for Arteta. With Viktor Gyökeres also clocking up plenty of playing time for Sweden, Arsenal have six players with at least 4,400 minutes for club and country since the start of last August.Chart showing Arsenal’s players with the most minutes for club and country since 1 August 2025This may have been a factor in Arsenal opting for a relatively low-key pre-season. They visited Asia last summer, but the trip to Catalonia to play Girona is the furthest they will travel this year. Arsenal also have games in Dublin (against Real Betis) and Cardiff (the Community Shield against City) sandwiching home friendlies against Borussia Dortmund and Como.With players still recovering from their World Cup exertions, it may be some time before we see the true Arsenal. A combination of fatigue, injuries and potential squad additions means the process could take far longer than would be ideal.Explore more on these topicsArsenalfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Field and French flourish for Wigan to boost title charge with victory at Leigh | Super League | The Guardian
description: Tries from Jai Field and Bevan French sparked Wigan’s 20-8 victory at Leigh to move them up to second in Super League and boost their title credentials
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Tries from Jai Field and Bevan French sparked Wigan’s 20-8 victory at Leigh to move them up to second in Super League and boost their title credentials
Content: Bevan French enjoys his try for Wigan in their comeback victory at Leigh.Photograph: Ed Sykes/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBevan French enjoys his try for Wigan in their comeback victory at Leigh.Photograph: Ed Sykes/SWpix.com/ShutterstockSuper LeagueField and French flourish for Wigan to boost title charge with victory at LeighSuper League: Leigh 8-20 WiganWigan move up to second within two points of LeedsAaron BowerFri 31 Jul 2026 17.08 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are moments inSuper Leagueseasons, marathons as they are, which can often prove to be sliding doors occasions for both teams involved. And as the full-time hooter sounded in Leigh and Wigan celebrated another statement win with their travelling support, it was not difficult to imagine how one particular moment from this derby could swing the seasons of both teams.For nearly 40 minutes, Leigh had done something no team had managed to do to Wigan for quite some time: make them appear second best. The Warriors, on a run of nine consecutive wins which began with theirChallenge Cup triumph at Wembleyin May, had been completely outplayed by their local rivals and their own coach admitted they were lucky to be only 8-0 behind.Kitchen magnate finds recipe for Wakefield joy in historic rugby league cityRead moreBut great teams, and great players, find a way to win. Leigh’s first real mistake came two minutes before half-time, when they turned their backs on Jai Field after conceding a penalty, expecting Wigan to kick for touch. Instead, Field tapped the ball and raced 90m downfield to reduce the deficit to just two points by half-time. Just like that, it turned.When Leigh produced another error three minutes after the restart, the Warriors’ other talisman, Bevan French, pounced to inexplicably move Wigan ahead in a game they had been dominated in to that point. Two more Leigh knock-ons followed soon afterwards and once again, the visitors scored tries from both of them.Nobody knows how this would have ended had Leigh led more convincingly at half-time. If the Leopards had won, they would have inserted themselves into the picture for the top two. Instead, they are now sitting sixth and looking nervously over their shoulders. Wigan,meanwhile, march on– they are now second and just two points behind the league leaders, Leeds.Perhaps in a way it was a lesson as to the step Leigh still need to take to compete with a side like Wigan. But the Warriors, frustrated as they will be by the level of this performance, should take great heart from the fact that if they can be this below par with the ball and still win against a playoff rival, imagine what they can do if it clicks in a playoff tie this autumn.View image in fullscreenJai Field dives over for Wigan’s first try of the night in their victory.Photograph: Ed Sykes/SWpix.com/Shutterstock“We needed to improve because in that first half we were second best,” their coach, Matt Peet, said. “We’ve managed our way out of a situation there. There was nothing wrong with our effort but they were very good. You don’t want to win this way every week but it’s good to know it’s in the locker.”Leigh deservedly led by eight points early on thanks to Innes Senior’s outstanding try and two goals from the boot of Adam Cook, but there was no doubting the big moment here – Field’s breakaway try – left a mark on them. The Leopards will hope it does not leave any long-lasting damage in their push to make the playoffs again.“I went in and tried to lift them at half-time but it felt like that moment was a bit of an implosion,” Leigh’s coach, Adrian Lam, said. “It was hard to watch in the second half but we were awesome in that first half. It was unbelievably good, and we are very close to being very good. A bit of negativity crept in and our gameplan just fell apart.”Field’s and French’s tries turned an eight-point deficit into a lead either side of half-time. When Leigh turned possession over cheaply again, Zach Eckersley was the third grateful recipient of a momentary lapse from the Leopards. Then as the hour mark struck, Noah Hodkinson was afforded the same opportunity to make it 20-8 and from there, Wigan were wise enough defensively to close out a crucial win.But this was a captivating and engrossing derby. With the National Rugby League’s bid for control of Super League incoming over the next few days, this was an advert for everything that is great about the competition. A sold-out stadium, a local rivalry and star talent proving to be the difference when it mattered most.Yet for all the change potentially coming Super League’s way off the field, one constant is that it would take a brave man to back against Wigan prevailing at Old Trafford again in October.Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueLeigh LeopardsWigan WarriorsRugby leaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Charley Hull doubles down on caddie prank after strong start to Women’s Open | Women's Open | The Guardian
description: Charley Hull, who finished five behind the second-round leader Ryu Hae-ran, said her caddie was unfazed by her £100,000 scratchcard joke
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Charley Hull, who finished five behind the second-round leader Ryu Hae-ran, said her caddie was unfazed by her £100,000 scratchcard joke
Content: Charley Hull says her caddie Adam Woodward loved her prank before the Open began.Photograph: Jon Super/APView image in fullscreenCharley Hull says her caddie Adam Woodward loved her prank before the Open began.Photograph: Jon Super/APWomen's OpenCharley Hull doubles down on caddie prank after strong start to Women’s OpenEnglish player’s actions called ‘extremely cruel’Ryu Hae-ran leads on seven-under at halfway markEwan Murrayat Royal Lytham & St AnnesFri 31 Jul 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNews that Charley Hull had slept for only three hours before her second round at the Women’s Open fuelled an obvious conclusion. With noisy fallout continuing fromthe 30-year-old’s prank on her caddie, it was assumed to be affecting her off the course. Not so, as it transpired. In typically emphatic style, Hull urged those who cannot accept criticism to “grow a pair of balls” after signing for a resilient 71 at Royal Lytham & St Annes.After Hull tricked her bag man Adam Woodward into believing he had won £100,000 from a fake scratchcard, some of the reaction was fierce. Laura Davies, one of the greats of women’s golf, called Hull’s actions “extremely cruel”. After round one at Lytham, Hull told her detractors to “loosen up”. That, too, fuelled castigation of the Englishwoman. Rather than back down, she has doubled down.“You put yourself in the limelight so you would be silly to think there will not be comments like that,” said Hull of the disapproval towards her.View image in fullscreenCharley Hull reacts after chipping in at the 17th hole during the second round.Photograph: Jon Super/AP“I think you see some people saying: ‘I really struggle from these comments.’ They’re almost looking for sympathy. You’re in such a good position in life. There are people way worse off in life and you’re moaning about what people are saying about you.“I just think like, I don’t know, grow a pair of balls and just forget about it. Because if that’s the worst thing in life, people saying bad stuff about you, you really have not got life that bad. My boyfriend said to me last night: ‘Free publicity is good publicity. Today’s newspaper is tomorrow’s fish-and-chip paper.’ I was like, yeah, true. Then we just laughed it off and then we haven’t really spoken about it since.”To everyone on the outside, though, this is an ongoing theme.It must be recognised that Woodward, Hull’s long-time caddie, has shrugged off the episode. “What people don’t understand is mine and Adam’s relationship,” Hull added. “We’re very, very close. He’s like a big brother to me. He is one of my best friends. He came to Wimbledon with me the other week.“He’s always taking the mickey out of me. He thought the joke was brilliant himself. He was showing it. He was laughing hard about it. Then when you hear comments, so many people saying how bad it is, just lighten up. You obviously don’t get my humour and I don’t care if you don’t get my humour.View image in fullscreenSouth Korea’s Ryu Hae-ran is seeking her third major title of the year and leads at halfway.Photograph: Jon Super/AP“My friends get my humour and that’s why they’re my friends. I wouldn’t do it to a random person that I knew wouldn’t take it very well. We all knew Adam, he is the king of pranks. The amount of pranks he and his caddie mates have are way worse than that. So he’s pretty chill. People need to chill out about that. Adam is loving the attention from it. He texted me last night saying this has been one of the funniest weeks ever because of that prank.”Lost in this melee is the fact Hull is well-placed to win her first major title. She may well remain the story of this tournament for different reasons than has been the case thus far.The highlight of day two was her bunker shot from greenside at the 17th, which found the bottom of the cup. A hole earlier and with her ball in a fairway divot, Hull twice backed off her approach after being distracted by a fidgety cameraman.“Everyone makes mistakes sometimes,” said Hull. “Bless him.” Life around this golfer is never dull.In tougher conditions than Thursday, Hull’s minus-two aggregate left her five adrift of the leader, Ryu Hae-ran. Ryu is seeking a third major win in as many starts. Shiho Kuwaki is one adrift at six under. Hull’s short sleep proved little hindrance.“I slept 12 hours the night before,” Hull said. “After a late finish it takes me a while to wind down. I had a lot of adrenaline going through me. When you know you’ve got to be up early you’re like: ‘I want to go to sleep’ and then you can’t sleep because you’re thinking about going to sleep.“I’m quite weird, I can sleep for 16 hours straight. I’ve slept for 20 hours before.”Hull’s total has been matched, somewhat extraordinarily, by the Spanish amateur Paula Martín Sampedro. When asked if she can win, the 20-year-old was admirably defiant. “I think I can,” she said. “If I play my best, I definitely can.” Top amateur honours at least should be a formality in this form.View image in fullscreenPaula Martin Sampedro, the Spanish amateur, said she can win the Open after an impressive first two rounds.Photograph: Jon Super/APJeeno Thitikul’s 73 slid her back to five under par. A missed cut for Georgia Hall at the venue where she won the 2018 Women’s Open surely ends any lingering hopes of reaching this year’s Solheim Cup.Team Europe will be confirmed on Monday, with the event taking place in the Netherlands in September. Megan Khang also headed for an early flight out of Lancashire with Miyu Yamashita, the 2025 champion, another to last only 36 holes.Explore more on these topicsWomen's OpenGolfnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tour de France Femmes under pressure to reroute Ventoux stage amid wildfire risk | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: The Tour de France Femmes is facing pressure to re-route part of its key stage to the summit of Mont Ventoux next Friday because of the wildfires threat in Provence
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: The Tour de France Femmes is facing pressure to re-route part of its key stage to the summit of Mont Ventoux next Friday because of the wildfires threat in Provence
Content: The inclusion of Mont Ventoux on this year’s Tour de France Femmes route underlines the race’s growth in stature.Photograph: Tim Ireland/PAView image in fullscreenThe inclusion of Mont Ventoux on this year’s Tour de France Femmes route underlines the race’s growth in stature.Photograph: Tim Ireland/PATour de France FemmesTour de France Femmes under pressure to reroute Ventoux stage amid wildfire riskAuthorities want stage altered if risk is ‘extreme’2025 champion Ferrand-Prévot faces sterner challengeJeremy Whittlein LausanneFri 31 Jul 2026 13.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTour de France Femmesis facing pressure to reroute part of its key stage to the summit of Mont Ventoux next Friday because of the wildfires threat in Provence.The women’s Tour, which begins in Lausanne on Saturday, is expected to keep the famous climb to the top of the “Giant of Provence”, but the current routing of the stage through the Ventoux’s foothills could be affected.‘I’m just a different type’: Demi Vollering gears up for Tour de France Femmes tiltRead moreIn a statement on its website, the Vaucluse prefecture said: “At a time when forest areas are at a peak risk of fire, the prefecture has asked the organisers of the Tour to consider an alternative route. Following a fire risk assessment on Tuesday 4 August, an alternative route will be implemented should the wildfire risk be considered extreme.”Three stages of the men’s Tour de France, whichfinished in Paris last Sunday, were disrupted by wildfires, extreme heat and the deployment of French emergency services to assist with the wildfire crisis in the country’s south-west.“We are in constant touch with the prefecture and we will adapt, just as the men’s Tour de France did,” said Marion Rousse, the Tour de France Femmes race director.“We have to deal with the real world – this is a bike race and the real world always takes priority. There will still be a climb of the Ventoux, but we have several options. We are ready to work with the emergency services and the government.”Few things demonstrate the fast‑track growth of women’s racing more than the inclusion of Mont Ventoux on the route for this year’s race. “There is no mountain that is too difficult for women,” Rousse said. “The level is now more and more consistent and they ride faster each time. Each year the progress is huge.”View image in fullscreenThe defending champion, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, did not attend the top riders’ media conference on Friday.Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/Keystone/APThe legendary climb is the standout stage in a race route that is bolder and bigger than it has been since the race was reintroduced in 2022 as a tentative bolt-on to the end of the men’s Tour de France.Over nine stages, including an individual time trial and stages through the Jura, Massif Central and Provence Alps, 147 riders will wend their way to the Côte d’Azur for a testing finale in the hills inland from Nice.Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, the defending champion, was a no-show at the top riders press conference on Friday afternoon, with her highly rated French teammate Marion Bunel, third overall in this year’s Vuelta Femenina, surprisingly taking her place.Ferrand-Prévot was said to have already fulfilled plenty of media obligations, but her absence from a top table that included past winners and her main rivals, Demi Vollering and Kasia Niewiadoma, did not go unnoticed.Ferrand-Prévot’ssuccess last Julywas hailed in France, but she faces more rivals this year than she did 12 months ago, with the 23-year-old Spanish rider Paula Blasi, who sealed victory in the Vuelta on the brutal climb of the Angliru, a leading contender.Elsewhere there are signs that others too, as Rousse suggested, have upped their game. The Swiss rider Marlen Reusser, who said she has had a “love-hate” relationship with the Tour Femmes in the past, is expected to shine in the individual time trial on stage four, while the long climb to the Ventoux is likely to feature the 2023 winner, Vollering, and the defending champion, Ferrand-Prévot, going head to head.View image in fullscreenMarlen Reusser is expected to excel in the stage four time trial.Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/EPAReusser, the world time trial champion, has had a series of false starts in the French race. “This is the first year that I’m here and feel healthy and good,” she said. “It’s special to finally be here in that way.”Ferrand-Prévot’s victory in last year’s race made her a household name in France and, after a long wait to see a home rider win the yellow jersey, drew crowds to the roadside in their thousands.“Now women’s cycling in France is doing well and men’s cycling in France is also doing very well,” Rousse, said by way of tribute to Ferrand-Prévot’s success.“We felt a real sense of patriotism with Pauline’s victory. Whether it was in the men’s or the women’s race, it’s been some time that we’ve been waiting for a French winner.“Pauline gives a lot. To the public, her charisma has done cycling a lot of good. All those little girls who dream one day of becoming like Pauline. People are interested in her because she is so likable.”Rousse is confident that Ferrand‑Prévot, despite a muted spring, will put up a staunch defence of her title. “There will be a great rivalry between her and Vollering,” she said. “I think that Pauline has increased her level in comparison to last year – she’s really gone up.”Elsewhere, the upward trajectory of the race continues. The number of women riding the amateur Étape du Tour Femmes is higher than those who rode the Étape du Tour, on Alpe d’Huez, with 27% of all participants in the Étape Femmes being female.“It shows that women put a lot less obstacles in their way than before, especially since the creation of the Tour de France Femmes,” Rousse said.Saturday’s opening 138km stage in Switzerland features a hilly loop based on Lausanne, through the Cantons of Vaud and Fribourg, leading to a steep uphill finish on the Côte Saint-François, while on Sunday the peloton follows the northern shore of Lake Geneva before a lakeside finish, and a possible sprint, in Geneva.Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Justice department moves to dismiss its charges against Olympian over reflecting pool | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Lawyers now say damage to pool liner attributed to David Hearn instead is result of installation by contractor
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Lawyers now say damage to pool liner attributed to David Hearn instead is result of installation by contractor
Content: David Hearn (second from left) with attorney Norman Eisen, in Washington DC on 9 July 2026.Photograph: Rod Lamkey/APView image in fullscreenDavid Hearn (second from left) with attorney Norman Eisen, in Washington DC on 9 July 2026.Photograph: Rod Lamkey/APTrump administrationJustice department moves to dismiss its charges against Olympian over reflecting poolLawyers now say damage to pool liner attributed to David Hearn instead is result of installation by contractorEdward HelmoreFri 31 Jul 2026 19.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 19.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe justice department has moved to dismiss a criminal case charging former Olympian David Hearn with deliberately damaging the Lincoln Memorial‘ reflecting pool, instead blaming damage to the pool liner as “the result of flawed installation by the contractor”.Government lawyers said in a 20-page court filing in DC superior court on Friday evening that they had received information about a “rush to complete the project prior to events associated with the America 250 celebration in the weeks surrounding Independence Day 2026”.Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, said that her office had received documents from the Department of the Interior only “after the return of the indictment” showing that damage to the pool occurred prior to Hearn visiting the reflecting pool and put his hand in the water on 19 June. Hearn had denied administration claims of pool sabotage and the charge that followed.The documents “indicated a rushed and flawed installation process, with repeated failures of the lining during the installation process, and extensive peeling of the lining throughout the Reflecting Pool,” the motion said.“It was not until after these documents were produced,” Pirro’s office added, that her office “first became aware of information showing that the damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism as initially represented by DOI”.Attorneys for Hearn said the government “owes Mr Hearn an apology”.“The Trump administration’s case against Davey Hearn should have never been brought,” attorneys Norm Eisen, Mary Dohrmann and Steve Levinsaid on social media. “Its dismissal today does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong. The government’s approach was ready, fire, aim.”Hearn told the Associated Press that he had been detained by the national guard and US park police for five hours after stopping by during a bike ride. He said he briefly touched a chunk attached to the side.Hearn, 67, was one of seven people facing charges in what Donald Trump had claimed were efforts to sabotage the $15m renovation project.Hearn was the only person known to be facing a felony charge, rather than a misdemeanor. Hearnpleadednot guilty earlier in July to one felony count of property destruction – a charge that could have resulted in a 10-year prison sentence and a $1,000 fine.His trial had been scheduled to start on 28 September inWashington DCsuperior court.Last week, a witness in the case testified that the area of the pool liner had already been damaged and would have required repairs regardless of Hearn’s alleged actions.Lawyers for Hearn called on prosecutors to disclose the legal instructions they gave to grand jurors about the elements of the criminal charge handed up against him.“The grand jury transcripts disclosed to the defense thus far contain other irregularities that reflect a misleading presentation to the grand jury and a need for review of the entire grand jury record in this matter,” Hearn’s attorneys wrote.A National Park Service (NPS) official testified that the pool had already been damaged before Hearn allegedly touched it, couldn’t quantify any damage attributable to the accused and said the same repairs would have been required regardless of his alleged conduct, defense attorneys contended.“The witness’s testimony established that the pool had substantial preexisting damage requiring repair before any alleged conduct by Mr Hearn,” his lawyers wrote. “According to the witness, the pool was leaking more than one million gallons of water per week; its expansion joints had exceeded their service life; and the liner already contained a rip.”Hearnhad previously told NBC Newsthat “the condition of the reflecting pool was the same after I stepped away from the water as it was before I got there”.Efforts to fix the leaky pool, which is prone to algae blooms, before America 250 celebrations had been dogged by problems: the liner started separating, and the pool once again turned green after specialist aeration machines were turned off before a UFC fight on the White House lawn.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationWashington DCOlympic GamesLaw (US)US justice systemUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Daughter of British couple killed in Spanish wildfire rejects claim they ignored order to leave | Spain | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Danielle Kirton calls on Ed Miliband to help her get answers about why evacuation order came too late
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Exclusive: Danielle Kirton calls on Ed Miliband to help her get answers about why evacuation order came too late
Content: Danielle Kirton, right, with her mum, Fran.Photograph: Danielle KirtonDanielle Kirton, right, with her mum, Fran.Photograph: Danielle KirtonSpainDaughter of British couple killed in Spanish wildfire rejects claim they ignored order to leaveExclusive: Danielle Kirton calls on Ed Miliband to help her get answers about why evacuation order came too lateHelena HortonFri 31 Jul 2026 12.36 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 09.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe bereaved daughter of a British couple who died in a Spanish wildfire is calling on the foreign secretary,Ed Miliband, to get answers from Spain’s government about why her parents were not told to evacuate until it was too late.Severe wildfires haveburned across Spain and Francesince early July, killing people, destroying thousands of homes and forcing more than 300,000 people to flee.Pete and Fran Gillam, who lived in Bédar in Almería, died in mid-July while fleeing their home as a wildfire tore through the village. They wereamong 13 people killed in the fires, many of whom died in their cars as they tried to escape.View image in fullscreenPete and Fran Gillam. Danielle said a lone police officer was ‘frantically driving from house to house’ to tell people in the village to evacuate.Photograph: FacebookDanielle Kirton, 42, an assistant headteacher from Nottinghamshire, has spent the weeks since her parents died looking for answers. She knows her mother would have followed official advice had she have been given it.Though the fire alert came at 4.30pm, the evacuation order did not come until more than three hours later. Kirton said this was delivered by a lone police officer, who was “frantically driving from house to house” and Spain’s official emergency alert system, which plays a loud noise on mobile phones and tells people to evacuate, was not used.British couple named among 13 killed in Spanish wildfiresRead more“My mother sent me a video at 6.45pm showing the fire a considerable way away from the hill where they live,” Kirton said. “She didn’t sound worried or concerned. I kept in contact with her and she sent me a message saying at 7.53pm that they’d evacuated.”However, the decision to evacuate was made tragically late. “They stopped at a neighbour’s driveway to shout to a neighbour they needed to evacuate, but then they became trapped as the fire had jumped on both sides of the road.”View image in fullscreenThe remains of cars in Bédar. Many of the 13 killed in the fire died in their vehicles as they tried to flee.Photograph: Atlas/Reuters‘I had an incredible escape’: British woman tells of close encounter with Spanish wildfireRead moreThere are now other wildfires burning in much of Spain and south-west France, but there have been no civilian casualties so far. In the small village where her parents lived, 13 people died. “It would appear that somewhere within that system there has been a failure. If you look at the subsequent wildfires in Spain, there have been no casualties and the biggest difference is the emergency alert was used in subsequent wildfires,” Kirton said.She said her mother loved living in Bédar and as a retired headteacher took much joy in organising quiz nights to fundraise for the local school. She had a bag packed and she was ready to evacuate. “She was just waiting to be told what to do,” Kirton said.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of the wildfire in Bédar. Thirteen people died when the fire tore through the village.Photograph: Gregorio Marrero/APSpanish politicians have claimed that those who died ignored instructions. “My parents did not ignore instructions. My parents would have not had an issue with instructions in Spanish,” Kirton said. “My parents heeded advice to shelter in place, until they were then told that they needed to evacuate.“They took the correct route, and their only route, to the evacuation point. It is a weak and cowardly act to blame victims in the face of tragedy.”The response from the Foreign Office has been a “slap in the face”, she added. “The help from the consulate has been nonexistent. We got sent a link: ‘What to do when someone dies abroad.’ That is it. It is a slap in the face, to be honest.”Miliband has been visiting France and Spain to discuss wildfires and the climate crisis with political leaders. Kirton said: “As UK citizens, it is important to ask for his support in asking Spanish authorities to conduct a full and thorough investigation.”Danielle Kirton, right, with her dad, Pete, and her sister, Natalie. Kirton said the UK Foreign Office’s response to her parents’ death has been a ‘slap in the face’.Photograph: Danielle KirtonScientists say thefires have been worsened by the climate crisis, which has intensified the recent heatwaves. Kirton said this makes it more crucial that lessons are learned so no one has to go through what she has.“It’s vital for planning for the future that we see what exactly were the contributing factors in this case,” she said. “It’s a perfect storm, the weather, the climate, the vegetation, the wind. My parents weren’t concerned before – it isn’t something they felt fearful of, it wasn’t something that happened where they lived.”Kirton has been working every day since her parents died trying to get answers and a substantial response from the Spanish authorities. She said: “My mum and dad would have always spoken up for what’s right and if I can do anything for them it’s that we can ask for the truth and ensure this never happens again to any other families.”The Andalusian government has been contacted for comment.A Foreign Office spokesperson said that any investigation into the fire response is a matter for the Spanish government: “The foreign secretary has been in regular contact with his Spanish counterpart, including during his visit to Madrid on Wednesday.“They discussed how the UK could support Spain’s response, ensure British nationals receive the right advice and assistance, and agreed that lessons must be learned as climate change makes these dangerous wildfires more likely.“Staff at our embassy have been working with the British community in the affected area, collating their questions and concerns and raising them with the Spanish authorities. This work is ongoing.”Explore more on these topicsSpainWildfiresExtreme weatherExtreme heatEuropeEd MilibandClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Healey sets budget for late October, promising to ‘spread money and power’ around UK | Economic policy | The Guardian
description: Chancellor will have to find money for Burnham’s policies while sticking to fiscal rules as borrowing costs rise
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Chancellor will have to find money for Burnham’s policies while sticking to fiscal rules as borrowing costs rise
Content: Andy Burnham and John Healey on a visit to a family centre in Sheffield on Friday.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and John Healey on a visit to a family centre in Sheffield on Friday.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/ReutersEconomic policyHealey sets budget for late October, promising to ‘spread money and power’ around UKChancellor will have to find money for Burnham’s policies while sticking to fiscal rules as borrowing costs riseRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentFri 31 Jul 2026 11.43 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham’s government has set a date for a late October budget to “spread money and power” out of Westminster as the new prime minister pushes forward his tax and spending plans.Announcing an autumn budget for 28 October, the chancellor,John Healey, said Labour would stick to its fiscal rules with its agenda to give businesses and households stability for the future.Burnham has used his first two weeks in power to make ablitz of policy announcements, including a VAT cut on energy bills, slashing business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues, capping bus fares and promising to give England’s regional mayors a share of income tax.Pushing to turn around Labour’s faltering performance in opinion polls under Keir Starmer, the prime minister will however need to spell out how his change in direction is funded in a tricky autumn budget.The UK government has faced a sharp rise in borrowing costs on global financial markets in recent weeks as the economic fallout from the Iran war hits activity, stokes inflation and adds to the financial pressures for countries around the world.With elevated levels of annual borrowing and the UK national debt at its highest point since the 1960s, City investors warn that Burnham has limited room for manoeuvre in the public finances. The prime minister has also committed to stick to Labour’s manifesto promises, including ruling out an increase in income tax, national insurance or VAT.City traders had expressed unease over the potential appointment of Ed Miliband as chancellor and Burnham taking a looser approach to the public finances. While picking Healey for chancellor and pledging to retain Rachel Reeves’s fiscal rules – which require spending to be balanced by receipts – has eased concerns, investors still warn the government faces a delicate balancing act that may lead Burnham to consider tax rises.In his first weeks in office Burnham had initially suggested he could look at“any flexibility”in the fiscal rules. He has also faced calls to consider awealth taxand to overhaulproperty taxes, and hasnot ruled out tax rises to fund social care.On Friday, the Times reported that, in a joint letter with the prime minister, Healey has instructed cabinet colleagues that all new announcements, such as developing technical education and devolving more power to mayors, “must be funded from within existing budgets”.Approaching the budget, Labour has a raft of policy measures that willrequire funding details to be spelt out, including Burnham’s cost of living support, devolution plan and billions of pounds of cuts pencilled in by Starmer and Reeves to support a £15bn increase in defence spending over five years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHealey said Labour was “working fast to restore hope” with the government’s announcements and that he was pushing to “get on with the job” in his first budget as chancellor.“This will be a budget that moves money and power out of Westminster and into every postcode around Britain.“It will be built on fiscal discipline. It will meet our fiscal rules. It’ll give businesses and families some of the stability they need to plan for the future.”Explore more on these topicsEconomic policyAndy BurnhamBudgetJohn HealeyLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Hull funeral director who left bodies to rot in mortuary jailed for 20 years | Hull | The Guardian
description: More than 80 loved ones spoke of horrors of learning about Robert Bush’s crimes, including mother of a miscarried baby
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: More than 80 loved ones spoke of horrors of learning about Robert Bush’s crimes, including mother of a miscarried baby
Content: In the time he spent defrauding bereaved families, Bush spent more than £42,000 on holidays.Photograph: Danny Lawson/PAView image in fullscreenIn the time he spent defrauding bereaved families, Bush spent more than £42,000 on holidays.Photograph: Danny Lawson/PAHullHull funeral director who left bodies to rot in mortuary jailed for 20 yearsMore than 80 loved ones spoke of horrors of learning about Robert Bush’s crimes, including mother of a miscarried babyPriya BharadiaFri 31 Jul 2026 11.46 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 08.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA funeral director has been jailed for 20 years for leaving dozens of bodies – including a miscarried baby – “rotting” in his mortuary and giving bereaved families the wrong ashes.Robert Bush, the owner of Legacy Independent Funeral Services inHull, pleaded guilty to 67 offences spanning 12 years and affecting hundreds of families, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial.After Bush’s sentencing, the government said it planned to crack down on “rogue operators” in the funeral industry, including by developing proposals for formal regulation of the sector.The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said Bush’s actions “were utterly abhorrent and my thoughts are with all the bereaved families in Hull who have been so badly let down”.Over a five-day sentencing hearing at Hull crown court, more than 80 victims recounted their horror at learning their loved ones had been left “rotting away” inside his funeral parlour. Many broke down sobbing during their statements.Sentencing Bush, the judge, Mr Justice Hilliard, said: “The defendant was so preoccupied with his own enrichment that he behaved in a shocking and disgraceful way towards the deceased.“The awful truth is that anyone whose loved one went through Legacy at any time when it was operating can now have no confidence as to how they were treated or whose ashes they have. Unless, of course, they were one of the 30 bodies recovered in March 2024.“Culpability is of course high because of the gross breach of trust in respect of people who were vulnerable as they were bereaved.”View image in fullscreenA court artist drawing of Robert Bush appearing at Hull crown court for sentencing.Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PABush, 48, from Otley, West Yorkshire, showed little visible emotion while listening to the statements in the dock, but hung his head lower and lower as the week went on.Gasps and sobbing could be heard from the public gallery when prosecutors revealed the grimcondition of the deceased.The court heard that bodies had been found uncovered and lying on racks in varying states of decomposition. Damp and mould had spread to the coffins and ash boxes, while dried body fluids and faeces had been left on the floor.During the search, PC Jason Sutcliffe spotted a brown paper bag on the floor. He initially thought the item inside was a baby bird, before noticing two hospital wristbands wrapped around the waist, identifying the body as the “baby of Jasmine Beverley”.The baby,Sunny Beverley-Conlin, was miscarried at 18 weeks in May 2022. His parents believed he had been given a funeral and cremated. Instead, Bush had left his remains inside Legacy for almost two years.View image in fullscreenPolice outside the Hessle Road branch in March 2024 after reports of ‘concern for care of the deceased’.Photograph: Danny Lawson/PASunny’s mother, Jasmine, sobbed as she faced Bush in court. “I trusted Rob with the most precious and important person in my life,” she said. “The reality I now live with is that my baby boy Sunny has spent more time in your possession than he ever did with his own family.”In a statement, Sutcliffe described finding Sunny’s remains as “the worst experience of my career” and said it would “never leave my thoughts”.The ashes presented to Beverley and her family had been “consistent with baby remains in volume but had larger pieces of coarse bones” expected from an adult’s body, according to evidence heard in court.Some of the ashes presented to Lucy Ness, who lost her child just before 12 weeks, were said to have resembled “animal remains” in terms of size and texture, which prompted cries in the courtroom.The body of 94-year-old Norman Bridger was recovered at the Legacy premises 323 days after his death. “My lovely dad lay in a cardboard coffin for almost 11 months,” said his daughter Karen King. “It’s beyond belief. I’ll never know why. It feels like he was just forgotten.”Bush was arrested on 10 March while returning from a holiday in Arizona, US, a £3,000 trip funded by his funeral fraud. Arrest footage showed Humberside and Met police officers escorting a shocked Bush off a plane at Heathrow airport.Soon after his arrest, Bush told officers: “I fucked it all up, everything, my whole world.”View image in fullscreenBush was arrested while returning from a holiday in Arizona.Photograph: Humberside police/PAPolice officers found 35 bodies and more than 100 sets of ashes during a search of Legacy premises at Hessle Road in March 2024.Several families had had the wrong ashes turned into jewellery, and in one instance planned to incorporate some into a tattoo.David Gorbutt told the court he felt “abused” after learning that Bush had given him a stranger’s ashes rather than those of his late wife, Susan Gorbutt. He had scattered those ashes at the same site as her son’s, as per Susan’s wishes.“I have had the uncertainty of not knowing who or what I have scattered over the ashes of Susan’s son,” Gorbutt said. “Who was that? One person? More than one?”The state of Bush’s premises “did not meet industry standards” and represented a “wholly inadequate approach to care for the deceased”, according to evidence from Dr Richard Lloyd, a human anatomy centre manager at the University of Cambridge and Cranfield University. “Bodies were simply abandoned in the Hessle Road mortuary for nature to take its course,” his report stated.Containers of ashes were “stored in an undignified manner” across the premises, stacked “chaotically on shelves” or left on the floor, where “damp had caused mould to grow on the boxes”. Ash was also found on desk surfaces and, in one room, strewn across the floor. Officers found jewellery that ought to have been returned to families and a large number of photographs that should have been placed inside coffins.Bush stole money from funeral services intended for 12 separate charities, including Macmillan Cancer Support, Salvation Army and a local hospice. In addition, he sold false funeral plans to 226 people over nearly 12 years, totalling in value £562,117.In the time he spent defrauding bereaved families, Bush spent more than £42,000 on holidays, including his trip to Arizona, £21,000 on motorcycle racing and £17,400 on home improvements between 2017 and 2024. He spent more than £9,000 on camping expenses in 2022– the same year he failed to cremate baby Sunny.Bush’s barrister, Richard Wright KC, said his client wished to apologise to the families and accepted this was “likely to be rejected” by them. Wright added: “He is treated, completely understandably, as a pariah – hated and despised.”Explore more on these topicsHullCrimeEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: $2m crime novel deal collapses amid questions over AI use | Books | The Guardian
description: Agents withdraw Jerry Falade’s hotly anticipated debut after saying they can no longer authenticate ‘how the manuscript evolved’
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Agents withdraw Jerry Falade’s hotly anticipated debut after saying they can no longer authenticate ‘how the manuscript evolved’
