Content: Authors, agents and publishers are grappling with how to handle suspected AI use in manuscripts.Photograph: FreshSplash/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAuthors, agents and publishers are grappling with how to handle suspected AI use in manuscripts.Photograph: FreshSplash/Getty ImagesBooks$2m crime novel deal collapses amid questions over AI useAgents withdraw Jerry Falade’s hotly anticipated debut after saying they can no longer authenticate ‘how the manuscript evolved’Emma LoffhagenFri 31 Jul 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 13.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA high-profile publishing deal for a debut crime novel has collapsed after doubts emerged over whether artificial intelligence played a role in writing it.The hotly anticipated manuscript Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body, by Jerry Falade, was withdrawn from sale by its agent despite reportedly receiving an offer for more than $2m (£1.5m) from Minotaur, owned by Macmillan US, as part of a 14-way auction. The plan was to publish it in 2028.An email sent to publishers by Falade’s agents and seen by the Guardian said: “Jerry Falade produced an incredible manuscript that dazzled us and the top publishing professionals around the world. Unfortunately, we are no longer able to authenticate how the manuscript fully evolved from origin to completion.”It continued: “During the submission process we vetted the manuscript with Jerry for AI and felt trusting in his reassurance that it was written without utilising AI as a resource in the writing or editorial process. We can no longer substantiate that, and we are withdrawing the book.”The US auction was run by the author’s agent Marc Gerald of Europa Content, according tothe Bookseller.In the UK, Sandy Hodgman of Hodgman Literary is said to have secured several six-figure bids through a similarly competitive process. The Guardian has approached both agents for comment.Gerald told the Bookseller he first read the book in June, and that it was “stunningly good, everyone fell in love with it. It’s a book that appeals to absolutely everyone.”He said that halfway through the submissions process, an editor raised concerns that the book had signs of potential AI use. Gerald said Europa opted against using AI-detection software to check the manuscript, saying Falade was “clear and credible” in his explanation.However, after a meeting on 29 July, when “aspects of [Falade’s] story changed”, the agency decided to cut ties, citing the “need to have total faith”.“We feel terrible for putting this into the universe and the firestorm it has caused,” Gerald added. “The book itself is genius – however it came to be drafted, it’s amazing.”Falade’s case is the latest in astring of controversies to hit publishing this year,as authors, agents and publishers grapple with how to handle suspected AI use in manuscripts. Earlier this year, Hachette pulled the US release of Mia Ballard’s horror novel Shy Girl after rumourscirculatedonline that the author had relied on AI, something she denies.In a statement to the Guardian, Falade rejected claims that he had used AI and said the response reflected racial bias in publishing.He said: “Three Black authors received major publishing deals this year, and all three later had deals cancelled or disrupted following suspicions about AI. There seems to be a troubling assumption that when a Black writer produces work that attracts significant attention, the work could not possibly be their own. Meanwhile, there are popular white writers who have publicly mentioned using AI for their writing processes and they’re still doing fine.”Falade did not name other authors, but two Black authors in the US – Ballard and HM Wolfe, author of the viral romance Daggermouth – faced allegations of AI use this year. Wolfe also denies she used AI.Falade said: “In my case, rumours began circulating and, within six hours, I had been dropped by my agency, deals were paused, and press releases were being issued.” He added that AI-detection tools “are widely known to produce false positives”. He said the novel had “passed through first readers, second readers, editors, and acquisitions teams at numerous publishing houses … If the manuscript had shown genuine signs of being generated by AI, it is difficult to believe that every one of those experienced professionals would have failed to notice.”Explore more on these topicsBooksPublishingAI (artificial intelligence)Crime fictionnewsShareReuse this content

title: New solar panels in Great Britain at 15-year high as fossil fuel costs soar | Solar power | The Guardian
description: Boom in solar farms and home installations in first half of 2026 began shortly after start of US-Israel war against Iran
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Boom in solar farms and home installations in first half of 2026 began shortly after start of US-Israel war against Iran
Content: UK households will be able to fit balcony solar panels by the end of August after legislation was passed this month.Photograph: Climate CentralView image in fullscreenUK households will be able to fit balcony solar panels by the end of August after legislation was passed this month.Photograph: Climate CentralSolar powerNew solar panels in Great Britain at 15-year high as fossil fuel costs soarBoom in solar farms and home installations in first half of 2026 began shortly after start of US-Israel war against IranJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentFri 31 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreat Britain has recorded more new solar power installations in the first half of this year than in any six-month period since 2011, as households turn to rooftop panels to help cut their energy bills.An analysis of the government’s official figures shows that Great Britain added 142,536 solar installations in the first six months of the year, putting it on track to top last year’s record solar additions.The government data, which includes large ground-mounted solar farms and rooftop panels, showed that the half-year solar boom is second only to the record 167,316 installations recorded in the second half of 2011, when the first large-scale solar farm was built in Cornwall on the site of a disused tin mine.Most of the new solar installations recorded in the government’s official figures are on household rooftops, although these smaller solar systems make up slightly less than a third of the country’s total solar power capacity.‘Extremely effective’ organised campaigns against wind and solar undermining support for renewable energyRead moreMore households have fitted solar panels to their rooftops in recent years, hoping to cut their energy bills by generating their own low-cost electricity as fossil fuels have caused bills to rocket, according to energy companies.The government’s data shows that more households are taking up grants to replace their gas boilers with low-carbon heating alternatives. The total number of applications for the boiler upgrade scheme reached 4,512 last month, up by 21% compared with June last year.Heat pumps are expected to be in higher demand in the months ahead after the government raised its grant funding by 20% last week, from £7,500 to £9,000, to help cover the costs of replacing fossil fuel heating. Andy Burnham has also cutVAT on electricity bills from October, which makes running a heat pump cheaper.E.ON Next, which is expected to become theUK’s biggest energy retailer, said it has recorded a 151% rise in the number of homes installing solar panels in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year.“More and more households are realising just how much they can save by generating and storing their own energy,” said Phil Gilbert, a director atE.ONNext. Some of its customers have saved up to £600 a year on their annual energy bill when signed on to its solar and battery tariff, he said.“People want to engage with their energy use, take control of their bills and rely less on the grid – and solar gives them a practical way to do that,” Gilbert added.Octopus Energy, which is currently Great Britain’s biggest energy supplier, also noteda sharp increase in solar panel saleswithin weeks of the Middle East conflict causing oil and gas prices to soar. The supplier said sales increased by more than 54% in March compared with the month before. In total there are more than 2m solar installations across Great Britain.The 1.4 megawatt (MW) Wheal Jane solar farm is now easily dwarfed by newer projects, including the 373MW Cleve Hill project in Kent, which became Britain’s largest working solar development when it reached full power last summer, and the 800MW Springwell solar farm in Lincolnshire, which is expected to begin generating in 2029.By the end of August UK bill payers living in flats or rented properties will be able to join themillions of people across Europe using “balcony solar panels”to lower their bills, according to legislation passed this month.Explore more on these topicsSolar powerRenewable energyEnergyHousehold billsConsumer affairsHeat pumpsOctopus EnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Extremely scary findings’ show climate crisis is supercharging Europe’s wildfire weather | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Latest study says global heating has made hot, dry and windy conditions in Spain at least 20 times more likely
Author: Damian Carrington
Headline: Latest study says global heating has made hot, dry and windy conditions in Spain at least 20 times more likely
Content: Emergency services in the Gironde department of France work to contain wildfires this week.Photograph: Mael Dubiez/SDIS33/EPAView image in fullscreenEmergency services in the Gironde department of France work to contain wildfires this week.Photograph: Mael Dubiez/SDIS33/EPAWildfires‘Extremely scary findings’ show climate crisis is supercharging Europe’s wildfire weatherLatest study says global heating has made hot, dry and windy conditions in Spain at least 20 times more likelyDamian CarringtonEnvironment editorFri 31 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe extreme heat and drought stoking huge wildfires in Spain andFrancewere made far more likely by the climate crisis, a scientific analysis has found.Global heating made hot, dry and windy weather at least 20 times more likely in Spain and twice as likely in France, experts from theWorld Weather Attribution (WWA) consortium calculated. The finding is the latest to pin the blame for the continent’s sweltering and deadly summer firmly on the heating caused by the burning of oil, gas and coal.Theintense heatwave at the end of June, which is estimated to havekilled 20,000 people, could not have happened without the extra heat trapped by carbon pollution, a previous WWA study showed. Another found that the climate crisis-drivenheat was “sucking soils dry”as extreme drought spread across Europe.Searing heat and parched land led to very high “daily severity ratings”, the metric that was used in the new analysis and which measures how severe a wildfire will be if ignited. Studies of the2025 wildfiresalso found they were supercharged by the climate crisis.This year’s wildfires in western Europe have been made worse by a wet winter and spring, which boosted the growth of vegetation, which then dried out and provided fuel for the fires – so-calledwhiplashconditions. Global heating is making winters wetter and summers drier and hotter in Europe.View image in fullscreenA scorched landscape near Vila Vella, in Spain’s València province.Photograph: Damian Torres/APDr Clair Barnes, a research associate at Imperial College London and part of the WWA study team, said: “We’ve seen repeatedly how climate change increases hot, dry, flammable conditions that are extremely conducive to wildfires.“What’s unique about [the July fires inSpainand France] is that it’s still early in the season – and with another heatwave looming, these findings are extremely scary. What we’re seeing is a clear sign of the escalating impacts of [human-caused] warming.”Julie Arrighi, the director of programmes at Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, said: “What we are seeing now in Spain and France goes well beyond what we would expect from past events.”The wildfires have released huge plumes of toxic smoke. Dr Augustin Colette, at the French National Institute for Industrial Environment and Risks, said: “The smoke increased particulate [pollution] peak levels up to 20 times above what is considered ‘fair air quality’, and extremely poor air quality was felt up to 400 km away from the fires.” About1.5 million people a yearare estimated to have their lives shortened by wildfire smoke.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEurope burns: a visual guide to the wildfiresRead moreSevere wildfires haveburned across Spain and Francesince early July, killing people, destroying thousands of homes, and forcing more than 300,000 people to flee. The WWA analysis assessed the seven-day period with the highest daily severity ratings (DSR) for each country. The scientists used weather records and established statistical methods to estimate how much more likely a week of extremely high DSR is in today’s heated world compared with in the world before mass fossil-fuel burning raised the global temperature by 1.4C (2.5F).Big wildfires have also broken outin the UKandGreece, where three firefighters lost their lives.The UN’s climate chief, Simon Stiell, said: “These European megafires show how fast climate-driven extreme heat and dry landscapes can turn wildfires into devastating national disasters.“Humanity continuing to burn colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas is making these conditions more dangerous, and these megafires more deadly and destructive,” he said. “But the solutions are equally clear: all countries must move faster from fossil fuels to renewables and protect people from worsening climate impacts, from wildfires, to megastorms and floods, to droughts hitting food production.”The Guardian’s climate forum 2026On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington, and our panel of experts– including ProfAndy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh, Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman– for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening. Book ticketshereor atguardian.liveExplore more on these topicsWildfiresClimate crisisExtreme heatExtreme weatherGreenhouse gas emissionsFossil fuelsSpainnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s all right for them’: private schools and golf courses stay green despite England’s hosepipe bans | Drought | The Guardian
description: As parks turn brown and paddling pools go unfilled, exemptions mean sports pitches can stay lush – even in school holidays
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: As parks turn brown and paddling pools go unfilled, exemptions mean sports pitches can stay lush – even in school holidays
Content: The playing fields at St Paul’s school in Barnes.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe playing fields at St Paul’s school in Barnes.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianDrought‘It’s all right for them’: private schools and golf courses stay green despite England’s hosepipe bansAs parks turn brown and paddling pools go unfilled, exemptions mean sports pitches can stay lush – even in school holidaysHelena HortonFri 31 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 08.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter multiple punishing heatwaves, and no rain in parts for over a month, it seems the whole of the south ofEnglandis golden brown.But by Hammersmith Bridge in Barnes, south-westLondon, there is the unmistakable scent of damp soil. The playing fields of St Paul’s school, where fees are up to £57,000 a year, are a bright, lush green.The neatly trimmed grass, with water droplets clinging to each blade, looks like a mirage in the otherwise parched landscape. It has been a shock to appalled residents, who are under a hosepipe ban and have to let their own lawns die.In England, 40% of the population is under a hosepipe ban, with seven water companies – AffinityWater, Anglian Water, Cambridge Water, Southern Water, South East Water, Thames Water and South West Water – all restricting use. But there are exemptions for golf courses, sports pitches and school playing fields, meaning there are pockets of green while the vegetation in the public parks dies.View image in fullscreenThe grounds of Dulwich College, and surrounding area, showing some parts watered while others are going brown due to the summer’s drought.Photograph: Maxar/Vantor/DigitalGlobe/Getty ImagesIt seems the bans came too late; the lack of water across the country means half of England isnow in drought. This is despite the fact some parts of the country had thewettest start to the yearon record.Elsewhere in south-west London, families were desperately trying to keep their children cool during school holidays. Young children could be seen huddled under trees in the shade on Tooting Bec Common, which has been scorched by the sun to the extent that the grass has died, leaving bare, hard soil.Parents with young children are unable to fill paddling pools to keep them cool, as temperatures have hit 30C or above on 24 separate occasions so far this summer.‘People are scared their neighbours will call the police on them’: how the hosepipe ban got caught up in the culture warsRead moreThe school, despite being closed for the summer, is allowed to keep its lawns verdant because of a loophole that allows schools to water their pitches for “health and safety” reasons.View image in fullscreenChildren sheltering under a tree at Tooting Bec Common.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian“They should be under the same rules as the rest of us,” says 62-year-old Steve Barker, who was stopping to mop his brow while on a walk along the Thames. “Why are they watering the playing fields when they aren’t even using them? It isn’t term-time!“It definitely looks better than my grass – I’ve had to let it die, and it is probably too late to save it now. They must be using a lot of water to keep it all so green.”While the contrast between the lush green of St Paul’s and the withering hydrangeas of the local community gardens is sharp, it is by no means unique: similar tensions are at play across swathes of the south. On the coast of Sandwich Bay in Kent, there are patches of bright green among the parched heathland. This is the Royal St George’s Golf Club, which hosts the Open Championship. The exclusive club allows membership only by recommendation by other members.Visitors can attend on some occasions throughout the year for about £400 a day. South East Water customers in the county are under a hosepipe ban, and the parks in Kent have gone brown.View image in fullscreenSteve Barker.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianDulwich College in south London, the £67,000-a-year school that counts Nigel Farage among its alumni, has also been keeping its acres of sports pitches lush and green, using powerful sprinklers. The school has said it is “using water as conservatively as possible”.It broke up for summer earlier this month, but continues to keep its sports pitches well watered. The community gardens in nearby Brockwell Park, however, cannot be properly watered.That pattern has intensified calls for a change in the water system, to iron out these inequalities and stop the need for as many hosepipe bans. Helena Dollimore, the Labour MP for Hastings and Rye, said: “Hosepipe ban exemptions for golf courses and private school sports pitches symbolise everything wrong with our water system. How can it be right that a private school can use hundreds of litres of water to keep the grass green in the middle of the summer holidays, but children cannot play in their paddling pools?“These are the consequences of consecutive Conservative governments selling off our most precious resource to create a system that benefits shareholders. All the while my constituents in Hastings, Rye and the villages suffer water outages year on year due to decades of underinvestment in our pipes and infrastructure. It cannot be one rule for them and another for everybody else.”View image in fullscreenA person walking through parched grassland beside a dried-up stream in Richmond Park, London.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersCat Hobbs, founder and director of the campaign group We Own It, said the inequality was “shocking”. She added: “Private school playing fields are staying lush and green while everywhere else, flowers wilt, parks go brown and kids can’t stay cool in the padding pool.”Hobbs thinks that “public ownership is crucial to manage our water properly, cut leaks and stop unfair exemptions like this”.In Barnes, anger at the private school’s green lawns has reached fever pitch. The school is hurriedly writing a letter to its neighbours to explain why the water is being used. Danielle Pierce, the estates manager, said: “We are watering our sports pitches, not the wider grounds, in line with Thames Water’s published guidance. This water comes from a dedicated standpipe and is not mains drinking water. We’re also preparing a short note for local residents, going out this afternoon, which covers the same points.”Barker said: “The parks are all yellow and dry, too – they aren’t allowed to break the hosepipe ban even though more people use them.”View image in fullscreenThe estates manager at St Paul’s school said: ‘We are watering our sports pitches, not the wider grounds, in line with Thames Water’s published guidance.’Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianAt some community gardens in the area, the plants are suffering as they cannot be watered with a hosepipe, requiring those who tend them to make multiple trips with a watering can.Julith Jedamus, a writer and editor who lives in the area, helps tend a community garden. “It is very tough on the trees and non-perennials,” she said. “Our garden is going very brown. I have been using a watering can for the hydrangeas, which have been suffering.”She seemed disgusted by the water use at the school, where snaking pipes of irrigation systems can be seen crisscrossing the grounds. “What annoys me is schools like St Paul’s can water their grass all year long, even now when school is not in session.”View image in fullscreenJulith Jedamus.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianOne passing man shouted out: “It’s all right for them!” while gesturing at the green playing fields. Of his garden he said: “It’s not dead quite yet, but it’s getting there.”Scientists have said that allowing golf courses and playing fields to remain lush and green can undermine efforts to encourage households to save water.Prof Hannah Cloke, a natural hazards researcher at the University of Reading, said: “I would hope green keepers and grounds staff follow best advice about when to water, only watering areas that they need to. It does seem crazy to sprinkle drinking water over sports pitches that don’t need it, when others are facing severe shortages.”Explore more on these topicsDroughtWaterPrivate schoolsEnglandLondonInequalityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham signals he will scrap plans to curb jury trials | Trial by jury | The Guardian
description: Prime minister says he has concerns about one of most significant proposals from Keir Starmer’s government
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Prime minister says he has concerns about one of most significant proposals from Keir Starmer’s government
Content: Andy Burnham was speaking during a visit to a family centre in Sheffield on Friday.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/Pool PA/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham was speaking during a visit to a family centre in Sheffield on Friday.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/Pool PA/APTrial by juryAndy Burnham signals he will scrap plans to curb jury trialsPrime minister says he has concerns about one of most significant proposals from Keir Starmer’s governmentJosh HallidayandPeter WalkerFri 31 Jul 2026 11.27 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 08.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham is indicating he will scrap plans to curtail jury trials in England and Wales, abandoning one of the most significant overhauls from Keir Starmer’s government.In perhaps his biggest repudiation yet of the policies he inherited from his predecessor, the prime minister said he had concerns about the proposals and his instinct was to keep juries at the heart of the justice system.Speaking at a community centre in Sheffield on Friday, Burnham said his reluctance related to the Hillsborough disaster.“Ihave my concerns about the plan to restrict a jury trial, partly from my personal experience, particularly in Hillsborough,” he said. “So I want to really look in detail at that proposal, and my instincts are that we need to find ways of not reducing access to jury trial.”Burnham’s intervention is the strongest signal yet that the former justice secretary David Lammy’s proposals, which amounted to a historic departure in the judicial system, will be dropped.The prime minister has previously raised concerns about the struggle of Hillsborough victims to secure justice for what he has called “the greatest miscarriage of justice of our times”.Lammy announced in December that defendants who were likely to receive asentence of three years or lesswould no longer get a jury trial. He said the proposals could clear the backlog of nearly 80,000 cases clogging up the court system within a decade.However, the plans were met with a fierce backlash from legal bodies and some Labour MPs including Karl Turner, who wassuspendedover his criticisms of Lammy and Starmer.On Friday, Burnham said he had asked the chief whip, Anneliese Midgley, to speak to Turner about being readmitted to the parliamentaryLabourparty.Two other Labour MPs who had lost the whip for other reasons – Diane Abbott and Joani Reid – have already been readmitted after separate independent disciplinary processes.Measures under the courts and tribunals bill would leave defendants no longer able to choose a jury trial, and the ability to appeal to a crown court against a magistrates court verdict would also be limited.Magistrates’ powers would be extended from dealing with maximum sentences of one year to at least 18 months and a judge-only “swift” court would be established to hear cases without a jury.Ministers argued the move was necessary to halve the number of jury trials from 15,000 a year and to tackle the backlog of court cases that built up during the Covid pandemic.The idea wasset out a year agoby Sir Brian Leveson, who had been asked by ministers to come up with possible ways to tackle a backlog that has seen many defendants and victims wait years for cases to come to court.In his report, the former judge said he did not “rejoice in these recommendations” but warned they were essential to avoid “a real risk of total system collapse in the near future” and that an effective lack of consequence for lawbreaking could bring grave societal consequences.Leveson warned that – even if adopted in full – his proposals would take more than five years to clear the backlog.The idea of limiting jury trials brought a furious response from some Labour MPs, withone mass lettercalling it “madness” and something that “will cause more problems than it solves”.Another group of MPsproposedhijacking the plan by using an amendment to introduce the alternative idea of specialist courts for sexual offences with fixed dates for trial, ensuring victims of sexual crimes saw justice sooner.Under Starmer, Downing Street was adamant there was no other option, saying that given the scale of the backlogs, “merely tinkering at the edges is simply not enough”.There were, however, also vehement objections from lawyers.One lettercondemning the plans, organised by the Bar Council, was signed by 3,200 lawyers, including 300 senior barristers.Separately, the founder of Doughty Street Chambers, the legal base for Starmer as well as Richard Hermer, his attorney general,condemned the plans. Geoffrey Robertson called the proposals a “cure worse than the disease”, adding: “Attacking juries must be regarded as a betrayal of the values for which Labour purports to stand.”Explore more on these topicsTrial by juryUK criminal justiceAndy BurnhamDavid LammyLabourEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: British-Azerbaijani man arrested in Cyprus over alleged spying on UK airbase for Iran | Cyprus | The Guardian
description: Rashad Sultanov, from London, suspected of conducting hostile surveillance and passing information to Revolutionary Guards
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rashad Sultanov, from London, suspected of conducting hostile surveillance and passing information to Revolutionary Guards
Content: The arrest was part of an investigation into incidents at RAF Akrotiri between May and June last year.Photograph: Yiannis Kourtoglou/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe arrest was part of an investigation into incidents at RAF Akrotiri between May and June last year.Photograph: Yiannis Kourtoglou/ReutersCyprusBritish-Azerbaijani man arrested in Cyprus over alleged spying on UK airbase for IranRashad Sultanov, from London, suspected of conducting hostile surveillance and passing information to Revolutionary GuardsReutersFri 31 Jul 2026 04.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British-Azerbaijani national has been arrested ⁠in Cyprus on suspicion of spying on a British airbase on the Mediterranean island and passing information to Iran’s ⁠Islamic Revolutionary Guard ⁠Corps, the Metropolitan police ​said.Rashad Sultanov, 44, from Islington, north London, was arrested on 17 July by Cypriot authorities ⁠and is being held in custody as extradition proceedings continue, the police said in a statement on Friday.He was arrested as part ⁠of Britain’s first overseas National Security Act investigation, led by counter-terrorism police into incidents at ​Britain’s RAF Akrotiri base in ‌Cyprus between 11 May and ‌22 June last year, the statement said. Cypriot police did not immediately ‌return a request for comment.Sultanov allegedly conducted hostile surveillance on the base and is alleged to have then shared information with the IRGC, the Met said.Helen Flanagan, the head of counter-terrorism policing in London, said: “This case shows we are able to use the National Security Act overseas when British military bases are allegedly targeted by hostile state activity.”Earlier in July the IRGC threatened to attack any British military ​bases used by US forces to launch attacks on Iran.In March, an Iranian-type Shahed drone strike caused slight damage to facilities at Akrotiri. Soon afterwards, Britain said the base would not be part of its defensive agreement ⁠with the US over the use of UK bases.Also in ​March, Iran was ​reported to have fired two ​ballistic missiles at a US-UK military base on Diego Garcia, ​in the Indian Ocean, ‌though neither hit ​the target.Akrotiri is ​one of two bases Britain has retained in its former colony since Cyprus’s independence in 1960. It has been used for military operations in Iraq, Syria and Yemen.Explore more on these topicsCyprusIranEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Chinese super-embassy in London to go ahead after high court challenge dismissed | UK news | The Guardian
description: Royal Mint Court residents’ association, which sought to stop planning permission, says it will appeal against ruling
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: Royal Mint Court residents’ association, which sought to stop planning permission, says it will appeal against ruling
Content: The Royal Mint Court, the proposed site of a new Chinese super-embassy.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Royal Mint Court, the proposed site of a new Chinese super-embassy.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersUK newsChinese super-embassy in London to go ahead after high court challenge dismissedRoyal Mint Court residents’ association, which sought to stop planning permission, says it will appeal against rulingAmy HawkinsFri 31 Jul 2026 07.37 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 07.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConstruction of a controversialnew Chinese embassywas given the green light on Friday after the high court dismissed a challenge from neighbours.The Royal Mint Court residents’ association (RMCRA), which brought the case against the government, immediately announced plans to appeal against the decision, in a move that could cause further delays to the project. The debate over planning permission for the new embassy has been asore pointof British-Chinese relations in recent years.The RMCRA represents people and businesses who live and operate from properties in Royal Mint Court, the historic site that the Chinese government bought for £255m in 2018.The association argued that the government had been unlawful in granting planning permission and that it had failed to assess the human rights considerations of the project.In January the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Governmentgave permissionfor China to build the vast new diplomatic outpost, which would be Beijing’s biggest in Europe.The decision was delayed for months after the planning application was taken out of the hands of the local council, Tower Hamlets, which had originally rejected it on security grounds. Senior spy officials later advised the government that therisks to UK national securitycould be controlled and dealt with.The high court rejected the RMCRA’s arguments. It said there was no evidence of the Chinese government interfering with the human rights of the residents, “even though they had strongly objected to the proposed embassy and had been involved in protests”.The government said it “conscientiously and carefully had regard” to the residents’ concerns.Ricardo Paulo Gama, a solicitor at Leigh Day, the law firm representing the residents’ association, said he hoped a higher court would be “braver” in considering the grounds of appeal.The RMCRAraised more than £220,000to fund the legal challenge. The group is supported by the Inter-parliamentary Alliance on China (Ipac), a cross-party group of parliamentarians focused on China.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe future of AI hinges on openness and cooperation. China and Britain can gain much by working together | Zheng ZeguangRead moreLuke de Pulford, the executive director of Ipac, said: “We have together already prevented the Chinese Communist party from breaking ground at Royal Mint Court for more than seven months.“The fight continues and we all want to win this case and to stop the embassy.”Mark Nygate, a representative of the RMCRA, said: “While we were also disappointed with today’s judgment, we knew this was going to be a long [process], and we intend to go all the way through.”Nygate said that it was a battle of “David versus two Goliaths”, the British and the Chinese governments.The Chinese government was not a party to the legal challenge. It has criticised the delays to the project and Xi Jinping, China’s leader,raised the matter directlywith Keir Starmer, the then UK prime minister, during a phone call in 2024.Plans to redevelop the British embassy in Beijing have been blocked pending approval of the Chinese embassy’s new site inLondon.Explore more on these topicsUK newsLondonChinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Mahershala Ali on Marvel’s collapsed Blade reboot: ‘If they wanted to do it, we would’ve done it’ | Mahershala Ali | The Guardian
description: Two-time Oscar winner was to take on role of vampire-hunting antihero but said project is no longer happening
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Two-time Oscar winner was to take on role of vampire-hunting antihero but said project is no longer happening
Content: Mahershala Ali wears a hat to promote Blade at Comic-Con in 2019.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/Invision/APView image in fullscreenMahershala Ali wears a hat to promote Blade at Comic-Con in 2019.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/Invision/APMahershala AliMahershala Ali on Marvel’s collapsed Blade reboot: ‘If they wanted to do it, we would’ve done it’Two-time Oscar winner was to take on role of vampire-hunting antihero but said project is no longer happeningBenjamin LeeFri 31 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 13.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe two-time Oscar winnerMahershala Alihas confirmed that hisBladereboot is no longer going forward.The star of Moonlight and Green Book had been attached to play Marvel’s vampire-hunting antihero in 2019. The role had originally been played by Wesley Snipes in three films between 1998 and 2004.The reboot was then trapped in development hell with various directors and screenwriters attached.“If they wanted to do it, we would’ve done it,” Ali said ina new GQ interview.He later added: “I feel ready to move on from theBladequestions. Those questions are for them. They didn’t want to do it, so they should answer that question.”His comments come after the Marvel head, Kevin Feige,saidhe felt like a “gigantic loser” for not getting the project off the ground.The film was at one stage set to be directed by the Mogul Mowgli film-maker Bassam Tariq. Ali and Tariq have since worked together on the revenge thrillerYour Mother Your Mother Your Mother, which is premiering at this year’s Toronto film festival.Ali said he “didn’t feel great about the fact that things finished the way that they did” with the Blade reboot. He had provided his voice for the character in a post-credits sequence in 2021’s underperforming Marvel adventure Eternals.Ali also added on the Blade collapse: “The best way I can answer this question is, when I look at what is for me, is it was either this or that – and I’ll take this. No offence to them. I’ve been doing this professionally for pushing 30 years now, and one thing I’ve learned is that what is for you is for you and what is not is not. For whatever reason, that project is not for me.”Since winning two best supporting actor Oscars in 2017 and 2019, Ali’s movie roles have included Jurassic World Rebirth and Leave the World Behind as well as providing his voice in the Spider-Verse series. When asked about his lack of other big screen roles since, he said that “some of how quiet I’ve been is not really of my own choosing”.Ali’s voice will soon be heard in much-anticipated stop-motion animated adventureWildwoodalongside Carey Mulligan and Angela Bassett as well as in the delayed third Spider-Verse adventure.Explore more on these topicsMahershala AliBladeMarvelSuperhero moviesnewsShareReuse this content

title: HIV prevention drug could reduce cases globally but USAID cuts prevent access, say experts | Aids and HIV | The Guardian
description: Injectable PrEP drug holds promise but investment in HIV prevention has declined dramatically worldwide
Author: Hannah Harris Green
Headline: Injectable PrEP drug holds promise but investment in HIV prevention has declined dramatically worldwide
Content: People protest against funding cuts and drug patents during the 26th International Aids Conference in Rio de Janeiro on Monday.Photograph: Pablo Porciúncula/AFP via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople protest against funding cuts and drug patents during the 26th International Aids Conference in Rio de Janeiro on Monday.Photograph: Pablo Porciúncula/AFP via Getty ImagesAids and HIVHIV prevention drug could reduce cases globally but USAID cuts prevent access, say expertsInjectable PrEP drug holds promise but investment in HIV prevention has declined dramatically worldwideSign up for the Breaking News US newsletter emailHannah Harris Greenin Rio de JaneiroFri 31 Jul 2026 12.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew innovations in HIV prevention could dramatically reduce the number of newHIVcases around the globe, but US foreign aid cuts will mean that those that most need the new medication will be unable to access it, according to experts at the Aids 2026 Conference in Rio de Janeiro,Brazil.One year ago, the World Health Organizationrecommended that governments around the world prioritizeexpanded access to lenacapavir, an injectable version of the HIV prevention medication PrEP that requires only two injections annually. PrEP, which also comes in the form of daily oral medications and bimonthly injections, is 99% effective in preventing sexually transmitted HIV for people who take it consistently.In its announcement, the WHO noted that access to lenacapavir is limited outside clinical trials. But the organisation recommended that governments around the world prioritise scaling up availability of the injectable medication, because it could be gamechanging for populations that face considerable barriers to access for the medications that are currently available.Trump’s HIV funding cuts having ‘severe and devastating’ impact around the worldRead moreFor people who face poverty or stigma, or who live in rural areas that are far away from healthcare services, accessing a daily pill or an every-other-month injection can be close to impossible. Lenacapavir would provide strong protection against HIV while only requiring patients to access healthcare twice annually. Amathematical modeling studyfrom the WHO and the United Nations estimated that widespread availability of lenacapavir could prevent 41% of new HIV infections in South Africa, Zimbabwe and western Kenya.Notably, when the WHO recommended global investment in lenacapavir for HIV prevention in 2025, the Trump administration was already in the process of dissolving USAID, which provided 73% of donor-funded resources for HIV prevention globally,according to a studyin the Lancet Global Health.As of July 2026,multiple reportsshowthat investmentin HIV prevention has declined dramatically around the world.“We have these major achievements in prevention. On the other hand, we are facing these major funding cuts that are affecting deeply the delivery not only of these new prevention technologies but also decreasing the number of people engaged in care, engaged in prevention services,” said Beatriz Grinsztejn, president of the International Aids Society, during a press conference at the Aids 2026 Conference.Grinsztejn is also an infectious disease physician and researcher at the HIV prevention organisation Fiocruz in Rio de Janeiro.The funding cuts not only affect the availability of medications themselves, but also the ability of organisations to reach the people who need them.“When funding cuts came, one of the big things that’s been impacted is peer outreach workers, which are crucial to reaching people who use drugs, to building trust with people who use drugs and engaging them with services,” said Ailish Brennan, a policy analyst at Harm Reduction International.People who inject drugs are at a particularly high risk for contracting HIV, especially if they do not have access to clean syringes. Areport from the International Network of People Who Use Drugsfound that organisations were most likely to respond to the loss of funding by cutting outreach services.Brennan said that many harm reduction and HIV prevention organisations around the world were having to shut down locations, including mobile locations, which can mean clients at risk for HIV lose trust in the organisation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“But also just if they have to travel further they lose their local point of contact, and ultimately this means the innovations that we’re seeing, the long-acting injectables that have so much hope and opportunity, are not going to reach the people who need them most,” Brennan said.At the press conference, Grinsztejn noted that even before the dissolution of USAID, much of Latin America had been left out of agreements with US-based pharmaceutical companies to make innovative HIV prevention more affordable.Gilead Sciences provides generic versions of long-acting medications to low- and middle-income countries for far below sticker price, but justifies excluding countries such asBrazil, Colombia, Mexico, Peru and Argentina by classifying them as “upper middle-income countries”. HIV advocates dispute this justification, partly because people in these countries played a key role in clinical trials to test these medications.“We do have prevention technologies that are our dream,” Grinsztejn said during the conference, adding that it should be possible to fulfill the UNAIDS long-held goal of eliminating AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.Grinsztejn then added: “From my personal perspective, I think that it’s really hard that we will get to the targets given the current scenario.”Explore more on these topicsAids and HIVTrump administrationInfectious diseasesUS foreign policyDonald TrumpHealthBrazilnewsShareReuse this content

title: Florida woman’s autopsy report reveals extent of alligator attack | Florida | The Guardian
description: Brittany Clark struggled for her life before dying from brutal injuries in rare attack, autopsy report confirms
Author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
Headline: Brittany Clark struggled for her life before dying from brutal injuries in rare attack, autopsy report confirms
Content: An alligator in Florida.Photograph: Troy Harrison/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn alligator in Florida.Photograph: Troy Harrison/Getty ImagesFloridaFlorida woman’s autopsy report reveals extent of alligator attackBrittany Clark struggled for her life before dying from brutal injuries in rare attack, autopsy report confirmsRamon Antonio VargasFri 31 Jul 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman who was killed ina rare alligator attackwhile swimming with her boyfriend in Florida struggled for her life before dying from the brutal injuries inflicted on her by the animal, newly released autopsy results confirmed.The report containing the results of Brittany Clark’s autopsy, published on Thursday, also contained new details about the extent of the 28 June mauling that unfolded in Seminole county’s Little Big Econ state forest.Clark, 31, and her boyfriend – identified in the 11-page autopsy report as Chance Allison – were swimming in the Econlockhatchee River when an alligator attacked her, local officials had previously said.Allison desperately tried to free Clark from the alligator’s mouth, according to aFloridafish and wildlife conservation commission (FWC) spokesperson. Nonetheless, the attack led to the “near complete traumatic amputations” of Clark’s left arm at the shoulder as well as her right forearm, the autopsy report said.The autopsy report also said that Clark had teeth marks from the attack on her left shoulder blade and collarbone.Clark died from her injuries as emergency responders brought her to a hospital, the FWC had said. The autopsy report noted that it was Allison who identified her body at Orlando regional medical center that same day.The Orange county associate medical examiner Jenaye Mack subsequently conducted the autopsy and determined Clark died from the multiple blunt force injuries that she received from the alligator. Mack also ruled that Clark’s manner of death was an accident.The FWC said officials removed two alligators – 12ft and 13ft in length, respectively – from the river and euthanized them. DNA testing conducted on those alligators linked the longer of that pair to Clark, the FWC later announced.Alligator attacks on humans are rare in Florida, according to the FWC, which compiles reports of encounters with the state’s estimated 1.3 million gators. The agency in 2022 reported an average of about eight unprovoked alligator bites annually – and only 26 fatalities from those attacks since 1948.Clark’s onlineobituarysaid she financially supported herself by working as a heavy construction equipment operator, and she had attained the role of foreman before her death.“She was ready to settle down, start her own family and begin new adventures,” the obituary added.Clark’s survivors included her parents and two siblings, according to the obituary. A celebration of life honoring her was scheduled for 26 July at a ranch in Geneva, Florida.Explore more on these topicsFloridaAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Senators accuse Republican ‘gelatinous blobs’ of caving to Trump on Iran war | US news | The Guardian
description: Democrats Warren and Van Hollen attack Republican ‘rubber stamps’ in Congress for ceding authority to Trump
Author: Rachel Leingang
Headline: Democrats Warren and Van Hollen attack Republican ‘rubber stamps’ in Congress for ceding authority to Trump
Content: Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, right, with Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, in November 2022.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSenator Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, right, with Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, in November 2022.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesUS newsSenators accuse Republican ‘gelatinous blobs’ of caving to Trump on Iran warDemocrats Warren and Van Hollen attack Republican ‘rubber stamps’ in Congress for ceding authority to TrumpRachel Leingangin Davison, MichiganFri 31 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 08.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSenior Democrats accusedRepublicansin the US Congress of becoming “gelatinous blobs” who won’t stand up to Donald Trump and “rubber stamps” for his war on Iran.Elizabeth Warren, a US senator for Massachusetts, and Chris Van Hollen, a US senator for Maryland, argued that the Republican-controlled Congress had surrendered its constitutional authority to the president.In interviews with the Guardian, the senators urged their Republican colleagues to stand withDemocratsand assert Congress’s authority as a separate branch of the federal government–with power over declaring war.“The Republicans have all had their spines surgically removed,” Warren said in Michigan,while stumping for the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. “I mean, they’re just gelatinous blobs that kind of make it through the United States Senate.”The constitution sets up three separate branches of government to hold one another accountable, Warren noted – and the assumption was that each of the three branches would “jealously guard its own powers”.“But with Donald Trump in the White House, and a bunch of weak-kneed Republicans in the House [of Representatives] and the Senate, all of a sudden, we’ve lost the whole game,” she said.The US-Israel war on Iran, launched in February, has cost the US tens of billions of dollars. Hundreds of US service members have been wounded and 18have been killedsince the start of the operation. A tentative peace dealfractured in recent weeks.The latest congressional bid to rein in Trump’s attacks on the Middle East failed on Thursday, when a war powers resolution failed by 49 votes to 50 in the Senate.US Senate rejects bid to rein in Trump’s authority over Iran warRead moreThe controversial conflict rumbles on, as Trump faces a crucial political test with November’s US midterm elections. Democrats could win back power in the House, which is currently controlled by Republicans, and are also vying to retake control of the Senate.If there is a Democratic majority, Warren suggested that, coupled with the groundswell of opposition to the war among voters, could enable Congress to serve as a proper check on Trump.If that happens, “I think we are able to rein in Donald Trump and [defense secretary] Pete Hegseth,even if they havegallons of testosterone”, said Warren.Earlier this month, the Housepassed a war powers resolutionfor the second time that directed Trump to withdraw the US military from Iran–this time on a 214-208 vote,with four Republicans joining all Democrats in voting in favor. But in the Senate, the resolution failed 47-49.In June, a similar war powers resolutionpassedthe Senate. The resolution directs the USmilitary be removed from Iran without explicit approval from Congress. Van Hollen, who introduced the war powers resolution, said the situation in Iran was a “senseless war” that “should never have started”.“Ultimately, Congress will have to turn off the funding spigot for this war,” Van Hollen, also in Michigan to support El-Sayed, said. “And I will not vote for a dime for this illegal war,” adding that he wouldn’t support Hegseth’s request for more funding,deliveredto the appropriations committee earlier this month.“At some point, these Republican senators are going to have to explain to their constituents why they’ve contracted out their constitutional responsibilities to Donald Trump, because that’s what they’re doing,” saidVan Hollen. “So long as you have a majority of senators who are turning over their constitutional responsibilities to Donald Trump, then they’re just rubber stamps for Donald Trump’s illegal war.”Van Hollen said Democrats should continue to press for votes on the war powers resolution,to hold Republican senators accountable.The war is unpopular in the US, with 29% of Americans approving of Trump’s handling of the situation with Iran, and 69% disapproving, according to aWashington Post-Ipsos pollearlier this month.“I would rather see Republicans assert their constitutional duties and help us end the war now,” added Van Hollen. “But, you know, maybe they’ll get the message from their constituents.”Explore more on these topicsUS newsUS politicsUS-Israel war on IranUS CongressRepublicansDemocratsUS midterm elections 2026newsShareReuse this content

title: Washington Post’s opinion editor resigns after just one year in role | Washington Post | The Guardian
description: Adam O’Neal did not give reason for his departure at end of August in another major shakeup at US publication
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Adam O’Neal did not give reason for his departure at end of August in another major shakeup at US publication
Content: The Washington Post building sign in February 2026 during a rally outside the newspaper's offices following sweeping layoffs.Photograph: Mehmet Eser/Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Washington Post building sign in February 2026 during a rally outside the newspaper's offices following sweeping layoffs.Photograph: Mehmet Eser/Sopa Images/ShutterstockWashington PostWashington Post’s opinion editor resigns after just one year in roleAdam O’Neal did not give reason for his departure at end of August in another major shakeup at US publicationJeremy BarrFri 31 Jul 2026 13.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Washington Post had realized a state of relative calm in the five months since the paper was turned upside down in February, when nearly half the newsroom waslaid offand its unpopular publisher, Will Lewis,abruptlyresigned.But on Friday, staffers were shocked to find out that Adam O’Neal, a millennial hired last year to lead its opinion section, was already leaving.In a memo to colleagues in the paper’s opinion section titled “A Remarkable Year”, O’Neal gave no reason for his departure, only saying that he had decided to leave and that 31 August would be his last day. Opinion staffers had been given no indication that O’Neal was on the verge of leaving the publication.US judge throws out Trump’s $3.8bn defamation lawsuit against Washington PostRead more“It has been a remarkable year, and I’m very proud of everything we’ve accomplished together,” he wrote in the memo obtained by the Guardian. “While this was not an easy decision, I am leaving proud of how far the opinion section has come and optimistic that its best days lie ahead.”In the memo, O’Neal nodded to the controversial decision last year by owner Jeff Bezos toreorientthe paper’s opinion section to focus on championing free markets and personal liberties, a move that served toalienatemany subscribers.“I joined The Post to lead the opinion section as it began a new chapter, and we have made dramatic changes over the past year. We quickly embraced our mission of championing free markets and personal liberties while simultaneously putting Post Opinions on a sustainable footing,” he wrote.“Our work has become more relevant, accessible and consequential. We regularly publish world-class journalism that finds the audience where it is. This includes agenda-setting columns; news-breaking op-eds; highly influential editorials; and social media content that reaches millions of new people.”Still, one of the section’s top priorities, the launch of a new video podcast calledMake It Make Sense, drew backlash on social media for what seemed like warmed-over hot takes anddid not drawa large viewership despite generous investment and support from the Post.Following O’Neal’s announcement, Jeff D’Onofrio, who took over as the interim publisher after Lewis departed, emailed the entire staff with the subject line “Thank You Adam.”“This past year, under the leadership of Adam O’Neal, Post Opinions has become more balanced in perspective, more financially sustainable and more accessible to readers than ever before,” he wrote. “I want to thank him for his leadership and hard work in reimagining the section.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionABC argues that early license review by FCC is ‘retaliation’ for network’s coverageRead moreStill, it’s extremely unusual for a top Post leader to depart so quickly, particularly one who served as the face of a dramatic reorientation of the section. O’Neal’s predecessor, the veteran journalist David Shipley,resignedafter failing to convince Bezos to not move forward with his new mandate for the section, which made the work of many of its longtime writers no longer relevant. Many such writers wereencouragedto take a buyout in the summer of 2025 and leave the publication.Looking ahead, D’Onofrio said the Post would “work to transition Post Opinions leadership”, with more information to come at a later date.O’Neal, who was 33 years old when he was hired, was seen as an unusual selection, despite past work experience at the Economist and the Wall Street Journal’s opinion desk.Sensing he was not widely known to the Post’s staff, he introduced himself with a verticalvideoposted by the newspaper’s public relations account on X.“Now odds are, you’ve probably never heard of me, and you might be wondering, ‘Who am I?’” he said in the video at the time. “That’s actually kind of a deep and philosophical question, and I’m not sure I went to school long enough to understand it. But I’ve been a journalist for a while, and I’d like to share some of our plans with you.”Explore more on these topicsWashington PostMedia businessUS press and publishingNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Boss of £300m used-car firm was ousted after ‘orchestrated plan’ by investors, judge rules | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Multimillionaire Peter Waddell is also found to have been properly dismissed from Big Motoring World for gross misconduct
Author: Simon Goodley
Headline: Multimillionaire Peter Waddell is also found to have been properly dismissed from Big Motoring World for gross misconduct
Content: Multimillionaire Peter Waddell made his fortune selling cars.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMultimillionaire Peter Waddell made his fortune selling cars.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianAutomotive industryBoss of £300m used-car firm was ousted after ‘orchestrated plan’ by investors, judge rulesMultimillionaire Peter Waddell is also found to have been properly dismissed from Big Motoring World for gross misconductSimon GoodleyFri 31 Jul 2026 11.56 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 11.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA multimillionaire used-car salesman was ousted from his £300m company after “a pre-conceived and orchestrated plan” devised by private equity investors that had backed his business, a high court judge has ruled.Peter Waddell, 60, was forced out as the chief executive of the Kent-based dealershipBig Motoring World in 2024 in a coup that resulted in “more-or-less open warfare” at the car seller and caused “unfair prejudice” to the investment company that held Waddell’s majority stake.The judgment came despite Waddell also being found by Mr Justice Marcus Smith to have been “properly dismissed for gross misconduct” after allegations he made a series of racist and sexist remarks.However, the judge further concluded that Big Motoring World’s private equity investor, Freshstream, did not address Waddell’s behaviour in order to later trap him and then attempt to seize full control of the business without paying for the shares via a pre-agreed contract known as a call option.Smith said: “I have found the formation and execution of a pre-conceived and orchestrated plan which worked backwards from Freshstream’s aim of achieving permanent control of, and Mr Waddell’s removal from, the business withouthaving to exercise the call option.“Without question, there were matters that should – long before this point in time [2023] – have resulted in some form of disciplinary process against Mr Waddell, hopefully not resulting in dismissal but in imposing limits on someone who was (for all his serious faults) the gifted and duly appointed [chief executive] of Big.”The judge went on to say that Freshstream allowed Waddell’s behaviour “to continue, unchecked, until Freshstream was in a position to cause Mr Waddell’s exclusion from Big”.The tycoon, who is deaf and has dyslexia,has a backstoryinvolving a childhood spent in care and a spell of homelessness before building up his multimillion-pound car business from scratch.He ended up creating a company with 525 employees, revenues of £371m and profits of £6.6m, according to the 2021 annual accounts – a record that prompted Freshstream toacquire about a third of the businessin April 2022, with the option of eventually acquiring Waddell’s remaining shares.Waddell, who says that his manner of speaking was known to Freshstream before the company acquired its initial stake, claimed that a downturn in the company’s trading prompted his investors and colleagues to devise a plan to wrest control from him. Reflecting on the judgment he added that “justice had been done” and that he now wanted to reacquire the company.A spokesperson for Freshstream said: “We welcome the judge’s findings that Peter Waddell was rightly dismissed for gross misconduct, including repeated acts of bullying and harassment (including sexual harassment). Further, we are pleased that a number of Mr Waddell’s claims in respect of [the holding company’s] exercise of its rights under the shareholders’ documents have failed. Therefore, Freshstream remains in control of the business.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It is disappointing that the judge has made a number of findings … in relation to steps … to address Mr Waddell’s conduct, despite his obvious acts of racism, misogyny and bullying.”The spokesperson added that those accused of not taking action were “considering all available options with their legal teams”.Remedies will be decided at a future hearing.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryPrivate equityKentnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK petrol price hits Iran war high, adding to pressure on households | Petrol prices | The Guardian
description: Average pump price reaches 160p a litre, while diesel is up 14.5p to 179p and forecast to increase to 185p soon
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: Average pump price reaches 160p a litre, while diesel is up 14.5p to 179p and forecast to increase to 185p soon
Content: The RAC says the cost of filling a family-size car with unleaded petrol has gone up to £88, while a tank of diesel is £10 more.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenThe RAC says the cost of filling a family-size car with unleaded petrol has gone up to £88, while a tank of diesel is £10 more.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAPetrol pricesUK petrol price hits Iran war high, adding to pressure on householdsAverage pump price reaches 160p a litre, while diesel is up 14.5p to 179p and forecast to increase to 185p soonZoe WoodFri 31 Jul 2026 10.24 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 08.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe price of petrol has hit a newIran warhigh at UK forecourts, adding to the financial pressure on millions of households about to embark on their annual holiday.The RAC said that in “very unwelcome news for drivers” the average pump price had reached 160p a litre, reversing the fall to 151p in early July that followed the announcement of aMiddle East ceasefire.The price on Friday was the highest level since November 2022, when it soared in the aftermath of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.Diesel is up 14.5p to 179p but the price remains below the high of 192p in April, the RAC said.“This means the cost of filling a family-size car with unleaded has gone up to £88, while a tank of diesel is £10 more,” said Simon Williams, the motoring body’s head of policy. “The wholesale price of petrol eased very slightly this week but is not enough to make a difference at the pumps.”Williams added that diesel looked “set to keep on rising” and would probably reach 185p a litre in the next few weeks, barring any significant fall in the price of oil.Fuel prices had declined after the US and Iran reached amemorandum of understandingin mid-June that extended a ceasefire in the war by 60 days to allow the restoration of trade through the strait of Hormuz and create breathing space for further talks.However, Donald Trump has in recent weeks appeared to tire of the peace efforts, with the USagain striking Iran several times in recent days. This has prompted Tehran to retaliate against Washington’s allies in the Middle East.On Friday, Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose more than 1% to above $90 a barrel as Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had struck two tankers trying to pass through the strait of Hormuz under a US “air escort” and turned four other ships around.The increase in pump prices in the UK had come “at a very bad time”, said Luke Bosdet, an AA spokesperson. “AA polling indicates that 20.5 million UK drivers will take to the road in the third week of the holiday season. Among them, 2.2 million will cover 100 to 200 miles, 1.5 million will travel 200 to 300 miles and 1.3 million will go even further.”However, Bosdet said fuel prices appeared to be following wholesale prices more closely since May, when the government introduced a newfuel finderscheme that has forced all petrol stations to report prices publicly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFuel retailers have in the past faced accusations of “rocket and feather” pricing – when rapid price increases are followed by slower price cuts.“In early May, when wholesale costs shot up 3p to 6p for more than a fortnight, average petrol prices put on less than 2p,” Bosdet said. “Fuel Finder compliance started to be enforced at the beginning of the month and that likely had an impact.“When costs plummeted from late May onwards, pump prices followed rapidly, which was unlike previous years of ‘rocket and feather’ pump pricing.”Explore more on these topicsPetrol pricesUK cost of living crisisMotoringEnergy industryOilnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI labels to be compulsory on authentic-looking content under EU rules | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Companies must ensure people know when they are interacting with artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look real
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Companies must ensure people know when they are interacting with artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look real
Content: Screengrab of an AI-generated image of the French president, Emmanuel Macron, dancing in a 1980s nightclub.View image in fullscreenScreengrab of an AI-generated image of the French president, Emmanuel Macron, dancing in a 1980s nightclub.AI (artificial intelligence)AI labels to be compulsory on authentic-looking content under EU rulesCompanies must ensure people know when they are interacting with artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look realJennifer Rankinin BrusselsFri 31 Jul 2026 07.21 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 05.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom apparently conspiring to steal elections to abusing staff or performing embarrassing dance moves, the last few years have seen plenty of fake content made about politicians intended to malign its targets and mislead the public.Now EU rules aim to stem the flood of this deceptive content: starting from Sunday, artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look authentic must be labelled.The rules, devised under theEU’s landmark AI Act, mean companies must ensure people know when they are interacting with an AI-powered chatbot or viewing a manipulated image or AI-generated text.View image in fullscreenDeepfakes have included fake audio of the Slovakian opposition leader, Michal Šimečka, conspiring with a journalist to rig election.Photograph: Radovan Stoklasa/ReutersThe rules apply to new AI systems on the EU market from 2 August, while existing ones have an extra four months to comply.“It is a matter not only of customer protection, it’s also a matter of democracy protection,” the Green MEP Sergey Lagodinsky, who helped negotiate the AI Act, told the Guardian. “Making transparent this information is something which we need to preserve our democracy and the authenticity of facts online.”Under the rules, synthetic text, images, video and audio designed to look truthful must be visibly marked as AI-generated and contain a digital watermark to show the artificial origins of the content.Texts on matters of public interest must also be labelled as AI-made if there is no human editorial oversight.Companies are encouraged to label AI-generated content pre-dating the rules, although this is not compulsory. The rules will not apply to users’ personal content and there is an exemption for “evidently artistic”, satirical and fictional works.Failure to comply could result in fines of up to €15m (£12.8) or 3% of a company’s worldwide global turnover.The EU executive has created black-and-white labels anyone can use, although companies can design their own.View image in fullscreenEU symbols to be used on content using AI.Illustration: EUDeepfakes have includedaudio purporting to revealthe Slovakian opposition leader Michal Šimečka conspiring with a journalist to rig elections,mocked-up videosof the French president, Emmanuel Macron, dancing in a 1980s nightclub, andfake footageof the then UK Labour leader, Keir Starmer, abusing party staff.The tech industry says it supports the quest to make deepfakes visible, but fears the rules will be interpreted too broadly and overwhelm internet users with banners and labels.The Computer and Communications Industry Association argues that EU guidelines published in July have expanded the definition of a deepfake far beyond the 2024 AI Act.“The label was meant to flag deceptive content,” said CCIA Europe’s AI policy lead, Boniface de Champris. “That distinction has been removed, so now almost everything gets labelled – a landscape in an advert is the same as a manipulated political speech. Like cookie banners, once labels are everywhere, users stop noticing them. That doesn’t protect anyone, it just burdens commercial activity across the board.”He thinks the most visible change for the public will not be on social media, which “already labels most AI content” but “in areas where AI is already used at scale but people don’t know it – advertising, film, publishing”.“Expect a lot more labels in sectors not usually associated with AI, and the burden will fall hardest on those least versed in AI regulation,” De Champris said.Some of the world’s largest tech companies already have policies designed to inform users about AI-generated content.TikTok, for example, says it requires creators to label realistic AI-generated images, audio and video, and that it has helped label more than 3bn pieces of content. However, recent research has shown thatAI-generated doctors are gaining millions of views on TikTokby spreading dubious health advice.Misleading AI-generated doctors pose ‘huge danger to public safety’Read moreGoogle launched a tool called SynthID in 2023, which enables users to check if an image is AI-generated. The company says it has put an invisible digital watermark, which enables identification, on more than 100bn images and 60,000 years’ worth of audio.Google and Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, have signed a voluntary code of practice intended to help companies comply with the EU’s AI transparency rules.The European Commission said more than 180 organisations had signed the code, which was drawn up by independent experts under the supervision of the EU AI office.Signing the code is seen by regulators as a sign of good intent, while non-signatories must show they are meeting the rules in other ways.Meta launched policies in 2024 to help people identify AI-generated photo-realistic images. It says it has been developing industry-wide technical standards to identify AI audio and video.Announcing Meta’s intention to sign the EU code of practice earlier this week [28 July], its vice-president for public policy in Europe, Markus Reinisch, said: “We must avoid a situation where online content is subject to a growing array of different labels and disclosures that end up overwhelming people, while at the same time adding additional regulatory complexity for providers.”Lagodinsky, the EU lawmaker, said he believed the industry could find a way: “I have a deep respect for industry, but in all too many cases, they complain, and … then after things are implemented, it doesn’t look that burdensome to them. And there is always a solution.”The transparency rules are part of broader enforcement of the AI Act, starting from 2 August. The commission’s lead official on tech policy, Henna Virkkunen, said AI was a “transformative technology” that could bring “extraordinary benefits” but the most advanced models “create risks on an entirely new scale”.“Europe anticipated this development. With the AI Act, we established a clear, risk-based and durable framework for trustworthy AI —one that gives innovators legal certainty while protecting the public interest.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Social mediaEuropean UnionDigital mediaEuropeComputingInternet safetynewsShareReuse this content

title: Glen Hansard obituary | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Oscar-winning singer, songwriter, actor and founder of the Dublin rock band the Frames
Author: Robin Denselow
Headline: Oscar-winning singer, songwriter, actor and founder of the Dublin rock band the Frames
Content: Glen Hansard takes part in the annual Christmas Eve busk in Dublin in 2019.Photograph: Artur Widak/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenGlen Hansard takes part in the annual Christmas Eve busk in Dublin in 2019.Photograph: Artur Widak/NurPhoto/ShutterstockPop and rockObituaryGlen Hansard obituaryOscar-winning singer, songwriter, actor and founder of the Dublin rock band the FramesRobin DenselowFri 31 Jul 2026 12.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGlen Hansard, who has died aged 56 in a motorcycle accident, was one of Dublin’s musical heroes – a one-time busker who became an Oscar-winning international star, successful both as a singer-songwriter and as an actor.He had already built up a local reputation busking regularly on Grafton Street, Dublin, when he decided to form a band, the Frames, along with other musicians he had befriended on the streets.In the early days of the band he had a call from the film directorAlan Parker, asking him to play the guitarist Outspan Foster in the 1991 film version of Roddy Doyle’s book The Commitments, the story of a young unemployed Dublin music fan who starts a soul band. With his shock of curly red hair, Hansard was the ideal choice to play the laid-back guitarist – after all, he had lived the role himself. But the filming process was not easy for someone who put his real band first – there was conflict with Parker whenHansard insisted on rescheduling filmingso he could perform at a Frames gig.The film was nevertheless a big hit and Hansard seemed assured of stardom – especially as the band had been signed to Island Records. But it did not immediately work out. Their debut album, Another Love Song (1991), reached only No 77 in the Irish charts, and the label dropped them. But the Frames kept going, playing regularly at the Dublin venue Whelan’s, and began to build a strong following. Their second album, Fitzcarraldo (1995), released on ZTT, reached No 26, helped by the anguished lead single Revelate.View image in fullscreenPeople stop to listen as musicians play in memory of Glen Hansard on King Street in Dublin on Thursday.Photograph: Damien Eagers/PAFrom then on, the Frames became an Irish success story. Their fourth album, For The Birds (2001), reached No 6 in the Irish charts, while Burn The Maps (2004) went to No 1. The band kept going – their seventh and final album, Longitude, was released in 2015 – but Hansard now had other interests.He had begun working with the Czech-Icelandic pianist and singer Markéta Irglová in a duo, The Swell Season, whose self-titled debut album was released in 2006. They were approached by the director John Carney, who had played bass for the Frames until 1993 and directed some of their videos, to star in his feature film Once, playing struggling musicians who fall in love. They agreed, and also provided the soundtrack for what became a widely successful film, though it had been shot on a shoestring budget. The poignant Falling Slowly won the Oscar for best original song in 2008, and their music would later feature in a Broadway adaptation of the film.Hansard and Irglová became romantic partners on and off the screen, continuing to work together once the relationship had ended. They toured together and released two more albums, Strict Joy (2009) and Forward (2025).View image in fullscreenGlen Hansard and Markéta Irglová in Once (2006).Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyIn his later years, Hansard concentrated mostly on his solo career, which began with the album Rhythm and Repose (2012). His second solo set, the gently reflective folk-rock album Didn’t He Ramble (2015), was nominated for a Grammy, as best folk album, the following year.
