He followed up with Between Two Shores (2018), This Wild Willing (2019) and All That Was East Is West of Me Now (2023). His last release,Don+t Settle, was a two-volume live set in which he revisited songs from throughout his career, backed by his band.Despite his success, Hansard never forgot his early roots. From 2010 on, he returned to busking in Dublin every Christmas Eve, for what became theBig Buskevent outside the Gaiety theatre, near where he once used to sing on Grafton Street. But he was now busking in aid of the Simon Community, a charity that helps the homeless, and the event became an annual fixture that attracted other leading Irish musicians, including Bono, Damien Dempsey and Imelda May. As an activist concerned with homelessness,Hansard joined protestersoccupying Apollo House, a vacant building in the centre of Dublin in 2016, to draw attention to the problem in the city.View image in fullscreenGlen Hansard in 2017, getting ready to perform in a protest concert to raise awareness of homelessness in Dublin.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAIn December 2023 he was one of the celebrities who performed at the funeral of the Pogues’ singerShane MacGowan, and was joined byLisa O’Neillto sing MacGowan’s best-known song, Fairytale of New York.He made his final London appearance at the Roundhouse in May, on the last night of a UK and European tour. An often intense, bearded figure, he began with the Frames’ Revelate, and moved on to songs from his solo albums, including Didn’t He Ramble, Grace Beneath the Pines, and – of course – the Swell Season’s Oscar-winning Falling Slowly.Born in Ballymun, a suburb on the north side of Dublin, Glen was one of six children of Catherine (nee Cahill) and James Hansard, a carpenter and talented fiddle player who touredIrelandwith showbands in the 1930s and 40s, but was also a heavy drinker, prone to occasional violence. Hansard attended Our Lady of Victories national school in Ballymun, but became more interested in music than schoolwork. He acquired a guitar from an uncle who had been sent to prison, and taught himself songs by Dylan and Van Morrison.When he was in his early teens he quit school on the advice of a teacher, who suggested he should become a busker – an unusual career path that the young Hansard followed with relish. He said that busking was a “great leveller”, and that “the busking education sits at the core of everything I’ve done since”.He played at a trad session at the Wren’s Nest pub, in west Dublin, just hours before he died in a single-vehicle crash.He is survived by his wife, Maire Saaritsa, a Finnish poet whom he married in 2022, their son, Christy, and by three brothers.Glen James Hansard, singer-songwriter, musician and actor, born 21 April 1970; died 29 July 2026Explore more on these topicsPop and rockIrelandobituariesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was born without self-esteem’: Hannah Einbinder on Hacks, her buzzy queer horror – and being Hollywood’s most outspoken star  | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Hacks lead was cast in meta-slasher sensation Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma for her ‘deranged physicality’ – but it’s a fitting role for an actor who has made a point of confronting shame and speaking her mind
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: The Hacks lead was cast in meta-slasher sensation Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma for her ‘deranged physicality’ – but it’s a fitting role for an actor who has made a point of confronting shame and speaking her mind
Content: ‘Comedy was my way of feeling good – and for the most part, I really didn’t feel good’ … Hannah Einbinder.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Comedy was my way of feeling good – and for the most part, I really didn’t feel good’ … Hannah Einbinder.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The GuardianMoviesInterview‘I was born without self-esteem’: Hannah Einbinder on Hacks, her buzzy queer horror – and being Hollywood’s most outspoken starNadia KhomamiThe Hacks lead was cast in meta-slasher sensation Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma for her ‘deranged physicality’ – but it’s a fitting role for an actor who has made a point of confronting shame and speaking her mindFri 31 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘God is good all the time,” laughs Hannah Einbinder. She’s fresh off a plane from Los Angeles and curled up barefoot in an armchair. This, she says, is “a crazy time in life. Starring in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma in the midst ofHacksending … it’s definitely an embarrassment of riches.”Hacks is the HBO comedy that ended earlier this year; in May, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, Jane Schoenbrun’s queer meta-horror, became the breakout hit of this year’s Cannes film festival.Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma review – Gillian Anderson superb in queer slasher spectacularRead moreIn the film, Einbinder plays a film-maker, Kris, who becomes consumed by her obsession with Billy Presley, the reclusive star of the original Camp Miasma slasher franchise – played with hypnotic wit and sensuality byGillian Anderson. What begins as an attempt to persuade Presley to return to the series spirals into an ecstasy of sex, death, VHS tapes and junk food. Scene by scene, the lines between reality and fantasy begin to collapse.“When my agent sent me the script, I was blown away,” says Einbinder. “Its through-line of confronting shame and dealing with repression and dissociation was intriguing to me.” (It’s a theme Schoenbrun has said was inspired by their own process of learning to embrace sexuality after transition.)“We’re discouraged from discussing this stuff,” says Einbinder, “but it’s something I’m familiar with. I had to think: ‘How true is this for me?’ Like Kris, I had to mine my own experiences and confront things I didn’t want to see.” The film, she adds, helped her “be more open about desire”. It was also “a roadmap for how it’s supposed to feel and what one should feel comfortable with doing or saying, and when to say no”.Dressed in a floor-length black dress and a flowing white silk kimono, Einbinder cuts a more glamorous figure than I had expected. On screen, her style and comedy often veer towards the oddball; in person, she is refined, softly-spoken, and deliberately cautious.Her willingness to sit with discomfort feels characteristic of the actor, whose performances often hinge on the tension between awkwardness and emotional honesty. Schoenbrun has said they cast her in her Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma because they “found her deranged physicality exciting”.View image in fullscreenAs Ava Daniels, with Deborah Vance (Jean Smart), in Hacks.Photograph: HBO MaxMost immediately significant is Einbinder’s gift for creating electric chemistry with older female co-stars. In Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma and Hacks, she spends much of the time opposite another glamorous and formidable woman.In the long-running series, Einbinder played Ava Daniels, an aimless comedy writer hired to revive the career of Jean Smart’s Las Vegas standup legend, Deborah Vance. It became one of television’s sharpest comedies, but the key to its emotional force was the relationship between Ava and Deborah: two women who initially seem to have little in common, but who slowly become essential to one another.Their bond was built on insults, betrayals and power struggles, but also on a profound creative understanding – Ava pushes Deborah to confront what she has become, while Deborah teaches Ava the discipline and resilience she lacks.The experience of working on the show was profoundly important to her, says Einbinder, welling up. “I learned so much and I became a person – I became myself. I don’t know how I would have become who I am without it.”She takes a deep breath. “I started comedy because the only way that I could feel good was if I felt like other people felt good. When I was 24 and starting the show, I was just kind of a shell. I didn’t advocate for myself. I didn’t have boundaries. I was passive in a lot of ways.“I think I was just born without self-esteem. Even neutrality felt impossible, just to be cool with myself, let alone the idea of love for myself. Now I feel incredibly embodied and certain of myself in a way that I never thought was possible. And I do credit a lot of that to my experience working on Hacks.”View image in fullscreenEinbinder in London, June 2026.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The GuardianIt’s hard not to trace a similar trajectory to that of her character in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma: a woman forced to excavate the parts of herself she would rather avoid, to come out the other side stronger, more self-assured, and committed to advocating for herself and the causes she believes in.Einbinder grew up in Los Angeles in a progressive Jewish family, where comedy was “the main currency”. Her parents – original Saturday Night Live cast member Laraine Newman and actor Chad Einbinder – were always trying to make each other laugh, and she and her siblings quickly joined in. “That’s certainly the incubator for my approach to interacting with others.”At university, studying broadcast journalism, she joined an improv troupe and began performing standup at open mic nights. She applied to it the same discipline, she says, that she developed as a competitive cheerleader in high school. “I was determined to risk anything, even falling on my face, if it meant I’d get a moment of satisfaction and approval. Comedy was my way of feeling good – and for the most part, I really didn’t feel good.”View image in fullscreenBig break … on The Late Show With Stephen Colbert.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesBy 2019, she was touring as the opening act for comedian Chelsea Handler, and the following year she made her late-night debut on The Late Show With Stephen Colbert – an appearance that helped her land Hacks, despite having no acting credits. “It was the only thing that I had to show for myself,” she saysThe audition, in March 2020, required the character to break down in tears. Einbinder listened to other candidates sobbing through the walls; she had never learned how to cry on command. “I thought, I can’t do the tears, but I could throw in a joke.” It worked; in fact, the gag was such a hit that it made it on to the show.One of Hacks’ central storylines follows Deborah’s battle to break into late-night TV. It’s also where Einbinder got her break. I wonder what she makes of the current state of American comedy?“Colbert is gone,” she says, referring to Stephen Colbert’s departure from The Late Show. “CBS has been very clear in their directives. [Jimmy] Kimmel was suspended. There’s no question that these are political choices.” But what is frightening, she adds, is that these figures represent relatively mainstream voices rather than the radical fringe critics often accuse them of being.“To me, those are not bastions of true leftist thought. They are Democrat with a capital D guys who are, yes, poking fun at the right. But they’re rich white men being axed for pretty centrist and mild speech. So if that’s being censored, that’s a huge problem.”In recent years, Einbinder has developed a reputation for being one of the most outspoken actors in Hollywood. She has used awards speeches and social media to advocate about the climate crisis, immigration, ICE and the war in Gaza. At the Emmy awards last September, after winning outstanding supporting actress in a comedy series for Hacks, she closed her acceptance speech with a message that became one of the night’s most widely discussed moments: “Go Birds, fuck ICE, and free Palestine!”View image in fullscreenStatement win ... Einbinder at the 77th Primetime Emmy awards, 2025.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersShe traces that confidence back to college, when Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaign became “a political awakening”. By far the most difficult part of her political journey, she says, was “unlearning” the Zionism she was raised with. “Once I came to understand reality as it was, I just could not bear the idea of not shouting at any time, in any place, about how wrong and violent it was. How deeply it desecrates our people and what our religion is supposed to mean.”The humanitarian crisis in Gaza “haunts” her, she adds. “I’m just doing what I think is, frankly, the Jewish thing to do, which is to value human life and try to contribute to healing the world.”She adds: “I am incredibly privileged, because smears of being an anti-Semite don’t stick to me. I’m such a proud Jew. But I’m certain there are community members who hate me for this, many of them in my business, and they won’t work with me and want nothing to do with me.”Instead of feeling anger, she says she feels a sense of sadness and loss. “I am sad for them. They are trapped in an ideological prison that stops them from seeing other people’s humanity. They’re trapped because of the massive propaganda campaign waged against them since the moment they could understand language.” Her views have cost her familial relationships, too. “I don’t know that they will ever be repaired, but I have found a family elsewhere in the rich anti-Zionist Jewish community.”View image in fullscreenFormidable women … with Gillian Anderson in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.Photograph: Ryan Plummer/MubiFor Einbinder, politics is inseparable from lived experience. She is bisexual, has two transgender siblings and speaks about identity not as an abstract debate but as something woven into everyday life. “Everything is personal. Politics is the most personal thing. It’s not theoretical.”That refusal to separate the personal from the public is, in its own way, what took her into Camp Miasma in the first place. It was her first real chance to leave behind the creative family that had shaped her on Hacks and find out what she could do without them. “I was both excited and intimidated,” she says. “I was just like: ‘Fuck, can I do this? Can I do something that isn’t the safe environment that raised me, with the people who know exactly how to shape and mould me?’” Watching her talk, it’s clear she already has her answer.Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma is released in the UK on 21 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmGillian AndersonHorror filmsHacksinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ryan Gosling is entering the Marvel Cinematic Universe – on a motorbike, in flames, wearing a leather jacket. What could go wrong? | Movies | The Guardian
description: After coveting the role for years, Gosling has been announced as the new Ghost Rider – a superhero stunt rider with powers bestowed by Satan. Is this a smart move all round or has he sold his soul to the devil?
Author: Ben Child
Headline: After coveting the role for years, Gosling has been announced as the new Ghost Rider – a superhero stunt rider with powers bestowed by Satan. Is this a smart move all round or has he sold his soul to the devil?
Content: He could have chosen anyone … Ryan Gosling at this month’s Comic-Con in San Diego, where he was announced as the new Ghost Rider.Photograph: John Salangsang/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHe could have chosen anyone … Ryan Gosling at this month’s Comic-Con in San Diego, where he was announced as the new Ghost Rider.Photograph: John Salangsang/ShutterstockWeek in geekMoviesRyan Gosling is entering the Marvel Cinematic Universe – on a motorbike, in flames, wearing a leather jacket. What could go wrong?Ben ChildAfter coveting the role for years, Gosling has been announced as the new Ghost Rider – a superhero stunt rider with powers bestowed by Satan. Is this a smart move all round or has he sold his soul to the devil?Fri 31 Jul 2026 06.47 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 09.01 EDTShareSteven Spielberg once said: “If a person can tell me the idea in 25 words or less, it’s going to make a pretty good movie.” And Marvel’s most popular big-screen superheroes can be described using less than half that number. Iron Man is a tech bro in a tin suit; Spider-Man has the powers of an arachnid; Thor is a Norse god. Go and watch a film featuring any of these characters and you know exactly what you’re going to get.But then there is Ghost Rider, who, according toreports from San Diego Comic-Conlast week, will be the subject of a new Marvel Cinematic Universe film directed by Deadpool & Wolverine’s Shawn Levy, and starring Ryan Gosling. There is no quick way to explain what is going on with this guy. In the 1972 origin story, stunt motorcyclist Johnny Blaze sells his soul to Satan to save his adoptive father from cancer. The cure works but its beneficiary is killed almost immediately. The devil then tries to claim Johnny’s soul and, when that fails, binds him to the demon Zarathos. This, ifChristopher Marloweis to be believed, ought to result in corruption, despair and eternal, fiery damnation. Yet somehow our hero emerges from the arrangement with a cool flaming skull, vast supernatural powers and a motorbike capable of riding up buildings and across dimensions. Blaze regards the whole arrangement as a curse, but to the casual observer his principal penance is to roam the Earth passing judgment on people more wicked than he is, while looking good in a leather jacket.So what does Gosling, one of the biggest movie stars in the world right now, see in the role?Reports suggestthis was not simply a case of Marvel waving a blank cheque in his direction. Gosling has wanted to play Ghost Rider for years, and apparently approached Marvel president Kevin Feige with his own conception of the character,inspired by specific comic book runs. At this point in his career, the star of Project Hail Mary, Barbie and Blade Runner 2049 could presumably have asked to play almost anyone in the Marvel universe. He chose the infernal Evel Knievel whose face catches fire.View image in fullscreenNicolas Cage as Johnny Blaze, with Peter Fonda, in in the 2007 Ghost Rider film.Photograph: Jasin Boland/Columbia/Marvel Enterprises/Kobal/REX/ShutterstockPart of the attraction may be that there is little cinematic inheritance to worry about. The two films with Nicolas Cage in the role were memorable chiefly as demonstrations of the venerable old ham’s ability to chew the scenery.The firstarrived in 2007 looking as though somebody had attempted to build a superhero franchise from a heavy-metal album cover and a bottle of hair dye. The sequel,Spirit of Vengeance, made Ghost Rider seem like a character whose principal dramatic function was to drive towards the camera while screaming. Perhaps, in a way, the failure of those films now counts as a blessing; at least Gosling does not have to compete with an iconic performance.Another plus point may be that the actor will be entering the MCU at the furthest point from its centre. Blaze – or whichever version of Ghost Rider Gosling ends up playing – need not immediately be forced to join the Avengers in yet another climactic battle against an army of anonymous CGI henchmen. Nobody is waiting to see him square off against Thanos or explain the multiverse. Gosling has a much better chance of moulding the project exactly as he wants. But this, it must be said, is a long way from the formula Feige used to build Marvel into the world’s most potent fantasy storytelling machine. Robert Downey Jr was not a megastar when he was cast as Iron Man; he was a risky, diminished name. Chris Hemsworth was barely known when he was cast as Thor; Chris Evans was hardly considered a prestigious casting as Captain America.Yet the studio is in a very different era from the one in 2008, when Iron Man first hit cinemas. The release ofSpider-Man: Brand New Daythis week is predicted to once again see Marvel back on top at the box office, but there is no longer any guarantee that every movie it makes will zoom past the $1bn mark. On that basis, it is easy to see why Feige and his team might opt to hand the keys to the kingdom to an actor who seems to have Hollywood’s equivalent of the Midas touch – especially when the property he is interested in is something of a free hit. Handing a major star considerable creative freedom certainly worked with Ryan Reynolds on Deadpool & Wolverine.Perhaps this will end up being the perfect match after all. Marvel finally gets a new hero, and its new Ghost Rider gets the freedom to turn one of the studio’s daftest creations into something entirely his own.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekSuperhero moviesRyan GoslingGhost Rider: Spirit of VengeanceMarvelScience fiction and fantasy filmscommentShareReuse this content

title: Heretic to Love Me: the seven best films to watch on TV this week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Hugh Grant gives a gleeful, career-best performance in A24’s terrifying horror, while Kristen Stewart and Steven Yeun star in a fun post-apocalyptic love story
Author: Ellen E Jones
Headline: Hugh Grant gives a gleeful, career-best performance in A24’s terrifying horror, while Kristen Stewart and Steven Yeun star in a fun post-apocalyptic love story
Content: Fully in his villain era … Hugh Grant in Heretic.Photograph: Kimberley FrenchView image in fullscreenFully in his villain era … Hugh Grant in Heretic.Photograph: Kimberley FrenchThe seven best films to watch on TV this weekTelevision & radioHeretic to Love Me: the seven best films to watch on TV this weekHugh Grant gives a gleeful, career-best performance in A24’s terrifying horror, while Kristen Stewart and Steven Yeun star in a fun post-apocalyptic love storyEllen E JonesFri 31 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekHereticSophie Thatcher (Yellowjackets) and Chloe East (The Fabelmans) play a pair of unworldly Mormon missionaries who arrive at the door of an avuncular Englishman hoping to make a new convert. That Englishman, however, is played by Hugh Grant – once a foppish romcom idol, now deep into his villain era – and what at first seems like a playful willingness to debate religion turns into something much moreterrifying. With a script by A Quiet Place co-writers Scott Beck and Bryan Woods to work with (the two also co-direct), Grant commands the screen with glee. It’s a career-best performance, with enough dark miracles to fully restore your faith in A24’s waning horror output.Saturday 1 August, 9.35pm, Sky Cinema PremiereLove MeView image in fullscreenWaiting to connect … Steven Yeun and Kristen Stewart in Love Me.Photograph: NBC UniversalMillennia have passed since humanity’s extinction, and on Earth’s half-frozen ocean a smart-tech-enabled buoy (Kristen Stewart) floats alone, emitting a “waiting to connect” signal. One day this is answered by a passing satellite (Steven Yeun), and together the devices search the internet, hoping to derive an understanding of life and love from this oddly incomplete record. First-time film-makers Sam and Andy Zuchero combine animation and live action into awe-inspiring visuals – and there’s comedy too, in Stewart and Yeun’s portrayal of the YouTube influencer couple the devices choose for avatars.Saturday 1 August, 10.25am, Sky Cinema PremiereSingin’ in the RainView image in fullscreenSure to give you a cheer-up … Gene Kelly in Singin’ in the Rain.Photograph: BFI National ArchiveIf you’re one of the many devotees of Damien Chazelle’s 2016 Oscar-winnerLa La Land– or maybe just in need of a cheer-up – be sure to check out this foundational1952 Hollywood musical. Gene Kelly’s genius is on full display as Don Lockwood, a star of the silent era who is attempting to ride out the transition to sound cinema with his integrity intact. There are also glorious supporting turns from Donald O’Connor and Debbie Reynolds, while the defiant exuberance of that title song shines through every scene, and every rain cloud.Sunday 2 August, 8pm, Sky Cinema GreatsStand By MeView image in fullscreenThe ultimate coming-of-age movie … Jerry O’Connell, River Phoenix, Wil Wheaton and Corey Feldman in Stand by Me.Photograph: AP/Sony Pictures“I never had any friends later like the ones I had when I was 12.” With that closing line, this 1986 adaptation of a Stephen King novella cemented its status as the ultimate coming-of-age movie. Its1950s-set storyconcerns four boys (including an iconic performance from the late River Phoenix) who set out on a macabre journey to find the body of a missing classmate. Stand By Me was always a classic, but subsequent events – including the tragic death of much beloved director Rob Reiner – have invested rewatches with added poignancy.Tuesday 4 August, 3am, Sky Cinema GreatsAll That Heaven AllowsView image in fullscreenEnthralling … Rock Hudson and Jane Wyman in All That Heaven Allows.Photograph: Cinetext/Universal/AllstarThe lush melodramas of Douglas Sirk have influenced film-makers all over the world, including John Waters, Wong Kar-Wai, Pedro Almodovár and Todd Haynes, whose 2002 filmFar from Heaven, starring Julianne Moore and Dennis Haysbert, is a direct descendent of this1955 film. Jane Wyman plays Cary, a middle-aged widow whose suburban life is disrupted for ever when she falls for hunky, younger gardener Ron (Rock Hudson). It still enthrals with emotion as intensely vivid as its colour palette.Thursday 6 August, 4.50pm, Film4The Last HouseView image in fullscreenIntriguing … Greta Lee as Ann in The Last House.Photograph: NetflixThe population has been confined indoors because of a little-understood external threat, meaning parents must homeschool their children, supplies are rationed and communication with neighbours can happen only at a distance … sound familiar? The Last House comes on like a Covid lockdown flashback but it’s actually an intriguing sci-fi horror, with a plot reminiscent of 2007 film The Mist. It benefits greatly from the presence of charming leads Wagner Moura (The Secret Agent) andGreta Lee(Past Lives), as a couple forced to extremes for their family’s survival.Friday 7 August, NetflixHoardView image in fullscreenThrillingly distinctive … Saura Lightfoot Leon in Hoard.Photograph: PR undefinedIf a film-watching experience can be described as “fetid”, thenHoardis that – but in a good way. Writer-director Luna Carmoon was only 26 when she made her debut feature, announcing herself as a thrillingly distinctive talent in British cinema. Saura Lightfoot Leon stars as Maria, a young, care-experienced woman whose loving but unstable childhood is revealed in the detritus of her chaotic present. Hayley Squires (I, Daniel Blake) plays Maria’s bin-diving, hoarder mother and Joseph Quinn (Stranger Things) is her foster brother turned love interest.Friday 7 August, 11.05pm, BBC TwoExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioThe seven best films to watch on TV this weekfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ted Lasso to Monsters of God: the seven best shows to stream this week | Television | The Guardian
description: Jason Sudeikis’ football coach turns his hand to the women’s game. Plus, a wild new documentary from the maker of Tiger King – about exotic animal smuggling
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Jason Sudeikis’ football coach turns his hand to the women’s game. Plus, a wild new documentary from the maker of Tiger King – about exotic animal smuggling
Content: Excellent … (from left) Brendan Hunt and Jason Sudeikis are joined by Tanya Reynolds for the fourth season of Ted Lasso.Photograph: Colin Hutton/AppleView image in fullscreenExcellent … (from left) Brendan Hunt and Jason Sudeikis are joined by Tanya Reynolds for the fourth season of Ted Lasso.Photograph: Colin Hutton/AppleThe seven best shows to stream this weekTelevisionTed Lasso to Monsters of God: the seven best shows to stream this weekJason Sudeikis’ football coach turns his hand to the women’s game. Plus, a wild new documentary from the maker of Tiger King – about exotic animal smugglingPhil HarrisonFri 31 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekTed LassoAre we still in the mood for football with a side order of ripe American cheese? In the light of reservations about the recent World Cup (and, particularly, the final’s half-time show featuring Ted Lasso), it’s certainly up for debate. The premise of this fourthseriesis “back to basics” – which is the only way the show could conceivably still work as an underdog story. Ted (Jason Sudeikis) is in the US when he’s visited by Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham) and Keeley (Juno Temple). Can he be persuaded to manage their second-tier women’s team, Lady Greyhounds? The excellent cast – which now also includes Sex Education star Tanya Reynolds – keep the ball rolling.Apple TV, from Wednesday 5 AugustMonsters of GodView image in fullscreenCompelling … Tyler Nolen with an indigo snake in Monsters of God.Photograph: HBO MaxA rich, strange, largely unknown world usually makes for a compelling documentary series and film-maker Eric “Tiger King” Goode’s deep dive into exotic animal smuggling is no exception. Many of the people we meet here fall into the likable oddball category – it’s clear that their enthusiasm for snakes and lizards is entirely sincere. However, that’s not the whole story. Goode gets the lowdown on the huge money that can be made by liberating (or stealing, depending on your point of view) animals from sanctuaries and trafficking them to both zoos and private collectors.HBO Max, from Friday 7 AugustOne Hundred Years of SolitudeView image in fullscreenThe magic is never far away … One Hundred Years of Solitude.Photograph: Mauricio González A/NetflixBack to Macondo for the second part of this Gabriel García Márquez adaptation which does anadmirable jobof capturing the uncanny, earthy strangeness of theoriginal novel. And there’s worrying news: the era of the exploitative American United Fruit Company is upon us, so along with carefully measured bananas, the town is to be modernised in all the worst possible ways. The plotline inevitably gives this season a more socially conscious and polemical slant but as Úrsula Iguarán’s ancient curse begins to manifest, the magic at the heart of the realism is never far away.Netflix, from Wednesday 5 AugustBig Chicken: A Fast Food ConspiracyView image in fullscreenPoultry-related horror … Big Chicken: A Fast Food Conspiracy.Photograph: NetflixThe format for comicMo Gilligan’s investigation into the chicken industry is far from original: his attempt to live on nothing but fast-food chicken for 28 days is clearly derived from Morgan Spurlock’s 2004 filmSuper Size Me. However, there’s merit elsewhere as Gilligan reveals a catalogue of poultry-related horror: the exploitation of workers; the targeting of low-income communities; the terrible conditions faced by the chickens; and the lack of nutritional value in the food. This is an industry long overdue the scrutiny it receives here.Netflix, from Wednesday 5 AugustSterling PointView image in fullscreenVoyage of discovery … Ella Rubin as Annie and Bo Bragason as Oona in Sterling Point.Photograph: Sabrina Lantos/Prime VideoMore drama about the growing pains of wealthy American teens in this YA series which, in terms of atmosphere at least, has echoes ofThe Summer I Turned Pretty. The action pivots round a brother and sister who (in an infuriatingly casual way) inherit a lake island. Problems, problems. However, things are set to become more confusing still: when Annie (Ella Rubin) arrives at Sterling Point, she’s shocked to bump into a girl who is the absolute double of her late mother. Could she have a secret sister? An emotionally fraught voyage of discovery ensues.Prime Video, from Wednesday 5 AugustThe ShardsView image in fullscreenCo-created with Bret Easton Ellis … Hayes Warner as Debbie and Igby Rigney as Bret in The Shards.Photograph: Ray Mickshaw/FXA new series from TV’s most prolific purveyor of primary coloured pulp,Ryan Murphy. The Shards was co-created with Bret Easton Ellis and adapted from the author’ssemi-autobiographical novel, set in the early 1980s within a jaded, privileged friendship group at an elite LA school. The world of aspiring writer Bret (Igby Rigney) is thrown into chaos by the arrival of Homer Gere’s charismatic Robert. Is this just school politics? Maybe, but there’s a serial killer on the loose and he and Robert seem connected. Restraint and understatement aren’t really in the picture.Disney+, from Thursday 6 AugustAlley CatsView image in fullscreenMisguided … Diane Morgan as Olive in Alley Cats.Photograph: NetflixRicky Gervais’s latest misguided comedy venture is this animation set within the shadowy world of cats. Sadly, the animation is generic, the plotting almost non-existent and the voice acting – particularly that of Gervais himself, though Tom Basden, Kerry Godliman and Diane Morgan also feature – almost insultingly cursory. As has often been the case with Gervais’s output since The Office, it somehow manages to be gratuitously unpleasant and twee at the same time, with lots of swearing and sentimentality.Netflix, from Friday 7 AugustExplore more on these topicsTelevisionThe seven best shows to stream this weekTV streamingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was so self-assured in my early 20s. Then my frontal lobe hit’: Rachel Chinouriri, every pop star’s favourite UK pop star | Rachel Chinouriri | The Guardian
description: ​She faced racist bullying as a child – then pigeonholing as an artist. Now following up a hit debut album championed by the A-list, the Croydon singer-songwriter says she finally understands who she really is
Author: Olive Pometsey
Headline: ​She faced racist bullying as a child – then pigeonholing as an artist. Now following up a hit debut album championed by the A-list, the Croydon singer-songwriter says she finally understands who she really is
Content: ‘The fun obsessions or meet-ups I used to love  came from a place of desperation, loneliness and seeking validation’ … Rachel Chinouriri.Photograph: Yana Van NuffelView image in fullscreen‘The fun obsessions or meet-ups I used to love  came from a place of desperation, loneliness and seeking validation’ … Rachel Chinouriri.Photograph: Yana Van NuffelRachel ChinouririInterview‘I was so self-assured in my early 20s. Then my frontal lobe hit’: Rachel Chinouriri, every pop star’s favourite UK pop starOlive Pometsey​She faced racist bullying as a child – then pigeonholing as an artist. Now following up a hit debut album championed by the A-list, the Croydon singer-songwriter says she finally understands who she really isFri 31 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn October 2017, Rachel Chinouriri had her first panic attack. It couldn’t have come at a worse time. She’d just landed her first major gig as a professional musician, supportingCelesteat the London members’ club Laylow. Out of nowhere, she began to spiral. “I don’t know what happened,” she says. “I just started having a mental breakdown.” Her manager told her to go home, try again next time. But that only made things worse. “I started feeling like I was wasting everyone’s time,” she says. “I started feeling ashamed.” It would be better, she decided, to go on stage and sing, “half crying”.Tears were already a familiar response to Chinouriri’s performance anxiety: the first time she sang in front of her classmates at the Brit school – the performing arts institution that trained Adele, Amy Winehouse and more – she burst into sobs afterwards. A rather inconvenient habit for an aspiring pop star, but at least she front-loaded the humiliation at the start of her career. “That was a big milestone for me,” she says of the Celeste show. “The fact that I could stand up there completely embarrassed, with people looking at me like, ‘Don’t really know what’s up with this girl’, but I still got through it and everything was fine.” The experience taught her that the catastrophic scenarios in her head rarely come to pass. “I’d given myself this pressure of, ‘This is the music industry. If they think I’m rubbish, I’m never gonna perform again.’” Chinouriri rolls her eyes at herself.The 27-year-old’s triumph over stage fright has been more impressive than most. It’s a sweltering Friday in July – 30C outside and even hotter in the small restaurant she’s chosen for our interview – and Chinouriri is having an excellent week. On Sunday, she performed to a crowd of 45,000 at Wolf Alice’s homecoming show in Finsbury Park – the latest artists to select her as a support act, after Sabrina Carpenter, Olivia Rodrigo, Gracie Abrams, Florence + the Machine and more have all been drawn to the fearless, bare-souled lyricism that charges through her contemporary twist on indie music. Last night, her former Brit school headteacher handed her the trophy for best new music at the O2 Silver Clef awards: her first-ever award win, after nominations at the 2025 Brits and 2021 Ivor Novellos. Melanie C was at the ceremony and later followed her on Instagram (“I will absolutely message her straight after this”).View image in fullscreenRachel Chinouriri at Radio 1’s Big Weekend at Herrington Country Park, Sunderland, May 2026.Photograph: Joseph Okpako/WireImageHow did she celebrate her big win? “I put on my glasses and left! I was in the heaviest metallic dress and it was like a sauna in there. Looking back at all the images, I’m just, like,weton stage.” Today, Chinouriri is dressed in more appropriate heatwave attire: red micro shorts, a strapless top and flip-flops. She scans the breakfast menu, though she hardly needs to: Café Palestina is one of her favourite spots in London, a short ride from her home in Camden. She orders a Palestinian breakfast and an assortment of kibbeh and stuffed vine leaves to share, then leans back into her seat.There’s another reason for Chinouriri’s good mood: this afternoon, she’ll hand in the final version of her forthcoming second album, I Think I Spoke Too Soon. The title is quite literal. “In my early 20s, I was so self-assured of who I was, then my frontal lobe hit and I went: ‘Nah, I’m actually not that person,’” she says. Chinouriri says she has recently learned about her Saturn return, the astrological milestone said to upend your late-20s. “I feel the shift. I thought I knew myself. Now I look in the mirror and I’m like: ‘Is this actually who I am?’”It’s a big question, but not a new one for Chinouriri. Growing up in Croydon, she was the only one of five siblings to be born in the UK, after her family moved from Zimbabwe. Her mother ran a strict Christian household while caring for her sick father. Both parents had fought as child soldiers in Zimbabwe’s war for independence. In the UK, they struggled to make ends meet. “But they always turned it into a giggle,” she says – even when the power went out. “Games would start getting invented. You’d get given the electricity meter key and walk to the shop to put £5 on.” She smiles fondly at the memory of them all sprinting to complete the task. “They found a way to turn struggle into something beautiful in order to survive.”View image in fullscreen‘My first school taught me: don’t stay where you’re not wanted.’Photograph: Yana Van NuffelAt a majority white secondary school, Chinouriri faced her own battles, enduring racist bullying so extreme that one pupil was suspended and another excluded. She was spat on, called the N-word and tormented with monkey noises as she walked through the corridors. Eventually, Chinouriri enrolled herself at a more diverse school, pretending to be her mother on the application form. “The first school taught me: don’t stay where you’re not wanted,” she says. “I hit points where I felt like dying. But afterwards, I was like: ‘I can leave here with my head raised high.’”A few years later, she made it to the Brit school, the state-funded incubator for British pop stars and actors. Chinouriri was in the same school year as Olivia Dean and Cat Burns; Lola Young was just a few years below. “I wasn’t in any of their classes, but they were three names I heard constantly – the rumours were right!” At home, her musical tastes stuck out. Forbidden from listening to non-Christian music, she and her siblings would row over which TV music channels to watch while their parents were at work. “My sisters were big lovers of B2K, Brandy and Destiny’s Child. When I was in charge of the TV, it would be Oasis and Coldplay.” But at the Brit school, the singer found a place where being different was kind of the whole point. “There was a girl who used to paint herself like an anime character every single day and walked around the school like it was normal,” she says. “I loved that level of expression and freedom.”double quotation markMy sisters loved Brandy and Destiny’s Child. Me, it was Oasis and ColdplayWhen Chinouriri released her debut album, What a Devastating Turn of Events, in 2024, she laid everything bare. The title track recounts her cousin’s suicide after an unwanted pregnancy; another song wrestles with self-worth and body dysmorphia; on My Blood, she sings about self-harm. The candour resonated and its songs were streamed hundreds of millions of times. “All my songs feel a bit like a journal entry, even if I make it sound like a pop song,” she says. “It’s always deeply embedded in my thoughts.” It also resonates when her lyrics turn to romance: her song Dumb Bitch Juice has become an anthem for fans weathering toxic relationships. As Chinouriri’s friend and collaborator PinkPantheress tells me, “Her youthful, melodic approach truly encapsulates the state of modern romance among people our age. She makes heartbreak warm and tolerable, even in the most painful situations.”View image in fullscreenChinouriri at Roskilde festival in Denmark, 2025.Photograph: Matt Jelonek/Getty ImagesChinouriri is now in a healthy, long-term relationship. These days, she sings about heartbreak from a distance: reflecting on past flings to better understand herself, instead of “writing through something I’m trying to survive,” she says. “I began asking myself: ‘Why do I attract these people?’ The fun obsessions or meet-ups I used to love actually came from a place of desperation, loneliness and seeking validation.”When her album was released, much of the media attention focused on Chinouriri’s presence as a Black woman in indie music, a genre that’s historically associated with white men. This was partly her own doing. In 2022, she called out the industry’s inaccurate – and, frankly, racist – miscategorisation of her music as R&B or soul on Instagram: “You see my colour before you hear my music.” What a Devastating Turn of Events doubled down on guitar sounds to make a point. “That had to happen because I was really fighting for my place in indie pop,” she says. But still, I wonder, did she ever tire of answering questions about race?“I feel like …” Chinouriri squints upwards as if the answer might be hovering above the table, then begins to speak slowly. “It was an important and necessary part of the story to pave the way for myself in pop, indie and alternative music. I’m glad that I’ve played a part in that. I love going on TikTok and seeing a new Black pop or indie girl with 10,000 likes and no one’s questioning it.” So the industry’s made progress, then? Another pause. “I can say that there’s been progress because I’ve benefited from it. But when I look to my left and right at festivals, I’m still the only Black girl on the lineup – or it will be me and Cat [Burns]. The fact that two Black pop girls who went to the same school are [being booked] around the UK … That’s interesting.”View image in fullscreenChinouriri at Field Day festival in London, 2019.Photograph: Lorne Thomson/RedfernsI Think I Spoke Too Soon turns the conversation inward. “My first album was about how I was perceived as a Black woman in this space. Now it’s about how I perceive myself in this space,” she says.The record is a near-total gear shift from Chinouriri’s previous output, drawing from her longtime pop heroes, Madonna, Kylie Minogue, Donna Summer, Prince and LCD Soundsystem – influences that would have perhaps complicated her fight against pigeonholing during her last album rollout. “As much as I love indie sleaze, I love me some Madonna,” she says, laughing. “I wanted [to recreate] the level of carefreeness I got when I listened to songs like Hung Up for the first time.”Bright synths replace Britpop-inspired guitars; melancholy hooks are transformed into singalong sad bangers. There are still flickers of her old self: rich harmonies, confessional lyrics, the odd indie track thrown in for good measure. But as she sings on lead single, One Song Away from Crying, this is principally an album that’s designed to “work it out on the floor”.If anything, Chinouriri’s darkest moments are made all the more cathartic when contrasted with a danceable beat. When she confronts her relationship to alcohol on Broken Chair, for example, she sings its euphoric chorus from the perspective of pitying an abandoned piece of furniture on the side of the road: “You look lonely, but not me / I’ve got plenty of friends until the last call”. The same theme is explored on The Good Fight, one of the first songs she wrote for the album. Around the same time, she decided to go sober. “I didn’t have too much of an issue with drinking, but I just looked at myself and thought: ‘This is not my happy place,’” she says. Up until that point, her party-girl image had become a running joke with her fans. “I was out with a friend and she posted a selfie of us. My fans were like, she’s about to tweet: ‘I’m tipsy!’” Without seeing their prediction, she did exactly that. “It was pretty funny. They know me well.”Chinouriri replies to group chats with her fans more often than her family. Recently, her team analysed her audience and found it skews overwhelmingly queer. “I was like: ‘This is fantastic!’” She went straight to the group chat to deliver the news. “I was like: ‘Announcement: everyone in here is gay and this is beautiful.’”Chinouriri is looking ahead to a busy few months of concerts, including a slot at Rodrigo’s inaugural Daisy Chain Fields festival in California and supporting Abrams on tour across the US. She’s already briefing fans on what to wear to align with her new era: “Blue, silvers, purple, shimmy-shimmy iridescence. It’s going to be so fun.”‘The beast inside me wants to move!’ The smart, slapstick world of Audrey Hobert, the Steve Martin of popRead moreWhen supporting Carpenter on tour around Europe last year, Chinouriri “felt like I was travelling in this Sabrina universe”. Every billboard had Carpenter’s face on it; every person seemed to be wearing merch; every cafe was playing her music. “It was so cool to see how she’s thought about her fans, even at that level, and the community they’ve built. I’d love to have that one day.”At the Finsbury Park show, one fan held up a sign that read: “When I don’t belong, her music calls.” Perhaps that feeling is a happy byproduct of Chinouriri’s own fight to be heard. “Whatever happens, if I do get pigeonholed again, so be it. I fought really hard. I tried my best,” she says. “But I need to trust that it won’t happen because I have found a way to know who I am.” At least for now. “You can change who you are at any moment, as long as you reflect and forgive yourself first.”I Think I Spoke Too Soon is released on 16 October via Parlophone/Atlas ArtistsExplore more on these topicsRachel ChinouririPop and rockIndieDance musicRacefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the art-pop showtunes of Luki and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Combining grand melodrama with nuanced emotional character, Lucy Duncan and producer Niac’s collaboration sounds both timeless and true
Author: Claire Biddles
Headline: Combining grand melodrama with nuanced emotional character, Lucy Duncan and producer Niac’s collaboration sounds both timeless and true
Content: Wisdom and fallibility … Lucy Duncan AKA Luki.Photograph: Matthew Arthur WilliamsView image in fullscreenWisdom and fallibility … Lucy Duncan AKA Luki.Photograph: Matthew Arthur WilliamsAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the art-pop showtunes of Luki and the week’s best new tracksCombining grand melodrama with nuanced emotional character, Lucy Duncan and producer Niac’s collaboration sounds both timeless and trueClaire BiddlesandBen Beaumont-ThomasFri 31 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromHastings, UKRecommended if you likeMary Margaret O’Hara, Tori Amos, Fiona AppleUp nextOld Feelings EP out now, album to follow later in 2026The first time listening to Luki feels like a miraculous discovery of something timeless and true, as though they’ve been waiting patiently to be discovered in the noisy maelstrom of contemporary pop music. The collaborative alias of singer/composer Lucy Duncan and producer Niac, Luki write off-kilter showtunes performed as baroque art songs, embodying a seemingly contradictory combination of grand melodrama and nuanced emotional character.Luki’s debut albumWispswas released by the excellent Glasgow-based tape label GLARC in 2018, followed by a sporadic string of singles over subsequent years. With the new EPOld Feelings, the project appears to be building up to something more substantial. The title track feels like a climactic ballad from a lost, late-period Sondheim musical by way of 90s Celine Dion: all rolling pianos and wry regrets, with synth lines lingering like dry ice. Strong, direct and rich with character, Duncan’s voice shares the wisdom and fallibility that the great Mary Margaret O’Hara has in spades.Elsewhere on the EP, Luki’s take on Such a Small Love imagines Scott Walker remade by Sensual World-era Kate Bush. The eight minute long I Think I Know is tricksier, akin to the experimental edges of Tori Amos or Fiona Apple, meandering through sections of spoken word and textural electronics. Old Feelings is both a tantalising taster of a forthcoming album – due to feature collaborations with Robbie Ellen, AKA art-pop songwriterPersonnel– and a genuinely remarkable set of songs in its own right.Claire BiddlesThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenOn heavy form … Dis Fig.Photograph: Camille BlakeDis Fig – The Account (ft the Wind Between)We loved her thunderous collab album with the Body, and Felicia Chen is on equally heavy form here, singing trip-hop vox and letting off bassy depth charges under the Wind Between’s rapped existential screed.Blonde Redhead – Blood SpilledThe art-rockers’ one-off single is no casual interstitial release, but a genuine epic, expanding across six minutes like a hot air balloon in burnt-sunset hues that keeps filling and floating away: astoundingly beautiful.Jae Stephens – Sugar TrapAlready a fave among pop musos, the US artist feels as if she’s one step away from proper stardom thanks to high-tempo, dancefloor-flirtation snappers like this, full of strutting, mane-tossing energy.Prodigal – The DoorBlending Deftones-style seriousness with the kind of sicko riffage that compels your tongue out of your mouth, this majestic moshpit detonator demonstrates that this new UK band are the real deal.163Margs – Clock ItThis MC is one of the most sprightly in London’s post-drill marketplace – check 2024’s Superstar if you haven’t heard it – and here he dances his flow through dreamy flutes and strings.Kade Young – MetallicMake sure any glassware is away from the edges of shelves if you stick on the Baltimore producer’s maximally vibrational, awesomely designed sub-bass, topped here with footwork-ish chopped-up vox.Essence Martins – Red VelvetNamed after the type of cake loved by her ex, this track sees the UK singer-songwriter – admired by SZA – reflect on heartbreak, but the swell of beautiful Coldplay-ish sound suggests she’s being carried to a new chapter.Ben Beaumont-ThomasSubscribe to the title: Arca: XXXXX review – a wild, brilliant album that taps into our bodies’ most feral frequencies  | Arca | The Guardian
description: In the follow-up to her Kick series, Arca jumbles the building blocks of electronic music to create a beautiful, disorienting sound world
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: In the follow-up to her Kick series, Arca jumbles the building blocks of electronic music to create a beautiful, disorienting sound world
Content: Arca.Photograph: Cassandra AntoniadesView image in fullscreenArca.Photograph: Cassandra AntoniadesArcaReviewArca: XXXXX review – a wild, brilliant album that taps into our bodies’ most feral frequencies(XL)In the follow-up to her Kick series, Arca jumbles the building blocks of electronic music to create a beautiful, disorienting sound worldShaad D'SouzaFri 31 Jul 2026 04.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenXXXXX’s cover artXXXXX, the new album by Venezuelan producer-vocalist Arca, is reportedly laden with meaning: a press release claims that “suspended between posthuman augmentation and raw emotion, XXXXX exposes the mainframe”. But the reason Arca, real name Alejandra Ghersi, has become such a star of electronic music – and a mainstream-adjacent one at that – is not because she lets philosophy postgrads in Berlin write her marketing copy: it’s because, for well over a decade, she has been putting out records like XXXXX, which seem to tap into the body’s most primal, feral frequencies better than nearly anyone else. That ability has resulted in recent callups to collaborate onMadonna’s Confessions IIand remix pop singerAddison Rae, and she has amassed a large, loyal fanbase – uncommon for someone making such outre music.‘It was a way of processing violences I’ve survived’: how iconoclastic musician Arca beat burnout with frenzied paintingRead moreThe follow-up to her phenomenalKick series– five albums, each highlighting a different side of Arca’s work – XXXXX sometimes channels the frenetic feel of Aphex Twin (as on Everything) and zeroes in on the wild, footwork-y high-tempo club music she made her name with (like on Fxck, a breathless and grimy rebuke to patriarchy). But it also delves more deeply into worlds the musician has previously skirted around. The sound of a tolling bell on Willow rings into a song that’s harsh and uncompromising; Raver jumbles the building blocks of classic mainstream EDM into a piece of beautiful, disorienting sound design.The music on XXXXX often sounds like tracks from multiple Kick albums layered atop one another: elements of classical composition, deconstructed club music and pop all fight for dominance. The resulting album is one of Arca’s densest and best: music for the body and brain that is unrelenting and unerringly brilliant.Explore more on these topicsArcaElectronic musicExperimental musicalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Jacaranda by Gaël Faye review – the limits of forgiveness after Rwanda | Fiction | The Guardian
description: This bold family saga explores a search for healing and truth in the aftermath of the Rwanda genocide
Author: Rachel Seiffert
Headline: This bold family saga explores a search for healing and truth in the aftermath of the Rwanda genocide
Content: Gaël Faye.Photograph: Jean-François PagaView image in fullscreenGaël Faye.Photograph: Jean-François PagaBook of the dayFictionReviewJacaranda by Gaël Faye review – the limits of forgiveness after RwandaThis bold family saga explores a search for healing and truth in the aftermath of the Rwanda genocideRachel SeiffertFri 31 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow to forgive the unforgivable? How to live in the aftermath of atrocity? Following 2016’sSmall Country, French-Rwandan rapper and writer Gaël Faye takes on huge questions in his second novel, Jacaranda, which explores the seismic events of the Rwanda genocide and the aftershocks that continue to ripple through the generations.Structurally bold, the story opens in summer 1994 with Milan, Faye’s then 12-year-old protagonist, enjoying an extended break from school. Milan’s father is white French and the family’s life in Versailles is the embodiment of first world ease – their holiday that year, as usual, spent sailing at the Île de Ré. Milan’s mother, though, is Rwandan. Venancia arrived in the 1970s, establishing a life for herself, a successful clothing boutique, a family. However, she cannot share the French ease, much less her thoughts on the disturbing reports from Rwanda now making the evening news.Indeed, taciturn Venancia has never shared the reasons she left for Europe, and Milan only learns he has extended Rwandan family when his “cousin” Claude arrives at the end of the holidays, out of the blue, and terribly injured by a machete. Small and so traumatised he can barely speak, Claude has been brought to France for treatment. While Venancia takes him in under obligation, young Milan quickly takes him to heart, and the boys’ developing bond over the autumn is tenderly described. But once his wounds are improving, Claude returns as abruptly as he arrived, and with just as little explanation, and the hole he leaves in Milan’s life refuses to heal.In part two we jump to 1998. Milan is 16, his parents’ marriage is faltering, and so are his studies, and he travels to Rwanda for the first time. In Kigali, Milan finds an alternative mother figure in Eusébie, a childhood friend of Venancia’s. A fellow Tutsi, and a survivor of the 1994 genocide, she is now a campaigner for justice and healing. The jacaranda of the title grows in her garden, providing shade for her elderly mother Rosalie and her newborn daughter Stella, the sibling Milan has been craving. When he holds the child, she smiles her first smile.double quotation markIn Milan and his family, in Claude, Stella, Sartre and Eusébie, Faye gives face and voice to the human capacity for enduranceMuch to his joy, Milan also finds Claude again, and through him meets the pivotal character Sartre, who lives in Le Palais, a ramshackle compound far from Eusébie’s leafy neighbourhood. Here, at the height of the violence, he gave shelter to dozens of Tutsi children, orphans of the genocide, becoming a Fagin of sorts. A scavenger of considerable discernment, Sartre has established an extensive library of books and music; Milan learns much about Rwanda under his tutelage, and from the many now almost-adult orphans – not least that, here, he is considered white. He finds a home from home among them regardless. Having stared death in the face, the young residents of Le Palais spend their days grafting and their nights partying, and Milan is inspired by their defiance.His grandmother is less welcoming. Milan finds Mamie much like Venancia: withheld and withholding. But he does begin to see that the 1994 violence had long and tangled roots, as does the Hutu-Tutsi divide; Claude was not the first in their family to suffer, but exactly why and how they fled remains shrouded.Milan will return to Rwanda many more times, and for longer and longer periods. Adrift, he will seek out Sartre, and the oblivion of partying in Le Palais; in search of shelter, he will turn to Eusébie and the now grown Stella; under the shade of the jacaranda, he will discover that she seeks answers too.The book’s most painful chapters describe thegacacacourts, which ran until 2012: mass open-air hearings, gathering testimonies from across the victim-perpetrator divide; public confessions and accusations that campaigners like Eusébie hoped would provide truth and reconciliation.But some truths are hard to take – perhaps impossible – and in some revelations, Milan sees forgiveness reach its limits. Venancia will not be the only one to have withheld her story, and neither will Claude have been alone in masquerading as someone he’s not. Who can Milan trust after all that he’s heard? Where can he find peace when even the shade of the jacaranda will not provide refuge?In Milan and his family, in Claude, Stella, Sartre and Eusébie, Faye gives face and voice to the human capacity for endurance. Perhaps above all, he sees the harm in the divides we make between victim and perpetrator, Tutsi and Hutu, parent and child, black and white, Europe and Africa. Jacaranda is a bold and uncompromising book.Jacaranda by Gaël Faye, translated by Sarah Ardizzone, is published by Chatto & Windus (£18.99). title: Jacqueline Crooks: ‘Toni Morrison’s voice made me want to find my own’ | Books | The Guardian
description: The novelist on learning empathy from Charles Dickens, the playfulness of Irenosen Okojie and avoiding Jane Austen
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The novelist on learning empathy from Charles Dickens, the playfulness of Irenosen Okojie and avoiding Jane Austen
Content: ‘There’s something deeply reassuring about returning to Walter Mosley’ … Jacqueline Crooks.Photograph: David Levenson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘There’s something deeply reassuring about returning to Walter Mosley’ … Jacqueline Crooks.Photograph: David Levenson/Getty ImagesThe books of my lifeBooksJacqueline Crooks: ‘Toni Morrison’s voice made me want to find my own’The novelist on learning empathy from Charles Dickens, the playfulness of Irenosen Okojie and avoiding Jane AustenJacqueline CrooksFri 31 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy earliest reading memoryI was eight when I was given The Water-Babies by Charles Kingsley, after being moved from my grand­mother’s care to live with my mother and her husband, who I barely knew. The story is about leaving one world, adapting to another. Surviving. It gave shape to unnamed feelings and developed my survival imagination: imagining beyond my circumstances.My favourite book growing upDavid Copperfield by Charles Dickens. I followed David’s journey from exclusion to belonging. Dickens vivifies his characters; you grow alongside them. The novel taught me empathy, and that some relationships sustain us while others must be left behind.The book that changed me as a teenagerI read Wuthering Heights when I was 12 or 13. Heathcliff fascinates me: enigmatic, brooding, never fully explained. Emily Brontë taught me landscape is character. The moors are a living force, mirroring Cathy and Heathcliff’s emotional lives. That shaped my writing: I’m drawn to unknowable characters and psychologically alive places.The writer who changed my mindI was in my 40s when a writing tutor suggested I read The Tempest while writing my story collection The Ice Migration. The island setting, themes of displacement and longing for return resonated, and made me realise Shakespeare could speak to my life.The author who made me want to be a writerI can’t remember which Toni Morrison novel affected me most: The Bluest Eye, Tar Baby or Jazz. Her worlds are familiar, dreamlike, grounded yet on the edge of the unknowable. Morrison showed me that Black lives and characters from marginalised worlds are worthy of being centred within literature. Her voice made me want to find my own.The book or author I came back toWhen I first read Wilson Harris, his writing felt demanding. Returning to it in my 40s, I was captivated by his Guyanese landscapes. Harris showed me landscape can carry history, memory, imagination. I learned to value my cultural inheritance and bring Jamaica’s landscapes on to the page.The book I rereadI first read Irenosen Okojie’sNudibranchin 2019 and return to it often. She does extraordinary things with language and image; at times, the writing creates its own imaginative vocabulary. It is a masterclass in inventiveness, playfulness and creative courage.The book I could never read againPride and Prejudice by Jane Austen. I studied it at school. I’ve always questioned respectability politics. The world of courtship and dinner parties feels confining. I respect Austen’s skill, but I’m drawn to books about characters who cross boundaries, venture into the unknown rather than finding their place within the social order.The book I discovered later in lifeI discovered Xiaolu Guo’s Radical in 2023. What struck me was its freedom. Guo combines memoir, philosophy, visual art and language, using Chinese script to guide the reader. I admire its fierce independence: a woman stepping outside prescribed roles to pursue creativity on her own terms. Guo isn’t writing to be liked; she is writing to push boundaries.The book I am currently readingI’m reading Cosmic Music: The Life, Art and Transcendence of Alice Coltrane by Andy Beta. Coltrane’s music has long been a muse for my writing and influenced my new novel, Sky City. Her music is spiritual, hopeful. As a writer, books about music help me to listen for rhythm and pace.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy comfort readThere’s something deeply reassuring about returning to Walter Mosley’s Always Outnumbered, Always Outgunned. And Socrates Fortlow is so familiar, he feels like family. His resourcefulness, humour and care for others, even in the face of hardship, remind me of people I’ve known throughout my life. I always come away believing that kindness, dignity and transformation are still possible, no matter what is going on in the world.Sky City by Jacqueline Crooks is published by Jonathan Cape. title: What we’re reading: writers and readers on the books they enjoyed in July | Books | The Guardian
description: Max Porter, Daisy Johnson, Avni Doshi and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the comments
Author: Daisy Johnson
Headline: Max Porter, Daisy Johnson, Avni Doshi and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the comments
Content: View image in fullscreenWhat we're readingBooksWhat we’re reading: writers and readers on the books they enjoyed in JulyMax Porter, Daisy Johnson, Avni Doshi and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the commentsMax Porter,Daisy Johnson, Avni Doshi and Guardian readersFri 31 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMax Porter, writerGrief is the Thing With Feathers: why Max Porter’s strange but ‘magnificent’ debut keeps inspiring adaptationsRead moreI recently readGaining GroundbyJoan Barfoot. It’s one of the best novels I’ve ever read about what it means to live with others, or decide not to; what we owe the people we love, the natural world, and ourselves. I also really enjoyedRobert Frost, by Robert Frost and Stacy Skolnik. It’s notthatRobert Frost; it’s an itinerant young American Robert Frost who jots down his thoughts and observations on homelessness, food, value, music, drugs, the philosophical wastelands of contemporary life, and Stacy Skolnik has turned them into these delightful, oddly profound, poems. Also, coming soon,End Times Fascismby Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. Everyone should read it. It tells us exactly what’s going on.Max Porter is the author of books includingShyandGrief Is the Thing With FeathersRichard, Guardian readerI am readingHeadlightsby the American horror writer CJ Leede. This is her third novel. I think she has the potential to be the 21st century’s Stephen King – she’s that good! Headlights is a pitch-black horror novel with overtones of Silence of the Lambs and Osgood Perkins’ fabulous filmLonglegs. It is also a love letter to King’s The Shining and has a strong environmental message too, concerning man’s uneasy and destructive relationship with the natural world. Leede is such a wonderful writer of prose. Her characters are three-dimensional and you care about them almost immediately (which makes what she does to some of them all the more horrible!). She has an obvious love of the American landscape and describes it beautifully, and the book’s relationship with The Shining will have horror lovers squealing with delight – there are little Easter eggs peppered throughout the book.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDaisy Johnson, writerDaisy Johnson: ‘I wasn’t a fan of David Szalay, but Flesh is a masterpiece’Read moreLately I am to be found loudly and excitedly recommendingThe Corner That Held Themby Sylvia Townsend Warner, first published in 1948. Set over 200 years and taking in the Black Death, the Great Revolt of 1381 and much bickering, the novel follows a convent of nuns living in the British Fenlands. I’ve also loved readingThe Empusium, an equally claustrophobic book by Olga Tokarczuk which, thrillingly, is described as “a health resort horror story” on the cover. It follows a young man with failing health who visits a sanatorium in the mountains to recover. It is a rather glorious and surreal romp.Long Wave by Daisy Johnson is published by Jonathan Cape (£18.99). To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may applySarah, Guardian readerThis month (perhaps not so subconsciously) I seem to have been drawn mostly to both fiction and nonfiction featuring women facing personal challenges. In fiction,Tamarinby Priya Hein andUnder Waterby Tara Menon have been favourites this month, and I think the books pair well together: both feature women who return to their homeland after life-changing experiences. In nonfiction,My Cantopop Nightsby Emma-Lee Mosswas a thoroughly enjoyable read about one woman’s search to find home and her identity in Hong Kong. Her experiences of motherhood resonated with me, and I was transported back to my own time spent in Hong Kong a decade ago. Finally, a hybrid of the two genres:Said the Deadby Doireann Ní Ghríofa. I devoured this book, which vividly brings to life the stories of a number of women who inhabited a psychiatric hospital in Ireland in the 1890s and early 20th century, the result of obsessive research by the author.Avni Doshi, writerView image in fullscreenAuthor Avni Doshi.Photograph: Aranka IsraniWhile researching for my next novel, in which one of the characters is an artist, I came across a brilliant book calledColourby Victoria Finlay. Finlay dives deep into the fascinating history of where colour comes from. It reads like an adventure into the painter’s palette. Expect intrigue, beetles and dead bodies.Andrea Bajani’sThe Anniversarywas also a recent favourite. The story follows a grown man unpicking the web of his painful childhood. A slim book written in crisp prose, there isn’t a word out of place. I read it in one sitting. I also loved and have been widely recommendingA Splinteringby Dur e Aziz Amna, in which a cunning and ambitious woman from a village in Pakistan reshapes the future that was set for her. Rarely have I read a character so ruthless and irresistible. Her hunger growls on the page.The First Houseby Avni Doshi is published by Hamish Hamilton (£16.99).
