title: The best recent poetry – review roundup | Poetry | The Guardian
description: Small Birds Singing by Matthew Welton; The Channel by Jana Prikryl; Stepmother by Helen Mort; Drunken Driving by Martina Evans
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Small Birds Singing by Matthew Welton; The Channel by Jana Prikryl; Stepmother by Helen Mort; Drunken Driving by Martina Evans
Content: The city through the seasons in Small Birds Singing.Photograph: Cavan Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe city through the seasons in Small Birds Singing.Photograph: Cavan Images/AlamyPoetry roundupPoetryReviewThe best recent poetry – review roundupSmall Birds Singing by Matthew Welton; The Channel by Jana Prikryl; Stepmother by Helen Mort; Drunken Driving by Martina EvansPhilip TerryFri 31 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSmall Birds Singingby Matthew Welton (Carcanet, £12.99)Written in unrhymed couplets that shrink and grow across the page like a concertina going through its scales, Welton’s poems focus attention on the city through the seasons: weeds through concrete, wasps emerging from the gaps between bricks, frozen towels on a clothesline, the shadows of jackdaws on a lawn. His gaze is neutral, and it often falls on that which we’d normally turn away from, things slightly out of place, or that disturb our sense of propriety: “more cardboard in the recycling bin / than the recycling bin can contain”. This is a poetry of things, like the poetry of Francis Ponge, but as Welton says: “no thinginess without thought”. Welton’s thoughts – though whether they are his or whether they emerge from his surroundings or from the act of writing itself, it is impossible to say – are couched in deliciously riddling couplets: “it is not the habit of patterns / to emphasise the pattern of habits”. He reminds us forcefully that poetry is all around us and within us, that anything can go in a poem: a sandwich, a desiccated lump of duck shit, the pile of junk left outside a house during a refurbishment. Poems can mirror our world in all its messiness, and in doing so let us see it a little bit better.View image in fullscreenThe Channelby Jana Prikryl (Faber, £12.99The casual violence of King Lear, the greed, the bureaucracy, and the indifference to human life, make the play particularly resonant to contemporary audiences. In her fourth collection, Prikryl channels the voice of Cordelia to think back through her own family story of displacement from the Czech Republic. Shakespeare’s Lear becomes “a document of fact / of things that happened and keep happening”, enabling Prikryl to explore her own separation from friends and family and her experiences of migration, where home is nowhere. In Dover Calais a ferry trip to France is meshed with the story of Cordelia’s exile, morphing into an account of a ferry disaster which in turn cuts to a scene where refugees make for shore in small boats: “Waves / unreal, and driving rain, the two-year-old / left face-down on a beach nine years ago / came up for me”. Like the scissored-off hospital undershirt in In the Mould, Prikryl’s language cuts off, ending abruptly: “or was the famous sweetness / of grandmother a bluff / which through and through was too”. This rewiring of the sentence creates dazzling leaps of thought, jumping from refugee camps to Shakespeare’s Fool battling with a tsunami of text messages to dissident window cleaners out of the novels of Milan Kundera to tender moments shared with her father. It’s a bold “stepping out of form” that turns its back on the neatness of the lyric, and by doing so creates a new poetic language which, like the language of Calvino in Invisible Cities, is able to connect everything to everything.View image in fullscreenStepmotherby Helen Mort (Chatto & Windus, £12.99)The ubiquity of the stepmother in fairytales has been explained by psychoanalyst Bruno Bettelheim as enabling the child to keep the image of the good mother intact. Marina Warner reminds us that their presence is historically connected to the high mortality rate of mothers in childbirth, though today women are more likely to find themselves in the role as a result of divorce. Here Mort explores her own experience of this neglected dimension of maternity alongside its representation in myth. “Better a serpent than a stepmother,” said Euripides, and the sentiment is reinforced across a range of stories where we witness stepmothers abandon their children in forests or simply decapitate them to be rid of them once and for all. Mort shows how traditional images of bad stepmothers are perpetuated in news stories and film, but she finds the modern experience repeating history in more subtle ways: she is jealous of her stepdaughter’s figure, distantly echoing the stepmother in Snow White, or, in an inversion of the way Cinderella is treated, it is the stepmother who finds herself pushed to the edge of her own household by photographs of the husband’s first marriage. Mort’s poems are a vivid compendium of stories, but they also offer ways of escaping the trap of myth: “You did not pick your stepchildren. Nor did they pick you. / But every day you can choose to love each other.”View image in fullscreenDrunken Drivingby Martina Evans (Carcanet, £12.99)This electrifying sequel to Evans’s 2023 sonnet sequence The Coming Thing is set 10 years on. Imelda, having put the Cork punk scene behind her, is now a young mother, married to Carl, working shifts at Pentonville prison and learning to negotiate the spiderweb crossroads of London in her red Astra. Appropriately for this carceral environment, the sonnets come cuffed with quotations taken from prison protocols, driving manuals and the novel Dracula: “With strained ears, I listened, and heard downstairs the grinding of the key in the great lock and the falling back of the heavy door.” Immediately we are plunged into a world of dangerous driving, vampiric warders, overcrowding and casual racism. Conversation within the prison walls is frowned upon but outside the banter flies between Imelda and her father Justin: “When I said Pentonville was a Chamber / of Horrors, Justin said, You’ve got an imagination. I’ll give you that. / But I don’t need one! I said. Half of Madame Tussaud’s waxworks were / hanged there. Justin snorted, Highly-strung, like yourself?” Pumped up with adrenaline, fuelled by alcohol, and peppered with razor-sharp observations, this reads like Porridge on steroids.Explore more on these topicsPoetryPoetry roundupreviewsShareReuse this content

title: SingStar Take That anyone? The strange joy of charity shop video games | Games | The Guardian
description: Hidden gems can be unearthed, but you have to dig deep into the bargain bins of countless outdated Fifas, Wii Fits without the controllers and partially finished quizshow games
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Hidden gems can be unearthed, but you have to dig deep into the bargain bins of countless outdated Fifas, Wii Fits without the controllers and partially finished quizshow games
Content: Shelf discovery … video games in a charity shop.Photograph: Keith Stuart/The GuardianView image in fullscreenShelf discovery … video games in a charity shop.Photograph: Keith Stuart/The GuardianGamesSingStar Take That anyone? The strange joy of charity shop video gamesHidden gems can be unearthed, but you have to dig deep into the bargain bins of countless outdated Fifas, Wii Fits without the controllers and partially finished quizshow gamesKeith StuartFri 31 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 19.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs an eternally optimistic charity shop fan, I hold on to the fantasy that one day I’ll walk into my local Oxfam and find a pristine copy of theSegaSaturn shooter Burning Rangers for £1.50. Or perhaps a box full of old Neo Geo carts for a quid each. Sadly, this is now unlikely. Charity shops have caught on to the fact that old video games – like old vinyl albums – are highly collectible, and so they’re putting the good stuff on eBay. That’s fine, it’s their job to raise money, not to provide opportunist swine like me with bargains. But what gamescanyou find tucked away in your local branch of Barnardo’s? To find out I visited about 40 charity stores across the country. Here is what I discovered on the shelves … And please do share your own charity shop gaming finds in the comments!Old versions of annual sports gamesView image in fullscreenSome good seasons, and hilarious commentary … old sports games.Photograph: Keith Stuart/The GuardianBy far the biggest category. Almost every store I entered had a selection of Fifa, Pro Evolution Soccer and Madden titles from years gone by, most of them on Xbox 360, and usually going for 50p each or less. There were a few decent outliers: I picked up a copy of tennis sim Top Spin 3 for £1 and was tempted by Major League Baseball 2K5 for the original Xbox, but was put off by the fact that it was missing its instruction booklet – and also, I don’t own an original Xbox. Are any others worth buying? Well, Fifa had a really good streak from 2010-2015 – super-fast gameplay, great licensed soundtracks, so if you don’t care about the latest squads, they’re entertaining for the money. I’d also recommend Pro Evolution Soccer 4-6 on thePlayStation2 – a true golden era of footie simulation and unintentionally hilarious commentary.Brain-training and quiz gamesTitles such as Dr Kawashima’s Brain Training and Big Brain Academy sold in their millions on the DS and Wii in the mid-00s, accelerated by smart,celebrity-crammed TV advertising. Naturally, there were reams of imitators – seemingly all of which have ended up on charity shop shelves. The original Brain Training is still challenging and compelling – although if you grab a copy, be careful to check any saved game files still left in the cart’s memory. I got a copy for a quid, and when I loaded it up, one of the stored usernames was “Martin’s Sex Bitch” (brain age: 35). Steer well clear of all the TV quiz show games that clogged up the DS library. One charity shop I went into had just a single game: Golden Balls, based on the daytime gameshow presented by Jasper Carrott. Reader: I did not buy it.Music and fitness games – without the required peripheralsView image in fullscreenBoard not available in my branch of Oxfam … Wii Fit.Photograph: Itsuo Inouye/APThis was another ubiquitous category. No matter where I went, charity shops were filled with copies of Dance UK, SingStar andWiiFit, but all lacked the necessary controllers to make them work. There were Kinect games with no Kinect and PlayStation EyeToy games with no camera. Out of all of them, I’d be tempted most by PlayStation 2 SingStar titles – it’ll only cost about £12 on eBay to buy the microphones and adaptor, then you can pick up the dozens of SingStar instalments for a few pounds (Rock Ballads! Motown! Sing along with Disney!) – hey presto, karaoke heaven. Wii Fit is also OK if you’re happy to pay £10 for a balance board on eBay that hasn’t been pounded to death.Kids’ gamesOnce again, these proliferated on the family-friendly Wii and DS consoles and as they hold little replay value, they show up in great numbers. Peppa Pig, Pirates of the Caribbean, lots of pet games – one store I found in Brighton had at least five horse sims, including Horse Life and Pippa Funnell. Ubisoft’s range of job sims including Imagine: Fashion Designer and Imagine: Teacher were in abundance, though sadly, I didn’t find a copy of Imagine: Journalist, which would have been useful. One title in this genre that was present in at least 65% of the shops I visited was CarnivalGamesfrom 2K Play, a wretched collection of fairground mini-challenges including duck shoot, ring toss and balloon darts. The motion controls are appalling and the player avatars are terrifying, dead-eyed monstrosities. If the backrooms had a games area, this would be playing.Blockbuster games from previous console generationsSome games sold so well, they have absolutely no value in the secondhand market. You can always count on finding a number of Call of Duty, Assassin’s Creed or Gears of War instalments as well as many copies of GTA V. Some of these are worth rediscovering. The campaign modes in Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare, Modern Warfare 2 and Infinite Warfare are exciting nonsense, while Assassin’s Creed Brotherhood, Origins and Odyssey are all worth playing – as is Assassin’s Creed 2. I’d also buy Gears of War 2 and Halo 2 for the campaign modes if you’ve not played them. The Mass Effect and Dragon Age titles are often knocking about and still have a lot of charm.PC gamesView image in fullscreenCD-Rom drive anyone … some old PC games.Photograph: Keith Stuart/The GuardianThese are still clogging the shelves of charity shops everywhere, despite (or perhaps because of) the fact that a lot ofPCowners no longer have CD-Rom drives, and even if they did, they’re likely to face compatibility issues trying to load ancient copies of, say, The Sims 2 or saucy adult adventure title, Leisure Suit Larry: Box Office Bust (the latter might still be in the Frome branch of the Cats and Dogs charity shop if you’re interested). With digital stores such as Steam and GOG stuffed with retro titles at teeny prices, there’s little reason to buy disc PC games now – unless you stumble across an ancient “big box” copy of Doom, Half-Life or Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders. Which you won’t.The odd gemView image in fullscreenOpportune moment … Time Crisis gamesPhotograph: Keith Stuart/The GuardianThey’re still out there, especially at pop-up charity shops and smaller independent stores. I bagged a copy of the rare Japanese role-playing adventure Koudelka at the Rotary Club shop in Frome for a pound, and feel a little guilty about it. I also recently acquired the light gun titles Time Crisis II (PS2) and Time Crisis: Razing Storm (PS3) for £3 each – and I even have a G-Con 2 and PlayStation Move controller to play them with. Elsewhere, I’ve regularly spotted copies of Dead Rising, Bulletstorm, FEAR and Project Gotham Racing – all great fun. Oh and fellow games contributor Jordan Erica Webber recently found Tiger Electronics’ handheld LCD game Poke Ball at the Cats Protection shop in Leamington Spa. I’d have snapped that up.But if youdofind a copy of Burning Rangers on the Sega Saturn it is completely worthless and terrible and you should just send it straight to me.Explore more on these topicsGamesRetro gamesSports gamesQuiz and trivia gamesPuzzle gamesWiiPlayStationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A universal human story’: Clean Start’s thought-provoking tidying sim tells immigrant’s tale | Games | The Guardian
description: Playing as recent arrival Lena, your challenges include learning a new language and uncovering family secrets – its developer hopes it will spread ‘a little more compassion’
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Playing as recent arrival Lena, your challenges include learning a new language and uncovering family secrets – its developer hopes it will spread ‘a little more compassion’
Content: Clean Start.Photograph: Serious Sim, Amplified GamesView image in fullscreenClean Start.Photograph: Serious Sim, Amplified GamesSummer games previewsGames‘A universal human story’: Clean Start’s thought-provoking tidying sim tells immigrant’s talePlaying as recent arrival Lena, your challenges include learning a new language and uncovering family secrets – its developer hopes it will spread ‘a little more compassion’Keith StuartFri 31 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 09.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe cosy house-sorting sim has become a much-loved staple of the PC indie scene. Titles such asUnpacking,A Little to the Leftand Momento charm players with their detailed interiors and quiet narratives of lives lived and shared within the same four walls. For Clean Start, Polish developer Serious Sim has taken a different approach – here you play as domestic cleaner, Lena, an immigrant who has arrived in an unspecified western country with little knowledge of the local language, and a family to support back home.From here, you’re tasked with cleaning a series of houses and apartments, polishing tables, tidying shelves and scrubbing muddy pawprints from kitchen floors. It seems you’re able to rearrange the rooms, giving them a personal feel, which is after all one of the most pleasing elements of the genre. You can also, we are reassured, pet the dog.View image in fullscreenPersonal feel … Clean Start.Photograph: Serious Sim, Amplified GamesFor artist and game director Katarzyna Haptaś the game has personal meaning. “It is largely inspired by the stories my mother told about working abroad as a domestic cleaner,” she says. “But that experience was shared by many members of my family, as well as my friends’ families. Back in the 90s, there was always some kid who had a parent working elsewhere, sending packages home for Christmas. I was blessed to hear stories from my grandmother as well. She went to America with only a few dollars in her purse and no confirmation that anyone would be waiting for her at the airport. All of that at a time when there was no internet or cellphones.”Haptaś has drawn on her own experiences, too. Working as a cleaner in a local cinema taught her how people interact with cleaning staff. The team researched the experiences of those coming to her home country to seek work. “During the pre-production phase of the prototype, we managed to have an interview with an immigration centre worker in Poland,” she says. “She shared many insights on immigrants working in Poland at the time, mainly from war-torn Ukraine.”Interestingly, the game uses language as a key part of its challenge. While chatting to Lena, her employers use unfamiliar words that she can learn through interacting with the environment. Owners will also ask you to find specific objects, usually with sentimental value or family stories and dramas attached. “By interacting with certain objects, players can piece together clues about what’s happening in each client’s life,” says Haptaś. “Often, these items help the clients realise something important or uncover a secret that was kept from them. Depending on what the player finds, there are different lines of dialogue commenting on it. Finding the right combination of items will reveal the full story to the player.”Clean Start isn’t just a cosy house-tidying sim – instead, it is using this genre to explore themes of connection, comfort and closure. Immigration has become such a polarising debate, there is value in such a quiet depiction. “I hope this is a universal human story,” says Haptaś. “I hope that people will see each other as human beings, with all of our shared hopes and fears. Leaving home to work in a foreign country with limited knowledge of the language is never an easy decision. It wasn’t easy in the 90s and it isn’t easy today. Ultimately, I hope that players will leave with a little more compassion and patience for those who are simply doing their best to work and communicate.”Clean Start is released on PC on 5 November, a demo isavailable on SteamExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tao of Glass review – stage magic as McDermott meditates on the minimalist master | Stage | The Guardian
description: This multifaceted and intensely personal homage to – and collaboration with – composer Philip Glass is a transcendent tapestry suffused with joy and wonder.
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: This multifaceted and intensely personal homage to – and collaboration with – composer Philip Glass is a transcendent tapestry suffused with joy and wonder.
Content: Music as a river … Phelim McDermott in Tao of Glass.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMusic as a river … Phelim McDermott in Tao of Glass.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianStageReviewTao of Glass review – stage magic as McDermott meditates on the minimalist masterSoho Place theatre, LondonThis multifaceted and personal homage to – and collaboration with – composer Philip Glass is a transcendent tapestry suffused with joy and wonder.Alexandra CoghlanFri 31 Jul 2026 11.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 11.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAshow that doesn’t happen (and one that’s never seen); a shattered coffee table; the I Ching; Maurice Sendak; a flotation tank; Deep Democracy. Just some of the disparate fragments that are lovingly assembled by the Tao of Glass into what writer and co-director Phelim McDermott has called “a storytelling tapestry – part concert, part performance”. Premiered at2019’s Manchester International festival, this beguiling meditation now makes its London debut – albeit without the figure who looms tousle-haired and scowling behind it: composer Philip Glass.Glass’s music has been, McDermott explains, a “river” through his life. The award-winning director’s fascination started as a teenager, lying on his bedroom floor listening to Glassworks on repeat, later crystallised by a little light stalking (the young McDermott follows Glass through the streets of Covent Garden) and professional collaborations on the composer’s operas.But it’s a show they never made together – an adaptation of Maurice Sendak’s In The Night Kitchen, derailed by the author’s death – that becomes the catalyst for a series of theatrical vignettes for McDermott, a trio of puppeteers and quartet of musicians, each set to a specially composed piece by Glass. All coalesce around Glass’s own question: where does music come from?View image in fullscreen‘A fool’s motley of sheet music and sticky-tape.’Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianFor “music” read art, inspiration, life. This is theatre about theatre, a monologue that uses all the genre’s tricks and techniques to magic McDermott – initially discovered sitting in the front row – from the stalls to the stage, from childhood wonder to adult maker. If that sounds solipsistic then it fails to take into account the creative delight, the humour and joy distilled into a monologue that makes a hooded Chinese philosopher out of a sheet of manuscript paper, turns the inner mechanism of a piano into the New York skyline, and kitchen utensils into an orchestra. There’s a tear-jerker, a fourth wall in tatters, even a jump-scare. It’s all here.Don’t expect a linear narrative. This is a homage to Glass, after all, and McDermott and co-director Kirsty Housley’s structure is a mirror to the composer’s own: images, gestures and themes looping, echoing, rhyming, evolving through repetition. What looks baggy and absurd – like McDermott himself, covered in a fool’s motley of sheet music and sticky-tape – is anything but. There’s no breadcrumb dropped that doesn’t lead us home, no seed planted that doesn’t swell.Glass’s music, meanwhile, is the river running through the show – frenetic, churning over a jagged bed of percussion in Newspaper, wistful and yearning in twining violin and clarinet in Maurice. The 89-year-old composer might not appear as he did in Manchester, but his ghost-presence in Coma (no spoilers) is at once the simplest and most electrifying stage-magic. Tao of Glass starts by asking us where music comes from, but ends up showing where it can take us to.AtSoho Place, London, until 12 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatrePhilip GlassreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Beguiling beauties, designs to be sat on and giant corn dollies – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Gwen John’s singular poetic world, Enid Marx’s signature designs for the London Underground and the rural gothic of LR Vandy – all in your weekly dispatch
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: Gwen John’s singular poetic world, Enid Marx’s signature designs for the London Underground and the rural gothic of LR Vandy – all in your weekly dispatch
Content: Gwen John, Girl with Bare Shoulders, c 1910.Photograph: SCALA Archives/© Digital image, The Museum of Modern Art, New York, Scala, FlorenceView image in fullscreenGwen John, Girl with Bare Shoulders, c 1910.Photograph: SCALA Archives/© Digital image, The Museum of Modern Art, New York, Scala, FlorenceArt Weekly newsletterArt and designBeguiling beauties, designs to be sat on and giant corn dollies – the week in artGwen John’s singular poetic world, Enid Marx’s signature designs for the London Underground and the rural gothic of LR Vandy –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 31 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekGwen John: Strange BeautiesThis excellent and moving encounter with the Welsh modern painter, touring from Wales’s National Museum, takes you deep into John’s silent, poetic world.Modern Two, Edinburgh, from 1 August until 4 JanuaryAlso showingThe Pattern of Life: Enid Marx and Modern British DesignCreator of the London Underground’s seat coverings and other classic fabrics, Marx is presented here as a major modern designer.Compton Verney, Warwickshire, until 3 JanuaryEast of the Aldgate PumpA survey of contemporary artists working in east London, including Rene Matić and Denzil Forrester.Whitechapel Gallery, London, until 6 SeptemberLR Vandy:RiseGiant corn dolly-like sculptures arranged round a Maypole offer a draft of rural gothic for summer.Yorkshire Sculpture Park, until 13 SeptemberRanti Bam: Sacred GrovesThe mysterious power of clay to connect nature with the human body is explored by this British Nigerian artist.South London Gallery, until 23 AugustImage of the weekView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Saul LeiterEra-defining photographs from the likes of Alfred Stieglitz, Dorothea Lange and this image from uptown Manhattan in 1960 by Saul Leiter showcase the US cityscape, from midnight crime scenes to gloomy corridors. They are part of a major new show in London.See our full galleryWhat we learnedThe fight to save the world’s only women’s sculpture park from becoming a generic space for VIP events and cocktails is onGunter von Hagens died this week, but his plastinated horrors will endureNearly 20 Georgia O’Keeffe works inspired by her New Mexico will show in the UK for the first timeCharles Rennie Mackintosh’s iconic Glasgow School of Art faces ‘curated decay’Startling unseen work by the late Brett Whiteley has been found at his studioKyiv wants to erect a statue of a Cossack chief in place of ‘enemy of humanity’ Leninskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArtists find creative haven in Côte d’Ivoire’s ‘calm and soothing’ Grand BassamMasterpiece of the weekThe Water Cistern (‘La Fontaine’) byJean-Siméon Chardin, 1733 or laterView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Heritage Images/National galleryWe can’t see this young woman’s face as she bends to release water from a bronze tank into a wooden bucket. She’s dressed in simple clothes and doing exhausting work so we assume she’s a servant in a grand house or on a farm. That’s as much of a story as you can extract from Chardin’s painting, for it expands one moment in time, the little drama of the water splashing from the tap and the silent attentiveness of the servant. Life, in the eyes of this early 18th-century painter of the humble and factual, is made up of such moments. This painting is in a line of quietness observed that leads from Vermeer’s Milkmaid to Gwen John’s portraits of women reading in solitude. As the maid fills her bucket, we notice a red and white slab of meat hanging in the shadows: this hunk of flesh might add a carnal hint to the scene, or make you think of mortality. For this peaceful routine takes place, the slaughtered animal reminds us, in a world of violence and desire that always threaten to destroy Chardin’s treasured calm.National Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get in TouchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsLondon UndergroundfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A World Elsewhere review – chaotic thrills as kids sail, fight and fall through trap doors | Children's theatre | The Guardian
description: Family show brings gleeful playfulness to the story of a 12-year-old whose escape into extravagant daydreams has begun to alarm him
Author: Miriam Gillinson
Headline: Family show brings gleeful playfulness to the story of a 12-year-old whose escape into extravagant daydreams has begun to alarm him
Content: Larks … Kerry Frampton as Sarah, Tanvi Virmani as Cobweb and Kyle Ndukuba as Cass in A World Elsewhere at Shakespeare's Globe.Photograph: Manuel HarlanView image in fullscreenLarks … Kerry Frampton as Sarah, Tanvi Virmani as Cobweb and Kyle Ndukuba as Cass in A World Elsewhere at Shakespeare's Globe.Photograph: Manuel HarlanChildren's theatreReviewA World Elsewhere review – chaotic thrills as kids sail, fight and fall through trap doorsSam Wanamaker Playhouse, LondonFamily show brings gleeful playfulness  to the story of a 12-year-old whose escape into extravagant daydreams has begun to alarm himMiriam GillinsonFri 31 Jul 2026 06.28 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 07.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe more children you bring along to this new family show – the latest co-production from the Globe theatre and Splendid Productions – the more fun you’ll have. It’s ostensibly about a 12-year-old school boy, Cass, who is struggling with his doubts and fears and considering reining in his imagination altogether. However, what makes this stubbornly ambitious production so special is the gleeful sense of playfulness it ignites in the young audience, as well as the parents watching alongside them.View image in fullscreenCracking make-believe … Kerry Frampton as Sarah and Kyle Ndukuba as Cass in A World Elsewhere.Photograph: Manuel HarlanThe story unfolds in young Cass’s imagination; a place populated by a host of cracking make-believe characters. There’s classical Shakespearean actor Sarah, played with a twinkling sense of pomposity by Kerry Frampton (also a co-writer on the show). Then there’s Tanvi Virmani’s plucky Cobweb - a minor Shakespearean character who has stuck around in Cass’s mind thanks to a brilliant production of A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Finally we have Zachary Willis’s Big Guy, one of Cass’s favourite TV characters, who spends most of his time enacting very silly and very funny play-fights.Much of the show is spent larking around with the gang, while Cass (Kyle Ndukuba) sulks moodily on the edges of the action. Together we sail the seas, summon up huge swaying forests and battle monsters, all directed with a lovely light touch from Lucy Cuthbertson. As Cass’s anxiety grows stronger, Rose Revitt’s design sparks into thrilling life. Actors are swallowed up by trap doors, smoke billows through the theatre and a huge, looming shadow-puppet threatens to engulf us all.It’s all effortlessly captivating until the second half, when things get a touch too meta-theatrical and ultimately pretty confusing. There’s a complicated strand about the importance of messiness and fear, and a slightly buried idea about just how boring our lives, stories and Shakespeare’s plays would be without a little bit of chaos. It’s a lot to fold in to a loosely constructed family show, and the younger children’s eyes begin to glaze over. But it isn’t long before the fun begins again and we’re reviving Cass’s friends with some magic dust, singing and tickling – all thanks to suggestions happily bellowed out from the audience.At Globe theatre, London,until 30 AugustExplore more on these topicsChildren's theatreTheatreShakespeare's GlobereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘If a space is cared for, everything improves’: Meet four gardeners transforming their urban communities | Gardens | The Guardian
description: From improving biodiversity to managing antisocial behaviour, the benefits of greening towns and cities are massive. These names are leading the charge…
Author: Matt Collins
Headline: From improving biodiversity to managing antisocial behaviour, the benefits of greening towns and cities are massive. These names are leading the charge…
Content: Paint the town green … The garden at Hepworth Wakefield.Photograph: Jason IngramView image in fullscreenPaint the town green … The garden at Hepworth Wakefield.Photograph: Jason IngramGardens‘If a space is cared for, everything improves’: Meet four gardeners transforming their urban communitiesFrom improving biodiversity to managing antisocial behaviour, the benefits of greening towns and cities are massive. These names are leading the charge…Matt CollinsFri 31 Jul 2026 06.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe importance of green space in Britain’s increasingly urban landscape – from city parks to community gardens and allotments – is unequivocal. Public Health England reports that regular exposure to green spacereduces stress and improves wellbeingand physical fitness, while the Natural History Museum has highlighted its value incooling city infrastructure and reducing pollution. Functional cities depend on functional greenery, yet the upkeep of these vital environments remains precarious. With parks and green spaces classified as non-statutory services, local authorities continue to slash their funding, relying increasingly on volunteer groups to maintain them.A leading voice advocating for change is John Little ofCare Not Capital, a community interest company offering free training for gardeners working in the public sphere so that they can have a greater influence on the spaces they maintain and those who govern them. “Green spaces are not sustainable unless you have someone looking after them,” says Little. “Yet in the public realm, the investment is often about infrastructure – overly designed landscapes and extravagant architecture – and rarely the ongoing care.” Investment in skilled gardeners, he argues, leads to positive outcomes far beyond good horticultural upkeep, from biodiversity increase and climate crisis mitigation to better community engagement and reduced antisocial behaviour.Little partnered with garden designer Susanna Grant to launch Care Not Capital last year, enlisting experts to deliver free training across a series of study days held at his much-celebrated garden Hilldrop in Essex. The inaugural course in 2025 saw 18 professional public-space gardeners develop skills in habitat creation, biodiversity surveying and community engagement. “By training gardeners to work in more creative, ecological and biodiverse ways, we make green spaces more engaging, more inclusive, and more valuable to their communities.”Much of the inspiration behind Care Not Capital stems from Little’s experience as a contractor for a social housing estate in Hackney, east London, in the early 2000s. Working alongside his brother, maintaining the estate’s formerly neglected green areas, Little saw how the presence of an enthusiastic, creative gardener yielded unexpected results. “Initially, we just started to make the place look like someone cared,” he says, but, listening to what the estate’s diversity of residents actually wanted from their green space ultimately led to Little sowing wildflowers, creating 60 new food growing allotments and planting specific fruit trees and shrubs culturally valued by residents of differing ethnicities, including medlars and grape vines. It led to far more interaction between residents, he tells me. “The role of a gardener can have such a huge impact on both places and people. If a space is cared for, everything improves.”With Care Not Capital now completing its second year of training, I spoke with four public space gardeners transforming their local communities.AccessibilityKaty Merrington, The Hepworth WakefieldView image in fullscreen‘To have this really top-class garden free and accessible is wonderful’: Katy Merrington.Photograph: Jason IngramWhen the Hepworth gallery in Wakefield decided to convert the derelict land on its doorstep into an ornate public garden accessible for all, employing a skilled, full-time gardener was a central priority. Katy Merrington, whose title is “cultural gardener”, was in place when the garden opened in 2019: it’s a four-season tapestry of colourful perennials intersected by weaving paths and breakout spaces designed by landscape architect Tom Stuart-Smith. Leading a team of volunteers, Merrington is a regular presence in the garden, which has become a place of inspiration, respite and social interaction.“One of the Hepworth’s missions is to inspire positive change locally,” Merrington tells me. “So to have this really top-class garden free and accessible in the city is wonderful – gardens like this typically charge an entrance fee, or you need a car to get to them.”A 2019 study by the University of Sheffield found that the visible presence of a gardener makes visitors feel safer and more comfortable using green spaces. Merrington agrees: “Your presence makes the place feel inhabited; people love to see you working it. That study also proved that a badly kept public park adversely affects health outcomes – a park full of litter doesn’t lift your spirits, but if it’s well cared for the health outcomes are substantial.”BiodiversityBenny Hawksbee, Eden Nature Garden, LondonView image in fullscreen‘For zone 2 London, the species list is quite cool’: Benny Hawksbee.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianGardener Benny Hawksbee looks after the Eden Nature Garden, a public pocket park in Clapham, south London. Employed by St Paul’s church, in whose grounds the garden resides, Hawksbee has developed the space into a haven for people and wildlife alike, from sparrowhawks to solitary mining bees. “For zone 2 London, the species list is quite cool,” he says. “We’ve had the second British recorded sightings of thread-waisted wasps from the Americas,Isodontia mexicana.”Regularly gardening the space has allowed him to experiment with habitat provision (“adding things like leaf stacks, stem bundles, standing water”), and to monitor the garden’s biodiversity using the citizen science apps iNaturalist and iRecord. “Gardeners are the best people for recording wildlife, because they’re in the same place every week, nurturing and observing. Over time they could end up recording more data than entomologists and ecologists, even.”CommunityShereen Chung-Blake,Londonskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘The garden’s had a tangible effect on community cohesion’: Shereen Chung-Blake (right).Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianAt a council estate in Camberwell, south London, resident Shereen Chung-Blake took public greening into her own hands, converting a disused patch of public lawn into a thriving community garden and allotment. “It was just grass before, and a lot of antisocial behaviour,” she tells me. “The trees were used to train bully dogs, there was fly-tipping.”Initially, Chung-Blake – who is project coordinator for theFuture Gardenerscourse, a free horticultural training scheme for individuals with barriers to employment – sought council funding for five food-growing beds, under Southwark’s Allotment Expansion Guarantee. “I knocked on doors and managed to get enough people involved to go ahead.”That was 2023; the garden is now alive with birdsong and skipping butterflies; there is a pond, a rainwater capturing shed, and a significant expansion of the original allotments. As the garden’s ongoing manager, Chung-Blake volunteers her weekends and evenings in the garden. “With a green space you need someone to lead it and keep that forward momentum,” she says.“But the garden’s had a tangible effect on community cohesion. It acknowledges the cultural richness of the many people living here, for whom growing food is part of their culture. When I talk to people over the wall, I hear all the time, ‘Oh, I used to grow that in my country,’ or ‘This reminds me of home.’ This place is becoming like a food forest, it’s really special.”Climatecrisis mitigationOwen Hayman,the Green Estate, SheffieldView image in fullscreen‘At its heart, Grey to Green is about managing flood water’: Owen Hayman (left).Photograph: Alastair Johnstone/Climate VisualsSheffield city council’s Grey to Green scheme is a leading example of city greening. Conceived in response to dramatic flooding in 2007, a mile of sustainable drainage system (SuDS) planting beds capture rainwater runoff, mitigating the effects of the increasingly volatile climate while providing a green corridor in the city centre. Comprising complex ecological plantings, the scheme is maintained by the Green Estate, a social enterprise focused on urban and environmental regeneration.Owen Hayman, the Green Estate’s horticulture innovation manager, tells me: “At its heart, Grey to Green is about managing flood water, but then it has the biodiversity and economic regeneration benefits, the green transport route, walking and cycling. Gardeners understand all the different functions the planting is playing, and help support them – but it takes time, observation and knowledge.”Explore more on these topicsGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Skincare staple or expensive gimmick: do you really need an LED face mask? | Skincare | The Guardian
description: They promise clearer, younger-looking skin, but is your money better spent elsewhere? Dermatologists and experts weigh in
Author: Sarah Matthews
Headline: They promise clearer, younger-looking skin, but is your money better spent elsewhere? Dermatologists and experts weigh in
Content: These scary-looking, space-age devices have become a staple in many a skincare routine.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThese scary-looking, space-age devices have become a staple in many a skincare routine.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianThe FilterSkincareSkincare staple or expensive gimmick: do you really need an LED face mask?They promise clearer, younger-looking skin, but is your money better spent elsewhere? Dermatologists and experts weigh inHow to build the perfect skincare routineSarah MatthewsFri 31 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Countless faddy products have crossed my desk over the years I’ve been reviewing beauty tech, from app-connected toothbrushes to AI-poweredhair dryers. Few, however, have held such sustained interest asLED face masks.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.At first glance, I assumed these scary-looking, space-age skincare devices would fizzle out of favour as quickly as they appeared. Instead, they’ve become a staple in some people’s skincare routines, including my own.LED masks use a process called photobiomodulation (PBM), where different light wavelengths are used to trigger specific processes in the body, as light stimulates the mitochondria – the “powerhouses” responsible for generating energy–in our cells.The first forms of light therapy usedconcentrated light to treat tuberculosis– and then, as its skin-rejuvenating properties were discovered, slowly evolved into the LED masks used today. “With consistent use, at-home LED therapy can lead to gradual, modest improvements in the skin, although results vary depending on the concern being treated,” says consultant dermatologistDr Derrick Phillips. “In general, LED works by supporting the skin’s natural repair processes. Red light can help reduce inflammation and stimulate collagen production over time, which may translate into subtly smoother, firmer-looking skin. Blue light, on the other hand, targets acne-causing bacteria and can help to reduce the frequency of breakouts in some people.”When you put it like that, the tech sounds like a painless, risk-free miracle treatment – something that feels rare and desirable in an age dominated byplastic surgery and “tweakments”. It’s not surprising that people have found these claims hard to resist: “Sales for LED masks were up 102% year on year in 2025,” says Lauren Starkey, a senior buying manager at Lookfantastic. And it’s a trend that has shown no sign of slowing in 2026.But with masks costing between £100 and £500, it’s sensible to question if you really need one, or if something more affordableor less time-consuming will have a bigger impact on your skin. You’ll also need to consider how often you’ll use it, as consistency is key to achieving results, and there’s no point buying gadgets only for them to gather dust in the corner.Can good skincare give the same results as an LED mask?View image in fullscreen‘Don’t even think about buying an LED face mask for anti-ageing if you don’t wear daily SPF.’Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian“LED masks can be a useful addition, but they’re not a substitute for the basics,” says Phillips. “In most cases, your money is better spent getting the [skincare] fundamentals right first, and then considering devices as an add-on once that foundation is in place.”I would add that my staunch commitment to skincare has bolstered the results of my LED mask use. I reach for mycleanserandmoisturiserevery evening, no matter how late it is or how many cocktails are coursing through my system. Admittedly, skincare isn’t always affordable, but Masters agrees that “topical actives often deliver stronger visible results per pound”.“Topical skincare and LED therapy work in slightly different ways, but there is some overlap in what they are trying to achieve,” says Phillips. “LED light can penetrate into the skin to trigger cellular responses involved in repair and regeneration.” This process can’t be exactly replicated using creams and serums.“Topical skincare tends to act more at the level of the epidermis,” says Phillips, but not all skincare is strictly surface level. “There are well-evidenced ingredients that can influence how skin cells behave,” he adds. Before you try an LED mask, he suggests looking into retinoids,vitamin Cand peptides, since they’re “designed to signal to the skin in a similar way”.As a rule, I’d recommend opting for a retinal serum at night for anti-ageing. I have usedMedik8 Crystal retinal, which is available in various strengths, so you can start low and increase the dosage when your skin acclimatises (beauty writer Sali Hughes alsorecommendsit). Peptides are a gentler alternative if you’re worried about the irritation retinoids can cause. I love theMedik8 peptide creamandthe Ordinary GF 15% serum. For spot-prone skin, invest in a product with salicylic acid. I keep a bottle ofPaula’s Choice BHA 2% tonerin my cupboard and use it sparingly as an on-the-spot treatment.Don’t even think about buying an LED face mask for anti-ageing if you don’t wear dailySPF: that’s like trying to bail out water using a colander. Sun damage is a leading cause of premature skin ageing – not to mention the risk of skin cancer – and active ingredients make your skin more vulnerable to the sun’s rays. I recommend theBeauty of Joseon Relief Sun SPF50 sunscreenas it has a silky texture that belies its affordable price, and it sits brilliantly under makeup.Before you jump in and raid the skincare aisle, try speaking with a dermatologist. This will arm you with tailored skincare recommendations, saving you from experimenting and wasting products and money.When integrating any new actives into your routine, it’s best to exercise caution. Always start using each active once or twice a week for a few weeks, then gradually increase the frequency. Any irritation, stinging or burning is a sure-fire sign that you should stop treatment.Are there cheaper alternatives to LED face masks?View image in fullscreenLED patches are more affordable than LED masks.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianIf you want a more affordable option, consider buying LED patches. They use the same LED technology but cover only a small, targeted area, and they’re cheaper than full masks, better for travel, and can be used all over the body. For acne-prone people, I recommend theLustre Solo patches,which use blue light to eliminate acne-causing bacteria and worked wonders on clearing my breakouts in my tests.Facial massage using a gua sha stone or facial roller can also help stimulate blood flow, reduce puffiness, and help the face appear more lifted. Some claim it may improve collagen production, too,although evidence is limited. This is a more active process than plopping on a face mask while flumped on the sofa – but you can pick up agua sha stone for as little as £15.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat are the benefits of an LED face mask?View image in fullscreen‘Daily treatments using blue, near-infrared and red light have reduced my breakouts.’Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian“People do not ‘need’ an LED face mask,” says Phillips, “but rather they are an optional extra to support skin health.” He advises that they can be particularly useful for anyone “looking to manage mild acne, reduce low-grade inflammation, or maintain overall skin quality between in-clinic treatments”.That aligns with my experience with LED face masks, which I’ve been using since 2024. My main concerns are blemish control and brightening my skin tone, and daily treatments using blue, near-infrared and red light have reduced my breakouts and ensured they heal faster than they did before.However, blue-light treatments aren’t suitable for everyone. “People with pigmentation and melasma need to be careful with blue light, since it can cause more inflammation,” warns facialistJustine Masters.“Use an LED mask as a maintenance tool, not a miracle device,” she continues. “Results are modest, and many cheap models lack sufficient power to deliver results.” In-clinic treatments are likely to use more powerful lights, although the cost of them can add up.Does spending more get you a better-quality LED mask?View image in fullscreenShark’s CryoGlow is a multitasking LED light therapy mask.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianIn my time testing LED masks, it’s become clear that cost isn’t always a prerequisite for quality. I’ve tried a£60 mask from Revolutionthat was wildly uncomfortable to wear, while a£700+ Foreo maskstarted to fall apart after a week and locked many of its preset treatments behind a subscription paywall in the “free” app.Having tested 15 for my roundup of thebest LED masks, my favourite overall is theCurrentBody Multi Light Therapy mask. It has a comfortable fit, brilliant facial coverage, a high-quality build, and a simple 10-minute treatment time. Or if you’re just in it for anti-ageing, I recommend theCurrentBody Series 2 mask. If you can’t justify spending that much, theShark CryoGlowcan help with both blemish busting and anti-ageing. Its three preset treatments are intuitive, and it has cooling pads to help reduce puffiness under the eyes.The best affordable option is theSilk’n Facial LED 100 mask. It feels marginally less sturdy than its high-end competition, but it’s comfortable and great for treating blemishes and early signs of ageing.For more, readSali Hughes’s pick of thebest anti-ageing creams, serums and treatmentsSarah Matthews is a consumer journalist who specialises in health and beauty reviews. In her four years of product testing, she’s worked her way through countless hair styling tools, hair removal, light therapy and skincare innovations. She’s seen beauty trends come and go, and can sniff out a fad from a gamechanger (that doesn’t mean she’s disciplined enough to always follow her own advice, though)Explore more on these topicsSkincareThe FilterBeautyGadgetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Benjamina Ebuehi’s summer berry dutch baby recipe | Summer food and drink | The Guardian
description: Think giant sweet yorkshire pud filled with a lake of summer berry compote
Author: Benjamina Ebuehi
Headline: Think giant sweet yorkshire pud filled with a lake of summer berry compote
Content: Benjamina Ebuehi's Summer berry dutch baby.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenBenjamina Ebuehi's Summer berry dutch baby.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.The sweet spotSummer food and drinkBenjamina Ebuehi’s summer berry dutch baby recipeThink giant sweet yorkshire pud filled with a lake of summer berry compote … that’s some brunch!Benjamina EbuehiFri 31 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis pancake/yorkshire pudding hybrid is nothing if not fun. The edges crisp and puff up in the most dramatic way, making for a very impressive brunch centrepiece that makes a change from regular pancakes. Although delicious just with some icing sugar, I’ve filled this one with a quick fruit compote to make the most of summer berries. The juices soak into the base, making way for my favourite part of a yorkshire: the slightly soggy bottom.Summer berry dutch babyWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep5 minRest20 minCook40 minServes4For the berry compote100gstrawberries,hulled and roughly chopped100g blackberries50g raspberries1 tbsp lemon juice2 tbsp caster sugarFor the batter110g plain flour25g caster sugar¼ tsp salt3 large eggs240mlwhole milk20g salted butterTo serve250ml double cream2 tbsp maple syrup,plus extra to serve½ tspvanilla bean pasteIcing sugar,to dustStart by making the compote. Add all the ingredients to a small pan and heat gently for a few minutes, until the fruits have softened but still hold their shape. Remove from the heat, set aside to cool completely, then chill until needed.Whip the double cream, maple syrup and vanilla together until soft peaks form; chill until you’re ready to serve.To make the batter, add the flour, sugar and salt to a large jug and mix to combine. Add the eggs and whisk to a thick mixture, then slowly pour in the milk, mixing again until the batter is smooth. (Alternatively, add everything to a blender.) Let the batter rest at room temperature for 20 minutes.Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7 and put a 25cm cast-iron pan in the oven to heat. Once hot, add the butter to the pan, carefully swirling it around, then put the pan back in the oven for one to two minutes, until the butter is melted and bubbling.Remove the pan from the oven, pour in the batter and bake for 15-20 minutes, making sure not to open the oven door in the first 15 minutes. The dutch baby is done when the edges are puffy and crisp, and there’s no wobble in the middle.Let the dutch baby cool for five minutes before spooning on the whipped cream, berry compote, an extra drizzle of maple syrup and a dusting of icing sugar. Serve straight away, because the dutch baby will begin to deflate.Explore more on these topicsSummer food and drinkThe sweet spotFoodDessertFruitBrunchrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Here comes the alt-bride: wedding gowns enter a more experimental era  | Wedding dresses | The Guardian
description: Celebrities including Charli xcx and Gabbriette and avant-garde brands honour tradition while also rejecting it
Author: Lauren Cochrane
Headline: Celebrities including Charli xcx and Gabbriette and avant-garde brands honour tradition while also rejecting it
Content: Charli xcx wore a minidress and sunglasses for her  wedding last year.Photograph: charlixcx/TikTokCharli xcx wore a minidress and sunglasses for her  wedding last year.Photograph: charlixcx/TikTokWedding dressesHere comes the alt-bride: wedding gowns enter a more experimental eraCelebrities including Charli xcx and Gabbriette and avant-garde brands honour tradition while also rejecting itLauren CochraneFri 31 Jul 2026 09.55 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 09.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf a wedding day brings to mind a bride dressed in a big white dress, the styles coming down the aisle in the near future may strike you as a little different. Whether it is through celebrity references, or new brands, wedding gowns are entering a more experimental era.For Charli xcx’s marriage to the 1975 drummer George Daniel last year,the bride wore a minidress and sunglasses.In July, the model and influencer Gabbriette married the 1975 singer, Matty Healy, wearing gothic makeup and a Victorian-style gown with bustle by Matières Fécales, the brand that has also dressed Lady Gaga and Zendaya despite the fact its name translates to “faecal matter”.View image in fullscreenWedding designs by the London fashion week designer Dilara Findikoğlu.Photograph: Dilara FindikoğluEmma Roberts, meanwhile, married fellow actor Cody John. If her dress was unremarkable, the lace veil falling across her eyes brought an artiness to her big day.View image in fullscreenA bridal design by Wed.There are a growing number of brands catering to the non-trad bride. This week, Dilara Findikoğlu – a London fashion week stalwart known for ornate corsets and references towards the occult – launched bridal wear. This followsWeddings& Funerals, the brand from Susie Cave, the founder of Vampire’s Wife, which only sells white and black dresses suitable for these two big life occasions.Joining the trend is Wed. Set up in 2019 by the Central Saint Martins graduates Amy Trinh and Evan Phillips, the brand sells dresses that suit the coquette trend along with short minis and designs with transparent panels.Speaking about her wedding dress toVogue, Gabbriette said: “Bridal is whatever you want it to be.” Findikoğlu echoes this sentiment: “[Women] don’t necessarily want to leave their personality behind on their wedding day. They want their bridal look to feel like an extension of who they already are, rather than becoming someone completely different for one day.”The dresses, therefore, reflect the look of the rest of Findikoğlu’s brand. “They carry our sense of rebellion,” she says. “They’re not perfectly polished in the way conventional wedding dresses often are.” Wed, meanwhile, began because Trinh was getting married and could not find anything she wanted to wear. Seven years later, the brand has proved there is a gap in the market. “It’s not always the creative types,” says Trinh. “We have people who work in tech, who are lawyers, who work in finance … They know what they like, and they’re quite sure of themselves.”View image in fullscreenElizabeth Taylor’s yellow wedding dress from 1964 shows the alternative trend is not new.Photograph: Hulton Archive/GettyEmma Firth, the writer and host of the Rejection is Romantic literary salon, says these dresses reflect a less fixed idea of marriage now. “Before there was a sense of you had to be with a person for a certain amount of time, if you were in your early 30s, that’s a good time to do it,” she says. “I think we’ve moved on from that quite rigid societal expectation.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenYoko Ono wore white sneakers for her marriage to John Lennon in Gibraltar in March 1969.Photograph: APAlternative bridal wear is not new. Firth points toElizabeth Taylorgetting married in yellow to Richard Burton in 1964, and Yoko Ono wearing sneakers for her marriage to John Lennon in 1969. Bridget Dalton, the head of Truth Futures at the brand consultancy Truth Consulting, cites Zoe Ball on her wedding day in 1999, wearing ripped jeans and carrying a bottle of Jack Daniel’s.The alt bride trend of 2026, however, comes at a time when marriage is less common. A report by theCentre for Social Justicefrom February found there were about 224,000 marriages in 2023, compared with more than 400,000 in 1970. Among younger people, 3.9% of women and 2.1% of men married before the age of 25, compared with 81.8% and 62.5% respectively in 1975.Even if these designer dresses are probably out of the price range of potential young brides, could the rise of alternative bridal wear – not to mention the nuptials of more rock’n’roll celebrities such as Gabbriette andCharli xcx– potentially put the institution back on the radar of gen Z?Dalton says it allows a foot in each camp. “It’s all about disavowing the saccharine sacredness, giving the finger to the infantilising princessness of former bridal aspiration. But nonetheless, you are still a bride, you’re still in the ecosystem of convention.”Trinh and Phillips are wary of any celebrity becoming a blueprint for a woman’s big day. “There’s something in culture that tells you if you’re not wearing that style, then your wedding’s not going to be cool,” says Phillips. “Whereas actually the coolest thing is when a bride puts a dress on, any dress, and they’re like ‘this is me’.”Explore more on these topicsWedding dressesWeddingsCharli xcxThe 1975Elizabeth TaylorYoko OnofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Luxury is coming for our teeth – but should we really be paying £20 for a tube of toothpaste? | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Minty fresh flavours are out, gold plated toothbrushes are in, and dental experts are sceptical
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: Minty fresh flavours are out, gold plated toothbrushes are in, and dental experts are sceptical
Content: Toothbrushes and toothpaste are moving from the tumbler behind the sink to the forefront of social media sink shots.Photograph: Klaus Vedfelt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenToothbrushes and toothpaste are moving from the tumbler behind the sink to the forefront of social media sink shots.Photograph: Klaus Vedfelt/Getty ImagesFashion Statement newsletterFashionLuxury is coming for our teeth – but should we really be paying £20 for a tube of toothpaste?Minty fresh flavours are out, gold plated toothbrushes are in, and dental experts are scepticalDon’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereChloe Mac DonnellFri 31 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.First it came for handwash. Then deodorant. Now, the fancification trend has claimed its next victim: dental products. From £20 toothpastes to bottles of mouthwash that sound more like a perfume than a breath freshener, a new wave of oral care is blurring the lines between function and fashion.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Rather than being shoved in an old tumbler on the back of the shelf, today’s iterations of toothbrushes and pastes are at the forefront ofsocial media sink shots, proudly displayed alongside a three-wick candle and curated pile of skincare.A recent report from the marketing insights firmVLMdescribed the mouth in grander terms than we’re perhaps, used to, calling it “the new centre of gravity for beauty, longevity and self-expression”, and highlighting a shift in oral care from “a hygiene necessity into a pillar of holistic wellness”.With the emergence of brands that treat toothpaste more like a perfume, mint is no longer the default flavour. The French brandLe Bonworks with an aroma house in Grasse to create its offering, which includes everything from blackcurrant to rose and orange blossom in packaging that could be mistaken for a hand cream. The Swedish brandSelahatineven includes flavour notes in its descriptions. It recently teamed up with the fashion designer Rick Owens on a limited-edition line of products including a toothpaste with top notes of Madagascan vanilla and base of black pepper, which it describes as capturing “the quiet act of transformation”.Unsurprisingly, what you pop your pea-size amount of toothpaste on has also become a signifier.Apirorisells brushes with asymmetric bristle pads, designed for effective cleaning of the tooth surface, but its striking colour choices and signature gold accent are just as arresting. The Swiss brandAurezzitakes it one step further with 24k gold-plated handles, yours for £49. Elsewhere,Machetesells brushes hand-sculpted from Italian acetate, which it describes as a “design moment for your bathroom”, while vintage fans will love Acca Kappa’sretro designs. On the cheaper end of the scale, Curaprox’s £5.90 brushes come in a range of 31 different colours. Electric toothbrushes are also pivoting from harsh whites to gentle pastel shades that look soothing rather than shouty in a bathroom shelfie.Dr Brandon Nejati, founder of the Nejati Clinic in London, says the trend shows how wellness is encroaching all parts of our daily routines. “People are no longer looking at the body in isolation,” he says. “They increasingly understand that the mouth is not separate from overall health, but one of the body’s most important protective barriers and a gateway to the rest of the body.” Along with his co-founder and wife, Dr Mahsa Nejati, the duo have developed their own range of oral products, Mahsa, that consists of toothpastes and mouthwashes that they say aim to “support the oral microbiome, reduce inflammation and promote long-term oral wellness”.View image in fullscreenStylish but impractical?Photograph: ApioriNejati says the trend is helping to change the way people think about dental care. “People are far more likely to maintain habits that feel enjoyable, thoughtful and purposeful,” he says. Selahatin’s founder, Kristoffer Vural, meanwhile describes the brand as transforming “the most ordinary act into a rite of taste, memory and emotion”, which is certainly something to mull over during your two minutes of brushing.The trend is also having a knock-on effect on the dentist chair with clinics offering treatments beyond the basic polish and scale. Many now provide LED light therapy and lasers that may help reduce inflammation, while others offer complementary treatments such as acupuncture that may help with jaw issues.“For decades, oral care was largely focused on preventing cavities or whitening teeth,” Nejati says. “Today, there is growing recognition that maintaining a healthy oral microbiome, reducing chronic inflammation and preserving the integrity of the oral barrier may have implications far beyond the mouth. As the science has evolved, so too has consumer awareness.”However, with many people in the UK struggling to even get basic dental treatment due to ascarcity of NHS dentists, the maintenance of a smile is quickly becoming an even brighter status symbol.Not every dental expert is thrilled with this new luxury or holistic spin. Some upscale toothpaste brands, such as the US-founded labelTheodent, don’t contain fluoride, which the British Dental Association cautions against. “The introduction of fluoride toothpaste in the mid-20th century has had a transformative impact on oral health in the UK by significantly reducing tooth decay rates,” says its chair, Eddie Crouch. “It achieves this by remineralising weakened enamel, slowing mineral loss, and hindering plaque bacteria acids. The BDA would not recommend any toothpaste without it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCrouch is also critical of the trend’s high price tags. “You can find perfectly decent toothpaste at a pound shop,” says Crouch. “Ultimately the deciding factor isn’t whether your next tube comes with ‘notes of vanilla’, but whether it has the necessary fluoride to protect your teeth.”Nejati compares the trend to skincare where the efficacy varies widely. “Elevating the daily experience encourages consistency, but the products must also deliver genuine scientific value,” he says. “The difference should never simply be branding – it should be the underlying science, formulation and philosophy. If a product is genuinely designed to support the oral microbiome, help reduce inflammation, preserve the oral barrier and encourage healthier long-term habits, then it represents a fundamentally different proposition.”View image in fullscreenLeave it in the packet ... Selahatin x Rick Owens dental care travel set.Photograph: Rick OwensBut perhaps dental experts shouldn’t be too concerned. Just like Aesop handsoap pump bottles are often refilled with cheaper dupes, it appears some dental products may be treated as for display purposes only. In a Reddit thread dedicated to the Rick Owens x Selahatin collaboration, one user wrote: “I treat it more like a collectible.” They’re not the only one. Despite the manual toothbrush priced at £50 and toothpaste at £40, both items are now out of stock and fetching triple their original prices on resale sites. Expect to find them pride of place (and most likely unused) in the fanciest bathrooms sometime soon.To read the complete version of this newsletter – complete with this week’s trending topics in The Measure –subscribe to receive Fashion Statementin your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFashionFashion Statement newsletterDentistsnewslettersShareReuse this content
