title: Literary escapes: your favourite trips inspired by books | Top 10s | The Guardian
description:
From Dervla Murphy’s Northern Ireland to Elena Ferrante’s Naples, readers share the stories that inspired them to travel

• Tell us about a trip to Europe’s lakes and mountains – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From Dervla Murphy’s Northern Ireland to Elena Ferrante’s Naples, readers share the stories that inspired them to travel• Tell us about a trip to Europe’s lakes and mountains – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher
Content: The Giant's Causeway.Photograph: Chiara Salvadori/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Giant's Causeway.Photograph: Chiara Salvadori/Getty ImagesReaders' travel tipsTop 10sLiterary escapes: your favourite trips inspired by booksFrom Dervla Murphy’s Northern Ireland to Elena Ferrante’s Naples, readers share the stories that inspired them to travelTell us abouta trip to Europe’s lakes and mountains– the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 31 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 06.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWinning tip: Northern IrelandInspired by Dervla Murphy’s A Place ApartDervla Murphy’sA Place Apartpersuaded me to see Northern Ireland differently. Cycling through the country during the Troubles, she looked beyond headlines to find generosity and ordinary lives. Following in her footsteps, you can walk the walls of Derry and stand beside the Giant’s Causeway, where the landscapes are every bit as striking as she described. Yet it is the people you remember most. Conversations begin easily in pubs and cafes, with local people quick to recommend a favourite beach or walk. I went looking for the places Murphy described. I left with the conversations she promised I’d find.JamesProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Sarajevo, Bosnia and HerzegovinaInspired by Priscilla Morris’s Black ButterfliesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Aleksandr Medvedkov/ShutterstockI readBlack Butterfliesby Priscilla Morris during a long, hot Covid afternoon and was immediately intrigued by the city of Sarajevo. The book is set during the siege, but I was captivated by the description of the buildings mixing east and west. Last year, I finally went and experienced the beautiful city for myself. The surrounding mountains and the old town, mixed with haunting memories unapologetically left in view by way of bullet holes in buildings and “roses” in the pavement [to mark where mortars fell], gave off a unique atmosphere. There are hints of old Eastern European glamour, Middle Eastern rituals and precious hope for the richness of a hard peace to remain in place. It’s a place that took my heart and showed me that it’s OK, things change but we carry the memories for a reason.LouisePorquerolles, FranceInspired by Georges Simenon’s My Friend MaigretView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Telly/ShutterstockAs a Georges Simenon fan, I had always enjoyed the novelMy Friend Maigret, set on the island of Porquerolles off the French Mediterranean coast. Nearing 80 years old, I decided it was now or never to visit and resolved to travel by train. So, it was Eurostar to Gare du Nord, RER across Paris to Gare de Lyon, then on to Toulon (despite missing my booked train), a slow train to Hyères, a bus to the port and a boat to Porquerolles. Visiting the sites described in the novel was such a pleasure. I became “Porquerolled” and an addict of the unique atmosphere (and the island wine).LeighSan FranciscoInspired by Armistead Maupin’s Tales of the CityView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Chris LaBasco/ShutterstockIt has to be Armistead Maupin’sTales of the Cityseries. Originally a daily serial in the San Francisco Chronicle, these wonderful novels paint the city as a place of kindness, beauty and pleasure. It made me and my wife Nic commit to two years of saving so we could live like the Barbary Lane gang for a fortnight. San Francisco didn’t disappoint. Weird, gorgeous and fascinating, it’s a city that rewards ambling and curiosity, just as Maupin suggests.FraserOrkney, ScotlandInspired by Amy Liptrot’s The OutrunView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Harald Schmidt/ShutterstockI readThe Outrunby Amy Liptrot and went on to have a wonderful three-week holiday in Orkney and Shetland. I travelled solo and met the best of people. I stayed in Amy’s mum Jane’s B&B and she took me birdwatching. It was a time to recover from a challenging year and enjoy the peace and beauty of the islands while never feeling lonely. I spent a week in the Papay hostel and walked all around the island. My sister lives in Shetland now and I plan to return soon.AmandaBognor Regis, EnglandInspired by RC Sherriff’s The Fortnight in SeptemberView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Eye Ubiquitous/AlamyThe Fortnight in Septemberby RC Sherriff, written in the heyday of British seaside holidays, harks back to a time when resorts like Bognor Regis were magical summer destinations that an ordinary family would look forward to all year. The descriptions of the bandstand, beach and lovely walks inspired a trip to Bognor to retrace the family’s steps. Bognor may have seen better days, but it was a perfect base for days out in the Sussex countryside, and there’s still little to beat a stroll along the promenade of this fading seaside town, sun shining and ice-cream in hand.PatriciaProvence, FranceInspired by Émile Zola’s Contes ChoisisView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Serts/Getty ImagesWhile studying French A-level back in the 80s, I read Émile Zola’s Contes Choisis short stories, which made me long to explore Provence. I loved the book, and its visual descriptions made me hanker to see the area for myself. More than 10 years later, I finally got to visit the area, by which time I’d also discovered the works of Cézanne and Matisse. Provence was a glorious feast for all the senses. I have visited a few times now and am always impressed by the beauty. I still have my book, and it is a wonderful reminder of the inspiration of A-levels.SandraThe Apennines, ItalyInspired by Eric Newby’s Love and War in the ApenninesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: REDA/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesEric Newby’sLove and War in the Apenninesinspired me and my wife to spend a month hiking in the mountainous area running the length of central Italy. Newby’s praise for the brave honest people who sheltered him, as a fleeing prisoner of war, in stone cottages and freezing farmyard barns was uplifting. They helped him learn Italian, and the book also delights in showing how he met his wife Wanda, an Italian-Slovenian woman, while hiding from the Nazis. Newby depicts loving, tight communities in towns like Fiumalbo, which we enjoyed visiting and where we were given a warm welcome. When we mentioned Signor Newby and showed his book, we were met with smiles by local people. It felt like we were part of an appreciative, heartfelt legacy created by the writer and those he met.PeterNaplesInspired by Elena Ferrante’s My Brilliant FriendView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alessandro Tortora/Getty ImagesIn 2018, after devouring the novelMy Brilliant Friendby Elena Ferrante, my lifelong friend and I decided to visit Naples. The book explores two childhood friends who bonded and grew up in various edgy neighbourhoods around Naples in the 50s, exploring social class and poverty. Naples has always had a bad press, focusing on crime and shabbiness. We had wonderful times visiting the places mentioned in the book. We felt safe, were welcomed and fed. Chiaia is mentioned in the book as a waterfront renowned for its promenade along Via Francesco Caracciolo.CarolPrince Edward Island, CanadaInspired by LM Montgomery’s Anne of Green GablesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: James Schwabel/AlamyMy favourite childhood books, read countless times, were theAnne of Green Gablesseries by LM Montgomery, set in a rural community on Prince Edward Island, Canada. The snowy winters, enchanting woods, winding country lanes, and red sandstone cliffs along the coast captured my imagination, leaving a lasting impression. At the age of 44, I made the journey there myself. My first day was a bitter disappointment, with torrential rain and thick mist obscuring the island’s beauty from dawn until dusk. However, the second day more than made up for it. Under clear skies, I enjoyed a perfect coastal boardwalk, a truly magical visit to Green Gables itself, and finished the day with a wonderful lobster meal.KatharineView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsTop 10sReaders' travel tipsCultural tripsFictionTravel writingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Experience: I drive a bus for dogs | Life and style | The Guardian
description: I worked with children for years, so the noise doesn’t bother me. You know you’ve done a good job if they’re quiet on the way home
Author: Kate Chapman
Headline: I worked with children for years, so the noise doesn’t bother me. You know you’ve done a good job if they’re quiet on the way home
Content: Sharon Telford in the dog bus she drives around Leeds.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSharon Telford in the dog bus she drives around Leeds.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianExperienceLife and styleExperience: I drive a bus for dogsI worked with children for years, so the noise doesn’t bother me. You know you’ve done a good job if they’re quiet on the way homeSharon TelfordFri 31 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve been a bus driver for 25 years. Before that, I worked in engineering sales and was on the road a lot, but it became impractical once I had young children. I took my kids to soft play centres and I thought: “I could run a place like this.” I opened my own centre in a Victorian shopping arcade in Otley, West Yorkshire,in 1995. It was great as my daughters could come with me. Then, a customer told me about play buses – vehicles converted into soft play centres with slides, ball pits and climbing frames. I liked the idea.I went to an exhibition to look at some and bought a doubledecker that had already been converted. My uncle drove it home, because I couldn’t. I had to learn quickly as it was parked outside my house. It had no power steering and a ratchet handbrake. I threw up during my first lesson because I was so scared, but driving it soon became second nature. I passed my test within six months.I loved working on the bus. I drove it to different places for play sessions and met different people every day. Eventually, I gave the play centre up and focused on taking the bus to weddings, christenings and birthdays.In April 2025, after 25 years, I sold my bus. I was looking for something else to do and spotted a job advert seeking drivers for a new bus service. It said applicants must like animals, because the passengers would be dogs. I was intrigued.I called Laura Mohan, who was launchingBilly’s Bus, to find out more. She explained that the bus – named after her cavapoo, Billy – would collect dogs and take them to her private dog park for exercise when their owners couldn’t walk them themselves.I love animals. I’ve always had dogs – I have a rescue whippet – and have cats and horses, too. My first thought was that the bus was a mad idea, but it sounded fun. Laura reminded me of myself when I started my play bus.After an interview and a trial shift, I began driving in October 2025. It’s been great – people smile and wave when they see a yellow bus full of dogs.double quotation markSome have a favourite seat. One will bark at any dog sitting in theirsView image in fullscreenThe bus has been adapted for its canine passengers who sit in raised pods with harnesses and water bowls.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianAt first, I just drove the bus. Now I supervise dogs in the field, too. My day starts with vehicle checks at 10am, then I collect our passengers. We cover a 10-mile radius of Leeds.We can have up to 15 dogs on board. The bus has been adapted – the seats have been removed, and each dog sits in its own raised pod with safety restraints, harnesses and water bowls, with views out the window. All the dogs have a trial to make sure they’re suited to the service and get along with each other. We have people in the back talking to them and reassuring them. There’s a ratio of one person to six dogs.The dogs all love the bus, and they know the routine. As soon as we turn on to a particular road and cross over the cattle grid, they start barking. They can’t wait to get to the field. I worked with children for years, so the noise doesn’t bother me.We clip a tunnel on to the side of the bus to get the dogs off and into the field. They run free or play on the seesaw, swing and trampoline, which they go bonkers for. We stay for a couple of hours before going home.Back on the bus, the dogs get treats and puppuccinos. They’re usually quiet on the return – you know you’ve done a good job if they’re worn out.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome have a favourite seat on the bus. One poodle has a meltdown if another dog is in her pod on the front row. She stands there, barking at them, so we tend to let her sit there.Experience: I live as a craneRead moreI adore my job – it’s so joyful and it doesn’t feel like work. Some of the dogs can be a bit aloof at first, but when they relax and take a treat off you, it gives you a real buzz.My role has involved some more unusual work, too – I drove the bus in the Ilkley Carnival parade in Bradford, with 10 dogs on board and another 30 following behind. We also filmed an advert in a cinema to mark the release of the Disney film Hoppers. We had 10 dogs sitting in the seats and watching the beginning of the movie. I was behind them, holding the leads and trying to make sure they all sat still.The business has evolved since I started – there are plans for the service to go national. I’m 56 now, and I never thought I’d end up driving a bus for dogs, but it’s such good fun – I can’t see myself doing anything else.As told to Kate ChapmanDo you have an experience to share? title: ‘It ain’t the same’: inside the bitter battle to free Ben & Jerry’s | Business | The Guardian
description: Ben Cohen says his ice-cream company has been silenced by corporate ownership – and a boycott of Magnum brands could force a sale
Author: Heather Timmons
Headline: Ben Cohen says his ice-cream company has been silenced by corporate ownership – and a boycott of Magnum brands could force a sale
Content: Ben Cohen says there are ‘millions of people who support Ben and Jerry’s and support its social mission’.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBen Cohen says there are ‘millions of people who support Ben and Jerry’s and support its social mission’.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesBusiness‘It ain’t the same’: inside the bitter battle to free Ben & Jerry’sBen Cohen says his ice-cream company has been silenced by corporate ownership – and a boycott of Magnum brands could force a saleHeather TimmonsFri 31 Jul 2026 14.48 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBen & Jerry’s ice-cream in the tub is still great, but the brand’s newest chocolate-covered ice-cream bar on a stick?“It ain’t the same,” Ben Cohen, the company co-founder, told the Guardian. Sure, the chocolate coating is still thick enough, but the ice cream itself is “kinda fluffy”, Cohen said – an insult in the ice-cream world that suggests extra air was added to cut costs.The criticism is surprising coming from Cohen, who opened his eponymous ice-cream shop in Burlington, Vermont, with childhood friend, Jerry Greenfield, in 1978. But it’s perhaps an apt metaphor of how he feels amid a simmeringfightto take back Ben & Jerry’s from a parent company he says has silenced the brand’s trademark activism.For Cohen, 75, the battle is legal and existential. Ben & Jerry’s social and economic value was protected for decades, he says, by an independent board with final say on the brand’s voice, values and ice-cream quality.But that independence has all but disappeared, Cohen said. In November 2024, Ben & Jerry’s boardsued parent company Unilever, claiming it was blocked from voicing support for Gaza, and accusing Unilever of breaching their agreement. The lawsuit is still making its way through federal court.In September 2025, after Unilever said it would spin off its ice-cream brands into the Magnum Ice Cream Company, Cohenstartedhis campaign to “Free Ben & Jerry’s” – asking Magnum to sell the brand so it can be independently owned and operated.Social activism is a core part of why people buy Ben & Jerry’s, Cohen says. “What consumers want above all is authenticity and attitude,” he said.Ben & Jerry’s could be valued at $1bn or more, Cohen estimates, but says Magnum won’t give him or potential investors numbers that could help value it more accurately.Magnum has insisted Ben & Jerry’s is not up for sale, so Cohen is amping up his campaign. In recent weeks, Cohen has started calling for a boycott of Magnum’s other brands, including Yasso, Breyers, Talenti and Klondike, with the idea that tanking the company’s overall sales will pressure it to sell back the company.“We didn’t want it to have to come to this,” he said of the boycott, but Magnum is “destroying a brand” that stands for values its customers believe in.What Cohen is trying to do – force an $11bn conglomerate into divesting a star brand – is highly unusual, and unlikely to succeed, some industry and management experts predict.“Most boycotts fail because people get distracted,” said Maurice Schweitzer, a management professor at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania. US and European consumers just may not have the long-term attention span for the sustained collective action that it would take to pressure management, Schweitzer said.But Cohen believes the company’s loyal followers are on his side.“Consumers want to vote with their dollars,” he said, insisting that support for the brand must continue. “We want Ben & Jerry’s to remain strong because we plan on eventually owning it.”The flavors of conflictIt’s been nearly three decades since Cohen and Greenfield sold their company to Unilever for $326m in 2000. The unique deal was built around an independent board andlauded by the Wharton Schoolfor preserving thecompany’s pledgeto try to “make the world a better place” while also committing to making great ice-cream and turning a profit.Under Unilever, Ben & Jerry’s was vocally supportive of social issues. The company criticized George W Bush’s war in Iraq, was a pioneering supporter of same-sex marriage, and called to “dismantle white supremacy” after George Floyd was murdered.But now, the divide between the brand’s founders and the company’s corporate owners is deep and bitter.Cracks first opened after an independent board overseeing the company said in 2021 that selling Ben & Jerry’s ice cream in occupied Palestine was “inconsistent with our values”, sparking outrage in Israel. Unileversold off the Israeli trademarkto a local businessman who is now selling a“Milk & Honey” flavor.The board firstsued Unileverin 2024, accusing the company of silencing its activism over Palestine, including vocal support for Gaza and calls to stop US aid to Israel.Then in 2025, UnileveroustedDavid Stever, the Ben & Jerry’s CEO, in a move Ben & Jerry’s said was designed to stifle its social mission, including aboard-approved planto sell a watermelon flavor to support Palestine that was quashed.In a statement to the Guardian, Unilever said Stever’s role was re-evaluated because of the spinoff, not the social mission, and that he turned down a role in the larger company and chose to quit.Co-founder Greenfieldquitsoon after, stepping away from the company for the first time in 50 years, saying it had lost its independence. Currently, the board has just two Unilever veterans after Magnum imposed new term limits.Though the campaign to buy back Ben & Jerry’s has been led by Cohen, Greenfield said in his resignation letter that leaving the board was one of the “hardest and most painful decisions” he had ever made.“It is profoundly disappointing to come to the conclusion that that independence, the very basis of our sale to Unilever, is gone,” he said. “If the company couldn’t stand up for the things we believed, then it wasn’t worth being a company at all.”Earlier in July, Ben & Jerry’s philanthropic foundationsaid it was forced to closeafter Magnum cut its funding. Magnum says an investigation found “governance and conflict-of-interest issues”.In an interview with the Guardian, Magnum’s chief corporate affairs and sustainability officer Victoria McKenzie-Gould said it invited trustees of the foundation to partner on a stronger corporate governance framework, but they declined.“Our focus remains where it belongs: on supporting the Ben & Jerry’s team and its three-part mission while making great ice-cream and campaigning on the causes the brand cares about – and the team is doing a fantastic job,” McKenzie-Gould said.‘Not for sale’Throughout Cohen’s months-long fight to buy back his company, Magnum has said it has no intention of selling.“Ben is a great campaigner, but Ben & Jerry’s is not for sale, and we are confident in the future because Ben & Jerry’s is thriving as part of the Magnum Ice Cream Company,” McKenzie-Gould said.Magnum doesn’t break out sales by brand, but called Ben & Jerry’s one of its “top four”, with 3% organic sales growthin 2025;about 35% of Magnum’s €7.9bn ($9.1bn) 2025 revenue came from the Americas, traditionally Ben & Jerry’s largest market.Salesgrew 9.2%in the second quarter, “powered by innovation”, Ben & Jerry’s CEO, Jochanan Senf, said on Thursday, adding that all three parts of the company’s mission – social, product and economic – must “thrive equally in a way that commands deep respect for individuals in and outside the company”.Since it was acquired in 2000, Ben & Jerry’s “footprint has grown from four to over 40 countries, [and] revenue has grown more than fivefold,” McKenzie-Gould said. The company’s overall social mission has received €500m ($576m) from the parent – more than the original purchase price.The brand had spoken out recently on “ICE;refugee support in Europe;cannabis justiceand voting rights”, a corporate spokesperson for the Ben & Jerry’s brand told the Guardian, including a new flavor –Razz Up!– that encourages midterm voting.The spokesperson disagreed with Cohen’s criticism of the new ice-cream bars, saying the product was approved by the independent board in 2024 and used the same design standards as every product.“More than one-third of bar buyers in the last year are completely new fans to Ben & Jerry’s,” Senf said with second-quarter results.Cohen’s calls for a boycott comes as many Americans are angry at companies and frustrated over US policies. Americansupport for Palestiniansand criticism of Donald Trump have grown, and there’s agrowing frustrationwith big companies over shoddy products and bad service.But the headwinds for a successful boycott are stiff. There’s awar against“woke capitalism”, andshareholder supportfor environmental, social and governance resolutions has plummeted. Many of the social media platforms Cohen needs to spread his message are controlled by conservative billionaires, leaving him at the mercy of their algorithms.“I do think this is going to get lost in the shuffle of so many other causes,” said Schweitzer.Plenty of fans seem to think Cohen’s expectations are naive. “Did you really think a giant company wouldn’t exploit you? When has an international company ever had social values?” wrote Base_Art, a painter, on Instagram.But Cohen has also gathered about 200,000 signatures and lots of encouraging social media messages. “Occasionally, I ate the vegan coffee Talenti,” former model Christie Brinkley recently wrote on Instagram. But without an independent board of directors, she said: “No more!”Cohen acknowledges the hurdles, but says he believes longtime, loyal fans will help overcome them.“I think that there’s millions of people who support Ben and Jerry’s and support its social mission,” Cohen said. “I’m going to take it until we win.”Explore more on these topicsBusinessVermontnewsShareReuse this content

title: At least 57 people die as tens of thousands cross to Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco | Spain | The Guardian
description: Pedro Sánchez decries ‘violation of territorial integrity’ as other EU countries criticise Madrid over incident
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Pedro Sánchez decries ‘violation of territorial integrity’ as other EU countries criticise Madrid over incident
Content: People try to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on Thursday.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/APView image in fullscreenPeople try to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on Thursday.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/APSpainAt least 57 people die as tens of thousands cross to Spanish enclave of Ceuta from MoroccoPedro Sánchez decries ‘violation of territorial integrity’ as other EU countries criticise Madrid over incidentSam Jonesin Madrid,Angela Giuffridain Rome andJakub KrupaFri 31 Jul 2026 13.52 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 03.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 57 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after as many as 50,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco in what Spain’s prime minister,Pedro Sánchez, called “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”.The huge influx, which took place over the course of just 24 hours, overwhelmed the city of 85,000 people, triggered a political crisis for Madrid and led to a mixed reaction from other EU countries, including calls forSpainto be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.3:37Tens of thousands of migrants cross into Spanish enclave Ceuta from Morocco - videoSánchez, who arrived in Ceuta on Friday morning, said he would use all the resources at his disposal to guarantee the safety of the city’s population.He attributed the mass crossing to “human trafficking mafias” that had taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta, or Spain’s other north African enclave of Melilla, could not be summarily returned under special rules.Sánchez said: “That has spread like wildfire during these last few hours through the networks of mafias that traffic in human beings and has produced an avalanche of the characteristics and dimension that we experienced yesterday.”Sánchez said a temporary reception centre would be established to facilitate the documentation, registration, triage and “expedited” expulsion of people with no legal claim to be in Spain.Hundreds of migrants run and cheer as they enter Spain’s enclave of CeutaHe also said the government would erect a visible barrier – a line of buoys – near the breakwater at Ceuta’s Tarajal beach to make it clear where the border was, and to legally comply with the court’s ruling.Although the Spanish government said about 50,000 people had crossed the border on Thursday and in the early hours of Friday, the president of Ceuta put the figure at about 60,000.Spain’s interior ministry, which has deployed additional police officers and soldiers to the enclave, said more than 48,300 people had voluntarily returned toMoroccoby 6pm on Friday.The Irish presidency of the EU has convened a meeting of member states on Saturday, under the Integrated Political Crisis Response mechanism.EU sources said this will provide experts from member states with an opportunity “to discuss the movements into Ceuta over the last two days, the numbers of people who have returned to Morocco today, the supports being provided by the EU to Spain and diplomatic engagement with Morocco”.A further meeting of EU ambassadors has been called in Brussels on Monday.The latest incident dwarfs the last mass border crossing in May 2021, when Morocco loosened its border controls, allowing about 10,000 people to enter the territory over the course of two days.Map showing location of Ceuta between Spain and Morocco, and another map showing location of Tarajal breakwater in CeutaThat crossing came amid heightened tensions between Madrid and Rabat over Spain’s decision to allow the leader of the Western Sahara independence movement, the Polisario Front, to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. Morocco and the Polisario Front both lay claim to Western Sahara, which was under Spanish rule until 1975, when colonial authorities handed over the territory to Morocco and Mauritania.That diplomatic crisis ended in 2022 when Madrid reversed its longstanding policy of neutrality and backed Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara – a move that had caused a diplomatic rift between Spain and Algeria, which had supported the Polisario group.Sánchez visited Algiers on 20 July – the first such visit by a Spanish head of government in four years – marking a thaw in relations with Algeria.Moroccan government sourcestold the Europa Press news agencythat the surge of people entering Ceuta was down to “criminal organisations” and insisted that Rabat’s cooperation with Spain remained “exemplary”.Morocco’s ambassador to Spain, Karima Benyaich, was quoted by the Associated Press as saying that “we have always prioritized legal, orderly and safe migration for all” and indicated that the situation had developed against Rabat’s wishes.View image in fullscreenSpain’s interior ministry said more than 48,300 people decided to return to Morocco from the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on Friday.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/APRachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers’ association representing officers of the Spanish Guardia Civil – which patrols Spain’s borders – described the situation as a “serious humanitarian crisis”.Without shelter, thousands of people, including unaccompanied children, had been left sleeping in parks and on pavements, while others roamed the streets aimlessly. “It’s chaotic,” said Sbihi.Among those who died, many drowned, but some were killed in a crush to cross the breakwater fence at Tarajal beach, Sbihi said.View image in fullscreenPeople waiting on the Moroccan side of the border for a chance to cross to Ceuta.Photograph: ReutersVideo footage on Thursday showed crowds of people walking around the breakwaters at Tarajal beach on to local roads. While most appeared to be young men, there were also families with women and small children.Ceuta and Melilla have the E​U’s only land border with ​Africa. ‌Both cities ​periodically ​experience surges in attempted crossings by people seeking to reachEurope.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCrowds in downtown Ceuta on Friday after making the crossing.Photograph: Fabian Bimmer/ReutersThe events in Ceuta led some EU countries to issue strong threats or rebukes.Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, summoned Italy’s ambassador to Madrid on Friday after Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, blamed the situation in Ceuta on the Sánchez government’s decision to offer a now closed schemeto regularise the statusof more than 1 million undocumented migrants and asylum seekers. He said the programme had incentivised human trafficking and was “profoundly wrong”.Tajani’s remarks prompted a sharp response from Albares, who said the comments were “unbecoming” and accused Italy of “partisan demagoguery”.Italy announced on Friday evening that it would be suspending its Schengen arrangements with Spain, but the practical impact of the move was not immediately clear.Meloni said the measure would be kept in force only as long as needed, adding: “In parallel, Italy is ready to support every European initiative to assist Spanish institutions as needed to restore full control of the union’s external borders and to address the ongoing situation with determination.”View image in fullscreenSpanish soldiers patrolling the Spanish-Moroccan border in Ceuta on Friday.Photograph: Fabian Bimmer/ReutersResponding to Italy’s unilateral decision, aEuropean Commissionspokesperson said a member state “may exceptionally and temporarily reintroduce internal border control as a matter of last resort, to address serious threats to public order or national security”. But they added that the member state would need to notify the commission and explain how the situation in Ceuta constituted such a threat.The Guardian understands that Italy has not yet formally notified any of its EU partners of its decision.The Swedish prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, urged Spain to “act swiftly to regain control of the situation and fulfil its commitments within Schengen cooperation”.The Finnish interior minister, Mari Rantanen,saidthat as Spain had “completely failed to protect the Schengen area’s external border”, all EU countries should support Italy’s proposal to suspend its Schengen status.However, in a statement later on Friday, the European Commission said Ceuta and Melilla were subject to special Schengen rules that prevented onward movement within the zone.View image in fullscreenBelongings float in the sea after they were left behind by people crossing from Morocco into Ceuta.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/APThe EU’s migration commissioner, Magnus Brunner, called the situation in Ceuta “unacceptable” and said he was in close contact with the Spanish authorities. But he also confirmed there was no onward route from Ceuta given the enclave’s unique status under the Schengen rules.He said: “The Schengen borders code provides for special rules that apply to Ceuta and Melilla. Border checks on persons departing from Ceuta and Melilla remain in force.”But there were also shows of unity. The European Council president, António Costa, expressed his “solidarity with Spain in the current situation of illegal migration in Ceuta”.The French president, Emmanuel Macron, said he had been in touch with the Spanish government to express his solidarity and to offer assistance to Spain. But, as a precautionary measure, Macron said he had asked the interior ministry to strengthen the French controls on its border with Spain with four mobile units and drones.In Spain, the opposition People’s party (PP) called on Sánchez to come up with a tough response, saying the military and police reinforcements announced on Thursday night were insufficient.In a post on X, the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, wrote: “People have continued to arrive in Ceuta throughout the night, and those on the ground describe an occupied city, with nothing sufficient being done to prevent it.” The far-right Vox party called the incident “an invasion”.On Friday evening, hundreds attended an anti-migrant rally outside the Moroccan embassy in Madrid, with images showing some protesters performing Nazi salutes and waving flags with far-right insignia.Explore more on these topicsSpainMoroccoPedro SánchezEuropean UnionEuropean CommissionMigrationItalynewsShareReuse this content

title: Archbishop of Canterbury vows to support £100m pledge helping communities affected by enslavement | Anglicanism | The Guardian
description: During visit to Ghana, Sarah Mullally expresses regret and says controversial fund symbolises Christian belief in repentance
Author: Eromo Egbejule
Headline: During visit to Ghana, Sarah Mullally expresses regret and says controversial fund symbolises Christian belief in repentance
Content: The archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, walking with the bishop of Asante Mampong, Cyril Kobina Ben-Smith, in Mampong.Photograph: Francis Kokoroko/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, walking with the bishop of Asante Mampong, Cyril Kobina Ben-Smith, in Mampong.Photograph: Francis Kokoroko/ReutersCotton Capital: ongoing seriesAnglicanismArchbishop of Canterbury vows to support £100m pledge helping communities affected by enslavementDuring visit to Ghana, Sarah Mullally expresses regret and says controversial fund symbolises Christian belief in repentanceEromo Egbejulein Cape CoastFri 31 Jul 2026 07.38 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 10.57 EDTShareAt a former British castle where thousands of enslaved Africans were held before being shipped across the Atlantic, the archbishop of Canterbury expressed “lament” for the Church of England’s involvement in transatlantic chattel slavery and reaffirmed her commitment to a controversial £100m fund for affected communities.Sarah Mullally made the comments during a visit to the Cape Coast castle, a 17th-century fortress built by Swedish traders, but occupied by the Danish and the Dutch, before the British seized it in 1664.It was part of a 10-day tour ofGhanaand Cameroon at the invitation of the head of the Anglican church’s west Africa province, the archbishop Cyril Kobina Ben-Smith.“Being at Cape Coast castle today and seeing the horrific conditions that thousands of people were kept in, it is impossible not to feel the weight of the immense evil that drove the transatlantic slave trade,” Mullally said on Thursday.She was shown the dungeons used to keep enslaved people, before praying in a former Anglican chapel above them. She also visited the “Door of No Return”, where enslaved people were loaded on to ships and ferried across the Atlantic. It has since been renamed the “Door of Return”.View image in fullscreenThe archbishop of Canterbury at the former ‘Door of No Return’ at Cape Castle in Ghana.Photograph: Nana Osei Adu-Boahene / Lambeth PalaceHer trip began in the Ghanaian capital of Accra, about 90 miles (145km) east of Cape Coast on Sunday. There, Mullally visited four local parishes and delivered the sermon at a special Eucharistic service at St Joseph the Worker Anglican church in the Kaneshie area. According to local reports, the service was officiated by an all-female clergy from the Anglican church of Ghana.Mullally, who in March became the 106th head of the 492-year-old denomination and the only woman to do so, also met the Ghanaian president, John Mahama, earlier in the tour, along with her husband, Eamonn Mullally.Since the government launched theYear of Return schemein 2019 to help Africans and their descendants in the diaspora reconnect with their roots, Ghana has had a surge in visitors. As part of Mullally’s visit, she laid a foundation stone for a hostel belonging to the local church’s culture resort initiative, to accommodate pilgrims from the diaspora wanting to engage in the scheme.The archbishop also preached at a service of more than 1,000 nurses in the town of Mampong, where she commissioned a new campus clinic named after her. On Friday, she was heading to Yaoundé, the Cameroonian capital, and will then proceed to Douala and the English-speaking cities of Buea and Limbe.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |MonthlySign up toCotton CapitalStarting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the worldPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat is Project Spire and why is it dividing the Church of England?Read moreGhana has been spearheading a global campaign to seek reparative justice and last month hosted alandmark conferenceattended by more than 80 heads of state.The archbishop’s visit comes three years after her predecessor Justin Welby formally apologised for the church’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, including using a fund for poor clergy to invest in enslaving Africans. “It is a stain on the wider church that some Christians did not see their brothers and sisters as created in the image of God, but as objects to be exploited,” he said.The church set up a £100m fund committed to “a programme of investment, research and engagement” in communities affected by slavery, promptingdiverse reactions. At the time, an independent oversight group argued that the amount was insufficient to address the generational damage slavery had caused and urged the church to expand that commitmentto £1bn. Upon Mullally’s ascension to the role of archbishop, a committee of Conservative MPs urged her to spend the money on wages for the church’s clergy.View image in fullscreenAsantehene Otumfuo Osei Tutu II with Archbishop of Canterbury Sarah Mullally at the Manhyia Palace.Photograph: Francis Kokoroko/ReutersHowever, on Thursday, the archbishop reaffirmed her commitment to the fund. “We played a part in the transatlantic slave trade … part of the Christian belief in repentance is about action, so we are putting in place action to support those communities that feel the legacy of the slave trade,” she said.Across Ghana, the mood has largely been celebratory. On a visit to the palace of the Asantehene, the traditional ruler of the Asante people, in the city of Kumasi on Wednesday, Mullally wore a special cassock and cape lined with kente cloth that pleased palace chiefs.Among the less enthused was Accra-based accountant Kenneth Mordzro, who said he believes the church can play a greater role in reparation efforts. “They should bring back the gold and artefacts they stole from our ancestors during the colonial days,” he said, referring to items looted by the British government during the Anglo-Asante wars of the 19th century.Explore more on these topicsAnglicanismCotton Capital: ongoing seriesReparations and reparative justiceGhanaChristianityAfricaReligionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ebola outbreak in DRC the fastest growing in the history of the virus | Global development | The Guardian
description: As the death toll rises to almost 1,500, and with a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain potentially still months away, health workers face a battle to slow the outbreak
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As the death toll rises to almost 1,500, and with a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain potentially still months away, health workers face a battle to slow the outbreak
Content: An Ebola treatment centre in Rwampara, Ituri, DRC, 20 June 2026. There have been 3,360 confirmed cases of the virus in the east of the country.Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/EPAView image in fullscreenAn Ebola treatment centre in Rwampara, Ituri, DRC, 20 June 2026. There have been 3,360 confirmed cases of the virus in the east of the country.Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/EPAGlobal developmentEbola outbreak in DRC the fastest growing in the history of the virusAs the death toll rises to almost 1,500, and with a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain potentially still months away, health workers face a battle to slow the outbreakSupported byAbout this contentProsper Heri Ngorora in BuniaFri 31 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe latest numbers of confirmed cases of Ebola in theDemocratic Republic of the Congohas made this latest outbreak the fastest growing in the known history of the virus.At3,360 confirmed cases, the disease is now affecting people in five provinces in the east of the DRC, with 1,487 deaths recorded, representing an overall case fatality rate estimated at about 45%, according to Congolese health officials. Health responses to the outbreak have been badly hampered by conflict in many of the affected areas.“I fear that at some point, life may come to a standstill here in our province of Ituri,” said Deborah Nzuva, a mother of four who lives in Rwampara, one of the affected regions. “We were already in a precarious situation before theEbolavirus disease, which continues to claim its victims.”Since officially declared by the Congolese authorities on 15 May, theBundibugyo strain of the virus has spread fasterthan any of the country’s 16 previous Ebola outbreaks – and the numbers are approaching the previous worst toll, in2018-2020 when 3,470 people in DRCwere infected.Prof Pierre Akilimali, from the country’s public health institute (NPHI), is in charge of the Ebola response. He emphasises that the disease continues to spread and that it is still difficult to know when it will reach its peak. According to him, there is a way to go and the road to bringing the outbreak under control is a long one.View image in fullscreenMembers of a Congolese Red Cross team in Bunia carry the body of a woman suspected of having died from Ebola, 7 June.Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty Images“Here in Ituri, we have the issues of insecurity, mining and high population density, which make the current outbreak more complex than previous ones,” he said.The Congolese authorities say they have taken a number of measures to limit spread, including strengthening surveillance through community liaison officers, building more than 20 Ebola treatment centres, and setting up local laboratories for testing. “The public must also play their part by seeking medical advice at the slightest suspicion of infection,” Akilimali said. “This will help us to respond effectively to the disease.”He said cases continue to rise in the Bunia and Rwampara health zones, with between 100 and 150 new confirmed infections each week.Annabelle Nissi, a clothing trader in Bunia, said people were living in fear.“This outbreak is causing us great distress. Our hope lies solely in God’s hands. It continues to disrupt our lives and has brought our development projects to a standstill,” she said.Dr Justus Nsio, field incident manager for theAfricaCentres for Disease Control and Prevention, said it was a race against time.First patients enrolled in record-breaking Ebola treatment trial in DRCRead more“All the experts monitoring this outbreak agree that it was detected too late. When detection is delayed, we have to work hard to make up for what we missed earlier in order to contain the disease,” he said.“What is certain is that, with the commitment of the movement and our partners, the outcome will be favourable.”View image in fullscreenHealth workers prepare for a safe burial operation in the community of Mongbwalu, Ituri, DRC, in May.Photograph: Michel Lunanga/Getty ImagesClinical trials began in early July of a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no standard treatment.As of 15 July, about 20 people had been enrolled in these trials, which could last up to four months, according to Prof Placide Mbala, head of laboratory operations for the Ebola response in the DRC.Uganda, which this week declared the Ebola outbreak over on its territory, 12 days after its last case was reported, has sent experts to the DRC to work alongside their Congolese counterparts, particularly in the border regions of Tchomia and Kasenyi.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentEbolaInfectious diseasesDemocratic Republic of the CongoAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: HIV prevention drug could reduce cases globally but USAID cuts prevent access, say experts | Aids and HIV | The Guardian
description: Injectable PrEP drug holds promise but investment in HIV prevention has declined dramatically worldwide
Author: Hannah Harris Green
Headline: Injectable PrEP drug holds promise but investment in HIV prevention has declined dramatically worldwide
Content: People protest against funding cuts and drug patents during the 26th International Aids Conference in Rio de Janeiro on Monday.Photograph: Pablo Porciúncula/AFP via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople protest against funding cuts and drug patents during the 26th International Aids Conference in Rio de Janeiro on Monday.Photograph: Pablo Porciúncula/AFP via Getty ImagesAids and HIVHIV prevention drug could reduce cases globally but USAID cuts prevent access, say expertsInjectable PrEP drug holds promise but investment in HIV prevention has declined dramatically worldwideSign up for the Breaking News US newsletter emailHannah Harris Greenin Rio de JaneiroFri 31 Jul 2026 12.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew innovations in HIV prevention could dramatically reduce the number of newHIVcases around the globe, but US foreign aid cuts will mean that those that most need the new medication will be unable to access it, according to experts at the Aids 2026 Conference in Rio de Janeiro,Brazil.One year ago, the World Health Organizationrecommended that governments around the world prioritizeexpanded access to lenacapavir, an injectable version of the HIV prevention medication PrEP that requires only two injections annually. PrEP, which also comes in the form of daily oral medications and bimonthly injections, is 99% effective in preventing sexually transmitted HIV for people who take it consistently.In its announcement, the WHO noted that access to lenacapavir is limited outside clinical trials. But the organisation recommended that governments around the world prioritise scaling up availability of the injectable medication, because it could be gamechanging for populations that face considerable barriers to access for the medications that are currently available.Trump’s HIV funding cuts having ‘severe and devastating’ impact around the worldRead moreFor people who face poverty or stigma, or who live in rural areas that are far away from healthcare services, accessing a daily pill or an every-other-month injection can be close to impossible. Lenacapavir would provide strong protection against HIV while only requiring patients to access healthcare twice annually. Amathematical modeling studyfrom the WHO and the United Nations estimated that widespread availability of lenacapavir could prevent 41% of new HIV infections in South Africa, Zimbabwe and western Kenya.Notably, when the WHO recommended global investment in lenacapavir for HIV prevention in 2025, the Trump administration was already in the process of dissolving USAID, which provided 73% of donor-funded resources for HIV prevention globally,according to a studyin the Lancet Global Health.As of July 2026,multiple reportsshowthat investmentin HIV prevention has declined dramatically around the world.“We have these major achievements in prevention. On the other hand, we are facing these major funding cuts that are affecting deeply the delivery not only of these new prevention technologies but also decreasing the number of people engaged in care, engaged in prevention services,” said Beatriz Grinsztejn, president of the International Aids Society, during a press conference at the Aids 2026 Conference.Grinsztejn is also an infectious disease physician and researcher at the HIV prevention organisation Fiocruz in Rio de Janeiro.The funding cuts not only affect the availability of medications themselves, but also the ability of organisations to reach the people who need them.“When funding cuts came, one of the big things that’s been impacted is peer outreach workers, which are crucial to reaching people who use drugs, to building trust with people who use drugs and engaging them with services,” said Ailish Brennan, a policy analyst at Harm Reduction International.People who inject drugs are at a particularly high risk for contracting HIV, especially if they do not have access to clean syringes. Areport from the International Network of People Who Use Drugsfound that organisations were most likely to respond to the loss of funding by cutting outreach services.Brennan said that many harm reduction and HIV prevention organisations around the world were having to shut down locations, including mobile locations, which can mean clients at risk for HIV lose trust in the organisation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“But also just if they have to travel further they lose their local point of contact, and ultimately this means the innovations that we’re seeing, the long-acting injectables that have so much hope and opportunity, are not going to reach the people who need them most,” Brennan said.At the press conference, Grinsztejn noted that even before the dissolution of USAID, much of Latin America had been left out of agreements with US-based pharmaceutical companies to make innovative HIV prevention more affordable.Gilead Sciences provides generic versions of long-acting medications to low- and middle-income countries for far below sticker price, but justifies excluding countries such asBrazil, Colombia, Mexico, Peru and Argentina by classifying them as “upper middle-income countries”. HIV advocates dispute this justification, partly because people in these countries played a key role in clinical trials to test these medications.“We do have prevention technologies that are our dream,” Grinsztejn said during the conference, adding that it should be possible to fulfill the UNAIDS long-held goal of eliminating AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.Grinsztejn then added: “From my personal perspective, I think that it’s really hard that we will get to the targets given the current scenario.”Explore more on these topicsAids and HIVTrump administrationInfectious diseasesUS foreign policyDonald TrumpHealthBrazilnewsShareReuse this content

title: FTSE 100 on track for best month since first US attacks on Iran five months ago – as it happened | Business | The Guardian
description: Live, rolling coverage as London’s biggest companies defy Middle East disruption and UK petrol prices rise to around £1.60 per litre, the highest since Donald Trump ordered renewed strikes
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Live, rolling coverage as London’s biggest companies defy Middle East disruption and UK petrol prices rise to around £1.60 per litre, the highest since Donald Trump ordered renewed strikes
Content: 12h ago10.10 EDTClosing summary: FTSE 100 limps to end of month, but share prices still upTheFTSE 100is losing a bit of momentum as the month crawls to its end, but it is still a much more positive picture than might have been expected during the turmoil of March.The index reached anew recordearlier this morning and – barring a significant worsening in the next hour or so – will finish the month up by about 3.5% at around 10,840 points. It was down 0.5% after 3pm BST.That came after a year low below 9,700 points at the worst point of the rout triggered by the attacks on Iran ordered by Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu.View image in fullscreenThe FTSE 100 has reached new record highs, although it dipped on Friday.Photograph: LSEGThe broader European Stoxx 600 index is up 1.2% this month, after dropping 8% in March.In other business and economics news today:BPhas put itsNorth Sea oil and gas business up for saleas it looks to end six decades of production from the basin.Theprice of petrolhashit a new Iran War highat UK forecourts, adding to the financial pressure on millions of households about to embark on their annual holiday.Morrisonshas revealed losses widened to £926m last year and itcut almost 5,000 jobsas it struggles with heavy debts and competition.Sainsbury’shasagreed to sell theArgosretail chainfor £120m to allow it to concentrate on its core food business.Great Britain has recordedmore newsolar power installationsin the first half of this year than in any six-month period since 2011.Economic uncertaintydampenedUK house pricegrowthin July as prospective buyers remained cautious about interest rates during the Iran war in what should be the peak housebuying season.That’s it for this week’s live coverage of business, economics and financial markets. Thanks for reading today, and please do join us on Monday for August. JJShare

title: Missing Australian hiker found dead in Wyoming, officials say | Wyoming | The Guardian
description: Body of William Standish discovered in Teton mountains as investigators say fatal fall likely cause of death
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Body of William Standish discovered in Teton mountains as investigators say fatal fall likely cause of death
Content: William Standish lost contact with his family as he was hiking in Wyoming.Photograph: Teton county search and rescueView image in fullscreenWilliam Standish lost contact with his family as he was hiking in Wyoming.Photograph: Teton county search and rescueWyomingMissing Australian hiker found dead in Wyoming, officials sayBody of William Standish discovered in Teton mountains as investigators say fatal fall likely cause of deathEdward HelmoreFri 31 Jul 2026 17.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 17.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 28-year-old Australian hiker who lost contact with his family while hiking the Continental Divide Trail between Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks inWyominghas been found dead, according to authorities.The man, identified as William Standish, was discovered by rescuers on Wednesday morning in the Wigwams, a series of rocky peaks on the west slope of the Teton mountain range, the Teton county coroner said. Investigators say it was likely he suffered a fatal fall.Standish had been attempting a thru-hike of the Continental Divide Trail between the Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks when he disappeared after contacting his family on 23 July, according toa statementfrom Teton county rescuers.Evidence suggests Standish may have fallen from a steep ridgeline that separates Grand Teton and the Jedediah Smith wilderness, officials said.Standish was discovered by a helicopter team after it spotted an orange backpack – and then saw his remains below the ridge.His family said it had stopped receiving updates from him via a Garmin GPS device and Facebook Messenger on 23 July, leading to a search being mounted by Teton county rescue crews.On 19 July, Standish gave an update from a location near Old Faithful, and described his planned route in the Tetons, Gros Ventre wilderness, the Wind River range, and the Divide Basin.Four days later, the family received a Garmin check-in without coordinates or a message. There was also a Facebook Messenger video that they believe placed him in the Wigwams.The Teton county search and rescue team said it “sends its sincere condolences to the family and friends of the deceased”. It also expressed gratitude to federal agencies who assisted in searching for Standish.Standish had reportedly been following a popular thru-hike, or end-to-end through-hike, starting in Canada, the most northern point of the 3,100-mileContinental Divide Trail– which passes down through Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, and New Mexico.There have been other hiking-related deaths in North America recently.The Colorado Sunreported that a 15-year-old boy died after being struck by lightning on the state’s Mount Blue Sky on Monday. Sheriff’s officials identified the boy as Levi Strobel. Four other people were seriously injured, including Levi’s younger brother.In Arizona, a man died during a hike on Phoenix’s South Mountain. Richard Fletcher, 61, left his home early on Saturday morning. Investigators later said his death was consistent with a heat-related or medical event, authorities toldlocal media.A 62-year-old man died in New Hampshire when he suffered a medical emergency in the state’s Welch-Dickey trail in the White Mountains. He was evacuated by national guard helicopter and later pronounced dead, according toNew Hampshire Public Radio.Two hikers also died in Canada’s Banff national park. One was a woman in her 20s after falling from a mountain near Marvel Peak on Tuesday. Three days earlier, a 65-year-old from Calgary fell from Mount Temple, also in Banff, theCBCreported.Explore more on these topicsWyomingnewsShareReuse this content

title: NSW should compensate elderly woman whose public housing was inundated with sewage, ombudsman finds | New South Wales | The Guardian
description: Ombudsman finds Homes NSW acted unreasonably and recommended additional payment for distress and suffering
Author: Achol Arok
Headline: Ombudsman finds Homes NSW acted unreasonably and recommended additional payment for distress and suffering
Content: File photo: The NSW Ombudsman has identified ‘inadequate policies and procedures’ regarding how Homes NSW deals with tenants’ complaints.Photograph: Dean Sewell/AAPView image in fullscreenFile photo: The NSW Ombudsman has identified ‘inadequate policies and procedures’ regarding how Homes NSW deals with tenants’ complaints.Photograph: Dean Sewell/AAPNew South WalesNSW should compensate elderly woman whose public housing was inundated with sewage, ombudsman findsOmbudsman finds Homes NSW acted unreasonably and recommended additional payment for distress and sufferingGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAchol ArokFri 31 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn elderly public housing tenant whose home was damaged by sewage overflows will be fully compensated by theNew South Walesgovernment after it disposed of her personal belongings without her consent and failed to properly support her insurance claim.The NSW Ombudsman on Friday published its report after an investigation in which it found Homes NSW acted unreasonably in how it handled the tenant’s contaminated belongings and “failed to provide full and accurate information to the insurer”.The woman, whose name and suburb were not made public, had lived in the unit for more than 15 years. She reported three successive sewage overflows within three months, which saw raw sewage enter the property.After the third incident she was relocated, but her belongings remained in the contaminated unit for two months before being boxed up and moved to a vacant property.‘I would just like to see more people housed’: inside NSW’s social housing changesRead moreThe furniture, household items, and family heirlooms were not cleaned nor returned to her, despite Homes NSW telling her “she would be actively involved in the decision to keep or dispose of any items”.She was later told “she would be adequately compensated” through an insurance claim, according to the report. When the claim was lodged, the insurer denied liability and offered a small “goodwill” payment.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe report found Homes NSW’s failure to provide the insurer with “full and accurate information” which contributed to the rejection of the claim.The Ombudsman’s recommendations included an apology and full compensation “in accordance with her itemised compensation claim”. It also recommended an additional payment for “the distress and suffering she experienced while trying to resolve her claim over more than five years”.Homes NSW has accepted all of the recommendations and will implement them by next month, according to the report.The senior deputy ombudsman for complaints and investigations, Kate Anderson, said the findings and recommendations come after identifying “inadequate policies and procedures in place”.“There were several points where there was inadequate communication to her about … what next steps were going to follow and then those steps were ultimately not followed,” she said.Anderson said the case demonstrated the importance of ensuring agencies were able to “listen to their complainants”, particularly when they should “have engaged with this particular individual to reach a conclusion on this complaint far earlier”.“This individual actually had very good record of the possessions that she had and the respective value of them, which ultimately was not taken into consideration,” she said.“At all points, people should be treated with courtesy and respect and the situation that materialised here really demonstrated that ultimately by the time it had come to us, the tenant had been trying to resolve it herself with Home NSW for a number of years and hadn’t been able to get an effective resolution.”A spokesperson for Homes NSW said it “sincerely apologises to the tenant affected” and acknowledged “the distress, inconvenience and impact the situation has had on them”.Homes NSW has since introduced “a number of changes to how we deliver maintenance and repairs with the aim of improved tenant satisfaction, including establishing an in-house call centre to manage repair requests”, the spokesperson said.Explore more on these topicsNew South WalesSocial housingHousing (Australia news)Housing (Society)newsShareReuse this content

Content: 13.27 EDTClosing summaryJakub KrupaAnd, on that note,we will be closing the blog for today.At least 57 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after as many as 60,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco(17:33).At least 57 people die as tens of thousands cross to Spanish enclave of Ceuta from MoroccoRead moreSpain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called it a “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”(12:51) and blamed on misleading narratives spread by human traffickers (12:54,13:17).In response,Italy has moved to suspend its free-travel Schengen arrangements with Spain by sea and air(18:26), claiming it was necessary to safeguard the security of its citizens (19:02,19:07).
