title: BP puts North Sea oil and gas business up for sale | BP | The Guardian
description: Move will end six decades of production in area, as new CEO tries to simplify company and cut debt
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: Move will end six decades of production in area, as new CEO tries to simplify company and cut debt
Content: BP believes its North Sea business would ‘be better positioned as part of another company’.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenBP believes its North Sea business would ‘be better positioned as part of another company’.Photograph: ReutersBPBP puts North Sea oil and gas business up for saleMove will end six decades of production in area, as new CEO tries to simplify company and cut debtBusiness live – latest updatesGraeme WeardenFri 31 Jul 2026 13.06 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 03.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBP has put its North Sea oil and gas business up for sale as it looks to end six decades of production from the basin.The firm announced on Friday morning it had launched a formal process to market its North Sea business for a potential sale. The move comes as BP’s new chief executive, Meg O’Neill, tries to simplify the company and cut its debt levels.O’Neill said: “The North Sea remains integral to the UK’s energy system. However, as we focus our portfolio and direct capital to our highest-value opportunities, we believe our North Sea business will be better positioned as part of another company.”She said Britain would “continue to play an important role” in BP’s future, adding: “We’re proud of the jobs we create, the contribution we make to the UK economy and the work we do to keep energy flowing every day.”North Sea oil begins to flow – archive, 3 November 1975Read moreBP’s involvement in the North Sea dates back to 1964, when it was granted its first UK North Sea exploration licence. The company discovered the West Sole gasfield in the winter of 1965, followed by its largest discovery in the area, the giant Forties field, in 1970.BP’s planned exit from the North Sea comes as the climate crisis leads to wildfires and drought conditions acrossEurope. Angharad Hopkinson, a political campaigner at Greenpeace UK, called BP’s withdrawal from the North Sea “the canary in the coalmine for a toxic, declining basin”.She said: “If the North Sea really were the saviour of jobs, opportunity and energy security that the fossil fuel lobby claims, its biggest beneficiaries wouldn’t be heading for the exit.”Chart showing expected production and demand for North Sea oilOn Thursday, Andy Burnham said he wouldtake a “pragmatic” approachto oil and gas drilling in the North Sea, adding that the government could not ignore the potential energy resources it held.Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, described BP’s North Sea sale as “a watershed moment”.“It says a lot when BP isn’t prepared to stick around to see if the new government can re-energise the UK’s energy policy,” Beauchamp said. “Clearly BP thinks it will take too long at a time when the need to exploit new energy fields is pressing, and waiting around for Whitehall to move is not a prudent use of resources.”The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said she was in close contact with BP over its plans.“The North Sea is a vital national asset and we will take a pragmatic approach, recognising that oil and gas will be part of our energy mix for years to come,” she said. “I’m in close contact with BP and have made clear that my priority is ensuring that the workers and local community are protected during this sale process.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSince drilling began in the North Sea in the 1960s, 47.7bn barrels of oil equivalent (BOE) have been produced from the UK continental shelf as of the end of 2024.The North Sea Transition Authority estimated there to be 2.9bn BOE of UK oil and gas reserves left in the North Sea at the end of 2024. There is also an estimated 6.2bn BOE of contingent resources – petroleum estimated to be recoverable from known deposits but not ready for commercial development.Chart showing expected production and demand for North Sea gasThere is an estimated 4.6bn BOE of “prospective resources” as well. These are undiscovered, potentially recoverable resources in mapped leads and prospects that have not yet been drilled. Those reserves could be extracted with government approval, if energy companies believed it was commercially viable.BP has been cutting its exposure to the UK this year. In May, itannounced plans to sell stakesin two large carbon capture and storage projects in the north-east of England.The company said it would retain its UK aviation fuel distribution business, retail sites, UK-based trading desk and London headquarters.O’Neill took over as BP’s chief executive on 1 April. Less than two months later, the companyremoved its chair, Albert Manifold, citing serious concerns about “important governance standards, oversight and conduct”, which he denies.Explore more on these topicsBPOil and gas companiesOilGasEnergy industryEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Daughter of British couple killed in Spanish wildfire rejects claim they ignored order to leave | Spain | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Danielle Kirton calls on Ed Miliband to help her get answers about why evacuation order came too late
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Exclusive: Danielle Kirton calls on Ed Miliband to help her get answers about why evacuation order came too late
Content: Danielle Kirton, right, with her mum, Fran.Photograph: Danielle KirtonDanielle Kirton, right, with her mum, Fran.Photograph: Danielle KirtonSpainDaughter of British couple killed in Spanish wildfire rejects claim they ignored order to leaveExclusive: Danielle Kirton calls on Ed Miliband to help her get answers about why evacuation order came too lateHelena HortonFri 31 Jul 2026 12.36 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 09.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe bereaved daughter of a British couple who died in a Spanish wildfire is calling on the foreign secretary,Ed Miliband, to get answers from Spain’s government about why her parents were not told to evacuate until it was too late.Severe wildfires haveburned across Spain and Francesince early July, killing people, destroying thousands of homes and forcing more than 300,000 people to flee.Pete and Fran Gillam, who lived in Bédar in Almería, died in mid-July while fleeing their home as a wildfire tore through the village. They wereamong 13 people killed in the fires, many of whom died in their cars as they tried to escape.View image in fullscreenPete and Fran Gillam. Danielle said a lone police officer was ‘frantically driving from house to house’ to tell people in the village to evacuate.Photograph: FacebookDanielle Kirton, 42, an assistant headteacher from Nottinghamshire, has spent the weeks since her parents died looking for answers. She knows her mother would have followed official advice had she have been given it.Though the fire alert came at 4.30pm, the evacuation order did not come until more than three hours later. Kirton said this was delivered by a lone police officer, who was “frantically driving from house to house” and Spain’s official emergency alert system, which plays a loud noise on mobile phones and tells people to evacuate, was not used.British couple named among 13 killed in Spanish wildfiresRead more“My mother sent me a video at 6.45pm showing the fire a considerable way away from the hill where they live,” Kirton said. “She didn’t sound worried or concerned. I kept in contact with her and she sent me a message saying at 7.53pm that they’d evacuated.”However, the decision to evacuate was made tragically late. “They stopped at a neighbour’s driveway to shout to a neighbour they needed to evacuate, but then they became trapped as the fire had jumped on both sides of the road.”View image in fullscreenThe remains of cars in Bédar. Many of the 13 killed in the fire died in their vehicles as they tried to flee.Photograph: Atlas/Reuters‘I had an incredible escape’: British woman tells of close encounter with Spanish wildfireRead moreThere are now other wildfires burning in much of Spain and south-west France, but there have been no civilian casualties so far. In the small village where her parents lived, 13 people died. “It would appear that somewhere within that system there has been a failure. If you look at the subsequent wildfires in Spain, there have been no casualties and the biggest difference is the emergency alert was used in subsequent wildfires,” Kirton said.She said her mother loved living in Bédar and as a retired headteacher took much joy in organising quiz nights to fundraise for the local school. She had a bag packed and she was ready to evacuate. “She was just waiting to be told what to do,” Kirton said.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of the wildfire in Bédar. Thirteen people died when the fire tore through the village.Photograph: Gregorio Marrero/APSpanish politicians have claimed that those who died ignored instructions. “My parents did not ignore instructions. My parents would have not had an issue with instructions in Spanish,” Kirton said. “My parents heeded advice to shelter in place, until they were then told that they needed to evacuate.“They took the correct route, and their only route, to the evacuation point. It is a weak and cowardly act to blame victims in the face of tragedy.”The response from the Foreign Office has been a “slap in the face”, she added. “The help from the consulate has been nonexistent. We got sent a link: ‘What to do when someone dies abroad.’ That is it. It is a slap in the face, to be honest.”Miliband has been visiting France and Spain to discuss wildfires and the climate crisis with political leaders. Kirton said: “As UK citizens, it is important to ask for his support in asking Spanish authorities to conduct a full and thorough investigation.”Danielle Kirton, right, with her dad, Pete, and her sister, Natalie. Kirton said the UK Foreign Office’s response to her parents’ death has been a ‘slap in the face’.Photograph: Danielle KirtonScientists say thefires have been worsened by the climate crisis, which has intensified the recent heatwaves. Kirton said this makes it more crucial that lessons are learned so no one has to go through what she has.“It’s vital for planning for the future that we see what exactly were the contributing factors in this case,” she said. “It’s a perfect storm, the weather, the climate, the vegetation, the wind. My parents weren’t concerned before – it isn’t something they felt fearful of, it wasn’t something that happened where they lived.”Kirton has been working every day since her parents died trying to get answers and a substantial response from the Spanish authorities. She said: “My mum and dad would have always spoken up for what’s right and if I can do anything for them it’s that we can ask for the truth and ensure this never happens again to any other families.”The Andalusian government has been contacted for comment.A Foreign Office spokesperson said that any investigation into the fire response is a matter for the Spanish government: “The foreign secretary has been in regular contact with his Spanish counterpart, including during his visit to Madrid on Wednesday.“They discussed how the UK could support Spain’s response, ensure British nationals receive the right advice and assistance, and agreed that lessons must be learned as climate change makes these dangerous wildfires more likely.“Staff at our embassy have been working with the British community in the affected area, collating their questions and concerns and raising them with the Spanish authorities. This work is ongoing.”Explore more on these topicsSpainWildfiresExtreme weatherExtreme heatEuropeEd MilibandClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI labels to be compulsory on authentic-looking content under EU rules | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Companies must ensure people know when they are interacting with artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look real
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Companies must ensure people know when they are interacting with artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look real
Content: Screengrab of an AI-generated image of the French president, Emmanuel Macron, dancing in a 1980s nightclub.View image in fullscreenScreengrab of an AI-generated image of the French president, Emmanuel Macron, dancing in a 1980s nightclub.AI (artificial intelligence)AI labels to be compulsory on authentic-looking content under EU rulesCompanies must ensure people know when they are interacting with artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look realJennifer Rankinin BrusselsFri 31 Jul 2026 07.21 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 05.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom apparently conspiring to steal elections to abusing staff or performing embarrassing dance moves, the last few years have seen plenty of fake content made about politicians intended to malign its targets and mislead the public.Now EU rules aim to stem the flood of this deceptive content: starting from Sunday, artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look authentic must be labelled.The rules, devised under theEU’s landmark AI Act, mean companies must ensure people know when they are interacting with an AI-powered chatbot or viewing a manipulated image or AI-generated text.View image in fullscreenDeepfakes have included fake audio of the Slovakian opposition leader, Michal Šimečka, conspiring with a journalist to rig election.Photograph: Radovan Stoklasa/ReutersThe rules apply to new AI systems on the EU market from 2 August, while existing ones have an extra four months to comply.“It is a matter not only of customer protection, it’s also a matter of democracy protection,” the Green MEP Sergey Lagodinsky, who helped negotiate the AI Act, told the Guardian. “Making transparent this information is something which we need to preserve our democracy and the authenticity of facts online.”Under the rules, synthetic text, images, video and audio designed to look truthful must be visibly marked as AI-generated and contain a digital watermark to show the artificial origins of the content.Texts on matters of public interest must also be labelled as AI-made if there is no human editorial oversight.Companies are encouraged to label AI-generated content pre-dating the rules, although this is not compulsory. The rules will not apply to users’ personal content and there is an exemption for “evidently artistic”, satirical and fictional works.Failure to comply could result in fines of up to €15m (£12.8) or 3% of a company’s worldwide global turnover.The EU executive has created black-and-white labels anyone can use, although companies can design their own.View image in fullscreenEU symbols to be used on content using AI.Illustration: EUDeepfakes have includedaudio purporting to revealthe Slovakian opposition leader Michal Šimečka conspiring with a journalist to rig elections,mocked-up videosof the French president, Emmanuel Macron, dancing in a 1980s nightclub, andfake footageof the then UK Labour leader, Keir Starmer, abusing party staff.The tech industry says it supports the quest to make deepfakes visible, but fears the rules will be interpreted too broadly and overwhelm internet users with banners and labels.The Computer and Communications Industry Association argues that EU guidelines published in July have expanded the definition of a deepfake far beyond the 2024 AI Act.“The label was meant to flag deceptive content,” said CCIA Europe’s AI policy lead, Boniface de Champris. “That distinction has been removed, so now almost everything gets labelled – a landscape in an advert is the same as a manipulated political speech. Like cookie banners, once labels are everywhere, users stop noticing them. That doesn’t protect anyone, it just burdens commercial activity across the board.”He thinks the most visible change for the public will not be on social media, which “already labels most AI content” but “in areas where AI is already used at scale but people don’t know it – advertising, film, publishing”.“Expect a lot more labels in sectors not usually associated with AI, and the burden will fall hardest on those least versed in AI regulation,” De Champris said.Some of the world’s largest tech companies already have policies designed to inform users about AI-generated content.TikTok, for example, says it requires creators to label realistic AI-generated images, audio and video, and that it has helped label more than 3bn pieces of content. However, recent research has shown thatAI-generated doctors are gaining millions of views on TikTokby spreading dubious health advice.Misleading AI-generated doctors pose ‘huge danger to public safety’Read moreGoogle launched a tool called SynthID in 2023, which enables users to check if an image is AI-generated. The company says it has put an invisible digital watermark, which enables identification, on more than 100bn images and 60,000 years’ worth of audio.Google and Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, have signed a voluntary code of practice intended to help companies comply with the EU’s AI transparency rules.The European Commission said more than 180 organisations had signed the code, which was drawn up by independent experts under the supervision of the EU AI office.Signing the code is seen by regulators as a sign of good intent, while non-signatories must show they are meeting the rules in other ways.Meta launched policies in 2024 to help people identify AI-generated photo-realistic images. It says it has been developing industry-wide technical standards to identify AI audio and video.Announcing Meta’s intention to sign the EU code of practice earlier this week [28 July], its vice-president for public policy in Europe, Markus Reinisch, said: “We must avoid a situation where online content is subject to a growing array of different labels and disclosures that end up overwhelming people, while at the same time adding additional regulatory complexity for providers.”Lagodinsky, the EU lawmaker, said he believed the industry could find a way: “I have a deep respect for industry, but in all too many cases, they complain, and … then after things are implemented, it doesn’t look that burdensome to them. And there is always a solution.”The transparency rules are part of broader enforcement of the AI Act, starting from 2 August. The commission’s lead official on tech policy, Henna Virkkunen, said AI was a “transformative technology” that could bring “extraordinary benefits” but the most advanced models “create risks on an entirely new scale”.“Europe anticipated this development. With the AI Act, we established a clear, risk-based and durable framework for trustworthy AI —one that gives innovators legal certainty while protecting the public interest.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Social mediaEuropean UnionDigital mediaEuropeComputingInternet safetynewsShareReuse this content

title: British-Azerbaijani man arrested in Cyprus over alleged spying on UK airbase for Iran | Cyprus | The Guardian
description: Rashad Sultanov, from London, suspected of conducting hostile surveillance and passing information to Revolutionary Guards
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rashad Sultanov, from London, suspected of conducting hostile surveillance and passing information to Revolutionary Guards
Content: The arrest was part of an investigation into incidents at RAF Akrotiri between May and June last year.Photograph: Yiannis Kourtoglou/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe arrest was part of an investigation into incidents at RAF Akrotiri between May and June last year.Photograph: Yiannis Kourtoglou/ReutersCyprusBritish-Azerbaijani man arrested in Cyprus over alleged spying on UK airbase for IranRashad Sultanov, from London, suspected of conducting hostile surveillance and passing information to Revolutionary GuardsReutersFri 31 Jul 2026 04.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British-Azerbaijani national has been arrested ⁠in Cyprus on suspicion of spying on a British airbase on the Mediterranean island and passing information to Iran’s ⁠Islamic Revolutionary Guard ⁠Corps, the Metropolitan police ​said.Rashad Sultanov, 44, from Islington, north London, was arrested on 17 July by Cypriot authorities ⁠and is being held in custody as extradition proceedings continue, the police said in a statement on Friday.He was arrested as part ⁠of Britain’s first overseas National Security Act investigation, led by counter-terrorism police into incidents at ​Britain’s RAF Akrotiri base in ‌Cyprus between 11 May and ‌22 June last year, the statement said. Cypriot police did not immediately ‌return a request for comment.Sultanov allegedly conducted hostile surveillance on the base and is alleged to have then shared information with the IRGC, the Met said.Helen Flanagan, the head of counter-terrorism policing in London, said: “This case shows we are able to use the National Security Act overseas when British military bases are allegedly targeted by hostile state activity.”Earlier in July the IRGC threatened to attack any British military ​bases used by US forces to launch attacks on Iran.In March, an Iranian-type Shahed drone strike caused slight damage to facilities at Akrotiri. Soon afterwards, Britain said the base would not be part of its defensive agreement ⁠with the US over the use of UK bases.Also in ​March, Iran was ​reported to have fired two ​ballistic missiles at a US-UK military base on Diego Garcia, ​in the Indian Ocean, ‌though neither hit ​the target.Akrotiri is ​one of two bases Britain has retained in its former colony since Cyprus’s independence in 1960. It has been used for military operations in Iraq, Syria and Yemen.Explore more on these topicsCyprusIranEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: World-renowned climber Nirmal Purja among 11 struck by avalanche on Pakistan mountain | Mountaineering | The Guardian
description: Rescuers say four bodies found in search for team caught in Broad Peak avalanche, after trackers showed rapid descent
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Rescuers say four bodies found in search for team caught in Broad Peak avalanche, after trackers showed rapid descent
Content: Nirmal Purja had been leading an expedition on Broad Peak along with climbers from Nepal, Pakistan, Oman, China and the US.Photograph: Nirmal Purja/PAView image in fullscreenNirmal Purja had been leading an expedition on Broad Peak along with climbers from Nepal, Pakistan, Oman, China and the US.Photograph: Nirmal Purja/PAMountaineeringWorld-renowned climber Nirmal Purja among 11 struck by avalanche on Pakistan mountainRescuers say four bodies found in search for team caught in Broad Peak avalanche, after trackers showed rapid descentPeter BeaumontandShah Meer Balochin IslamabadFri 31 Jul 2026 11.35 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 22.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world-renowned Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja – a former British special forces member – is among 11 climbers caught in a deadly avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak.The Alpine Club of Pakistan said “seven climbers have been spotted via aerial drone footage” adding that “their identities and condition cannot yet be verified”.Rescuers had said earlier on Friday that four bodies had been foundand efforts were under way to retrieve them despite the harsh weather. Three of the dead have been identified: Pur Bahadur Gurung, a Nepali citizen, Nadhira Alharthy, who was the first Omani to climb Everest, and US climber Mallory Geis. Their bodies have been transported to a hospital.Purja, also known as Nims Dai, made history in 2019 afterclimbing all of the world’s 14 peaks over 8,000 metresin just over six months, cutting years off the previous record. He later led the first team to summit K2, the world’s second-highest mountain in winter, a highly coveted achievement.View image in fullscreenNirmal ‘Nims’ Purja and his Project Possible team are congratulated after successfully scaling all 14 mountains above 8,000 metres in just over six months.Photograph: Skanda Gautam/Zuma Wire/Rex/ShutterstockPurja has also attracted controversy, however, includinga high-profile claim, which he denied, of sexually inappropriate behaviour.Also among those missing are the US climber Mallory Geis, a Chinese national, Wang Zhong, and Pakistani and Nepali high-altitude workers.As night fell on the mountain on Friday, visual searches for any survivors, including with the use of drones, were halted. Search efforts have been hampered by the weather and the fact that unlike in Nepal, where there is a well-established network of private helicopter search and rescue operations, helicopters are less available in Pakistan and run by the military.Map showing location of Broad PeakTrackers carried by the climbers showed a rapid loss of altitude, suggesting the team had been caught in an avalanche. Purja’s tracker, however, shifted location after the initial rapid descent.The GPS data suggested the avalanche occurred close to 9am local time at 6,579 metres (21,585ft), between camp two and camp three on the mountain’s west ridge, the most popular ascent route.According toClimbing magazine, Geis’s tracker showed a sudden descent of 543 metres, while Alharthy’s tracker showed a much-larger descent of 1,651 metres.View image in fullscreenBroad Peak, on the border of Pakistan and China, is the 12th highest mountain in the world at 8,047 metres.Photograph: Naveed Hussain/AlamyCommenting on the rescue efforts, a spokesperson for police in the mountainous Gilgit-Baltistan region said “preliminary reports indicate that four bodies have so far been recovered”, adding that the condition of the remaining climbers was still being verified.A statement by the Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP) suggested an avalanche had struck a group of climbers around midday on Thursday. “The entire team has been out of communication since the avalanche,” the statement said, as teams with helicopters and drones were sent to help with rescue efforts.The statement added: “Every possible effort is being made to ensure that helicopter support and all available rescue resources are mobilised at the earliest opportunity, subject to weather and operational conditions.”Irfan Arshad Khan, the ACP’s president, said: “We can confirm the death of three climbers, as we received two dead bodies and a body part of another climber.”Purja’s business partner, Mingma Gyabu Sherpa, who is also a member of the Nepali house of representatives, said data appeared to show continuing movement from Purja’s tracking device after the initial incident.“Initially, it appeared that he had been swept downhill by the avalanche,” he told the Nepali news site Kantipur. “But after the point where the tracking had stopped, the location appears to have shifted again.”Mingma added that one Pakistani and one Nepali climber had set out overland towards the suspected avalanche site to check reports that one climber’s location appeared to be near the base of the mountain.“We have received information that one person’s location appears to be near the foot of the mountain. A search team has gone there to verify it,” he said.Mingma cautioned that they did not have any indication of Purja’s condition, simply that the location of the tracker had shifted.In person, Purja wasstriking for his confidence and self-belief. His rapid chain of ascents of the world’s tallest mountains demonstrated strength and a talent for logistical organisation, using the exploit to showcase what he felt were the overlooked abilities of Nepali climbers.His profile was boosted after he starred in a 2021 Netflix documentary on the feat. The previous record for climbing all 14 was seven years; his record was surpassed in 2023.View image in fullscreenPurja, after being part of the all-Nepali mountaineering team that became the first to scale K2 in winter, arrives at Tribhuwan international airport in Kathmandu in January 2021.Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/APPurja was leading an expedition for his company, Elite Exped, on Broad Peak, the world’s 12th-highest mountain at 8,047 metres, when the avalanche occurred.The ACP received “deeply concerning” reports on Thursday that an avalanche had struck the team.‘It’s not about ego’, says speed climber who tamed world’s 14 highest peaksRead moreThe expedition includes five Nepali climbers, as well as US, Pakistani, Omani and Chinese nationals. Another foreign climber was also part of the group, said the ACP’s vice-president, Karrar Haidri.“The club prays for the safety and successful rescue of all the climbers and stands in solidarity with their families and the international mountaineering community during this difficult time,” the ACP said in a statement.View image in fullscreenNims Purja on Manaslu, the world’s eighth-highest mountain, in NepalPhotograph: SuppliedPurja, who is also a British citizen after joining the British army in 2003, opted to use supplementary oxygen for his ascents, justifying his choice by the huge size of the challenge he had set himself.Purja had written on X this week that he was close to becoming the first person to climb all 14 mountains over 8,000 metres twice without oxygen. “Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down,” he wrote. “I take zero mountains for granted. Not one. The moment my foot leaves basecamp, it’s 100%. Always has been. Always will be.“My purpose has never been about me. It’s about what I represent. It’s about showing YOU that your own mountains – whatever they are – are climbable.”Explore more on these topicsMountaineeringPakistanNepalOmanChinaSouth and central AsiaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran strikes tankers under US escort in Hormuz strait as Trump gathers cabinet to discuss war | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Energy prices have soared again since fighting between US and Iran resumed two weeks ago as conflict spreads across Middle East
Author: William Christou
Headline: Energy prices have soared again since fighting between US and Iran resumed two weeks ago as conflict spreads across Middle East
Content: Donald Trump en route to Camp David where he and his cabinet are meeting to discuss the war and its fallout.Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump en route to Camp David where he and his cabinet are meeting to discuss the war and its fallout.Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/APUS-Israel war on IranIran strikes tankers under US escort in Hormuz strait as Trump gathers cabinet to discuss warEnergy prices have soared again since fighting between US and Iran resumed two weeks ago as conflict spreads across Middle EastWilliam Christouin BeirutFri 31 Jul 2026 10.48 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 10.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran has said it struck two tankers trying to pass through the strait of Hormuz under the escort of the US military asDonald Trumpgathered his cabinet to discuss the stalling war and rising prices as midterm elections in the US loom.Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Friday that the “non-compliant oil tankers … were struck and brought to a halt, while four other oil tankers quickly changed course and returned to their previous positions”. The military body said the ships had tried to pass through the strait via an “undeclared route” and under US aerial escort.Iran and the US have said ships should pass through the strait via two competing routes, with Iran bombing ships that take the southern route, close to the coast of Oman, and the US bombing ships that violate its blockade of Iranian ships and ports.View image in fullscreenVessels in the strait of Hormuz near Oman. The strait has been almost completely closed to traffic for the last two weeks.Photograph: ReutersThe strait has been almost completely closed to traffic since Iran and the US returned to fighting two weeks ago, sending energy prices soaring. On Thursday, the price of crude oil pushed past $90 a barrel when the US struck Iran in retaliation for its targeting of US bases in Jordan.Fighting continued on Friday, with the Kuwaiti defence ministry reporting that it had shot down Iranian drones targeting “vital and military facilities” without any casualties.In Lebanon, the Israeli military carried out a huge detonation overnight near the ancient Beaufort Castle. It said it was targetingHezbollahtunnels and infrastructure. The explosion was heard across south Lebanon and covered nearby towns in ash, while photos showed the affected area levelled by the force of the blast.Lebanese officials accusedIsraelof violating the ceasefire by carrying out the detonation. The Israeli military said it was ensuring the security of its northern residents.View image in fullscreenSmoke rises behind Beaufort Castle in Lebanon after an Israeli military strike in June. The area was hit by Israel again on Friiday in a massive explosion that covered towns in ash.Photograph: Léo Corrêa/APTrump has tried to open the strait of Hormuz by force, butincreasingly intense US strikes on Iran have yielded few results. The price of gas and groceries remain high in the US as a result of the energy disruption, complicating Republicans’ chances at the ballot box in November’s midterm elections.On Friday, Trump brought his cabinet together at the Camp David retreat in Maryland to try to chart a path forward for the war. The White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, said at a briefing last week that the cabinet meeting would be “a lot of fun and something different for the cabinet to experience together”.Top of the agenda will be the Iran war, which Trump promised would last a few weeks but has now dragged on for five months. A Reuters-Ipsos poll this week found that one in three Americans support the war, the lowest polling since the war began.View image in fullscreenA gas station in Miami. Energy companies have posted record profits as a result of the war in Iran.Photograph: Marta Lavandier/APSupport in Congress is also waning, with the US Senate narrowly rejecting a symbolic vote to express disapproval of the war. The war powers resolution asking the president to stop the war failed in a 49-50 vote.Inflation caused by the war is a boon for Democrats, who are hoping to wrest control of the house from the Republicans.Energy companies have posted record profits as a result of the conflict, with ExxonMobil’s profits doubling and Chevron reporting more than five times its profits in the same time period last year.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranStrait of HormuzTrump administrationDonald TrumpIranUS politicsMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump says ‘complete disarmament’ of Hamas agreed in Gaza but Israel yet to accept | Gaza | The Guardian
description: US president hails breakthrough but Israeli far-right minister says ‘only solution’ is ‘encouraging emigration and destroying Hamas’
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: US president hails breakthrough but Israeli far-right minister says ‘only solution’ is ‘encouraging emigration and destroying Hamas’
Content: Israel has pointed to Hamas’s failure to disarm as justification for its continued strikes on Gaza.Photograph: Hatem Khaled/ReutersView image in fullscreenIsrael has pointed to Hamas’s failure to disarm as justification for its continued strikes on Gaza.Photograph: Hatem Khaled/ReutersGazaTrump says ‘complete disarmament’ of Hamas agreed in Gaza but Israel yet to acceptUS president hails breakthrough but Israeli far-right minister says ‘only solution’ is ‘encouraging emigration and destroying Hamas’Middle East crisis – live updatesWhat is Trump’s Board of Peace and who is involved?Julian BorgerSenior international correspondentFri 31 Jul 2026 10.09 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 20.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has declared a breakthrough in negotiations over the disarmament of Hamas in Gaza and the withdrawal of Israeli forces, issues that have so far stalled the implementation of last October’s ceasefire, but Israel has yet to respond officially to the plan and government officials have voiced scepticism over the deal.Announcing the agreement in a social media post on Thursday night, Trump said it involved the “complete disarmament” ofHamasand other armed groups in Gaza and was “a monumental step toward ending the fighting”.Israel has pointed to Hamas’s failure to disarm as justification for its continued strikes and refusal to allow any reconstruction in Gaza, and for Israeli forces’ steady edging forward from the demarcation line agreed in October.9:32Can Trump’s Hamas disarmament plan work and will Israel agree to withdraw from Gaza? - The LatestAfter months of negotiations in Cairo, the Board of Peace (BoP), set up by Trump last year, managed on Thursday to secure Hamas’s agreement to a “roadmap” for phased disarmament, in parallel with Israeli withdrawal, and alongside a transfer of power inGazafrom Hamas to a Palestinian interim administration of technocrats, supported by specially trained Palestinian police and an international stabilisation force (ISF).The 14-point plan,posted by the BoP on Xon Friday, urges Israel, Hamas and other Palestinian factions to halt all military operations, and calls for an international verification committee (IVC) to be set up. It outlines a 14-day period after all parties have accepted the roadmap, with a timetable and implementation mechanisms to be worked out.View image in fullscreenSmoke rises after an Israeli strike in Gaza. The Israeli military has continued to expand ​its area of occupation.Photograph: Jehad Alshrafi/APControl of Gaza would then be handed to a National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, a panel of Palestinian professionals and experts set up by the BoP in January who have been waiting in Cairo since then to take over. The NCAG would take over all administrative functions, backed by the new police force and the ISF. That would enable a “process to decommission and store heavy weapons, military production sites, depots of weapons, and tunnels”.The disarming of Hamas and other groups would be “gradual, sequential and time-bound” and would be “linked to an Israeli withdrawal, in phases, from the areas under its control in Gaza”. The ISF would operate between NCAG and Israeli-controlled areas of the territory, while internal security would be the responsibility of the NCAG and its police force.What is Trump’s Board of Peace and who is involved?Read moreNickolay Mladenov, a Bulgarian diplomat appointed as the BoP’s high representative for Gaza, said: “Today, agreement has been reached on the decommissioning of weapons and civilian transition in Gaza. It took months of very difficult negotiations to get here. There were several points when I did not believe we would make it.“What the agreement says matters. What happens next matters even more. Implementation and verification have to be real. Withdrawal must move in lockstep with decommissioning.”There was no confirmation from the Israeli government by Friday afternoon that it accepted the agreement. The far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, dismissed it as “unacceptable”.“The assassinations in Gaza must continue, the encouragement of immigration must happen, Israel must win,” Ben-Gvir said on the Telegram messaging platform.Hours after Trump announced the Hamas agreement, Israel carried out an airstrike on Gaza, wounding several people. Israeli forces have killed more than 1,000 Palestinians in Gaza since the October ceasefire.View image in fullscreenA Palestinian man cycling past the rubble of buildings destroyed by Israeli strikes in Khan Younis, Gaza.Photograph: Abdel Kareem Hana/APAn Israeli official told Reuters: “Israel demands the complete disarmament of Hamas, including ​the removal of weapons from Gaza and the complete demilitarisation of the strip as a precondition for ‌any process.” They said the plan under discussion did not “provide a satisfactory response to these demands and Israel conveyed its objections”.Hamas said it agreed to the roadmap on condition that disarmament was carried out at the same time as Israeli withdrawal. “We will not take any action regarding disarmament prior to Israel’s withdrawal from the strip,” Ghazi Hamad, a member of the Hamas negotiating team, told ​Al Jazeera.Hamad told Agence France-Presse in a separate interview: “The agreement contains a clear provision stating that Israel must commit to and implement its obligations. If Israel does not implement the agreement, neither will we.”By agreeing to Mladenov’s roadmap, Hamas has increased the pressure on Israel to fulfil the commitments it made in the October ceasefire. A US official who briefed the press on Thursday night acknowledged that Israel was “very sceptical that Hamas will ‌disarm” but added that Trump would be “very, very disappointed” if Israel did not meet its obligations under the agreement.It is unclear how long the agreement would take to implement. The 13 members of the NCAG have so far been barred by Israel from entering Gaza, the special training of Palestinian police has yet to start, and troops from the countries volunteering to support the ISF, such as Morocco and Kosovo, have yet to arrive.“The whole point of this is the sequencing, the verification and the reciprocity, less [about] timetables,” a BoP official told the Guardian. “If something isn’t adhered to, the next step isn’t compelled. If something requires more time, the IVC allots more time. There is a recognition that this won’t be easy. There will be challenges, and things may take more or less time.”Hamas had previously said it was ready to disarm but had insisted it would not agree to any new deal before Israel had fulfilled Hamas’s obligations under the first phase of the ceasefire: stopping the bombing and pulling back to the agreed demarcation line.View image in fullscreenDisplaced Palestinians shelter at a tent camp in Gaza City.Photograph: Dawoud Abu Alkas/ReutersMuhammad Shehada, a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said Hamas relented as it was facing increasing resentment inside Gaza.“Hamas is eager to get rid of the governing burden of Gaza, having to pay the salaries of 35,000 employees. They see this as a burden,” Shehada added. Hamas leaders had hoped Iran would make the Gaza ceasefire a condition for its June memorandum of understanding with the US, but this did not happen.“There is disappointment with Iran, as Gaza was not mentioned explicitly,” Shehada said. “The other reason is the fear that Israel would relaunch the war back to its full might.”There was little optimism in Gaza that the agreement would be carried out, he said.“As a precondition, Israel would have to fulfil a number of minimal obligations, like 600 trucks of aid in a day, suspending military operations, withdrawing to the [agreed demarcation] line,” Shehada said. Before Israeli elections, that would “be seen from the Israeli government’s perspective as political suicide”.Explore more on these topicsGazaHamasPalestineIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaTrump administrationUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: India’s monsoon rains in danger as UN chief warns planet is ‘on fire’ | El Niño southern oscillation | The Guardian
description: António Guterres says strengthening El Niño will help push the world’s climate crisis into ‘uncharted territory’
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: António Guterres says strengthening El Niño will help push the world’s climate crisis into ‘uncharted territory’
Content: People wading through a waterlogged street in Ahmedabad last week.Photograph: Ajit Solanki/APView image in fullscreenPeople wading through a waterlogged street in Ahmedabad last week.Photograph: Ajit Solanki/APEl Niño southern oscillationIndia’s monsoon rains in danger as UN chief warns planet is ‘on fire’António Guterres says strengthening El Niño will help push the world’s climate crisis into ‘uncharted territory’Fiona HarveyEnvironment editorFri 31 Jul 2026 13.37 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndia’s monsoon is in danger and hotter, drier conditions are forecast across much of the world as a stronger El Niño weather system is taking hold, weather experts have warned.António Guterres, the UN secretary general, said the strengthening El Niño was “adding fuel to a planet already on fire” and pushing the world into “uncharted territory”.The El Niño system will strengthen from August to October, which will bring higher temperatures globally, with increasing rainfall in some regions while others suffer drought, according to data andforecastsreleased by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) on Friday.Marine heatwaveshave already shocked scientists this year and are set to intensify: the WMO said temperatures were likely to exceed 2.9C above normal in several regions.“The Pacific waters driving it have never been this warm this early in an El Niño, and temperatures are still increasing,” Guterres said. “[This year] risks shattering every seasonal record, and driving even more severe effects worldwide. We are in uncharted territory.”The risk of a weakened monsoon, which brings the rain on which Indian farmers rely, was highlighted as the forecast gave an “enhancement in the probability for below-normal rainfall”, which would produce increased drought, floods and wildfire risk around the Indian Ocean basin. Drier conditions are also likely across parts of equatorial Africa to the west of the Horn of Africa, across the south and east of Australia, large parts of South America and in North America.Higher than normal rainfall is expected in southern Europe, central Asia and the Horn of Africa and south-eastern South America.Extreme weather has already caused havoc around the world this summer, withrecord-breakingheatwaves beginning in May in the UK, andwildfires across France and Spainthat have destroyed villages and displaced hundreds of thousands of people.View image in fullscreenA destroyed house after wildfires in the village of Le Porge, Gironde, France.Photograph: Catalina Martin-Chico/The GuardianScientists have warnedthis year of the development of an El Niño, a weather system in the Pacific that frequently affects temperatures and rainfall around the world. Some El Niño years in the past have been relatively mild, but scientists have said that this year’s has been supercharged by the climate crisis.Warmer waters – earlier in the year than usual and with water temperatures still increasing – have led to predictions of a “super El Niño” forming. The WMO does not use this term, but has said that the weather system developing is likely to be significantly stronger and more intense than usual. Friday’s forecasts were the organisation’s latest update, covering August to October.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA rain festival with no rain: the Indian farmers bracing for a ‘super’ El Niño as monsoon arrives lateRead moreCeleste Saulo, the secretary general of the WMO, called on governments to make preparations to help people affected by the heat, drought and potential floods that are likely in the months ahead.“El Niño is one of the most closely monitored climate phenomena in the world,” she said. “But forecasts in themselves do not prevent hazards, people do. This El Niño, developing against the backdrop of unprecedented ocean heat and rising temperatures, provides governments and communities with a window of opportunity to anticipate risks and act before impacts unfold. The decisions we make today will shape the impacts we experience tomorrow.”Guterres warned of the impacts on Friday and called for governments to take action on fossil fuels. “Two months ago, I warned that El Niño was arriving on our doorstep. Now it is inside the house, and turning up the heat,” he told reporters in New York.He added:“El Niño is strengthening – adding fuel to a planet already on fire with scorching heat domes, apocalyptic wildfires and record hot seas. Fossil fuels are fanning the flames of this crisis. Expansion must stop.”Guterres warned particularly of the risks to workers: “Heat is claiming lives on a growing scale, day after day, in every region of the world. It is also putting an enormous share of the global workforce at risk, exposing billions of people to dangers and often life-threatening conditions.”Separately, studies have shown that theextreme weather Europe is experiencingand theincreasing likelihood of drought and wildfireshave been “supercharged” by the climate crisis.Explore more on these topicsEl Niño southern oscillationIndiaSouth and central AsiaExtreme weatherClimate crisisDroughtnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour wins decisive victory in Greater Manchester mayoral byelection | Mayoral elections | The Guardian
description: Bev Craig succeeds Andy Burnham and wins back support in areas where Reform made gains in May
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Bev Craig succeeds Andy Burnham and wins back support in areas where Reform made gains in May
Content: Bev Craig defeated Reform UK by 66.3% to 33.7% in the second round of the Greater Manchester mayoral byelection.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBev Craig defeated Reform UK by 66.3% to 33.7% in the second round of the Greater Manchester mayoral byelection.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianMayoral electionsLabour wins decisive victory in Greater Manchester mayoral byelectionBev Craig succeeds Andy Burnham and wins back support in areas where Reform made gains in MayJosh HallidayNorth of England editorFri 31 Jul 2026 18.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLabour has stormed to a decisive victory in theGreater Manchestermayoral byelection, seizing back areas that recently fell to Reform UK and the Greens.Labour’s Bev Craig, theManchestercity council leader, will now succeed Andy Burnham and hold one of the most powerful political positions outside Westminster.Labour won 47% of first-preference votes, withReform UKway behind on 21% and the Greens in third on 12%.The contest took place under the supplementary vote system, meaning that, as no candidate achieved more than 50%, voters’ second preferences were counted.When voters’ second choices were counted and other parties were eliminated, Labour’s share rose to 66.3% and Reform UK’s to 33.7%.In her victory speech at Co-op Live in Manchester, Craig urged society to “move away from divisive politics that try to pit neighbour against neighbour”.The scale of the victory is a significant boost for the new prime minister, suggesting Labour can win back both left- and right-leaning voters who deserted the party under Keir Starmer.It also poses troubling questions for Nigel Farage, whose party has surrendered its year-long lead in the national polls and is in a deepening crisis over questions about its funding.A poll last month had Labour and Reform UK virtually neck and neck in the battle for the mayoralty.In the May elections, Farage’s party won more than 100 seats across Greater Manchester, including all but one of the 25 up for grabs in Wigan – the borough of Burnham’s new constituency – and 18 out of 19 in Tameside, both once solidly Labour areas.However, Farage scuppered the party’s mayoral campaign when he announced he was standing down as an MP in order to fight aself-imposed parliamentary byelectionin Clacton after scrutiny over his funding.Before the result was officially declared, Labour sources said it had won in every ward in boroughs including Bury, Tameside and all but one in Trafford, where both Reform UK and the Greens made inroads in May.In Oldham, where Reform UK gained 13 councillors and ended Labour’s 15-year grip on power two months ago, Labour won 17 of the 20 wards in the mayoral contest, it is understood. Sources said Labour had won every ward in Gorton and Denton, the constituency won by the Green party’s Hannah Spencer in February.One senior Labour source said it looked as if Reform UK had “massively underperformed” and that the result was a combination of Burnham’s prime ministership signalling “you can vote Labour again” and voters feeling confident they could vote for Craig.‘This is the dream job’: Labour’s Bev Craig on the battle to be Greater Manchester mayorRead moreThe result will also worry Reform UK as its hard-right rival Restore Britain won 8.7% of the vote to beat the Conservatives into fourth place.Rupert Lowe’s anti-immigration party, which only launched six months ago, focused its campaign on child sexual abuse gangs and its approach appeared to pay off, taking a share of Reform UK’s vote while potentially galvanising lapsed voters who might otherwise have stayed at home.Its support was strongest in more deprived outer boroughs like Tameside, where Restore got 14% of the vote – almost 6,000 voters – and Rochdale and Oldham where it won 12%.Speaking from the podium after the result was announced just after 11pm on Friday, Craig said that during the campaign she had met “fantastic people doing incredible things against the odds every single day – rejecting the politics of hate but standing with their neighbours, looking out for each other”.For the Greens, which won 7% of the vote against Burnham when the Greater Manchester mayoralty was last contested in 2024, the result may be a disappointment after its recent electoral successes.Geraldine Coggins, the Green party candidate, said she was pleased with its campaign and that there had been a “surge” of support for the party under Zack Polanski’s leadership.She claimed the result was “not a ringing endorsement” of Craig, comparing her 47% vote share with Burnham whonever won less than 60% of the vote in each of his three victories since 2017.“The fact this has even gone to the second round is devastating for them,” Coggins said. “To have lost this much support in the honeymoon period of a new prime minister is not a positive sign for them.”The contest was triggered by Burnhamwinning the Makerfield byelectionon 18 June, meaning he had to step down as mayor of the most powerful combined authority outside London.The byelection was the biggest contest of its kind in British political history, with more than 2 million eligible voters.However, the turnout was down on previous Greater Manchester mayoral contests – only 25%, the third lowest of any mayoral byelection to date – due to a combination of low voter awareness and it taking place in the summer holidays.Explore more on these topicsMayoral electionsGreater ManchesterBev CraigLabourManchesterReform UKGreen partynewsShareReuse this content

title: High court clears way for clinical trial giving puberty blockers to children | Transgender | The Guardian
description: Legal challenge to King’s College London research study claimed it could harm participants but was rejected
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Legal challenge to King’s College London research study claimed it could harm participants but was rejected
Content: King's College London says particular care will be taken over the safety of participants, who will be aged between 11 and 16.Photograph: camberwell.camera/AlamyView image in fullscreenKing's College London says particular care will be taken over the safety of participants, who will be aged between 11 and 16.Photograph: camberwell.camera/AlamyTransgenderHigh court clears way for clinical trial giving puberty blockers to childrenLegal challenge to King’s College London research study claimed it could harm participants but was rejectedKevin RawlinsonFri 31 Jul 2026 13.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA clinical trial of drugs that can delay puberty can go ahead after a high court judge threw out a legal challenge on Friday.Campaigners had launched the attemptto halt the planned research into puberty blockers, to be run by researchers at King’s College London (KCL), on the grounds that they believed it could harm the children taking part.But Mr Justice Chamberlain refused the application for a judicial review, saying none of their claims had a realistic chance of success in court. He said each patient involved in the Pathways trial would have been assessed over “many months” by specialist doctors who would have “formed the opinion that a child has a reasonable prospect of receiving a clinical benefit from the treatment”.The university welcomed the court’s decision on Friday, saying particular care would be taken over the safety of participants of the trial, which will start recruiting more than 220 children aged between 11 and 16 years old from 1 August.But opponents, including the psychotherapist James Esses and Keira Bell, who began taking puberty blockers as a teenager before later detransitioning, expressed sadness at the ruling.Bell told the BBC: “It’s a tragedy that the court has refused permission for this challenge to proceed. The medical profession and morality do not always walk hand in hand. If they did, this trial would be out of the question.”The Bayswater Group, which works with parents of gender-questioning children and was also part of the legal challenge, said:“We remain of the view that the Pathways trial does not meet the legal and ethical thresholds required for research on children.“The design and scale of the study, the known and potential harms of the intervention, and the absence of a sufficient prior evidence base of benefit raise fundamental questions about whether the protective framework for minors has been properly implemented.”A spokesperson for KCL said: “Pathways trial is a carefully designed study to give much needed evidence about the potential benefits and risks of puberty suppression to improve NHS care.“A small number of young people with long-term gender incongruence, who have already received comprehensive psychological and social support through NHS gender services, will be eligible.”The spokesperson added that the study would have “strict eligibility requirements” and that the trial’s design had been “carefully reviewed by independent researchers and has been approved by the UK’s health research regulators, the HRA and MHRA”.The study was originally commissioned in response to a 2024 review of gender identity services by Dr Hilary Cass, which found that gender medicine was an “area of remarkably weak evidence” and“built on shaky foundations”. Initially used to treat early onset puberty,puberty blockershad been prescribed off-label to children with gender dysphoria until the NHS banned their use last year after the Cass review.Explore more on these topicsTransgenderChildrenMedical researchYoung peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Sam Fender and Olivia Dean’s Rein Me In breaks 73-year record to become longest-running UK No 1 single | UK charts | The Guardian
description: Duetting stars surpass record set in 1953, when crooner Frankie Laine hit the top with I Believe
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Duetting stars surpass record set in 1953, when crooner Frankie Laine hit the top with I Believe
Content: Sam Fender and Olivia Dean, performing Rein Me In.View image in fullscreenSam Fender and Olivia Dean, performing Rein Me In.UK chartsSam Fender and Olivia Dean’s Rein Me In breaks 73-year record to become longest-running UK No 1 singleDuetting stars surpass record set in 1953, when crooner Frankie Laine hit the top with I BelieveBen Beaumont-ThomasFri 31 Jul 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSam Fender and Olivia Dean have scored the longest running UK No 1 single in history withRein Me In, beating a record that has stood since 1953.Back then, the UK singles chart had been running for less than a year and contained just 12 songs when I Believe, a bombastic ballad by US crooner Frankie Laine, hit No 1 and spent a total of 18 weeks on the chart.There have been other songs that have come close to beating him since, such as Bryan Adams’s (Everything I Do) I Do It For You, which spent 16 weeks at the top in 1991, and Wet Wet Wet’s Love is All Around, which had 15 weeks in 1994. Both were gooey power ballads launched off the back of major movie placements – and both prompted just as much exasperation as celebration with every passing week at No 1. More recently, Drake’s One Dance had a 15 week stint at No 1 in 2016, and Ed Sheeran’s Shape of You scored 14 weeks in 2017.But Fender and Dean have clung on to clock up an amazing 19 weeks at the summit – made all the more impressive by chart rules introduced in recent years to prevent this length of run from ever happening.On hearing the news, Fender said he was “completely lost for words. Thank you so much toOlivia Deanand the fans for making this song the juggernaut that it is.”Fender wrote Rein Me In for his albumPeople Watching, which was released in February 2025. He released five other singles from the album prior to Rein Me In, including the title track, which seemed like it would be the biggest hit, reaching No 4 and hanging around the Top 100 for 43 weeks.That title song is an obvious anthem: high tempo with strident guitars, euphoric synths and a Springsteen-esque sense of grandeur. Rein Me In, on the other hand, is a gentler and less obviously commercial proposition, rooted in Fender’s love of British folk and given a slower, rollicking rhythm. The beautiful music belies a bleak, heart-rending story of someone who spins into alcohol and drugs, “working myself up to a nice warm bliss”, after self-destructively ending a relationship.Sam Fender: People Watching review | Alexis Petridis’s album of the weekRead more“I’m talking about substance abuse and drinking too much to get the reason back, the reason for going through your day,” Fender has said. “It’s loosely based on my own life, this song, but also, I always kind of take parts of my own life and put it into characters and embellish it, ‘cause all good stories deserve embellishment. The ‘rein me in’ part kind of [means] your friends are gonna rein you in from drinking too much and going off the rails because you’re heartbroken and you’re dealing with it in a bad way.”The song went from album track to hit single after being re-recorded with a new verse by Dean, who has had her own huge solo success in tandem with Rein Me In, thanks to her hit second album,The Art of Loving. Her verse voices the woman who Fender’s protagonist walked away from, singing to him: “You’re so afraid of that heart inside your chest.”Released in June 2025, the new version of Rein Me In took 36 weeks to reach No 1, and has been on and off the top spot since February, interrupted by short spells from Harry Styles, Olivia Rodrigo, Ariana Grande and Taylor Swift before wresting the No 1 place back each time. This week, the song held off competition from Shakira and Burna Boy, who remain at No 2 with their official World Cup song, Dai Dai.View image in fullscreenFender and Dean at the 2026 Brit awards.Photograph: JMEnternational/Getty ImagesRein Me In has also managed to buck a rule introduced in 2017 called “accelerated decline”, which was created to make more songs flow through theUK charts, sweeping away older ones that had been sticking around. Once a song has been on the charts for 10 weeks, if its streaming numbers drop three weeks in a row, the value of its streams are then halved – generally causing a precipitous drop down the charts, even if it remains popular in real terms.Rein Me In’s relatively up-and-down, slow burn path to the top has helped it avoid that fate, along with its sheer songwriting quality and emotional impact, which has given it appeal right across the tastes of British pop fans.Hard work, romance and bell hooks: how Olivia Dean became British pop’s newest megastarRead moreJo Twist, chief executive of the UK music industry’s leading trade association, the British Phonographic Institute (BPI), said: “In an evolving world where we all consume music globally, it’s a truly remarkable feat for Rein Me In to resonate with fans in such a profound way. The British public have taken the song to their hearts, and we should all be proud and celebrate this special moment in our music heritage.”The duet version of Rein Me In also won song of the year at the 2026 Brit awards.Adams’s (Everything I Do) I Do It For You still has the longest consecutive run at No 1: its 16 weeks were unbroken, before being dethroned by U2’s The Fly.There was another British record broken this week on the albums chart, as Charli xcx becomes the first British female artist to have two No 1 albums in the same year. Her new album,Music, Fashion, Film, reached the top just five months after her previous one, hersoundtrackto Emerald Fennell’s film adaptation ofWuthering Heights.The Guardian’s rock and pop critic Alexis Petridis on Rein Me InView image in fullscreenAlexis Petridis.Photograph: Alicia Canter/the GuardianWhenSam Fenderand Olivia Dean launched their re-recorded version of Rein Me In last summer – Dean appearing on stage to perform the song during Fender’s run of British stadium shows – it seems highly unlikely either of them thought they were sitting on a record-breaking single that would still be lodged at No 1 a year later.Rein Me In certainly doesn’t have the obvious blockbusting qualities of previous long-term chart toppers such as Everything I Do (I Do It for You), Bohemian Rhapsody, or Meat Loaf’s I’d Do Anything For Love (But I Won’t Do That). It’s got a singalong chorus, but even by the standards of Fender’s more anthemic Springsteen-inspired material – Seventeen Going Under or Hypersonic Missiles – it’s understated; a sweet tune with a vaguely country-ish lilt. The guitar part sounds like a banjo and the piano has a metallic “tack” sound, familiar from saloon-bar players in old westerns.Even so, it’s the kind of track that works well in a climate dominated by streaming. It’s pretty, mellifluous, well-written, and sounds amiable in a way that is at odds with its subject matter. It sits somewhere between genres – a bit folky, a bit rocky, a bit country, plus a hint of soul thanks to Dean’s vocal – and it bears repeated listening because it’s not so striking that anyone would tire of it quickly.Perhaps its shelf life was extended by the fact that the balance between the two artists who made it has gradually shifted over the last year. In summer 2025, Fender was giving a mid-ranking British singer some stadium-level exposure, but with the release of The Art of Loving – a huge global hit, bolstered by a string of massively successful singles, the billion-streaming Man I Need among them – Dean’s career rocketed. A song that began life very much as Sam Fender featuring Olivia Dean has, over the course of its success, gradually become something else: a collaboration between two huge stars.Explore more on these topicsUK chartsSam FenderOlivia DeanPop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s OK to mess around’: how ‘mop man’ stole the show at Glasgow’s Commonwealth Games | Commonwealth Games | The Guardian
description: CJ Miller from West Lothian has delighted global audiences with ‘sheer stupidity’ of his half-time routines
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: CJ Miller from West Lothian has delighted global audiences with ‘sheer stupidity’ of his half-time routines
Content: CJ Miller, the man behind the mop, says he is enjoying ‘a lovely 50 minutes of fame’.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCJ Miller, the man behind the mop, says he is enjoying ‘a lovely 50 minutes of fame’.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianCommonwealth Games‘It’s OK to mess around’: how ‘mop man’ stole the show at Glasgow’s Commonwealth GamesCJ Miller from West Lothian has delighted global audiences with ‘sheer stupidity’ of his half-time dancesPriya BharadiaFri 31 Jul 2026 12.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe 2026Commonwealth Gamesin Glasgow have already provided plenty of highlights. But fans across the world have been dazzled by one particular breakout star: the “mop man”.When a cleaner came out at half-time during a netball match to wipe down the court before the restart, everything appeared normal. But as the cleaner swept, and the first bars of Queen’s I Want to Break Free rang out in the venue, he went from sweeping to a standing split.A full dance routine set to the 1984 hit then followed, much to the surprise and delight of the audience at the OVO Hydro. The crowd watched him do the worm, splits and front handsprings. He has since entertained crowds during breaks in play at a number of other events and clips of his performances have gone viral online.View image in fullscreen‘It’s Doris the mop now’: CJ Miller isn’t the only one to have been given a surprising nickname.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAThe man behind the mop is CJ Miller, 25, from Livingston, West Lothian, a trained dancer who was hired by the Games to keep crowds entertained during intermissions.He considers himself more of an introvert than his cleaning alter ego. “I’m an anxious and paranoid queen,” said Miller. “And I’m so grateful for the turn of events. It’s been a lovely 50 minutes of fame. I wish I’d had a haircut before it happened.”Miller was initially told he would be part of a flashmob at the Games with other dancers. “Then it was, ‘oh, here’s a mop. Here’s the song.’ It wasn’t until the Tuesday before the Games I found out it was gonna be Boo Boo the Fool here, on his own,” Miller laughed, pointing to himself.View image in fullscreenFreddie Mercury in Queen’s video for I Want to Break Free, the song Miller dances to.Photograph: QueenWhen choreographing the routine, Miller was inspired by “the concept of a volunteer … a cleaner that had been possessed by the music and just exploded.”But the character soon took on a life – and fanbase – of his own. “People have messaged being like, ‘Thank you for making me smile, I really needed that today.’”For Miller, the universal charm of his performance comes from “the sheer stupidity, the sheer bonkersness of it all”. “It just made people feel like it’s OK to mess around,” he said. “Sometimes, people need to be reminded to just take a break. Just take a minute to smile at someone else being so bloody ridiculous.”Miller’s performance was soon picked up by broadcasters and newspapers around the world. There was particular praise for the unexpected chemistry with his dance partner: Doris the mop.“Phil [Goodlad] from the BBC had named the mop Doris – so I didn’t even name the bloody mop!” said Miller. “He asked me, and I went: ‘The mop is a mop, Phil.’ And he was like: ‘I think it looks like a Doris.’ I went: ‘Brilliant. It’s Doris the mop now, Phil, spectacular.’”Did he have a name in mind for his other dance partner, the vacuum? “It was a Vax vacuum, so I think the vacuum should be called Vaxtina – like Xtina. You can write that one down.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA new start after 60: stuck in a hospital bed, I decided to retire. Now I’m a tap dancerRead moreGoing into the Games, Miller felt nervous about performing in front of a sports crowd for the first time. “Basketball, for me, was a scary one. I was like: ‘I don’t think the basketball crowd are going to want to see my flamboyant ass, giving them a dance to Freddie Mercury. And I was wrong. The basketball crowd were incredible.”View image in fullscreenMiller with his dance partner, Doris the mop.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian“It was a lesson for me to check my own prejudice,” he said. “It doesn’t excuse the point of view I had of sports fans, and that has been changed now from the immense support I’ve received from the sports fans at the Commonwealth. Thank you for proving me wrong, sports fans.”Going forward, Miller is soon to join Newcastle College as a dance tutor and continue building his career as a choreographer. But will the world ever see more of mop man?“I think it would be fun,” said Miller, who has been approached by one company about taking his performance further. “If I were to do it again, let’s get some other professions in there,” said Miller. “Referee, waiter, bloody construction worker. Let’s get inventive with it.”While mop man’s performances may have come to an end, Miller hopes viewers can be inspired by his character’s self-confidence and sense of whimsy. “Be messy, fail, screw up,” he said. “That’s what makes us human. Get your mop and shake your ass, you know what I mean?”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth GamesCommonwealth Games 2026DanceQueenScotlandGlasgownewsShareReuse this content

title: Pilot ejects from F-35B jet crash near San Diego marine base, officials say | US military | The Guardian
description: Unidentified pilot of F-35B fighter jet receives treatment for non-life-threatening injuries after crash near Miramar
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Unidentified pilot of F-35B fighter jet receives treatment for non-life-threatening injuries after crash near Miramar
Content: Fire crews spray down the wreckage of an F-35B fighter jet after it crashed near Miramar air base in San Diego.Photograph: Sandy Huffaker/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFire crews spray down the wreckage of an F-35B fighter jet after it crashed near Miramar air base in San Diego.Photograph: Sandy Huffaker/AFP/Getty ImagesUS militaryPilot ejects from F-35B jet crash near San Diego marine base, officials sayUnidentified pilot of F-35B fighter jet receives treatment for non-life-threatening injuries after crash near MiramarAssociated PressFri 31 Jul 2026 19.17 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn F-35B fighter jet crashed near a US Marine Corps base inSan Diegoon Friday morning, sparking a small fire that first responders doused.The pilot, who has not been publicly identified, sustained non-life-threatening injuries, according to a statement from the Marine Corps Miramar air base. “The pilot ejected, was transported to a local medical facility in stable condition for evaluation and treatment of non-life-threatening injuries,” the Marine Corps said in an updated statement.It’s unclear what led to the crash, which officials characterized as a “Class A mishap”. That’s the most severe mishap category, used when the damage totals more than $2m, an aircraft is destroyed or a service member killed.Democrats demand answers over treatment of wounded US troops after Iran strikeRead moreA single F-35B fighter jet costs about $109m.Candace Hadley, a spokesperson for San Diego Fire, said firefighters were on scene to respond to a vegetation fire that sparked near the crash site. She referred additional questions to Miramar.The F-35B is one of several versions of the advanced stealth fighter jet that is flown by the Marine Corps, navy and air force. The “B” version has an engine that is designed for short takeoffs and is capable of vertical landings.At least seven other military aircraft mishaps have happened in the US this year, according to the Flight Safety Foundation’s Aviation Safety Network database.Mishap investigations reportedly can take several months.The F-35s are considered the safest and most capable fighter jets the military has in its fleet, according to the Lexington Institute thinktank that focuses on defense technology and national security.There have been fewer crashes involving any of the F-35 models since the jet was adopted in 2015 compared with other fighter jets when those planes were new – and fatal crashes are rare in F-35s.Explore more on these topicsUS militarySan DiegoCaliforniaWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: San Francisco pitbull rescued after two days trapped in railway tunnel | San Francisco | The Guardian
description: Pup named Roo, who ran away from home, was found curled up next to rail track – and was ‘thrilled’ to be rescued
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Pup named Roo, who ran away from home, was found curled up next to rail track – and was ‘thrilled’ to be rescued
Content: Roo has since been reunited with his owner.Photograph: San Francisco department of animal care and controlView image in fullscreenRoo has since been reunited with his owner.Photograph: San Francisco department of animal care and controlSan FranciscoSan Francisco pitbull rescued after two days trapped in railway tunnelPup named Roo, who ran away from home, was found curled up next to rail track – and was ‘thrilled’ to be rescuedUwa Ede-OsifoFri 31 Jul 2026 19.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA two-year-old pitbull who ran away from home braved two days in a dimSan Franciscorailway tunnel before being rescued.Caltrain operators spotted the pup named Roo on his first day in the tunnel. Looking at the dog’s unmoving body, they had assumed he had been fatally struck by a train, according to a recent social media post from the San Francisco animal care and control shelter.On the second day, after Roo was seen moving, police officers set out on foot in the tunnel with a flashlight.View image in fullscreenCaltrain operators helping the pup named Roo.Photograph: San Francisco Department of Animal Care & ControlThey found Roo, lying curled next to a rail track, and led the dog out of the dark into the light of day.“He was terrified at first, then was thrilled to be rescued,” the animal shelter wrote in the post. The pup is a recent adoptee, who ran away after being “spooked”.Fortunately, Roo was microchipped. He has since been reunited with his owner.The San Francisco area has rallied around other dogs in distress as of late.Menlo Park firefighters rescued a missing dog that was found swimming in the San Francisco Bay, as seagulls followed in pursuit.Explore more on these topicsSan FranciscoCaliforniaWest CoastAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Illinois officer who killed Sonya Massey denied medical release from prison | Sonya Massey | The Guardian
description: Sean Grayson, diagnosed with colon cancer, was sentenced to 20 years for killing Massey in Springfield in 2024
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sean Grayson, diagnosed with colon cancer, was sentenced to 20 years for killing Massey in Springfield in 2024
