Content: Sonya Massey in this undated photo provided by the family’s lawyers.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenSonya Massey in this undated photo provided by the family’s lawyers.Photograph: APSonya MasseyIllinois officer who killed Sonya Massey denied medical release from prisonSean Grayson, diagnosed with colon cancer, was sentenced to 20 years for killing Massey in Springfield in 2024Associated PressFri 31 Jul 2026 17.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former Illinois sheriff’s deputy won’t get an early medical release from his two-decade prison sentence for killingSonya Masseyinside her home after the Black woman called 911 about a possible prowler, state officials decided on Friday.Sean Grayson had been diagnosed with colon cancer prior to the 2024 shooting, and his attorney noted in January that the cancer had advanced to his liver and lungs.The three-memberIllinoisprisoner review board voted unanimously on Friday to deny Grayson’s application for early medical release, panel spokesperson Liz Mitchell said in an email.Grayson, who is white, was convicted in October of second-degree murder for Massey’s killing, a case that sparked protests over systemic racism and a US justice department review.View image in fullscreenBodycam footage shows Sonya Massey and Sean Grayson outside her home in Springfield.Photograph: Illinois state police/APBody-camera footage showed Grayson and another deputy enter Massey’s home in Springfield, Illinois. Minutes later, Grayson shot the 36-year-old single mother in the face as she moved a pot of hot water from the stove and told him: “I rebuke you in the name of Jesus.”Grayson wasgiven20 years, the maximum possible sentence, in January.He filed for early release from prison in May, six months into his sentence, according to a copy of his application published by Capitol News Illinois. Grayson apologized for Massey’s death at his January sentencing but in the release application wrote she had “attacked me with a pot of boiling water”.Attorney Daniel Fultz, who has represented Grayson, declined to comment.In a letter to the board opposing Grayson’s release, Sangamon county state’s attorney John Milhiser said the former deputy’s medical condition was already considered at sentencing.“To release Grayson under these circumstances would be a miscarriage of justice,” he wrote, “and an insult to Sonya Massey’s memory and family.”Representing Massey’s family, attorneys Ben Crump and Antonio Romanucci said on Friday that the board “made the right decision”.“The board recognized what this family has said from the start,” they said in a statement. “No one is above accountability, and a badge does not provide an early way out.”Democratic governor JB Pritzker said in a statement that Illinois law requires the prisoner review board to consider medical release requests. He called Massey’s killing “a profound loss”.“Sonya was innocent, unarmed, and calling law enforcement for help,” he said. “It was a painful reminder that too many innocent Black Americans have faced this kind of violence – and they deserve justice.”Explore more on these topicsSonya MasseyUS crimeUS policingIllinoisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jurors in Lindsay Clancy murder trial visit home where children were killed | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: Defense lawyers say Clancy was ill with postpartum psychosis when she killed three children in January 2023
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Defense lawyers say Clancy was ill with postpartum psychosis when she killed three children in January 2023
Content: A police barricade stands outside the former home of Lindsay Clancy in Duxbury, Massachusetts, on 31 July.Photograph: Rodrique Ngowi/APView image in fullscreenA police barricade stands outside the former home of Lindsay Clancy in Duxbury, Massachusetts, on 31 July.Photograph: Rodrique Ngowi/APMassachusettsJurors in Lindsay Clancy murder trial visit home where children were killedDefense lawyers say Clancy was ill with postpartum psychosis when she killed three children in January 2023Associated PressFri 31 Jul 2026 15.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 18.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJurors walked through the Massachusetts home whereLindsay Clancystrangled her three children, a rare visit on Friday that let them see first-hand the place where an outwardly ordinary family lifeunraveled into tragedy.After being driven past two businesses relevant to the narrative of the January 2023 killings, jurors were escorted in groups of six to view the inside of the house, including the basement where the children died.During the roughly 40-minute visit, the jury also saw the yard where Clancy was found after jumping from a second-story window.Journalists were kept away by a police barricade, but court officers could be seen through the trees escorting jurors to and from the bus along the site of the Clancy family’s former driveway. The home now has a new owner.Lindsay Clancy’s husband told police children were dead, court hearsRead moreClancy herself did not attend the visit to the home, which she has not seen since the day of the killings. Her lawyers say Clancy was in the grip ofpostpartum psychosis, a rare mental illness linked to the stress, sleep deprivation and hormonal changes that follow childbirth.Jurors in US criminal cases often are expressly told not to visit the scene of the events in question. There are a number of rationales for not doing so – among other things, the site may have changed in the interim between an alleged crime and a trial.But courts sometimes allow juries to make a supervised excursion as a group, for reasons that can include assessing distances or features not thought to come across fully in photos.Such excursions have happened in a number of high-profile cases, including the 2023murder trialof the South Carolina attorneyAlex Murdaugh; the 2022sentencing trialof Parkland, Florida, school shooterNikolas Cruz; the 2015 Massachusettsmurder trialof former New England Patriots playerAaron Hernandez; and the 1995murder trialofOJ Simpson.Jurors in Clancy’s trial retraced the route her ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, took when she asked him to pick up takeout food and medicine for Cora, their five-year-old, on the night of the killings. He returned to find the children dead and Clancy badly injured and bleeding in the yard.The panel was driven past the restaurant – about 5.5 miles from the family’s former home in Duxbury, a suburb south of Boston – and the pharmacy, about a mile from the house.Lindsay Clancy’s ex-husband testifies about day she killed their three childrenRead moreProsecutors say the errands were a ruse to get her husband out of the house. They say Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, acted intentionally and is criminally responsible for the deaths of children Cora, five; Dawson, three; and Callan, eight months.Her lawyers do not dispute that Clancy killed the children, but they say she had bipolar disorder and her condition worsened when she took antidepressants prescribed after the birth of her third child. Clancy believed a voice was telling her to “kill the children so you can kill yourself”, according to her lawyers.Lindsay Clancy is paralyzed from the waist down after trying to kill herself that night.Clancy faces life in prison without parole if convicted of murder. If found not guilty due to a lack of criminal responsibility, she would be committed to a state mental health facility.In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsMassachusettsUS crimeMental healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Washington Post’s opinion editor resigns after just one year in role | Washington Post | The Guardian
description: Adam O’Neal did not give reason for his departure at end of August in another major shakeup at US publication
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Adam O’Neal did not give reason for his departure at end of August in another major shakeup at US publication
Content: The Washington Post building sign in February 2026 during a rally outside the newspaper's offices following sweeping layoffs.Photograph: Mehmet Eser/Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Washington Post building sign in February 2026 during a rally outside the newspaper's offices following sweeping layoffs.Photograph: Mehmet Eser/Sopa Images/ShutterstockWashington PostWashington Post’s opinion editor resigns after just one year in roleAdam O’Neal did not give reason for his departure at end of August in another major shakeup at US publicationJeremy BarrFri 31 Jul 2026 13.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Washington Post had realized a state of relative calm in the five months since the paper was turned upside down in February, when nearly half the newsroom waslaid offand its unpopular publisher, Will Lewis,abruptlyresigned.But on Friday, staffers were shocked to find out that Adam O’Neal, a millennial hired last year to lead its opinion section, was already leaving.In a memo to colleagues in the paper’s opinion section titled “A Remarkable Year”, O’Neal gave no reason for his departure, only saying that he had decided to leave and that 31 August would be his last day. Opinion staffers had been given no indication that O’Neal was on the verge of leaving the publication.US judge throws out Trump’s $3.8bn defamation lawsuit against Washington PostRead more“It has been a remarkable year, and I’m very proud of everything we’ve accomplished together,” he wrote in the memo obtained by the Guardian. “While this was not an easy decision, I am leaving proud of how far the opinion section has come and optimistic that its best days lie ahead.”In the memo, O’Neal nodded to the controversial decision last year by owner Jeff Bezos toreorientthe paper’s opinion section to focus on championing free markets and personal liberties, a move that served toalienatemany subscribers.“I joined The Post to lead the opinion section as it began a new chapter, and we have made dramatic changes over the past year. We quickly embraced our mission of championing free markets and personal liberties while simultaneously putting Post Opinions on a sustainable footing,” he wrote.“Our work has become more relevant, accessible and consequential. We regularly publish world-class journalism that finds the audience where it is. This includes agenda-setting columns; news-breaking op-eds; highly influential editorials; and social media content that reaches millions of new people.”Still, one of the section’s top priorities, the launch of a new video podcast calledMake It Make Sense, drew backlash on social media for what seemed like warmed-over hot takes anddid not drawa large viewership despite generous investment and support from the Post.Following O’Neal’s announcement, Jeff D’Onofrio, who took over as the interim publisher after Lewis departed, emailed the entire staff with the subject line “Thank You Adam.”“This past year, under the leadership of Adam O’Neal, Post Opinions has become more balanced in perspective, more financially sustainable and more accessible to readers than ever before,” he wrote. “I want to thank him for his leadership and hard work in reimagining the section.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionABC argues that early license review by FCC is ‘retaliation’ for network’s coverageRead moreStill, it’s extremely unusual for a top Post leader to depart so quickly, particularly one who served as the face of a dramatic reorientation of the section. O’Neal’s predecessor, the veteran journalist David Shipley,resignedafter failing to convince Bezos to not move forward with his new mandate for the section, which made the work of many of its longtime writers no longer relevant. Many such writers wereencouragedto take a buyout in the summer of 2025 and leave the publication.Looking ahead, D’Onofrio said the Post would “work to transition Post Opinions leadership”, with more information to come at a later date.O’Neal, who was 33 years old when he was hired, was seen as an unusual selection, despite past work experience at the Economist and the Wall Street Journal’s opinion desk.Sensing he was not widely known to the Post’s staff, he introduced himself with a verticalvideoposted by the newspaper’s public relations account on X.“Now odds are, you’ve probably never heard of me, and you might be wondering, ‘Who am I?’” he said in the video at the time. “That’s actually kind of a deep and philosophical question, and I’m not sure I went to school long enough to understand it. But I’ve been a journalist for a while, and I’d like to share some of our plans with you.”Explore more on these topicsWashington PostMedia businessUS press and publishingNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It ain’t the same’: inside the bitter battle to free Ben & Jerry’s | Business | The Guardian
description: Ben Cohen says his ice-cream company has been silenced by corporate ownership – and a boycott of Magnum brands could force a sale
Author: Heather Timmons
Headline: Ben Cohen says his ice-cream company has been silenced by corporate ownership – and a boycott of Magnum brands could force a sale
Content: Ben Cohen says there are ‘millions of people who support Ben and Jerry’s and support its social mission’.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBen Cohen says there are ‘millions of people who support Ben and Jerry’s and support its social mission’.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesBusiness‘It ain’t the same’: inside the bitter battle to free Ben & Jerry’sBen Cohen says his ice-cream company has been silenced by corporate ownership – and a boycott of Magnum brands could force a saleHeather TimmonsFri 31 Jul 2026 14.48 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBen & Jerry’s ice-cream in the tub is still great, but the brand’s newest chocolate-covered ice-cream bar on a stick?“It ain’t the same,” Ben Cohen, the company co-founder, told the Guardian. Sure, the chocolate coating is still thick enough, but the ice cream itself is “kinda fluffy”, Cohen said – an insult in the ice-cream world that suggests extra air was added to cut costs.The criticism is surprising coming from Cohen, who opened his eponymous ice-cream shop in Burlington, Vermont, with childhood friend, Jerry Greenfield, in 1978. But it’s perhaps an apt metaphor of how he feels amid a simmeringfightto take back Ben & Jerry’s from a parent company he says has silenced the brand’s trademark activism.For Cohen, 75, the battle is legal and existential. Ben & Jerry’s social and economic value was protected for decades, he says, by an independent board with final say on the brand’s voice, values and ice-cream quality.But that independence has all but disappeared, Cohen said. In November 2024, Ben & Jerry’s boardsued parent company Unilever, claiming it was blocked from voicing support for Gaza, and accusing Unilever of breaching their agreement. The lawsuit is still making its way through federal court.In September 2025, after Unilever said it would spin off its ice-cream brands into the Magnum Ice Cream Company, Cohenstartedhis campaign to “Free Ben & Jerry’s” – asking Magnum to sell the brand so it can be independently owned and operated.Social activism is a core part of why people buy Ben & Jerry’s, Cohen says. “What consumers want above all is authenticity and attitude,” he said.Ben & Jerry’s could be valued at $1bn or more, Cohen estimates, but says Magnum won’t give him or potential investors numbers that could help value it more accurately.Magnum has insisted Ben & Jerry’s is not up for sale, so Cohen is amping up his campaign. In recent weeks, Cohen has started calling for a boycott of Magnum’s other brands, including Yasso, Breyers, Talenti and Klondike, with the idea that tanking the company’s overall sales will pressure it to sell back the company.“We didn’t want it to have to come to this,” he said of the boycott, but Magnum is “destroying a brand” that stands for values its customers believe in.What Cohen is trying to do – force an $11bn conglomerate into divesting a star brand – is highly unusual, and unlikely to succeed, some industry and management experts predict.“Most boycotts fail because people get distracted,” said Maurice Schweitzer, a management professor at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania. US and European consumers just may not have the long-term attention span for the sustained collective action that it would take to pressure management, Schweitzer said.But Cohen believes the company’s loyal followers are on his side.“Consumers want to vote with their dollars,” he said, insisting that support for the brand must continue. “We want Ben & Jerry’s to remain strong because we plan on eventually owning it.”The flavors of conflictIt’s been nearly three decades since Cohen and Greenfield sold their company to Unilever for $326m in 2000. The unique deal was built around an independent board andlauded by the Wharton Schoolfor preserving thecompany’s pledgeto try to “make the world a better place” while also committing to making great ice-cream and turning a profit.Under Unilever, Ben & Jerry’s was vocally supportive of social issues. The company criticized George W Bush’s war in Iraq, was a pioneering supporter of same-sex marriage, and called to “dismantle white supremacy” after George Floyd was murdered.But now, the divide between the brand’s founders and the company’s corporate owners is deep and bitter.Cracks first opened after an independent board overseeing the company said in 2021 that selling Ben & Jerry’s ice cream in occupied Palestine was “inconsistent with our values”, sparking outrage in Israel. Unileversold off the Israeli trademarkto a local businessman who is now selling a“Milk & Honey” flavor.The board firstsued Unileverin 2024, accusing the company of silencing its activism over Palestine, including vocal support for Gaza and calls to stop US aid to Israel.Then in 2025, UnileveroustedDavid Stever, the Ben & Jerry’s CEO, in a move Ben & Jerry’s said was designed to stifle its social mission, including aboard-approved planto sell a watermelon flavor to support Palestine that was quashed.In a statement to the Guardian, Unilever said Stever’s role was re-evaluated because of the spinoff, not the social mission, and that he turned down a role in the larger company and chose to quit.Co-founder Greenfieldquitsoon after, stepping away from the company for the first time in 50 years, saying it had lost its independence. Currently, the board has just two Unilever veterans after Magnum imposed new term limits.Though the campaign to buy back Ben & Jerry’s has been led by Cohen, Greenfield said in his resignation letter that leaving the board was one of the “hardest and most painful decisions” he had ever made.“It is profoundly disappointing to come to the conclusion that that independence, the very basis of our sale to Unilever, is gone,” he said. “If the company couldn’t stand up for the things we believed, then it wasn’t worth being a company at all.”Earlier in July, Ben & Jerry’s philanthropic foundationsaid it was forced to closeafter Magnum cut its funding. Magnum says an investigation found “governance and conflict-of-interest issues”.In an interview with the Guardian, Magnum’s chief corporate affairs and sustainability officer Victoria McKenzie-Gould said it invited trustees of the foundation to partner on a stronger corporate governance framework, but they declined.“Our focus remains where it belongs: on supporting the Ben & Jerry’s team and its three-part mission while making great ice-cream and campaigning on the causes the brand cares about – and the team is doing a fantastic job,” McKenzie-Gould said.‘Not for sale’Throughout Cohen’s months-long fight to buy back his company, Magnum has said it has no intention of selling.“Ben is a great campaigner, but Ben & Jerry’s is not for sale, and we are confident in the future because Ben & Jerry’s is thriving as part of the Magnum Ice Cream Company,” McKenzie-Gould said.Magnum doesn’t break out sales by brand, but called Ben & Jerry’s one of its “top four”, with 3% organic sales growthin 2025;about 35% of Magnum’s €7.9bn ($9.1bn) 2025 revenue came from the Americas, traditionally Ben & Jerry’s largest market.Salesgrew 9.2%in the second quarter, “powered by innovation”, Ben & Jerry’s CEO, Jochanan Senf, said on Thursday, adding that all three parts of the company’s mission – social, product and economic – must “thrive equally in a way that commands deep respect for individuals in and outside the company”.Since it was acquired in 2000, Ben & Jerry’s “footprint has grown from four to over 40 countries, [and] revenue has grown more than fivefold,” McKenzie-Gould said. The company’s overall social mission has received €500m ($576m) from the parent – more than the original purchase price.The brand had spoken out recently on “ICE;refugee support in Europe;cannabis justiceand voting rights”, a corporate spokesperson for the Ben & Jerry’s brand told the Guardian, including a new flavor –Razz Up!– that encourages midterm voting.The spokesperson disagreed with Cohen’s criticism of the new ice-cream bars, saying the product was approved by the independent board in 2024 and used the same design standards as every product.“More than one-third of bar buyers in the last year are completely new fans to Ben & Jerry’s,” Senf said with second-quarter results.Cohen’s calls for a boycott comes as many Americans are angry at companies and frustrated over US policies. Americansupport for Palestiniansand criticism of Donald Trump have grown, and there’s agrowing frustrationwith big companies over shoddy products and bad service.But the headwinds for a successful boycott are stiff. There’s awar against“woke capitalism”, andshareholder supportfor environmental, social and governance resolutions has plummeted. Many of the social media platforms Cohen needs to spread his message are controlled by conservative billionaires, leaving him at the mercy of their algorithms.“I do think this is going to get lost in the shuffle of so many other causes,” said Schweitzer.Plenty of fans seem to think Cohen’s expectations are naive. “Did you really think a giant company wouldn’t exploit you? When has an international company ever had social values?” wrote Base_Art, a painter, on Instagram.But Cohen has also gathered about 200,000 signatures and lots of encouraging social media messages. “Occasionally, I ate the vegan coffee Talenti,” former model Christie Brinkley recently wrote on Instagram. But without an independent board of directors, she said: “No more!”Cohen acknowledges the hurdles, but says he believes longtime, loyal fans will help overcome them.“I think that there’s millions of people who support Ben and Jerry’s and support its social mission,” Cohen said. “I’m going to take it until we win.”Explore more on these topicsBusinessVermontnewsShareReuse this content

title: BTS are back: return of K-pop superstars sparks US economic boom | BTS | The Guardian
description: Cities in North America hosting 14 concerts in August and September – and economic impact is set to be significant
Author: Jenna Zaza
Headline: Cities in North America hosting 14 concerts in August and September – and economic impact is set to be significant
Content: Fans at a BTS exhibition in Seoul in March.Photograph: Soo-hyeon Kim/ReutersView image in fullscreenFans at a BTS exhibition in Seoul in March.Photograph: Soo-hyeon Kim/ReutersBTSBTS are back: return of K-pop superstars sparks US economic boomCities in North America hosting 14 concerts in August and September – and economic impact is set to be significantJenna ZazaFri 31 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBTS’s “Army” fanbase is descending onNew Yorkthis weekend as the K-pop supergroup continues their first world tour after a four-year hiatus, sparking an economic boom wherever they land.After shows in South Korea and Europe, the group are back in North America, with 14 shows in six US cities in August and September.Following the rollout of BTS’s sixth album, Arirang, in March, fans have proved they are willing to spend. In Las Vegas, concertgoers who attended four sold-out shows in May generated an estimated $340m in economic activity, witheventsat huge hotels on the strip and at tiny Chinatown cafes.HYBE, the group’s label, has partnered with local businesses and cultural centers for the “BTS The City – Arirang” project in select cities, offering exclusiveBTSprogramming for concertgoers.Ahead of two concerts at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium on 1 and 2 August, fans can follow amapof activities, landmarks and eateries that celebrate the group.Manhattan’s Koreatown is bracing for thousands of fans. Theeconomic impact of BTS concertgoersis expected to match that of soccer fans who crowded MetLife Stadium for the World Cup final – which included a BTS performance – a few weeks ago.BTS will “easily compare [to] or even exceed Fifa’s economic impact just on average spending”, said Michael Mariano, head of economic development at Tourism Economics.The group’s return has been a boon for HYBE, whichreporteda record-high revenue of $993m this past quarter.View image in fullscreenBTS merchandise at a pop-up store in Seoul.Photograph: Kim Hong-Ji/ReutersThe Korean Cultural Center New York will serve as the hub for fan activities. Participants who nabbed a coveted reservation can try on K-beauty products, sample desserts from Tous les Jours, a South Korean bakery chain, and customize the light sticks they’ll bring to the concert, known as “Army bombs”.“K-pop can serve as a gateway to learning the Korean language and discovering Korean beauty, food, technology, tourism and other aspects of Korean culture,” said Bora Yoon, visual arts manager at the center.The Arte Museum, which houses large-scale digital art, is hosting a special BTS exhibit that will feature music and digital art celebrating the group’s music. The museum expects a high demand for the exhibit, which will immerse BTS fans in “all five senses”, said Sang Jin Lee, head of the creative team and vice-president of d’strict, a creative design company that owns the Arte Museum.“It’s about sharing our culture, great heritage and Korean contemporary digital art through the lens of BTS, using an enduring folk song that is continually reinterpreted by every generation,” Lee said in Korean, referring to Arirang, the centuries-old folk song that inspired the name of BTS’s new album.View image in fullscreenBTS fans pose for pictures as they gather at HMV on Oxford Street in London.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersNew Wonjo, the oldest Korean barbecue restaurant in New York, is also featured on the map, and plans to serve a special menu inspired by the members of BTS and the foods they miss most on tour, including kimchi fried rice, pork belly and jajangmyeon, or black bean noodles.The menu was developed “with intention, and is rooted in Korean culture, rather than just pasting ‘BTS’ on a regular menu item”, said Jacob Baik, art director of New Wonjo. “We hope that some guests who might initially visit because of the ‘BTS The City’ project leave with a genuine interest in the restaurant, the food and Korean culture more broadly.”The map also features bingsu, a type of South Korean shaved ice dessert, offered by Seoul Bingsu – a pop-up version of Seoul-based Tokyo Bingsu, known for its tomato flavor of the dessert. For its limited 10-day New York run, Seoul Bingsu will offer special bookmarks, pins and stickers for those who order from its special Arirang menu.Ara Go, the Seoul-based owner of Seoul Bingsu, said BTS “has truly helped introduce Korean culture to the world”.“Food and desserts are a huge part of Korean culture, and I saw this as a wonderful opportunity to promote not only our food but our country with a broader audience,” Go said in Korean.View image in fullscreenBTS fans in New York.Photograph: JNI/Star Max/GC ImagesBefore the spot’s collaboration with BTS, Angela May, 18, had never heard of bingsu. May, a BTS fan for nearly six years, traveled to Manhattan fromNew Jerseyto try it.“Just having BTS written on the menu or the window will bring a lot of attention to the place,” May said.Asli Penaeo, 22, grew up in New York and has been a fan for seven years, yet she has never been to most of the collaborating restaurants.“This event is finally giving me a chance to go to some of these restaurants, try new items, but also make new memories with fellow Army [fans],” she said, sipping on a BTS-branded Tous Les Jours strawberry lemonade.Sunmi Lee, 40, an interior designer, said she was considering taking a BTS-themed double-decker bus tour to visit New York landmarks – even though she lives in the city.“It’s about celebrating Korean culture,” she said. “Trying authentic local spots, and feeling connected to something bigger than just a concert.”Explore more on these topicsBTSNew YorkNew JerseyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fifa scraps proposal to sell off stakes in World Cup after widespread backlash | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Gianni ⁠Infantino has said Fifa ​has scrapped plans to ⁠sell a stake in the World ⁠Cup to private ​investors ‌after widespread ‌backlash
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Gianni ⁠Infantino has said Fifa ​has scrapped plans to ⁠sell a stake in the World ⁠Cup to private ​investors ‌after widespread ‌backlash
Content: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has said plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup have been scrapped after a furious backlash.Photograph: Buda Mendes/FIFA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFifa president Gianni Infantino has said plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup have been scrapped after a furious backlash.Photograph: Buda Mendes/FIFA/Getty ImagesFifaFifa scraps proposal to sell off stakes in World Cup after widespread backlashGianni ⁠Infantino issues statement on controversial plan‘This proposal will not proceed,’ confirms Fifa presidentNick AmesFri 31 Jul 2026 19.55 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGianni Infantino’s proposal to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors has sensationally collapsed, with the Fifa president admitting the project “has created divisions of a nature that are no longer of the interest of the objective”, amid widespread anger globally.The plan had caused ructions within football around the world, leading Uefa to threaten a boycott of futureFifatournaments if it was not shelved. Other confederations had also come out in opposition while one of Infantino’s senior advisors, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned on Friday in protest at the scheme. The Fifa chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, had also aimed a scathing rebuke at Infantino’s “serious lack of respect” in seeking to force it through with minimal consultation.Andy Burnham calls on Infantino to resign over ‘outrageous’ World Cup plansRead moreIt has led Infantino to back down amid speculation the venture capital firm Thrive Capital, which was leading the proposed investor group, had also expressed doubts after a week that threatened to tear the sport apart. Infantino’s previously secure presidency has come under severe pressure and it remains to be seen whether his climbdown will be enough to save his position.“Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place,” Infantino said in a statement.“Our purpose has always been – and will always be – to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed. Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support.”The proposed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), unveiled earlier this week, had been intended to raise hundreds of millions of dollars by selling a significant stake in the commercial rights of the men’s and women’s World Cups, and the Club World Cup, to investors. It promised an increase in distribution to “over $10bn” (£7.5bn) being spread back among Fifa’s 211 member associations. A deadline of 19 September had been set for member associations to sign up to the scheme, which offered an optional $20m (£14.8m) to those participating.But the plan was roundly rejected by European countries’ FAs, who agreed upon a boycott at an emergency meeting on Thursday. Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation, the latter with a stinging statement on Friday morning, had also made their distaste clear. While Infantino retains a stronghold in Africa he was left with nowhere to go, the numbers to push through the plan in any credible form having eluded him.Attention will now turn to Infantino’s future given the scale of the internal revolt within Fifa and the severe hit his standing has taken elsewhere. It is unlikely his withdrawal of the plan will sway member associations who had already become deeply disenchanted by his handling of the Folarin Balogun affair, which unfolded three weeks previously during the World Cup. But some observers have wondered whether recourse to Fifa’s reserves, which stand at around $4bn (£2.97bn), for the promised FFE cash would convince enough federations to save his skin.Uefa and other confederations have stepped up their search for candidates to run against Infantino in next year’s Fifa election, in which he had been expected to comfortably win a fourth term. Their appetite is unlikely to change and time will tell whether Infantino can turn his fortunes around after an episode that has had a shattering impact on his credibility.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tony Romo placed on leave from CBS Sports after OWI arrest in Wisconsin | NFL | The Guardian
description: Tony Romo has been placed on leave from his role as the lead analyst on CBS’ NFL coverage following his arrest last week on suspicion of operating a vehicle while under the influence
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tony Romo has been placed on leave from his role as the lead analyst on CBS’ NFL coverage following his arrest last week on suspicion of operating a vehicle while under the influence
Content: Tony Romo (right) has been the lead game analyst for CBS’ NFL coverage since 2017 after making four Pro Bowl appearances during a career that ran from 2004-16.Photograph: Tony Gutierrez/APView image in fullscreenTony Romo (right) has been the lead game analyst for CBS’ NFL coverage since 2017 after making four Pro Bowl appearances during a career that ran from 2004-16.Photograph: Tony Gutierrez/APNFLTony Romo placed on leave from CBS Sports after OWI arrest in WisconsinCBS sidelines Romo indefinitely after arrestJJ Watt promoted to lead booth in absenceArrest followed Wisconsin OWI traffic stopAgenciesFri 31 Jul 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTony Romo has been placed on leave from his role as the lead analyst on CBS’NFLcoverage following his arrest last week on suspicion of operating a vehicle while under the influence.CBS Sports announced Friday that the former Dallas Cowboys quarterback was on leave “until further notice”. JJ Watt will join Jim Nantz and Tracy Wolfson as CBS Sports’ lead NFL team during Romo’s absence.Romo, 46,was arrested on 23 Julyafter he was stopped while driving south on Interstate 43 in Wisconsin. According to the Milwaukee County Sheriff’s Office report, Romo performed poorly on field sobriety tests before getting taken into custody, booked and released.He has a court date set for 21 September.CBS Sports’ announcement comes after citations released by the Milwaukee County Sheriff’s Office indicated an open bottle of an alcoholic beverage was found in the passenger’s side of Romo’s black Jeep during an inventory before it was towed.According to the citations, police stopped Romo after he was seen passing cars in a gore area, which separates interstate traffic from cars entering from an on-ramp. Police said Romo questioned what a gore area was during the stop.Body camera footage released earlier this week showed Romo telling deputies he had been coming from a golf course and was on his way “to visit grandma and grandpa” when he was stopped. A deputy told Romo he suspected him of being impaired because he had “red glassy eyes” and an “odor of an intoxicating alcoholic beverage”.Romo went to high school about 35 miles from Milwaukee in Burlington, Wisconsin.He has been the lead game analyst for CBS’ NFL coverage since 2017 after making four Pro Bowl appearances during an NFL career that ran from 2004-16 and was spent entirely with Dallas.Romo remains the Cowboys’ franchise leader in career touchdown passes with 248. He held the franchise record for career passing yards (34,183) until Dak Prescott overtook him last season.Watt joined CBS in 2023. He was an analyst on The NFL Today for two seasons before teaming with Ian Eagle on the network’s No 2 crew beginning last season.Romo wasn’t expected to have his first game until the opening Sunday of the regular season on 13 September. CBS will air a preseason game between the Cincinnati Bengals and Philadelphia Eagles on 28 August.CBS likely will reveal its game assignments and announcer pairings for the first three weeks of the regular season in the next couple of weeks.Explore more on these topicsNFLUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: How does MLS pick up the World Cup mantle? Casemiro helps, but it’ll take much more | Inter Miami | The Guardian
description: Casemiro’s arrival is another statement signing for MLS, but Sebastian Berhalter’s departure highlights the league’s bigger challenge after a landmark World Cup
Author: Chris Smith
Headline: Casemiro’s arrival is another statement signing for MLS, but Sebastian Berhalter’s departure highlights the league’s bigger challenge after a landmark World Cup
Content: Casemiro was introduced at a Thursday event at Inter Miami’s home ground.Photograph: Anissa DimiltaView image in fullscreenCasemiro was introduced at a Thursday event at Inter Miami’s home ground.Photograph: Anissa DimiltaInter MiamiHow does MLS pick up the World Cup mantle? Casemiro helps, but it’ll take much moreThe World Cup gave MLS unprecedented momentum. Keeping it will depend less on signing aging icons than convincing America’s best young players to stayChris Smithin MiamiFri 31 Jul 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Thanks World, we’ll take it from here,” is Major League Soccer’s message to the American public. Yet two moves in the last week were emblematic of the issues the league faces in taking on the mantle of North America’s hosting of the game’s grandest stage.A rising, under-the-radar homegrown player left for Europe, and a veteran with immense pedigree arrived, likely to close out his career. Sebastian Berhalter’s swapped title-chasing Vancouver Whitecaps for Middlesbrough of the EFL Championship. Free agent Brazil legend Casemiro traded Manchester’s Old Trafford for Nu Stadium in Miami.TheMLSCup holders unveiled their new No 5 on Thursday. They called it The Arrival. Season ticket holders filled the seats around the players’ tunnel as their rhythm section formed a guard of honor, welcoming the new signing onto the field.Here he was. A World Cup star who has captained Brazil. A five-times Champions League winner with Real Madrid and a popular figure at Man United. Now striding on to the turf at Inter Miami’s dazzling new arena wearing a T-shirt emblazoned with the club’s motto: “Freedom to Dream”. He’d had other great offers from Europe, but Casemiro only wanted Miami, both player and ownership enthused at the event.“We have to keep growing, keep evolving and that’s why I’m here too,” Casemiro told the Guardian. “Not only to help Inter Miami and my teammates, but also the league, and the country. To transmit the values of what football is and the greatness of football. MLS can count on me. I want to help.”However, there was an unfortunate irony in the 34-year-old’s unveiling coming on the day Brazil manager Carlo Ancelotti called time on his 91-cap international career.Ancelottitold Globoin Brazil: “I think that this World Cup brings a generation of very important players to an end. Starting with Neymar, also Danilo and Casemiro, all of these players who were over 30 at the World Cup. We are going to look at new players who can come in.”Can the arrival of players like Casemiro alone propel the domestic league forward and capitalize on the World Cup momentum? It helps maintain excitement levels, but it keeps the league in a holding patten where the most marketable names are all born in the last century.Up the road in Orlando, Antoine Griezmann is another recent star acquisition. Robert Lewandowski has arrived in Chicago. Son Heung-min at LAFC and Timo Werner at San Jose have been standout performers in the western conference.Inter Miami have enjoyed a conveyor belt of players with name value coming to play alongside Leo Messi. Sergio Busquets ended his career here. Luis Suárez (39) and Jordi Alba (37) are likely to follow suit. Casemiro joins 32-year-old Rodrigo de Paul in Inter’s midfield.During the introductory press conference – which managing owner Jorge Mas began with 10 minutes ofdefending Inter Miami against tampering allegations– Casemiro added: “A lot of people think MLS is a league that still has a long way to grow, but you have to remember the best player of the last World Cup plays in this league. Leo was the best player of the World Cup, and he’s in MLS.”Messi’s presence is a source of immense pride for Miami and MLS. Had Argentina won the World Cup final, another Ballon d’Or and another landmark distinction for the league would have surely followed. There is no other Messi. And the GOAT is on borrowed time.Efforts to bring in new fans after “the Fifa” travel through the lens of what energized the American public this summer – elite stars like Messi performing at their absolute best, the colorful cultures of visiting fans, and the hope inspired by a likable and talented States team.Erling Haaland captivated, Kylian Mbappe mesmerized and Jude Bellingham’s NBA-like athleticism stood out. Those players at the peak of their powers are not realistic targets for MLS. Miami owner Mas likes to say: “We’re not competing with other MLS teams for this level of athlete. We are competing in a global marketplace.” However, that only applies in these situations with veteran players. And, as is often the case inUS sports, the stars trump the wider galaxy.View image in fullscreenMLS can’t live on aging superstars alone if it wants to own soccer’s post-World Cup moment.Photograph: Anissa DimiltaAlexi Lalas’ assertion that Spain “went under the radar” relied solely on the notion that a half-fit Lamine Yamal had not been as impactful. Lalas is a tough watch, but his voice can be representative of the fan MLS would love to introduce to stadiums around the league.“Their biggest star, Lamine Yamal, he’s a world champion, but did he star throughout the tournament? In his own unique way but not compared to the other stars in this tournament,” the Fox Sports pundit said. Yet Spain’s marvelous ensemble cast had not flown under the radar. Their World Cup campaign bordered on mastery of the sport.Much of the domestic enthusiasm derived from American team and that Country Roads spirit. The last-32 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina was the most-watched English-language soccer game in US history, with 26.4m tuning in.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEight (soon to be six) of Mauricio Pochettino’s 26-man squad represented MLS clubs. 13 others were MLS homegrown players or came through MLS academies. Of his preferred XI, only goalkeeper Matt Freese and 38-year-old team captain Tim Ream are currently MLS-based.Of the challenges ahead, outgoing commissioner Don Garber said this week (viaSBJ): “We’ve got to evolve our roster rules. We’ve got to re-engage our thinking on homegrown player development programs. We’ve got to continue to sign players like Antoine Griezmann and Robert Lewandowski and find ways to keep the best young American players here in the United States.”That last point is key. While it’s heartening to see the US team composed of impressive talents who are important players at major European clubs, that doesn’t really help MLS. Nor does standout homegrown talents like 15-year-old Benji Flowers (Chelsea) and 16-year-old prodigy Cavan Sullivan (Man City) being plucked from MLS academies. Both will leave for England when they’re legally able.Sebastian Berhalter did represent MLS at the tournament. The 25-year-old impressed with Western Conference leaders Vancouver Whitecaps prior to the break, with six goals and four assists. At the World Cup, he appeared in all five US games, racking up 185 minutes. He’s off to play in England’s second tier.“This is where I want to be,” Berhalter, 25, said in a sobering message for the league. “I want to keep getting better as a player and person, and this is a great place to do it.”New fans wondering where they can see Christian Pulisic or Tyler Adams or Weston McKennie or Antonee Robinson or Brenden Aaronson must look beyond these shores. For better or worse, the enduring symbol of the American World Cup effort was Folarin Balogun, and he’s in Monaco. It’s akin to a new fan becoming enthralled by the US Olympic basketball squad, and learning only a couple played in the NBA. It’s a bummer.Twenty-five-year-old Columbus Crew wingback Max Arfsten’s only World Cup action was a minute in the 4-1 loss to Belgium. He was the first Crew player to represent the US at a World Cup since Brian McBride in 2002. He is also finalizing a move to Middlesbrough to join Berhalter, The Athleticreportedon Friday.Back-up keeper Chris Brady of the Chicago Fire didn’t play in the tournament. Matt Turner deputized for Freese against Turkey with group stage qualification already guaranteed. Miles Robinson and Christian Rodlan are good pros and have spent their entire careers in MLS. Robinson played the 90 minutes against Turkey. And didn’t feature otherwise. Rodlan made the squad but did not play a World Cup minute, just like in 2022.As Garber says, the challenge for MLS is keeping the best American players here. Bringing the current crop home with their prime years still intact would be great too. Casemiro, Griezmann and Lewandowski help short term, but there will always be more players of that profile arriving every year.The league has grown exponentially in other ways. The expansion of teams, and purpose-built arenas. The increases in attendance and TV viewing audiences (thanks to a global TV deal with Apple). They’re all markers of a league truly on the rise. However, to “take it from here” and join the world’s elite leagues, MLS needs more.Explore more on these topicsInter MiamiMLSUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ayami Sato, the greatest pitcher in women’s baseball, is ready for her American debut | Baseball | The Guardian
description: The most decorated pitcher in women’s baseball history begins a new chapter with the Los Angeles Queens as the WPBL launches in the United States
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The most decorated pitcher in women’s baseball history begins a new chapter with the Los Angeles Queens as the WPBL launches in the United States
Content: Ayami Sato pitches during a Women's Pro Baseball League exhibition game in March.Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/APView image in fullscreenAyami Sato pitches during a Women's Pro Baseball League exhibition game in March.Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/APBaseballAyami Sato, the greatest pitcher in women’s baseball, is ready for her American debutA six-time world champion and three-time World Cup MVP, Japan’s Ayami Sato joins the new Women’s Professional Baseball League hoping to help build the sport’s futureFrankie de la CretazFri 31 Jul 2026 11.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 11.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Ayami Sato takes the mound as the starting pitcher for the Los Angeles Queens on Saturday, it will be the culmination of a professional career that has spanned 16 years and three countries. The right-handed hurler is largely considered the best pitcher in the history of women’s baseball. She has the awards and experience to prove it, and now she’s taking on America when she makes her debut in the Women’s ProfessionalBaseballLeague, the first pro women’s baseball league in the United States since the 1950s.Even though most Americans tuning into the WPBL may not have heard of her, Sato’s resume speaks for itself. Sato’s fastball has been clocked at nearly 80mph and her curveball has a devastating spin rate that is higher than many Major League Baseball pitchers. As a member of the Japan National Team since 2010, Sato has won six gold medals. She is the only player in Women’s Baseball World Cup history to win three consecutive MVP awards. As a member of the now-defunct Japan’s Women’s Baseball League, Sato led the league in strikeouts in three of the last four seasons. And most recently, in 2024 she became the first woman to play pro baseball in Canada as a member of the Toronto Maple Leafs of the Intercounty Baseball League.Now, she is bringing her talent to the US and the WPBL. “This is a brand new league for all of us,” Sato tells the Guardian through a translator. “So I also want to approach it with the mindset of a rookie –staying curious, paying attention to everything around me, and embracing this new challenge with an open mind.”The league will play all its games in a centralized location for its first season, at Robin Roberts Stadium in Springfield, Illinois. There are four teams – the Queens, the New York Heights, the San Francisco Firebells and the Boston Hunters. And the best players from all over the world will take the field together for the first time as one league, including at least nine players from the US women’s national baseball team. On the Queens, Sato will play alongside USA star third baseman Ashton Lansdell and Little League World Series star Mo’ne Davis.View image in fullscreenAyami Sato pitches during tryouts for the Women’s Professional Baseball League at the Washington Nationals Youth Baseball Academy last August in Washington DC.Photograph: Win McNamee/Getty ImagesWPBL co-founder and commissioner Justine Seigel says it was always the plan to recruit internationally for the league. “We want many of the best players, and to have many of the best players, you have to go out into the world and find the best shortstop in Venezuela, and who’s pitching in Japan,” Seigel says. “It’s also fun because baseball is baseball, but it’s also got its own little nuances country-to-country, and it’s kind of fun to see in a game, as well.”Sato is from Amami Ōshima island in Kagoshima prefecture. She began playing baseball as a girl, at first as a way to hang out with her older brother, but by third grade she was taking the sport seriously. She took to pitching almost immediately, after the manager of the boys’ baseball team she was on noticed that she liked to throw and told her that she had a strong shoulder.In Japan, Sato explains that there is a strong emphasis on mastering the fundamentals like proper throwing mechanics and learning to move your body the right way. While it’s something that Sato has always liked about the way she was trained, she’s gained even more appreciation for her country’s emphasis on the fundamentals because she believes they have contributed to the longevity of her career.“One thing that I hope fans recognize is that great performances don’t just happen, they come from a lot of preparation,” Sato says. “I spend a great deal of time getting ready, physically and mentally, before I ever step onto the field, so I’ll be very happy if people notice not only how I play, but also the preparation that I do and mindset behind it.”“I got to catch her bullpen, which was surreal,” New York Heights and USA catcher Denae Benitessaidat one of the WPBL tryout sessions. “She’s a legend in the game and last year I got to face her as a hitter in a World Cup and I think she did get me twice. So now I’m learning her secrets, I’m learning her pitches. But that was a truly incredible moment.”Despite all the accolades and stats that Sato has racked up over the course of her career, she’s humble. For as excited as the other players are to play alongside her, she is just as excited to play with (and against) them.“I’ve always considered the American players to be the biggest rivals against Japan,” Sato says. “They constantly challenged me and made things very difficult for me, but because they were such strong opponents, they also pushed me to improve and made me want to become a better player.”She says after watching the documentary See Her, Be Her about women who played baseball (including Sato herself), she stopped seeing the USA players just as opponent-athletes and more as people who had had many of the same experiences that she has faced.“Now I’ll have the chance to play in the same league with the players I’ve come to understand on a deeper level and we will be fellow players building something together,” she says. “I feel nothing but excitement, and I really cannot wait.”View image in fullscreenLast year’s tryouts were the first women’s professional baseball tryouts to be held in over 80 years since the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League in 1943.Photograph: Jess Rapfogel/Getty ImagesAnd because Sato is such an experienced player, she can bring that veteran leadership to the Queens. She hopes she can teach her teammates how to slow down and never let the game get away from them, to take the game pitch-by-pitch, and to work hard so that they can be the best version of themselves that they can be.”Sato is so hyperfocused on baseball that sometimes it can be hard for her to think of herself outside of that. When asked what she wanted fans to know about her off-the field, she regularly came back to her baseball training or philosophy. She found it to be a difficult question to answer, describing herself as a person. Her partner and translator, Mayo Hirano, was happy to offer insight into Sato’s personality.“She has a unique ability to take control of the game and set the tone for everyone around her,” Hirano says. “Once she steps onto the mound, she creates an atmosphere that only Ayami can create – calm, focused, and quietly powerful.Off the field, though, she is completely different. She is one of the purest and most genuine people I know. She lives life at her own pace, and it’s a very slow one – sometimes it even tests my patience! She loves drawing and singing, and she finds joy in the simple things.”In many ways, Sato has been building towards the WPBL through her entire career. That this league has come to be at a time when Japan’s women’s league no longer exists and while Sato is still playing is, in some ways, kismet. Sato will have yet another opportunity to show the world why she is the best at what she does. And she’ll get to do it on her own terms, bringing all the lessons she’s learned throughout her career to the mound in Springfield.“I think the combination of bringing together the American style of enjoying the game and having fun with the Japanese approach of building a strong foundation – if you could combine those two, I think you have the base of the best of both worlds.”Explore more on these topicsBaseballUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Can We Kick It?: new doc is timely take on Black history, pay-to-play and future of US soccer | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Akbar Majeed’s new feature tells the story of the sport through a Black lens and asks hard questions about the barriers facing the game’s breakthrough
Author: Matthew Hall
Headline: Akbar Majeed’s new feature tells the story of the sport through a Black lens and asks hard questions about the barriers facing the game’s breakthrough
Content: Can We Kick It? examines why soccer has struggled to cut into Black American culture.Photograph: Rise Sport EntertainmentView image in fullscreenCan We Kick It? examines why soccer has struggled to cut into Black American culture.Photograph: Rise Sport EntertainmentSoccerCan We Kick It?: new doc is timely take on Black history, pay-to-play and future of US soccerAkbar Majeed’s new feature tells the story of the sport through a Black lens and asks hard questions about the barriers facing the game’s breakthroughMatthew HallFri 31 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAkbar Majeed takes a deep breath as he considers the legacy of the 2026 World Cup and, in particular, the effect of the US team’scollapseagainst Belgium for a last-16 exit.“Unfortunately, that performance in the last game did not help at all,” he says.“You have to be careful what you ask for, right?” he says. “You want people to watch the sport. You got the most people in America to watch that game and that is the product we put out there? It reinforced a lot of the thoughts about soccer.”Arsène Wenger: US soccer development will depend on ‘consistency’ and ‘education’Read moreMajeed has a lot of thoughts about soccer. As the director of Can We Kick It?,a feature documentaryreleased this summer, he has also heard the thoughts about soccer from a cast of players, coaches, administrators, parents and fans. The project explores how the sport has engaged – and often not engaged – with Black communities in the United States.Can We Kick It? delivers an honesty often missing in conversations about soccer in the US. The film tells the story of the sport through a Black lens and with Black voices and asks hard questions about why the sport – from grassroots to elite professional levels – has struggled to cut into Black American culture.The documentary tells the story of Howard University, a historically Black university in Washington, beingcontroversially strippedof a 1971 NCAA title but rebounding to take the 1974 championship undefeated. It reminds that American soccer’s real “shot heard around the world” was not Paul Caligiuri’s mythologized qualifying goal for the 1990 World Cup but Joe Gaetjens’s winner against England at the 1950 World Cup. Soccer, the film argues, may be the world’s game but in the United States, one community has been left out of its story and growth.Majeed, inspired by conversations he has had for decades about the cultural, structural and economic barriers facing the game’s reach into urban America, suggests the sport’s failure to connect with urban audiences is part of a larger discussion on how the sport engages with wider American culture.“African Americans were part of the game from the very beginning and we were at the 1950 World Cup,” he says. “I grew up playing in North Carolina in the 80s and I didn’t see a lot of people like me playing the sport – particularly as I got better.“I didn’t see a soccer match until I was 19. We played a game that we didn’t see on TV. I had a soccer book with all the greats in it. So it was a book that got me into the game.”Following grad school, Majeed launched a basketball academy and as an American traveling abroad discovered something present in much of the rest of the world, but not yet in the US.“The biggest grassroots sport in the world is soccer,” he explains. “Basketball is the most grassroots sport in the US but globally it is not. There is a void in the US. Soccer is not accessible to vast parts of the community and it is not reaching parts of the community that would enjoy it.”In 2008, driven to bring grassroots sports into communities, Majeed converted an ice skating rink in Charlotte, North Carolina, into an indoor soccer field. “That thrust me back into the conversation about what is wrong with American soccer. We excel at every other sport in the world but not soccer.”One issue, according to Majeed, is the connection between grassroots soccer and the elite level. The US men’s team at this summer’s World Cup was more diverse than in years past, he says, but scratch the surface and glaring gaps still exist.“There are definitely more Black faces on the team and a lot of them represent immigrant families so [the team does represent] that part of America but there is a huge immigrant population that is being left out. The population that plays soccer the most is Latino. If we were really engaged with the population that loves and engages with soccer, it is the Latino population, and the national team definitely did not represent that part of the country.“If we talk about socioeconomic backgrounds the team definitely does not represent the [total] population. The vast majority of the Black players are coming from means and that is what you are seeing in the men’s and women’s side. There is still socioeconomic space that is being excluded when it comes to soccer in America.”View image in fullscreenDon Cogsville, who earned six caps with the US national team in 1988, is among the interviewees in Can I Kick It?.Photograph: Rise Sport EntertainmentWhich brings us to the three words of the moment in the post-World Cup discussion:pay-to-play. The phrase describes the established American system in which competitive youth soccer for boys and girls – and the pathway that can lead to a potential professional career or college soccer opportunities – often requires families to pay in excess of $3,000 per year to participate on a team. With travel to tournaments that require mandatory stays at expensive hotels, travel expenses and equipment, thecost of youth soccercan blow out to $15,000 per player.No one needs to be an economist to figure out who is priced out of participating in organized youth soccer. Not everyone is opposed to the system, though. Alexi Lalas, who came to fame as a player with the US during the 1994 World Cup and is now a Fox Sports presenter,is a defenderof the pay-to-play system.“Youth soccer (youth sports) is a competitive market with businesses selling a product that obviously customers are willing to pay for,” Lalas wrote on social media earlier this month. “I’d love if soccer was free to all. But who is going to pay for all this free soccer?“Millions benefit. It’s a business catering to a market willing to pay for the product. Soccer (like piano lessons) is not an inalienable right. Free soccer costs money. Someone has to pay. So who will pay for all this free soccer?”Can We Kick It? dives into pay-to-play. Majeed says Lalas can be right and very wrong at the same time.“His statement is very disingenuous and very elitist and very American arrogance and American arrogance is one of the reasons America is in the position it is when it comes to soccer,” he says.“I don’t think pay-to-play is going anywhere. This is America. America is about the money and international soccer is trying to figure out how to do more with America. But if you are concerned about a real competitive US soccer team then that comment is foolish. If you care about continuing to make the money that US soccer is making, then I understand why you make that comment.”Majeed believes soccer can only make the full leap into mainstream American culture by authentically embracing urban communities – and not just for marketing purposes.“Soccer still isn’t accepted across America,” Majeed says. “It is not culturally part of American sports values. The World Cup did some work in bridging that gap, mainly because the tournament was here, mainly because of social media, and the world also did a great job coming to America and exposing America to the world.“NBA players hanging out with soccer players is cool but then [we need to talk about] access to the game itself. Where can I play it? We do engagement very well because people put their kids in soccer at 4, 5 or 6 years old but there is clearly a perception where [soccer] isn’t competitive, so if I want to get my kids into a sport where they can go somewhere [in life] you transition them into another sport very quickly.”The title of Majeed’s film is borrowed from the 1990 hip-hop classic by A Tribe Called Quest famed for the lines“Can I kick it? Yes, you can!”The US’s disappointing World Cup finish contradicts that optimism but that’s not necessarily a bad thing. The larger legacy of the 2026 World Cup won’t be revealed for many years. Majeed believes soccer has the potential to be all-inclusive for the American population but until that happens the conversations about US soccer’s social, economic and cultural divides will continue.“Because of that performance against Belgium, people are going to see what you are going to do [about those challenges],” he says.“I don’t care if the coach stays or leaves. A new coach is not going to change that image of we got beat and we got beat bad, and we got embarrassed on home soil. The conversation around Can We Kick It? continues for another four years. You have to show us four years from now if anything happened. And if not, it’s going to continue that question.”Explore more on these topicsFootballUS sportsUSAfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Chess: Bodhana Sivanandan, 11, breaks another world age record at Dole Trophy | Chess | The Guardian
description: The Harrow schoolgirl eclipses the legend Judit Polgar as the youngest girl ever to score an international master result
Author: Leonard Barden
Headline: The Harrow schoolgirl eclipses the legend Judit Polgar as the youngest girl ever to score an international master result
Content: Bodhana Sivanandan beat Judit Polgar’s record for achieving a first international master result by almost five months.Photograph: Micha Walusza/Walusza Fotografia/FideView image in fullscreenBodhana Sivanandan beat Judit Polgar’s record for achieving a first international master result by almost five months.Photograph: Micha Walusza/Walusza Fotografia/FideLeonard Barden on chessChessChess: Bodhana Sivanandan, 11, breaks another world age record at Dole TrophyHarrow schoolgirl eclipses legend Judit Polgar as youngest girl ever to score international master resultLeonard BardenFri 31 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland’s 11-year-old talent Bodhana Sivanandan fought her way to another world age record last Saturday. Sivanandan ended the Dole Trophy in Aix-en-Provence, France, with a historic first international master result.Judit Polgar, the all-time No 1 woman, achieved her first IM norm in April 1988 in the International B section of the New York Open at 11 years and nine months. Sivanandan had a harder route to beating Polgar’s age record by almost five months.After her first-round win against the reigning French champion, Marc’Andria Maurizzi, she slipped to 2/5, against opposition that included two more grandmasters and an IM, before producing a late surge in the last four rounds.View image in fullscreen4035:Fabiano Caruana v Ruslan Ponomariov, Dortmund 2014. White to move and win.A correction to last week’s column: the previous youngest to beat a 2600+ opponent was not Polgar but the all-time No 2 woman, Hou Yifan, who defeated Nikita Vitiugov at Aeroflot Moscow 2007 when aged 12 years and 11 months. Polgar’s win was against the GM Lajos Portisch’s nephew Gabor Portisch.Sivanandan’s ninth and final round game, against the rising US international master Samrug Narayanan, proved to be an epic draw. A queen’s pawn opening developed into a marathon rook and minor piece ending where the 11-year-old was on the defensive. At one point the IM had a difficult win, but missed it. It was a long, grinding encounter which took 99 moves and six hours to complete. At the end, they were the last players out of 150 boards to remain in the tournament hall.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: X.comThe minimum performance rating for an IM norm is 2450 and, as the table above shows, Sivanandan performed at 2463 against a 2420 field. She also surpassed the 2400 requirement for her second women’s grandmaster norm. The organisers remembered to give her two norm certificates.A third WGM norm before age 12 years and four months would give Sivanandan the WGM title, breaking the age record set by Russia’s Kateryna Lagno.Further record opportunities could lie ahead this weekend and in September, when Sivanandan competes in the British Championship in Coventry, then plays in the England women’s team of five at the 200-nation Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan.Fury as UK’s only all-female chess team promoted – then told they must recruit a manRead moreAn intriguing question is how Sivanandan improved in the space of a few weeks from a disappointing sub-2200 performance in the European Women’s Championship at Batumi, Georgia. In that event she had losing positions in nine of her 11 games, although thanks to her own ingenuity and errors by her opponents she ended up with 5.5/11. Her performance level improved nearly 300 Fide points between Batumi and the Dole Open.Her father, Sivanandan Velayutham, said that her online coach was unavailable during this period, while she also had end-of-term school activities and a French and maths competition.The explanation is likely a phenomenon observed by Professor Arpad Elo – he of the Elo rating system – in his seminal work The Rating of Chessplayers, Past and Present. Elo claimed that improvement among young talents occurs more often in a series of quantum jumps, followed by periods of consolidation and partial retracement, rather than in a straight line.Currently, Sivanandan receives limited support for coaching and tournament expenses from Evren Ucok, a wealthy Turkish investor whose main interest is naturally his country’s own rising star, Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus, 15. Erdogmus recently became the world’s youngest ever 2700-rated player.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSivanandan is clearly England’s outstanding junior prospect, and as such she merits priority when funds from the government’s new £250,000 a year grant for elite chess are allocated.She was personally invited to 11 Downing Street before theSupporting Elite Chess Fundwas launched in April by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, while the announcement itself refers to “improving inclusivity” and “creating and sustaining a pipeline of new female talent”.Fide has announced that the 2026 world championship match between Gukesh Dommaraju, the Indian title holder, and Javokhir Sindarov, the Uzbek challenger, will take place in Geneva, Switzerland,from 25 November to 15 December. Full details are here.The participants will both be 20 at the start of the match, although Sindarov will turn 21 on 8 December, which will make it the youngest world championship encounter since title matches started in 1886.It could also turn out among the most one-sided contests in championship history. Gukesh’s form this year has been dreadful, with poor results in Wijk aan Zee and Prague followed by outright last in Oslo and his home city, Chennai, where he drew four games and lost three. He has dropped to 30th place in the live ratings and to 26th in Fide’s July monthly list.Meanwhile, Sindarov, who won the Candidates impressively in Cyprus to become the official challenger, continued his vintage form on Monday when hedefeated the world No 3, Hikaru Nakamura, in a brilliant 22-move miniature at the USA v Uzbekistan rapid and blitz match in Miami. USA won the match 14-10.The annual British championships start at the University of Warwick on Saturday. Michael Adams, the holder, is aiming for his 10th national title, equalling Jonathan Penrose’s record, while Sivanandan will aim to become the youngest ever British Women’s Champion. There is a record entry of more than 1,750 competitors across all sections, although this includes many who are also playing rapid and blitz sections.4035:1 Re7! Qxe7 2 Ba6! Kxa6 3 Qa8 mate.Explore more on these topicsChessLeonard Barden on chessnewsShareReuse this content

title: New York sues Kalshi prediction market alleging ‘illegal gambling operation’ | New York | The Guardian
description: Calling it an ‘illegal, unlicensed gambling operation’, state seeks to halt Kalshi’s operations and force it to forfeit profits
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Calling it an ‘illegal, unlicensed gambling operation’, state seeks to halt Kalshi’s operations and force it to forfeit profits
Content: An advertisement for Kalshi in Washington DC on 1 April 2026.Photograph: Allison Robbert/APView image in fullscreenAn advertisement for Kalshi in Washington DC on 1 April 2026.Photograph: Allison Robbert/APNew YorkNew York sues Kalshi prediction market alleging ‘illegal gambling operation’Calling it an ‘illegal, unlicensed gambling operation’, state seeks to halt Kalshi’s operations and force it to forfeit profitsMaya Yangand agenciesFri 31 Jul 2026 10.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe state ofNew Yorkhas filed a lawsuit against Kalshi, accusing the prediction market operator of “running an illegal gambling operation”.The lawsuit, filed on Friday, wasannouncedby Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, and Letitia James, the state attorney general. It seeks to force the New York-based company to forfeit its profits, provide restitution to harmed consumers and pay fines equal to three times its profits.“Kalshi has chosen to ignore New York’s gaming laws, which exist to protect consumers, prevent problematic gambling, deliver funding for critical public services, and ensure that every company plays by the same rules,” Hochul said, adding: “This choice has consequences … no company is above the law.”James, who in Aprilfiled a similar lawsuitagainst Coinbase and Gemini, echoed those remarks, saying: “New York’s gambling laws protect children from underage betting and help combat gambling addiction. No matter what they call themselves, prediction markets like Kalshi are gambling platforms, plain and simple. By ignoring our laws, Kalshi is running an illegal operation and harming New Yorkers in the process. We are taking them to court to uphold our laws and protect New Yorkers.”The lawsuit claims that Kalshi’s prediction markets are a form of gambling because users bet on uncertain events they cannot control. It also alleges that Kalshi operates without a license from the New York state gaming commission, allowing it to avoid taxes that licensed casinos and sports betting platforms are required to pay. Revenue from regulated gambling helps fund public schools, youth sports programs and problem gambling prevention and treatment.Prediction markets surge in US as public health advocates call for support to combat gamblingRead moreThe lawsuit also alleges that Kalshi allows 18- to 20-year-olds to use its prediction markets, even though New York law requires users to be at least 21 to place mobile sports bets.Responding to the lawsuit, the Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana said: “It’s sad to see this type of political theater from the leadership in our own state. States can’t just shut down a federally licensed exchange. This would also hurt New Yorkers, who would be driven offshore. We love New York, we love New Yorkers, and New Yorkers love our product.”Prediction market platforms say they operate differently than gambling operations because consumers are trading against other consumers – much like how stock markets work. Prices are based on trading, and the platforms only take a fee from the trading, they say.The platforms also argue federal law gives the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) exclusive jurisdiction to regulate transactions offered in the prediction market. In February, Trump’s appointee atop the federal commission declared that the agency “will no longer sit idly by” while states aim to regulate or ban prediction markets and “undermine the agency’s exclusive jurisdiction”.States counter that the vast majority of the business on prediction market platforms is sports betting, which they are empowered to regulate, and that is completely different from the commodities and futures contracts that the commission regulates.On Monday, a federal judge temporarily blocked Minnesota’s first-in-the-nation law banning prediction markets just days before it was to take effect – dealing a setback for states trying to outlaw or regulate the platforms.In April, Arizona’s attorney generalfiled criminal chargesagainst Kalshi, alleging that the company is illegally allowing users to bet on elections.“Kalshi may brand itself as a ’prediction market’, but what it’s actually doing is running an illegal gambling operation and taking bets on Arizona elections, both of which violate Arizona law,” Arizona’s attorney general, Kris Mayes, said at the time.In response, Kalshi called Arizona’s case “paper-thin”, arguing that it should not be “overseen by a patchwork of inconsistent state laws”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKalshi to offer betting on drug trial results and FDA regulatory decisionsRead moreMore than 20 federal lawsuitshave been filedacross the US over whether prediction market operators including Kalshi should be federally regulated as financial exchanges or as gambling businesses subject to state gambling laws. In April, the federal governmentsuedArizona, Connecticut andIllinoisover their attempts to regulate prediction markets.Unlike traditional sportsbooks, which can only operate in states where sports betting is legal, companies such as Kalshi are regulated at the federal level. They classify their products as “event derivatives” under commodities law, with users trading against one another rather than against a traditional “house”. As a result, they are overseen by the CFTC and can offer their services nationwide to users aged 18 and older.Yet despite prediction markets not being regulated as gambling platforms, experts warn that they are just as addictive.Speaking tothe Guardian in May, Lia Nower, the director of Rutgers University’s center for gambling studies, said: “The more people gamble, the more activities they gamble on, and the more ways they gamble, the more likely they are to develop a problem.“So, on average, unregulated markets like Kalshi andPolymarketwill have an additive effect to the legal forms of gambling.
