title: Georgia Hunter Bell outruns Odira to win Commonwealth Games 800m gold | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Hunter Bell clocked 1min 59.51 to beat the world champion in Glasgow, a victory that secured a full set of major medals for the English woman
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Hunter Bell clocked 1min 59.51 to beat the world champion in Glasgow, a victory that secured a full set of major medals for the English woman
Content: Georgia Hunter Bell takes in her achievement after winning the women's 800m final in Glasgow.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGeorgia Hunter Bell takes in her achievement after winning the women's 800m final in Glasgow.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Georgia Hunter Bell outruns Odira to win Commonwealth Games 800m goldHunter Bell clocks 1min 59.51 to beat world championWin secures full set of major medals for English runnerSean Ingleat Scotstoun StadiumFri 31 Jul 2026 17.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are late developers in sport, and then there is the brilliant Georgia Hunter Bell, who continues to defy sporting gravity at the age of 32.And on Friday night under the Glasgow lights, she gave a tactical masterclass to outwit – and then outpace – the 800m world champion Lilian Odira and complete her set of global medals.Commonwealth Games 2026: Hunter Bell wins 800m gold; athletics and boxing on day eight – liveRead moreIncredibly it was only two years ago that she made her international debut here in Scotland’s biggest city. Back then she was a part-time runner working in tech. Now, staggeringly, she is one of Britain’s biggest sports stars and the proud owner of Olympic, World, European and now Commonwealth medals.“There were some tears on the podium,” Hunter Bell said afterwards. “That showed me how much that meant.”Hunter Bell’s story loses nothing in its retelling. As a teenager she was among the best runners in Britain. Then came a series of injuries, setbacks and heartaches. By her mid-20s she had retired. Then came a second act not even Hollywood would dare write.It started with long cycle rides during lockdown, then a series of parkruns in Bushy Park. By November 2022 Hunter Bell had got in contact with her old coaches, Trevor Painter and Jenny Meadows, who guided Keely Hodgkinson to glory and had regarded Hunter Bell as “the one who got away”. Soon her injuries were long behind her – along with most of her opponents.By March 2024 she was wearing her first GB vest in the world indoor championships in Glasgow. That August she won an Olympic 1500m bronze medal in a British record 3min 52.61sec. Since then she has given up her job and got even better. This medal, in an England vest, was her sixth time on a global podium.“Lots of people reflect on being a kid and doing it for the kid version of yourself,” she said after. “But I ­actually think of the young woman version of myself, who was like 23, 24, and gave up and really didn’t know what she was doing with her life.“I feel sorry for that girl, and then I feel proud of making it through that and coming back here,” she added. “That’s what makes me emotional.”View image in fullscreenGeorgia Hunter Bell crosses the finishing line well clear of Lilian Odira and Sarah Billings.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APGoing into the final, most thought that Odira, the Kenyan who had defied Hunter Bell and Hodgkinson to win gold at last year’s world championships, was the one to beat.But Hunter Bell had other ideas, leading from tape to gun, to take an easy victory in 1min 59.51sec. Odira took silver, more than a second back, with the Australian Sarah Billings claiming bronze.“I felt calm,” Hunter Bell said. “I really feel like I was composed. It didn’t go to plan as in the race. I did not think I would go gun-to-tape and lead it for the whole thing. I wanted to lead with 200m to go. But I found myself at the front, and so I thought ‘I’ll just control it, keep it relaxed, not too fast’, and then when I feel that pressure on me with the move being made, I’ll be ready to go.”The thing is nobody came. They were through halfway in a slow 60.32sec, and the race had barely sped up when Hunter Bell finally powered clear with 200m to go. At this point Odira was five metres back and had no chance of closing.“I’m really happy with that, it worked perfectly,” Hunter Bell said. “I really felt my legs were going in the last few steps and I couldn’t see where anyone was, but the crowd really pulled me home. It was great.”There were also two silver medals for England on the night through Emily Newnham and Jake Minshull in the women’s and men’s 400m hurdles. But this was a night that belonged to Hunter Bell.Elsewhere, Adaejah Hodge of the British Virgin Islands gave a small hint of her talent by storming to the women’s 200m title in 22.07.The 20-year-old has already run 10.63 for the 100m this year, making her the fifth fastest woman in history. For good measure she has a personal best of 21.68 for the 200m, putting her joint-ninth of all time. But on a cold night in Glasgow, a more modest time was enough as she took gold ahead of Shaniqua Bascombe, of Trinidad and Tobago, with Jamaica’s Alana Reid picking up bronze.In the men’s javelin Sri Lanka’s Rumesh Pathirage continued his annus mirabilis by winning gold with a huge throw of 89.75m, ahead of India’s Olympic champion, Neeraj Chopra.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s Georgia Baker joins select cycling club with fifth Commonwealth Games gold  | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Bakers adds to haul with scratch race win while there was heartbreak for judoka Josh Katz in 60kg final
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Bakers adds to haul with scratch race win while there was heartbreak for judoka Josh Katz in 60kg final
Content: Georgia Baker of Australia after winning gold in the women's 10km scratch race final.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPView image in fullscreenGeorgia Baker of Australia after winning gold in the women's 10km scratch race final.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPCommonwealth Games 2026Australia’s Georgia Baker joins select cycling club with fifth Commonwealth Games goldBaker adds to haul with scratch race winHeartbreak for judoka Josh Katz in 60kg finalAustralia Associated PressFri 31 Jul 2026 16.12 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 15.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorgia Baker has joined a select club in Australian cycling, winning her fifth Commonwealth Games gold medal.Baker joins sprinters Anna Meares and Matt Glaetzer and pursuit specialist Brad McGee on five gold medals after capping faultless teamwork to claim the scratch race win.After three golds at the Birmingham Games in 2022 and the team pursuit win in Glasgow, Baker can add to her haul in the women’s points and elimination events over the last two days at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.In contrast, Australian judoka Josh Katz was left crying on the shoulder of his coach and older brother Nathan after falling short of gold in the men’s 60kg final after India’s Harsh Singh nailed a waza-ari throw in the final minute of their bout.View image in fullscreenJoshua Katz of Australia grapples with India’s Harsh Singh in the 60kg judo final.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPKatz took silver ahead of teammate Pedro Antun Neto, who beat Botswana’s Tumiso Phuthego via ippon for bronze.Katz was not the only Australian to suffer heartbreak in Glasgow, with defending 2022 champion Tinka Easton and Games debutant Vas Middleton falling short of the podium.Katz, a Paris Olympian, was out to win gold with his brother after both siblings claimed bronze medals in 2022.Josh Katz took men’s 60kg bronze at the Birmingham Games, where older brother Nathan, now aged 31, finished third in the 66kg event.View image in fullscreenPedro Carlos Antun Neto of Australia after winning bronze in Glasgow.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP“A bit gutted,” an emotional Josh Katz said after the final, having recorded three earlier wins in Glasgow.“I felt really good today and super confident that I could win gold. Coming off straight away after losing a final that I felt like I could win, it hurts, for sure.“You know you got to wait a really long time (to fight for gold again), maybe never.“I don’t know how many more opportunities I’m going to have.”Holding back tears as he spoke, Katz joked he was awaiting a spray from Nathan.“He just gave me a hug, and I was crying a little on his shoulder,” Katz said. “It makes me a little bit emotional.“We were looking at some pictures from four years ago, and we really wanted to try to make some more memories today.“We did. There were a few times today, we looked at each other and just laughed and smiled, like, ‘oh yeah, like this is a pretty cool place to be’.“It’s hard now, and I’m sure he’ll spray me out the back when I go back for losing the final. I wish we could have changed the colour of the medal.”Easton was also in tears after a devastating loss by ippon to Cameroon’s Marie Celine Baba Matia in their women’s 52kg bronze-medal bout.View image in fullscreenTinka Easton of Australia after her loss in the women’s 52kg bronze medal contest.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPThe 30-year-old was defeated earlier in her semi-final by eventual gold medallist Evelyn Beaton, losing to the Canadian by yuko.“I wanted to make magic happen again and reclaim my title. So it’s a very, very disappointing end to the competition,” Easton said.Middleton lost by yuko to Cypriot judoka Petros Christodoulides in their men’s 66kg bronze-medal match.Middleton’s older sister Saya will also compete in Glasgow, fighting to reach the podium in the women’s -63kg event.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Australia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Infantino under huge pressure after plan for World Cup sell-off sparks resignation and rebuke | Fifa | The Guardian
description: The walls started closing in on Gianni Infantino after another dramatic day that saw one of his senior advisoers resign and brought a scathing rebuke from Fifa’s own chief operating officer
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: The walls started closing in on Gianni Infantino after another dramatic day that saw one of his senior advisoers resign and brought a scathing rebuke from Fifa’s own chief operating officer
Content: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has seen two key members of his inner circle distance themselves from him.Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPAView image in fullscreenFifa president Gianni Infantino has seen two key members of his inner circle distance themselves from him.Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPAFifaInfantino under huge pressure after plan for World Cup sell-off sparks resignation and rebukeCordeiro quits as senior adviser to Fifa presidentLamour: sell-off plan ‘defies belief and imagination’Nick AmesandMatt HughesFri 31 Jul 2026 14.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 17.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe walls started closing in onGianni Infantinoafter another dramatic day that saw one of his senior advisers resign and brought a scathing rebuke from Fifa’s own chief operating officer.Infantino is under huge pressure after hisplan to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investorsmet a tide of opposition from around the globe. European countries have alreadypromised to boycott Fifa competitionsif he does not shelve the scheme but Friday’s developments, which led to two key members of his inner circle distancing themselves from him, may prove equally damaging to any prospects of salvaging his presidency.Fifa rapidly accelerates plan to expand World Cup to 64 teams from 2030 tournamentRead moreMeanwhileUefaand other confederations are actively seeking candidates to run against Infantino in next year’s Fifa election, in which he had been expected to comfortably win a fourth term. The pressure that has built since this week’s revelations casts doubt on whether the previously unassailable Swiss, who has doubled down on the proposals, will be able to cling on for that long.The resignation of Carlos Cordeiro, one of Infantino’s senior advisers since 2021, struck a fresh blow upon Infantino hours after Uefa’s 55 members had unanimously threatened a boycott. Cordeiro, a former US Soccer chief, said Infantino had proposed “a bad deal for Fifa’s member associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game”. He questioned the lack of transparency in Fifa’s process and pointed out that the governing body is sitting on vast debt-free reserves that could be used to fund development.“Why this deal?” he asked. “Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football?”But an extraordinary statement later in the day by Kevin Lamour, Fifa’s current chief operating officer, may have inflicted a more serious wound. Lamour, a close associate of Infantino at Fifa and during their previous spells at Uefa, said staff and other stakeholders had been “deceived” by the president and said he would tolerate being sacked for expressing his views.double quotation markWe all want to be proud to work for Fifa, and today, unfortunately, it seems that is no longer the case for many of usKevin Lamour, Fifa chief operating officer“What has been announced in recent days and what has been happening behind the scenes in recent months defies belief and imagination,” Lamour said. “To put it very clearly and directly: the project that has sparked so much controversy and debate is not a Fifa project. It is even less a project of Fifa’s administration. It is the project of one person.“The Fifa vice-presidents, the members of the Fifa Council, the confederations, the federations, the players, the leagues, the clubs, and the fans were not the only ones who were ignored. Fifa’s own administration was also deceived.“This lie by omission over many months and this unilateral exercise of power are not trivial. They are indicative of a lack of trust, a lack of transparency, a lack of discernment, a lack of good governance. And a serious lack of respect.”Lamour said Fifa’s mission is “not to serve the personal interests of a person who, unfortunately, believes he embodies Fifa when he is supposed to be at its service”. He stated that his colleagues “deserve better than contempt and intimidation”, adding: “My feeling is that we all want to be proud to work for Fifa, and today, unfortunately, it seems that is no longer the case for many of us.”Infantino appears to be shedding allies and there was no succour to be taken from a strongly worded statement from the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), which backed Uefa and Concacaf in their opposition to the privately funded Fifa Forward Enterprise plan. The AFC stopped short of matching Uefa’s boycott but was clear in saying the proposal should be scrapped.View image in fullscreenCarlos Cordeiro (left) with Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino in the Oval Office in 2018.Photograph: Evan Vucci/AP“The fact that the situation has reached the point where the real possibility of a FifaWorld Cupboycott has entered public discourse should concern everyone who cares about the future of our game,” it said. “The AFC believes that the proposed FFE cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward.”It called upon Fifa to “undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework”, echoing its peers’ complaints about a lack of consultation regarding key decisions such as World Cup hosting arrangements.A further revelation on Friday that Fifa has opened a tender for research companies to assess the economic benefits ofexpanding the World Cup to 64 teams, demanding a hugely accelerated timescale, has only increased such concerns in football’s corridors of power.Uefa is minded to play a waiting game after securing a united front in opposing Infantino’s plan. It will assess how Fifa reacts, although early signs suggest little change of tack. Overnight Fifa hadattempted to blame media reportingfor such widespread opposition, claiming its commitment to “an open and democratic consultation”, although that intervention has cut no ice among its opponents.It is unlikely any mechanism to depose Infantino will be triggered immediately although in theory an extraordinary Fifa Congress, and subsequent vote of confidence, could be convened if 43 countries make such a request. The priority around Uefa and beyond is to see off the FFE plan before taking further steps. Any Europe-backed candidate for the Fifa presidency election in March is likely to hail from a different continent, with the Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, and AFC president, Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa, among possible contenders. The latterlost narrowly to Infantino in the 2016 election.Fifa continues to lobby federations to accept their project and have stuck by the 19 September deadline originally given for those who wish to sign up.Late on Friday night the South American soccer body ⁠Conmebol said it had ⁠requested further ⁠information ​from Fifa on its proposal to ⁠sell a stake in its tournament business, including ⁠the World Cup, and ​launched ‌a consultation ‌process with its member ‌associations.Conmebol said it had requested further information and clarifications from Fifa on the proposal’s scope, structure, ‌governance and potential effects, and would continue ​to analyse it before taking a position.“We recognise that the development ⁠of football requires commercial and ​financial ​decisions. However, ​such decisions must always ​serve ‌football ​and ​never take precedence over its very essence,” Conmebol said in a statement.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoWorld CupWorld Cup 2026UefaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tour de France Femmes under pressure to reroute Ventoux stage amid wildfire risk | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: The Tour de France Femmes is facing pressure to re-route part of its key stage to the summit of Mont Ventoux next Friday because of the wildfires threat in Provence
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: The Tour de France Femmes is facing pressure to re-route part of its key stage to the summit of Mont Ventoux next Friday because of the wildfires threat in Provence
Content: The inclusion of Mont Ventoux on this year’s Tour de France Femmes route underlines the race’s growth in stature.Photograph: Tim Ireland/PAView image in fullscreenThe inclusion of Mont Ventoux on this year’s Tour de France Femmes route underlines the race’s growth in stature.Photograph: Tim Ireland/PATour de France FemmesTour de France Femmes under pressure to reroute Ventoux stage amid wildfire riskAuthorities want stage altered if risk is ‘extreme’2025 champion Ferrand-Prévot faces sterner challengeJeremy Whittlein LausanneFri 31 Jul 2026 13.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTour de France Femmesis facing pressure to reroute part of its key stage to the summit of Mont Ventoux next Friday because of the wildfires threat in Provence.The women’s Tour, which begins in Lausanne on Saturday, is expected to keep the famous climb to the top of the “Giant of Provence”, but the current routing of the stage through the Ventoux’s foothills could be affected.‘I’m just a different type’: Demi Vollering gears up for Tour de France Femmes tiltRead moreIn a statement on its website, the Vaucluse prefecture said: “At a time when forest areas are at a peak risk of fire, the prefecture has asked the organisers of the Tour to consider an alternative route. Following a fire risk assessment on Tuesday 4 August, an alternative route will be implemented should the wildfire risk be considered extreme.”Three stages of the men’s Tour de France, whichfinished in Paris last Sunday, were disrupted by wildfires, extreme heat and the deployment of French emergency services to assist with the wildfire crisis in the country’s south-west.“We are in constant touch with the prefecture and we will adapt, just as the men’s Tour de France did,” said Marion Rousse, the Tour de France Femmes race director.“We have to deal with the real world – this is a bike race and the real world always takes priority. There will still be a climb of the Ventoux, but we have several options. We are ready to work with the emergency services and the government.”Few things demonstrate the fast‑track growth of women’s racing more than the inclusion of Mont Ventoux on the route for this year’s race. “There is no mountain that is too difficult for women,” Rousse said. “The level is now more and more consistent and they ride faster each time. Each year the progress is huge.”View image in fullscreenThe defending champion, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, did not attend the top riders’ media conference on Friday.Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/Keystone/APThe legendary climb is the standout stage in a race route that is bolder and bigger than it has been since the race was reintroduced in 2022 as a tentative bolt-on to the end of the men’s Tour de France.Over nine stages, including an individual time trial and stages through the Jura, Massif Central and Provence Alps, 147 riders will wend their way to the Côte d’Azur for a testing finale in the hills inland from Nice.Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, the defending champion, was a no-show at the top riders press conference on Friday afternoon, with her highly rated French teammate Marion Bunel, third overall in this year’s Vuelta Femenina, surprisingly taking her place.Ferrand-Prévot was said to have already fulfilled plenty of media obligations, but her absence from a top table that included past winners and her main rivals, Demi Vollering and Kasia Niewiadoma, did not go unnoticed.Ferrand-Prévot’ssuccess last Julywas hailed in France, but she faces more rivals this year than she did 12 months ago, with the 23-year-old Spanish rider Paula Blasi, who sealed victory in the Vuelta on the brutal climb of the Angliru, a leading contender.Elsewhere there are signs that others too, as Rousse suggested, have upped their game. The Swiss rider Marlen Reusser, who said she has had a “love-hate” relationship with the Tour Femmes in the past, is expected to shine in the individual time trial on stage four, while the long climb to the Ventoux is likely to feature the 2023 winner, Vollering, and the defending champion, Ferrand-Prévot, going head to head.View image in fullscreenMarlen Reusser is expected to excel in the stage four time trial.Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/EPAReusser, the world time trial champion, has had a series of false starts in the French race. “This is the first year that I’m here and feel healthy and good,” she said. “It’s special to finally be here in that way.”Ferrand-Prévot’s victory in last year’s race made her a household name in France and, after a long wait to see a home rider win the yellow jersey, drew crowds to the roadside in their thousands.“Now women’s cycling in France is doing well and men’s cycling in France is also doing very well,” Rousse, said by way of tribute to Ferrand-Prévot’s success.“We felt a real sense of patriotism with Pauline’s victory. Whether it was in the men’s or the women’s race, it’s been some time that we’ve been waiting for a French winner.“Pauline gives a lot. To the public, her charisma has done cycling a lot of good. All those little girls who dream one day of becoming like Pauline. People are interested in her because she is so likable.”Rousse is confident that Ferrand‑Prévot, despite a muted spring, will put up a staunch defence of her title. “There will be a great rivalry between her and Vollering,” she said. “I think that Pauline has increased her level in comparison to last year – she’s really gone up.”Elsewhere, the upward trajectory of the race continues. The number of women riding the amateur Étape du Tour Femmes is higher than those who rode the Étape du Tour, on Alpe d’Huez, with 27% of all participants in the Étape Femmes being female.“It shows that women put a lot less obstacles in their way than before, especially since the creation of the Tour de France Femmes,” Rousse said.Saturday’s opening 138km stage in Switzerland features a hilly loop based on Lausanne, through the Cantons of Vaud and Fribourg, leading to a steep uphill finish on the Côte Saint-François, while on Sunday the peloton follows the northern shore of Lake Geneva before a lakeside finish, and a possible sprint, in Geneva.Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Infantino increasingly embattled after senior adviser resigns over World Cup sell-off plans | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Gianni Infantino’s authority has been dealt a fresh blow after Carlos Cordeiro, one of his senior advisers, resigned with immediate effect in protest at proposals to sell a stake in the World Cup
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Gianni Infantino’s authority has been dealt a fresh blow after Carlos Cordeiro, one of his senior advisers, resigned with immediate effect in protest at proposals to sell a stake in the World Cup
Content: Gianni Infantino is facing calls for an urgent review of Fifa’s governance.Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPAView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino is facing calls for an urgent review of Fifa’s governance.Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPAFifaInfantino increasingly embattled after senior adviser resigns over World Cup sell-off plansInfantino’s role as president under increasing pressure143 of Fifa’s 211 members now stand against schemeMatt HughesandNick AmesFri 31 Jul 2026 06.18 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 00.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGianni Infantino’s authority has been dealt a fresh blow after Carlos Cordeiro, one of his senior advisers, resigned with immediate effect in protest at proposals to sell a stake in the World Cup.In the latest embarrassment for Infantino, who saw European FAs threaten to boycott futureFifatournaments on Thursday, the former US Soccer chief Cordeiro criticised “a bad deal for football” and pointed out that the global governing body already sits on huge amounts of debt-free reserves.Uefa have formed a rare but fragile united front against Fifa in battle for football’s future | Nick Ames and Matt HughesRead more“I cannot stand by while Fifa considers selling a stake in the World Cup,” Cordeiro said in his resignation statement. “I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally. It is a bad deal for Fifa’s member associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game.”Cordeiro has worked for Fifa since 2021 as senior adviser to Infantino. He also operated as a senior adviser to the White House taskforce on this summer’s World Cup.In resigning he said Fifa “already has the financial capacity to provide [additional financial] support from existing resources”. He added that Fifa would be “mortgaging football’s future without any compelling justification” if it sold off a permanent stake.In addition, Cordeiro questioned the lack of transparency in Fifa’s process. “Why this deal?” he asked. “Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football?”Cordeiro’s exit was followed by hefty criticism of Infantino from Fifa’s chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, who told the Associated Press: “It is the project of one person. Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions.”It adds to the pressure growing on Infantino and Fifa, which is facing calls for an urgent review of its governance after insisting that the planned World Cup sell-off will continue despite the threat of a boycott from all 55 European members.View image in fullscreenCarlos Cordeiro with Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino at the White House in 2018.Photograph: Evan Vucci/APIn a strongly worded statement issued on Friday morning, the Asian Football Confederation backedUefa’s and Concacaf’s oppositionto the creation of a new commercial company, Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), saying it “cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward”, and urging Fifa to “undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework”.Fifa had attempted to double down on its position overnight,releasing a statement at 4am UK timesaying “we will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA [member association] has the ability to express its vote based on facts,” but it is now clear Infantino is facing united opposition to his proposals from around the globe.Uefa, Concacaf and the AFC constitute 143 of Fifa’s 211 members, so if their coalition remains united there is no prospect of Infantino getting the votes he needs. The 56-year-old’s position as Fifa president is also under threat for the first time since he was elected in 2016, unless he backs down quickly.While stopping short of matching Uefa’s boycott the AFC went further than Concacaf in clearly stating that the FFE proposal should be dropped. “The AFC stands in solidarity with Uefa and Concacaf in expressing serious concerns over Fifa’s proposal to introduce private investment into Fifa’s flagship competitions and the decision-making process around FFE,” its statement read. “The fact that the situation has reached the point where the real possibility of a Fifa World Cup boycott has entered public discourse should concern everyone who cares about the future of our game.“Football should never have been placed in such a position. Against this backdrop, and in light of the clear positions expressed by Uefa and Concacaf as well as the unprecedented divisions that have emerged across the football world, the AFC believes that the proposed FFE cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward.“The Fifa World Cup is the pinnacle of global football and derives its strength from the participation of all Confederations and the world’s leading football nations. Any proposal that risks undermining the unity and universal character of the competition must be reconsidered.”The AFC echoed Uefa and Concacaf’s complaints about alack of consultation from Fifa, making clear that it is not the first time confederations and the Fifa council have been excluded from major decisions, most notably hosting arrangements for the 2030 and 2034 World Cups.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The AFC sees this moment as a catalyst for strengthening institutional practices,” the statement continued. “While every Fifa MA must have the opportunity to consider and determine proposals affecting the future of world football, meaningful democracy is not measured solely by the opportunity to vote.“It begins with transparent governance, timely consultation, informed deliberation and genuine participation throughout the decision-making process.“The AFC calls upon Fifa to undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework to ensure that proposals of global significance are developed through proper consultation, meaningful engagement and appropriate oversight by Fifa’s statutory bodies.”View image in fullscreenThe hosts for the 2030 World Cup were announced at the Fifa Congress in Zurich in 2024.Photograph: Sergio Pérez/EPAFifa had attempted to blame media reporting for the widespread opposition to its scheme, but it is now clear that will not wash with most of its member associations.“We respect the feedback and concern aired in public and reaffirm our commitment to an open and democratic consultation,” a Fifa statement read. “Our planned consultation process was disrupted by incorrect media reports. We will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA has the ability to express its vote based on facts.“FFE has been proposed solely to ensure that all Fifa member associations have the opportunity to take meaningful ownership of the commercial opportunity of football in their respective countries, and that this does not come at the cost of either the spirit or the governance of Fifa or football itself.“Nobody is selling football. This is not something Fifa would ever entertain. Everyone has the right to express their opposition and to seek further clarification but no single entity can claim to represent all 211 MAs around the world. Each MA should be allowed to review the proposal and have a say in shaping their own future. These are the democratic principles of Fifa.”If Fifa was to refuse to back down, the first step of the threatened European boycott would come at next month’s Under-20 Women’s World Cup in Poland, with senior Women’s World Cup qualifiers to follow in October.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsUefaUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI labels to be compulsory on authentic-looking content under EU rules | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Companies must ensure people know when they are interacting with artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look real
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Companies must ensure people know when they are interacting with artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look real
Content: Screengrab of an AI-generated image of the French president, Emmanuel Macron, dancing in a 1980s nightclub.View image in fullscreenScreengrab of an AI-generated image of the French president, Emmanuel Macron, dancing in a 1980s nightclub.AI (artificial intelligence)AI labels to be compulsory on authentic-looking content under EU rulesCompanies must ensure people know when they are interacting with artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look realJennifer Rankinin BrusselsFri 31 Jul 2026 07.21 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 05.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom apparently conspiring to steal elections to abusing staff or performing embarrassing dance moves, the last few years have seen plenty of fake content made about politicians intended to malign its targets and mislead the public.Now EU rules aim to stem the flood of this deceptive content: starting from Sunday, artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look authentic must be labelled.The rules, devised under theEU’s landmark AI Act, mean companies must ensure people know when they are interacting with an AI-powered chatbot or viewing a manipulated image or AI-generated text.View image in fullscreenDeepfakes have included fake audio of the Slovakian opposition leader, Michal Šimečka, conspiring with a journalist to rig election.Photograph: Radovan Stoklasa/ReutersThe rules apply to new AI systems on the EU market from 2 August, while existing ones have an extra four months to comply.“It is a matter not only of customer protection, it’s also a matter of democracy protection,” the Green MEP Sergey Lagodinsky, who helped negotiate the AI Act, told the Guardian. “Making transparent this information is something which we need to preserve our democracy and the authenticity of facts online.”Under the rules, synthetic text, images, video and audio designed to look truthful must be visibly marked as AI-generated and contain a digital watermark to show the artificial origins of the content.Texts on matters of public interest must also be labelled as AI-made if there is no human editorial oversight.Companies are encouraged to label AI-generated content pre-dating the rules, although this is not compulsory. The rules will not apply to users’ personal content and there is an exemption for “evidently artistic”, satirical and fictional works.Failure to comply could result in fines of up to €15m (£12.8) or 3% of a company’s worldwide global turnover.The EU executive has created black-and-white labels anyone can use, although companies can design their own.View image in fullscreenEU symbols to be used on content using AI.Illustration: EUDeepfakes have includedaudio purporting to revealthe Slovakian opposition leader Michal Šimečka conspiring with a journalist to rig elections,mocked-up videosof the French president, Emmanuel Macron, dancing in a 1980s nightclub, andfake footageof the then UK Labour leader, Keir Starmer, abusing party staff.The tech industry says it supports the quest to make deepfakes visible, but fears the rules will be interpreted too broadly and overwhelm internet users with banners and labels.The Computer and Communications Industry Association argues that EU guidelines published in July have expanded the definition of a deepfake far beyond the 2024 AI Act.“The label was meant to flag deceptive content,” said CCIA Europe’s AI policy lead, Boniface de Champris. “That distinction has been removed, so now almost everything gets labelled – a landscape in an advert is the same as a manipulated political speech. Like cookie banners, once labels are everywhere, users stop noticing them. That doesn’t protect anyone, it just burdens commercial activity across the board.”He thinks the most visible change for the public will not be on social media, which “already labels most AI content” but “in areas where AI is already used at scale but people don’t know it – advertising, film, publishing”.“Expect a lot more labels in sectors not usually associated with AI, and the burden will fall hardest on those least versed in AI regulation,” De Champris said.Some of the world’s largest tech companies already have policies designed to inform users about AI-generated content.TikTok, for example, says it requires creators to label realistic AI-generated images, audio and video, and that it has helped label more than 3bn pieces of content. However, recent research has shown thatAI-generated doctors are gaining millions of views on TikTokby spreading dubious health advice.Misleading AI-generated doctors pose ‘huge danger to public safety’Read moreGoogle launched a tool called SynthID in 2023, which enables users to check if an image is AI-generated. The company says it has put an invisible digital watermark, which enables identification, on more than 100bn images and 60,000 years’ worth of audio.Google and Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, have signed a voluntary code of practice intended to help companies comply with the EU’s AI transparency rules.The European Commission said more than 180 organisations had signed the code, which was drawn up by independent experts under the supervision of the EU AI office.Signing the code is seen by regulators as a sign of good intent, while non-signatories must show they are meeting the rules in other ways.Meta launched policies in 2024 to help people identify AI-generated photo-realistic images. It says it has been developing industry-wide technical standards to identify AI audio and video.Announcing Meta’s intention to sign the EU code of practice earlier this week [28 July], its vice-president for public policy in Europe, Markus Reinisch, said: “We must avoid a situation where online content is subject to a growing array of different labels and disclosures that end up overwhelming people, while at the same time adding additional regulatory complexity for providers.”Lagodinsky, the EU lawmaker, said he believed the industry could find a way: “I have a deep respect for industry, but in all too many cases, they complain, and … then after things are implemented, it doesn’t look that burdensome to them. And there is always a solution.”The transparency rules are part of broader enforcement of the AI Act, starting from 2 August. The commission’s lead official on tech policy, Henna Virkkunen, said AI was a “transformative technology” that could bring “extraordinary benefits” but the most advanced models “create risks on an entirely new scale”.“Europe anticipated this development. With the AI Act, we established a clear, risk-based and durable framework for trustworthy AI —one that gives innovators legal certainty while protecting the public interest.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Social mediaEuropean UnionDigital mediaEuropeComputingInternet safetynewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic’s AI Claude hacked into three organizations during cybersecurity test | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: Company says it discovered unauthorized access during ‘proactive review’ after rival OpenAI revealed rogue agent
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Company says it discovered unauthorized access during ‘proactive review’ after rival OpenAI revealed rogue agent
Content: ‘Claude gained ‌unauthorized access to the ‌systems after a misconfiguration.’Photograph: AnthropicView image in fullscreen‘Claude gained ‌unauthorized access to the ‌systems after a misconfiguration.’Photograph: AnthropicAnthropicAnthropic’s AI Claude hacked into three organizations during cybersecurity testCompany says it discovered unauthorized access during ‘proactive review’ after rival OpenAI revealed rogue agentReutersThu 30 Jul 2026 20.22 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 20.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthropic ⁠said on Thursday its AI Claude model hacked ⁠systems of ⁠three ​organizations during testing,days after rival OpenAI⁠revealed a rogue agent had gone on a days-long ⁠hacking spree at the AI ​firm Hugging ‌Face.Claude gained ‌unauthorized access to the ‌systems during cybersecurity evaluations after a misconfiguration allowed the models to reach the internet from testing environments that ‌were supposed to be isolated,Anthropicsaid.The company said ​it identified the incidents after reviewing 141,006 cybersecurity evaluation runs, a process it ⁠launched following OpenAI’s disclosures.The ‌breaches signal that AI’s expanding capabilities are already fueling the security threat experts have long feared ‌and that even top developers can be caught off-guard by flaws their models can exploit.“Claude compromised the ​impacted ​organizations’ infrastructure using ​basic techniques, such as ​exploiting ‌weak passwords and ​unauthenticated ​endpoints,” it said.Anthropic said the incidents involved three separate models: Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Mythos 5 and an internal research model. The earliest cases dated back to April and ‌occurred in evaluation environments that lacked what the company described as standard safeguards.The breaches occurred during the so-called “capture the flag” exercises, in which models were tasked with finding ​hidden information in simulated networks. The company said its prompts told the models they had no internet access, but a misunderstanding with its evaluation partner Irregular left the systems connected to the public internet.Two of the organizations were ​unaware of the activity ‌before being contacted, Anthropic ​said, adding that ​it was still trying to reach the third.“We discovered these incidents after a proactive review of our cybersecurity evaluation transcripts,” the company said in a statement.The findings underscore the need for stronger controls in both internal and third-party testing environments as AI models become increasingly capable of carrying out real-world cyber activities, Anthropic said.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Could AI take your job? Some workers in China already know the answer | China | The Guardian
description: Across the country, workers are fearful about the impact of AI on their livelihoods in an increasingly fragile labour market
Author: Yu-chen Li
Headline: Across the country, workers are fearful about the impact of AI on their livelihoods in an increasingly fragile labour market
Content: Workers and a robot prepare tea beside each other at a booth at the 2026 Zhongguancun Forum earlier this year. China’s rollout of artificial intelligence has sparked concerns about the future of the jobs market.Photograph: Jessica Lee/EPAView image in fullscreenWorkers and a robot prepare tea beside each other at a booth at the 2026 Zhongguancun Forum earlier this year. China’s rollout of artificial intelligence has sparked concerns about the future of the jobs market.Photograph: Jessica Lee/EPAChinaCould AI take your job? Some workers in China already know the answerAcross the country, workers are fearful about the impact of AI on their livelihoods in an increasingly fragile labour marketAmy Hawkinsin WuhanThu 30 Jul 2026 22.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 11.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the tree-lined streets of Wuhan, where cars jostle for space with mopeds and cargo trucks, the malfunctioning of a new type of vehicle has recently been causing chaos on the city’s roads.In March, several cars from a fleet of driverless taxisstopped abruptlyin the streets. The “system malfunction” left distressed riders stranded for hours. The robotaxis, known as Apollo Go and powered by artificial intelligence (AI), were taken off Wuhan’s streets for months for investigations.But the outage was a boon for 45-year-old taxi driver Yao Xinnong. His wages, which had fallen by about 40% since Apollo Go launched in 2022, jumped back up as customers returned.“I don’t really like them, to be honest,” Yao says of the driverless cabs operated by the tech giant Baidu. “Their impact has been huge”.China is encouraging the deployment of AI at a scale unseen in the west. The technology is being rolled out at a staggering rate in an increasingly precarious labour market, and the Wuhan episode helped to highlight the social tensions it is causing.View image in fullscreenA Baidu driverless robotaxi on the streets of Wuhan in 2024.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesGig workers like Yao are fearful about the impact of AI on their livelihoods, while recent incidents of white-collar workers being replaced by AI have also sparked a debate over whether workers should embrace the technology – or try to compete with it.Addressing Shanghai’s World AI Conference in July, China’s leader, Xi Jinping, said that AI should be “an important driver for shared prosperity and common security”.But that goal is being pursued amid an increasingly fragile labour market. As well as suffering from high levels of unemployment, China has seen tens of millions of workers drop out of formal employment into the gig economy. According to one thinktank, the number of people in flexible employment will rise to 320 million this year, up from 160 million in 2019. That is about 44% of China’s workforce.China’s gig economyTaxi drivers are one part of this huge cohort. Across the country, as previously heavyweight industries such as real estate and education have floundered, workers have turned to ride-hailing apps to make ends meet. But now the rollout of robotaxis, one of the most popular applications of AI that is already in use in China, is threatening their livelihoods.“If the state really took you into consideration, Apollo Go would never have gone on the market,” says one Wuhan driver.“If things keep going this way in the future, sure, rapid development and scientific progress are great, but ordinary people like us will have no place to survive,” she adds.In 2024, taxi drivers in Wuhan protested against the rollout of Apollo Go in their city. It is unclear how many people took part, because news of the protests were quickly censored. Several drivers interviewed in Wuhan said they had heard about the protests but denied being involved.That year, a Wuhan taxi company, took the rare step of publicly criticising the government’s policy to allow automation on to the city’s streets.“The recent rise of autonomous ride-hailing vehicles has allowed technology to monopolise resources and take away the livelihoods of people at the bottom of society,” the letter said.View image in fullscreenTaxis wait for fares outside the airport in Wuhan, China.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAuthorities in China do not take kindly to public criticism. When the Guardian visited the taxi company’s office in July, an employee declined to be interviewed, citing an agreement with the police to refuse interviews and the risk of detention if he violated the agreement.But two years later, the government is echoing some of the same concerns first voiced by the Wuhan drivers.An editorial published in the state-run Workers’ Daily said that employment rights were “facing new challenges” in the age of AI. The article warned of a “collision between traditional employment rules and the iteration of AI technology”.The government recently pledged to “comprehensively address the impact of changes in the external environment and the development of new technologies such as artificial intelligence on employment”.Selina Xu, a China technology analyst, said there had been a “major vibe shift” from Beijing.She says that after the success of local AI modelDeepSeeklast year, China was “very pro AI development”.“This year, if you look at certain new guidelines that have been published … there has been a lot more emphasis placed on AI for boosting employment and people-first approaches,” Xu says.Cheng Wanhui, an official for the local government in Beijing’s hi-tech zone of Zhongguancun, says that the authorities are “paying close attention to the social issues AI brings, as well as potential ethical concerns.”“The key is for everyone to shift their mindset, see AI as a tool, and learn how to apply it in their future work,” Cheng says.Recent court rulings have awarded compensation to white-collar workers laid off by their firms to be replaced by AI. But many workers fear the AI uptake will be a barrier to them being offered a job in the first place.Tian Zemin, a cinematographer who works in Beijing, has worked in the film industry for nearly two decades. But now he’s out of work. “I spent six gruelling years working my way up to become a cinematographer, only to be replaced by a piece of software,” he wrote in a social media post about AI.“I thought I would spend my whole life in this industry. But the emergence of AI has made me feel a huge shock for the first time,” he tells the Guardian.Many of Tian’s peers are losing out as AI becomes more widely adopted across the film industry. His own rate as a freelancer is now 40% of what it was in 2019.Tian said he’s been shocked at AI’s progress. Last year, it made shonky, weird looking avatars. Now it can make convincing digital clones who have the range to carry a feature length film. “We have barely had time to react,” Tian says.Many analysts believe that China, where the government exerts significant control over the private sector, will be better placed than the US to contain the fallout from AI-related job losses. Beijing could for example instruct companies to comply with hiring quotas, Xu says.But for Tian, protections may not come soon enough. “We could be replaced at any moment,” he says. “Perhaps the only thing we can do is adapt as quickly as possible, and try to find the corner that AI still cannot replace – but that corner is getting smaller and smaller.”Additional research by Yu-chen LiExplore more on these topicsChinaAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: FTSE 100 on track for best month since first US attacks on Iran five months ago – as it happened | Business | The Guardian

Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Live, rolling coverage as London’s biggest companies defy Middle East disruption and UK petrol prices rise to around £1.60 per litre, the highest since Donald Trump ordered renewed strikes
Content: 12h ago10.10 EDTClosing summary: FTSE 100 limps to end of month, but share prices still upTheFTSE 100is losing a bit of momentum as the month crawls to its end, but it is still a much more positive picture than might have been expected during the turmoil of March.The index reached anew recordearlier this morning and – barring a significant worsening in the next hour or so – will finish the month up by about 3.5% at around 10,840 points.
