title: Drones offer alternative to balloons for weather research | Drones (non-military) | The Guardian
description: Pre-programmed flights gather data at different altitudes then return to bases to recharge and download
Author: David Hambling
Headline: Pre-programmed flights gather data at different altitudes then return to bases to recharge and download
Content: Weather balloons, in regular use since the 1930s, sometimes get mistaken for UFOs.Photograph: Miguel Roberts/APView image in fullscreenWeather balloons, in regular use since the 1930s, sometimes get mistaken for UFOs.Photograph: Miguel Roberts/APWeatherwatchDrones (non-military)Drones offer alternative to balloons for weather researchPre-programmed flights gather data at different altitudes then return to bases to recharge and downloadDavid HamblingFri 31 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWeather happens in the boundary layer, the atmosphere from ground level to a few thousand metres, but this can be difficult to study in detail: weather stations are too low, and aircraft are expensive. Instrumented weather balloons are the traditional solution, and thousands are released every day. But these are at the mercy of the wind and use irreplaceable helium.Drones offer an alternative and the US company Meteomatics has taken the idea further withMeteobase, a base station on the ground with a drone that can be launched and recovered automatically. It carries out a pre-programmed flight, gathering data at different altitudes, then returns to recharge and download data which the Meteobase sends to researchers.The base is highly weather resistant and keeps the drone at a comfortable temperature. It can send out one data-gathering mission a day, or multiple flights to monitor fog, icing, an advancing weather front, or other fast-changing conditions. Such a setup could potentially replace labour-intensive and expensive balloon launches.Weather balloons carrying instruments have been in regular use since the 1930s. They have become part of popular culture, partly because they sometimes get mistaken forUFOs, or are used as a throwaway “explanation” for UFO sightings. Future flying saucer spotters may be equally well entertained by weather drones bearing flashing lights.Explore more on these topicsDrones (non-military)WeatherwatchUFOsMeteorologynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A universal human story’: Clean Start’s thought-provoking tidying sim tells immigrant’s tale | Games | The Guardian
description: Playing as recent arrival Lena, your challenges include learning a new language and uncovering family secrets – its developer hopes it will spread ‘a little more compassion’
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Playing as recent arrival Lena, your challenges include learning a new language and uncovering family secrets – its developer hopes it will spread ‘a little more compassion’
Content: Clean Start.Photograph: Serious Sim, Amplified GamesView image in fullscreenClean Start.Photograph: Serious Sim, Amplified GamesSummer games previewsGames‘A universal human story’: Clean Start’s thought-provoking tidying sim tells immigrant’s talePlaying as recent arrival Lena, your challenges include learning a new language and uncovering family secrets – its developer hopes it will spread ‘a little more compassion’Keith StuartFri 31 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 09.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe cosy house-sorting sim has become a much-loved staple of the PC indie scene. Titles such asUnpacking,A Little to the Leftand Momento charm players with their detailed interiors and quiet narratives of lives lived and shared within the same four walls. For Clean Start, Polish developer Serious Sim has taken a different approach – here you play as domestic cleaner, Lena, an immigrant who has arrived in an unspecified western country with little knowledge of the local language, and a family to support back home.From here, you’re tasked with cleaning a series of houses and apartments, polishing tables, tidying shelves and scrubbing muddy pawprints from kitchen floors. It seems you’re able to rearrange the rooms, giving them a personal feel, which is after all one of the most pleasing elements of the genre. You can also, we are reassured, pet the dog.View image in fullscreenPersonal feel … Clean Start.Photograph: Serious Sim, Amplified GamesFor artist and game director Katarzyna Haptaś the game has personal meaning. “It is largely inspired by the stories my mother told about working abroad as a domestic cleaner,” she says. “But that experience was shared by many members of my family, as well as my friends’ families. Back in the 90s, there was always some kid who had a parent working elsewhere, sending packages home for Christmas. I was blessed to hear stories from my grandmother as well. She went to America with only a few dollars in her purse and no confirmation that anyone would be waiting for her at the airport. All of that at a time when there was no internet or cellphones.”Haptaś has drawn on her own experiences, too. Working as a cleaner in a local cinema taught her how people interact with cleaning staff. The team researched the experiences of those coming to her home country to seek work. “During the pre-production phase of the prototype, we managed to have an interview with an immigration centre worker in Poland,” she says. “She shared many insights on immigrants working in Poland at the time, mainly from war-torn Ukraine.”Interestingly, the game uses language as a key part of its challenge. While chatting to Lena, her employers use unfamiliar words that she can learn through interacting with the environment. Owners will also ask you to find specific objects, usually with sentimental value or family stories and dramas attached. “By interacting with certain objects, players can piece together clues about what’s happening in each client’s life,” says Haptaś. “Often, these items help the clients realise something important or uncover a secret that was kept from them. Depending on what the player finds, there are different lines of dialogue commenting on it. Finding the right combination of items will reveal the full story to the player.”Clean Start isn’t just a cosy house-tidying sim – instead, it is using this genre to explore themes of connection, comfort and closure. Immigration has become such a polarising debate, there is value in such a quiet depiction. “I hope this is a universal human story,” says Haptaś. “I hope that people will see each other as human beings, with all of our shared hopes and fears. Leaving home to work in a foreign country with limited knowledge of the language is never an easy decision. It wasn’t easy in the 90s and it isn’t easy today. Ultimately, I hope that players will leave with a little more compassion and patience for those who are simply doing their best to work and communicate.”Clean Start is released on PC on 5 November, a demo isavailable on SteamExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My family is coming apart – so it’s time for one last video game session | Games | The Guardian
description: I wanted our last family games night to be the best fun we’ve ever had. Maybe we should have stuck with Mario Kart …
Author: Dominik Diamond
Headline: I wanted our last family games night to be the best fun we’ve ever had. Maybe we should have stuck with Mario Kart …
Content: ‘Games remind us that we always have more things in common than we sometimes feel’ …Photograph: Interfoto/Alamy Stock PhotoView image in fullscreen‘Games remind us that we always have more things in common than we sometimes feel’ …Photograph: Interfoto/Alamy Stock PhotoGamesMy family is coming apart – so it’s time for one last video game sessionDominik DiamondI wanted our last family games night to be the best fun we’ve ever had. Maybe we should have stuck with Mario Kart …Fri 31 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 19.16 EDTShareIt is the end of an era for the Diamond family. For 20 years, there have been five of us living together. It has not been easy. Militant vegan daughters, sons who have inherited Scottish tempers, and a youngest child who attracts trouble like an industrial magnet, have meant our house has been conflict-laden at times. Throw in the fact that we are beset with all manner of mental health bobbins and chronic illnesses that resulted in two of our three kids almost dying in hospitals and you get a family that is combustible – but extremely close.Through it all, we had games. They always brought us back together. Not just us all hunkering over Super Mario Kart like some kind of UN-mandated family therapy, but the conversations that happen when any of us spy another playing something new.Gamesare a cultural touchstone that helped us crack through the veneer of disagreements and distrust and remind us that we have more things in common than we sometimes feel.View image in fullscreen‘UN-mandated family therapy’ … Mario Kart 8 Deluxe.Photograph: NintendoBut now we are moving out of the house we have shared for years. My wife has to go back to the UK for family reasons, #1 Child is moving in with her boyfriend and youngest child is moving in with a friend. This leaves the Son and I – we are moving into an apartment for the next few months, which Charlie is already dubbing the bro-tel. (I am filled with equal parts excitement and dread about this.)So I wanted one last family games night to remind us of simpler times before we all go our separate ways. I wanted it to be the best fun we have ever had. I wanted … Quiplash!Quiplash is one of the most important games in the history of our family, because I view it as the game that trained my kids to be funny. Seeing them all become fairly high-level comedy beings has been the greatest thrill of my life as a dad.It’s a simple “fill in the blanks or answer the question with something funny to get the most votes” game, the beauty of it being you can play using mobile phones as controllers and five people can play. That’s why I have it as a go-to. Getting any family together to do anything is like herding particularly wilful sheep, and when was the last time you saw a shepherd try that while hunting for 10 working batteries for gaming controllers? Exactly.It’s not just the genuinely funny answers that get votes: there is also a lot of love for old family running gags, most of which are at my expense, usually my baldness or my rigidity with rules.However, while I am impressed by my grownup kids’ quick-thinking quippery, I am still appalled by some of their spelling. So for our final game, I introduce a rule that you can only vote for answers spelt correctly. This rule is not just ignored but aggressively mocked with answers that are part punchline and part Welsh street name.I am in last place because they can tell which answers are from me. So, I start deliberately entering badly spelt answers to confuse them, so they give up trying to play the game seriously and while I am writing quality punchlines such as “God said ‘wrong door’” (you had to be there), I am faced with answers from them such as “pee pee poo poo”.And then the rows break out. My two youngest kids work at the same trendy bar/restaurant, and they have issues with each other. One suggested a role for the other there that they are not happy about, so they declare they never want to work in the same place together again. Impressively, during the argument, my son still manages to answer “skittle flavour that just missed the cut” with “narly Netenyahu nectarine”. Which almost got my vote until I noticed that neither Netanyahu nor gnarly are spelt like that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe row escalates. Wife and #1 Child have reverted to doomscrolling on their phones instead. No one wants to play. It’s all falling apart. Not just this desperate attempt at one final family gaming session, but the family itself. In one week, our matriarch, the most important one of us, will be on the other side of the Atlantic. In a couple of months, #1 Child could be the only one still actually living on this side of it.View image in fullscreenMemories flooded back … Kirby’s Return to Dream Land Deluxe.Photograph: NintendoMemories start flooding back: the summer I spent playing Super Mario Sunshine with #1 Child when she was five. Evading guard dogs in the snow with my son on Call of Duty: Modern Warfare when he wasn’t much older. Seeing my youngest child fall in love with Kirby. The years of Mario Kart, Mortal Kombat and Just Dance. The conversations. The debates. The windups. There is such joy in those moments but now they are spilling through my fingers like water.I think of all the times in recent years when one of the kids has asked me if I want to play a game with them. And I’ve been “too busy”. I wish I had all those moments back to create more memories.My wife, ever the peacemaker of the family, declares the next day that we will have one more go at this the night before she goes back to Blighty. That prospect seems as good as it gets right now.Explore more on these topicsGamesFamilycommentShareReuse this content

title: SingStar Take That anyone? The strange joy of charity shop video games | Games | The Guardian
description: Hidden gems can be unearthed, but you have to dig deep into the bargain bins of countless outdated Fifas, Wii Fits without the controllers and partially finished quizshow games
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Hidden gems can be unearthed, but you have to dig deep into the bargain bins of countless outdated Fifas, Wii Fits without the controllers and partially finished quizshow games
Content: Shelf discovery … video games in a charity shop.Photograph: Keith Stuart/The GuardianView image in fullscreenShelf discovery … video games in a charity shop.Photograph: Keith Stuart/The GuardianGamesSingStar Take That anyone? The strange joy of charity shop video gamesHidden gems can be unearthed, but you have to dig deep into the bargain bins of countless outdated Fifas, Wii Fits without the controllers and partially finished quizshow gamesKeith StuartFri 31 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 19.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs an eternally optimistic charity shop fan, I hold on to the fantasy that one day I’ll walk into my local Oxfam and find a pristine copy of theSegaSaturn shooter Burning Rangers for £1.50. Or perhaps a box full of old Neo Geo carts for a quid each. Sadly, this is now unlikely. Charity shops have caught on to the fact that old video games – like old vinyl albums – are highly collectible, and so they’re putting the good stuff on eBay. That’s fine, it’s their job to raise money, not to provide opportunist swine like me with bargains. But what gamescanyou find tucked away in your local branch of Barnardo’s? To find out I visited about 40 charity stores across the country. Here is what I discovered on the shelves … And please do share your own charity shop gaming finds in the comments!Old versions of annual sports gamesView image in fullscreenSome good seasons, and hilarious commentary … old sports games.Photograph: Keith Stuart/The GuardianBy far the biggest category. Almost every store I entered had a selection of Fifa, Pro Evolution Soccer and Madden titles from years gone by, most of them on Xbox 360, and usually going for 50p each or less. There were a few decent outliers: I picked up a copy of tennis sim Top Spin 3 for £1 and was tempted by Major League Baseball 2K5 for the original Xbox, but was put off by the fact that it was missing its instruction booklet – and also, I don’t own an original Xbox. Are any others worth buying? Well, Fifa had a really good streak from 2010-2015 – super-fast gameplay, great licensed soundtracks, so if you don’t care about the latest squads, they’re entertaining for the money. I’d also recommend Pro Evolution Soccer 4-6 on thePlayStation2 – a true golden era of footie simulation and unintentionally hilarious commentary.Brain-training and quiz gamesTitles such as Dr Kawashima’s Brain Training and Big Brain Academy sold in their millions on the DS and Wii in the mid-00s, accelerated by smart,celebrity-crammed TV advertising. Naturally, there were reams of imitators – seemingly all of which have ended up on charity shop shelves. The original Brain Training is still challenging and compelling – although if you grab a copy, be careful to check any saved game files still left in the cart’s memory. I got a copy for a quid, and when I loaded it up, one of the stored usernames was “Martin’s Sex Bitch” (brain age: 35). Steer well clear of all the TV quiz show games that clogged up the DS library. One charity shop I went into had just a single game: Golden Balls, based on the daytime gameshow presented by Jasper Carrott. Reader: I did not buy it.Music and fitness games – without the required peripheralsView image in fullscreenBoard not available in my branch of Oxfam … Wii Fit.Photograph: Itsuo Inouye/APThis was another ubiquitous category. No matter where I went, charity shops were filled with copies of Dance UK, SingStar andWiiFit, but all lacked the necessary controllers to make them work. There were Kinect games with no Kinect and PlayStation EyeToy games with no camera. Out of all of them, I’d be tempted most by PlayStation 2 SingStar titles – it’ll only cost about £12 on eBay to buy the microphones and adaptor, then you can pick up the dozens of SingStar instalments for a few pounds (Rock Ballads! Motown! Sing along with Disney!) – hey presto, karaoke heaven. Wii Fit is also OK if you’re happy to pay £10 for a balance board on eBay that hasn’t been pounded to death.Kids’ gamesOnce again, these proliferated on the family-friendly Wii and DS consoles and as they hold little replay value, they show up in great numbers. Peppa Pig, Pirates of the Caribbean, lots of pet games – one store I found in Brighton had at least five horse sims, including Horse Life and Pippa Funnell. Ubisoft’s range of job sims including Imagine: Fashion Designer and Imagine: Teacher were in abundance, though sadly, I didn’t find a copy of Imagine: Journalist, which would have been useful. One title in this genre that was present in at least 65% of the shops I visited was CarnivalGamesfrom 2K Play, a wretched collection of fairground mini-challenges including duck shoot, ring toss and balloon darts. The motion controls are appalling and the player avatars are terrifying, dead-eyed monstrosities. If the backrooms had a games area, this would be playing.Blockbuster games from previous console generationsSome games sold so well, they have absolutely no value in the secondhand market. You can always count on finding a number of Call of Duty, Assassin’s Creed or Gears of War instalments as well as many copies of GTA V. Some of these are worth rediscovering. The campaign modes in Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare, Modern Warfare 2 and Infinite Warfare are exciting nonsense, while Assassin’s Creed Brotherhood, Origins and Odyssey are all worth playing – as is Assassin’s Creed 2. I’d also buy Gears of War 2 and Halo 2 for the campaign modes if you’ve not played them. The Mass Effect and Dragon Age titles are often knocking about and still have a lot of charm.PC gamesView image in fullscreenCD-Rom drive anyone … some old PC games.Photograph: Keith Stuart/The GuardianThese are still clogging the shelves of charity shops everywhere, despite (or perhaps because of) the fact that a lot ofPCowners no longer have CD-Rom drives, and even if they did, they’re likely to face compatibility issues trying to load ancient copies of, say, The Sims 2 or saucy adult adventure title, Leisure Suit Larry: Box Office Bust (the latter might still be in the Frome branch of the Cats and Dogs charity shop if you’re interested). With digital stores such as Steam and GOG stuffed with retro titles at teeny prices, there’s little reason to buy disc PC games now – unless you stumble across an ancient “big box” copy of Doom, Half-Life or Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders. Which you won’t.The odd gemView image in fullscreenOpportune moment … Time Crisis gamesPhotograph: Keith Stuart/The GuardianThey’re still out there, especially at pop-up charity shops and smaller independent stores. I bagged a copy of the rare Japanese role-playing adventure Koudelka at the Rotary Club shop in Frome for a pound, and feel a little guilty about it. I also recently acquired the light gun titles Time Crisis II (PS2) and Time Crisis: Razing Storm (PS3) for £3 each – and I even have a G-Con 2 and PlayStation Move controller to play them with. Elsewhere, I’ve regularly spotted copies of Dead Rising, Bulletstorm, FEAR and Project Gotham Racing – all great fun. Oh and fellow games contributor Jordan Erica Webber recently found Tiger Electronics’ handheld LCD game Poke Ball at the Cats Protection shop in Leamington Spa. I’d have snapped that up.But if youdofind a copy of Burning Rangers on the Sega Saturn it is completely worthless and terrible and you should just send it straight to me.Explore more on these topicsGamesRetro gamesSports gamesQuiz and trivia gamesPuzzle gamesWiiPlayStationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Will Trump be Burnham’s undoing, or the making of him? The answer lies in Europe | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: In an increasingly dangerous world, Europe is finding safety in numbers – but Britain is on the outside. The new PM’s task is to change that, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: In an increasingly dangerous world, Europe is finding safety in numbers – but Britain is on the outside. The new PM’s task is to change that, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Shutterstock/APView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Shutterstock/APOpinionAndy BurnhamWill Trump be Burnham’s undoing, or the making of him? The answer lies in EuropeJonathan FreedlandIn an increasingly dangerous world, our European neighbours are finding safety in numbers – but Britain is on the outside. The new PM’s task is to change thatFri 31 Jul 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 13.54 EDTShareThere is an orange cloud in the sky. I’m not referring to the wildfires ravaging parts of Europe and East Anglia, though they are connected. I mean the looming pall from across the Atlantic that threatens to spoil the sunny start to the premiership of Andy Burnham – and whose name isDonald Trump.Burnham’s first 10 days or so in office have gone about as well as he or any of his team could have dared hope. His net approval rating has risen by 17 points, according toone early poll,gaining groundwith every category of voter except supporters of Reform UK, though they too like some of what they see. His easy manner, no-notes speech-making and agility on social media have won plaudits, including from a usually sceptical press.But the new prime minister will know that all this could be upended at a stroke, with a single move by the man in the White House. Keir Starmer watched as the earliest green shoots of economic growth emerged earlier this year, only to be crushed by Trump’s decision to combine with Israel and attack Iran. What can Burnham do to ensure he does not suffer that same fate? As it happens, the answer to that question answers another: what might constitute a Burnham foreign policy that would match the spirit and ethos of the agenda he has set out at home?So far most of the discussion in this area has concentrated on how the new PM should handle his counterpart in Washington. Some suggest his best bet is to emulate Starmer: swallow your pride, ladle on the flattery, avoid overt confrontation. Maybe tickle Trump’s tummy by promising to drill in the North Sea, even as Suffolk is engulfed in the flames of the climate breakdown. Others say the US president is a bully who only respects strength: therefore, stand up to him, even if that means a row.All this owes more to the realm of animal psychology than political analysis. Different world leaders have tried both approaches – nice guy and tough guy – and both have failed. And sometimes succeeded. Trump has an attention span measured in seconds; he is erratic and impulse driven; he changes his mind without warning, logic or consistency.Those at the sharp end have come to understand this, which helps explain the muted reaction to Trump’s announcement late on Thursday of a breakthrough in Gaza. “There is scepticism and cautiousness among Palestinians,” reported Al Jazeera after Trump said Hamas was ready to disarm in return for an Israeli withdrawal from the territory. As anyone who has followed his zigzagging engagement with the Middle East has come to learn, the safest response to any development heralded by the US president is: don’t hold your breath.Faced with such a man, it’s foolish to imagine a British prime minister can have much impact on American decisions. Even senior US administration officials have been known to admit privately that they have next to no sway over Trump, so why would a British PM fare any better? Brits do have access – I’m told that national security adviser Jonathan Powell is in regular contact with Trump’s personal envoy and golfing buddy Steve Witkoff – but that is not the same as influence.The remedy, then, is not to hope to change a president who won’t change, but rather to be less exposed to his whims. And that points to a much larger strategy, one that makes sense in terms of both policy and politics – and which just so happens to fit Burnham’s approach to a T.The prime minister’s opening pitch has been that he will speak to voters candidly, that he will confront the big problems that his predecessors ducked and that he is ready to break from orthodoxies that have held too long. He has already made a start in that vein domestically, withhis promise this weekto tackle social care. But why not extend it to the international realm?It would begin with a stark admission that the foundation of postwar UK foreign policy is no longer stable – that we cannot rely on the US as the guarantor of our security. A US president who muses out loud about abandoning Nato, whothreatens to seize the territory(Greenland) of a Nato ally (Denmark) and whose support for a country (Ukraine) invaded by an enemy (Russia) is so inconstant, is less a guarantor than a danger. It is clearly reckless to remain in a state of dependence on such a power.Luckily, there is a group of allies close at hand who have reached that same conclusion and are already acting on it. Our European neighbours are coming together to defend themselves, without relying on Washington. They are borrowing money collectively, which makes it cheaper, and pooling resources, which makes arms spending more efficient. Add theSafe loan programme, funding joint defence procurement to the tune of €150bn (£128bn), to the EU arming of Ukraine, and you can see why Mark Leonard, director of the European Council on Foreign Relations, tells me: “The EU is becoming a security community.”It is security broadly defined too. Witness joint EU action on energy, to plug the gap previously filled by Russian gas; vaccines during the Covid pandemic; cybersecurity and election interference; the climate crisis and immigration. In an increasingly dangerous world, the Europeans are finding safety in numbers. And we, though they are our nearest neighbours, are on the outside.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is an economic dimension to this. Spending your defence budgets closer to home, rather than on US-made hardware, serves pretty well as what Burnham might call a reindustrialisation strategy. The French have long understood that; the Germans increasingly so. Not for nothing has Berlin decided to spendonly 8%of its massive €80bn rearmament drive on US weapons. As the EU moves to a “buy European” approach, it will be European industry that benefits – but not us.The economic dimension goes further, because our security is threatened in that sphere too. As Mark Carney of Canada correctly diagnosed in hisDavos speech, globalisation, and the economic interdependence it entails, can easily be turned into a weapon. Trump’s US wields it through the imposition of tariffs, China by controlling access to rare earth metals. The best way for a country to protect itself is to stop being dependent on either of those two titans. The UK’s only shot at such independence is, perhaps paradoxically, to be part of a group large enough to aim for resilience and self-sufficiency – and that means the EU.It will look politically daring, but that’s only if you adopt the view from Westminster – where Brexit seems untouchable and all anyone can see are red lines. Among the people of Britain, it’s a very different picture.A major survey by the ECFRin June found that Britons now regard Brexit as a “disaster”, with three-quarters wanting a closer relationship with the EU. One striking number: when asked to choose, 63% said they would prioritise the relationship with the EU over the US, with only 19% making the opposite choice. A plurality even favours the creation of that one-time tabloid spectre: a European army with British troops in it. As Leonard puts it: “The waters are much warmer than people realise.”This, then, is what Burnhamism could look like abroad – a willingness to face the world as it now is, to break from the old, Atlanticist default setting and to pursue a new approach that will make us both militarily and economically more resilient. The answer is no longer to put our trust in a single, unreliable friend – but rather to combine with our nearest neighbours. The new prime minister has so much to do, but he can do almost none of it without challenging a status quo that has done so much damage in a single decade. He will have to undo the folly of 2016 – and look to Europe.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionEuropeEuropean UnionDonald TrumpForeign policyDefence policyBrexitcommentShareReuse this content

title: A World Cup with no participants – it could be Gianni Infantino’s boldest move yet | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: You’ve got to admire the Fifa president’s chutzpah in trying to flog off football’s greatest prize. If only Uefa wasn’t being so pesky about it all, says Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: You’ve got to admire the Fifa president’s chutzpah in trying to flog off football’s greatest prize. If only Uefa wasn’t being so pesky about it all, says Marina Hyde
Content: Fifa president Gianni Infantino during the World Cup 2026 play-offs draw in Zurich, Switzerland, 20 November 2025.Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPAView image in fullscreenFifa president Gianni Infantino during the World Cup 2026 play-offs draw in Zurich, Switzerland, 20 November 2025.Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPAOpinionGianni InfantinoA World Cup with no participants – it could be Gianni Infantino’s boldest move yetMarina HydeYou’ve got to admire the Fifa president’s chutzpah in trying to flog off football’s greatest prize. If only Uefa wasn’t being so pesky about it allFri 31 Jul 2026 08.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 08.48 EDTShareImagine a plan so distasteful that even the Americans and a Middle Eastern nepo-royal football boss can’t be doing with it. Such is the status of Fifa president Gianni Infantino’s scheme tosell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors. More historically, perhaps, the 55 nations that make up Uefa have reacted to this horror show byvoting unanimously to boycott Fifa tournaments, including World Cups, if Infantino presses ahead. That would mean Spain and Portugal boycotting their own men’s World Cup next time around, which you’d think – not to call it too soon – would come off as slightly bad vibes.A testing moment, then, for the haunted cue-ball. Again. Can it really already be time to turn to Infantino once more, even after he appeared in this spotonly on Tuesday, after his 15-page Instagram crash-out about his haters? Yes. Yes, I’m afraid it can. Demanding the federations of the world sell off the World Cup to some fund led byDonald Trump’s son-in-law’s brotherwill regrettably draw attention to you in ways that will prove difficult to control. As indicated, the Fifa president’s plan has contrived to appear vulgar to the North American confederation, Concacaf, as well as the Asian Football Confederation (AFC).Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, the Bahraini royal who leads the AFC,has issued a statement, declaring that “the AFC is deeply concerned that Fifa’s unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football, which are based on solidarity, cooperation and transparency”. He went on to call for “the highest standards of ethics and good governance”. And certainly, it’s always a pleasure to take an ethics lesson from a guy like this. A number of human rights organisations claim that during the Arab spring,Salman busied himself with identifying dissident players and other athletes, many of whom were imprisoned and tortured. (He denies this.) Yet even he simply cannot force himself through Infantino’s latest show of full-spectrum amorality.It’s hard to escape the sense of gathering momentum against not only Infantino’s plan but the man himself, even from federations he has showered with disproportionate amounts of development cash over the years. A hotly defensive new statement declaring that “Nobody is selling football” emanated overnight from Fifa, which, to repeat, is proposing literally selling stakes in football to private investors.It’s a testing moment, too, for one of the most extravagant pieces of corporate bullshit of our entire era – the post-binfire promise: “We will learn from this.” And so to the involvement of JP Morgan in Infantino’s scheme. Five years ago, JP Morgan ended up apologising to fans after its part in the imploded plan to create a breakaway European Super League.Back then, it said: “We clearly misjudged how this deal would be viewed by the wider football community and how it might affect them in the future.” Then, it was time to deploy the mother lode: “We will learn from this.” Will you though? JP Morgan evidently regards time as a great healer, because it is once again the bank at the centre of the firestorm, having been working with Fifa to raise $4.2bn with the new commercial vehicle.At time of writing, Infantino was still insisting that he was pressing ahead with the scheme despite Uefa’s boycott pledge, which is certainly bold, given he would be trying to sell stakes in a tournament in which most of the best sides would not be playing. One intervention that has yet to materialise is any comment on the idea from Trump. The US president has, of course, been quite taken up over the past few days with his Middle East peace manoeuvres, creditinghis “historic” agreement to disarm Hamasand other militant groups in Gaza to the machinations of his Board of Peace – a body whose inauguration, you might recall, Infantino showily attended. Perhaps the most excruciatingly on-brand move for the Fifa president now would be to post a 15-page Insta meltdown about how he was way more concerned with the slightly more important matter of Middle East peace as brought about by his special friend, than about trifling matters such as flogging the World Cup to private equity. Certainly wouldn’t put it past him.But it is hard not to conclude that it is too much time with his special friend that has caused Infantino to overplay his hand in precisely the way he has. Maybe the real Trump derangement syndrome is the betas who suck up to the alpha in the apparent belief they will somehow osmotically absorb his unique characteristics and political gifts, and then themselves get away with the sort of stuff that only he has historically been able to pull. It’s personality cult as cargo cult.We see it in Nigel Farage, a man who threw a byelection to which no one turned up, and is now having to chomp his way through a long hot summer of wasting time and money. And we see it in Infantino, a man who has spent the past year or two getting as up close and personal as possible with Trump, and presumably concluded that the US president’s ability to defy various laws of politics had rubbed magically off on him. But that isn’t how it has worked at all, as he is now finding out, presumably to his own bemusement. The first rule of politics, famously, is to learn how to count – and Infantino’s failure to do so now suggests his own days are numbered.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMarina Hyde is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoOpinionFifaUefaFootball politicsDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m a Haitian TPS holder. Over 330,000 of us hold our breath as Congress decides our future | Josiane Valsaint | The Guardian
description: Temporary protected status allowed me to rebuild my life. Now thousands like me help keep this country running
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Temporary protected status allowed me to rebuild my life. Now thousands like me help keep this country running
Content: ‘Our Haitian neighbors, like our other community members, are business owners, workers, and church members, parents, students, caretakers and farm workers.’Photograph: Adam Gray/APView image in fullscreen‘Our Haitian neighbors, like our other community members, are business owners, workers, and church members, parents, students, caretakers and farm workers.’Photograph: Adam Gray/APOpinionUS CongressI’m a Haitian TPS holder. Over 330,000 of us hold our breath as Congress decides our futureJosiane ValsaintTemporary protected status allowed me to rebuild my life. Now thousands like me help keep this country runningFri 31 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 08.31 EDTShareRight now, across the country, there aremore than 330,000 Haitianscollectively holding their breath over the future of lifesaving immigration protections provided through temporary protected status (TPS). Three hundred and fifty thousand is a big, meaningful number – but for many, it’s still just a number.In the case ofDonald Trumpand his supporters in Congress, the number of lives at stake has mattered little. Trump has been incessant in his efforts to eliminate TPS for Haitians. In doing so, he’s broken with a bipartisan tradition dating back to 1990 of prioritizing the safety of people from other countries who cannot return home because of dangerous conditions. And it’showhe’s done it, too: without consideration for theongoing violence,civil unrest, lack of infrastructure, and political instability in Haiti. But what Trump has also failed to acknowledge are the lives built here by that same huge number of people.‘We’re human beings’: Haitians in the US fear family separation and deportation to violenceRead moreWhen I hear the figure, I think of all the Haitians I met on my long journey to the US. I think of the people who, forced to first pass through several other countries, lost their lives before they could find safety and stability in this country. Mothers, fathers, kids, young couples – all seeking safety, protection and a better life for themselves and their families, no different from anyone else. I think inevitably, though it brings me great pain, of theHaitiI was forced to leave behind more than 16 years ago before starting a new life in San Diego.A magnitude-seven earthquake ravaged my homeland in 2010,killing more than 220,000 peopleand displacing millions. It remains one of the deadliest natural disasters in the history of the western hemisphere and has left an indelible mark on all Haitians, both those who fled and those who couldn’t.In Haiti, the tremors we felt after the earthquake weren’t just tectonic; they were political, psychological, even existential – and they can still be felt today. The past decade and a half has seen Haiti taken over by widespread food insecurity, hurricanes, rampant gang violence and a full-blowncholera epidemicthat has consumed part of the country. It’s why I made the difficult decision to leave everything behind and flee with my son, who was a toddler at the time.I joined family members in the US, making a home in San Diego. Thanks to TPS, which wasdesignated in 2010and thenredesignated in 2011, I obtained the stability needed to build a home and give back to the community that welcomed me with such warmth and kindness. I learned English and became a caregiver and then a nursing assistant. For a while, things started to get so much better with TPS that it almost felt like those familiar tremors – which followed Haitians like me across thousands of miles – had gone away. But not for long.‘Each day feels like the last’: Haitians with TPS on edge as confusion clouds US work statusRead moreBecause the Trump administration refused to redesignate TPS for Haitians, thousands of people were left without legal status and vulnerable to callous immigration raids. My husband was one of those people. Our young children still say that they never got to say goodbye to their dad. If TPS isn’t renewed for Haitians, they could lose their mother to the very same system.Thankfully, there’s a glimpse of light and hope. In April, the House of Representativesvoted to extendTPS for Haitians for three more years. The bill,S.4814, awaits a vote in the Senate; it’s why I am calling on our elected officials there to do the right thing, just as I’m calling on the public to stand up for our Haitian neighbors.The Senate must stand with families and protect the stability of communities. Our Haitian neighbors, like our other community members, are business owners, workers, and church members, parents, students, caretakers and farm workers.We work hard, we pay our taxes, we give back to our communities and we are a big part of the engine that keeps the United States workforce in many essential industries moving.We deserve to stay here, with our families and loved ones.Josiane Valsaint is a TPS recipient and advocate for Haitian nationals who risk being deported by the Trump administrationExplore more on these topicsUS CongressOpinionHaitiCaribbeanAmericasUS SenateUS domestic policycommentShareReuse this content

title: McCarthyism has returned to the United States – and this time it’s even more dangerous | Judith Levine | The Guardian
description: Trump’s campaign of repression echoes the red scare. But now the government has bigger ambitions and more powerful tools
Author: Judith Levine
Headline: Trump’s campaign of repression echoes the red scare. But now the government has bigger ambitions and more powerful tools
Content: ‘The scope of this administration’s ambitions; its armies of enforcers; the technological and legal tools at its disposal; and the dearth of principled actors to obstruct it make this McCarthyism far more dangerous.’Photograph: Byron Rollins/APView image in fullscreen‘The scope of this administration’s ambitions; its armies of enforcers; the technological and legal tools at its disposal; and the dearth of principled actors to obstruct it make this McCarthyism far more dangerous.’Photograph: Byron Rollins/APOpinionTrump administrationMcCarthyism has returned to the United States – and this time it’s even more dangerousJudith LevineTrump’s campaign of repression echoes the red scare. But now the government has bigger ambitions and more powerful toolsFri 31 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.10 EDTShareThere are many parallels between the first McCarthy era, roughly 1946 to 1956, and Trump’s campaign of political repression, his own updated McCarthyism.Both regimes crafted a monster of quasi-facts and innuendo and fed it with fear: an enemy within, well-organized and financed, secretive and violent, allied with evil foreigners and bent on overthrowing capitalism, democracy and Christian morality. Both used flagrantly unconstitutional means to cleanse the nation of the spectral menace.Each time, federal employees were targeted first. President Harry S Truman’sFederal Loyalty Programscreened 5 million workers for communist affiliation; 2,700 lost their jobs, 12,000 resigned. Schools, unions and Hollywood fell in line; blacklists outlasted their makers. The Trump administrationpurgedthe federal agencies of his equivalent of the cold war communist, the “woke”. Applicants for civil service jobs wereasked to identifytheir favorite administration policies and explain how they would advance them if hired. The federal employees’ union correctly called this request a “loyalty question”.Then as now,law firmsquailed,mediacompaniescapitulated,universitiescollaborated. Artists andperformers– Zero Mostel, Jimmy Kimmel – were exiled from film and television. In the 1940s and 50s, the attorney general compiledlistsof supposedly subversive organizations, which, along with communists and socialists, included groups from the National Negro League to the Nature Friends of America. Trump’s justice department is investigating progressive non-profits, includingActBlue, a chief funding source for Democratic candidates, theSouthern Poverty Law Center, and theOpen Society Foundations, funded by George Soros, best known for supporting democracy movements in the former Soviet Union.In both eras, the standard bearers were full of ideological passion. “Can there be anyone who fails to realize that ... this is the time for the showdown between the democratic Christian world and the communist atheistic world?” McCarthy thundered to theSenatein 1950.Trump believes in nothing but himself. But like McCarthy and his confederates, the intellectuals behind this repression are true believers. “When the leftist – who does not believe in freedom, who does not believe in civil rights, who does not believe in any ordinary notion of justice – protests that we are violating his rights, understand that he is lying to try to persuade people who are not closely following the political scene that some injustice has perpetrated against him,” Trump’s policy adviser Stephen Millersaid in a speech. “We must stay the course and be completely unflinching in the pursuit of justice against these enemies of civilization.”McCarthy and his more powerful and enduring co-conspirator, the FBI director J Edgar Hoover, ruined countless lives and crippled progressive movements. But the scope of this administration’s ambitions; its armies of enforcers inside a gargantuan carceral state; the technological and legal tools at its disposal; and the dearth of principled government actors to obstruct it make this McCarthyism far more dangerous.Global ambitionsWhile McCarthy claimed that American communists were puppets of the Soviet Union, and the CIAconspiredto undermine progressive organizing in Europe, today’s attempt toenlist foreign governmentsin a coordinated fight against “far-left terrorism” potentially extends the administration’s repressive reach around the globe.On 22 September 2025, Trump issued an executive orderdesignating the non-organization “antifa”a “domestic terrorist organization”. Three days later it issuedNational Security Presidential Memo-7on “countering domestic terrorism and organized political violence”.Brett Kavanaugh has become Trump’s chief enabler on the supreme court | Sidney BlumenthalRead moreInvoking Charlie Kirk’s murder, the assassination attempts against Trump and the supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, and “riots in Los Angeles and Portland” – but not the January 6 insurrection or the 2019 El Paso, Texas,massacreof 23 Chicano shoppers by a young white supremacist – the memo is as much manifesto as battle plan. “This political violence,” it says, “is a culmination of sophisticated, organized campaigns of targeted intimidation, radicalization, threats, and violence designed to silence opposing speech, limit political activity, change or direct policy outcomes, and prevent the functioning of a democratic society. A new law enforcement strategy that investigates all participants in these criminal and terroristic conspiracies – including the organized structures, networks, entities, organizations, funding sources, and predicate actions behind them – is required.”But if a war on the US left inside US borders were not enough, on 16 July the White Houseannounceda “global campaign to crush radical left terrorism”. The secretary of state, Marco Rubio, invited representatives of more than 60 countries to a “summit”, where he named four European “far-left terrorist organizations” and offered$10mfor information on their financing. Hepromised: “There will be more [terrorist] designations soon.” At the same time, the US implemented newvisa restrictionstargeting people who have allegedly “supported or incited acts of terrorism”.Europe has expressedskepticismthat leftwing terrorism is a big problem. Still, some countries are cooperating. The US requested theextraditionfrom Spain of a wealthy American who has donated to humanitarian aid efforts in Palestine – which the administration views as support for Hamas. Spanish authorities are detaining him while they decide whether to send him home or release him.Unlike the US criminal code on domestic terrorism, the laws on combatting foreign terrorism offer “many more tools” to pursue not just people planning or committing violent acts, but also those within “two to three degrees of separation” from the act, Mike German, a former FBI special agent, toldDemocracy Now. The purpose of the 16 July summit, he said, was “to reframe the discussion around domestic terrorism to imagine that it has these foreign connections that justify the use of these much more aggressive tools”.Laws passed since 11 September 2001, make this sleight of hand easier. The 1947National Security Actcreated a wall between the CIA and the FBI, between international and domestic intelligence gathering. But the USA Patriot Act, written and signed hastily after al-Qaida’s attacks on US soil, broke down thatwall.Civil libertarianshave long argued – and whistleblowerEdward Snowdenproved in 2013 – that the collection of communications to, from or about a foreign target can sweep up tons ofprivate informationabout Americans. “The most acute danger” of “uncontrolled sharing of criminal investigative information with intelligence agencies”, argued the ACLU at a 2005 congressional hearing, “is that federal prosecutors and law enforcement agents … concerned with preventing and punishing criminal activities” will become “a domestic spy network directed at unpopular religious and political organizations”.In fact, after September 11, that is what happened. George W Bush’s administrationmaligned and shut downUS Muslim and Arab charities and non-profits under the suspicion that they were supporting a vaguely defined foreign terrorist enemy.ICE’s surveillance app is a techno-authoritarian nightmare | Moustafa BayoumiRead moreGerman continued, citing current investigations into progressive non-profits like the Southern Poverty Law Center: “This effort to designate left-wing groups as foreign terrorists … using these broad terms like ‘antifa’ will allow them to go after people who are not committing violence, but who are simply engaging in the political process.”Extreme policingIn June, the administration circulated apress releaseboasting of the blows it had delivered the “violent anarchist network” antifa. It cited crackdowns from coast to coast – from Spokane, Washington, where “multiple Antifa insurgents were convicted on federal conspiracy charges for their roles in a violent attack at [an] ICE facility”, to Newark, New Jersey, where “Antifa thugs violently laid siege” to an immigrant detention center, “resulting in dozens of arrests and federal charges”. For the record, the Spokane protestersblocked an ICE van. The New Jersey public defender hasfileda motion to dismiss the charges against 40 protesters, which “contain nearly identical, generalized allegations and fail to identify the specific conduct attributed to each individual”.It makes sense that an administration that criminalizes immigration and sends federal agents to detain and deport law-abiding gardeners, shopkeepers, mothers and toddlers will use the same tactics to suppress protest against that brutality. A carceral system that locks up millions and imposes extraordinarilyharshsentences functions in concert with these enforcement tactics to intimidate would-be dissenters and punish those who openly dissent.The charges often don’t stick. TheNew York Timesreviewed hundreds of cases involving charges of assaulting or impeding federal immigration officers and found that most of them unraveled, due to federal agents’ “extensive misconduct”, from “attacking protesters” to “misrepresenting facts in court”.But when they stick, the damage can be devastating. Case in point: thetrial and convictionof nine participants in a 4 July 2025, action outside ICE’s Prairieland detention facility in Alvarado, Texas. Some brought guns, which is legal in Texas. Benjamin Song fired at a police officer – he said he aimed at the ground – who was injured. Others scrawled graffiti on cars and shot off fireworks.View image in fullscreenProtesters hold up signs with faces of Prairieland defendants outside of the Eldon B Mahon US courthouse in Fort Worth, Texas, on 1 July.Photograph: The Dallas Morning News/Hearst Newspapers/GettyImagesSong was convicted of attempted murder, the other eight on charges of riot and explosives (the fireworks) and material support for terrorism; the prosecutionpresented a claimthat their black clothing and use of Signal are antifa tactics. Daniel Sanchez-Estrada, who was not there,was convictedof conspiracy to conceal documents for moving a box of zines.The prisonsentencesthey received wereextremeby any measure: 100 years for Song, 30 for Sanchez-Estrada; 50 to 70 years for the others. The justice department proudly broadcast the total:450 yearsfor a “terrorist attack” on an ICE facility. The woman who attempted to assassinate supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh goteight years.By comparison, between 1941 and 1957 hundreds of communists and others were prosecuted under theSmith Act, which made it a crime to “advocate, abet, advise or teach the … desirability or propriety of overthrowing the Government of the United States or of any State by force or violence” – all constitutionally protected speech. Eleven leaders of the Communist party convicted in onemajor trialwere sentenced to three to five years.Techno-surveillanceAt the counter-terrorism summit, Millerdescribedefforts to “disrupt, identify, defund, debank, arrest and prosecute these political terrorists that are operating in our country”. Aided by technology and undeterred by watchdogs, they can do it.View image in fullscreenStephen Miller speaks during a ministerial meeting on political violence at the state department in Washington DC on 16 July.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersMcCarthy relied on wiretapping, spies, informants and human bureaucrats digging through paper files to identify his targets. He managed to find thousands. But late 21st-century technology, including artificial intelligence, which enables the state to conduct surveillance on millions andcollate datafrom government agencies at all levels, makes Hoover’s witch-hunt look like a game of hide-and-seek.The examples are myriad. ICE has anew $25m-a-year contractwith a subsidiary of thedata brokerThomson Reuters to provide “continuous monitoring” of such things as potential government fraud and the arrival of unaccompanied immigrant minors. It also does “academic risk flagging”, whatever that is.The agriculture department has contracted withPalantirto provide an AI-empowered return-to-office tracking tool, whichcriticssaycan be used for other kinds of employee surveillance. The White House has mandated the installation of an app on federal workers’ phones that “gives all Americans direct access” to administration news alerts, social media posts and policy announcements. A “text President Trump” option pre-populates a message praising him. What happens to the worker who wants to criticize him?Police are using surveillance tech to stalk love interests. Dystopia, here we come | Arwa MahdawiRead moreThose antiterrorist visa restrictions are determined through theideological vettingof travelers bypulling social media contentinto government databases using AI-powered monitoring tools; the process continues after the person enters the country.Trump’s friendly relationswith tech companies that amass mountains of customer data constitute an incalculable asset to the repressive regime.Submissive WashingtonOn 2 December 1954, the Senate, led by three Republicans,censuredJoe McCarthy. Its resolution described the senator’s hunt for suspected communists in the federal government as “contrary to senatorial traditions”. Quaint as that sounds, it initiated his undoing. Throughout the 1950s, Chief Justice Earl Warren’s supreme court dismantled the tools of McCarthyism piece by piece,fortifyingthe fifth amendment against self-incrimination andreining inCongress’s power to call witnesses when testifying would “unjustifiably” abridge their right to privacy or “liberty of speech, press, religion or assembly”.Now, cowed by their vengeful and fickle commander-in-chief, the Republican Congress has relinquished its powers – of appropriation and regulation, declaration of war or removal of a corrupt, incompetent or emotionally unstable president. While the lower federal judiciary has ruled frequently against Trump, the supreme court’s majority has upheld the president’s prerogative to reshape the federal government according to his whim. The recentrulingthat allowed his no-cause dismissal of the Federal Trade commissioner Rebecca Slaughter – andoverturneda 91-year-old decision limiting such executive authority – reverberates throughout the federal workforce, politicizing the public sector and reopening the door to the ruinous inquests of the McCarthy era.What will be the next frontier of political repression? Will the postal inspector be deputized to open packages in search of abortion pills bound for red states? Will Trump send ICE or the national guard to intimidate voters at the polls?A president without a moral compass and advisers whose true north is the extreme right, helming a government with unparalleled legal, technological and financial resources, can implement a regime of political repression that Joe McCarthy – or even Big Brother – could not have dreamt of.Judith Levine is a Brooklyn-based journalist and frequent contributor to the Guardian. title: I study the boreal forest. This summer wildfires came for my home | Julee Boan | The Guardian
description: Here are things that will – and will not – help us fight the threat of wildfires
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Here are things that will – and will not – help us fight the threat of wildfires
Content: ‘The smoke is telling us where the real work is. It is at our doorsteps.’Photograph: Emma Da Silva/APView image in fullscreen‘The smoke is telling us where the real work is. It is at our doorsteps.’Photograph: Emma Da Silva/APOpinionClimate crisisI study the boreal forest. This summer wildfires came for my homeJulee BoanHere are things that will – and will not – help us fight the threat of wildfiresFri 31 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 13.55 EDTShareIhave spent much of my career studying boreal forests and I know fire is part of how they renew themselves. That knowledge did nothing for the lump in my throat last week as wildfires closed in on my community in northwestern Ontario.Over 150 fires were burning in the region almost at once, displacing at least 1,800 people from more than a dozen communities, most of them Indigenous. Namaygoosisagagun First Nation burned to the ground, its residents narrowly escaping by boat.Thunder Bay, the regional hub for evacuees, ran out of hotel rooms. The Red Cross arrived to set up cots in hockey arenas. Living rurally just northwest of Thunder Bay, I joined my neighbors to watch the sky turn black and wondered how quickly we could move our livestock. If even breathing was extremely hazardous, with toxic air readings beyond the scales used to report them, where would we be safe?As the smoke drifted south, the loudestresponse from the Trump administrationwas a threat to sanction Canadian officials until these forests are “cleaned up”. But there is no “raking” our way out of this problem. We are living in a new era of fire where smoke is reshaping air‑quality across Canada and the United States.Yet this future is not hopeless. We can lower the threats to communities and to our lungs. In looking for answers and solutions, our best path lies in addressing three things we keep refusing to face.The first is to acknowledge that climate change has almost certainly made extreme fire weather — the hot, dry, windy conditions that allow fires to ignite and spread — more common and more intense in many parts of the world.Northern Ontario hit a record 40 degrees Celsius, that’s 104 degrees Fahrenheit, this summer after weeks with almost no rain. This is a part of the world where few, until recently, owned air conditioners. Add a series of “dry” thunderstorms — minimal rain but abundant lightning — and high winds, and our region ignited almost at once. Under these conditions, Trump is pointing his finger in the wrong direction.The United States emits roughly 6 billion tons of greenhouse gases a year. Astudy published in Naturethis spring put the global economic damage from US emissions since 1990 at $10tn, with a quarter of those losses inside the United States itself.The Trump administration is also actively working to make the climate crisis worse, taking at least 97 actions that weaken or eliminate curbs on carbon pollution or undercut the USA’s ability to cope with the consequences. This ranges from gutting tailpipe pollution standards to rolling back the phase down of climate super pollutants used in refrigeration. For an administration glib about the genuine risks from a changing climate, the smoke crossing our shared border is not an export. It is a receipt.Canada has also been recently downplaying the impacts of expanding oil and gas exports, putting short term gains over long term costs. Our per‑capita greenhouse‑gas emissions are roughly three times the world average, yet, federal and provincial governments have made several recent commitments to new pipelines that, if built, will further increase our emissions.The second is to acknowledge what is and isn’t within our control when it comes to managing forests. Everyone who lives or works in the boreal knows that humility is required. It stretches across roughly 750 million acres — more than 400 million soccer fields — and its sheer scale lays clear that we will never engineer our way out of fire.But that doesn’t mean forest management is irrelevant. In forests near communities, management can focus on planting swaths of deciduous trees – natural speed bumps for fire – and clearing brush and thinning dense stands around homes and evacuation routes.Intensive management in these near-community forests could help to slow fires down and give people more time in wildfire emergencies. In forests far from communities, there can be opportunities to rebuild the forest’s natural resilience by enhancing tree diversity with more fire resistant species, protecting areas least likely to sustain high‑intensity fire, and supporting Indigenous nations whose cultural burning practices have shaped these landscapes for millennia.These actions won’t stop all fires, nor would we want them to as fire is a necessary part of forest renewal, but they can help to shape where forests burn and how much smoke reaches the places where people live.The third is that, while the fires grow across Canada and the US, governments on both sides of the border need to do more preparing and less reacting. In Canada, Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s government has beencriticizedover its insufficient wildfire budgets, forcing emergency overspending, limiting preparedness, and contributing to slow or insufficient support for vulnerable communities — especially First Nations.In 2026, his government allocated $150m to wildland firefighting, far short of the $271m it actually spent responding to last year’s fires.While Ford claims that his government “won’t spare a penny” fighting fires now, firefighters have described logistical failures — too few helicopters, delayed resource acquisition, and inability to act preemptively — all tied to inadequateupfrontfunding.On the US side, the Trump Administration is dismantling the very public agencies Americans need to study and mitigate wildfires and instead investing in industrial activities that worsen the problem.The US Forest Service lost nearly 6,000 employees in 2025, about 16% of its workforce, according to the USDA’s inspector general. Its latest budget request would cut the agency’s discretionary funding by roughly 75% and eliminate major firefighting programs.The agency plans to close 57 of its 77 research facilities, the source of much research on how homes ignite and forests respond to a hotter world. Fewer firefighters, fewer scientists, more smoke. That is a choice, and it is the wrong one at the worst moment.When the rain finally came to our region, small as it was, people danced with relief. For the moment, some respite is here and the rebuilding will soon begin. But every year more communities, everywhere, are impacted. We must do more. Prepare our communities, cut the emissions, fund the people who fight and study these fires. The smoke is telling us where the real work is. It is at our doorsteps, and in our climate policy, not deep in the woods.Julee Boan is Partnerships Director, Global Nature, International, at the Natural Resources Defense CouncilExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionNatural disasterscommentShareReuse this content

title: Sydney, you were a dream of warmth and ease. When I returned to wintry Melbourne, time collapsed – and the city was still romantic | Brigid Delaney | The Guardian
description: A few years after graduating, I moved north and got lucky. It was like riding a smooth, perfect wave that would never hit the shore …
Author: Brigid Delaney
Headline: A few years after graduating, I moved north and got lucky. It was like riding a smooth, perfect wave that would never hit the shore …
Content: ‘Sydney – particularly in 2001 in its post-Olympics glow – was easy to fall in love with,’ Brigid Delaney writes.Photograph: Mark Evans/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Sydney – particularly in 2001 in its post-Olympics glow – was easy to fall in love with,’ Brigid Delaney writes.Photograph: Mark Evans/Getty ImagesOpinionSydneySydney, you were a dream of warmth and ease. When I returned to wintry Melbourne, time collapsed – and the city was still romanticBrigid DelaneyA few years after graduating, I moved north and got lucky. It was like riding a smooth, perfect wave that would never hit the shoreFri 31 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 11.01 EDTShareIwent to a wedding in Sydney when I was 12, arriving from the gloomy and windswept south-west coast ofVictoria, and even though it was only two days I never forgot it. First time on a plane, first time eating poached salmon, first time realising people could actually live like this, drenched in sunlight, homes right on the cliffs, goldilocks weather where you could be in the ocean before work and on weekends go sailing.2001A few years after graduating, I moved north. I found a six-week sublet at an apartment in Paddington with a stranger and a job in recruiting, and thought I’d give my dream a shot.Late summer and the air was warm and fragrant. In the dusk it would crackle with electricity and sudden, almost violent storms. The footpaths of Paddington were covered in skin-soft frangipani blossoms, like a wedding procession had just passed through, and the trees were full of strange, loud, colourful birds that we didn’t have down south.Sydney – particularly in 2001 in its post-Olympics glow – was easy to fall in love with. I adored it all over again.Could I endure a frigid Canberra winter? Not in my wildest, electric dreams | Brigid DelaneyRead moreI presumed the sublet would be some featureless box but it was gorgeous – art deco with dark wood, and charming, strange-shaped rooms, looking out on to an enormous gum tree.My new housemate was a formal young man in his early 20s. While I was dozing off on my first evening he came home from work, into my room and loomed above me in a dark suit, leaning on the handle of an expensive-looking umbrella, before sticking out a hand and introducing himself. Patrick.We drank heavily at the Paddington Inn, spent all our money on imported Iranian seedless grapes at an upmarket grocer and made plans to one day make this six-week housemate arrangement more permanent.I had got lucky. Circles of friends expanded to include me. It didn’t matter that I had a job in recruiting that was hard to explain and boring, or that I went to parties with only the thinnest connection to anyone there. Along with the pleasant climate, an entire experience of ease was beginning to characterise my time in Sydney. It was all my 12-year-old self had dreamed of.I stayed in Sydney, moving to Redfern. Summer gave way to the mildest of winters. The ease – the luck – continued. I sat an exam and did a range of interviews, and landed a highly sought-after position at Sydney Morning Herald as a trainee journalist. I met people there who would become lifelong friends. I found a vocation that would, in one form or another, stay with me for the rest of my life. And over the years in Sydney I also got lucky with houses (I even moved in with Patrick again, to a place in Potts Point). The homes were mostly by the water, in the east. And they were mostly cheap. When I had years of living precariously as a freelancer, or focused on writing books, somehow the city took care of me.This luck – the ease – continued for such a long stretch that I thought it wouldn’t end, like riding a smooth, perfect wave that would never hit the shore.double quotation markOn still nights I could smell the salt and hear the water and the shouts from party boats. The next day small bags containing cocaine residue would wash up in the poolThis year I realised with a jolt that it had been 25 years since that first night in Paddington. It wasn’t totally unbroken. I had stints in Canberra,Melbourne, London, Berlin, Castlemaine and New York. But I always came back. If things didn’t work out in other places or I was spat out, Sydney was a bath that was always warm, that was always beckoning me to sink back in.But when I booked a removalist and packed up the truck to head back down the Hume in June, the break felt different. The perfect wave had finally hit the shore, the bathwater had gone cold, the dream run had ended. It was over.Joan Didion in her farewell letter to New York, Goodbye to All That, wrote: “It is easy to see the beginnings of things, and harder to see the ends.”But Icouldsee the end of my time in Sydney. It had arrived abruptly at dinner one night three months ago, at a friend’s house in Bronte. It was Holy Thursday and the email came in the middle of the meal. It was an official document on a government letterhead and forwarded by my real estate agent. Three months notice to vacate. I was being turfed. The owners wanted to move back in.View image in fullscreen‘I was being let in on a Sydney secret.’Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianIn 2026 can you be a freelance writer, living on one income, who is renting in a walkable Sydney neighbourhood? Not any more.I looked around for new places but they were $200, $300, $400 a week more expensive than what I was paying. People told me the deal I’d had for the last five years was ridic, unreal, stuck in Covid-era pricing. I had not been in sync with the market and now I was.Wake up! Wake up! The dream is over.2021When I first saw the apartment it had been empty for a while and the owners were prepared to drop the price. I moved in the day Sydney locked down for the second time.The building was art deco with a charming row of letterboxes, a board with residents’ names and an attractive, sparkling foyer. The apartment itself had huge ceilings, thick walls, timber floorboards, an impractical bachelor’s kitchen with an ancient Kooka gas stove and tiles with native Australian animals. The building sat on the water’s edge, and a long window in the lounge room looked directly on to Sydney Harbour.But the jewel in the crown of this apartment building was the harbour swimming pool.What would our lives look like if we no longer had to work? As a thought experiment I tried to imagine | Brigid DelaneyRead moreThe real estate agent had mentioned it as an afterthought – “Oh, there’s a harbour pool” – but it wound up being the prime attraction.I never even knew such a thing was possible, for buildings to have their own private harbour pools, but apparently there are 78 of them dotted around the harbour.I loved living so close to the water. On still nights I could smell the salt and hear the water and the shouts from party boats. The next day small bags containing cocaine residue would wash up in the pool.Some days friends would come over and we’d sit on a blanket, feet hanging off the harbour wall, drinking wine and watching golden hour.Other mornings we got the paddleboard out and puttered around the bay. It was as though I was being let in on a Sydney secret. A whole new way of being in the city opened up.The first two years, and the last year of my time in that apartment, I was a freelancer who worked from home (the years in between I worked in politics and moved between Sydney and Canberra, depending on sitting weeks).Much of this freelance time, it felt as though I had won the lottery and retired, seeing out my days in this gorgeous resort, hanging out in the garden and in the pool, wandering down to the marina in Beare Park for coffee. Despite being quite broke in those shoulder years, living article by article, my lifestyle was of the super-rich. Idle hours – there I’d be at 2pm on sunny days, with a book and ice rattling around my cold-brew coffee in a glass tumbler.double quotation markBy 2025 I had stopped feeling that the harbourside dream on a writer’s income was still possible … I had snuck in through the palace gates and was on borrowed timeThe area, including Potts Point and Kings Cross, had long been the home of writers and artists because of cheaper, smaller apartments, including lots of studios and one-bedroom places. By my last year there, things were changing.Small apartments were being torn down to create large luxury apartment blocks, with a Potts Point Preservation Group report highlighting six current or proposed redevelopments in Potts Point, Elizabeth Bay and Rushcutters Bay thatwould reduce the 209 existing apartments to just 85– a 58% net loss of housing stock.As I walked each day to the marina, the streets were increasingly filled with cranes and gaping holes where entire apartment blocks had once been. In their place, new blocks promised luxury living with house-sized floor space. Where would all the old residents go? Who could afford to live here except for the mega-rich?View image in fullscreen‘As I stepped out, walking across the intersection … I suddenly felt a peculiar, not-unpleasant sensation.’Photograph: EschCollection/Getty ImagesIt’s an old Sydney story that property is destiny – but destiny goes two ways. It can welcome you into the dream (you are 12 taking your first bite of poached salmon in Cammeray and realising that this could be your adult life) or throw you out of it.By 2025 I had stopped feeling that the harbourside dream on a writer’s income was still possible in these traditionally bohemian pockets of Sydney and instead started to feel as though I had snuck in through the palace gates and was on borrowed time.And Iwas.Iwas born in Melbourne and spent my formative years – 18 to 24 – in the city in the 90s. Because I was young, those years seemed longer and more densely packed than the almost six years that have just passed in Elizabeth Bay. They were also some of the best years of my life. The city may have been ostensibly struggling then (there was an economic depression and a heroin epidemic) but, if you were very young, the edginess was the point. Everything was romantic.In those years we were obsessed with the photographs of Bill Henson. We could see ourselves and our city in them; moody winter light, enormous clouds tinged with gold, industrial landscapes, being young and in the darkness, merging with it somehow.Now – decades later – in my first week back in Melbourne, I stayed with a former housemate from those years. She dropped me off at the station one morning on her way to the school run and I took the train to Flinders Street.It was a still, foggy, grey morning and, as I stepped out, walking across the intersection through thin blades of cold, gold light, I suddenly felt a peculiar, not-unpleasant sensation. It was of time collapsing. The Sydney years were a dream and I was back there in the 90s, my friend, the station, the winter gloom, nothing changed – and everything was still romantic.The time in between vanished like a spire in the fog, like a figure in a Henson portrait who disappears into the darkness at the centre of the frame. The sensation was vertiginous.I was home. I had never left. The swimming pools, and bags of Iranian seedless grapes, and the schooners of beer at the Paddington Inn, and the nights on the 27th floor of the Sydney Morning Herald, watching the Balmain ferry pull into Darling Harbour, and the lockdown days swimming in the harbour pool, and all the books I wrote in that apartment, all those nights being lulled to sleep by the creak of boats by my window, seemed to have happened to a different person.It was a dream, imagined by a 12-year-old girl.Brigid Delaney is the author of five books, including The Seeker and the Sage.
