title: Will Burnham fix our barbaric prisons – or cave to rightwing populism? The answer is a tragedy | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: England and Wales’s prisons are overcrowded, drug-infested and barbaric. Labour has halted a once-in-a-generation effort to change that sorry state, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: England and Wales’s prisons are overcrowded, drug-infested and barbaric. Labour has halted a once-in-a-generation effort to change that sorry state, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: Prisoners in Pentonville prison being released early in September 2024, as part of the attempt to tackle overcrowding issues.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenPrisoners in Pentonville prison being released early in September 2024, as part of the attempt to tackle overcrowding issues.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAOpinionPrisons and probationWill Burnham fix our barbaric prisons – or cave to rightwing populism? The answer is a tragedySimon JenkinsEngland and Wales’s prisons are overcrowded, drug-infested and barbaric. Labour has halted a once-in-a-generation effort to change that sorry stateFri 31 Jul 2026 06.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.18 EDTShareAndy Burnham’s“pausing”of the Starmer government’s prisoner release scheme and theresignation of its architect, James Timpson, are disasters. They indicate a Downing Street that puts populism ahead of policy. England and Wales’s prisons are a total disgrace. Timpson was the first justice minister in 15 years prepared to handle them. Now he has gone. Although he said it had been an “honour” to serve in the government, it is reasonable to assume he resigned in disgust.InAugust 2024, the prison population in England and Wales hit a record high. The following March, a savagereport from the public accounts committeewarned that prisons, already full to bursting, could not cope with such numbers and would overflow by the start of 2026.Theearly release of 16,000 prisoners in the last three months of 2024eased pressure on the system, but now another crisis is forecast for this November. Under Timpson’s law passed in January, a surge in electronic tagging was being frantically prepared for another bout of early releases in September. But pressure fromprobation unions, parliamentary opponents and victim groups, backed by the rightwing press, has persuaded Burnham to call a halt.Chaos beckons.Victims of crime may deserve sympathy and support, but they should not dictate justice policy.Kemi Badenoch, meanwhile, should not do anything but apologise for her party in government reducing prisons to their current state.The facts cannot be repeated too often. England and Wales’s penal policy is the most backward in western Europe. They imprisonroughly twice the proportion of the population as Germany, and three times as many as Italy and Spain. Prisoner numbers in England and Wales havedoubled in 30 years.In 2024, a quarter of prisoners in England and Wales were having toshare cells designed for one person. Two-thirds were estimated to spend most of their days in their cells with little to occupy them, fuelling reports from prisoners of mental health problems and self-harm. In the 21st century, this is indefensibly primitive.Prisoners are some of the nation’s most assiduous consumers of drugs. About 40% of prisoners in England and Wales say it iseasy to access drugs while inside, cells are simplyawash in illegal substances. As for training and rehabilitation to prepare for release, curbed budgets and staff shortages have seen them collapsing.Half of short-term prisoners reoffendas a result. Rehabilitation – the one sure way to cut reoffending – is a farce. Community sentences such as Timpson’s favouredintensive supervision courtsoffer an alternative but are still in their infancy.As for England and Wales’s fixation with incarcerating women, in December 2024, aquarter of thosein prison were on remand, awaiting what might not have been imprisonment at all. Most need help, not separation from their families and loved ones, with many said to be victims of worse crimes than they commit. The Prison Reform Trust has pleaded for sentences totake account of family stability, but to no effect. Even Reform UK’sColin Sutton, the new police and crime commissioner for Norfolk, has said most women in custody should be released.To allow prisons policy to be led by public opinion is absurd. It should be led by evidence of what works. Manynon-violent prisoners will be drug and alcohol addictschronically in need of effective treatment in the community. There are also the kind of prisoners I used to visit prisons in the London area. They are victims of family or personal breakdown, poverty, homelessness or sheer misfortune. Above all they needed hostels and help.Nothing more infuriates the pro-prisons lobby than mention of Norway. The reason is thatNorway’s prisons work. In the 1990s, the country suffered a dire 70% recidivism rate. It examined evidence and opted for drastic reform. This tied new “correction centres” to local communities, relating rehabilitation to local jobs and family ties. Prisoners were treated with dignity. Reoffending plummeted and Norway’s prison population has been drastically reduced.The late Ann Widdecombe, a former Tory prisons minister, boldly went to Norway in 2020 with a television crew to see what she calledThe World’s Most Luxurious Prison.She called it a holiday camp. She admitted it “worked” but was appalled at the absence of what she regarded as penal retribution. Loss of liberty was combined with a total lack of humiliation.Nothing more typified the British approach to social policy than Widdecombe’s reaction. Foreigners must be wrong, even if she could not explain why. To her, as to many of her compatriots, the survival of our Dickensian prisons embodied justice. Their harshness was an appropriate response to crime. Even if they did not “work”, they must be right.A liberal society must be able to look abroad, examine evidence and be open to reform. Even in the prison-loving US, states from Texas to Oregon and North Dakota have visited Norway and are professing tolearn from it.They know it makes no sense to imprison but not rehabilitate.Our justice policy is crippled by changes of leadership. Catherine McKinnell, appointed as Timpson’s replacement, is the 13th prison minister in the past decade – a ludicrous number, as if it was a hobby rather than a job. Policy is left at the mercy of rightwing sentiment, fed by victims groups and the press. They are now joined by the prime minister. Beware the autumn.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsPrisons and probationOpinionUK criminal justiceLabourJames TimpsonAndy BurnhamCrimecommentShareReuse this content

title: The Burnham bounce is eclipsing the Green surge – and Zack Polanski’s radical hope is being tested | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: The new PM is enjoying a honeymoon period but the Greens have the freedom to say whatever Labour won’t, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: The new PM is enjoying a honeymoon period but the Greens have the freedom to say whatever Labour won’t, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Zack Polanski, leader of the Green party, 10 July 2026Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/LNPView image in fullscreenZack Polanski, leader of the Green party, 10 July 2026Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/LNPOpinionGreen partyThe Burnham bounce is eclipsing the Green surge – and Zack Polanski’s radical hope is being testedGaby HinsliffThe new PM is enjoying a honeymoon period but, longer-term, the Greens have the freedom to say whatever Labour won’tFri 31 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 03.11 EDTShareCackling happily into their pints, the two most powerful men in the country scoff their way through a selection of pub snacks.Pork scratchings or scampi fries? Or maybe old-school peanuts? It’s hardly the toughest choice currently facing Andy Burnham andthechancellor, John Healey, so some may find this week’s made-to-go-viral Instagram reel of themgleefully ranking crispsa bit silly. (I’m writing this, laptop balanced on my knee, beside a hospital bed; right now I couldn’t care less whether the chancellor likes bacon fries.) But I do care, intensely, about a government that ispromising once-in-a-generation reform of care for elderly peoplewinning the public’s confidence for long enough to actually carry out that promise, and weirdly in 2026 that means chomping crisps on camera to establish your bona fides with people who’d scroll straight past conventional political content.Pulling off this kind of freewheeling, seemingly casual content actually takes surprising skill, as the compulsively online Green leader, Zack Polanski – until now the reigning king of leftwing British TikTok – has just inadvertently demonstrated. On Wednesday, the policecleared Polanski of any wrongdoingover reposting a picture of a man in a T-shirt emblazoned with a guillotine and the words, “We’re only making plans for Nigel”. (Polanski says it was among a bunch of images he uploaded without looking properly first, and he deleted it as soon as he realised.) An innocent mistake but a sloppy one, coming days after the alleged murder of the Reform spokeswoman Ann Widdecombe; the kind he can no longer afford to make too often.The unexpected resurgence of hope, joy and radical energy in the Labour party over the last week and a half poses an unmistakable threat to the leader who until now has had a virtual monopoly on those things. Hardened Green voters – those for whom Burnham’s “business-friendly socialism” will never be socialist enough, or who see the new prime minister’s support for more drilling in the North Sea as environmental vandalism – are going nowhere. But newcomers who migrated to the Greens because they felt Keir Starmer’s government had lost its moral compass, or become too relentlessly miserable, are now squarely in Burnham’s sights. Interestingly, the More in Common poll this week, whichput Labour back in the leadfor the first time since last March, found that “Burnham bounce” coming if anything more at the Greens’ expense than Reform’s.When the new prime ministerapologisesfor the way his predecessor approached the Gaza war, orcondemnswhat he calls 40 failed years of neoliberalism, he’s signalling that it’s safe for those lost Labour voters to come home. When he’s messing about on Instagram, he’s reaching out to younger people unused to seeing Labour politicians doing anything interesting on Green-dominated feeds. And when heholds cross-party talkson fixing social carewithout either Polanski or Farage, then intentionally or not, he is sending a message about who he takes seriously. Polanski,whose partner works in palliative care, has spoken movingly about the issue. But it was only the Lib Dems and the Tories, Downing Street says, who actually wrote to the prime minister expressing interest in his call for a non-partisan approach to this difficult issue.It would be ridiculous, of course, to think this Labour honeymoon can last. Keir Starmer was popular, right up until his first spending cut.The Green surgemay be receding for the moment but it’s only five months since they left Labour for dust in theGorton and Denton byelection, and it would be a surprise if they don’t at least improve on their 2024 performance in this week’s Manchester mayoral elections.Yet something has clearly shifted. As recently as early May, 22% of Britons thought Polanski would be a better prime minister than Starmer, according to YouGov. Butonly 9% now prefer him to Burnham. The guillotine T-shirt affair, meanwhile, was merely the latest in a string of mistakes – from Polanski’sfailure to register to votein May’s local elections, toconfusion over whether he paid enough council taxwhile living on a houseboat in London, to a spate ofantisemitism allegationsinvolving Green candidates at the local elections – that together raise questions about Polanski’s readiness for the remorseless scrutiny that wannabe main parties of the left inevitably face.The Greens’ defence is to argue that only they can offer a “full fat” socialist revolution, not some watered down Burnhamite version. If he won’t imposerent controlsor newproperty taxes– both ideas circulating around the sprawling Burnham camp that have died an unceremonious death since he entered Downing Street – then they will. Unconstrained by the realities of government, their freedom to say whatever Labour won’t could easily become a powerful weapon again given time and the inevitable disappointments of office, though it’s unclear how much time Burnham intends to give them. (He has publiclyruled out a snap election, but the current strategy – a blitzkrieg of exciting but vague announcements, starving Reform and the Greens of political oxygen but without giving them much to fight him on – wouldn’t half be good preparation for one.)But for the next few weeks at least, it’s Burnham on whom the fickle political sun shines: Burnham who has the priceless opportunity to actuallydosomething about what ails the country, rather than simply talk – however fluently or winningly – about it. Political careers, as he should know, are notoriously short these days. He should make the most of every moment while it lasts.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsGreen partyOpinionZack PolanskiAndy BurnhamSocialismcommentShareReuse this content

title: Think our basic rights are safe? In the age of oligarchs and corporate lobbying, think again | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: The global assault on our freedoms is coming ever closer to home. Just look at the sinister prosecution of UK lawyer Rajiv Menon, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: The global assault on our freedoms is coming ever closer to home. Just look at the sinister prosecution of UK lawyer Rajiv Menon, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Illustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianOpinionLawThink our basic rights are safe? In the age of oligarchs and corporate lobbying, think againGeorge MonbiotThe global assault on our freedoms is coming ever closer to home. Just look at the sinister prosecution of UK lawyer Rajiv MenonFri 31 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 03.11 EDTShareNo more resistance in the US. The era of human rights is over, and dissent is once more forbidden. This is what certain billionaires and their concierges want, and this is the model they’re also seeking to project across the world. If we fail to resist, if our new prime minister is as weak and suggestible as the last one, this is what we will get. In fact, we are halfway there already.Why? Because successive governments in the UK have succumbed to a global campaign to cancel our fundamental freedoms, a campaign led by oligarchs and corporations, the media they own and the junktanks they fund. A campaign that has become definitional for the second Trump presidency.At aglobal summitconvened by the US government earlier this month, the Trump administration officials Marco Rubio, Stephen Miller and Scott Bessent explained that they were redirecting counterterrorism efforts away from Islamic jihadism and towards “the political left”. Most of the examples they cited to justify this shift were more than 30 years old. Several times they had to dig down to the 1970s to find a sufficiently menacing threat. You could hear the barrel being scraped.Without producing a shred of evidence, Rubio, the secretary of state, claimed that the Cuban government is “inextricably linked to the far-left groups and movements across and beyond the west”. The following week, his department sought to justify this claimwith a reportcontaining a long list of leftwing legislators, journalists and activists that attempted tolink them to Cubain ways that ranged from the tenuous to the hilarious. This is a well-honed tactic, used prolificallyby the Nazisamong others: they claimed dissenters, by definition, were part of an international communist conspiracy. They insisted, as Rubio did, that “it is time to crush this evil for ever”.That wasn’t the only crude reminder. Miller, Donald Trump’s deputy chief of staff, maintained that when you see antifascist protests, “not one of the people that is demonstrating looks like a normal person. Not one looks normal. They’re all deformed in some way – in their appearance, in their dress, in their mannerism … their outer appearance becomes a manifestation of their inner hatred.” I’m just surprised he didn’t say “untermenschen”. The US government, by contrast, promotes “normal, healthy, ordered living”.But what hit me even harder was Miller’s attack on “jury nullification”: jurors acquitting people who, he said, were “obviously guilty”. Shutting down this possibility has been an aim of illiberal governments and conservative judges around the world. We saw it in the UK in theprosecution of Trudi Warnerand others for holding signs that state an ancient principle in English law: “Jurors have an absolute right to acquit a defendant according to their conscience.”View image in fullscreenRajiv Menon KC, who is facing prosecution for contempt of court.Photograph: Garden Court ChambersWe see it in theastonishing prosecution, being pursued at the moment, of Rajiv Menon KC, who reminded jurors of this right at the trial of the Palestine Action campaigners he was defending. He became, as a result, the first lawyer in English history to becharged with contempt of courtfor a closing speech. If convicted, he faces up to two years’ imprisonment and will be struck off. Prosecuting lawyers for defending their dissident clients is more or less the definition of authoritarianism.We also saw it in the assault Keir Starmerlaunched on jury trialsas a whole, greatly curtailing, without any coherent justification, our strongest defence against injustice.Starmer was a weak man, without a clear vision of his own, who was rolled by any powerful state or corporate lobby. He was no match for a well-funded and highly effective international campaign. A network of groups such as theAmerican Legislative Exchange Council, funded by corporations and billionaires, has been producing “model legislation”. The groups test these laws in sympathetic jurisdictions. If they are found to work, they then press for their adoption elsewhere. The result is a sustained assault on our rights to protest, to political equality and to ahabitable planet.The globalisation of this attack on our fundamental rights is a key conservative aim. As capital operates everywhere, so should its ability to crush our objections. The long series ofvicious anti-protest lawsin the UK is an outcome of sustained lobbying by junktanks, the media and other governments. The result is a country that now keepshundreds of political prisoners, a country in which you can getsix months in jailfor marching slowly down the street.These oppressive laws have culminated – so far – in an act of parliament passed in April that enables the police to shut down any protestthey deem to havea “cumulative” impact on the community. The only protests that have ever succeeded are those with acumulative impact. Protest is acceptable as long as it’s useless. Let the people have their say, but only if we can’t hear them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne day, your life and future may depend on a jury. The integrity of that legal process is in peril right now | Imran KhanRead moreThe new laws have been accompanied by that age-old trick, traditionally associated with fascist regimes, of smearing leftwing dissidents as terrorists. As the rights groupLiberty has pointed out, the definition of terrorism here has greatly expanded, to incorporate tactics formerly regarded as civil protest. This is what enabled Starmer’s government toban Palestine Action.The judge who referred Menon for contempt, Mr Justice Johnson, was also the first – at the same trial – to use theextraordinary powersquietly inserted by the Conservatives into the Sentencing Act 2020. These enable someone tried for one crime to be sentenced for another. The four Palestine Action protesters were convicted of ordinary crimes. But, without informing the jury, Johnson marked the case as having a “terrorist connection”. He then sentenced them for terrorist offences, which means much more prison time.Already, his example has been followed by another judge: a different group of pro-Palestine protesters, who sprayed red paint and broke some windows of a branch of Barclays Bank, are about to besentenced as terrorists, though neither they nor the jurors were told of this possibility during their trial for criminal damage. This means, of course, that they were unable to defend themselves against this far more serious charge.Nothing is safe from the billionaire assault on humanity. None of our rights, however ancient and familiar, are impregnable. Fight for them now or lose them, perhaps for ever.George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: After teargas, protests and legal strife, Turkey has a new opposition party. Is this the man who can defeat Erdoğan? | Kaya Genç | The Guardian
description: Under Özgür Özel, the CHP became Turkey’s most popular party. Now his Yeni (New) movement is growing fast, says the Istanbul-based novelist Kaya Genç
Author: Kaya Genç
Headline: Under Özgür Özel, the CHP became Turkey’s most popular party. Now his Yeni (New) movement is growing fast, says the Istanbul-based novelist Kaya Genç
Content: Özgür Özel, former leader of Turkey’s CHP opposition party, now leader of the Yeni (New) party, Ankara, 24 July 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenÖzgür Özel, former leader of Turkey’s CHP opposition party, now leader of the Yeni (New) party, Ankara, 24 July 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionTurkeyAfter teargas, protests and legal strife, Turkey has a new opposition party. Is this the man who can defeat Erdoğan?Kaya GençUnder Özgür Özel, the CHP became Turkey’s most popular party. Now his Yeni (New) movement is growing fastFri 31 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 05.15 EDTShareIn May this year, police in Ankara stormed the headquarters of the Republican People’s party (CHP), the oldest political party in Turkey. Officersused teargas to enforcea controversial appeal court decision that reinstated the CHP’s 77-year-old former leader Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu–seen as less of a threat to the ruling Justice and Development party (AKP). CHP members aligned with Kılıçdaroğlu’s successor, Özgür Özel, placed furniture at the building’s entrance, creating a barrier to prevent police from entering. It didn’t work. Hours later, party members loyal to Özel were physically removed from the premises.Entering the offices of Turkey’s leading opposition party in such a fashion was a spectacular act with historic consequences. Last Friday, Özel and 90 CHP deputiesresigned from their partyand declared the founding of the New (Yeni) party. The CHP had served as Turkey’s main opposition since 2002. But not any longer: with the exodus of members to the New party, the CHP is reduced to just 44 legislators in the 600-seat parliament, its third smallest party out of seven.Over the past week, Turkey’s new main opposition, with its 91 legislators, enjoyed strong winds in its sails. Throughout Turkish political history, those who have suffered legal injustices have gone on to benefit from them at the ballot box. In 1999,Recep Tayyip Erdoğanhimself spent four months in prison. Four years later, he was prime minister. If managed well, the ousting of Özel from the CHP will probably boost the popularity of Turkey’s progressives overall.But what of the CHP itself? This is the party MustafaKemal Atatürkfounded in 1923, which played a crucial role in establishing the modern republic of Turkey. In the past 18 months, it has witnessed a stunning reversal of fortunes.At Turkey’s nationwide local elections in March 2024, the CHP was Turkey’smost popular political party. Özel’s leadership engineered that success: the CHP won37.8% of the vote, beating Erdoğan’s AKP on 35.4%. This was the first national election since the AKP’s establishment in 2001 in which it wasn’t the largest party – a decisive moment in Turkish politics and one with worrying implications for Erdoğan in the run-up to 2028’s presidential elections. The CHP victory, on a platform of municipal socialism, has raised the profile of a generation of young, charismatic leftwing mayors who, like Zohran Mamdani in New York, won office in Turkey’s wealthiest and most populous cities: Istanbul, Ankara, İzmir.Their proximity to power must have raised concerns among the country’s ruling elites, who have profited from an economic order that prioritises the construction, defence and tourism industries. Three weeks after he announced his candidacy for the presidential elections, in March last year, Istanbul’s CHP mayor, Ekrem İmamoğlu, wasremoved from office. He has been accused of142 offences, including accepting bribes, unlawfully obtaining personal data, racketeering, leading a criminal organisation, interfering with public tenders and aiding the outlawed Kurdistan Workers’ party (PKK). His charges could lead to 2,430 years behind bars, and it looks extremely unlikely that he will be able to run for president in 2028. Writing inthis newspaper from jaillast September, İmamoğlu claimed Erdoğan was “weaponising the courts against the democratic opposition”. (The government has denied putting pressure on the courts to prosecute CHP mayors.)Since İmamoğlu’s arrest, a different CHP city or district mayor has beenarrested almost every month. One after another, politicians have been sent to jail or threatened with prosecution. Several detained CHP mayors have since been released, including İnan Güney, the suspended mayor of Istanbul’s touristic hub, Beyoğlu.View image in fullscreenA protest against the arrest and imprisonment of then mayor of Istanbul, Ekrem İmamoğlu, 25 March 2025.Photograph: Francisco Seco/APOver time these developments led to apathy among opposition supporters: for months, it felt almost impossible to keep up with CHP’s legal troubles, which dominated the Turkish media.When İmamoğlu was arrested in March 2025, ittriggered nationwide protests, the largest in Turkey in more than a decade. But since then, court cases against the CHP have largely been met with silence. In April, I went tofollow İmamoğlu’s casein a courtroom in Silivri, 83km (52 miles) away from Istanbul’s city centre; I saw no supporters inside or outside the courtroom. The cab driver who took me to the court that day said he wished to see the CHP mayor of Silivri in jail next. While holidaying on Büyükada island off the coast of Istanbul two months later, I heard of theSilivri mayor’s arrest. By the end of June, Büyükada’s CHP mayor had been jailed too.After his reinstatement as party leader, Kılıçdaroğlu implied, in a public statement, that those CHP mayors could indeed be guilty. Likening the CHP to a tree, he said: “The shade of this mighty tree can never, ever be a refuge for the forbidden and the polluted. When necessary, it knows how to purify itself and conduct its inner accounting.” Kılıçdaroğlu’s call for purification has led to fury among opposition supporters, protests and an exodus of party members.Despite the excitement over Özel’s New party, it faces challenges: it lacks CHP’s resources, personnel, history and financial support from Turkey’s treasury. Breakaway parties have often suffered defeat in Turkish politics: the Good party, established in 2017 by disgruntled Turkish nationalists, has little support among the electorate. The Future party and the Democracy and Progress party (DEVA), founded by former AKP leaders in 2019 and 2020, fared poorly in elections, failing to distinguish themselves from the AKP.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI was elected mayor of Istanbul, but I write this from jail: Turkish democracy is under grave threat | Ekrem ImamoğluRead moreThe CHP is a similar colossus, with an unsurpassable brand name in Turkish politics. It is the Republic of Turkey’s founding party, the party of Atatürk, and its history carries a lot of weight.Özel has defined the New party as “social democrat”, and theparty programmeacknowledges Turkey’s different religions, ethnicities and languages. It also references gender and sexual orientation, terms that have become taboo in Turkey in recent years. The New party embraces full membership of the EU and promises to increase Turkey’s role at the Council of Europe and Nato.If Özel can position his party as not just another splinter party but the new CHP, that would be an attractive proposition. A century ago, the CHP implemented a flurry of social, cultural and political reforms across Turkey, from the abolition of the caliphate to significant advancements in women’s rights. In the 1960s and 1970s it found support from students, the underprivileged and the marginalised with its leftist turn.The New party should promise an equally bold and progressive agenda. That way it won’t just emerge as the victor of the 2028 elections but will be in a position to truly transform Turkey.Kaya Genç is a novelist and essayist from Istanbul, and the author ofThe Lion and the Nightingale: A Journey Through Modern TurkeyExplore more on these topicsTurkeyOpinionRecep Tayyip ErdoğanEuropeKemal AtatürkcommentShareReuse this content

title: A man has been found guilty of rape but we can’t say who he is. Why are there exceptions to open justice? | Richard Ackland | The Guardian
description: It is not entirely surprising the ‘well-connected Melbourne businessman’ has so far managed to have his name protected
Author: Richard Ackland
Headline: It is not entirely surprising the ‘well-connected Melbourne businessman’ has so far managed to have his name protected
Content: The accused, who has been found guilty of two counts of rape and one of sexual assault, has been described in news bulletins as a ‘well-connected Melbourne businessman’.Photograph: Dave Hunt/AAPView image in fullscreenThe accused, who has been found guilty of two counts of rape and one of sexual assault, has been described in news bulletins as a ‘well-connected Melbourne businessman’.Photograph: Dave Hunt/AAPOpinionAustralian lawA man has been found guilty of rape but we can’t say who he is. Why are there exceptions to open justice?Richard AcklandIt is not entirely surprising the ‘well-connected Melbourne businessman’ has so far managed to have his name protectedThu 30 Jul 2026 23.11 EDTLast modified on Thu 30 Jul 2026 23.13 EDTShareVictoria has the sorry distinction of being the national capital for court-imposed gag orders.The courts and tribunals of that state issue more than half the tally of suppressions for all the other states and territories combined.A count of these orders is religiously kept by Gina McWilliams, a senior legal counsel at News Corp. Her tally for 2025 totalled 1,226 suppression and no-publication orders Australia-wide.Victoria, including the civil and administrative tribunal, issued 640 – under the ambit of the Orwellian-named Open Courts Act.Raw data doesn’t explain the reason for this. Maybe there are simply more applications of this type south of the Murray than in the rest of the nation, or quite possibly the judges in that jurisdiction are more predisposed to keeping proceedings and identities hidden.Some of that tally would be reduced by subsequent court orders to lift the veil of secrecy – and that would also apply in all the other jurisdictions.It was not entirely surprising that the accused in a high-profileMelbournerape case managed to have his identity protected by a county court suppression order.Well-connected Melbourne man found guilty of raping former stafferRead moreQuite apart from the case attracting attention in the media and elsewhere, the accused himself was also repeatedly described in news bulletins as a “well-connected Melbourne businessman”.On Tuesday a jury found him guilty of two counts of rape and one of sexual assault of a former employee visiting his home. An intention to appeal has been flagged by his lawyers – in fact his defence counsel said that his client has been the subject of a “gross miscarriage of justice” and that there was a prospective application to stay the sentencing.His psychiatrist has given evidence about his mental health. In 2024, after the high-profile individual was charged, she told the court that he had a series of inpatient admissions related to mental distress as a result of being charged and prospectively being identified in the media. A suicide attempt was self-reported.She had been told by her patient: “If I’m guilty, put it on the front page.” Among many in Melbourne his identity is an open secret.Clearly, there are balls in the air that are yet to land. Despite the verdict, the suppression order on his identity remains in place to be revisited in court on Monday, where his lawyers could apply to extend the order.The psychiatrist is expected to give further evidence next week.This could well be a situation where a person is clinging to their business and social standing, which already has been jettisoned.The familiar shibboleth trotted out at judicial conferences is that justice is open, the courts have to be seen to be doing their work, otherwise who knows what monkey business judges might get up to.Yet, like everything else in life, there are exceptions to the rule. Various statutes proclaim that the names of children caught in the cruel machinery of the courts cannot be published, also litigants in family court cases, so too complainants in sexual assault trials, and people afflicted by serious mental health problems.The judges themselves have the power to dish out suppression or non-publication orders for a variety of reasons, broadly swept up in the “administration of justice”. For instance, reporting of proceedings that could prejudice the fairness of other proceedings are generally forbidden.When it comes to the shame of being dealt with by the criminal justice system, former high court justice Michael Kirby has said that personal embarrassment should not be a deciding factor to issue a gag order – open justice must prevail.But it seems exposure, embarrassment and mental health are all closely aligned, requiring great judicial agility to determine the relevant basis for open justice.Swirling speculation also surrounds the identity of a man whose name has been suppressed by a Cairns magistrate. The online gossip mill tells us that the man is a prominent “Queensland figure” and that his identity was used as leverage by another man to extort a former female partner, who may or may not have been closely involved with the unmentionable “Queensland figure”.It sounds too salacious for the wider public to be told anything more, for now.Bruce Lehrmann also got an identity suppression order in relation to two counts of rape before the district court in Toowoomba. His lawyers raised concerns about self-harm if his name was published in connection to the case. His condition was described as potentially “catastrophic”.However, this did not prevent him engaging with the media in self-serving TV interviews and suing Network Ten for defamation.Later, supreme court justice Peter Applegarth upheld a decision to reverse an earlier order protecting his identity.It is not entirely a special area of the law for prominent people who are accused of rape. The Nine newspapers, for example, at the beginning of the year lost a battle for a 50-year suppression order to stop publication of the details of a deed of settlement with a woman who appeared as a witness in the Ben Roberts-Smith defamation case and who accused the former soldier of assaulting her while they were having an affair – something which he denies.Again, the utility of a mainstream media suppression order is rendered meaningless when the secret gems were out there already on the internet.It is one of the curiosities of the law that, after very contained and limited reports of the guilty verdict in the Cardinal Pell trial, major Australian media organisations were being prosecuted for contempt while full details of the jury’s decision were published by major international online news organisations.Members of the legal profession itself are in a rarefied category of judicial protection. In several states and territories misconduct proceedings against lawyers are conducted with their identity anonymised.Quaintly, this is to protect their professional “reputation”. There is one Sydney barrister who “behaved badly” with a young women at a bar dinner and is enjoying an order to hide his name – the duration of which will see out the lifetime of most living newspaper reporters.Court suppression applications can be readily thrown around, a bit like confetti. Due to the sensitivities at stake, the reasons for granting them are often shrouded in mystery. There are so many of them made on a daily basis that the media cannot possibly be on hand with submissions to protect the public interest.Richard Ackland publishesSpilled Inkand the law journalJustinianIn Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.org. In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor.Explore more on these topicsAustralian lawOpinionMelbourneVictoriacommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Change is happening! I can cut off my hair and misbehave’: Vicky Krieps on rage, rebellion, and rejecting Hollywood | Movies | The Guardian
description: After her star turn in Phantom Thread, everyone expected a move to Tinseltown – but the actor embraced indie European films instead. It’s because of a lifelong instinct to be bold, she says
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: After her star turn in Phantom Thread, everyone expected a move to Tinseltown – but the actor embraced indie European films instead. It’s because of a lifelong instinct to be bold, she says
Content: Risky business … Vicky Krieps.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRisky business … Vicky Krieps.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty ImagesMoviesInterview‘Change is happening! I can cut off my hair and misbehave’: Vicky Krieps on rage, rebellion, and rejecting HollywoodFiona SturgesAfter her star turn in Phantom Thread, everyone expected a move to Tinseltown – but the actor embraced indie European films instead. It’s because of a lifelong instinct to be bold, she saysFri 31 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 09.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBack when she was a rising actor, Vicky Krieps had her fill of people telling her what not to do. When she got pregnant in her 20s, she was advised not to have the baby as it would derail her career, but she did it anyway. When, after playing a fashion designer’s muse in Paul Thomas Anderson’sPhantom Thread, she went back to making low-budget French films, she was, she says, “actually laughed at. It just seemed absurd to these people that I would turn my back on Hollywood and invest so much energy and passion in something that wasn’t giving me money.”Yet Krieps’s determination to forge her own path has reaped rewards. For the last decade she has had one foot in the Hollywood mainstream, appearing in Fede Álvarez’s The Girl in the Spider’s Web and M Night Shyamalan’sOld, while keeping the other firmly in independent cinema where she has freedom to experiment. Krieps also does her utmost to avoid the pantomime of red-carpet events. On the occasions she does make an appearance, she will stick out her tongue or give photographers the finger. “I always smile when I’m doing it. But I’m telling them: ‘Guys, this is really ridiculous and the shouting is a bit much. Just talk nicely to me.’”It comes as no surprise to learn that Krieps, 42, who was born and raised in Luxembourg and speaks four languages, has declined to make the obligatory move to Los Angeles. For the past 15 years, she has lived in Berlin – though, when we speak over video call, she is in Greece, which she regularly visits since marrying her husband, the Greek film production assistant Lazaros Gounaridis, last year. (They met on the set of the 2023 film Hot Milk.)Sporting a pixie cut and a crisp white shirt, Krieps is open, thoughtful and speaks with unusual seriousness and candour about her job which, for her, is all-consuming. “Sometimes I feel less like an actor and more like a scientist who is experimenting on my own body,” she says.View image in fullscreenKrieps in Love Me Tender.Photograph: Peccadillo PicturesThis immersive approach can take a toll. Two weeks after wrapping her forthcoming film Love Me Tender, in which she plays a woman who loses custody of her young son, Krieps began feeling “really bad in my body. I was lying on my bed, and I couldn’t move my arms and my neck. I thought I had a serious disease.” She saw doctors and had an MRI, and found everything was fine but the pain itself was real. “I think I had assembled so much psychological pain that it became physical. You know the saying ‘My heart is aching’? I feel that in my whole chest.”Directed by Anna Cazenave Cambet and based on the autobiographical novel by Constance Debré, Love Me Tender challenges the unfair expectations foisted upon mothers. Krieps plays Clémence, who has given up a well-paid legal career to write books. After separating amicably from her husband, Laurent, she gives away most of her belongings, immerses herself in the club scene and explores her sexuality. When she eventually tells Laurent that she is dating women, he appears to accept it. But afterwards, he makes dark allegations about her and questions her mental stability in a bid to secure sole custody of their eight-year-old son, Paul.“Laurent,” says Krieps, “is an example of when the male ego starts to rage because it is hurting and doesn’t understand what is happening. He’s thinking: ‘Why am I not included in this? Why did this train leave without me?’” When “there is no real dialogue between men and women, men like this can become mean, sour and self-righteous”.As their case creaks through the courts, Clémence is denied permission to see Paul. When they finally meet after nearly 18 months apart, it’s for an hour every fortnight under supervision. Those meetings, where Clémence must hold in her grief and keep it together for her son, are devastating. The tension of those scenes, Krieps realised, “caused me to hit a wall. But it was good for me to learn that the next time I work on something like this I will need to look after myself and take longer breaks while filming.”View image in fullscreenCouture club … Krieps with Daniel Day-Lewis in Phantom Thread.Photograph: Focus Features/AllstarKrieps has spent much of her career playing women trying to break out of the boxes that others have put them in. In Phantom Thread, she is Alma, a serving maid who is expected to remain meek in front of Daniel Day-Lewis’s dictatorial dressmaker but instead stands her ground and answers back. In 2022’s terrificCorsage, she is Elisabeth, Empress of Austria, celebrated in the 19th century for her beauty and her tiny waist (made tinier by ruthless corsetry), who rebels against her tightly controlled existence. In Emily Atef’sMore Than Ever, she is a terminally ill woman fighting for the right to live out her days on her own terms.“I talked to Charlotte Rampling about this after we worked on the Jim Jarmusch movieFather Mother Sister Brother,” Krieps reflects. “We realised what we have in common is that we are constantly drawn to exploring the edge of a [character], the place where it starts to hurt. I think I take this to every part.”Where possible, Krieps tries to work with female directors – or rather, she clarifies, directors who preside over “feminine sets. I’ve worked with men where the set was not masculine and there was no male ego. And there are female directors who unfortunately operate with a male ego. A lot of film sets are run like the military and are very hierarchy-driven. It’s incredibly loud and it’s about pushing. But take a director like [Corsage’s] Marie Kreutzer: her set is extremely quiet and calm. No one is shouting. And the positive side to that is when you create silence, you start hearing each other.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPicking apart societal roles and rejecting authority is in Krieps’s blood. Her grandfather was in the resistance during the second world war and survived internment at Dachau. He later became a socialist politician in Luxembourg and successfully mounted a campaign to abolish the death penalty. “Knowing that someone so close almost lost his life to fight for humanity, this is something you can’t forget,” reflects Krieps. Meanwhile, her mother “is just a crazy hippy, in the best way, and raised me to question everything: how do I know this is what they say it is? I think this made me dare to be brave and risk my livelihood.”That daring surfaced when a teenage Krieps attended her school graduation ceremony and thanked her teachers for giving her “proof that I know how to learn off by heart, that I know how to copy and how to shut my mouth”. The incident made the papers in Luxembourg. It is also evident in her habit of tweaking the words and actions of her characters mid-scene. In Corsage, she launched herself out of a window in frustration at her onscreen husband (she emerged unscathed; the scene was filmed on the ground floor). The moment was not in the script but nonetheless made the final cut, with Krieps’s character sustaining a fracture from the fall. “These things are not premeditated but sometimes you just feel something that feels like the truth, and it wants to come out,” Krieps says.True to her straddling of popular and arthouse entertainment, this autumn Krieps can be seen in Ryan Murphy’s series Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story playing the Borden family’s maid Bridget Sullivan. She has also just finished work on Emma Doucet, a film by the French director Élise Girard about a single mother who falls in love with the French prime minister and which, she says, is “close to a poem. It’s very nouvelle vague.”Krieps acknowledges that her questing spirit and single-mindedness as an actor wouldn’t have been possible even 20 years ago. “You wouldn’t have a woman who’s allowed to do all these different movies, and not give a fuck, cut off her hair and generally misbehave. The fact that I exist shows me change is happening and is possible.”Love Me Tender is in UK and Irish cinemas from7August.Explore more on these topicsFilminterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Alien erotica, football coaching and making Meryl Streep cry: Ted Lasso’s new star Tanya Reynolds opens up | Television | The Guardian
description: She lit up screens as Sex Education’s steamy sci-fi writer, wowed Streep in the West End and now she’s starring in the return of TV’s feelgood footie hit. The star talks about pretending to be sporty – and why she’s a total cheese string
Author: Lucinda Everett
Headline: She lit up screens as Sex Education’s steamy sci-fi writer, wowed Streep in the West End and now she’s starring in the return of TV’s feelgood footie hit. The star talks about pretending to be sporty – and why she’s a total cheese string
Content: ‘The thought of me being tough is hilarious’ … Tanya Reynolds, photographed in London for the Guardian.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The thought of me being tough is hilarious’ … Tanya Reynolds, photographed in London for the Guardian.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianTelevisionInterviewAlien erotica, football coaching and making Meryl Streep cry: Ted Lasso’s new star Tanya Reynolds opens upLucinda EverettShe lit up screens as Sex Education’s steamy sci-fi writer, wowed Streep in the West End and now she’s starring in the return of TV’s feelgood footie hit. The  star talks about pretending to be sporty – and why she’s a total cheese stringFri 31 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy the time its third season came to an end in 2023, Ted Lasso was a Big Deal. The cosy comedy about an indefatigably positive American football coach gee-whizzing his way into the hearts of a London football team had won 13 Emmys and racked up more than 25bn minutes ofviewing.Contributing exactly zero minutes to this staggering stat wasTanya Reynolds, who joins the series in its fourth season as Ted’s assistant coach, Alice.“I don’t know where I was!” she tells me with a helpless shrug as we chat. “I mean, I am a bit of a hermit. I do sort of live under a rock, so it’s not surprising I missed it.” She had heard of it, she assures me, and accepted the invitation to audition because it was “so unlike anything I’ve done before. I just was like: ‘Football coach. Mad. Yeah, OK.’” A week after sending her tape and thinking nothing more of it “because I didn’t think it was very good”, Tanya had a Zoom with the show’s co-creator, writer and titular star, Jason Sudeikis, who offered her the part on the spot. She swiftly watched all three seasons and realised “I really want to be part of this world”.She’s speaking from her north London home on a Monday morning – every hermit’s favourite time to meet a prying journalist who is snooping at your background (I spot candles, books – Tanya recommends her favourites on Instagram – and a huge painting of sunflowers, which she swings her camera towards so I can get a better look). In a sleeveless red top, her hair in a scrunchy, Reynolds is blissfully free of media-training gloss – her answers are peppered with pauses and rephrasings (or perhaps they’re just a result of her being a “nervous person”). She is also warm, never far from a face-splitting laugh and, like all self-respecting Brits, mocks herself routinely and expertly.View image in fullscreen‘I am a bit of a hermit. I do sort of live under a rock’ … says Reynolds.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianAs we settle, amid apologies about her whirring washing machine (“I’m hoping it chills out. You know when it goes mental?”), I ask aboutMeryl Streep and Martin Shortcoming to see1536, the play she is starring in when we speak, with Margot Robbie as co-producer.“We’d known they were coming for weeks. We actually graffitied it backstage: MERYL STREEP IS COMING ON THE TENTH!” she says. “We all stood on the stage, lined up like …” she does her best impression of an old-timey family portrait, “and couldn’t speak. But they were so kind … We all cried. Meryl cried. It was lovely.”She adds that “Margot’s input has been huge … It’s so wonderful that someone with that amount of power is championing really important work, new work.” And how beautiful is she in real life, on a scale of one to obscene? Reynolds laughs. “She’s like a painting that’s come to life.”1536 is the latest entry on Reynolds’s impressive theatrical CV, which also includes playing Masha inThe Seagulllast year opposite Cate Blanchett, and being nominated for an Olivier award in 2024 for her performance inA Mirrorat the Almeida. But many will still know her best for her breakout role in Netflix’sSex Educationas Lily Iglehart – the space-bun sporting, cosplaying teen writer of alien erotica (The Trial of Glenoxi: Fucklord of the Universe being one of her efforts). The show proved a hotbed for young talent, with Ncuti Gatwa and Aimee Lou Wood among the cast. “I remember feeling in my very first days: ‘I am in the presence of superstars,’” says Reynolds.View image in fullscreenReynolds with Siena Kelly in 1536.Photograph: Helen MurrayShe has since become a TV fixture, starring in Netflix’s bubonic plague rompThe Decameron, in which she stole the show as wild maid turned “noblewoman” Licisca, and the BBC’sThe Other Bennet Sister, where she played a deliciously disdainful Caroline Bingley (pleaseGoogle the primrose-eating scene). There have been films, too, including Alice Lowe’s era-hopping comedy Timestalker.Encouraged by Lowe, Reynolds wrote her own film,Dog Person, which she will direct (“I’m definitely terrified, for sure”) and star in, alongside Hugh Bonneville and James Norton. “Hopefully” shooting this year, it follows a thirtysomething woman, exhausted by life’s pressures, who “discovers this desire to be a dog”. (As if by magic, her own dog, a shaggy rescue called Borage, pads in at this point, after a trip to the vet).Born in Hemel Hempstead into “not a theatrical family at all” (her Italian dad was a builder and her mum a sign painter – both were “quite quiet and quite shy”), Reynolds decided, aged four “or maybe six”, to be an actor. Where did that come from?“I don’t.Know,”she enunciates. “I was always showing off and I remember my mum saying: ‘You’re brilliant at acting,’ and something in my brain was like: ‘Oh, I’ll do that.’ My parents, even though they we were not even adjacent to that world … never made it seem like it would be hard.” She was the first person in her family to go to university before winning a fully funded scholarship to the Oxford School ofDrama– the only way she could afford to go.Given that she “never had a backup plan”, what does she think about thedecline of drama in schools? “It’s crazy to me that drama’s even on the chopping block of the curriculum,” she says. “That breaks my heart … The drama department was always my safe space. It’s so upsetting to me that there are kids that may not be able to explore that side of themselves because of government cuts. What is happening? It’s absolutely mad.”If there is a through-line in Reynolds’s career, it is refreshingly complex characters – flawed, forthright, spiky, violent. Playing Licisca, she says, helped her find her “feral” side. “It’s always been there but it never comes out – unless in a medieval costume!”View image in fullscreenReynolds with Jason Sudeikis in Ted Lasso’s fourth season.Photograph: Colin Hutton/AppleCoach Alice is another complicated proposition. She glowers through much of my allotted four episodes, eyeing Ted’s proffered high fives as if she might catch rabies, or worse, fun. But there are glimmers of an unfurling. “I was quite scared at the thought of playing someone tough. The thought of me being tough is hilarious. Because I am a cheese string,” she laughs. “[But] she’s almost performing at the beginning … Particularly in fields that have been historically male-dominant, I think women can often feel they have to present as the opposite to what is typically regarded as feminine. Alice is trying to be this sturdy, unemotional, humourless machine. But what the show is so good at is showing that, beneath any exterior, no matter how tough or spiky, there’s complexity and depth and tenderness.”Indeed, the show is still a wholesome delight: reliably funny, big on cockle-warming, and this season with a great dollop of female empowerment thanks to its new storyline, in which Ted coaches Richmond’s women’s team. It is also a welcome break from the incessant violence against women on our screens, and indeed in all art forms. I mention last month’s revelation that nine out of 10 bestselling novels in the UKfeature a murdered woman. “Yes!” shouts Reynolds, head in hands in exasperation.“A big part of why I loved Ted Lasso so much was that it’s exactly the kind of TV I want to watch right now,” she says. “Personally, and maybe this is because of my own slightly nervous, anxious disposition …” a pause, “or maybe it’s because I’m justfuckingexhausted, like so many women out there are just exhausted of ... yeah,” she trails off, rubbing her eyes wearily. “But I can’t watch things that are violent, and especially violent towards women. I just can’t,” she concludes.“1536,” she adds, “is basically a play about how history is repeating itself [and asking] how far have we moved on from that time that a king [Henry VIII] decided to start changing the laws so he could kill his wives.” A gallows laugh. “Take us out of our huge dresses and put us in jeans, and you could have the same script, essentially.” She adds: “Ted Lasso is very different but its whole thing is about optimism and positivity and … communicating with each other. That’s the kind of telly I’m craving.”Others who have been craving Ted will be pleased to see many of the original cast returning. In fact, outside of the footballers, Reynolds is the only new lead. How was her first day on set?“I was so nervous. And they write as they go, so it wasn’t like we had 10 scripts in advance. By the time I started, I had read two,” she says. “They know where they would like to go but they’re also so open to collaboration and they write for the actors, so everything’s getting built as you’re going.”A lot of her scenes were with “genius improvisers” Sudeikis and Brendan Hunt (the co-creator and writer who plays Coach Beard). “So much of the improv was just them being hilarious, and me trying not to laugh. The whole shoot felt like an exercise in ‘Don’t laugh. Just don’t laugh.’”They also helped Reynolds find her footballing feet. “Like a lot of people, I definitely have gotten into women’s football in the last couple of years but I had to up the ante getting this [job].” Despite watching “more football than I’ve probably ever watched”, the match scenes proved tricky. “They filmed the coaches separately, so we’re not actually watching any football. The lads would improv and shout things out. I just was like ‘Er, kick! Go on, um, kick the ball!’ I had to constantly ask Brendan and Jason: ‘What’s a good football-coachy thing to say?’”The release of Ted Lasso will no doubt catapult Reynolds to a new level of stardom. But despite being “obnoxiously sure of [herself]” at primary school, she has been dogged by imposter syndrome throughout her career. Surely it’s getting better with all her successes, I ask?“To be honest, I think it’s maybe getting worse!” she laughs a ‘what you gonna do?’ laugh. “It gets worse every year. The way I’m dealing with it currently is to take every job as it comes, do my best with it, and then afterwards I don’t watch anything. I just think: ‘I’m just gonna keep going until they tell me I can’t.’”Ted Lasso is on Apple TV from5 August.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionDramaTV comedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘He lived here a long time, so it feels poignant’: Nick Cave thrills Brighton passersby with secret rooftop gig | Nick Cave | The Guardian
description: Prior to playing huge outdoor show in city’s Preston Park, Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds set up on a record shop balcony – and play to fans visiting from across the world
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Prior to playing huge outdoor show in city’s Preston Park, Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds set up on a record shop balcony – and play to fans visiting from across the world
Content: Onstage commitment is his trademark … Nick Cave performing with the Bad Seeds on the roof of Resident Records in Brighton.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOnstage commitment is his trademark … Nick Cave performing with the Bad Seeds on the roof of Resident Records in Brighton.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/The GuardianNick Cave‘He lived here a long time, so it feels poignant’: Nick Cave thrills Brighton passersby with secret rooftop gigPrior to playing huge outdoor show in city’s Preston Park, Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds set up on a record shop balcony – and play to fans visiting from across the worldAlexis PetridisFri 31 Jul 2026 12.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNick Cave and the Bad Seeds’ only advertised UK live performance of 2026, a show in Brighton’s Preston Park, arrives with other events across the city attached. The Duke of York’s Picturehouse cinema is hosting a weekend-long Nick Cave takeover, featuring films curated and introduced by the singer-songwriter. There is a pop-up shop replete with exclusive merchandise, and a postbox where physical letters can be sent toThe Red Hand Files, the website Cave started in 2018 where he answers fans’ questions on topics ranging from faith and grief to his favourite brand of hair dye (L’Oreal, apparently). Even the announcements at the train station have been changed: arrivals are temporarily greeted by the sound of Nick Cave welcoming them to Brighton.All these have been well-publicised, but judging by the crowd gathering in Kensington Gardens, a narrow pedestrian road in North Laine – not far from Jubilee Street, the subject of a Cave song – word also seems to have leaked out about a theoretically secret event: a live performance on the roof of Resident Records, which is hosting the two-dayNick Cavepop-up shop.View image in fullscreenBy 10.30am the street is packed … the view of Resident Records, with the band performing on the balcony.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/The GuardianA substantial group has already assembled, an hour before the performance is scheduled to begin. Some have been tipped off in advance (“My mate told me about it last night, he’s very well connected”). Others simply arrived in order to avail themselves of an exclusive Cave picture disc. (It sold out yesterday and there are already copies on eBay for £60, one disgruntled punter notes, before suggesting that the enterprising soul behind the eBay listing is “a bastard”.) After seeing the musical equipment on the roof, they put two and two together.By 10.30am, the street is packed. A security guard manages to keep a narrow flow of pedestrians moving through its centre, but no one seems to have considered Snoopers Paradise, the vintage market across the road. The crowd jams its doorways and shoppers can’t get out: “What’s going on?” asks a plaintive voice. “Oh, I can’tstandNick Cave.”Said voice is clearly in the minority. The startling thing about the crowd is that it largelyisn’tcomprised of curious locals: there are people here from Germany, Norway, France, all of whom have flown in specially for the Preston Park gig. There is talk of visitors from the US and east Asia. A couple from Oslo are enjoying what they call “a Nick Cave summer”, following the Bad Seeds around Europe: “Well, we’re going to four shows – he’s playing 32”. TheBrightonshow has extra appeal, says Lisa, who has travelled down from Edinburgh with her partner because it’s a kind of a hometown gig, although “former adopted hometown” gig would be more accurate. “He lived in Brighton for a long time – he moved when his son died,” she says, referring to Arthur Cave, who fell from a cliff in Ovingdean in 2015. “So it feels quite poignant.”View image in fullscreenEclectic and winningly chaotic … Nick Cave.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/The GuardianThe distance some people in the crowd have travelled reflects Cave’s ongoing purple patch. The music he has released in the last decade – most notably 2019’s extraordinary mediation on loss,Ghosteen– has been some of the most acclaimed of his career. The harrowing documentary filmOne More Time With Feelingmet with similar acclaim, as didFaith Hope and Carnage, a book containing an astonishingly frank series of interviews with journalist Sean O’Hagan.Cave has courted controversy over his opposition to the cultural boycott of Israel, although it doesn’t seem to have impacted his popularity. Improbably, the Bad Seeds began playing arena-sized venues at the exact moment their music took a turn towards the abstract, with 2016’sSkeleton Tree, although Lisa suggests the crowds may have been swelled by those only familiar with his most famous songs. “I think there were a lot of Peaky Blinders fans in the audience when he played Glasgow,” she says, “just waiting to hear Red Right Hand.” She wrinkles her noise, irritably. “They were quite chatty during the rest of it.”By the time Cave and the Bad Seeds arrive, there are people gathered not just on the street but on the roofs of adjacent shops. The set is eclectic – lurching from the apocalyptic clatter of 1985’s Train Long Suffering to a piano-led cover of T Rex’s Cosmic Dancer – and winningly chaotic, as perhaps any performance involving seven musicians and four backing singers on a tiny balcony is wont to be.View image in fullscreenFans on Kensington Gardens watching Nick Cave.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/The GuardianCave occasionally grins at the absurdity of it all (“Fucking Brighton!” he smiles at one point) or issues frantic instructions to his bandmates mid-song, but the really striking thing is how committed his performance is, despite the peculiar circumstances. He hangs precariously over the balcony to conduct the crowd in call-and-response vocals. Singing Henry Lee as a duet with Janet Ramus, he performs it as if wracked by a desire for both the backing vocalist and his wife, Susie, who is watching from an adjacent balcony. Then again, onstage commitment regardless of the circumstances is something of a Cave trademark, as our Norwegian friends enjoying their summer of Nick note. “In Antwerp, the show was in the middle of a heatwave and he played for two and a half hours wearing a three-piece suit.”It ends with a version of Papa Won’t Leave You, Henry. The police arrive shortly afterwards – one suspects the gig was not officially sanctioned – but the crowd are already dispersing, most of them in the direction of Preston Park. It’s hours before the Bad Seeds are due on stage, but the real lure seems to be the opportunity to outwit the bastards on eBay: a rumour suggests remaining copies of the exclusive picture disc are on sale there, and people scurry off.Explore more on these topicsNick CavePop and rockBrightonShareReuse this content

title: Ariana Grande: Petal review – calm, controlled anger at exes, fans and the media | Ariana Grande | The Guardian
description: Casting herself as a flower trampled underfoot, the superstar’s eighth album swaps the ​glitz of her Wicked years ​f​or dark blooms of haunted electronics
Author: Katie Hawthorne
Headline: Casting herself as a flower trampled underfoot, the superstar’s eighth album swaps the ​glitz of her Wicked years ​f​or dark blooms of haunted electronics
Content: Measured neutrality … Ariana Grande.Photograph:  Katia TemkinView image in fullscreenMeasured neutrality … Ariana Grande.Photograph:  Katia TemkinAriana GrandeReviewAriana Grande: Petal review – calm, controlled anger at exes, fans and the media(Republic)Casting herself as a flower trampled underfoot, the superstar’s eighth album swaps the ​glitz of her Wicked years ​f​or dark blooms of haunted electronicsKatie HawthorneFri 31 Jul 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 13.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Tell me who’s to blame?”Ariana Grandeasks, exasperated, on the title track of her eighth album, Petal. “Is it the people or myself?” As bleary, fuzzed-up drums threaten to drown her out, this shadowy carousel-ride of a song cycles through more questions than answers. Does her success only make her need more of it? Can her new record of No 1 singles stave off heartbreak? Does Grande’s life shape her music, or does her music shape her life?View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Petal.Photograph: Republic Records/APMoody and muted, Petal is a riposte to the glitz and sparkle of the pop star’s Oscar-nominated turn inWickedand the theatre kid energy of her last album, 2024’sEternal Sunshine. She describes this record as one of “unfiltered rage”, and there’s plenty Grande could be angry about: just this weekshe filed a lawsuitagainst hackers who allegedly stole and sold numerous unreleased songs.Intrusive fans are raked over the coals on the icily aloof lead single Hate That I Made You Love Me – a huge global hit since its release in May – while whispery Oh Well casually dispatches “bad guys” (read: exes) to hell. Like I Do opens with panicky gasps, stylised as a vocal exercise, and ruminates on co-dependence with the press – along with a possible dig at years of clickbait headlines pedalling faux concern about her weight: “I’ve got shit to talk, keeps me well fed.”The album’s central metaphor of a petal on the pavement – something delicate getting trampled underfoot – is mirrored in production that is unusually dark by Grande’s standards. Written and produced by Grande and longtime collaborator Ilya Salmanzadeh, Petal buries her soft, sparkling voice under bass, rattling percussion and a raft of crackling, distorted electronic textures. It sounds lonely: a haunted house of a pop record with Grande’s usual R&B vocal fireworks locked in the basement.Dread-soaked opener Kiss Me is a crisis of faith, with Grande’s gleaming voice the only light in the dark as she demands, vampirically, for a lover to “bring her to life”. Water drips from the ceiling on Hate That I Made You Love Me, as if her chilly dismissal of her fans’ obsession was recorded in some kind of sewer.Snatches of shuffling UKG percussion suggest that Kelela’s eerie fusion of club, R&B and alt-rock has replaced Mariah Carey’s glam on Grande’s mood board, but there’s still a shiny, theatrical bent to her new grunge. Sirens wee-woo melodramatically on Never Get Over Me, which threatens another ex over campy, villainous piano. In a similar vein, Big Feelings claims femme fatale status via generically stomping synths and a wide-eyed rendition of a line from Rizzo’s big ballad in Grease: “There are worse things that I could do.”Through it all, Grande maintains a measured neutrality to her voice. Shelving the powerhouse vocal runs she’s famous for, she leans towards lacy, translucent harmonies and stacked layers (in the vein of her longtime inspiration Imogen Heap), which turn into ghostly cathedrals of sound. The closest we get to an old-school Ariana moment is on interlude Warning Signs, which escalates into a rare outburst: “I wish someone could hear me,” she cries, before the track cuts out.Ariana Grande review - glittering hits and powerhouse vocals in stunning return to stageRead morePetal is an album of quiet, controlled, vetted anger; there’s no rush of blood to the head. Maybe it’s because Grande is rehashing familiar topics – it’s far from the first time she’s dissected fame, romance or self-worth in her music – that she sounds numb to it, tired of treading the same ground. Or maybe it’s because performing anger in public is a new challenge for her. While singing the title track live for the first time this week, she clenched her fists: Anger 101. But as she demanded those answers – from herself, from a sea of screaming fans and phone screens – her voice had real bite.Explore more on these topicsAriana GrandePop and rockR&Balbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hold the front page! Marilyn Monroe is Dakota Johnson’s ninth cousin three times removed | Movies | The Guardian
description: The vogue for celebrity ancestors can be traced back to Robert Pattinson descending from Dracula and Benedict Cumberbatch being related to just about everyone
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The vogue for celebrity ancestors can be traced back to Robert Pattinson descending from Dracula and Benedict Cumberbatch being related to just about everyone
Content: Family resemblance? … Dakota Johnson as Marilyn Monroe in Flesh ImpactView image in fullscreenFamily resemblance? … Dakota Johnson as Marilyn Monroe in Flesh ImpactMoviesHold the front page! Marilyn Monroe is Dakota Johnson’s ninth cousin three times removedThe vogue for celebrity ancestors can be traced back to Robert Pattinson descending from Dracula and Benedict Cumberbatch being related to just about everyoneStuart HeritageFri 31 Jul 2026 10.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 10.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.To mark Marilyn Monroe’s 100th birthday, a short film will premiere at this year’s Venice film festival. Entitled Flesh Impact, the film has been written and directed by Maggie Gyllenhaal, and will star two versions of Monroe. The first, played by Ellen Burstyn, will apparently be “a version of Monroe the world never got to see”, while Dakota Johnson will play Monroe in her pomp.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Ahead of its premiere, a photo of Johnson dolled up as Monroe has been released. And it has to be said that the resemblance is actually pretty good. This could be down to one of two reasons. The first is that Monroe is so iconic that you could slap a wig and a beauty spot on Phil Mitchell and you’d immediately see who he was trying to emulate. Or it could be because Marilyn Monroe andDakota Johnsonare literally related.View image in fullscreenBig news … Monroe in Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953).Photograph: 20th Century Fox/AllstarNo, really. A new press release from MyHeritage has revealed that Marilyn Monroe is Dakota Johnson’s ninth cousin three times removed. According to the release, “their shared ancestry traces back to Richard and Charity Tydings, 17th-century English settlers in Maryland. Marilyn descends from their daughter Pretitia, while Dakota and [her father] Don Johnson descend from her younger sister, Mary.”This is incredible news indeed. What a scoop, casting one of Marilyn Monroe’s own relatives in a film about Marilyn Monroe. And a close relative, too. Ninth cousins three times removed. Take that, anyone who is only the 12th cousin six times removed of Marilyn Monroe. This is the real deal.However, if you can believe such a thing, Johnson and Monroe are not the only miraculous relatives in Hollywood. For example, in the 2017 BBC seriesGunpowder, Kit Harington played Robert Catesby, the leader of a Catholic group who planned the failed gunpowder plot in 1605. It’s a great, grim character to play – spoiler, he ends with his head on a spike – but the biggest news about the series was the fact that Harington was a descendant of Catesby. The website Famouskin claims that Harington isCatesby’s sixth cousin 11 times removed, although it’s worth pointing out that Harington’s family is so well to do that his10th great-grandfather was James I– meaning that he is simultaneously related to a failed assassin and the assassin’s intended victim.Another actor related to royalty is Benedict Cumberbatch. In 2016, Cumberbatch playedRichard III in The Hollow Crown, a year after genealogists revealed that the actor was Richard’ssecond cousin 16 times removed. However, it turns out that Cumberbatch is also related to basically every other character he has ever played.View image in fullscreenBenedict Cumberbatch as Alan Turing in The Imitation Game.Photograph: Black Bear Pictures/Sportsphoto/AllstarAfter appearing inSherlock, Ancestry revealed that Cumberbatch was the16th cousin twice removed of Arthur Conan Doyle. When the Alan Turing biopicThe Imitation Gamewas released in 2014, Ancestry went to work again, declaring thatCumberbatch and Turing were 17th cousins, sharing an ancestor in the first Earl of Somerset. You may also remember that Cumberbatch starred in12 Years a Slave. While not directly related to his character, Cumberbatch’s fifth great-grandfather Abraham was nevertheless an enslaver with a Barbados sugar plantation in his name.As you can see, Ancestry really comes into its own on matters like this. For example, just one month after Taylor Swift announced her 2024 albumThe Tortured Poets Department, the website managed to discover that Swift was in fact related to a notoriously tortured poet, being thesixth cousin three times removedof Emily Dickinson. Last year, it was also claimed that Swift was theeighth cousin 11 times removedof King Louis XIV of France. Perhaps this will be a link covered in a future album called The Hubristic Monarchs Department.View image in fullscreenTaylor Swift and her sixth cousin three times removed, Emily Dickinson.Composite: Getty Images for TAS Rights Management, Culture ClubBut being related to royalty is boring. Being related to something supernatural, on the other hand, is much more fun. And so it came to pass in 2009 that Emma Watson, famous for playing a witch in the Harry Potter films, is actually related to a witch. The news came out of yet another Ancestry deep dive, revealing that Watson’sdistant ancestor was Joan Playle, a woman who was convicted of witchcraft in 1592. Although she wasn’t executed for her crimes, Playle was nevertheless excommunicated from the church, although it might be worth pointing out that the evidence for her being a witch essentially begins and ends with the fact that she was unmarried.Finally, the greatest ancestral link of them all. Shortly before the release of The Twilight Saga: Eclipse, Ancestry managed to work out that Robert Pattinson, who played a vampire in the film, wasdistantly related to Vlad III, known as Vlad the Impaler or Vlad Dracula. Being a screen vampire who is literally related to Dracula is quite a flex, although it should also be pointed out that other relatives of Vlad include Prince William and Prince Harry, and George W Bush, so hopefully they’ll band together for any further sequels.Explore more on these topicsFilmDakota JohnsonMarilyn MonroeBenedict CumberbatchKit HaringtonRobert PattinsonTaylor SwiftfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was so self-assured in my early 20s. Then my frontal lobe hit’: Rachel Chinouriri, every pop star’s favourite UK pop star | Rachel Chinouriri | The Guardian
description: ​She faced racist bullying as a child – then pigeonholing as an artist. Now following up a hit debut album championed by the A-list, the Croydon singer-songwriter says she finally understands who she really is
Author: Olive Pometsey
Headline: ​She faced racist bullying as a child – then pigeonholing as an artist. Now following up a hit debut album championed by the A-list, the Croydon singer-songwriter says she finally understands who she really is
Content: ‘The fun obsessions or meet-ups I used to love  came from a place of desperation, loneliness and seeking validation’ … Rachel Chinouriri.Photograph: Yana Van NuffelView image in fullscreen‘The fun obsessions or meet-ups I used to love  came from a place of desperation, loneliness and seeking validation’ … Rachel Chinouriri.Photograph: Yana Van NuffelRachel ChinouririInterview‘I was so self-assured in my early 20s.
