Then my frontal lobe hit’: Rachel Chinouriri, every pop star’s favourite UK pop starOlive Pometsey​She faced racist bullying as a child – then pigeonholing as an artist. Now following up a hit debut album championed by the A-list, the Croydon singer-songwriter says she finally understands who she really isFri 31 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn October 2017, Rachel Chinouriri had her first panic attack. It couldn’t have come at a worse time. She’d just landed her first major gig as a professional musician, supportingCelesteat the London members’ club Laylow. Out of nowhere, she began to spiral. “I don’t know what happened,” she says. “I just started having a mental breakdown.” Her manager told her to go home, try again next time. But that only made things worse. “I started feeling like I was wasting everyone’s time,” she says. “I started feeling ashamed.” It would be better, she decided, to go on stage and sing, “half crying”.Tears were already a familiar response to Chinouriri’s performance anxiety: the first time she sang in front of her classmates at the Brit school – the performing arts institution that trained Adele, Amy Winehouse and more – she burst into sobs afterwards. A rather inconvenient habit for an aspiring pop star, but at least she front-loaded the humiliation at the start of her career. “That was a big milestone for me,” she says of the Celeste show. “The fact that I could stand up there completely embarrassed, with people looking at me like, ‘Don’t really know what’s up with this girl’, but I still got through it and everything was fine.” The experience taught her that the catastrophic scenarios in her head rarely come to pass. “I’d given myself this pressure of, ‘This is the music industry. If they think I’m rubbish, I’m never gonna perform again.’” Chinouriri rolls her eyes at herself.The 27-year-old’s triumph over stage fright has been more impressive than most. It’s a sweltering Friday in July – 30C outside and even hotter in the small restaurant she’s chosen for our interview – and Chinouriri is having an excellent week. On Sunday, she performed to a crowd of 45,000 at Wolf Alice’s homecoming show in Finsbury Park – the latest artists to select her as a support act, after Sabrina Carpenter, Olivia Rodrigo, Gracie Abrams, Florence + the Machine and more have all been drawn to the fearless, bare-souled lyricism that charges through her contemporary twist on indie music. Last night, her former Brit school headteacher handed her the trophy for best new music at the O2 Silver Clef awards: her first-ever award win, after nominations at the 2025 Brits and 2021 Ivor Novellos. Melanie C was at the ceremony and later followed her on Instagram (“I will absolutely message her straight after this”).View image in fullscreenRachel Chinouriri at Radio 1’s Big Weekend at Herrington Country Park, Sunderland, May 2026.Photograph: Joseph Okpako/WireImageHow did she celebrate her big win? “I put on my glasses and left! I was in the heaviest metallic dress and it was like a sauna in there. Looking back at all the images, I’m just, like,weton stage.” Today, Chinouriri is dressed in more appropriate heatwave attire: red micro shorts, a strapless top and flip-flops. She scans the breakfast menu, though she hardly needs to: Café Palestina is one of her favourite spots in London, a short ride from her home in Camden. She orders a Palestinian breakfast and an assortment of kibbeh and stuffed vine leaves to share, then leans back into her seat.There’s another reason for Chinouriri’s good mood: this afternoon, she’ll hand in the final version of her forthcoming second album, I Think I Spoke Too Soon. The title is quite literal. “In my early 20s, I was so self-assured of who I was, then my frontal lobe hit and I went: ‘Nah, I’m actually not that person,’” she says. Chinouriri says she has recently learned about her Saturn return, the astrological milestone said to upend your late-20s. “I feel the shift. I thought I knew myself. Now I look in the mirror and I’m like: ‘Is this actually who I am?’”It’s a big question, but not a new one for Chinouriri. Growing up in Croydon, she was the only one of five siblings to be born in the UK, after her family moved from Zimbabwe. Her mother ran a strict Christian household while caring for her sick father. Both parents had fought as child soldiers in Zimbabwe’s war for independence. In the UK, they struggled to make ends meet. “But they always turned it into a giggle,” she says – even when the power went out. “Games would start getting invented. You’d get given the electricity meter key and walk to the shop to put £5 on.” She smiles fondly at the memory of them all sprinting to complete the task. “They found a way to turn struggle into something beautiful in order to survive.”View image in fullscreen‘My first school taught me: don’t stay where you’re not wanted.’Photograph: Yana Van NuffelAt a majority white secondary school, Chinouriri faced her own battles, enduring racist bullying so extreme that one pupil was suspended and another excluded. She was spat on, called the N-word and tormented with monkey noises as she walked through the corridors. Eventually, Chinouriri enrolled herself at a more diverse school, pretending to be her mother on the application form. “The first school taught me: don’t stay where you’re not wanted,” she says. “I hit points where I felt like dying. But afterwards, I was like: ‘I can leave here with my head raised high.’”A few years later, she made it to the Brit school, the state-funded incubator for British pop stars and actors. Chinouriri was in the same school year as Olivia Dean and Cat Burns; Lola Young was just a few years below. “I wasn’t in any of their classes, but they were three names I heard constantly – the rumours were right!” At home, her musical tastes stuck out. Forbidden from listening to non-Christian music, she and her siblings would row over which TV music channels to watch while their parents were at work. “My sisters were big lovers of B2K, Brandy and Destiny’s Child. When I was in charge of the TV, it would be Oasis and Coldplay.” But at the Brit school, the singer found a place where being different was kind of the whole point. “There was a girl who used to paint herself like an anime character every single day and walked around the school like it was normal,” she says. “I loved that level of expression and freedom.”double quotation markMy sisters loved Brandy and Destiny’s Child. Me, it was Oasis and ColdplayWhen Chinouriri released her debut album, What a Devastating Turn of Events, in 2024, she laid everything bare. The title track recounts her cousin’s suicide after an unwanted pregnancy; another song wrestles with self-worth and body dysmorphia; on My Blood, she sings about self-harm. The candour resonated and its songs were streamed hundreds of millions of times. “All my songs feel a bit like a journal entry, even if I make it sound like a pop song,” she says. “It’s always deeply embedded in my thoughts.” It also resonates when her lyrics turn to romance: her song Dumb Bitch Juice has become an anthem for fans weathering toxic relationships. As Chinouriri’s friend and collaborator PinkPantheress tells me, “Her youthful, melodic approach truly encapsulates the state of modern romance among people our age. She makes heartbreak warm and tolerable, even in the most painful situations.”View image in fullscreenChinouriri at Roskilde festival in Denmark, 2025.Photograph: Matt Jelonek/Getty ImagesChinouriri is now in a healthy, long-term relationship. These days, she sings about heartbreak from a distance: reflecting on past flings to better understand herself, instead of “writing through something I’m trying to survive,” she says. “I began asking myself: ‘Why do I attract these people?’ The fun obsessions or meet-ups I used to love actually came from a place of desperation, loneliness and seeking validation.”When her album was released, much of the media attention focused on Chinouriri’s presence as a Black woman in indie music, a genre that’s historically associated with white men. This was partly her own doing. In 2022, she called out the industry’s inaccurate – and, frankly, racist – miscategorisation of her music as R&B or soul on Instagram: “You see my colour before you hear my music.” What a Devastating Turn of Events doubled down on guitar sounds to make a point. “That had to happen because I was really fighting for my place in indie pop,” she says. But still, I wonder, did she ever tire of answering questions about race?“I feel like …” Chinouriri squints upwards as if the answer might be hovering above the table, then begins to speak slowly. “It was an important and necessary part of the story to pave the way for myself in pop, indie and alternative music. I’m glad that I’ve played a part in that. I love going on TikTok and seeing a new Black pop or indie girl with 10,000 likes and no one’s questioning it.” So the industry’s made progress, then? Another pause. “I can say that there’s been progress because I’ve benefited from it. But when I look to my left and right at festivals, I’m still the only Black girl on the lineup – or it will be me and Cat [Burns]. The fact that two Black pop girls who went to the same school are [being booked] around the UK … That’s interesting.”View image in fullscreenChinouriri at Field Day festival in London, 2019.Photograph: Lorne Thomson/RedfernsI Think I Spoke Too Soon turns the conversation inward. “My first album was about how I was perceived as a Black woman in this space. Now it’s about how I perceive myself in this space,” she says.The record is a near-total gear shift from Chinouriri’s previous output, drawing from her longtime pop heroes, Madonna, Kylie Minogue, Donna Summer, Prince and LCD Soundsystem – influences that would have perhaps complicated her fight against pigeonholing during her last album rollout. “As much as I love indie sleaze, I love me some Madonna,” she says, laughing. “I wanted [to recreate] the level of carefreeness I got when I listened to songs like Hung Up for the first time.”Bright synths replace Britpop-inspired guitars; melancholy hooks are transformed into singalong sad bangers. There are still flickers of her old self: rich harmonies, confessional lyrics, the odd indie track thrown in for good measure. But as she sings on lead single, One Song Away from Crying, this is principally an album that’s designed to “work it out on the floor”.If anything, Chinouriri’s darkest moments are made all the more cathartic when contrasted with a danceable beat. When she confronts her relationship to alcohol on Broken Chair, for example, she sings its euphoric chorus from the perspective of pitying an abandoned piece of furniture on the side of the road: “You look lonely, but not me / I’ve got plenty of friends until the last call”. The same theme is explored on The Good Fight, one of the first songs she wrote for the album. Around the same time, she decided to go sober. “I didn’t have too much of an issue with drinking, but I just looked at myself and thought: ‘This is not my happy place,’” she says. Up until that point, her party-girl image had become a running joke with her fans. “I was out with a friend and she posted a selfie of us. My fans were like, she’s about to tweet: ‘I’m tipsy!’” Without seeing their prediction, she did exactly that. “It was pretty funny. They know me well.”Chinouriri replies to group chats with her fans more often than her family. Recently, her team analysed her audience and found it skews overwhelmingly queer. “I was like: ‘This is fantastic!’” She went straight to the group chat to deliver the news. “I was like: ‘Announcement: everyone in here is gay and this is beautiful.’”Chinouriri is looking ahead to a busy few months of concerts, including a slot at Rodrigo’s inaugural Daisy Chain Fields festival in California and supporting Abrams on tour across the US. She’s already briefing fans on what to wear to align with her new era: “Blue, silvers, purple, shimmy-shimmy iridescence. It’s going to be so fun.”‘The beast inside me wants to move!’ The smart, slapstick world of Audrey Hobert, the Steve Martin of popRead moreWhen supporting Carpenter on tour around Europe last year, Chinouriri “felt like I was travelling in this Sabrina universe”. Every billboard had Carpenter’s face on it; every person seemed to be wearing merch; every cafe was playing her music. “It was so cool to see how she’s thought about her fans, even at that level, and the community they’ve built. I’d love to have that one day.”At the Finsbury Park show, one fan held up a sign that read: “When I don’t belong, her music calls.” Perhaps that feeling is a happy byproduct of Chinouriri’s own fight to be heard. “Whatever happens, if I do get pigeonholed again, so be it. I fought really hard. I tried my best,” she says. “But I need to trust that it won’t happen because I have found a way to know who I am.” At least for now. “You can change who you are at any moment, as long as you reflect and forgive yourself first.”I Think I Spoke Too Soon is released on 16 October via Parlophone/Atlas ArtistsExplore more on these topicsRachel ChinouririPop and rockIndieDance musicRacefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘An intermission is a must’: why Greek cinemas are adding a loo break to The Odyssey | Movies | The Guardian
description: In Athens’ picturehouses, an interval is always a ‘non-negotiable’ – a chance to buy a beer, nip to the toilet – or pop the question
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In Athens’ picturehouses, an interval is always a ‘non-negotiable’ – a chance to buy a beer, nip to the toilet – or pop the question
Content: Critical revenue … a crowd outside Laura cinema in Athens.Photograph: Daniel MaurerView image in fullscreenCritical revenue … a crowd outside Laura cinema in Athens.Photograph: Daniel MaurerMovies‘An intermission is a must’: why Greek cinemas are adding a loo break to The OdysseyIn Athens’ picturehouses, an interval is always a ‘non-negotiable’ – a chance to buy a beer, nip to the toilet – or pop the questionRelease schedule: when to wee and when to wait during this summer’s biggest moviesDaniel MaurerFri 31 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the lights rose during a recent screening ofThe Odysseyat the Arian open-air cinema on the Athens riviera, nervous laughter floated into the breeze. Moments earlier, Odysseus’s men had morphed into pigs during a grotesque feeding frenzy fuelled by drugged cheese and wine. Now, as the Bangles’ Eternal Flame played on the house speakers, no one seemed especially tempted by the concession stand’s hotdogs.This is presumably the sort of scenario Christopher Nolan hoped to avoid when he decided against an intermission in his nearly three-hour-long adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey. In the epic’s country of origin, however, directors do not get the final word.“InGreece, the intermission is a must,” said Fotis Georgopoulos, whose family has run Cine Foivos, a movie house in the Athens suburb of Peristeri, for 72 years. “People want to smoke, they want to go to the toilet, they want to discuss the movie. And they don’t want to lose even five minutes of it.”At Foivos, The Odyssey’s interval came during a more elegant moment, as Odysseus sailed away from Circe’s island. Outside, Gina Alexopoulou, 24, welcomed the chance to tell her boyfriend that Nolan’s Laestrygonians were the work of seven-foot actors rather than CGI. Nearby, brothers Giorgios and Panagiotis Liolias, both in their 30s, were also having a smoke, though they would have preferred to watch the film uninterrupted.View image in fullscreen‘They don’t want to lose even five minutes of the film’ … an intermission card at Arian Urban Openair Cinema.Photograph: Daniel MaurerUntil recent years, intermissions were standard practice at cinemas in Athens. In the early days, orchestras and theatrical troupes sometimes entertained audiences as projectionists changed reels. By 1960, when the city had at least 350 movie theatres, the intermission had become a social affair.The tradition faded somewhat as multiplexes arrived in the late 1990s, independent theatres transitioned to digital projection in the 2000s, and Covid regulations briefly prohibited intermissions altogether. Now, customers who prefer the breaks – typically five to 10 minutes – often check for them at the box office or ticketing site.At the city’s longstanding summer cinemas, it’s a different story. At the halfway point of most any movie shown outdoors, patrons still shoot the proverbial breeze as they queue for cheese pies, homemade sour cherry juice and the ubiquitous Domino’s Pizza.double quotation markObsession was interrupted right as the unhinged protagonist urinated on the floor – the perfect cue to use the looIntermissions are still deployed, though increasingly less so, in countries including Switzerland, Egypt, and Turkey, and are de rigueur in India, where Bollywood films are scripted with the interval in mind.In Greece, they are crucial to cinemas’ survival. When Dafni Bechtsi took over Athens’ troubled Alexandra theatre in 2024 (now the Cinobo Patision), a midway break for refreshments was essential to her business model. Greek cinemas receive “no support from the government or anything, and they’re really struggling”, she said. “The revenue you get during the break, from food and drink, even if it might not be so much, is super critical.”After winter, cinemas like the Cinobo Patision close for the season to make way for the city’s dozens of open-air ones. The interval becomes a chance to enjoy the bamboo-lined, Cyclades-style terrace at Cine Dexameni, or the view of the Acropolis from the rooftop Cine Paris. Seats are sometimes substituted with hammocks, sunbeds, or garden swings.View image in fullscreenA summer tradition … an open-air cinema with beanbags on the beach.Photograph: Daniel MaurerIn one of the world’s most nocturnal cities, a midnight intermission can also be an opportunity to re-evaluate one’s night altogether and determine whether it’s worth watching the rest of a dud rather than joining friends at a concert or late dinner. Maybe it isn’t just a coincidence that the Greeks refer to the intermission as adiáleimma.However some audience members remain sceptical. At the Electra, a loud grumble of “for fuck’s sake” greeted a bathroom break that shattered the tension ofBackrooms. Other cuts are Oscar-worthy. At the open-air cinema abutting the War Museum, where ushers hand out blankets and pillows during the interval,Obsessionwas interrupted right as the unhinged protagonist urinated on the floor – the perfect cue to use the loo.Projectionists have varying approaches to inserting restroom respites. Anastasia Kottaki, who works at Trianon, jumped straight to the middle of The Odyssey’s digital file to identify a suitable scene change. At Cine Alsos, a 61-year-old cinema tucked inside a wooded park, staff watched the movie in its entirety to choose the best moment and avoid stepping on any action sequences.Mid-screening sales account for about 30% of the Alsos’s profits. Yet owner Giannis Chatzidimitriou insists that the social value of the intermission is equally important. A few years ago, he helped a customer pop the question by screening a proposal video during the interlude. The couple received a standing – and leg-stretching – ovation.View image in fullscreenOscar-worthy timing … an open-air cinema in Athens.Photograph: Daniel MaurerMore than one marriage has blossomed over popcorn andpassatempo, Greece’s beloved salted pumpkin seeds. Vrasidas Karalis, author of A History of Greek Cinema, recalls a friend meeting her future husband while queueing at the snack bar during Bernardo Bertolucci’s 1900. “Their hands touched, and they started talking about the upcoming revolution and the end of capitalist cruelty,” he says.Release schedule: when to wee and when to wait during this summer’s biggest moviesRead moreKaralis, who grew up in the Greater Athens area and now lives in Australia, says he misses the conversations that unfolded with old-timers working the canteen. “Most of them still are real eccentrics with something interesting to suggest about other films.”Peggy Ringa, an archaeologist turned cinema-owner, counts herself among those enthusiasts. At her open-air cinemas – the Riviera, Vox and Athinaia – intermissions are “non-negotiable”. Longer films even get two of them. But they can still take visitors unaware.While Béla Tarr’s two-and-a-half-hour-long Werckmeister Harmonies premiered in the country, said Ringa, the director was alarmed by the sight of audience members filing out of the auditorium halfway through. “The Greek distributors had a very difficult time convincing him that this was perfectly normal.”Explore more on these topicsFilmThe OdysseyFilm industryGreeceEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was born without self-esteem’: Hannah Einbinder on Hacks, her buzzy queer horror – and being Hollywood’s most outspoken star  | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Hacks lead was cast in meta-slasher sensation Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma for her ‘deranged physicality’ – but it’s a fitting role for an actor who has made a point of confronting shame and speaking her mind
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: The Hacks lead was cast in meta-slasher sensation Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma for her ‘deranged physicality’ – but it’s a fitting role for an actor who has made a point of confronting shame and speaking her mind
Content: ‘Comedy was my way of feeling good – and for the most part, I really didn’t feel good’ … Hannah Einbinder.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Comedy was my way of feeling good – and for the most part, I really didn’t feel good’ … Hannah Einbinder.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The GuardianMoviesInterview‘I was born without self-esteem’: Hannah Einbinder on Hacks, her buzzy queer horror – and being Hollywood’s most outspoken starNadia KhomamiThe Hacks lead was cast in meta-slasher sensation Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma for her ‘deranged physicality’ – but it’s a fitting role for an actor who has made a point of confronting shame and speaking her mindFri 31 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘God is good all the time,” laughs Hannah Einbinder. She’s fresh off a plane from Los Angeles and curled up barefoot in an armchair. This, she says, is “a crazy time in life. Starring in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma in the midst ofHacksending … it’s definitely an embarrassment of riches.”Hacks is the HBO comedy that ended earlier this year; in May, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, Jane Schoenbrun’s queer meta-horror, became the breakout hit of this year’s Cannes film festival.Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma review – Gillian Anderson superb in queer slasher spectacularRead moreIn the film, Einbinder plays a film-maker, Kris, who becomes consumed by her obsession with Billy Presley, the reclusive star of the original Camp Miasma slasher franchise – played with hypnotic wit and sensuality byGillian Anderson. What begins as an attempt to persuade Presley to return to the series spirals into an ecstasy of sex, death, VHS tapes and junk food. Scene by scene, the lines between reality and fantasy begin to collapse.“When my agent sent me the script, I was blown away,” says Einbinder. “Its through-line of confronting shame and dealing with repression and dissociation was intriguing to me.” (It’s a theme Schoenbrun has said was inspired by their own process of learning to embrace sexuality after transition.)“We’re discouraged from discussing this stuff,” says Einbinder, “but it’s something I’m familiar with. I had to think: ‘How true is this for me?’ Like Kris, I had to mine my own experiences and confront things I didn’t want to see.” The film, she adds, helped her “be more open about desire”. It was also “a roadmap for how it’s supposed to feel and what one should feel comfortable with doing or saying, and when to say no”.Dressed in a floor-length black dress and a flowing white silk kimono, Einbinder cuts a more glamorous figure than I had expected. On screen, her style and comedy often veer towards the oddball; in person, she is refined, softly-spoken, and deliberately cautious.Her willingness to sit with discomfort feels characteristic of the actor, whose performances often hinge on the tension between awkwardness and emotional honesty. Schoenbrun has said they cast her in her Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma because they “found her deranged physicality exciting”.View image in fullscreenAs Ava Daniels, with Deborah Vance (Jean Smart), in Hacks.Photograph: HBO MaxMost immediately significant is Einbinder’s gift for creating electric chemistry with older female co-stars. In Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma and Hacks, she spends much of the time opposite another glamorous and formidable woman.In the long-running series, Einbinder played Ava Daniels, an aimless comedy writer hired to revive the career of Jean Smart’s Las Vegas standup legend, Deborah Vance. It became one of television’s sharpest comedies, but the key to its emotional force was the relationship between Ava and Deborah: two women who initially seem to have little in common, but who slowly become essential to one another.Their bond was built on insults, betrayals and power struggles, but also on a profound creative understanding – Ava pushes Deborah to confront what she has become, while Deborah teaches Ava the discipline and resilience she lacks.The experience of working on the show was profoundly important to her, says Einbinder, welling up. “I learned so much and I became a person – I became myself. I don’t know how I would have become who I am without it.”She takes a deep breath. “I started comedy because the only way that I could feel good was if I felt like other people felt good. When I was 24 and starting the show, I was just kind of a shell. I didn’t advocate for myself. I didn’t have boundaries. I was passive in a lot of ways.“I think I was just born without self-esteem. Even neutrality felt impossible, just to be cool with myself, let alone the idea of love for myself. Now I feel incredibly embodied and certain of myself in a way that I never thought was possible. And I do credit a lot of that to my experience working on Hacks.”View image in fullscreenEinbinder in London, June 2026.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The GuardianIt’s hard not to trace a similar trajectory to that of her character in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma: a woman forced to excavate the parts of herself she would rather avoid, to come out the other side stronger, more self-assured, and committed to advocating for herself and the causes she believes in.Einbinder grew up in Los Angeles in a progressive Jewish family, where comedy was “the main currency”. Her parents – original Saturday Night Live cast member Laraine Newman and actor Chad Einbinder – were always trying to make each other laugh, and she and her siblings quickly joined in. “That’s certainly the incubator for my approach to interacting with others.”At university, studying broadcast journalism, she joined an improv troupe and began performing standup at open mic nights. She applied to it the same discipline, she says, that she developed as a competitive cheerleader in high school. “I was determined to risk anything, even falling on my face, if it meant I’d get a moment of satisfaction and approval. Comedy was my way of feeling good – and for the most part, I really didn’t feel good.”View image in fullscreenBig break … on The Late Show With Stephen Colbert.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesBy 2019, she was touring as the opening act for comedian Chelsea Handler, and the following year she made her late-night debut on The Late Show With Stephen Colbert – an appearance that helped her land Hacks, despite having no acting credits. “It was the only thing that I had to show for myself,” she saysThe audition, in March 2020, required the character to break down in tears. Einbinder listened to other candidates sobbing through the walls; she had never learned how to cry on command. “I thought, I can’t do the tears, but I could throw in a joke.” It worked; in fact, the gag was such a hit that it made it on to the show.One of Hacks’ central storylines follows Deborah’s battle to break into late-night TV. It’s also where Einbinder got her break. I wonder what she makes of the current state of American comedy?“Colbert is gone,” she says, referring to Stephen Colbert’s departure from The Late Show. “CBS has been very clear in their directives. [Jimmy] Kimmel was suspended. There’s no question that these are political choices.” But what is frightening, she adds, is that these figures represent relatively mainstream voices rather than the radical fringe critics often accuse them of being.“To me, those are not bastions of true leftist thought. They are Democrat with a capital D guys who are, yes, poking fun at the right. But they’re rich white men being axed for pretty centrist and mild speech. So if that’s being censored, that’s a huge problem.”In recent years, Einbinder has developed a reputation for being one of the most outspoken actors in Hollywood. She has used awards speeches and social media to advocate about the climate crisis, immigration, ICE and the war in Gaza. At the Emmy awards last September, after winning outstanding supporting actress in a comedy series for Hacks, she closed her acceptance speech with a message that became one of the night’s most widely discussed moments: “Go Birds, fuck ICE, and free Palestine!”View image in fullscreenStatement win ... Einbinder at the 77th Primetime Emmy awards, 2025.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersShe traces that confidence back to college, when Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaign became “a political awakening”. By far the most difficult part of her political journey, she says, was “unlearning” the Zionism she was raised with. “Once I came to understand reality as it was, I just could not bear the idea of not shouting at any time, in any place, about how wrong and violent it was. How deeply it desecrates our people and what our religion is supposed to mean.”The humanitarian crisis in Gaza “haunts” her, she adds. “I’m just doing what I think is, frankly, the Jewish thing to do, which is to value human life and try to contribute to healing the world.”She adds: “I am incredibly privileged, because smears of being an anti-Semite don’t stick to me. I’m such a proud Jew. But I’m certain there are community members who hate me for this, many of them in my business, and they won’t work with me and want nothing to do with me.”Instead of feeling anger, she says she feels a sense of sadness and loss. “I am sad for them. They are trapped in an ideological prison that stops them from seeing other people’s humanity. They’re trapped because of the massive propaganda campaign waged against them since the moment they could understand language.” Her views have cost her familial relationships, too. “I don’t know that they will ever be repaired, but I have found a family elsewhere in the rich anti-Zionist Jewish community.”View image in fullscreenFormidable women … with Gillian Anderson in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.Photograph: Ryan Plummer/MubiFor Einbinder, politics is inseparable from lived experience. She is bisexual, has two transgender siblings and speaks about identity not as an abstract debate but as something woven into everyday life. “Everything is personal. Politics is the most personal thing. It’s not theoretical.”That refusal to separate the personal from the public is, in its own way, what took her into Camp Miasma in the first place. It was her first real chance to leave behind the creative family that had shaped her on Hacks and find out what she could do without them. “I was both excited and intimidated,” she says. “I was just like: ‘Fuck, can I do this? Can I do something that isn’t the safe environment that raised me, with the people who know exactly how to shape and mould me?’” Watching her talk, it’s clear she already has her answer.Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma is released in the UK on 21 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmGillian AndersonHorror filmsHacksinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: BTS are back: return of K-pop superstars sparks US economic boom | BTS | The Guardian
description: Cities in North America hosting 14 concerts in August and September – and economic impact is set to be significant
Author: Jenna Zaza
Headline: Cities in North America hosting 14 concerts in August and September – and economic impact is set to be significant
Content: Fans at a BTS exhibition in Seoul in March.Photograph: Soo-hyeon Kim/ReutersView image in fullscreenFans at a BTS exhibition in Seoul in March.Photograph: Soo-hyeon Kim/ReutersBTSBTS are back: return of K-pop superstars sparks US economic boomCities in North America hosting 14 concerts in August and September – and economic impact is set to be significantJenna ZazaFri 31 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 12.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBTS’s “Army” fanbase is descending onNew Yorkthis weekend as the K-pop supergroup continues their first world tour after a four-year hiatus, sparking an economic boom wherever they land.After shows in South Korea and Europe, the group are back in North America, with 14 shows in six US cities in August and September.Following the rollout of BTS’s sixth album, Arirang, in March, fans have proved they are willing to spend. In Las Vegas, concertgoers who attended four sold-out shows in May generated an estimated $340m in economic activity, witheventsat huge hotels on the strip and at tiny Chinatown cafes.HYBE, the group’s label, has partnered with local businesses and cultural centers for the “BTS The City – Arirang” project in select cities, offering exclusiveBTSprogramming for concertgoers.Ahead of two concerts at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium on 1 and 2 August, fans can follow amapof activities, landmarks and eateries that celebrate the group.Manhattan’s Koreatown is bracing for thousands of fans. Theeconomic impact of BTS concertgoersis expected to match that of soccer fans who crowded MetLife Stadium for the World Cup final – which included a BTS performance – a few weeks ago.BTS will “easily compare [to] or even exceed Fifa’s economic impact just on average spending”, said Michael Mariano, head of economic development at Tourism Economics.The group’s return has been a boon for HYBE, whichreporteda record-high revenue of $993m this past quarter.View image in fullscreenBTS merchandise at a pop-up store in Seoul.Photograph: Kim Hong-Ji/ReutersThe Korean Cultural Center New York will serve as the hub for fan activities. Participants who nabbed a coveted reservation can try on K-beauty products, sample desserts from Tous les Jours, a South Korean bakery chain, and customize the light sticks they’ll bring to the concert, known as “Army bombs”.“K-pop can serve as a gateway to learning the Korean language and discovering Korean beauty, food, technology, tourism and other aspects of Korean culture,” said Bora Yoon, visual arts manager at the center.The Arte Museum, which houses large-scale digital art, is hosting a special BTS exhibit that will feature music and digital art celebrating the group’s music. The museum expects a high demand for the exhibit, which will immerse BTS fans in “all five senses”, said Sang Jin Lee, head of the creative team and vice-president of d’strict, a creative design company that owns the Arte Museum.“It’s about sharing our culture, great heritage and Korean contemporary digital art through the lens of BTS, using an enduring folk song that is continually reinterpreted by every generation,” Lee said in Korean, referring to Arirang, the centuries-old folk song that inspired the name of BTS’s new album.View image in fullscreenBTS fans pose for pictures as they gather at HMV on Oxford Street in London.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersNew Wonjo, the oldest Korean barbecue restaurant in New York, is also featured on the map, and plans to serve a special menu inspired by the members of BTS and the foods they miss most on tour, including kimchi fried rice, pork belly and jajangmyeon, or black bean noodles.The menu was developed “with intention, and is rooted in Korean culture, rather than just pasting ‘BTS’ on a regular menu item”, said Jacob Baik, art director of New Wonjo. “We hope that some guests who might initially visit because of the ‘BTS The City’ project leave with a genuine interest in the restaurant, the food and Korean culture more broadly.”The map also features bingsu, a type of South Korean shaved ice dessert, offered by Seoul Bingsu – a pop-up version of Seoul-based Tokyo Bingsu, known for its tomato flavor of the dessert. For its limited 10-day New York run, Seoul Bingsu will offer special bookmarks, pins and stickers for those who order from its special Arirang menu.Ara Go, the Seoul-based owner of Seoul Bingsu, said BTS “has truly helped introduce Korean culture to the world”.“Food and desserts are a huge part of Korean culture, and I saw this as a wonderful opportunity to promote not only our food but our country with a broader audience,” Go said in Korean.View image in fullscreenBTS fans in New York.Photograph: JNI/Star Max/GC ImagesBefore the spot’s collaboration with BTS, Angela May, 18, had never heard of bingsu. May, a BTS fan for nearly six years, traveled to Manhattan fromNew Jerseyto try it.“Just having BTS written on the menu or the window will bring a lot of attention to the place,” May said.Asli Penaeo, 22, grew up in New York and has been a fan for seven years, yet she has never been to most of the collaborating restaurants.“This event is finally giving me a chance to go to some of these restaurants, try new items, but also make new memories with fellow Army [fans],” she said, sipping on a BTS-branded Tous Les Jours strawberry lemonade.Sunmi Lee, 40, an interior designer, said she was considering taking a BTS-themed double-decker bus tour to visit New York landmarks – even though she lives in the city.“It’s about celebrating Korean culture,” she said. “Trying authentic local spots, and feeling connected to something bigger than just a concert.”Explore more on these topicsBTSNew YorkNew JerseyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Boy George pulls out of Jesus Christ Superstar after releasing pro-Israel song | Boy George | The Guardian
description: The 80s star will no longer appear in role of Herod in London Palladium run, with manager saying decision is ‘in the best interests of my artist’
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: The 80s star will no longer appear in role of Herod in London Palladium run, with manager saying decision is ‘in the best interests of my artist’
Content: Boy George performing with Culture Club at Uptown festival.Photograph: Lorne Thomson/RedfernsView image in fullscreenBoy George performing with Culture Club at Uptown festival.Photograph: Lorne Thomson/RedfernsBoy GeorgeBoy George pulls out of Jesus Christ Superstar after releasing pro-Israel songThe 80s star will no longer appear in role of Herod in London Palladium run, with manager saying decision is ‘in the best interests of my artist’Ben Beaumont-ThomasFri 31 Jul 2026 05.08 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBoy George has pulled out of a forthcoming London production of Jesus Christ Superstar, days after he releaseda controversial songvoicing support for Israel’s military action against Palestine.The song, entitled עוד נרקוד alongside its English translation We Will Dance Again, addresses critics of Israel, whose military campaign has been been described as genocidal by a UN commission. “You say genocide, I say war / When you’re attacked, that’s what the army’s for,” read the lyrics. “Does it get ugly? You bet it does / When I know you wanna kill every last one of us.”‘You say genocide, I say war’: Boy George releases pro-Israel song, We Will Dance AgainRead moreThe singer’s manager Paul Kemsley wrote on Instagram that he had “decided, in my capacity as Boy George’s manager, that he will no longer be appearing in Jesus Christ Superstar at the London Palladium”.He did not make specific reference to the new song, but added: “George has never been afraid to stand by his personal convictions, and I have always respected him for that. Equally, I believe it is my responsibility to make decisions that are in the best interests of my artist while also showing respect to others. In this instance, I felt it was right to step aside, allowing the production to remain the focus, while ensuring everyone involved can move forward with mutual respect and goodwill.”Boy George was to have played King Herod in the Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice musical, which tells the story of the persecution and crucifixion of Jesus.Kemsley apologised to ticketholders who hoped to see Boy George in the role, and thanked the show’s producers and creative team “for the professionalism and understanding they have shown throughout”.With Eurovision star Sam Ryder as Jesus, the Herod role was being shared by five actors: Boy George, Julian Clary, Jesse Tyler Ferguson, Layton Williams and Richard Armitage, the last of whom will now cover Boy George’s performances.Alluding to his departure from the production, Boy George posted an AI image of himself with a Groucho Marx moustache, and said: “To quote Groucho Marx I would never want to be part of any club that would have me as a member!”Elsewhere in his new song, Boy George had criticised other musicians who voiced support for Palestine – “You condemn the Jews, with selective memory / Musicians holding flags, mouthing like sheep / Propaganda fuelled by the internet feels so weak” – and sang about the attack by Hamas on the Nova music festival at the outset of the war.There were calls for protests outside the Palladium over his Jesus Christ Superstar appearances, and widespread condemnation of the song on social media.Martyn Ware, one of Boy George’s 80s pop peers who was in the Human League and Heaven 17, described the song as an “overtly pro-genocide, anti-Palestinian piece of musical propaganda” and that Boy George should be “ashamed”.Boy George responded to his critics on X, writing: “It doesn’t matter what I think or what you think. When will you realise you’re doing NOTHING! … I am even falling out with Jewish friends. The madness knows no bounds.”On Threads he wrote: “I’m afraid we all struggle with the inability to live peacefully with each other. Until we do, we are doomed. I accept that many people disagree with my point of view but that is what is great about democracy. As imperfect as it is!”The phrase “we will dance again” has been used by Israelis to voice resilience during the conflict, referring back to the dance music played at the Nova festival. Boy George added: “I saw the slogan ‘we will dance again’ and it resonated. Writing has to reflect the world we live in. Why not put the word ‘genocide’ in a song? Why are people suddenly uncomfortable with that word?”He also said the reggae-backed song had been created with AI: “I call it ‘AI for good’. Truthfully, I would struggle to write this with a human!”Boy George has frequently voiced support for the UK’s Jewish community, including after the knife attack on two men in Golders Green in April.He also remained in the Eurovision song contest this year, as a guest artist in San Marino’s entry, after there were calls to boycott it over Israel’s inclusion. “I feel very connected to the Jewish people,” he said. “I’m not necessarily connected to Israel. I don’t really have an opinion on that. But the mission of music is to unite people.”Explore more on these topicsBoy GeorgePop and rockMusicalsShareReuse this content

title: From Felix the Cat to MTV: MoMA explores a century of animation | Art | The Guardian
description: Exhibition It’s Alive follows the evolution of animation in the 100 years before digital technology changed the game
Author: Veronica Esposito
Headline: Exhibition It’s Alive follows the evolution of animation in the 100 years before digital technology changed the game
Content: Buzzco Productions/Buzzco Associates - MTV cel setup: Astronauts. c. 1983.Photograph: Buzzco/Perpetual Motion Collection, Gift of Buzzco Associates IncView image in fullscreenBuzzco Productions/Buzzco Associates - MTV cel setup: Astronauts. c. 1983.Photograph: Buzzco/Perpetual Motion Collection, Gift of Buzzco Associates IncArtFrom Felix the Cat to MTV: MoMA explores a century of animationExhibition It’s Alive follows the evolution of animation in the 100 years before digital technology changed the gameVeronica EspositoFri 31 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlthough the word “animation” may bring to mind rascally, anthropomorphic bunnies, cats and ducks doing outlandish things, the truth of the medium’s diversity goes far beyond these few recognizable brands. According to MoMA curator Ron Magliozzi, whose new show covering 100 years of animation, It’s Alive!, debuts this week, the field may have emerged with character-based, Disney-fied offerings, but it took a hard turn in 1946 when the visionary director John Hubley released a manifesto titled Animation Warrants a New Language.“It’s very short, but it essentially talks about going beyond pigs and bunnies,” Magliozzi told me, “basically leaving behind that first generation and doing the kind of animation that can do much more.”‘Flight originated from the imagination’: how artists have captured space travelRead moreInvigorated by the creative demands of the second world war – and buoyed by his work creating an animated film to promote Franklin Roosevelt in the 1944 election – Hubley aspired to animation that was driven by independent-minded creators who could engage deeply with important social issues and profound artistic questions.Although It’s Alive! engages both parts of animation’s history, with a black-and-white gallery offering such prewar characters as Gertie the Dinosaur, Felix the Cat (in a film where he plays “Romeeow”), and Raggedy Ann & Andy, where the show really ignites is in its postwar, in-color gallery, documenting some of the strangest and most fascinating animations you’ll ever see.View image in fullscreenWinsor McCay – Gertie the Dinosaur animation drawing #28, 1914.Photograph: Robert N Brotherton Collection, Gift of Betty Adam BrothertonWhile Magliozzi noted the inherent challenges to introducing a range of widely unknown and decidedly ambitious animations, he had early signs that he was hitting the mark when one particular constituency gave him glowing feedback.“Most of the art is going to be unfamiliar to most people,” he explained, “but I know it’s exciting stuff because we’ve gotten very good feedback from the installation so far. When the guards stop by to see what you’re doing, you know you’re on the right track.”Take, for instance, the American artist and Oscar–winning film-maker Jerome Hill, whose The Sand Castle is a Jungian fantasia that begins as a black-and-white film about a boy’s trip to the beach and ends as a remarkable stop-motion animation into a dreamlike version of the titular castle. The animated section comes complete with a bizarre dining room sequence and a ballroom fantasia – according to an interview with Hill conducted by Jonas Mekas, Jung himself inspired all of this creativity when the great psychologist told Hill: “Don’t put me in the film; let my ideas be shown in a film.”In another bit of gorgeous whimsy, Magliozzi has chosen to exhibit the legendary Sesame Street animator Jane Aaron. The show has many of the hundreds of amazing letters of the alphabet that she created for the show, as well as her visuals of famous artists and art works, among them Vincent Van Gogh and Picasso’s Girl Before a Mirror – in Aaron’s animation, these figures are taking note of their own nose, eyes and mouth, making for striking visuals to accompany the Sesame Street standard Right in the Middle of My Face. “Jane is one of the primary animators from Sesame Street,” Magliozzi said. “Audiences might know of her work but not necessarily know who she was. So it’s a special thing to be able to showcase her here.”View image in fullscreenJane Aaron – Right in the Middle of My Face Picasso sneeze animation drawing, 1993.Photograph: Jane Aaron Collection, Gift of Skip Blumberg, 2023.MoMA has dedicated holdings of 13 different forms of animation – among them stop-motion, cel, rotoscope, pinscreen and pixilation – giving Magliozzi a true treasure trove to draw from. Having worked at MoMA for nearly 50 years, Magliozzi was able to participate in acquiring many of these collections, and he was excited to have another opportunity to exhibit them. “We have such a wealth of animation here, so that really was the inspiration for this show.”In an effort to make the artistry behind these films more accessible to audiences, It’s Alive! will screen 20 films within the gallery space, offering viewers a chance to get a closeup view of these striking sights. Making an innovative move, Magliozzi has chosen to screen these films without sound, granting viewers space to pay full attention to the remarkable visuals.“The sound is distracting, and so without sound people really focus differently,” Magliozzi explained. “There will be an app that folks can have on their phone to listen to the sound. So it’s possible to not miss out on that if you want it, but I think most people will experience them without sound, which is the way I want them to experience it.”If there’s one animated short in It’s Alive! that audiences will be likely to know, it’s MTV’s I Want My MTV! ad campaign from the channel’s rise to prominence in the early 1980s. Featuring animated versions of era superstars like Cyndi Lauper, Billy Idol, Paul McCartney and Pat Benatar, the ad helped etch MTV into the stratosphere of 80s pop culture, while burning the catchphrase into the minds of a generation.A film accompanying the MTV portion of the show offers outtakes of the filming sessions where some of the 80s’ most famous rock stars endlessly utter “I want my MTV!”, trying to get the catchphrase just right. “It’s people like Cyndi Lauper, the Police, Peter Wolf just saying it over and over again. I want people to hear ‘I want my MTV!’ over and over again in the gallery!” Magliozzi laughed.It’s Alive! ends with the advent of digital, which Magliozzi sees as a fundamental shift of the medium, comparing it to streaming music versus listening to it on vinyl. “A film print is a mechanical object, when it goes into a projector it’s alive, viewers can feel it,” he said. “With many of the films we’re screening for the show, we had a choice between digital print or a 35mm print, and in most cases we’re going with the 35 because people can just sense it, it’s a physical thing.”Beyond being a buffet of a century’s worth of incredible animation, Magliozzi hopes that It’s Alive! will be a way of bringing generations together. Whether you watched Sesame Street in the 1970s or the 2010s, you can come to MoMA’s galleries and be dazzled by something that’s probably quite new and thrilling, hopefully connecting with others outside of your age group. “It’s a very cross-generational thing,” Magliozzi. “Children love it, adults love it. It’s a bonding experience, so it’s really fun to do for that reason.”It’s Alive! A Century of Animation from the Collection is on display at theMuseum of Modern Artin New York from 1 AugustExplore more on these topicsArtAnimation in filmMuseum of Modern ArtExhibitionsMuseumsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a great comedy drama about a flawed Muslim American | Television | The Guardian
description: Ramy Youssef’s excellent show finally returns to UK terrestrial TV. Plus: a post-apocalyptic origin story. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Ramy Youssef’s excellent show finally returns to UK terrestrial TV. Plus: a post-apocalyptic origin story. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Ramy Youssef and Julian Sergi in Ramy.Photograph: Jon Pack/HULUView image in fullscreenRamy Youssef and Julian Sergi in Ramy.Photograph: Jon Pack/HULUTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: a great comedy drama about a flawed Muslim AmericanRamy Youssef’s excellent show finally returns to UK terrestrial TV. Plus: a post-apocalyptic origin story. Here’s what to watch this eveningHannah J Davies,Alexi Duggins,Jack Seale,Hollie RichardsonandSimon WardellFri 31 Jul 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRamy12.10am, Channel 4Four years on from its release, the third season of Ramy Youssef’s great comedy drama about a deeply flawed Muslim American gets a UK terrestrial airing. The good news is that it has aged rather brilliantly: in particular, the second episode of this double bill featuring a disastrous Tinder date.Hannah J DaviesElgar at the Proms7pm, BBC FourA night celebrating the great British composer. Ryan Wigglesworth leads the BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra through Elgar’s First Symphony, plus there’s archive footage of Sheku Kanneh-Mason’s earlier Proms performance of the composer’s much loved Cello Concerto.Alexi DugginsGranite Harbour8pm, BBC OneA workmanlike Scottish crime drama now in its third season, with the bones of the story becoming visible in this, the middle of three episodes. The discovery of a murder weapon leads DC Lindo (Romario Simpson) and team to think they know what they’re dealing with, but then further information leads them down an even darker path.Jack SealeStation Eleven9pm, Sky AtlanticView image in fullscreenDrawing inspiration … Miranda (Danielle Deadwyler) in Station Eleven.Photograph: StarzplayThis adaptation of the bestselling post-apocalypse novel starts with a flashback episode to 2005 – and it shows the origins of the Station Eleven graphic novel. In Chicago, Miranda (Danielle Deadwyler) is drawing first sketches of Dr Eleven when an actor, Arthur (Gael García Bernal), takes an interest.Hollie RichardsonAnn Droid9.30pm, BBC OneMore funny, and at times deeply touching, comedy about a widow and her socially awkward robot. Sue (Sue Johnston) and her carer droid Linda (Diane Morgan) go on a trip to the seaside, where a fortune-teller gives Sue a message from her late husband, telling her to have fun!HRGrimsburg9.30pm, Sky OneJon Hamm’s gravelly tones voice a pot-bellied police detective in this silly adult cartoon. Marvin Flute returns to his home of Grimsburg – “The town I left behind like a perfectly timed elevator fart” – to solve bizarre cases.HRFilmView image in fullscreen‘Delicious incongruity’ … Bob Odenkirk in Normal.Photograph: Ent-movie/AlamyNormal (Ben Wheatley, 2025),8.25am, 8pm, 1.10am,Sky Cinema PremiereIf you’ve seen Bob Odenkirk in the black ops caper Nobody you’ll know what to expect from Ben Wheatley’s spry thriller. The actor plays Ulysses Richardson, the temporary sheriff of the small town of Normal, Minnesota. There’s nothing normal about Normal, of course, which Ulysses discovers when a bank heist goes wrong and he realises it’s not the robbers he has to be worried about. The slapstick gunplay of Wheatley’s own Free Fire mingles with the deadpan drama of Fargo and the still delicious incongruity of Odenkirk packing heat.Simon WardellExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What we’re reading: writers and readers on the books they enjoyed in July | Books | The Guardian
description: Max Porter, Daisy Johnson, Avni Doshi and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the comments
Author: Daisy Johnson
Headline: Max Porter, Daisy Johnson, Avni Doshi and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the comments
Content: View image in fullscreenWhat we're readingBooksWhat we’re reading: writers and readers on the books they enjoyed in JulyMax Porter, Daisy Johnson, Avni Doshi and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the commentsMax Porter,Daisy Johnson, Avni Doshi and Guardian readersFri 31 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMax Porter, writerGrief is the Thing With Feathers: why Max Porter’s strange but ‘magnificent’ debut keeps inspiring adaptationsRead moreI recently readGaining GroundbyJoan Barfoot. It’s one of the best novels I’ve ever read about what it means to live with others, or decide not to; what we owe the people we love, the natural world, and ourselves. I also really enjoyedRobert Frost, by Robert Frost and Stacy Skolnik. It’s notthatRobert Frost; it’s an itinerant young American Robert Frost who jots down his thoughts and observations on homelessness, food, value, music, drugs, the philosophical wastelands of contemporary life, and Stacy Skolnik has turned them into these delightful, oddly profound, poems. Also, coming soon,End Times Fascismby Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. Everyone should read it. It tells us exactly what’s going on.Max Porter is the author of books includingShyandGrief Is the Thing With FeathersRichard, Guardian readerI am readingHeadlightsby the American horror writer CJ Leede. This is her third novel. I think she has the potential to be the 21st century’s Stephen King – she’s that good! Headlights is a pitch-black horror novel with overtones of Silence of the Lambs and Osgood Perkins’ fabulous filmLonglegs. It is also a love letter to King’s The Shining and has a strong environmental message too, concerning man’s uneasy and destructive relationship with the natural world. Leede is such a wonderful writer of prose. Her characters are three-dimensional and you care about them almost immediately (which makes what she does to some of them all the more horrible!). She has an obvious love of the American landscape and describes it beautifully, and the book’s relationship with The Shining will have horror lovers squealing with delight – there are little Easter eggs peppered throughout the book.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDaisy Johnson, writerDaisy Johnson: ‘I wasn’t a fan of David Szalay, but Flesh is a masterpiece’Read moreLately I am to be found loudly and excitedly recommendingThe Corner That Held Themby Sylvia Townsend Warner, first published in 1948. Set over 200 years and taking in the Black Death, the Great Revolt of 1381 and much bickering, the novel follows a convent of nuns living in the British Fenlands. I’ve also loved readingThe Empusium, an equally claustrophobic book by Olga Tokarczuk which, thrillingly, is described as “a health resort horror story” on the cover. It follows a young man with failing health who visits a sanatorium in the mountains to recover. It is a rather glorious and surreal romp.Long Wave by Daisy Johnson is published by Jonathan Cape (£18.99). To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may applySarah, Guardian readerThis month (perhaps not so subconsciously) I seem to have been drawn mostly to both fiction and nonfiction featuring women facing personal challenges. In fiction,Tamarinby Priya Hein andUnder Waterby Tara Menon have been favourites this month, and I think the books pair well together: both feature women who return to their homeland after life-changing experiences. In nonfiction,My Cantopop Nightsby Emma-Lee Mosswas a thoroughly enjoyable read about one woman’s search to find home and her identity in Hong Kong. Her experiences of motherhood resonated with me, and I was transported back to my own time spent in Hong Kong a decade ago. Finally, a hybrid of the two genres:Said the Deadby Doireann Ní Ghríofa. I devoured this book, which vividly brings to life the stories of a number of women who inhabited a psychiatric hospital in Ireland in the 1890s and early 20th century, the result of obsessive research by the author.Avni Doshi, writerView image in fullscreenAuthor Avni Doshi.Photograph: Aranka IsraniWhile researching for my next novel, in which one of the characters is an artist, I came across a brilliant book calledColourby Victoria Finlay. Finlay dives deep into the fascinating history of where colour comes from. It reads like an adventure into the painter’s palette. Expect intrigue, beetles and dead bodies.Andrea Bajani’sThe Anniversarywas also a recent favourite. The story follows a grown man unpicking the web of his painful childhood. A slim book written in crisp prose, there isn’t a word out of place. I read it in one sitting. I also loved and have been widely recommendingA Splinteringby Dur e Aziz Amna, in which a cunning and ambitious woman from a village in Pakistan reshapes the future that was set for her. Rarely have I read a character so ruthless and irresistible. Her hunger growls on the page.The First Houseby Avni Doshi is published by Hamish Hamilton (£16.99). title: The best recent poetry – review roundup | Poetry | The Guardian
description: Small Birds Singing by Matthew Welton; The Channel by Jana Prikryl; Stepmother by Helen Mort; Drunken Driving by Martina Evans
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Small Birds Singing by Matthew Welton; The Channel by Jana Prikryl; Stepmother by Helen Mort; Drunken Driving by Martina Evans
Content: The city through the seasons in Small Birds Singing.Photograph: Cavan Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe city through the seasons in Small Birds Singing.Photograph: Cavan Images/AlamyPoetry roundupPoetryReviewThe best recent poetry – review roundupSmall Birds Singing by Matthew Welton; The Channel by Jana Prikryl; Stepmother by Helen Mort; Drunken Driving by Martina EvansPhilip TerryFri 31 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSmall Birds Singingby Matthew Welton (Carcanet, £12.99)Written in unrhymed couplets that shrink and grow across the page like a concertina going through its scales, Welton’s poems focus attention on the city through the seasons: weeds through concrete, wasps emerging from the gaps between bricks, frozen towels on a clothesline, the shadows of jackdaws on a lawn. His gaze is neutral, and it often falls on that which we’d normally turn away from, things slightly out of place, or that disturb our sense of propriety: “more cardboard in the recycling bin / than the recycling bin can contain”. This is a poetry of things, like the poetry of Francis Ponge, but as Welton says: “no thinginess without thought”. Welton’s thoughts – though whether they are his or whether they emerge from his surroundings or from the act of writing itself, it is impossible to say – are couched in deliciously riddling couplets: “it is not the habit of patterns / to emphasise the pattern of habits”. He reminds us forcefully that poetry is all around us and within us, that anything can go in a poem: a sandwich, a desiccated lump of duck shit, the pile of junk left outside a house during a refurbishment. Poems can mirror our world in all its messiness, and in doing so let us see it a little bit better.View image in fullscreenThe Channelby Jana Prikryl (Faber, £12.99The casual violence of King Lear, the greed, the bureaucracy, and the indifference to human life, make the play particularly resonant to contemporary audiences. In her fourth collection, Prikryl channels the voice of Cordelia to think back through her own family story of displacement from the Czech Republic. Shakespeare’s Lear becomes “a document of fact / of things that happened and keep happening”, enabling Prikryl to explore her own separation from friends and family and her experiences of migration, where home is nowhere. In Dover Calais a ferry trip to France is meshed with the story of Cordelia’s exile, morphing into an account of a ferry disaster which in turn cuts to a scene where refugees make for shore in small boats: “Waves / unreal, and driving rain, the two-year-old / left face-down on a beach nine years ago / came up for me”. Like the scissored-off hospital undershirt in In the Mould, Prikryl’s language cuts off, ending abruptly: “or was the famous sweetness / of grandmother a bluff / which through and through was too”. This rewiring of the sentence creates dazzling leaps of thought, jumping from refugee camps to Shakespeare’s Fool battling with a tsunami of text messages to dissident window cleaners out of the novels of Milan Kundera to tender moments shared with her father. It’s a bold “stepping out of form” that turns its back on the neatness of the lyric, and by doing so creates a new poetic language which, like the language of Calvino in Invisible Cities, is able to connect everything to everything.View image in fullscreenStepmotherby Helen Mort (Chatto & Windus, £12.99)The ubiquity of the stepmother in fairytales has been explained by psychoanalyst Bruno Bettelheim as enabling the child to keep the image of the good mother intact. Marina Warner reminds us that their presence is historically connected to the high mortality rate of mothers in childbirth, though today women are more likely to find themselves in the role as a result of divorce. Here Mort explores her own experience of this neglected dimension of maternity alongside its representation in myth. “Better a serpent than a stepmother,” said Euripides, and the sentiment is reinforced across a range of stories where we witness stepmothers abandon their children in forests or simply decapitate them to be rid of them once and for all. Mort shows how traditional images of bad stepmothers are perpetuated in news stories and film, but she finds the modern experience repeating history in more subtle ways: she is jealous of her stepdaughter’s figure, distantly echoing the stepmother in Snow White, or, in an inversion of the way Cinderella is treated, it is the stepmother who finds herself pushed to the edge of her own household by photographs of the husband’s first marriage. Mort’s poems are a vivid compendium of stories, but they also offer ways of escaping the trap of myth: “You did not pick your stepchildren. Nor did they pick you. / But every day you can choose to love each other.”View image in fullscreenDrunken Drivingby Martina Evans (Carcanet, £12.99)This electrifying sequel to Evans’s 2023 sonnet sequence The Coming Thing is set 10 years on. Imelda, having put the Cork punk scene behind her, is now a young mother, married to Carl, working shifts at Pentonville prison and learning to negotiate the spiderweb crossroads of London in her red Astra. Appropriately for this carceral environment, the sonnets come cuffed with quotations taken from prison protocols, driving manuals and the novel Dracula: “With strained ears, I listened, and heard downstairs the grinding of the key in the great lock and the falling back of the heavy door.” Immediately we are plunged into a world of dangerous driving, vampiric warders, overcrowding and casual racism. Conversation within the prison walls is frowned upon but outside the banter flies between Imelda and her father Justin: “When I said Pentonville was a Chamber / of Horrors, Justin said, You’ve got an imagination. I’ll give you that. / But I don’t need one! I said. Half of Madame Tussaud’s waxworks were / hanged there. Justin snorted, Highly-strung, like yourself?” Pumped up with adrenaline, fuelled by alcohol, and peppered with razor-sharp observations, this reads like Porridge on steroids.Explore more on these topicsPoetryPoetry roundupreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A World Elsewhere review – chaotic thrills as kids sail, fight and fall through trap doors | Children's theatre | The Guardian
description: Family show brings gleeful playfulness to the story of a 12-year-old whose escape into extravagant daydreams has begun to alarm him
Author: Miriam Gillinson
Headline: Family show brings gleeful playfulness to the story of a 12-year-old whose escape into extravagant daydreams has begun to alarm him
Content: Larks … Kerry Frampton as Sarah, Tanvi Virmani as Cobweb and Kyle Ndukuba as Cass in A World Elsewhere at Shakespeare's Globe.Photograph: Manuel HarlanView image in fullscreenLarks … Kerry Frampton as Sarah, Tanvi Virmani as Cobweb and Kyle Ndukuba as Cass in A World Elsewhere at Shakespeare's Globe.Photograph: Manuel HarlanChildren's theatreReviewA World Elsewhere review – chaotic thrills as kids sail, fight and fall through trap doorsSam Wanamaker Playhouse, LondonFamily show brings gleeful playfulness  to the story of a 12-year-old whose escape into extravagant daydreams has begun to alarm himMiriam GillinsonFri 31 Jul 2026 06.28 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 07.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe more children you bring along to this new family show – the latest co-production from the Globe theatre and Splendid Productions – the more fun you’ll have. It’s ostensibly about a 12-year-old school boy, Cass, who is struggling with his doubts and fears and considering reining in his imagination altogether. However, what makes this stubbornly ambitious production so special is the gleeful sense of playfulness it ignites in the young audience, as well as the parents watching alongside them.View image in fullscreenCracking make-believe … Kerry Frampton as Sarah and Kyle Ndukuba as Cass in A World Elsewhere.Photograph: Manuel HarlanThe story unfolds in young Cass’s imagination; a place populated by a host of cracking make-believe characters. There’s classical Shakespearean actor Sarah, played with a twinkling sense of pomposity by Kerry Frampton (also a co-writer on the show). Then there’s Tanvi Virmani’s plucky Cobweb - a minor Shakespearean character who has stuck around in Cass’s mind thanks to a brilliant production of A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Finally we have Zachary Willis’s Big Guy, one of Cass’s favourite TV characters, who spends most of his time enacting very silly and very funny play-fights.Much of the show is spent larking around with the gang, while Cass (Kyle Ndukuba) sulks moodily on the edges of the action. Together we sail the seas, summon up huge swaying forests and battle monsters, all directed with a lovely light touch from Lucy Cuthbertson. As Cass’s anxiety grows stronger, Rose Revitt’s design sparks into thrilling life. Actors are swallowed up by trap doors, smoke billows through the theatre and a huge, looming shadow-puppet threatens to engulf us all.It’s all effortlessly captivating until the second half, when things get a touch too meta-theatrical and ultimately pretty confusing. There’s a complicated strand about the importance of messiness and fear, and a slightly buried idea about just how boring our lives, stories and Shakespeare’s plays would be without a little bit of chaos. It’s a lot to fold in to a loosely constructed family show, and the younger children’s eyes begin to glaze over. But it isn’t long before the fun begins again and we’re reviving Cass’s friends with some magic dust, singing and tickling – all thanks to suggestions happily bellowed out from the audience.At Globe theatre, London,until 30 AugustExplore more on these topicsChildren's theatreTheatreShakespeare's GlobereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the art-pop showtunes of Luki and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Combining grand melodrama with nuanced emotional character, Lucy Duncan and producer Niac’s collaboration sounds both timeless and true
Author: Claire Biddles
Headline: Combining grand melodrama with nuanced emotional character, Lucy Duncan and producer Niac’s collaboration sounds both timeless and true
Content: Wisdom and fallibility … Lucy Duncan AKA Luki.Photograph: Matthew Arthur WilliamsView image in fullscreenWisdom and fallibility … Lucy Duncan AKA Luki.Photograph: Matthew Arthur WilliamsAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the art-pop showtunes of Luki and the week’s best new tracksCombining grand melodrama with nuanced emotional character, Lucy Duncan and producer Niac’s collaboration sounds both timeless and trueClaire BiddlesandBen Beaumont-ThomasFri 31 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromHastings, UKRecommended if you likeMary Margaret O’Hara, Tori Amos, Fiona AppleUp nextOld Feelings EP out now, album to follow later in 2026The first time listening to Luki feels like a miraculous discovery of something timeless and true, as though they’ve been waiting patiently to be discovered in the noisy maelstrom of contemporary pop music. The collaborative alias of singer/composer Lucy Duncan and producer Niac, Luki write off-kilter showtunes performed as baroque art songs, embodying a seemingly contradictory combination of grand melodrama and nuanced emotional character.Luki’s debut albumWispswas released by the excellent Glasgow-based tape label GLARC in 2018, followed by a sporadic string of singles over subsequent years. With the new EPOld Feelings, the project appears to be building up to something more substantial. The title track feels like a climactic ballad from a lost, late-period Sondheim musical by way of 90s Celine Dion: all rolling pianos and wry regrets, with synth lines lingering like dry ice. Strong, direct and rich with character, Duncan’s voice shares the wisdom and fallibility that the great Mary Margaret O’Hara has in spades.Elsewhere on the EP, Luki’s take on Such a Small Love imagines Scott Walker remade by Sensual World-era Kate Bush. The eight minute long I Think I Know is tricksier, akin to the experimental edges of Tori Amos or Fiona Apple, meandering through sections of spoken word and textural electronics. Old Feelings is both a tantalising taster of a forthcoming album – due to feature collaborations with Robbie Ellen, AKA art-pop songwriterPersonnel– and a genuinely remarkable set of songs in its own right.Claire BiddlesThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenOn heavy form … Dis Fig.Photograph: Camille BlakeDis Fig – The Account (ft the Wind Between)We loved her thunderous collab album with the Body, and Felicia Chen is on equally heavy form here, singing trip-hop vox and letting off bassy depth charges under the Wind Between’s rapped existential screed.Blonde Redhead – Blood SpilledThe art-rockers’ one-off single is no casual interstitial release, but a genuine epic, expanding across six minutes like a hot air balloon in burnt-sunset hues that keeps filling and floating away: astoundingly beautiful.Jae Stephens – Sugar TrapAlready a fave among pop musos, the US artist feels as if she’s one step away from proper stardom thanks to high-tempo, dancefloor-flirtation snappers like this, full of strutting, mane-tossing energy.Prodigal – The DoorBlending Deftones-style seriousness with the kind of sicko riffage that compels your tongue out of your mouth, this majestic moshpit detonator demonstrates that this new UK band are the real deal.163Margs – Clock ItThis MC is one of the most sprightly in London’s post-drill marketplace – check 2024’s Superstar if you haven’t heard it – and here he dances his flow through dreamy flutes and strings.Kade Young – MetallicMake sure any glassware is away from the edges of shelves if you stick on the Baltimore producer’s maximally vibrational, awesomely designed sub-bass, topped here with footwork-ish chopped-up vox.Essence Martins – Red VelvetNamed after the type of cake loved by her ex, this track sees the UK singer-songwriter – admired by SZA – reflect on heartbreak, but the swell of beautiful Coldplay-ish sound suggests she’s being carried to a new chapter.Ben Beaumont-ThomasSubscribe to the
