title: Arca: XXXXX review – a wild, brilliant album that taps into our bodies’ most feral frequencies  | Arca | The Guardian
description: In the follow-up to her Kick series, Arca jumbles the building blocks of electronic music to create a beautiful, disorienting sound world
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: In the follow-up to her Kick series, Arca jumbles the building blocks of electronic music to create a beautiful, disorienting sound world
Content: Arca.Photograph: Cassandra AntoniadesView image in fullscreenArca.Photograph: Cassandra AntoniadesArcaReviewArca: XXXXX review – a wild, brilliant album that taps into our bodies’ most feral frequencies(XL)In the follow-up to her Kick series, Arca jumbles the building blocks of electronic music to create a beautiful, disorienting sound worldShaad D'SouzaFri 31 Jul 2026 04.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenXXXXX’s cover artXXXXX, the new album by Venezuelan producer-vocalist Arca, is reportedly laden with meaning: a press release claims that “suspended between posthuman augmentation and raw emotion, XXXXX exposes the mainframe”. But the reason Arca, real name Alejandra Ghersi, has become such a star of electronic music – and a mainstream-adjacent one at that – is not because she lets philosophy postgrads in Berlin write her marketing copy: it’s because, for well over a decade, she has been putting out records like XXXXX, which seem to tap into the body’s most primal, feral frequencies better than nearly anyone else. That ability has resulted in recent callups to collaborate onMadonna’s Confessions IIand remix pop singerAddison Rae, and she has amassed a large, loyal fanbase – uncommon for someone making such outre music.‘It was a way of processing violences I’ve survived’: how iconoclastic musician Arca beat burnout with frenzied paintingRead moreThe follow-up to her phenomenalKick series– five albums, each highlighting a different side of Arca’s work – XXXXX sometimes channels the frenetic feel of Aphex Twin (as on Everything) and zeroes in on the wild, footwork-y high-tempo club music she made her name with (like on Fxck, a breathless and grimy rebuke to patriarchy). But it also delves more deeply into worlds the musician has previously skirted around. The sound of a tolling bell on Willow rings into a song that’s harsh and uncompromising; Raver jumbles the building blocks of classic mainstream EDM into a piece of beautiful, disorienting sound design.The music on XXXXX often sounds like tracks from multiple Kick albums layered atop one another: elements of classical composition, deconstructed club music and pop all fight for dominance. The resulting album is one of Arca’s densest and best: music for the body and brain that is unrelenting and unerringly brilliant.Explore more on these topicsArcaElectronic musicExperimental musicalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: John Tilbury: At Home album review – an eclectic and extraordinary treasure trove | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The great interpreter of Morton Feldman and a towering figure of experimental music signs off with four discs of intimate, revelatory recordings
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The great interpreter of Morton Feldman and a towering figure of experimental music signs off with four discs of intimate, revelatory recordings
Content: Experimental music … John Tilbury, whose final release gathers intimate home recordings made over eight years.View image in fullscreenExperimental music … John Tilbury, whose final release gathers intimate home recordings made over eight years.Classical musicReviewJohn Tilbury: At Home album review – an eclectic and extraordinary treasure troveJohn Tilbury(Another Timbre, four CDs)The great interpreter of Morton Feldman and a towering figure of experimental music signs off with four discs of intimate, revelatory recordingsClive PagetFri 31 Jul 2026 02.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 02.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFew have made a more significant contribution to the fields of contemporary, improvised and experimental music than John Tilbury. When, at 82, he decided to end his live appearances, Simon Reynell, founder of Another Timbre, asked if he might occasionally visit the pianist’s home in Deal, on the Kent coast, and record whatever happened to be on his mind. Eight years later, Tilbury has decided to hang up his hat for good, hence this four-disc set celebrating a unique artist and musical pioneer.View image in fullscreenJohn Tilbury: At Home.Photograph: Another TimbreMorton Feldman admired the “swagger” of Tilbury and the British avant garde, and the pianist went on to become perhaps the US composer’s leading interpreter. His recording of Madame Press Died Last Week at Ninety is authoritative, a masterclass in spontaneous phrasing and sonic sensitivity.Feldman’s vaunted restraint hovers over several works here, including music by friends from Tilbury’s time with Cornelius Cardew’s revolutionary Scratch Orchestra. Highlights include John Lely’s hypnotic Sycamore, five pensive nocturnes by Mark R Taylor and Dave Smith’s Al Contrario, a brooding contrapuntal fantasy honouring maverick French composer Charles-Valentin Alkan. For Samuel Beckett, an improvisation with pianist Sebastian Lexer taken from a 2005 concert, is one of several archival recordings included here and perhaps the most purely beautiful music in the box.More quirky contributions include Guillaume de Machaut arranged by Kurtág, and an extraordinary recording made by Klaus Filip of Swiss dust particles, combined with an inside-piano improvisation captured in Deal. A handful of pieces were written for Tilbury’s sea-air-weathered clavichord, its deliriously plinkety-plonk tuning left to the whims of nature. Christopher Hobbs’ Five Pieces, for example, sounds like a baroque suite written for the Mad Hatter’s tea party.An eclectic treasure chest of discoveries.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: My family is coming apart – so it’s time for one last video game session | Games | The Guardian
description: I wanted our last family games night to be the best fun we’ve ever had. Maybe we should have stuck with Mario Kart …
Author: Dominik Diamond
Headline: I wanted our last family games night to be the best fun we’ve ever had. Maybe we should have stuck with Mario Kart …
Content: ‘Games remind us that we always have more things in common than we sometimes feel’ …Photograph: Interfoto/Alamy Stock PhotoView image in fullscreen‘Games remind us that we always have more things in common than we sometimes feel’ …Photograph: Interfoto/Alamy Stock PhotoGamesMy family is coming apart – so it’s time for one last video game sessionDominik DiamondI wanted our last family games night to be the best fun we’ve ever had. Maybe we should have stuck with Mario Kart …Fri 31 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 19.16 EDTShareIt is the end of an era for the Diamond family. For 20 years, there have been five of us living together. It has not been easy. Militant vegan daughters, sons who have inherited Scottish tempers, and a youngest child who attracts trouble like an industrial magnet, have meant our house has been conflict-laden at times. Throw in the fact that we are beset with all manner of mental health bobbins and chronic illnesses that resulted in two of our three kids almost dying in hospitals and you get a family that is combustible – but extremely close.Through it all, we had games. They always brought us back together. Not just us all hunkering over Super Mario Kart like some kind of UN-mandated family therapy, but the conversations that happen when any of us spy another playing something new.Gamesare a cultural touchstone that helped us crack through the veneer of disagreements and distrust and remind us that we have more things in common than we sometimes feel.View image in fullscreen‘UN-mandated family therapy’ … Mario Kart 8 Deluxe.Photograph: NintendoBut now we are moving out of the house we have shared for years. My wife has to go back to the UK for family reasons, #1 Child is moving in with her boyfriend and youngest child is moving in with a friend. This leaves the Son and I – we are moving into an apartment for the next few months, which Charlie is already dubbing the bro-tel. (I am filled with equal parts excitement and dread about this.)So I wanted one last family games night to remind us of simpler times before we all go our separate ways. I wanted it to be the best fun we have ever had. I wanted … Quiplash!Quiplash is one of the most important games in the history of our family, because I view it as the game that trained my kids to be funny. Seeing them all become fairly high-level comedy beings has been the greatest thrill of my life as a dad.It’s a simple “fill in the blanks or answer the question with something funny to get the most votes” game, the beauty of it being you can play using mobile phones as controllers and five people can play. That’s why I have it as a go-to. Getting any family together to do anything is like herding particularly wilful sheep, and when was the last time you saw a shepherd try that while hunting for 10 working batteries for gaming controllers? Exactly.It’s not just the genuinely funny answers that get votes: there is also a lot of love for old family running gags, most of which are at my expense, usually my baldness or my rigidity with rules.However, while I am impressed by my grownup kids’ quick-thinking quippery, I am still appalled by some of their spelling. So for our final game, I introduce a rule that you can only vote for answers spelt correctly. This rule is not just ignored but aggressively mocked with answers that are part punchline and part Welsh street name.I am in last place because they can tell which answers are from me. So, I start deliberately entering badly spelt answers to confuse them, so they give up trying to play the game seriously and while I am writing quality punchlines such as “God said ‘wrong door’” (you had to be there), I am faced with answers from them such as “pee pee poo poo”.And then the rows break out. My two youngest kids work at the same trendy bar/restaurant, and they have issues with each other. One suggested a role for the other there that they are not happy about, so they declare they never want to work in the same place together again. Impressively, during the argument, my son still manages to answer “skittle flavour that just missed the cut” with “narly Netenyahu nectarine”. Which almost got my vote until I noticed that neither Netanyahu nor gnarly are spelt like that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe row escalates. Wife and #1 Child have reverted to doomscrolling on their phones instead. No one wants to play. It’s all falling apart. Not just this desperate attempt at one final family gaming session, but the family itself. In one week, our matriarch, the most important one of us, will be on the other side of the Atlantic. In a couple of months, #1 Child could be the only one still actually living on this side of it.View image in fullscreenMemories flooded back … Kirby’s Return to Dream Land Deluxe.Photograph: NintendoMemories start flooding back: the summer I spent playing Super Mario Sunshine with #1 Child when she was five. Evading guard dogs in the snow with my son on Call of Duty: Modern Warfare when he wasn’t much older. Seeing my youngest child fall in love with Kirby. The years of Mario Kart, Mortal Kombat and Just Dance. The conversations. The debates. The windups. There is such joy in those moments but now they are spilling through my fingers like water.I think of all the times in recent years when one of the kids has asked me if I want to play a game with them. And I’ve been “too busy”. I wish I had all those moments back to create more memories.My wife, ever the peacemaker of the family, declares the next day that we will have one more go at this the night before she goes back to Blighty. That prospect seems as good as it gets right now.Explore more on these topicsGamesFamilycommentShareReuse this content

title: Benjamina Ebuehi’s summer berry dutch baby recipe | Summer food and drink | The Guardian
description: Think giant sweet yorkshire pud filled with a lake of summer berry compote
Author: Benjamina Ebuehi
Headline: Think giant sweet yorkshire pud filled with a lake of summer berry compote
Content: Benjamina Ebuehi's Summer berry dutch baby.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenBenjamina Ebuehi's Summer berry dutch baby.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.The sweet spotSummer food and drinkBenjamina Ebuehi’s summer berry dutch baby recipeThink giant sweet yorkshire pud filled with a lake of summer berry compote … that’s some brunch!Benjamina EbuehiFri 31 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis pancake/yorkshire pudding hybrid is nothing if not fun. The edges crisp and puff up in the most dramatic way, making for a very impressive brunch centrepiece that makes a change from regular pancakes. Although delicious just with some icing sugar, I’ve filled this one with a quick fruit compote to make the most of summer berries. The juices soak into the base, making way for my favourite part of a yorkshire: the slightly soggy bottom.Summer berry dutch babyWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep5 minRest20 minCook40 minServes4For the berry compote100gstrawberries,hulled and roughly chopped100g blackberries50g raspberries1 tbsp lemon juice2 tbsp caster sugarFor the batter110g plain flour25g caster sugar¼ tsp salt3 large eggs240mlwhole milk20g salted butterTo serve250ml double cream2 tbsp maple syrup,plus extra to serve½ tspvanilla bean pasteIcing sugar,to dustStart by making the compote. Add all the ingredients to a small pan and heat gently for a few minutes, until the fruits have softened but still hold their shape. Remove from the heat, set aside to cool completely, then chill until needed.Whip the double cream, maple syrup and vanilla together until soft peaks form; chill until you’re ready to serve.To make the batter, add the flour, sugar and salt to a large jug and mix to combine. Add the eggs and whisk to a thick mixture, then slowly pour in the milk, mixing again until the batter is smooth. (Alternatively, add everything to a blender.) Let the batter rest at room temperature for 20 minutes.Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7 and put a 25cm cast-iron pan in the oven to heat. Once hot, add the butter to the pan, carefully swirling it around, then put the pan back in the oven for one to two minutes, until the butter is melted and bubbling.Remove the pan from the oven, pour in the batter and bake for 15-20 minutes, making sure not to open the oven door in the first 15 minutes. The dutch baby is done when the edges are puffy and crisp, and there’s no wobble in the middle.Let the dutch baby cool for five minutes before spooning on the whipped cream, berry compote, an extra drizzle of maple syrup and a dusting of icing sugar. Serve straight away, because the dutch baby will begin to deflate.Explore more on these topicsSummer food and drinkThe sweet spotFoodDessertFruitBrunchrecipesShareReuse this content

title: A bitter pill: are you wasting your money on supplements? | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: Will collagen make you look younger? Could magnesium help you sleep better? Or are the benefits overstated? A dietitian reveals which are worth taking
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Will collagen make you look younger? Could magnesium help you sleep better? Or are the benefits overstated? A dietitian reveals which are worth taking
Content: Photograph: Anil Akkus/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Anil Akkus/Getty ImagesHealth & wellbeingA bitter pill: are you wasting your money on supplements?Will collagen make you look younger? Could magnesium help you sleep better? Or are the benefits overstated? A dietitian reveals which are worth takingJosie PorterFri 31 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMultivitaminsMultivitamins are one of the most commonly used supplements worldwide – but for most people, there isn’t evidence of a huge benefit.One of the largest trials to date found a smallimprovement in memoryamong older adults taking a daily multivitamin. But the difference was tiny, amounting to roughly a quarter of a word in a 20-word recall test. Other outcomes such as mood, immune function and overall wellbeing have generally shown little to no improvement in people who are already meeting their nutritional needs through food.That doesn’t mean multivitamins are pointless. They may be helpful during life stages with higher nutrient requirements, such as pregnancy, or when intake or absorption is lower. But multivitamins are not standardised, so check with your doctor or dietitian what’s best for you.Your best return on investment will always come from real food. Aim to include fruits, vegetables, whole grains, beans, nuts, seeds, dairy (or fortified alternatives) and protein-rich foods every day in order to give your body a good blend of the vitamins, minerals, fibre and plant compounds that supplements can’t fully replicate.CreatineCreatine has been getting a lot of hype lately, even though it’s been around for years. It’s a compound that your body naturally produces, though you can also get very small amounts from red meat and fish.Creatine is stored in your muscles, where it helps provide energy during short bursts of high-intensity exercise. The effects of taking extra creatine are not dramatic, but when combined with training well, eating enough protein and prioritising recovery, it may help you modestlylift heavier weightsorsprint better.Unlike many nutrients, where dietary changes can often achieve similar results to supplementation, there isn’t a practical food-first way to maximise creatine stores.CollagenCollagen is the main structural protein in skin, tendons and connective tissue, and production starts to gradually decline from your mid-20s.Most collagen supplements come in the form of hydrolysed collagen peptides, meaning the protein has been broken down into smaller fragments that are easier to dissolve and digest. They are typically sold as powders that can be mixed into drinks or foods. Several randomised controlled trials suggest that taking these supplements daily for about three months may lead to smallimprovements in skin hydration and elasticity, particularly in women in their 40s and 50s.Collagen supplements are also being studied for tendon and joint health, with some trials suggesting modest improvements. However, these are best seen as a potential edge for very specific groups, such as people withexercise-related joint injuriesor those withhigher training loads, rather than a magic fix or a replacement for food-first strategies.Before thinking about supplements, it’s crucial to make sure you are eating enough protein overall, which for most people is about 30g per meal, to provide the amino acids needed for tissue repair and collagen production, including glycine and proline, alongside adequate vitamin C from fruit and vegetables, which is required for collagen synthesis.Vitamin DOur skin makes vitamin D from sunlight, but in the UK this only really works between late March and early October, when UVB is strong enough. Outside these months, even on bright or warm days, our exposure to the sun is too weak. This is why low vitamin D is more common in winter, and also more likely year-round in people with darker skin, older adults, those who cover their skin, and people who spend most of their time indoors.There are food sources, but they’re limited and usually not enough on their own, which is why it’s recommended to supplement10 micrograms (400 IU) dailyduring autumn and winter. This is mainly for bone health, supporting calcium absorption and reducing the risk of conditions such as rickets and osteomalacia. But more is not better – vitamin D is fat soluble and stored in the body, so avoid very high intakes as these can build up and may cause harm.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Yagi Studio/Getty ImagesMagnesiumMagnesium supplements are getting a lot of attention for improving everything from sleep and muscle cramps to blood pressure and brain health, but the evidence is more underwhelming than the marketing. Most benefits are seen in people with low magnesium intake. This is relevant because the National Diet and Nutrition Survey shows that many people in the UKfall below recommended intakes, largely due to low consumption of nuts, seeds, legumes, whole grains and leafy green vegetables.These foods, which are naturally high in magnesium, also contain other key nutrients from which we can benefit: fibre, healthy fats, vitamin E, or minerals such as iron.Meeting your recommended allowance is easier than it might seem. For example, a bowl of porridge with pumpkin seeds or wholewheat pasta with chickpeas and spinach can provide almost half of your daily magnesium needs.ElectrolytesElectrolyte supplements contain minerals such as sodium, chloride and potassium that help regulate fluid balance. They’re often marketed as a daily hydration essential, but for most people this isn’t supported by science.In reality, our body tightly regulates electrolytes, particularly sodium, which we lose when we sweat. Outside situations involving significant fluid loss, such as long endurance exercise, heavy sweating or illness, most people maintain electrolyte balance throughfood and simply drinking enough water.When sweating a lot, sodium and chloride are the main electrolytes we lose, and these can usually be replaced by adding salt to meals or drinks, which is far cheaper than supplements. As a rough guide, during heavy sweating, sodium losses are around the equivalent of 1g to 3g of salt per hour, which is roughly equivalent to between a couple of pinches and half a teaspoon.Omega-3In the UK, most people don’t meet the recommendation of at leastone portion of oily fishper week, which contains vital omega-3s, including eicosapentaenoic Acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic Acid (DHA), alongside protein, iodine, selenium and vitamin D. Good sources include mackerel, salmon, trout, sardines and anchovies.We can also get omega-3s from plant sources, known as alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), but this is a less efficient way of meeting our needs, as conversion to EPA and DHA is limited. For people who don’t eat fish, algae-based omega-3 supplements can be a practical alternative. Check the label for adequate levels of EPA and DHA, aiming for about 250-500mg combined.AshwagandhaAshwagandha is a herbal supplement with a long history in Ayurvedic medicine. The strongest evidence of any effectiveness relates to stress. People taking ashwagandha often report improvements in stress and sleep quality, alongsidereductions in cortisol levelsof about 10-30%.But most people in these studies don’t have high cortisol levels to begin with. And because cortisol naturally rises and falls throughout the day and plays an important role in the body, it’s not clear whether lowering it when it’s already within a normal range has any meaningful long-term health benefit.Before turning to supplements, it’s worth remembering that eating regular meals with enough protein and fibre helps provide steady fuel for the brain and body and supports more stable blood sugar levels, which can help combat energy dips, irritability and sudden pangs of “hanger”.Fibre (psyllium husk or blends)Fibre supplements can be useful in specific contexts, particularly for symptom management, with psyllium husk having good evidence for bothconstipation and diarrhoea, and modest improvements incholesterol levelslinked to heart health.Outside these targeted uses, we tend to benefit more when we get fibre from a wide range of plant foods. Large observational studies, including data from the American Gut Project, have found eating30 or more different plant foods a weekis associated with greater gut microbiome diversity.This is probably because whole plant foods such as fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds and whole grains provide fibre alongside a range of other compounds, including polyphenols, that aren’t present in isolated supplements. You don’t need to obsess over eating 30, as more research is needed to confirm this number. Just focus on eating as many plants as possible.IronIron is an essential mineral that’s most often low in menstruating women, endurance athletes and people following plant-based diets. It plays a key role in oxygen transport, energy production and cognitive function, so when levels are low, you can feel it.That said, symptoms such as fatigue can be down to many different factors, so a blood test is essential, as more iron is not better. Higher intakes can cause gastrointestinal side effects such as constipation, nausea and abdominal discomfort, and in rare cases can contribute to iron overload.Reduce your risk of deficiency by eating red meat, fish and poultry, and plant-based iron found in lentils, beans, tofu and fortified cereals. Iron from plants is less readily absorbed, but smart pairings with vitamin C-rich foods such as red peppers and kiwis canincrease absorption by up to 300%. Think beans on toast with tomatoes, or overnight quinoa with strawberries.How to build a balanced plateMost of your needs over time can be covered by a simple repeating structure: one protein (for maintenance and repair); two different-coloured plants (for micronutrients and fibre); one fibre-rich starchy carb (for energy); two flavour boosters such as herbs and spices (for polyphenols); and one source of fat (for vitamin absorption). This framework helps you quickly sense-check whether a meal is broadly balanced, without needing to track, measure or optimise every detail.Aim for protein variety across the week by rotating three to five sources – such as eggs, yoghurt or kefir, chicken or turkey, tofu or tempeh, fish, and beans or lentils – in your weekly shop. This also provides a balance of different vitamins, minerals and compounds.Curate a colourful freezer because frozen fruit, vegetables and herbs are often cheaper, just as nutrient-dense and require zero prep. Think mango chunks stirred into yoghurt, edamame added to salads or rice bowls, raspberries on porridge, spinach blended into sauces, or mixed veg folded into egg fried grains.Aim to try one new ingredient, recipe or meal combination each week. Small, repeated exposures to different foods is one of the simplest ways to naturally increase diversity in your diet and broaden your intake of micronutrients.HowNot toTakeSupplements:ADietitian’sGuide toThriving onRealFood by Josie Porterispublished byEburyat £17.99. Prop stylist: Davina MajiView image in fullscreenBanana, medjool date, tahini and sesame crumble muffins.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food stylist and recipe developer: Sonali Shah. Prop stylist: Davina MajiRecipes from FEEDJimi Famurewa’s banana, medjool date, tahini and sesame crumble muffins – recipeNew Guardian Food showFEED with Jimi Famurewatravels the UK in search of food trends. This bake is inspired by the flavours of ‘third culture bakery’ FarhaPaid for byAbout this contentJimi FamurewaFri 31 Jul 2026 05.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 05.06 EDTShareThis recipe is largely inspired by the sweet tahini crunch at the heart of east-London bakery Farha’s mega-selling banana brulee pastry. The savoury depth of tahini tempers the heady, perfumed sweetness of ripe bananas, which can be a little cloying, and also works well with the deep caramel notes of Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference medjool dates and the brown butter.Prep20 minCook30 minServes12100g unsalted butter150g Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference medjool dates,pitted and finely chopped5 tbsp Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference Jersey whole milk200g Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference Scottish whole rolled jumbo oats4 large ripe bananas,peeled60g soured cream1 tsp Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference Madagascan vanilla extract2 Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference free range golden yolk eggs½ tsp bicarbonate of soda1 tsp baking powder½ tsp ground cinnamon3 tbsp tahini3 tbsp Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference Canadian maple syrupCrumble topping1 tbsp Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference Scottish whole rolled jumbo oats1 tbsp sesame seeds1 tbsp demerara cane sugar12 Sainsbury’s cafe style muffin casesBanana, medjool date, tahini and sesame crumble muffinsTo start, heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and line a 12 hole muffin tin with your muffin cases.Add the butter to a small saucepan over a medium heat, and let it melt. Once melted, increase the heat to high and stir the butter regularly as it starts to brown. Once it begins to smell nutty, remove from the heat, pour into a large mixing bowl and leave aside to cool.Return the pan to a medium heat with the milk and the chopped medjool dates. Cook for 2-3 minutes, stirring often, or until the dates have softened completely. Leave aside to cool.Meanwhile, blend your oats in a high speed blender until you have a fine powder – this is your oat flour.Mash the bananas and browned butter in a bowl until smooth. Stir in the soured cream, vanilla extract, eggs and date mixture. Now mix in the oat flour, bicarbonate of soda, baking powder, cinnamon and a pinch of salt until well combined. Leave for 5 minutes. Meanwhile, mix your crumble topping in another bowl.Divide the batter between the muffin cases. Drizzle the tahini over the top of each one and use a skewer to swirl into the batter. Sprinkle the crumble topping over the muffins then put into the oven to bake for 25-30 minutes, or until golden brown and a skewer inserted into the muffins comes out clean.Remove from the oven. Drizzle the maple syrup evenly across the muffins then leave aside to cool in the tin.With thanks to Farha, 42 Leyton High Road, London E15 2BPJimi Famurewa’s banana, medjool date, tahini and sesame crumble muffins – recipeShop the full range of Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference ingredientsWatch the full episode of FEED with Jimi Famurewa onYouTubeandthe GuardianExplore more on these topicsRecipes from FEEDadvertisement featuresShareReuse this content

title: The best ice-cream makers in the UK for gelato, soft serve and sorbets – tested | Ice-cream and sorbet | The Guardian
description: Our writer spent the hottest weeks of the year churning through the top ice-cream makers, from compressor models to the cult favourite Ninja Creami. Here’s the scoop
Author: Danielle Amato
Headline: Our writer spent the hottest weeks of the year churning through the top ice-cream makers, from compressor models to the cult favourite Ninja Creami. Here’s the scoop
Content: View image in fullscreenThe FilterIce-cream and sorbetReviewThe best ice-cream makers in the UK for gelato, soft serve and sorbets – testedOur writer spent the hottest weeks of the year churning through the top ice-cream makers, from compressor models to the cult favourite Ninja Creami. Here’s the scoopKitchen gadgets top chefs can’t live withoutDanielle AmatoFri 31 Jul 2026 12.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Ilove a scoop or two of the good stuff, even more so when the mercury hits 30C and ice-cream starts feeling less like an indulgence and more like an essential survival tool. This is why owning an ice-cream maker has always made sense to me. I’ve been using the original Ninja Creami for years now, but before that I was spending a small fortune on gelato, fruity sorbets, frozen yoghurt and other such desserts from the frozen aisle.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Some might argue that the best ice-cream makers are a luxury, but if you’re a true dessert devotee, I believe they can earn their keep in no time. A tub of Häagen-Dazs will set you back almost £6 nowadays, which is an expensive habit if you’re getting through a pot a week during the hottest months of the year.With your own ice-cream machine, you get an endless supply whenever you fancy it, and you can get creative with flavours, tweaking as you go. It’s also ideal if you have allergies or follow a dairy-free diet, as good allergy-friendly ice-cream can be harder to find. Better still, making your own means you can skip the emulsifiers, artificial flavours, sweeteners and stabilisers found in many shop-bought tubs, so it’s a great option if you’re trying to move away from ultra-processed foods.But with so many options available, where do you start? I’ve taken one for the team – and no doubt my waistline – to test the best ice-cream makers available right now, from trendy soft-serve ice-cream machines to professional-style compressor models.At a glanceBest ice-cream maker overallCasoIceCreamer£278.97 at AmazonBest budget ice-cream makerCuisinartSolo Scoops£33.99 at AmazonBest freeze-first ice-cream makerNinjaCreami NC300£199.99 at SharkNinjaBest ice-cream maker for small freezersNutribulletChill£169.99 at CurrysBest soft-serve ice-cream makerGreenPanFrost ice-cream maker and slushie machine£328.99 at AmazonWhy you should trust meI’ve spent almost a decade researching, testing and reviewing kitchen appliances, which means I’m aware of the very best (and worst) the industry has to offer. I’ve seen appliance trends come and go, and I know what people actually want in their kitchens.I’m also an avid home cook and dinner party host. When I’m not in my kitchen testing appliances on the clock, I’m still there whipping up feasts for my willing partner and friends.How I testedView image in fullscreenWhipping up a storm … each ice-cream maker was assessed on everything from texture to ease of cleaning.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianThe research for this article meant making – and eating – a lot of ice-cream and sorbet (someone had to do it). I put 13 machines through their paces with three recipes on each: Felicity Cloake’sperfect vanilla ice-cream, herlemon sorbetand, where the machine allowed, a more basic throw-it-all-in recipe for strawberry ice-cream made with milk, cream, sugar and macerated strawberries. All the machines also came with their own recipe booklet or app, so I also tested one of these, usually a standard vanilla recipe with double cream.Testing a variety of recipes gave me a sense of how capable and versatile each machine really was, helping to decide whether it’s worthy of taking up precious space on your worktop.As well as making lots of ice-cream, I put on my technical hat to measure churning speeds, record noise levels using a decibel meter, and assess ice crystal formation, as well as the general taste and texture of the results after some time in the freezer.As a certified chore hater, I found that ease of assembly and cleaning were just as important. Waiting 24 hours to taste the results of your prep is one thing; spending another hour to disassemble and scrub clean the machine afterwards is quite another.All ice-cream makers sourced for this article will be donated to charity.The best ice-cream makers for your homeView image in fullscreenCool contenders … the ice-cream machines that went head-to-head in the tests.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianBest ice-cream maker overall:Caso IceCreamerCasoIceCreamerfrom£278.97£280 at Argos£278.97 at AmazonWhat we loveFamily-friendly and easy to useWhat we don’t loveIt’s a worktop hogView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£280 at Argos£278.97 at AmazonA real surprise standout, this model from the little-known brand Caso turned out to be not only the best compressor ice-cream maker, but also my favourite overall. It may be big and bulky, but that shouldn’t put you off (as long as you have the space).Why we love itCaso’s IceCreamer was the easiest machine I used, with very little that can actually go wrong. It has a generous two-litre capacity, and as it’s a compressor model, there was no need to prefreeze anything. Caso recommends chilling any mixture beforehand to improve churning times, but that can be as little as an hour – I’m impatient, and I still got great results after about 30 minutes.I was testing on one of the hottest June days on record, and so I wasn’t expecting miracles when it came to churn times. Impressively, though, the machine produced rich, velvety ice-cream in about 60 minutes using Felicity Cloake’s vanilla recipe. I imagine on a slightly cooler day it would have been even quicker. Unfortunately, the heat did mean my ice-cream began to melt almost instantly once out of the machine, but I managed to get it in the freezer before all the hard work was undone.Despite this, the ice-cream that initially emerged was well frozen yet buttery smooth and had few ice crystals. After a couple of days in the freezer in an airtight container, it still tasted fantastic. It also made light work of the lemon sorbet recipe in about 40 minutes.The IceCreamer has post-churn settings that keep the ice-cream at a frozen temperature for up to 60 minutes, or it just churns without freezing. It also comes with an ice-cream scoop and measuring cup. The bowl was easy to clean and, unlike some other machines here, there weren’t any fiddly parts to handle.It’s a shame that …it’s on the large side – and quite pricey, when not on offer.Machine type:compressorCapacity:2lAverage churn time:1hrNoise level: 67dBDimensions:43 x 28.5 x 28cm (WDH)Wattage:180WWarranty:two yearsCasoIceCreamerfrom£278.97£280 at Argos£278.97 at AmazonWhat we loveFamily-friendly and easy to useWhat we don’t loveIt’s a worktop hogBest budget ice-cream maker:Cuisinart Solo ScoopsCuisinartSolo Scoopsfrom£33.99£39.99 at Lakeland£33.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s compact and easy to useWhat we don’t loveStruggles to produce a good consistencyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£39.99 at Lakeland£33.99 at AmazonLet me temper your expectations here – if you’re spending this little on an ice-cream maker, you’d be silly to expect the world. However, I’m making a case for this mini motor-based machine because it’s so ridiculously simple to use.Why we love itIf you’re short on counter space or can’t justify the £200+ spend on a more premium machine, this is a great option. For occasional ice-cream indulgers who prefer to make their desserts from scratch – I’m thinking people with allergies and dairy-free dessert fans – the Solo Scoops is a compact, low-risk buy.The ice-cream maker comes with a small bowl that makes up to 475ml of ice-cream. It needs to be popped in the freezer for at least 24 hours before use, but takes up very little space. You’ll know it’s ready when you can no longer hear the liquid in the walls of the bowl moving around.Its small size is both a strength and a limitation. Because it relies on the frozen bowl staying cold for as long as possible (which proved a challenge in my furnace-like kitchen), I struggled to achieve the same firm, scoopable texture as the other models here despite using the same vanilla recipe throughout. With a little patience, though, you can get a soft-serve-style ice-cream in about 30 minutes. I got the best results by freezing the bowl for a minimum of 36 hours, chilling the ingredients first, and opting for sorbets over richer, higher-fat ice-creams.If you’re at all worried about longevity given the price (I was), the good news is that parts are easy to replace or repair. The Solo Scoops’ simple design means there’s less to go wrong, and replacement parts are available throughCuisinart’s website.It’s a shame that …while it’s not overly loud, the noise it makes is a bit grating.Machine type:freeze-firstCapacity:475mlAverage churn time:30minsNoise level:66dBDimensions:machine,25 x 21 x 21cm (WDH); bowl, 15 x 15 x 10cm (WDH)Wattage:12WWarranty:three yearsCuisinartSolo Scoopsfrom£33.99£39.99 at Lakeland£33.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s compact and easy to useWhat we don’t loveStruggles to produce a good consistencyBest freeze-first ice-cream maker:Ninja Creami NC300NinjaCreami NC300from£199.99£199.99 at SharkNinja£199.99 at CurrysWhat we loveMakes ice-cream easy; good for healthier optionsWhat we don’t loveIt’s noisy and freakishly tallView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£199.99 at SharkNinja£199.99 at CurrysNinja’s first iteration of the Creami might be getting on a bit now, with newer models featuring improved designs and new settings, but I’ve owned it for years, and it still produces good results.Why we love itNinja’s ice-cream makers are popular for a reason. While some find the brand’s products a little gimmicky (and some are, in my opinion), the Creami stands out because it makes homemade ice-cream genuinely achievable – even for the most reluctant cooks.Over the years, I’ve used my Creami to create all kinds of frozen desserts, from the brand’s signature strawberry ice-cream, which you’ll find in the accompanying booklet, to gelato-style mixes and even frozen smoothie bowls. Unlike other brands on this list, I really rate Ninja’s recipes, too.All recipes I tested, including Felicity’s sorbet and frozen vanilla ice-cream, were fully churned in about three minutes – a couple of minutes faster than the Nutribullet Chill below. I also like the Creami’s flat blade, as it allows it to get right to the end of the tub with ease. The compact tubs are also a plus, fitting easily into the freezer without taking up too much space.I found the Creami easy to clean, and some parts are dishwasher-safe. That’s not to say there aren’t any nooks where mixture can hide, but I haven’t had any problems as long as I’ve cleaned the machine straight away.The machine comes with two 493ml tubs as standard from SharkNinja, although some retailers offer three, and you canbuy more either directly from the manufactureror at otheronline retailers. Spare parts are available throughthe brand’s website, so if anything does go wrong, it’s usually easy to fix at home.It’s a shame that …it’s quite loud, and it’s unusually tall, so might not fit under some kitchen cabinets.Machine type:freeze-firstCapacity: 2 x 493mlAverage churn time:3minsNoise level:81dBDimensions:machine, 40.5 x 16.5 x 27cm (WDH); cup only, 11 x 11 x 10.31cm (WDH)Wattage:800WWarranty:two years (needs to be registered if bought from a third-party retailer)NinjaCreami NC300from£199.99£199.99 at SharkNinja£199.99 at CurrysWhat we loveMakes ice-cream easy; good for healthier optionsWhat we don’t loveIt’s noisy and freakishly tallBest ice-cream maker for small freezers:Nutribullet ChillNutribulletChillfrom£169.99£169.99 at Currys£169.99 at AmazonWhat we loveEasy to use and comes with two tubsWhat we don’t loveIt’s ear-shatteringly loudView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£169.99 at Currys£169.99 at AmazonNutribullet’s Ninja Creami-esque machine makes ice-cream, sorbet and frozen yoghurt with minimum fuss after 24 hours of freezing the mixture in the tub. I was won over by its simple design, and much like the Caso, it was an underdog that surprised me in testing.Why we love itThe Nutribullet Chill isn’t your classic churning ice-cream maker, but it’s easy to use and produced great results with my vanilla ice-cream and lemon sorbet test mixtures. You make and prefreeze your mixture in a compact 470ml tub, then the machine uses a powerful blade to churn it all up from frozen.The texture isn’t quite the same as a classic compressor machine – it’s less velvety – but for its compact size and ease of use, the trade-off is one I’d be happy to make.In performance, it’s similar to the Ninja Creami. The vanilla ice-cream and sorbet recipes came out as expected – less smooth than a compressor but still delicious – although I did find that the recipes in Nutribullet’s accompanying booklet and app do need a little tweaking. Using too much fat in your recipe will give you grainy, greasy-tasting results, as the fat from the cream isn’t stable and solidifies. I had better luck swapping out the double cream in Nutribullet’s recipes with a 40:60 split of double and single cream. It also did a great job making vegan ice-cream.The Nutribullet Chill comes with two 470ml tubs, withextras available to buy. In addition, the blade comes away for easy cleaning, plus replacement parts are available for repairing at home.It’s a shame that …it’s ear-shatteringly loud: I found myself having to leave the room while noise levels were being measured. Something to bear in mind if you’re noise-sensitive like I am.Machine type:freeze-firstCapacity: 2 x 470mlAverage churn time:5minsNoise level:96dBDimensions:machine,19.6 x 20.5 x 43.1cm (WDH); cup only, 10.5 x 10.5 x 15cm (WDH)Wattage:500WWarranty:two years if you keep your receiptNutribulletChillfrom£169.99£169.99 at Currys£169.99 at AmazonWhat we loveEasy to use and comes with two tubsWhat we don’t loveIt’s ear-shatteringly loudBest soft-serve ice-cream maker:GreenPan Frost ice-cream maker and slushie machineGreenPanFrost ice-cream maker and slushie machinefrom£328.99£328.99 at Robert Dyas£328.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMakes soft serve, slushies, milkshakes and moreWhat we don’t loveExpensive and tiresome to cleanView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£328.99 at Robert Dyas£328.99 at AmazonLooking for an all-in-one appliance that will keep both kids and adults happy? Then GreenPan – best known for, well, itspans– turns out to make a surprisingly capable ice-cream maker, too.Why we love it:The GreenPanFrost really impressed in tests. I used it to make a custardy vanilla soft serve using Felicity Cloake’s recipe and a soft-serve “sorbet” – essentially, a lemon slushie. My chilled mixture achieved soft-serve consistency in about 25 minutes, but I did have to tweak the recipe a few times to get it right.Some research revealed that soft serve works best with an additional stabiliser, such as xanthan gum. I tested this with other batches and found it did indeed help the ice-cream hold its shape better. That said, it’s not essential if you’d rather skip it – you’ll simply get a more traditional soft-serve texture. The GreenPan Frost also has settings for making milkshakes, slushies (of the booze and booze-free variety) and similar treats.Unfortunately, one of the downsides of this style of machine is cleaning: it was definitely trickier to clean than others on this list. The Frost has a self-cleaning cycle, while its numerous parts can be disassembled for cleaning in the dishwasher – a bonus for convenience and repairability. My advice is to run the clean cycle with two to three rinses of warm water and a bit of washing-up liquid before taking apart the machine.It’s a shame that …it’s the priciest model on this list.Machine type:compressor/soft serveCapacity: 1.9lAverage churn time:30-40 minsNoise level:58dBDimensions:22.2 x 44.1 x 43.8cm (WDH)Wattage:150WWarranty:two yearsGreenPanFrost ice-cream maker and slushie machinefrom£328.99£328.99 at Robert Dyas£328.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMakes soft serve, slushies, milkshakes and moreWhat we don’t loveExpensive and tiresome to cleanThe best of the restView image in fullscreenSide by side … the Lakeland (right) excelled at gelato-style recipes, while the Cuisinart Frost Fusion (left) took more trial and error.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianLakeland Compressor ice-cream makerLakelandCompressor ice-cream maker£199.99£199.99 at LakelandWhat we loveMakes amazing ice-creamWhat we don’t loveControls aren’t very intuitiveView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£199.99 at LakelandBest for:gelato-style recipesThis is another great classic compressor machine – simple, with gentle churning that’s ideal for gelato. It performed well in tests, with results in about an hour. It’s also easy to clean.Unlike the Caso IceCreamer, the Lakeland Compressor machine doesn’t allow you to adjust the timing mid-cycle. When I set it to 40 minutes and realised halfway through that my mixture needed longer, I couldn’t simply press the “+” button to add more time – I had to stop and restart the machine instead.Thankfully, this didn’t affect the quality of the ice-cream – it was still excellent and held its texture well in the freezer. It was just frustrating that I had to use a workaround for something that should have been a simple adjustment.It didn’t make the final cut because …I found the controls counterintuitive and a pain to use. The Caso IceCreamer offered a slightly better user experience.Machine type:compressor;capacity:1.8l;average churn time:30-40mins;noise level:58dB;dimensions:49.8 x 38.6 x 30.4cm (WDH);wattage:150W;warranty:three yearsLakelandCompressor ice-cream maker£199.99£199.99 at LakelandWhat we loveMakes amazing ice-creamWhat we don’t loveControls aren’t very intuitiveCuisinart Frost Fusion soft-serve ice-cream maker and drinks machineCuisinartFrost Fusionfrom£199.99£299.99 at Lakeland£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMore affordable than some; easy to useWhat we don’t loveThe soft-serve recipe provided doesn’t workView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danielle Amato/The Guardian£299.99 at Lakeland£199.99 at AmazonBest for:familiesI had high hopes for this machine: it’s cheaper and easier to clean than the GreenPan, but I found it more difficult to achieve the right ice-cream consistency. It was always just a bit too soft, even after many tweaks to the recipe.I started with Cuisinart’s own soft-serve recipe from the accompanying booklet, which uses 100% double cream, sugar and vanilla. Unfortunately, the result was less soft serve, more homemade butter. I initially assumed it was my fault, particularly as I’d halved the quantity – but when it happened a second time, I realised something was up.Swapping to a 60:40 mix of single and double cream fixed this – as it did with other machines – but the whole experience was rather unpleasant. I wouldn’t recommend using your soft-serve maker to churn butter, by the way – it’s not particularly easy to clean.However, the slushies were amazing, and the standard vanilla recipe I used throughout testing was decent, although it lacked the structure I would have liked for soft serve. While there’s nothing catastrophically wrong with the machine itself, be prepared for a lot of trial and error.It didn’t make the final cut because …performance wasn’t up there with the GreenPan, although it is slightly more affordable.Machine type:compressor/soft serve;capacity:1.6l;average churn time:30-40mins;noise level:58dB;dimensions:16.4 x 41.4 x 41.8cm (WDH);wattage:150W;warranty:three years at LakelandCuisinartFrost Fusionfrom£199.99£299.99 at Lakeland£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMore affordable than some; easy to useWhat we don’t loveThe soft-serve recipe provided doesn’t workWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenWorth the wait: freeze-first machines, such as the Cuisinart Solo Scoops, need planning ahead, but can produce excellent ice-cream and sorbet.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianFreeze first vs compressor ice-cream makers – what’s the difference?There was a time when you could only get two types of ice-cream maker. The first was a classicfreeze-firstmodel, where you needed to prefreeze the coolant-filled bowl for at least 24 hours before starting. The other was acompressormodel, using a built-in refrigeration unit that freezes the chilled mixture as it churns, taking up to 60 minutes.While these two options are still popular today, others have joined the ice-cream-making party. These include soft-serve and slushie machines, which also use a compressor but churn faster to produce softer, Mr Whippy-style ice-cream. Another type is often described as a “frozen dessert maker” (such as the Ninja Creami, Nutribullet Chill, and so on). These machines require you to combine ingredients and prefreeze in a tub, after which the mix is processed from frozen with a sharp blade.These newer models are more flexible in terms of what you can make, but they require more experimentation to get the best results and are often trickier to clean.How to make ice-cream in an ice-cream makerI quickly learned during testing that many of the recipes in the ice-cream makers’ accompanying booklets aren’t very good. Most suggest using double cream exclusively, which doesn’t freeze that well and often creates a greasy, grainy texture when it does.My advice is to stick to tried-and-tested recipes that use stable, lower-fat ingredients. While you need some fat to achieve that delicious, creamy feel, if it’s too much, it goes the other way.Compressor machinesView image in fullscreenKeep your cool: compressor models often mean simply adding the chilled mixture and letting the machine do the rest.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianYou’ll get great results with most recipes – I found sorbet and custard-based ice-creams worked best. Simply chill the mixture, then throw it in. In general, mix-ins aren’t advised while freezing and should instead be added at the end using the “churn-only” setting, which simply spins the paddle.Freeze-first machinesThese require you to freeze the included bowl for at least 24 hours before making ice-cream (I found 36 hours works best as a minimum), as well as chill your mixture in the fridge separately. With this done, you can churn as usual – but, like compressor models, leave mix-ins until the end.Soft-serve and slushie machinesThese can be a bit trickier to master, especially if the recipes included with your machine aren’t quite right. For best results, stick to stable, medium-fat recipes (eg not just double cream); otherwise you risk making butter. You can use a chilled mixture straight from the fridge, though – it chills even quicker than a traditional compressor model, so no 24-hour waits.Blade machinesThese work a bit like freeze-first machines, but instead of freezing the bowl overnight, you freeze the mixture in the tub provided. Again, if it’s too high in fat, your mixture will become grainy, so stick to a custard or single-cream base. You can also freeze certain mix-ins directly within the ice-cream base with these models, as the blade will chop right through them.How repairable are ice-cream makers?Repairability varies. If you want a machine that lasts for years, look for one with easily replaceable parts and a simple design. Models with fewer hidden electronics or that can be disassembled into several pieces for cleaning are generally easier to repair at home or by a local professional. In that light, the Nutribullet Chill and Cuisinart Solo Scoops are two of the most easily repairable machines on this list in terms of the spare parts that are available.However, spare parts won’t always cover you for issues with electrical components. It’s always worth checking whether the manufacturer of your model offers a repair service. Some have dedicated support pages on their websites where you can buy replacement parts, and of course, don’t overlook warranties when you’re making a buying decision, for valuable peace of mind if anything should go wrong.For more, read thebest (and worst) chef’s knivesand thebest blenders for smoothies, soups and frozen dessertsDanielle Amato is a consumer reviews journalist with almost a decade of experience covering kitchen and home appliances. She’s an avid ice-cream and pasta enthusiast (not at the same time, though she wouldn’t judge) and loves nothing more than getting stuck into a new recipe or appliance in her unofficial test kitchenExplore more on these topicsIce-cream and sorbetThe FilterDessertFoodGadgetsfeaturesShareReuse this content
